Uniform Title: Puraścaryārṇava, Volume 3 Main Title: Puraścaryārṇavaḥ, Volume 3 Editor: Muralidhara Jhā
Description: Compiled by His Highness the Maharaja Pratapa Simha Sah Bahadur of Nepal.
Notes: The texts have been transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0, January 28, 2007.
Publisher: Prabhakari and Co.
Publication Year: 1901 Publication City: Benares Publication Country: India
The ten Mahāvidyās and their specific preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*) are now demonstrated.
And so it is said in the *Muṇḍamālā*:
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī. (9.1)
Vagalā, Siddhividyā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā—these ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the Siddhividyās. (9-2)
Therein, at the beginning, the first vidyā is proclaimed in the *Kumārītantra*.
Bhairava said:
"Indeed, there exists this one eternal knowledge, which is most secret."
For it is extremely secret and cannot be told at all. || 9-3 ||
"O beloved, I tell you this because you are exceedingly dear to me:
for this entire world, both gross and subtle, is indeed composed of Brahman. (4)
Indeed, without primordial nature (prakṛti), transmigratory existence does not arise;
therefore, no root cause of that primordial nature is ever perceived. (9-5)
O beautiful lady, there are many forms of Prakṛti;
among these, O Great Goddess, the form of Kālī is most enchanting. (9.6)
Especially in the Kali Yuga, she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others are her worshippers.
Indra, Sūrya, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Agni, and another; Durvāsas, Vasiṣṭha, Dattātreya, and Bṛhaspati. || 9-8 ||
What is the use of saying more here? All the gods are her devotees;
by the grace of Kālīkā, they partake in worldly enjoyment, liberation, and other such blessings.
I shall proclaim her mantra, by which one may protect the three worlds: the letter *ka* joined with fire (*ra*) and endowed with the essence of passion (*i*) and the bindu (*m*). (9–10)
Then one should utter the three qualities (triguṇa), followed by a pair of *kūrca* syllables, then a pair of *lajjā* syllables,
and finally "dakṣiṇe kālike" along with the previously mentioned seed-syllables.
O Śivā, this mantra of Kālikā is said to end with the wife of Vahni (svāhā);
it consists of twenty-two syllables and is declared to be the Siddhividya.
He states the meaning of the mantra in the *Saṃketatantra*:
"The universe has arisen from the letter *ka*; therefore, she is of the nature of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
The letter *ra* is the self of Rudra as the Fire of Time (*kālāgnirudra*); therefore, she is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). (9–13)
The vowel *ī* is Mahālakṣmī, the illuminator of the three worlds;
therefore, she is the power (*śakti*) that protects, and through the *bindu*, she is the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).
(In the Kālītantra:
Because of the letter *ka*, she is of the nature of Śiva and bestows all sovereignty;
through her union with the fiery syllable, she is auspicious and composed of all splendor. (9.15)
The Vindumālinī alone illuminates all the principles (tattvas);
because it is partless (niṣkala) due to the bindu, it bestows the fruit of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
The seed-syllable Kūrca alone illuminates all awakening;
it is the very form of consciousness, terrifying to the cycle of existence, and the bestower of liberation. (9.17)
The state of being illuminated by the sky (vyoman) and the state of devouring by fire (agni)—the emission (visarga) of these two, conjoined with the bindu, is considered the Tantric tradition. (9.18)
The Dakṣiṇā, free from the Siddhas, Sādhya-s, and others, bestows swift accomplishment.
Because she swallows time through the integration of time, she is Kālī. (9-19)
With the utterance "Svāhā," all sense objects are offered into the deity;
thus, in its universal form, it is the supreme, absolute power of consciousness alone.
"Consisting of all the gods, manifest as the very nature of Śabdabrahman—thus should the pure-souled one meditate, being himself liberated while living and Śiva. (9.21)
The *Bhairavītantra* speaks of the greatness of this knowledge:

"In this [practice], there shall be no impurity of mind, nor any affliction from enemies, friends, and the like; nor is there excessive exertion, such as [observing] rules (*samaya*) or prohibitions (*asamaya*). (9.22)
It involves neither great expenditure of wealth nor physical hardship;
it was taught by the gods for the attainment of divinity, and by the Siddhas for the attainment of moving through the sky.
It is always resorted to by serpents, Rākṣasas, mortals, sages seeking liberation, those driven by desire, those devoted to dharma, and those wishing for wealth. (9.24)
The practitioner who meditates upon her, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires, holds all supernatural powers (siddhi) forever in his hand; of this there is no doubt. (9.25)
Merely by the sight of him, the disputants are rendered lusterless;
even kings submit to servitude—what need be said of other people? (9.26)
He is capable of making fire cold, paralyzing the flow of water, stopping the movement of the sun, and even reversing day and night. (9.27)
And at the end, that man attains the state of being a Gaṇa of the Goddess, which is difficult to obtain;
having become equal to the moon and the sun, he shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.
Nothing is difficult to attain for one who remembers Ghorakālikā;
(in the Kālītantra) indeed, by the mere remembrance of her, the eight siddhis come to be. 9-29.
Thus, this queen of all sciences cannot be praised even by thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of tongues. (9.30)
The goddess Aniruddha-Sarasvatī is the bestower of all accomplishments;
therefore, indeed, accomplishments arise from the mere knowledge of her. 9.31
Likewise: "Even if there were a woman equal to you, and a man equal to me, a mantra equal to the Sarasvatī of Aniruddha would always exist. (9.32)
In another tantra:
"In the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī; in the Kali age, Kālī alone.
Kālikā has been accomplished by Kālanātha and is manifest in the Kali age. (9.33)
In the Kali age, whoever desires liberation while abandoning Kālī is surely like one who wishes to dispel hunger without food. (9.34)
In the Kali age, whoever seeks peace while abandoning Kālī is like one who resorts to the snowy mountains for the sake of removing the heat.
In the Kali age, whoever abandons Kālī and desires poetry will always commit sins for the sake of ending his suffering. (9.36)
The Śrī Mahākālikā Vidyā bestows complete fruit in the Kali age; for indeed, in the Kali age, [the age] performs worship at the feet of her servant. (9.37)
O Great Goddess, whether through ignorance or with knowledge, whether playfully or with mockery, Kālī bestows accomplishment even if remembered but once. (9.38)
Established through various divisions of knowledge, such as the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) and the Knowledge of Accomplishment (Siddhividyā),
Kālikā is present on earth through the distinctions of the secondary sciences (Upavidyā) and others.
All the sciences, beginning with Tārā, were born from Kālikā;
indeed, O Pārvatī, all sciences are established within Kālikā.
p. 727) Now, the ritual placement of the seer and so forth (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*) [as stated in the] *Kālītantra*:
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (*ṛṣi*); the *uṣṇih* meter is cited; the deity is declared to be Kālikā; and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is indeed the syllable of modesty (*lajjā*). (9.41)
The Śakti is the Kūrca-bīja, which is Aniruddha-Sarasvatī;
in the Kālī-krama, the Kīlaka is the first Bīja, which grants the accomplishment of the four aims of human life. (9.42)
In the *Kālītantra*,
for the purpose of poetic composition, there should be an application [of mantras] such as the visualization of the Ṛṣis and so forth;
the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) are now described correctly.
One should fashion [the mantra] with a seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels preceded by the *praṇava*;
(as it is said in the Vīra-tantra:
"One should fashion it with that which is preceded by the *praṇava* and joined with the six long vowels. (44)
Other nyāsas should be consulted in that very same [text].
Now, as for the meditation (*dhyāna*) [described] in the *Merutantra*: [one should visualize her] with a terrifying face, fierce, with disheveled hair, and four-armed.
Black, divine, with a sacrificial fee, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a sword, the gesture of fearlessness, a boon-granting mudrā, and a severed head in her hands;
possessing the luster of a great cloud, dark-complexioned, and likewise naked.
She had a garland of severed heads suspended from her neck, smeared with dripping blood,
and was adorned by pairs of corpses that served as her ear-ornaments.
She had terrible fangs and a gaping mouth, with full and elevated breasts;
she wore a girdle made from a multitude of corpses and possessed a laughing face.
Her face was dappled by streams of blood trickling from both corners of her mouth;
she was of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, and a dweller in the abode of the cremation ground.
She has prominent teeth, her loosened mass of long hair spreads to the right, and she is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse. (9.50)
It was surrounded on all four sides by auspicious jackals of terrible howls,
joined by Mahākāla, and occupied by those intent upon corpses.
One should thus meditate upon Kālī, who dwells in the cremation ground, whose lotus-like face is smiling, and who bestows boons with a joyful countenance. (9.52)
Likewise:

"Whatever fruit results from the gift of the earth filled with the jewels of tawny cows, that same fruit is obtained by meditating upon the Goddess, as is the fruit of a thousand million *koṭi*-sacrifices. (9.53)

By the recitation of this mantra, the practitioner is liberated from the murder of a Brahmin, as well as from the killing of one's father or mother, and what need is there to mention other trivial murderers? (9.54)
Now, regarding the removal of the curse in that context:
I shall proclaim the removal of the curse performed by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
having recited [the mantra] twenty-four hundred thousand times, he had cursed him out of anger. (9.55)
"From this day forward, O Goddess Kālikā, you who are the embodiment of Time, the accomplishment of your mantras shall come about only through great hardship. (9.56)
Having heard this, the Great Goddess appeared and, having propitiated him, said: "O son, why has this curse been bestowed in vain? (9.57)
O Lord of Munis, act in such a way that this fruit may not come to pass, for you have bestowed a knowledge that is difficult to attain and hard to master even for the gods. (9.58)
Then, having received with joy a boon endowed with knowledge and realization, he spoke with a delighted mind regarding the end of the curse during that crisis of mantras.
O Mother, I shall now declare the remedy spoken there in anger:
having first extracted the Praṇava, [one should place it] in the southern [position] as Ghorarūpā.
Having uttered "siddhiṃ kuru" twice, one should then say the word "Kālike," followed by:
"Grant me quickly my desired fruit and abundance of wealth. (9.61)
Having uttered the mantra at the beginning of the recitation, one should recite it again at the end of the recitation;
from that, O Supreme Goddess, success will arise without delay.
Now, the different types of seats are described in the *Matsyasūkta*: "Seated on soft grass or on other soft materials... (9.63).
Or, having settled upon a seat, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
The wise say that these characteristics [occur] right there within six months; they call it "mild" when the embryo has fallen away.
They know this [period] as "prior to the tonsure" (ācūḍaka), being devoid of both the tonsure ceremony and the initiation;
it is the time for a boy whose tonsure has been performed but who is yet devoid of initiation. (9.65)
They know that one who dies in the fifth year is indeed "tender" (komala). Likewise:
"O Goddess, that man who recites the mantra of Kālikā without the 'seat of death' (mṛtāsana)... (9.66)
He is to be known as a hell-being until the dissolution of the world (āhūtasaṃplava), provided he is one who [calls himself] "vīra" (hero); for such a seat is forbidden for an animal. (9-67)
In the absence of a soft seat or similar items, an alternative method is stated in the *Vīratantra*: "In the absence of a corpse, one should fashion a seat (*viṣṭara*) in the form of a corpse;
with fifty [blades of grass] there shall be Brahmā, and with half of that, the seat. (9.68)
(In the Kālītantra and other texts:
"In the absence of a corpse, one should prepare a seat in the form of *kuśa* grass.
Now listen as the nature of the practitioner's seat is described. (9.69)
That in which the leaves are indeed the elements is called *kuśa*;
it measures ten [units] in the hand and the foot, and ten times that in the pair of directions (the body) and in the heart-lotus.
The number twenty is proclaimed for the head, O bestower of all boons; [the number ten] is likewise for the secret place, the tongue, the mouth, the teeth, the nose, the ears, and the breasts. (9.71)
On the *liṅga* and the *caṇḍa*, one should place *kuśa* grass measuring a *yuga*;
thus is described this *viṣṭara*, which bestows all accomplishments.
O Supreme Goddess, the binding should be performed with kuśa grass or with a tube;
alternatively, it may be done with a thread mixed with blood or with silk thread.
Having then prepared a seat, one should perform the recitation upon it;
thus has the procedure for the ritual seat-lotus been declared by me to you. (9.74)
Then, having assumed the form of a Śava, a man shall become a poet and an eloquent speaker;
for the sake of attaining all perfections, the Sūtra spoken by Svayambhū must be performed.
In the absence of a corpse, however, the seat (viṣṭara) is proclaimed to have the form of a corpse;
the seat should be of the nature of Śiva, through the mental conception of it as one's own Śakti.
What on earth cannot be accomplished through the union of Śiva and Śakti?

Now, regarding the consecration of the seat (*viṣṭara-saṃskāra*): during the union with Śakti, one should perform the untying [of the thread] with the Gāyatrī and carry out the tying together with the root mantra. (9.77)
Having formed the resolve, the practitioner, grasping [the water] gently with the left hand using the *kūrca* seed-syllable,
should perform the sprinkling with the *astra* mantra.
Having uttered the Praṇava and Bhuvaneśī, one should say that:
"O you who have the form of a corpse, O great preta, grant me the eight siddhis."
Having thus praised him correctly, one should place him in the midst of *kuśa* grass;
indeed, upon his body, one should draw a triangle with red sandalwood paste.
Having drawn the Māyā situated in the center, one should fashion the outer mandala;
[reciting] "Oṃ Āḥ Surekhe Vajrarekhe" thereafter. (9.81)

The mantra for the mandala consists of the *kūrca* (hūṃ), the weapon (*astra*) [phaṭ], the wife of fire (*vahnivadhū*) [svāhā], the syllable *ā*, then *māyā* (hrīṃ), the syllable *kro*, and *haṃsa*. (9.82)
Having uttered the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), one should speak the word "śavaprāṇāḥ" (the life-breaths of the corpse).
Having spoken the word "iha prāṇāḥ" (here the life-breaths), one says "śavajīva iha sthitaḥ" (the life of the corpse is situated here).
The vital breaths, all the sense organs, speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and even pleasure have come here from that corpse and remained for a long time. (9.84)
Let the mantra for the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇa), joined with "svāhā," remain as it is; first, having uttered the Praṇava, one should then utter the word "Ādhāraśakti. (9.85)
One should worship him with the word *komalāsana* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*) followed by *namaḥ*.
The salutation consists of the syllable *Oṃ*, followed by *kāmapīṭhāya* and the word *namaḥ*. (9.86)
An image of the corpse should be fashioned from three *māṣa* of gold on a cloth;
having placed it at the end of the expansion, one should perform everything as previously described.

According to the statement "there is no state of death," even the *kuśa*-grass mat used as a substitute for a corpse is not permitted for the bound soul (*paśu*), because the right to a substitute belongs only to one who has the primary entitlement; thus say the authors of the *Sudhārṇava*.
Furthermore, the consecration of other types of seats is mentioned in the *Bhairavatantra*:
"Either *kuśa* grass, a tiger skin, or likewise a red woolen blanket."
Or one may also wrap a soft seat with a yellow cloth.
Having properly assumed the posture, one should then perform the purification;
one should duly perform the worship according to the procedure prescribed in the ritual manual.
"O Maheśvarī, having thus received the command of the Goddess, I purify the seat for the sake of worship with the root mantra and the heart mantra. (9.90)
Having sprinkled the seat with water and veiled it with the *kavaca* mantra,
and having protected it with the *astra* mantra, one should meditate upon [the deity] as resembling Sadāśiva.
There, one should devoutly recite the *pīṭha-mantra* one hundred and eight times, having worshipped Sadāśiva with whatever wealth and offerings are available. (9.92)
O Siddhiśvara Mahādeva, bestower of all accomplishments,
grant me my desired success through this very form of your seat.
Having recited this mantra and sat upon the seat,
one should then perform the ritual according to the rules and offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru.
Thus ends the consecration of the seat.
Now, regarding the locations (*phetkāriṇīye*):
in a place with a single *liṅga*, in a cremation ground, and in four empty houses.
Staying there, the yogi should accomplish the vidyā that liberates from the three worlds.

The definition of an *ekaliṅga* is stated in that very same [text]: "Where one does not see another *liṅga* within a distance of five *krośas*, that is declared an *ekaliṅga*; there, the highest accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained. (9.96)
The characteristics of the cremation ground and other such places have been described [in the *Triśaktiratnākara*]:
"Where lifeless bodies are burned amidst a multitude of corpse-stakes,
and which is surrounded by vultures, jackals, crows, and others greedy for flesh" (9.97).
That place is known as a cremation ground, frequented by hosts of piśācas,
filled with the nests of crows and other birds, and abounding in human skins, umbrellas, and the like.
That which has been abandoned from afar by the citizens, which causes distress to those who would dwell there,
and where grass and weeds have grown upon the mansions— that is called an empty house.
And where the conjunction of four [roads] occurs simultaneously, that is called a crossroads (catuṣpatha); at night, it bestows what is desired.
Each preceding method among these is recommended, while each subsequent one is considered inferior;
this may be performed in a thicket, on a mountain, in a deserted place, or at a crossroads.
In a temple devoid of deities, at the foot of a bilva tree, on a riverbank, in one's own home, in a deserted grove, or likewise in the vicinity of an aśvattha tree. (9-102)
(In the *Kumārītantra*):
In its absence, [one should worship] in a divine house marked with vermilion and other substances, and adorned with a sword, trident, mace, cleaver, chowrie, fan, and so forth. (9–103)
In a place filled with the smoke of canopies and well-scented with black agallochum,
beautified by the dancing of young courtesans intoxicated with wine.
In a house filled with the sound of conchs and bells and resplendent with rows of lamps— such being the setting— the worship of Kālikā is most beautiful.
Now, the procedure for *puraścaraṇa* (according to the *Vīratantra*):
At the outset, one should perform *puraścaraṇa* for the sake of accomplishing the mantra;
thereafter, the practitioner, possessing a perfected mantra, should accomplish the rites for specific desires. (9–106)
In the *Svatantra-tantra*,
a person, having become pure and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times during the day;
thereafter, O Dear One, he should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with sacrificial food consisting of one-tenth of that number.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with water from a sacred bathing place, or with milk, or even with clarified butter, or with honey, or with water mixed with sugar.
And one should consecrate the Goddess with water ten times the amount used for the grass;
O Dear One, one should then devoutly feed her ten times that amount of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
O Dear One, one should give sacrificial fees to the brahmins who know the Kālī-mantra and to the preceptor;
thereafter, O Beloved, listen to the Pāśava-kalpa, which is harsh and full of enmity.
Having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed ritual with offerings of meat and corpses at night,
one should then, while naked and even if covered in secretions, enjoy a naked woman.
Then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should perform the fire-oblation for the Goddess in a blazing fire situated within a *yonikuṇḍa*,
using clarified butter, meat, and liquor.
The practitioner should satisfy [the deities] with ten parts of liquor mixed with meat;
having performed the sprinkling with a tenth part of that satisfaction, he should [worship] her who consists of the entire world. (9.113)
One should feed a tenth part [of the offerings] to a virtuous practitioner who is dear to Kālikā;
one should cause wine, meat, fish, and solid food to be offered.
Then, O Beloved, one should gratify the Guru with devotion by means of gold and other gifts;
O Goddess, through these two kalpas, the mantra is certainly perfected.
In the *Kālītantra*:
"First, one should perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) according to rule and according to the prescribed method;
being pure and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) during the day, one should recite the mantra (*vidyā*) one hundred thousand times. (9–116)

Having his mouth filled with betel for nights while prostrating a hundred thousand times upon his bed, the practitioner of mantras then becomes one whose mantra is perfected and fit for ritual application; it is not otherwise.
(In the *Sādhanasamuccaya*):
Having performed the daily rites during the day, one should perform the worship at night;
at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform recitation, delighted by the tasting of the causal [essence]. (9-118)
By means of one hundred thousand recitations, the Kālī-vidyā is accomplished. (In the Bhairavatantra:
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food should recite it one hundred thousand times in a single day. (9-119)
Having become devoted to celibacy during the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*),
the mantra-practitioner should likewise recite the mantra one hundred thousand times at night while remaining intent upon sexual union.
Having performed this according to the sequence of conduct, one should accomplish the mantra for oneself;
then, by means of the ritual procedure, success will surely arise from the mantra alone—of this there is no doubt.
In the Bhairavayāmala:
"He who, having mastered the procedure for initiation from the presence of a guru and having received the mantra, recites it one hundred thousand times during the day..."
At night, that best of practitioners, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), with a mind unshaken by envy, passion, anger, greed, and the like— 9.122.
At night, at the conclusion of love-making with his own wives, Mahākāla— naked, with disheveled hair, and with his mind fixed upon you— [performs] a hundred thousand [prostrations].
(From the *Mahākālastuti*)
The self-controlled one, intent on consuming sacrificial food and devoted to meditating upon the pair of your feet during the day, mutters the mantra one hundred thousand times.

Furthermore, by means of the pleasure of amorous dalliance while naked at night, a person may recite a hundred thousand mantras; such a one shall become equal to the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) upon the surface of the earth.
(From the Merutantra:
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day, eating sacrificial food and remaining pure. (9-124)
And likewise, being impure at night, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should perform the fire-oblation with clarified butter ten times that number, and offer libations and perform consecrations.
Homa, libation (tarpaṇa), and worship must be performed especially;
thereafter, one should carry out the ritual applications (prayoga) for the attainment of desired results.
(In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*):
I shall describe the procedure for the practice, most wonderful in its secret convention, by the mere knowledge of which the state of a sky-farer (*khecaratva*) arises. (9.127)
One should perform the fire sacrifice with diligence using milk-rice or sesame seeds;
having bathed and wearing white garments, one should remain pure during the day while performing the daily rites.
One should perform worship at night according to the procedure for the five mudrās;
by this very procedure, the wise one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Placing one's own respective karma at the forefront, one shall become a lord of all accomplishments;
one should perform gestures, expressions, and the like, and seize the great vine of the *mahācīna* practice.
(From the *Śrutisiddhāntatantra*):
One should always perform libations, bathing, drinking, and so forth with that very [liquid].
The ritual procedure for the bound (*pāśava*) is on the right; however, the ritual procedure for the heroes (*vīra*) belongs to the left-hand practitioners (*vāmin*). 9.131.
Relying upon two kalpas, the mantra is quickly accomplished;
having received the command of the guru, one who has bathed, wears white garments, and is pure. (9.132)
During the day, one should recite the vidyā a hundred thousand times while observing celibacy;
and at night, having worshipped the Goddess of the lords of gods with offerings of the left-hand ritual (vāmopacāra).
Having worshipped the Śaktis according to the rules and performed the festival of sexual union,
he sits upon a soft seat, his limbs relaxed, naked as the directions.
With his mouth full of betel and his forehead marked with vermilion,
he should take up the secret rosary and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
This rule is proclaimed for those who have entered the path of the *kula*.

Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa and others maintain that for a Brāhmaṇa or a *paśu*, there is a recitation (*japa*) of one hundred thousand [mantras] during the day with the worship of the right side (*dakṣiṇopacāra*); whereas for a Śūdra or a *vīra*, there is a recitation of one hundred thousand characterized by the worship of the left side (*vāmopacāra*) at night.
This is their intention.
Food consisting of alms and other such regulated items is prescribed to be taken only once at night. || 9-136 ||
"A twice-born man performing the *puraścaraṇa* should perform the recitation (*japa*) during the day alone," according to the statement in the *Phetkāriṇī-tantra*.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, pure, and with a restrained mind— (9-137).
During the day, everything should be performed for the sake of accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha;
this is the rule proclaimed here for all twice-born men.
And according to the statement of the *Merutantra* regarding the *puraścaraṇa* performed by Brahmins and others:
"One should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions [of the day] and recite the mantra at the three junctions;
one must never touch the mantra or the rosary at night. (139)

This is because of the statement in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* belonging to the section on the state of the bound soul (*paśubhāva*): "In the *puraścaraṇa* performed by a bound soul, the time is indeed during the day.
And thus:
"For all twice-born [castes], the rule for the daytime is stated here."
And for Śūdras, it is likewise declared that entering [the temple] at night yields great fruit.
Thus, following the statement in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*,
regarding the *puraścaraṇa* performed by a Śūdra:
"When the first watch has passed, up until the third watch..."
It should be recited only during the night; one should not recite it when the night has passed.

Since it is established by the statement in the *Vīramuṇḍamālā* concerning the section on the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for heroes that the time for a hero’s preliminary rite is exclusively the night, [the following applies]:

"The practitioner recites the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the 'fettered' (*pāśava*) procedure, using the Vidyā obtained from the mouth of the Guru, which has the splendor of a dense mass of time. (142)
Having received the divine Kalikā from the mouth of a divine Guru,
the practitioner should always recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the Vīra-kalpa.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Kālīkulārṇava*:
"One devoted to one's own conduct should always recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times by day as a *paśu*;
or else, whether a *divya* or a *vīra*, one should perform the recitation one hundred thousand times at night. (144)

And because of the statement in the *Kālīkrama*, "In this system, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for all [mantras] is established as consisting of exactly one hundred thousand recitations": "One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times during the day, pure and eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*);
at night, with the mouth full of betel, one should recite it one hundred thousand times while lying on a bed. (145)
Having thus recited two hundred thousand [times], the knower of mantras, O Goddess, should perform ten thousand oblations with a tenth part of that number, distinguishing between day and night. (146)

Thus, the contradiction with the *Kumārītantra*—which prescribes for all [practitioners] the *puraścaraṇa* and other rites consisting of the recitation of two hundred thousand [mantras] according to their respective specific procedures—is unavoidable.
(In the *Niruttaratantra* as well,) the recitation is stated to be exactly two hundred thousand:
"One should recite the vidyā two hundred thousand times, distinguishing between day and night."

However, according to the *Sudhārṇava*—based on such statements as "having thus recited two hundred thousand [times]" from the *Kumārītantra* and other sources—it follows that for everyone, the appropriate recitation of two hundred thousand, consisting of one hundred thousand each day and night through distinct practices for day and night, is established:
"Devoted to his own conduct, a bound soul (*paśu*) should always recite one hundred thousand during the day. (147)

"Or else, a divine being or a hero should perform the recitation of a hundred thousand [mantras] at night"— by this statement from the *Kālīkrama*, [the rule of daytime practice] is set aside as an exception.
Likewise, for a heroic Brahmin as well, [the practice] at night is preceded by the consumption of wine and other [intoxicants].
A Brāhmaṇa who gives liquor is indeed deprived of his status as a Brāhmaṇa.

Thus, a recitation (japa) has been obtained that contradicts such statements and is opposed to the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, which prescribes the use of milk by Brāhmaṇas in the context of the Heroic State (*vīrabhāva*).
In that regard,
the rule for all twice-born men is intended here to apply during the daytime.
This is an exception to the rule. By this, even for a *vīra* Brahmin, the recitation of one hundred thousand [mantras] during the day is concluded by first partaking of *maireya* liquor and the like.
In this way, it also serves as an exception to the night-only recitation for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
And for Śūdras, it has been stated thus: "That which is performed at night yields great fruit. (9.149)
Thus ends the reply. Consequently, the statement from the *Kumārīkalpa* is established as referring specifically to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Since the general rule (*utsarga*) remains valid when the scope of its exceptions (*apavāda*) is excluded, the nocturnal sacrifice of animals (*rātri-paśu*) is indeed set aside by the statements in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* belonging to the section on the nature of sacrificial animals (*paśubhāva-prakaraṇīya*). Therefore, everything is faultless.
In reality, however—

Based on the statement from the *Kālīkulārṇava*, "Having received [the mantra] from the mouth of a Guru," and so forth, they say that for one who has received the mantra from a *paśu* (an uninitiated person), the practice is performed with the state of a *paśu*, while for one who has received the mantra from a *vīra*, it is performed with the state of a *vīra*. In the case of the former, there is one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), whereas in the reverse case, there are two hundred thousand recitations. Regarding this "reverse case," according to the method taught in the *Kumārītantra*, since two hundred thousand recitations must be performed, it is impossible to perform the practice with the state of a *paśu* for one who has received the mantra from a *vīra*. Therefore, it should be understood that the "reverse" consists precisely in performing the practice with the state of a *vīra* for one who has received the mantra from a *paśu*. On this point, the venerable Kṛṣṇabhaṭṭa says:

Thus, based on statements from the *Kumārītantra* and other sources such as "having recited two hundred thousand [times]," the recitation for all [categories of practitioners] is indeed limited to two hundred thousand. However, the statements from the *Kālīkulārṇava*, *Kālīkrama*, and others which prescribe a recitation of one hundred thousand for each of the *paśu*, *divya*, and *vīra* classes, refer specifically to those who have already attained mastery over the mantra (*siddhamantra*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Yāmala* and other texts:
"If a mantra accomplished by the Guru is obtained through good fortune..."
Then, having recited it one hundred thousand times, one should accomplish all rites. ||150||
In this regard, however, there is a distinction:
having worshipped the Goddess at night according to the prescribed ritual with meat and liquor,
[one should do so] while naked, embracing a naked woman— according to such statements from the *Svatantratantra* and other sources.

Even for a Brāhmaṇa, both of these are applicable: first, the giving of *maireya* liquor and so forth, which contradicts the statement of Mahākāla beginning with "having given wine to a Brāhmaṇa"; and second, sexual intercourse prior to night-time recitation (*rātrijapa*), which contradicts statements from the general section on preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) such as those found in the *Siddhāntasampradāya* beginning with "having approached one's own wife out of ignorance.
Both of these [apply].
A Brāhmaṇa should worship Śivā with materials that are purely of the nature of sattva.
Having thus summoned her— whether she be their own wife, another's wife, or a common woman— the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras should perform the recitation.
Thus it is set aside by the statement of the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"And likewise,
O Bhairava, one's own birth-flower and the causal substance [are required]."
Having touched [it] and likewise smelled it, one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow. ||153||

"Furthermore, one should not approach a woman with zeal except during her fertile period," and so forth. By such statements from the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* regarding the nature of the "beast-like state" (*paśubhāva*), both [the aforementioned practices] are indeed rejected even for a beast other than a Brahmin. As for the statement in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi* prohibiting nocturnal recitation for any beast whatsoever, it refers specifically to a beast who is a worshiper of a deity other than this [prescribed] deity.
One should recite [the mantra] even at night for that long, in order to pacify transgressions.

Thus, because the *Śrutisiddhāntatantra*—in the section concerning the optional rites performed by animal-sacrificers (*paśu*)—prescribes night-recitation even for an animal-sacrificer who worships this deity; and because of the statement:
"For Śūdras, it is likewise declared that what is performed at night yields great fruit" (p.
740), this text indicates a superior result for Śūdras when performing night-recitation, but it does not prohibit day-time recitation performed by Śūdras.
And likewise:

for both the *vīra* and *divya* [practitioners], there is one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) by day according to the *pāśava* ritual procedure, and one hundred thousand recitations at night according to the *vīra* ritual procedure. Furthermore, in that context, the direct use of *maireya* wine and so forth is for the *śūdra* alone; it is not the use of those substances even for a *vīra* who belongs to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*).
"The Brāhmaṇas are to be gratified with milk, and those born of the royal lineage with clarified butter. (9.155)
"By those of the Vaiśya caste with honey-wines (*mākṣika*), and by those born of the Śūdra caste with *āsava* liquors"—
from this statement in the *Bhairavatantra*. For this very reason, it is said in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
It is heard that the preeminence of the fruit therein arises first from the gift of liquor.
"For that is to be known as intended for Śūdras, and not for the twice-born, O beloved.

Regarding the animal [sacrifice], they say that the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) results in two hundred thousand recitations for everyone: one hundred thousand recitations by the right-hand path during the day, and one hundred thousand recitations by that same path at night.
However, this is how it appears to me:
The Pāśava ritual is for the right-hand path, while the Vīra ritual is for those on the left-hand path.

From such scriptural statements of the *Śrutisiddhāntatantra* as these, it is established that the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇamārgin*) has only the *pāśava-kalpa* (the fettered ritual procedure) as its sphere of authority, while the left-hand path (*vāmamārgin*) has only the *vīra-kalpa* (the heroic ritual procedure). Having thus described the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) according to the *pāśava-kalpa*, it is stated in that very same text: "This rule is proclaimed for those who have entered the path of the *Kula*."
In this manner, according to the sequence of family tradition, one should accomplish the mantra-nature.

Thus, from the statement in the *Bhairavatantra*: "The Kaula is endowed with the rites of both the right and the left, being a mixture of both," and from the statement in the *Ācāraprakaraṇa* of the *Vāḍavānala*: "By resorting to these two kalpas, the authority belongs to the Kaulika alone. From these [sources], it is understood that the Kaulika alone has the qualification for this.
And thus:

for those following the Southern Path (*dakṣiṇamārgin*), the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of reciting one hundred thousand mantras during the day according to the *Pāśava* method; for those following the Northern Path (*vāmamārgin*), it consists of reciting one hundred thousand mantras at night according to the *Vīra* method. For the Kaulika, the preparatory rite comprises both of these. Thus, there is a distinction in the preparatory rite as well, based on the division of the paths.

In the passage beginning with “of all the *dvijas*,” (*p. 741*), the word *dvija* refers to the *paśus* (bound souls) and not merely to the *vipras* (Brahmins), because the latter term denotes the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). For this very reason, the word “all” (*sarveṣām*) was employed to include both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; however, it was not included in the second half of the verse. Otherwise, as stated by the author of the *Sudhārṇava*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the expectation regarding the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas remaining unfulfilled. Furthermore, the *paśu* follows the Southern Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*). Likewise, in the second half of the verse, the word *śūdra* refers to those who follow the Northern Path (*vāmamārgin*). Therefore, it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"The accomplishment of those beginning with the Śūdras and ending with the Yavanas is established on the Left Path. || 9.159 ||

Regarding the passages "the divine [mantra] from the mouth of the Guru" and "whether divine or else heroic," the terms *divya* and *vīra* refer here to followers of the Vāmamārga and not to Kaulikas; for it will be stated later that each of these two possesses a twofold division based on the distinction between the Kaulika and Vāmamārga paths. Thus, the statements in texts such as the *Kālikulārṇava* which prescribe one hundred thousand recitations during the day are to be understood as referring to the Dakṣiṇamārga; the statements in texts such as the *Sādhanasamuccaya* which prescribe one hundred thousand recitations at night are to be understood as referring to the Vāmamārga; and the statements which prescribe two hundred thousand appropriate recitations by distinguishing between day and night are to be understood as referring to the Kulamārga. In this way, everything is rendered free of blemish.
Furthermore, one who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remains pure by day should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times;
likewise, being impure at night, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (160)

In these and other such passages, the wise should understand that there is a threefold preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) applicable to the threefold path. Now, one might ask: how can *paśus* (the bound souls) have the qualification for the worship of this deity? "One should not worship Kālī without the divine state (*divyabhāva*) or the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*);
if one worships her [otherwise], one goes to hell, suffering at every step. (161)
O Goddess, if one who relies on the state of a bound soul (paśu) should worship Kālī, he goes to the Raurava hell until the dissolution of all beings at the end of time. 162.

If it is argued that this is because of the prohibition in the statement from the *Niruttaratantra*, we say no; for statements such as "the divine state" (*divyabhāva*) belong to the section concerning the Left-hand Practice (*vāmācāra*), and thus their purpose is to prohibit those following the Left-hand Path from resorting to the animal state (*paśubhāva*).
Accordingly:
"One who follows the Left-hand Path shall not worship Kālī without the divine state."
The meaning is that if one should worship while remaining based on the state of a bound animal (paśu), then one goes to the Raurava hell.
As it has been said elsewhere: "One who follows the Vāmamārga should resort to the divine state (divyabhāva) or the heroic state (vīrabhāva). (9.163)
"By the mere contact with an animal, one shall go to the Raurava hell. Thus [it is said].
And so it is said:
"For the state of being a sacrificial animal (paśu) is considered by the wise to be conducive to their highest good. (9.164)
"Therefore, a Brahmin should worship Kālī according to the animal ritual," based on this statement from the *Śrutisiddhāntatantra*.
Thus, a Brahmin should worship Māyā by means of the Southern Path (*dakṣiṇamārga*). ||165||

And because of such statements as from the *Siddhāntasāra*, the eligibility of bound souls (*paśus*) for the worship of this deity remains entirely intact. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statement from the *Kālakulārṇava*: "A bound soul, having received [the teaching] from the mouth of the Guru...";
and with [the verse]: "Devoted to his own conduct, the bound soul should conquer a hundred thousand [times] day after day."
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of inconsistency with such statements as those in the *Kālīkrama*.
And thus:
"When the practitioner has attained agitation, the agitation of the Goddess arises. (9.166)
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
[otherwise], by eating meat, drinking liquor, or approaching a woman in her menses— || 9.167 ||
For one who recites [the mantra of] Dakṣiṇakālī, there shall be suffering at every step;
O Dear One, one should satisfy Kālikā by means of the yoga of the abode of Kalā.

One should understand that even such statements from the *Niruttara Tantra* as these refer to the *vīra*. Many [scholars] maintain that because the consumption of intoxicants (*maireya*) and the like is prohibited for a *vīra* who is a Brāhmaṇa, the aforementioned statements refer to a *vīra* other than a Brāhmaṇa.

In reality, however, the state of being a *vīra* and so forth is precisely what is forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa, since it has been stated: "For Brāhmaṇas, there is indeed the state of a *paśu* (the bound soul)."
Now, [one might object]: "A Brahmin, through the state of a hero (vīrabhāva), should offer liquor, fish, meat, the *mudrā*, and sexual union to Kālikā. (168)
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, according to their lineage, should worship Kālī with the five [offerings] if they are seekers of liberation in the Kali age. (169)
If it be argued that, based on such statements from the *Niruttara Tantra* as cited above, how could a Brāhmaṇa lack the qualification for the state of a hero (*vīra*), we say: it is not so.
"Brāhmaṇical vigor, likewise the field [of birth], and the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) originate from Brahmā;
through the practice of Brahmā and by means of the Brahma-knowledges, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa. (170)

Thus, among the five characteristics mentioned in the *Merutantra*, since the one who lacks four of these characteristics and is equal to a *śūdra*—namely, a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen away from all conduct—is qualified for the *vāmācāra*; and since such a Brāhmaṇa alone is qualified for the *kulācāra*; and because any other *vipra* is disqualified from both due to the prohibition of the state of a *vīra* [for them], it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"In whichever *vipra* even one of the aforementioned characteristics is observed..."
In this matter, the authority belongs solely to that Brāhmaṇa on the left. ||171||
Likewise:
"The paths such as the Kaulika and others belong to those who are devoid of the four characteristics. Likewise:
One who has fallen away from all proper conduct should take refuge in the conduct of his own family.
"One who has fallen away from the conduct of his family shall go to the Raurava hell.
For this very reason it is said in the *Bhāvanirṇaya*:
"A low-born man (*vṛṣala*) should never at any time resort to the state of a beast. (9.173)

"A Brāhmaṇa should not conceive of the state of a hero (*vīrabhāva*) even in his mind"—by the word "and" (*ca*) in this verse, the state of a divine being (*divyabhāva*) is also included. Thus, wherever a statement is found prescribing the consumption of liquor and so forth by a Brāhmaṇa, it should be understood that in each such instance the word "Brāhmaṇa" refers to a *vīra-brāhmaṇa* who lacks the four aforementioned characteristics. This is because, according to the Tantric view, the term "Brāhmaṇa" is applied even to such a person. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Merutantra*: "of that very Brāhmaṇa... (tasyaiva brāhmaṇasya).
It should always be drunk by Brāhmaṇas, and by Kṣatriyas when battle approaches.

The statement from the *Kulārṇava*, "Never [should it be drunk] by Vaiśyas engaged in monetary transactions, nor ever by Śūdras," is also consistent with the reading "sadā peyam" (always to be drunk) through the elision of the vowel 'a' (*akāra-praleṣa*), resulting in "sadā apeyam" (never to be drunk). Furthermore, this is because Harinātha Upādhyāya, in his *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* within the section on the duties of the Kali age, has stated the prohibition against taking the *surā* cup during the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice;
and because we have already demonstrated that the Brāhmaṇa qualified for the *Kula* tradition is distinct [from such ritual contexts].
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and according to family custom, a Brāhmaṇa may drink surā.
Thus, the statement regarding the conduct of the *samaya* is indeed consistent.
As for that which was said:
"In the Tretā age, the Goddess was worshipped with clarified butter by all castes."
In the Dvāpara age, she was worshipped with honey offerings by people of all castes.

"In the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped with *āsava* alone"—this is the statement from the *Yāmala*. In that context, the term "all castes" (*sarvavarṇa*) refers to those other than Brahmins.

A Brahmin who has performed the three Vedas and the sacrifice, who is a devotee of the Earth (*bhūdeva*), and who wears the triple-thread of the sacrifice, must never touch the young woman (*bālā*) nor offer her to the Goddess. (177)
Thus, because of the statement in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* that prohibits a Brāhmaṇa from ever giving liquor,
and likewise:
"In cases where the gift of wine is specifically prescribed as supreme..."
The Brahmin should pour the cow-derived liquor into a copper vessel. ||178||

Thus, the procedure for the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) mentioned in the *Bhairavatantra* also refers exclusively to the aforementioned heroic Brahmin (*vīrabrāhmaṇa*). No one other than him has the qualification (*adhikāra*) even for that. For there is a statement in another tantra: "If a Brahmin does not perform the secondary alternative, he shall fall into the state of a *caṇḍāla*."
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
At times, the twice-born may offer liquor to the Goddess according to the secondary rule. 9-179.
I shall tell you the intoxicants; listen closely, O Goddess. By taking equal parts of ginger and jaggery, one may produce *surā*.
Likewise, honey and cow's milk should be placed in a copper vessel;
coconut water in a bell-metal vessel; and palm juice in a tin vessel. (9.181)
Rasāla is the juice in the *raṅga* fruit, as is pānasa; madhūka is the grape in its pod, and [the term applies] to its flower and its leaf as well. (9.182)
Ciñcā juice on a lotus leaf, and *kāraka* drink on an *aśvattha* leaf—these, O fair-faced one, are the twelve types of intoxicants. (9.183)
If a twice-born man desires to give liquor, he should give these [substitutes] and not *surā*;
even these should not be given by those who are sattvic and fearful of violating the Dharma. (9.184)

Whether it be liquor or even an intoxicant, it does not receive the name "liquor" [in this context]; however, one does not become fallen merely by these [substances], nor does one fall in that same manner. (9.185)
In this context, the word *dvija* refers to those twice-born other than Brāhmaṇas, and not to Brāhmaṇas. For this very reason, it is stated in that same work:
"Water from a coconut in a bronze vessel, cow-products in copper, and likewise honey—these gifts are for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, but never for a Brāhmaṇa. (9.186)
"In this way, by the mere act of giving, a Brāhmaṇa may become short-lived.
And likewise:
"Even though she has been worshipped with devotion and an abundance of various offerings," (9.187)

"Kālikā is not pleased at all without the application of the letter *ma*," and so forth; such statements from the *Kularatnāvalī* should also be understood as referring to worship performed by Śūdras and others. This is because it is heard that in the case of worship performed by Brahmins and others, her satisfaction arises only through *sāttvika* utterances. All of this is explicit in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*.
For instance:
"While other objects remained present, which were pleasing to the queen. (9.188)
What is the use of this liquor, which is foul by nature and consists of wretched food— this meat mixed with pus intended for spirits, ghosts, and demons?
Therefore, it must not be given by a Brahmin to the goddess, nor indeed should it be eaten by her;
for she is not satisfied by this, or even if she were, she feels great loathing.
Therefore, being deeply distressed by that, a twice-born man must never give liquor;
for by doing so, the Veda is destroyed, Dharma is destroyed, and one's own world beyond is destroyed. (191)
The family is destroyed, the lineage is destroyed, and the status of a Brahmin is indeed destroyed by that fool who, considering himself wise, drinks liquor out of ignorance. (192)
What was done, what was accomplished, or what was acquired, that he has now lost it all through his indulgence in liquor? (9.193)
In this very way, one submerged in ignorance will quickly destroy even me;
Mahāmāyā herself would become agitated upon beholding that. (9.194)
[The same applies] for fishermen, outcasts, barbarians, dyers, and those who live by killing; for leather-workers, actors, elephant-drivers, and those who subsist on cane. (9.195)
Indeed, having offered me food that is foul-smelling, dried, and otherwise unwholesome, how could there not be a longing for the nectar-like [food] among those people who drink it? (9.196)
There are no other substances such as food offerings for the purpose of making an offering; what is untouchable, that the *kula* women bring and give to me. (9.197)
The Ṛg verses, Yajus formulas, Sāman chants, as well as the Atharva-Aṅgirasas,
and likewise the great mantras, are ten million times more numerous than the Vedas.
Those people who purify those dwelling in their bodies by filling them with liquors up to the neck will surely flood me as well; what wonder is there in that? (9.199)
I am truly satisfied by offerings that are pure and sattvic—by bulbs, flowers, fruits, and leaves; yet in their absence, I am pleased by sincere devotion and a true heart. (9.200)
Not with extensive offerings of liquor and meat, which are the food of pretas and rākṣasas;
for the mental sons of Brahmā, headed by Marīci, Atri, and Aṅgiras, [are his true progeny].
From these, thousands of others have likewise arisen in their lineage:
Kaśyapa, Durvāsas, Dattātreya, and Candramas.
Bṛhaspati, Viśravas, Śakti, Dakṣa, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu (Mārkaṇḍeya),
Nārada, Kapila, Vyāsa, Kālāgni, and the son of Jamadagni (Paraśurāma).
Dākṣa, Kavi, Atharvan, Śāṇḍilya, Gautama, Manu, Nāciketa, Bharadvāja, and Śvetāśvatara. (9.204)
Aurva, Dadhīci, Cyavana, Ṛcīka, and Parāśara;
Śātātapa, Lomaśa, Jaigīṣavya, and Devala. (9.205)
Paiṭhīnasi, Vītihavya, Saṃvarta, Agasti, Āsuri, Upamanyu, Mataṅga, as well as Vājasravas and Kaṭha. (9.206)
Uddālaka Āruṇeya, Āśvalāyana, Uttaṅka, Yavakrīta, Kātyāyana, and Ṛtaśravas. (9.207)
These and other sages, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
performed all the sacrificial rites with the prescribed fees fully completed.
Reciting all the Vedic hymns, performing difficult austerities,
meditating upon the partless Brahman, and chanting my mantra— (9.209)
They always worship me with purely sattvic offerings;
their hearts are perpetually offered unto me, and they are ever permeated by a state of goodness.
They have always come to me for refuge; they are peaceful, self-controlled, and have conquered their senses;
they subsist on air, or are without food, and are indeed those whose vital energy is drawn upward.
Such as they were, capable of causing even Śakra to fall by the power of their asceticism, why did they not inform me of the wine? (9.212)
Having recognized in this [woman] the great fault, her censurability, her being a cause of sin, her quality of provoking reproach, her causing one's downfall, and her state of putridity; (9.213)
It brings about the destruction of the next world, likewise serves as a cause for rebirth in hell, destroys the status of the Brahmin caste, and renders one equal to a barbarian. (9.214)
Therefore, having grasped this very path of the Vedas, they abandoned it;
for in this [other path], there is both freedom from defects and the quality of producing merit. (9.215)
If that were so, how is it that the twice-born did not give me liquor?
Having understood the established order of dharma in this way, other members of the twice-born caste as well [refrain from it]. (9.216)
They will by no means offer me any intoxicating liquor, even though they have been instructed in the meaning of the treatises and disregard my words. (9.217)
"Those whose minds are afflicted by greed will act out of delusion; whatever they do, Dharmarāja will surely punish them—of this there is no doubt. (9.218)
"By means of severe punishments and the falling into most terrible hells and the like"—thus did the Mother of the World truly speak to me in the past. (9.219)
Thereupon, O Goddess, I spoke with syllables emerging from the mouth of the Goddess: "Henceforth, listen to the Dharma and my very words. (9.220)

And for those twice-born who, transgressing the command of the Goddess, shall offer liquor, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) is their punisher; one should listen to that which is supreme for those who listen.
O beloved, a non-twice-born person should always offer liquor to the Goddess in secret,
and he himself should daily partake of the great grace (mahāprasāda).
One should always offer meat and burnt fish;
then Kālikā is immediately pleased with these [offerings] from Śūdras and others. (9.223)
O lady of excellent complexion, whatever censure has been described regarding the giving of liquor to the twice-born, that same amount of praise should be understood to apply to Śūdras. (9.224)
Therefore, a Śūdra should diligently offer liquor to the Goddess;
[he shall obtain] long life, freedom from disease, eloquence, and honor among kings. (9.225)
Furthermore, by means of liquor, a Śūdra attains the fulfillment of his desires for sons, fields, and a wife, and in the end, he reaches heaven and other celestial realms. (9.226)

O beloved, that abundance of fruit which is heard of in the Tantras and other scriptures resulting from the offering of liquor should be understood as referring specifically to Śūdras, and certainly not to the twice-born.
Whatever food one eats oneself, that same food belongs to one's deities and one's ancestors; such is the established rule of the Vedas. (9.228)
Among all classes of living beings, human birth is extremely difficult to obtain;
even among those with human bodies, the Śūdra is superior to those of the lowest castes. (9.229)
A Vaiśya is a hundred times superior to a Śūdra; a king is a thousand times superior to a Vaiśya;
and a Brahmin devoted to his own Vedic study should be known as ten million times superior to a king. (9.230)
For this very reason, having created the world of moving and non-moving beings at the beginning of the creation,
Brahmā took for himself whatever was the most essential substance from among them for the sake of the twice-born.
The Vedas, the six auxiliary sciences, forbearance, truth, austerity, fortitude, purity, self-control, compassion, righteousness, discernment, and sweet speech. (9.232)
Renunciation, tranquility, moral discipline, Vedic study, contemplation on the inner self, sacrifices with all kinds of oblations, cow’s milk, and pure food—these indeed [are the means]. (9.233)
He gave these things in their opposite form to the Śūdras alone;
consequently, he subjected all three of the [higher] castes to the state of servitude.
Livelihood through all types of crafts, the absence of mantras, lack of formal benedictions, impurity, and exclusion from the ritual row; || 9.235 ||
Untouchability, lack of eligibility for Vedic study, and likewise the prohibition against conversation; the consumption of liquor and meat, as well as the selling of them. (9.236)
The act of giving that [gift] to the gods, as well as the very production of it;
going to lands such as those of the Mlecchas, and indeed coming into contact with them. (9.237)
O Goddess, because of this great audacity and the very fact of not listening to the Vedas, by virtue of this boundary of the Vedas— || 9.238 ||
I declare that these alone have the authority regarding the offering of wine;
there is not even the slightest fault for them in giving liquor to the gods. (9.239)
Furthermore, an abundance of fruit is heard of in the Vedas and other scriptures;
therefore, a Śūdra should diligently offer what has been heard [of the ritual] to the Goddess.
A Brahmin should always avoid that very [gift], even at the risk of his own life;
for even after hearing of such faults, if he still desires to give it— (9.241)
He and she discern whether it be dharma or indeed evil.
(Also in the Agastyasaṃhitā:
"But we two, O Goddess of the Gods, [are satisfied] with flesh, blood, and even wine. (9.242)
Those who perform sacrifices without considering the dharma appropriate to their caste and stage of life become *brahmarākṣasas*, [beings] such as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*.
(Merutantra) Arisen together with nectar, wine becomes nectar in the proper place;
arisen even together with poison, by that [same principle] wine becomes poison. (9-244)
Likewise: "Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are designated as *surā* (intoxicant).
It is not desired for Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas; what then to say of the Brāhmaṇa? (9.245)
Now, the classification of the Vidyās (*Kālītantra*):
The *Kalīhṛdaya-vidyā*, the *Siddhi-vidyā*, and the *Mahodayā*.
By means of which [Vidyā] and in what manner [it] was previously recited, the gods attained perfection. (9.246)
The syllable of desire (KĀM) situated in fire (RA), together with Indirā (I), Nāda (Ū), and Bindu (M)—this is known as the King of Mantras, difficult for those of sinful minds to obtain. (9.247)
Indeed, this threefold [mantra] is especially the awakener of all scriptures;
there is no knowledge equal to this which bestows the gift of Sarasvatī.
"By means of this [mantra], one may accomplish attraction, subjugation, killing, and expulsion, as well as rites such as pacification and nourishment, without delay"— and so forth (9.249).
Likewise: "All [practices] such as meditation and worship, the means of accomplishment (sādhana), and the preliminary rites—all these are said to be identical for Aniruddha-Sarasvatī. (9.250)
p.
751) My recitation, worship, and so forth, as before, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through their specific excellence (in the Śrutisiddhānta).
Having first extracted one's own seed-syllable, [the mantra] is *kālike*, followed by *vahnigohinī*. (9.251)
This six-syllabled vidyā bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (In the Merutantra:
Its ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth are as previously described; however, it is considered specifically to grant worldly enjoyment. (9-252)
In that very same [text]:
"The three-syllabled mantra *krī hū hrī* is proclaimed as belonging to Kālī;
its recitation and so forth are as before, and it specifically bestows a continuous lineage. (9.253)
The seed-syllable of Kālī is *hūṃ*, and *māyā* is *huṃ*; the five-syllabled mantra is *phaṭ*.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth are as before; its specific power is the destruction of spirits (*bhūta*). (9.254)
Having uttered "krī hū hrī hu phaṭ," there is a seven-syllable mantra ending in "svāhā.
Then follow two *māyās*, a pair of *kūrca*s, ending with the *aindra* [vajra], and three *madana*s. (9.255)

One should extract the seven seed-syllables by means of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), beginning with the word "Kālike" on the right, joined with the Māyā-vowel (Ī) and the Viśvara (R). (9.256)
The mantra of Kālikā begins with Tārā and consists of twenty-one syllables. (Also in the Merutantra:
"Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] consisting of twenty-one letters. (9.257)
Oṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ hūḥ. The placement (nyāsa) of the pair of powers (śakti-yugma) and so forth is as before.
[He is] mounted upon a corpse at the root of a bilva tree, and likewise at the root of a vaṭa tree. (9.258)
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one shall become a master of all siddhis;
contemplating the fifth [mantra] as its representative, it bestows the siddhis of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
Likewise: "O Kālikā, svāhā!"—this is the supreme eight-syllable mantra. (p.
752) The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is as before; [one should meditate on] Śiva situated upon the corpse, which is the object of meditation and the mantra. (9.260)
[She is] intensely attached to Mahākāla and surrounded on all sides by Śivās;
likewise: "Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme mantra of the color of Śakra. (9.261)
*Krī hū hrī* is for Kālikā on the right; *krī hū hrī* is for Dahanapriyā.
The worship, including the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), meditation, recitation (*japa*), and so forth, is declared to be as previously described. (9.262)
This [mantra] is especially capable of attracting humans, gods, and others;
it consists of the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ* three times, *krī* twice, followed by *lajjāṃ svāhā*, possessing both specific forms and phonemes. (9.263)

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth are as before; however, there is a specific subjugation (*vaśīkṛti*) through the recitation (*japa*) of this [mantra]. Everything else, moreover, is as previously described. (9.264)
Having uttered *krī* *krī* *krī* *hū*, one should utter *hū* and the two *lajjās*. To the south, "O Kālikā, svāhā" is proclaimed as having fifteen syllables. (9-265)
This king of mantras has been declared; its worship should be performed as previously described.
Specifically, for those who have lost their kingdoms, this shall be the bestower of sovereignty. (9.266)
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this Gātrī has been stated in the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*:
"Having meditated thus upon Mahākālī, one should recite [her mantra] four hundred thousand times;
one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with bilva leaves smeared with red [substances] in a tenth part of that amount. (9-267)
Now, regarding the mantra of Mahākāla (in the Śaktisaṅgama),
the venerable Śiva said: "Listen to the determination of the Nityās, beginning with Mahākāla."
Mahākālī is most formidable, resembling the fire of universal destruction.
Śiva, who is born from the illusion (māyā) of Kālī and whose mind is fixed on Kālī,
is Mahākāla, the supreme Śambhu, the source of qualities that transcend even the highest.
I shall proclaim his mantra, by which one may protect the three worlds:
"Kūrcayugam, Mahākāla, prasīda"—these two phrases. (9.270)
The pair of *lajjās* (the two *hrīṃ*s) conjoined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*) constitutes the sixteen-syllable mantra;
these sixteen syllables are preeminent throughout the entire circle of the *śīcakra*. (9.271)
Likewise, this is proclaimed as Mahākāla at all times;
Kālikā is declared his seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is proclaimed as the meter (chanda). || 9.272 ||
The deity is Mahākāla, who possesses all forms and is stainless;
likewise, his seed-syllable is Kūrca (HŪM), and Māyā (HRĪM) is proclaimed as his Śakti. || 9.273 ||
The *svāhā*-kīla has been described; its application is for the purpose of Kālī.
Now hear, O fair-faced one, the six limbs performed with *māyā* and the visualization (*dhyāna*). (9.274)
Now, as for the meditation: [He is] radiant like the fire at the end of an aeon, four-armed and three-eyed, standing in the midst of eight cremation grounds, adorned by eight severed heads. (9.275)
The deity stands upon five corpses; he holds a trident and a hand-drum, as well as a sword and a skull-bowl, in his left and right hands respectively.
Bearing a beautiful body adorned with the ashes of the cremation ground,
he sports with various corpses while holding Kālikā within his heart.
Caressing her while intent on passion, devoted to fierce kissing, surrounded by vultures and jackals, and accompanied by a pack of female jackals. (9.278)
Richly adorned with the beauty of a mass of matted locks, he dwells in the abode of universal void;
Śiva has a serene countenance, is the universal void itself, and is adorned with a severed head.
The word "should meditate" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
having thus performed the worship, O Śivā, one should then recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform a fire sacrifice with *karavīra* flowers using one-tenth of that [number]. (9.280)

One should offer oblations with seeds consecrated by the Self-born One, or with those consecrated by the Cause; one should perform all rites—daily, occasional, and for specific desires—just as in the case of Kālī. (9.281)
Now, the mantra of Mahākālī (from the Merutantra): "Next, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Mahākālī:
Oṃ kṣaḥ kṣreḥ kṣreḥ kreḥ, then kreḥ, and one should utter 'grahāṇa paśum' (seize the victim). 9-282.
"Huḥ phaṭ svāhā" is declared to be the mantra of Śakra’s color; for this perfected mantra, no ritual placement (nyāsa) of sages and so forth exists. (9.283)
Having summoned Kālikā into a jar filled with black water,
the devotee should worship her together with the female messengers (dūtīs), beginning with Brāhmī.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon the goddess Caṇḍikā here in the home on the eighth day.
As for the meditation:
"She has five faces, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses three eyes in each face. (9.285)
The Goddess, adorned with serpent ornaments, holds in her right and left hands a spear, a trident, a bow, an arrow, a shield, a sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
the practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the left-hand practice (*vāmācāra*).
Thereafter, he should offer oblations of *picumarda* wood fuel sticks smeared with clarified butter.
Then, when fire has been kindled with a rope, one should perform the libations and other rites;
thus, the practitioner whose mantra is perfected shall slay the enemy before long. (9.288)
Now, the mantra of Bhadrakālī is given in that same place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme mantra of Bhadrakālī:
*Hauṃ Kālī*, Mahākālī; twice *Kiṇi*; *Phaṭ*—the beloved of the eight. (9.289)
The fourteen-syllable mantra of Bhadrakālī has been proclaimed;
one should fashion the six limbs, joined with the [seed] syllables of birth, by means of six words. (9.290)

(p. 755) Now, regarding meditation: This goddess Bhadrakālī, who inspires fear, emaciated by hunger and possessing sunken eyes, should always be meditated upon as she says, "I am not yet satiated. (9-291)
With a face like black soot, her hair disheveled, she was eager to devour the world;
with teeth resembling jambu fruits and a flickering tongue, she was terrifying.
Holding a trident, a skull-bowl, a goad, and a flaming noose—whatever has been taught in the Kālikā-tantra in its entirety, that is also here. (9.293)
The specific procedure for the placement of mantras (nyāsa) and its application is now stated:
having worshipped [the deity], one should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. (9.294)
A garland of *riṣṭa* beads should be fashioned for the purpose of recitation by one desiring success;
this goddess, the Great Goddess, is the subduer of enemies. (9.295)
She should be meditated upon with actions performed as one desires, for she bestows the accomplishment of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha.
Now I shall declare another mantra of Bhadrakālī, which is well-guarded in secret. (9.296)
"O Gṛdhrakarṇī, Virūpākṣī, Lambastanī, Mahodarī!
Produce [the state], cause [beings] to cross over!"—thus the word "pada" (foot/state) occurs twice in the latter part. 9-297.
It knows the word in two ways: *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, consisting of seven fire-colored syllables; Pippalāda is declared to be the sage, and the Nivṛt metre is cited. (9-298)
Bhadrakālī shall be the deity; "dvir utpādya" is remembered as the heart (hṛt).
"Uparibhyām" is declared to be the head (śiras), while "vettibhyām" is remembered as the crest-lock (śikhā).
The armor is proclaimed with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, and the weapon with *svāhā*.
Now, the meditation: She is exceedingly fierce, with great fangs, very long [in stature], and thin-waisted. (9.300)
With well-rounded eyes, heroic, long-nosed, and intoxicated with passion,
she possesses a smooth and deep resonance and resembles a dark blue cloud.
(756) Blazing with a jar of molten lead, terrifying with great fangs, her eyes copper-red with rage against her lips and tusks, and her long hair blood-stained; 9.302.
With her staff-like arms occupied by a trident, devouring the worms of hell,
the goddess is clad in exceedingly red garments and is fond of blood, flesh, and wine.
Her limbs adorned with a garland of heads, drinking the wine of blood,
she dances and laughs, attended by hosts of piśācas.
Having mounted the shoulder of a Piśāca, she wanders over the surface of the earth;
born from the mouth of Śaṅkara, she is a Yoginī beloved of Yoga.
Thus endowed, Bhadrakālī is surrounded by the Mothers. Now follows the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa):
having meditated correctly and having worshipped her thoroughly, the wise one should then recite the mantra. (9.306)
For the sake of attaining success in mantra, one intent on the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa) should perform ten thousand recitations;
likewise, an oblation of ghee (ghṛtahoma) should be performed, and one should carry out the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites.
And whatever has been taught in the *Dhūmāvatī* [Tantra], that too one should practice.
Now, the mantra of Siddhikālī (from the *Kālītantra*):
"Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the highly exalted Siddhavidyā. (9-308)
In ancient times, the Lord spoke of the Goddess known as Hṛdīśā;
having first uttered the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable Hṛllekhā.
The Vidyārājñī is proclaimed as being joined with two *ṭha* letters;
Bhairava is declared its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *virāṭ* meter is cited for it. (9.310)
Siddhikālī is the deity who is the form of Brahman, the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī);
her seed-syllable is *ratī*, and she is said to have *hṛllekhā* as her power (*śakti*).

One should fashion the six limbs with the *hṛllekhā* mantra, preceded by the *praṇava* and extended by the six long vowels; then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) and meditated upon the Goddess, one becomes Śiva. (9.312)
As for the meditative visualization (*dhyāna*):
Her body is drenched by the nectar flowing from the orb of the moon split open by a sword; three-eyed and with disheveled hair, she drinks the nectar dripping from a skull-cup held in her right hand.

Clad in the directions as her garment, girdled with a golden belt, adorned with a crown of jewels and other ornaments, with a flaming tongue, possessing the luster of a blue lotus, and with feet encircled by earrings shining like the sun and moon—may she protect us. (9.313)

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): the knower of mantras should recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times, together with an additional thousand; he should then perform a fire oblation (*homa*) with soft flowers using one-tenth of that number. (9.314)
Now, the mantra of Śmaśānakālī (from the *Svatantratantra*):
"O Śivā, listen attentively to the mantra of Śmaśānakālikā:
[the syllable] Vāṇī, Māyā, Tāra, Lakṣmī, and thereafter the seed-syllable of Kāma. (9.315)

O Goddess of gods, one should write the fourfold seed-syllables in their combined form according to the *kālika* method; this [mantra] consists of eleven syllables and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. (9.316)
The seer is Bhṛgu; the metre is Nivṛt; the deity is the supreme Kālikā;
she who dwells in the cremation ground and so forth is Vāṅmāyā; O Maheśvarī, she is the seed-syllable and the power. (9.317)
"The *kīlaka* is that which is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*)...
Thus [it is said]. With the four, four, three, and four *vidyā*-mantras, one performs the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*). (9.318)
Having performed the ritual placement, one should, with a concentrated mind, meditate upon the Goddess Kālikā,
who resembles a mountain of collyrium and dwells in the cremation ground.
She has three eyes, her hair is disheveled, and she is extremely terrifying with her emaciated flesh;
she has tawny eyes and holds in her left hand a skull-cup filled with wine.
I salute Śivā, who holds with her right hand a head recently severed,
whose face is ever smiling, and who is constantly intent on satiating herself with the flesh of the left side.
"One whose limbs are adorned with various ornaments, yet naked and always intoxicated by corpses"—
the remainder of the sentence is that "one should meditate in this manner.
Now, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and its tenth part—thus [it is said]. ||322||
Now, the mantra of Siddhilakṣmī (from the Kālānalatantra):
Oṃ hrīḥ huḥ hāḥ phreṃ kṣoḥ kroḥ namaḥ | Śruti, Caṭī, Dogdhrī, Śoṣiṇī, together with Śirā. (9-323)
Next, Dolā, then Mālūra, Sāmara, and Niratyaya;
at the end, Daṇḍa is to be recognized—this is the nine-syllable [meter] that has been described.
No mantra equal to this exists in the three worlds. Now, with another mantra, [he says] right there: "Now I shall extract the supreme sixteen-syllable mantra of the Goddess of the Gods. (9.325)
By reciting this once, one is liberated from the perils of birth:
HRĪḤ HŪṂ PHREṂ CHRĪḤ HSRAUḤ HRĪḤ KROṂ PHREṂ STRĪ ŚRĪ HO JŪ BLAU VRĪ SVĀHĀ. (9-326)
Caṭī, Dogdhrī, Śirasiddhi, Bhūmarddhi, and Prota;
then Phalī, Śiras, Retas, Prātar, and Āntra thereafter. (9.327)
The preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) consist of fire-oblations (*homa*) performed while wandering along the banks of a turbid lake;
this mantra is also remembered as the most excellent among all mantras.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and other elements for these two is stated in that very same place:
"For the mantra of Śrī Siddhilakṣmī, the seer is declared to be Nārada;
the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter, and Siddhilakṣmī is the deity. (9.329)

The seed-syllable (bīja) is thus declared to be Caṭī; effort (samīhā) is held to be Śakti; one should know that Prabandha is Kīlaka, [all] for the sake of the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha). (9.330)

O Nārada, the application (*viniyoga*) of this mantra has been told to you. Now follow the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*) for the hands and limbs: the assignment for the hands and limbs is taught by means of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) endowed with the six long vowels. (9.331)
Now, O bull among the twice-born, I shall explain this to you in an easy manner:
having first uttered the seed-syllable with the *śruti*, one should then [place it] on the feet with both thumbs. (9.332)
The *daṇḍa* [mudrā] is declared for the remainder; furthermore, one should describe two seeds.
When [the fingers are joined] by the two index fingers (*tarjanī*), it is designated there as the *daṇḍa*. (9.333)
Furthermore, where there are two seed-syllables, from those [comes] the middle mantra;
the staff is to be known in the remainder, and then that very same seed-syllable again. (9.334)
Then the staff (daṇḍa) is proclaimed from the two ring fingers;
from the two seeds [and] the two little fingers, the seed of the staff is remembered from the word "pad". || 9-335 ||
