Having performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*)— with the two seed-syllables on the palms and the back of the hands, and likewise on the staff— the wise practitioner should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
O Brahmin, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to this sequence;
having addressed the two ears, one should then utter the word "to the heart" (hṛdayāya).
Thereafter, O brahmin-sage, there is the *daṇḍa*, and likewise two further seed-syllables;
then the seed-syllable of the milch-cow (*dogdhrī*) is prescribed for the head and for the feet.
Having uttered those two seed-syllables and the word *śikhāyai*, one should utter the seed-syllable of Indra;
then one should speak the two seed-syllables again.
O Nārada, one should indeed utter the seed-syllable *dogdhri* after the word for the armor (*kavaca*),
and likewise, having recited the seed-syllable, [one says] "to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ."
The six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) has been described as the purification of the body for the purpose of worship.
Now, regarding meditation: O son of Aja, listen as I proclaim the meditation upon her. (9.341)
White in color, mounted upon a white corpse, with human skulls forming her earrings,
she has five faces, is exceedingly fierce, and possesses three eyes in each face.
Her waist was draped with a tiger skin, her limbs were adorned with dried [flesh], she wore a yogapaṭṭa tied around her, and her ornaments were made of human bones. (9.343)
With sixteen hands, she is radiant, her thick locks of hair disheveled;
she holds a sword, an arrow, a trident, a discus, a spear, and even a mace.
She holds a rosary and a knife in her right hands,
as well as a shield, a bow, a serpent-noose, and an axe.
She carries in her left hands a hand-drum, a jackal cub, and a skull-cup filled with human heads, while all her limbs are adorned with long ornaments.
This is the meditation for the nine-syllable mantra. Regarding the sixteen-syllable vidyā, another meditation is stated in that very same place:
"Lakṣmī consists of great splendor, with the radiance of ten million crores of rays;
she has five faces, ten arms, and is endowed with fifteen eyes. (9.346)
The goddess, resembling the color white, stands upon a great preta;
she resides in the midst of the eight Mātṛkās and is attended by those perfected in yoga.
With her gaping mouth, she was licking [the world], her flames obscuring the three worlds;
by the force of her exhalations and inhalations, she shook the great mountain ranges.
In some place, on some peak, or somewhere else, he may dissolve [the world] in an instant; in some place he may create and protect it, or he proceeds from his own sovereignty. (9.349)
Adorned with ornaments of serpents and decorated with the lords of snakes, the Goddess holds a noose and a goad, her lotus-like hands granting boons and fearlessness. 350.
In his right hand he holds a sword that causes the agitation of the three worlds;
in his left, an extremely fierce *khaṭvāṅga*, and in his right [other hand], an excellent trident.
In her left hand, however, she holds a divine flask filled with great jewels;
this is the goddess Pratyaṅgirā, the intoxicated one born from the body of space. (352)
The Great Goddess Pratyaṅgirā, the Fortune of Accomplishment who bestows victory, abides pervading the entire universe with her single self through manifold divisions. 353.

(paddhatau) Śivā, who appears with her excellent arms holding a skull-topped staff, a goad, a noose, a trident, a boon-granting gesture, a protection gesture, a vessel, a severed head, a jar, a sword, and a blazing [flame], [is worshipped].
I worship the Blessed Lady Śrī Siddhilakṣmī, who rests upon the shoulders of Rudra, who resembles the autumnal moon, who is beautiful with five faces, and who is adorned with fifteen eyes. 354.

Regarding the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for the two aforementioned mantras of Śrīsiddhilakṣmī, they should be understood as being like the "Secret Preliminary Rite" (*guhyāpuraścaraṇa*) described in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*.
As it is said in the *Kālānalatantra*:
"O twice-born one, just as Kāmakalā is Kālī, so too is Guhyakālī."
Just as Chinnā, just as Tārā, and just as Vajrakāpalinī.
Likewise, there is no difference whatsoever between the goddess Siddhilakṣmī and [the other];
O twice-born one, the worship is to be understood as one and the same, as are the ritual applications.
Whatever has not been stated here, as well as that which is in the Saṃhitā, they know it;
and because of the fear of making the book too voluminous, other things have not been told to you, O twice-born one. (9.357)
In brief, O best of men, everything concerning the signs of success for Siddhilakṣmī has been proclaimed to you;
it is also detailed at length in the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
O Nārada, recitation (*japa*), preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and proper conduct (*ācāra*) have been proclaimed in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* regarding the practice of the *Kāmakalā*. (9.359)
O Brahmin Nārada, by that very same path, all know the entirety of the fortune of spiritual perfection (*siddhi-lakṣmī*);
out of fear of redundancy, I shall not speak of it here.
Now, the mantra of Guhyakālī (from the Mahākālasaṃhitā):
"O Dear One, there are eighteen varieties of the mantras of Guhyakālī; they are to be kept secret in all the Āgamas and must never be disclosed. (9.361)
According to the distinctions among mantras, there are likewise various distinctions of meditations;
similarly, there are distinctions of yantras as well as distinctions of vehicles. (9.362)
O beloved, the traditional transmission (āmnāya) is proclaimed to be that mantra by which it was practiced,
as was done by Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise by Rāma.
Also by Hiraṇyākṣa, by Ugra, by Kuvera,
by Yama, by Bharata, by Daśāsya, by Bali, and by Vāsava.
She was worshipped by Viṣṇu, by other gods, and even by various lords of the Daityas, for the sake of attaining perfection, and she granted them abundant success.
She is proclaimed to have a hundred faces, eighty faces, and likewise sixty faces;
she is also described as having thirty-six faces and twenty faces.
Likewise, Kālikā has twenty faces, ten faces, five faces, three faces, two faces, and one face. (9.367)
O Dear One, Guhyakālī, who is worshipped by Bharata, resides in the center of that;
she has ten faces, sixteen syllables, and is endowed with fifty-four arms.
She is indeed remembered as the most preeminent among all the Guhyakālīs;
I shall first describe her, and thereafter I shall describe the others.
The sixteen-syllable mantra is both fixed and unfixed. Of these, I shall first speak of the fixed, and thereafter I shall speak of the unfixed. (9.370)
O Pārvatī, the meditation on the pin and the non-pin is indeed one and the same.
He states the extraction of the mantra: first, having extracted the beginning of the Veda, then the second letter of *pa*. (9.371)
One should join the letter *ra* beneath that [the letter *e*] along with the vowel *a* and the bindu;
then, having uttered the word "siddhi," one should designate "karālī. (9.372)
Recalling shame and anger, one should raise the left elbow;
then, one should join that [elbow] with the left eye, the bindu, the downward-facing fire (va), and the letter ta. (9.373)
Furthermore, one should extract the seed-syllable of the bride, which is the second seed of the mantra;
this sixteen-syllable mantra consists of the heart-mantra and the wife of fire (svāhā). || 9.374 ||
He states another method:
"Alternatively, one should first recollect Krodha from the seed-syllable of the beloved woman;
for this [goddess] is worshipped by Bharata and is also bound by a curse. (9.375)

The sixteen-syllable mantra worshipped by Bharata is of two kinds; therein, the first is "pinned" (kīlitā) while the second is "unpinned" (akīlitā)—this is the meaning. He speaks of the seventeen-syllable mantra:
"Therefore, I shall now describe the one consisting of seventeen syllables worshipped by Rāma;
that too was pinned by the sage Hārīta through the power of his asceticism. (9.376)
First, one should extract four syllables of that very mantra;
then, one should apply "hasakhaṃ" above the second seed-syllable.
Thus, the fifth seed-syllable is deprived of the sixth by means of *kha*;
and immediately after that, O Karālī, the seventh is devoid of *ha* and *sa*.
The seventh syllable is in the thirteenth and eleventh positions;
the fifth is in the twelfth position, and the second is in the fourteenth. (9.379)
One should perform the first [mantra] on the fifteenth day; this is the mantra of Vahnijayā, worshipped by Hārīta. Now hear about the one worshipped by Cyavana.
The transposition of its sixth and fifth [syllables] is proclaimed;
by this alone, the *cyāvanī* becomes one of very great fruit. (9.381)

In this context, the seventeen-syllable mantra worshipped by Rāma is twofold: that worshipped by Hārīta and that worshipped by Cyavana. Between these two, it should be understood that only the one worshipped by Hārīta is "pinned" (kīlitā), whereas the one worshipped by Cyavana is not pinned.
He states the seer and other details:
"Now I shall speak of the two distinct sixteen-syllable mantras."
Next, I shall tell you the seer and so forth of the seventeenth [chapter].
Atharvan is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Jagatī is said to be the meter (chandas).
The deity is Guhyakālī, and the second syllable is the pin (kīlaka). (9.383)
The Śakti is the tenth seed-syllable, and it becomes the ninth in the second [position];
this is the abiding state of desire for the sake of accomplishing the four aims of human life.
For the seventeenth mantra, Parameṣṭhin is considered the seer; the meter is called Sapratiṣṭhā, and the deity is Guhyakālikā. (9.385)
The fifth syllable is the *kīlaka*, and the seventh is said to be the *śakti*. That same [syllable], when reversed, is declared to be the *cyāvanī*.
The application for the sake of all accomplishments should be uttered during recitation;
now I shall tell you the extraction of other varieties of mantras.
Then, O Pārvatī, I shall describe their ṛṣis and so forth;
now, the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) therein is as follows:
two, five, three, two, two, and again two, and likewise [two] more.
One should place the phonemes and syllables of the Goddess Bhāratī in their respective locations;
one should place that many syllables, together with the Praṇava, in each of those places.
Whatever sequence of mantra-syllables constitutes the *cyāvanī*, those syllables situated between the two *tāra*s are indeed the *vī* syllables. (9-389)
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon those very locations in the *Manu* honored by Hārīta.
He states the meditation (*dhyāna*): "That which is remembered as being worshipped by Bharata and that which is worshipped by Rāma. (9.390)
Listen as I describe the single meditation common to both of them:
one should meditate upon an overflowing ocean of blood arising from the power of the Goddess. (9.391)
There, filling the quarters of space with exceedingly high waves,
was an island filled with red flesh and possessing red sands.
Surrounded by nine crores of Cāmuṇḍās and ten million Bhairavas, one should meditate upon the maṇḍala in its center, extending for ten thousand yojanas. (9.393)
One should visualize there a rampart composed of ten million Bhairavīs; in its center is a single cremation ground extending for a hundred yojanas.
One should visualize the circle of the constellations pervaded by surging flames of fire,
with the activity of millions of yoginīs clapping their hands.
With a steady mind, one should meditate upon Kālī stationed within that [maṇḍala], which has an archway garland fashioned from a string of human entrails and skulls.
One should meditate upon him holding a divine jeweled lion-throne made of diamonds, pearls, and other gems, at each of its four corners supporting a pair of Vedic verses.
The Kṛtayuga is the Ṛgveda, white in color, and situated in the east;
the Tretāyuga is the Yajurveda, yellow in color, and situated in the south. (9-398)
The Dvāpara age and the Sāmaveda are red, situated in the western direction;
the Kali age and the Atharvaveda are dark blue, situated in the northern direction.
Upon the head of the radiant Upaveda, a lion-throne is situated;
above that lion-throne is another great lion-throne.
One should meditate without weariness upon those who support the Goddess’s lion-throne, surrounded on all eight directions by [their respective] weapons and vehicles. 9-401.
Each remained occupying his own direction, most beautifully adorned; Indra was yellow, holding a thunderbolt, and stood atop Airāvata.
Pāvaka is red in color, seated upon a goat, and holds a spear in his hand;
Yama is black, seated upon a buffalo, and has a staff in his hand. (9.403)
And Varuṇa, with noose in hand, white in color, and having a makara as his vehicle;
and Vāyu, dark-complexioned, bearing a banner, seated upon a deer. || 9-404 ||
Gadādhara and Kuvera, with the luster of saffron, are situated upon a man;
and Īśāna, white in color and holding a trident in his hand, is situated upon a bull. (9-405)
And the third is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), O beloved, which is supported by five pretas;
[these are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These five great pretas are situated below the lion throne;
they are yellow, dark green, red, smoke-colored, and white, respectively.
Holding a staff, a discus, a spear, a trident, and a khaṭvāṅga,
they have three eyes with the index finger placed upon their mouths.
There are lions, elephants, and hyenas, terrifying with their howling cries;
above that seat, one should then meditate upon the fearsome one named Bhairava.
Dwarfish, very stout, formidable, black in color,
four-armed, five-faced, three-eyed, and adorned with ornaments of bones.

Holding a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and a flaying knife (kartṛkā) in his right hands, as well as a skull-cup (kapāla) and a hand-drum (ḍamaru), he is adorned with a garland of severed heads and is terrifying with the tips of his fangs.
Above that is a sixteen-petaled lotus prepared for sacrifice;
the Jyotiṣṭoma, Agniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, and the Ṣoḍaśin [are its parts]. (9.412)
The Cayana, the Puṇḍarīka, the Rājasūya, the Aśvamedha, the Bārhaspatya, the Viśvajit, the Gomedha, and the Naramedha. || 9-413 ||
The Sautrāmaṇi, the Ardhāsāvitrī, the Sun-gem (sūryakānta), and the Mountain-splitter (acalambhida)—
with these sixteen petals, a lotus is thus fashioned.
Thereupon, one should meditate above that upon the unsurpassed seat of Śiva, which is blue, joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and marked by the crescent moon. (9.415)
Adorned with ornaments of highly precious jewels, three-eyed, and of terrifying appearance,
he is Śivottama, whose teeth and claws are like adamant, seated upon the back of a lotus.
(767) He has a mass of tawny, fierce, single matted locks; he is two-armed and wears a snake as an ornament;
he is clothed in a tiger skin and carries a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff. || 9.417 ||
Above that is an eight-petaled lotus, which serves as the ninth seat;
Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya are located in the four directions.
Fame, solitude, desire, and liberation are located in the intermediate directions.
Thus, one should meditate upon Guhyakālī seated upon an eight-petaled lotus.
One should meditate on her who is dark as a blue lotus, possessing a luster like that of sapphire,
whose body shines like a dense rain-cloud, and who has the brilliance of a tender blade of dūrvā grass.
She stands in the midst of a circle of light, a mass of expanding rays of wisdom;
she is Guhyakālī with ten faces and twenty-seven eyes.
She has two eyes on each of her faces— the left, the right, and the front—
and is endowed with three eyes on each of her other seven faces.
The upper face is called Dvipaka, known as Caṇḍayogeśvarī;
below that is the lion-faced [face], white in color and terrifying.
Below that is a black jackal-face, the Trailokyadaṃmara;
then to the left is a monkey-face, intensely radiant with red light.
That face on the left should be known as human-faced, resembling Kirmīra, exceedingly fierce;
on the right, it should have the face of a bear, smoke-colored and terrifying.
Then, on the left, there is a face with the head of a garuḍa, tawny in color and possessing a beautiful beak; and on the right, a face with the head of a makara, proclaimed to be greenish in hue.
One should contemplate the elephant-faced [deity] on the left of Kālī, with a face like a cow, flowing with rut;
and the horse-faced [deity] on the right, who is dark-colored. (9.427)
They have great fangs that are terrifying, they possess dreadful sounds, they are filled with loud,
mocking laughter, and they are constantly dripping with blood.
And she bears on her face the auspicious Śivā, which possesses a trembling, beautiful tongue protruding and licking, and which quivers day and night. (9.429)
She was terrifying with a fearsome roar, her face contorted with frowns and eyebrows;
she wore a mass of tawny, upright matted locks, with the crescent moon serving as her crest-ornament.
Her head is adorned with various jewels fashioned from skulls and golden ornaments;
she wears a garland of stars made from a stream of blood flowing from human heads.
She was adorned with a garland of severed heads hanging from her neck down to her ankles, and she shone most brilliantly with a necklace and a collar made of white bone-beads.
Her chest was adorned with rows of fingers as long as a corpse,
and she possessed a pair of firm, tawny, and towering breasts.
Adorned with a hip-altar made of great emerald stones,
she possessed the expansive curve of broad hips and exceedingly slender waist-regions.
[He beheld] the Mother of the World, adorned with tinkling bells swinging from the heads of infants bound upon her,
and graced with fifty-four arms.
A jewel garland, a skull-cup, a hide, and likewise a noose;
a spear, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a severed head, a bhuśuṇḍī weapon, and a bow.
Then the wheel, the bell, the young preta, and after that the mountain;
Naraka, Kāla, Nakula, the serpent, Unmāda, and Vaṃśikā. (9.437)
A mallet, a fire-pit, a hand-drum, and likewise a small drum;
a sling, a pestle, a noose, and also a sharp-edged spear.
She holds a *śataghnī* and a *śivāpota* in her left hands;
then, in her right arms, she carries a jewel garland, a lute, and likewise a sword.
The threatening gesture, the goad, the staff, the jewel-pitcher, and the trident;
the five arrows of Paśupati—those which cause withering, intoxication, and fainting. (9.440)
Those who bear the names of the destroyers and bringers of death—namely Kunta, Pārijāta, Churikā, and likewise Tomara—(p. 769).
A garland of flowers, a small drum, a vulture, and a water-pot;
a piece of meat, a sacrificial ladle (*śruva*), a citron, and likewise a large sacrificial spoon (*śruc*).
Holding an axe, a mace, a staff, a fist, and a corpse-mutilating weapon, she was exceedingly fierce and the cause of the destruction of the world.
She wore a pair of anklets fashioned by the great serpent king, resembling the Java flower,
and was adorned with shimmering armlets made of Pāṭala-colored serpents.
She wears a broad waist-thread fashioned from a greyish snake,
and is adorned with earrings made from a very pale lordly serpent.
Her matted hair, bound with a white hooded serpent, is adorned with a crown;
she is clothed in a tiger skin and wears a leopard skin as an upper garment.
Richly adorned with a network of tinkling bells, sounding with the roar of heroic gongs,
charming with the jingling of anklets, and terrifying with a gurgling sound.
Adorned with the beauty of human bones fashioned into bracelets, armlets, and necklaces,
she wears a garland made of red lotuses that hangs down to her lotus feet.
She was resplendent with a girdle and a waist adorned by a golden belt,
her neck shining with the sacred thread, and she wore a meditation cloth as an upper garment.
She is adorned with both gentle and fierce ornaments, resplendent with eight serpents,
her ears graced by jeweled earrings, and she abides within the five-fold time and the fire of destruction.
The Goddess, seated upon a lotus, eternally manifest, dancing, comfortably seated in the lotus posture, the supreme deity of all gods. || 9-451 ||
One should visualize her flicking the tip of her tongue,
which has the form of a severed head, accompanied by nine crores of Cāmuṇḍās who possess the power of the three categories.
She is empowered by eighteen koṭis of great yoginīs, and she moves about and laughs together with sixty koṭis of ḍākinīs. (9-453)
She is surrounded by a retinue of eight hundred million Bhairavas,
and her body rises up, eclipsing the flames of ten million fires of cosmic destruction.
Resembling ten million suns at the time of the great dissolution, like lightning and clouds,
difficult to behold and most terrifying even for the gods and asuras led by Indra.
She who causes the destruction of the enemy faction, the destroyer of the Daityas and Dānavas;
she who is changeless, without appearance, immutable, and the playful manifestation of consciousness.
Non-dual, supreme bliss, eternal, pure, and stainless—
creation, maintenance, and dissolution are the unnameable manifestation of that which is designated by the word "pada" (the ground).
She is to be known through the Vedānta, whose nature is absolute liberation, who brings about final extinction (nirvāṇa),
who transcends the qualities (guṇas), and whose sphere of experience lies beyond the awakening to the nature of the self.
Thus should Mahākālī be meditated upon, possessing the bloom of fresh youth;
she is Guhyakālī Parameśvarī, situated in the midst of the five-faced one.
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) in that very context:
one should perform the supreme *puraścaraṇa* on a mountain, by a riverbank, in an empty house, in a temple of Śiva, on a sacred seat (*pīṭha*), or at a crossroads. (9.460)
In that regard, many observances (niyamas) must be diligently performed; through performing what is unrighteous, there will be a loss of accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. (9-461)
One should perform the ritual bath at the three times of day, eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) at night,
and one must not show one's own mantra or rosary even to the guru.
One should abandon malicious gossip and avoid slander; likewise, one should avoid the company of the wicked as well as conversation with women and Śūdras. (9.463)
O Great Goddess, the seat should consist of cloth, a mat of kuśa grass, a tiger skin, or even a human skull; furthermore, facing north is highly recommended.
Know that a beautiful rosary fashioned from pure crystal, rudrākṣa seeds, human skulls, or bones is increasingly more praiseworthy as one proceeds further up the list.
By means of this aforementioned procedure, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number, as well as the libation (tarpaṇa) and the consecration (abhiṣecana).
Then, O Dear One, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra should perform the ritual applications;
for this sixteen-syllable Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) is difficult to obtain even for the gods. (From the *Mahātharvaṇasaṃhitā*, 9.467)
O Kuleśānī, he by whom [this] has been obtained from the lotus-face of the true guru through great merits accumulated over ten million births and impelled by devotion— 9.468.
He is blessed and worthy of worship in all the worlds by the inhabitants of the three realms;
there exists no knowledge higher than this in the three worlds.
Therefore, with every effort, this sixteen-syllable vidyā should be recited by the best of practitioners; it should be meditated upon as Guhyakālī.
He by whom this vidyā has been accomplished is indeed that Sadāśiva.
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"That which was described by me to you as Guhyakālī with ten faces... (9.471).
That primordial nature (prakṛti), the Mother of the World belonging to the Kālīs, is to be fully known;
others are declared to be transformations (vikṛtis) according to the distinction between cause and effect.
Likewise:
"O lady of excellent limbs, she alone should be known as having the nature of the qualityless Brahman;
the entire world is under her control, and she is not subject to anyone else. (9.473)
She creates the entire universe, yet no one creates her; she sustains the world, yet no one sustains her. (9.474)
No one can withdraw her; she withdraws all this.
By her command the wind blows, and out of fear of her the sun shines. (9.475)
Out of fear of Him, fire cooks the food; out of fear of Him, death moves about.
(From the Atharvaveda Saṃhitā) Śrī Devī said:
O Supreme Lord, higher than the highest, who has the moon as your crest-jewel!
O Yogādiyogin, omniscient one, devoted to compassion for all beings,
I have heard from you the mantras that are concealed in all the tantras.
And there is also worship according to the rules through the sequences of the nyāsa and āvaraṇa rites;
[the goddesses] Tārā, Chinnamastā, and likewise Tripurasundarī.
Bālā, Vagalā, Tripurā, and likewise Bhairavī;
Kālī, Dakṣiṇakālī, Kubjikā, and Vivareśvarī.
Aghorā, Rājamātā, Siddhilakṣmī, Arundhatī, Aśvārūḍhā, Bhogavatī, Nityaklinnā, and Kukkuṭī. (9.480)
Kaumārī, Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Bhuvaneśī, as well as Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī and Caṇḍaghaṇṭikā. (9.481)
Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Guhyakālī, and likewise another—
these and other goddesses, along with their mantras, have indeed been described by you.
But you have not told me, O Lord, of Kāmakalākālī;
is that perhaps something to be hidden from me as well, O Supreme Lord? (9.483)
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever to be found in the three worlds that could not be told to me, even if it were more precious than my own life. (9.484)
Why then, O wise one, do you conceal from me this great divinity?
If I am worthy of your compassion, if I am honorable and a vessel of your affection. (9.485)
"I am worthy of favor; I am your beloved. Therefore, tell me now about this Goddess Kāmakalākālī, preceded by the mantras and meditations."
Śrī Mahākāla said:
"O beautiful lady, you are blessed and entirely favored by that very goddess,
since such an intention toward her has arisen in you."
"O Goddess, having taken an oath, I shall speak before you:
indeed, no such means for attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation exists upon this earth. (9.488)
"O Goddess, you have spoken the truth, and your state as a cowherd girl is indeed to be concealed in every way;
nevertheless, because of your exceptional devotion, I shall tell you—of this there is no doubt. (9-489)
One may give away a kingdom, one may give away wealth, and likewise one may give away a wife or even one's own head;
but one must never, under any circumstances, give away Kāmakalākālī to anyone.
She was formerly worshipped by Indra, who desired the sovereignty of the gods;
likewise by Varuṇa, by Kubera, and by Brahmā.
By Rāma, by Rāvaṇa, by Yama, by Vivasvat,
by Candra, by Viṣṇu, and likewise by other great ṛṣis.
By the mere remembrance of her, whether playfully or with grace, the fortune of knowledge, the fortune of sovereignty, and the fortune of fame remain under one's control. (9.493)
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking a kingdom obtains a kingdom; and one seeking a beloved obtains an auspicious woman. (9.494)
One who seeks fame attains renown; one who seeks liberation shall attain liberation;
and one who seeks the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇiman*, shall obtain the group of eight *siddhis*.
Likewise:
"If this knowledge is obtained through the full rise of the fortune of those ancestral men who have remained [in the lineage] up to the seventy-second generation," (9-496).
Then, considering himself to have accomplished his purpose, he should, without hesitation, accept [the gift] by giving away all his possessions, while touching the feet of the guru. (9.497)
Likewise: "If the gift of life were placed on one side and this offering on the other, and they were weighed together on a scale, this gift would be superior. (9.498)
Likewise:
"O Goddess of Gods, whether this is obtained through merits accumulated over ten million births or not, take an oath that this shall not be revealed anywhere."
"Truth, truth, my triple truth; therefore I shall speak, O Pārvatī.
If not, I shall not speak even to you; in that matter, she alone is my authority."
The Goddess said:
I swear by your lotus feet; I swear by the Himālaya mountain upon my head;
I swear by Skanda, the sole son of Śiva—if I speak of her to anyone else.
Or rather, I swear by that goddess whom you shall tell me of;
if I reveal her identity, she herself will turn away from me. (9.502)
Mahākāla said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate lady! Now I have full confidence in you;
since you have taken this oath, I shall therefore speak without hesitation."
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, remain composed and attentive;
O beloved, bind your hands in the añjali gesture and make your mind one-pointed.
Listen attentively to me regarding Kālī, preceded by Kāmakalā.
(p. 775) Likewise: That very Guhyakālī is this Kālī known as Kāmakalā. (9.505)
Through the differentiation of mantras and the differentiation of meditations, she becomes the essence of the Kāmakalā;
just as Tārā may be threefold, so too is Sundarī seventy-sevenfold.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be of five kinds; likewise, this Guhyakālikā arises in seven forms through meditation and mantra, possessing distinct appearances.
Just as the five-syllable mantra is known as the goddess Ekajaṭā,
so too the twenty-two-syllable mantra is the goddess Dakṣiṇakālikā.
Likewise, O beloved Goddess, among many other principal deities, the eighteen-syllable mantra of Kāmakalākālī is [the foremost]. (9.509)
Just as the sixteen-syllable [mantra] is considered primary when situated in the center of the entire Śrīcakra,
so too is this [mantra] always remembered as the most preeminent among the nine Kālīs.
The mantra known as Trailokyākarṣaṇa (the Attractor of the Three Worlds) has been proclaimed for her;
I shall now explain its extraction—listen with diligence, O Pārvatī. (9.511)
Having heard this, retain it for the sake of all auspiciousness.
He states the extraction of the mantra:
"The first letter of the first group [of consonants], conjoined with the left eye. (9-512)
On the head, with the head [of the letter *m*], that which is below the third yoke (*ya*) is cut around;
it is joined with the bindu and the left eye (*i*), and fire (*ra*) has the supreme ether (*ha*) as its head. (9.513)
The third [syllable] should be formed with the left ear and a half-moon, followed by the letter *sa*;
the imperishable [syllable] has the right shoulder, the upper teeth, and a bindu at its head.

The second letter of the labial class preceded by *ha*, followed by the lower lip (*adharoṣṭha*) and the bindu—having addressed these six syllables according to the sequence of their names as they stand. (9.515)
Having extracted those five seed-syllables in reverse order—
beginning indeed with the seed-syllable of the elements (bhūta) and ending with the seed-syllable of Māra (māra)— (9.516).
Indeed, this mantra of eighteen syllables is joined with the wife of Vaiśvānara;
by the mere recollection of it, whatever siddhis there may be [are attained]. (9.517)
They come before one of their own accord; what need is there to mention recitation and other such practices? There are seven secret mantras of Kāmakalākālī. (9-518)
Among all those mantras, this one is proclaimed as the foremost;
by the mere remembrance of this mantra, all the deities become transfixed.
Stunned and trembling, they rise up in extreme agitation;
becoming obedient to his commands, they behave like servants. (9.520)
O Queen of the Gods, what is the use of much speaking? I speak with truth from the outset, even if I were to have a thousand mouths, or a hundred thousand, or ten million mouths.
His greatness cannot be described by me even in ten thousand years;
understand it in general terms: whatever the practitioner desires, [he obtains]. (9.522)
It performs all those various deeds like another Prajāpati;
this mantra named Trailokyākarṣaka is the accomplisher of all goals. (9-523)
He states the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seers and so forth: "Henceforth I shall proclaim the meter, the seer, and the seed-syllable.
I am considered the seer of this mantra of Kāmakalākālī. (9.524)
Chanda is known as Bṛhatī, and she is proclaimed as the Goddess;
the first seed-syllable is the seed, while the syllable of wrath is indeed the Śakti.
The application of all this is always for the attainment of every success;
one should perform the six-limbed rite with those five seed-syllables, and also perform one with the Name.
O Pārvatī, the letters of her name should be assigned there one by one.
Now, as for the visualization:
I shall describe her visualization; focus your mind with single-minded concentration. (9.527)
Resembling a *japā* flower embraced by rising dark clouds,
possessing the luster of the eyes of an intoxicated cuckoo, and the brilliance of a ripe *jambū* fruit.
Her thick hair was long, powerful, hanging down, and disheveled;
she was adorned with three blood-red eyes that resembled glowing embers. || 9.529 ||
She has a face like a full autumn moon or a red lotus,
and her lotus-like mouth is terrifying with a pair of long fangs protruding upward.
She is terrifying with her beautiful tongue protruding to the length of a span,
and her circle of thirty-two teeth is visible because her mouth is wide open.
Her head was trembling incessantly; she was of terrible form, with a human skull resting upon her shoulder from whose cavernous mouth she drank blood.
She desired her pair of breasts, which were being bathed by the blood flowing from her two lips;
she desired the mass of blood gushing forth and clinging to the lotuses of her breasts.
She was making a hissing sound while sucking it, licking it with her tongue that knows its flavor,
and painting a design on her forehead with the thick blood of the nārāca arrow.
She has earrings made from human heads with blood dripping from them, severed just now; her hair is bound by sacred threads, and she wears ear-ornaments that hang down to her shoulders.
She was adorned with a garland of severed heads bound together by her hair, which hung from her neck down to her ankles, dripping continuously with streams of blood. || 9.536 ||
She was intensely radiant with a necklace of white bone-beads and a golden neck-ornament;
she remained firm upon her chest, which was adorned by a row of long fingers from a corpse.
She was endowed with a pair of firm, full, and high breasts,
and her hips were adorned with a pedestal of great emerald stones.
(778) She has broad hips and an exceedingly emaciated waist;
she is adorned with a circle of tinkling bells made from the heads of infants strung together with entrails. 9.539
She has sixteen well-developed arms, a great conch-shell earring, and bracelets made from the coiled coils of the veins of corpses. (9.540)
She wears a waist-cord made of garlands of strings woven from the hair of corpses,
and a girdle fashioned by weaving together rows of the hands of dead infants.
With finger-rings made of flesh, fat, marrow, and shining fingers,
[he holds] a sword, a trident, a discus, an arrow, and a goad.
And likewise, in her right [hands], she holds a lute, a knife, and a rosary;
and a noose, an axe, a serpent, a bow, and a mallet.
She holds in her left hand a skull-bowl containing a portion of Śiva, filled with fat, blood, and marrow, as well as a human head with long, hanging hair.
The Goddess, with her tinkling anklets, was adorned with strung skeletons of corpses and stood in the midst of the fierce flames of the blazing funeral pyres of the cremation ground.
She moves upon the back of a great, long, prostrate corpse with its face turned downward,
while the quarters of space are pervaded by the mass of flames of fire vomiting from her mouth.
Indeed, she stands having just arisen, with her feet in the *pratyālīḍha* posture,
roaring again and again from her left and right sides.
The Supreme Goddess was encircled by two Śivas of terrible form, who were vomiting great fire and whose limbs were the color of lightning and glowing embers.
She was constantly adorned by two jackals that were ever-attendant, gazing at the Great Goddess and terrifying her repeatedly. (9.549)
She was offering the brain situated within a skull to those two;
she was naked, with disheveled hair, and terrifying with her loud, boisterous laughter.
Adorned with a sevenfold-bound nārāca-yoga-bandage, she desires union together with Saṃhārabhairava himself. (9.551)
Kālī, who was excessively passionate, laughing, and short of stature,
her body rising up as if to suppress the flames of ten million fires of time.
[She is] like ten million suns at the time of the great dissolution, like lightning and clouds at the end of an aeon;
she is Kālī, the bringer of the end of the kalpa, possessing the form of Mahābhairava.
Extremely terrifying and difficult to behold even for the gods and asuras led by Indra,
it causes the destruction of the enemy faction and slays the Daityas and Dānavas.
One should meditate upon such a goddess, Kālī, who is designated as Kāmakalā.
Now, regarding the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for that very [deity]:
hereafter I shall explain the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa*.
In a single leaf-vessel, success shall be immediate;
the purification of the ground and the purification of the substances have already been described by me previously. (9.556)
Whatever restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) there may be for the rite of preliminary service (puraścaraṇa),
one should employ them all constantly, being intent upon devotion.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites in the morning, having completed the ritual of worship, and being pure,
he should bury human bone in the ground while reciting the Astra-mantra.
One should utter *tāram*, followed by *krodha-anu-hrīḥ*; then one should extract *pāśa-smara-bhūtān*.
Having pronounced *siddhim*, one should say *dehi* and then the pair *vahnayaṅganām*. (9.559)
The seed-syllable of the elements is *phr̥m*.
Likewise,
having spread out one's seat directly upon that, it should be well-prepared.
Having placed a human skull in front [of him], with a rosary made of human bones, || 9.560 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), remaining pure during the day;
likewise, one hundred thousand times at night while remaining impure. (9.561)
The practitioner of mantra should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth [of the recitations], and likewise perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the consecration (abhiṣecana).
Regarding both the fire-oblation and the libation, the procedure is said to be the same as that for worship.
O lady of pure smiles, whether in worship, in ritual application, in fire-offering, or in libation, everything should be performed according to the procedure of Guhyakālī. (9.563)
Whatever ritual procedure is not mentioned here, one should apply that which is prescribed for that [other] context;
and whatever remains unmentioned even there, the rule for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as stated in that [latter] context should be used.
Thus ends the first section on the Great Vidyā.
Now, regarding the second Vidyā, [as stated] in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
[He saw him] seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, resplendent with the crescent moon.
Seated upon his chest, the daughter of the mountain asked:
O Īśāna, how did those whose wealth is austerity obtain omniscience?
Having acquired what knowledge did the sages compose the *Bhārata* and other works? (9.566)
Having heard the words of the daughter of the mountain, the Supreme Lord laughed and, embracing his beloved, spoke while honoring her, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! (9.567).
Listen, O virtuous lady, to this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) which burns the fuel of ignorance;
having attained it, great-souled beings [succeed] in virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
The poets of pure intellect considered nothing to be impossible;
for in debate within the assembly, their words were capable of paralyzing their opponents.

O Goddess, that which causes the loss of knowledge for the wise through the offering of oblations (validāna), and which speaks even impure things for the amusement of the members of the assembly, [is such a woman]. (9.570)

One should bring even the disputant, the king, or the minister under one's control; that is, one should cause the disputant to speak. By merely knowing the mantra and through its recitation, one leads [the practitioner] to omniscience. (9-571)
He states the extraction of the mantra:

"Having first placed the letter *sa* together with its following [vowel], adorned with the fourth vowel, mounted upon the letter *ra*, radiant and shimmering, and endowed with the moon and the bindu. (9.572)
Then one should place the letter *tra*, adorned with the fourth vowel;
thereafter, one should join the letter *ha* conjoined with the long vowel *ū*.
And then one should utter the syllable *phaṭ*; thus the mantra is complete and perfected.
(From the Matsyasūkta:
Now I shall declare the unsurpassed extraction of the mantra of the Great Goddess. 9-574.
And having known that, a man shines like another Vācaspati;
[the mantra is formed] by extracting the seed-syllable of Māyā and likewise the first letter of the *tavarga* class.
The second supreme seed-syllable is joined with Rati, Bindu, and Vahni;
the third is the Kūrca seed-syllable, followed immediately by the syllable Phaṭ.
But the mantra with its full perfection is endowed with five rays;
the *praṇava* consists of five rays.
This has been stated in the *Tārārṇava*:
Immediately thereafter, one should extract the Māyottara-mantra from that [source].
The fifth *papañca* is joined with the five rays; it is proclaimed as follows:
the letter *a* is the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*), the letter *u* is the Superior Illusion (*māyottara*), and the letter *ma* is the fifth *papañca*.
(In the *Tattvabodha*).
*Tāraṃ lajjāṃ nakāmeśīṃ huḥ phaṭ*—this is the *Ugratārikā*.
One should worship with Māyā (Hrīm), Strī (Strīm), and ending with Hūm and Astra (Phaṭ) for Ekajaṭā;
this [mantra] devoid of the Astra is prescribed for Nīlasarasvatī.
The syllable *ī* is Kāmeśī;
this three-syllabled great mantra, ending with the word *phaṭ*, resides in the heart.
Endowed with five rays of light, it is the burner of the fuel of ignorance. (9.580)
(Matsyasūkta) The seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*), the seed-syllable of the bride (*badhūbīja*), and likewise the seed-syllable of the tuft (*kūrcabīja*) followed by *phaṭ*:
such is the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī vidyā*) that reveals the five elements. (9-581)
Likewise: "The three-syllable Mahānīla-Sarasvatī, devoid of the *tārā* weapon-mantra, is known as the *kulluka*; it is concealed within the three worlds. (9.582)
In the *Tārārṇava*, it is said:
"Because the fierce goddess worshipped by Vasiṣṭha does not grant swift results, a most terrible curse was therefore pronounced by that very sage. (9.583)
From that time forth, this vidyā has not been fruitful for anyone;
the seed-syllable of Śakti is joined above the seed-syllable situated within Trapā. (9.584)
From that time forth, this science has been like a glorious bride;
it is the fruit-bearing mother of all sciences, victorious for those who desire victory. (9.585)
This knowledge destroys poison and bestows immortality;
by the mere knowledge of this mantra, one becomes victorious on earth. (9.586)
The master of speech becomes mute, yet the man is born as the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati).

"The seed-syllable of Śakti" refers to the letter *sa*. The seed-syllable situated within *trapā* is the syllable *troṃ*. By that, "strīm" becomes the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*). The curse, however, lasts only until the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa; once the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa has occurred, he is again liberated from the curse. || 9-587 ||
Thus, from the statement of another tantra;
he states the meaning of the mantra (*Sādhanasamuccaya*):
"From the *praṇava*, she is the form of Brahman; 'So 'ham'—she is the very nature of reality."
The state of being illuminated by the void and the state of devouring by fire.
The visarga of those two [ta and ra] is considered the tantric *īkāra* when joined with the bindu.
The letter *ta* destroys all sins, and the letter *ra* reveals the true nature of reality (*tattva*). (9.589)
The *vindumālin* is the great seed-syllable that illuminates the *śabdabrahman*;
the *kūrca* is of the nature of awakening, and the *astra* is the destroyer of dullness. (9-590)
Thus, he who knows this is a pure self; he is indeed Maheśvara himself.
(In the *Matsyasūkta*):
When the Vidyā begins with the seed-syllable of Śrī, then Śrī faces in every direction. (9-591)
For this indeed is the Great Vidyā, beginning with Māyā, which grants all desired objects;
it begins with Vāgbhava, is the very nature of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), and consists of all speech.
Likewise:
the accomplishment of the pill, the vetāla, the pātāla, the vaṭayakṣiṇī, entry into another's body, and the power of command arise. (9.593)
Merely by contemplating [this] on the tongue, one will certainly become a knower of the three times;
that best of practitioners who contemplates the Vidyā without distinction [of time]. (9-594)
He becomes liberated while living and is certainly liberated at the end [of life] as well; (as stated in the *Brahmasaṃhitā* and the *Phetkāriṇī*):
"Nīlasarasvatī is always the swift bestower of grace upon the worlds. (9-595)
Especially in the Kali age, by my grace, there will be a practitioner who has mastered the mantra even upon the head of a fool. (9.596)
Having paid his fee, he quickly instructs him; he, in turn, should recite the verses.
[The teacher] instructs him, commanding: "Compose a verse.
And so it is.
Through the mere knowledge of the mantra, two types of supernatural power (anubhāva) arise. || 9-597 ||
Its poetry is spontaneous and its meaning is inscrutable to others.
Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers and so forth (in the *Merutantra*): the sage is named Akṣobhya, and its meter is said to be Bṛhatī. (9-598)
The seed-syllable of the goddess Tārā is *hrīḥ*, and *hūṃ* is proclaimed to be her power (*śakti*).
(From the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*):
Akṣobhya is the seer of this [verse], and the *bṛhatī* meter is declared for it. (9-599)
The goddess Nīlasarasvatī is concealed within the three worlds;
with *hūṃ* as her seed-syllable, she is the weapon and the power that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. (9.600)
In the *Saṃgraha* composed by Dāmodaramiśra:
"Akṣobhya is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], the Bṛhatī meter is declared for it, and the goddess Nīlasarasvatī is concealed within the three worlds. (9-601)

HŪṂ is the seed-mantra (bījamantra), Śakti is the power (śakti), and Māyā is remembered as the female [seed-syllable] (strī). O Goddess, the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life. || 9-602 ||

"Ugratārā is the deity" (in the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*). Now, for the placement [of mantras] on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*): first, regarding Ugratārā (in the *Tārākalpa*), the procedure for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgavidhi*) is proclaimed by means of the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*) with the six long vowels.
In the *Siddhasārasvata* [tantra] of Nīlasarasvatī, however, having uttered "the embodiment of all speech," one should say "namas" to the heart. (9.603)
"O beloved of Fire, having uttered 'to the head, [the goddess] whose form is the unbroken supreme speech,' and then 'to the tuft, vaṣaṭ, O you whose form is the speech of Brahmā.'"
Having uttered [the mantra] in the form of the speech of Viṣṇu, one should utter "huṃ" for the armor;
and likewise, [the mantra] in the form of the speech of Rudra for the three eyes, ending with "vauṣaṭ."
Having uttered the mantra of the form of all speech, one should recollect "Astrāya Phaṭ.
One should join those [syllables] with the seed-syllable (bīja) by means of the six long vowels, placing them at the end of the seed-syllable.
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, regarding Ekajaṭā:
at the end of the seed-syllable, "to Ekajaṭā" is proclaimed as the heart;
likewise, "to Tāriṇī" is the head, and similarly, "O Vajrodakā" is the crest-lock mantra. (9.607)
The armor is for Ugrajaṭā and likewise for Mahāparisara;
similarly, the eye-missile and the weapon-missile are proclaimed for Piṅgograikajaṭā. (9.608)
According to the tradition, this *nyāsa* is incompatible with the deities Ugratārā and Ekajaṭā.
Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*) [as stated in the Gandharva Tantra]:
Having visualized a cremation ground there, one should imagine a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) therein.
At its base is a jeweled pedestal, adorned with various kinds of gems.
On all sides, there were jackals rejoicing in the abundance of flesh and bones; in the four directions stood corpses, skulls, funeral pyres, charcoal, and bones as ornaments.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon the Goddess according to the yoga of meditation as described [in the *Nīlatantra*]:
"She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, is formidable, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads. (9.611)
She is short-statured, pot-bellied, and formidable, draped around her waist with a tiger skin;
she is endowed with fresh youth and adorned with the five mudrās.
Four-armed, with a protruding tongue, most terrifying, and bestowing boons;
she holds a sword and a flaying knife in her right hands, and carries a severed head and a blue lotus in her left.
One should meditate on her with a single tawny, fierce matted lock, adorned at the crown of her head by Akṣobhya,
and graced with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun.
She stands in the midst of blazing funeral pyres, her face terrifying with fangs,
smiling with intense absorption, and adorned with ornaments of bone.
Seated upon a white lotus within the waters that pervade the universe,
her two right and left hands are joined with a sword and a flaying knife (as described in the Śyāmārahasya and other texts).
"Endowed with a pair of right hands joined with a skull and a blue lotus"—this is the reading [in one version].
(In another tantra:
"The goddess holding a sword and a flaying knife, and bearing a skull and a blue lotus"—this is the reading. || 9-617 ||
(p. 786) (In the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*):
In the upper chamber of that [palace], one should visualize the Goddess—dwarfish, with the luster of a sapphire, pot-bellied, her hips draped in a tiger skin. ||618||
She possessed a mass of full and elevated breasts, with round red eyes;
she was most terrifying, with a lolling tongue and blazing with the tips of her fangs.
She wears a radiant garland of blue lotuses, has her hair tied in a topknot, and is terrifying;
she is adorned with five skulls joined by a band of white bones. || 9.620 ||
She has an earring made from a red serpent upon her forehead,
and she is most brilliantly radiant with a necklace fashioned from a very white great serpent.
She has a sacrificial thread made of a serpent as dark as a blade of dūrvā grass;
she is four-armed, with one fist adorned by a piece of red flesh.
Adorned with a mass of matted hair and a rosary,
she is beautified by a sharp-edged sword held aloft in her right hand, and she is the roaring heroine.
Below that, one should visualize the supreme goddess, adorned with a seed-vessel and a small knife;
she is beautiful in her nakedness, with a red stalk upon her left shoulder.
She holds a blue lotus, and beneath that, a skull-cup;
she holds [the skull] which is like a jasmine flower, yet joined with the dullness of the worlds.
Her arms were quickly adorned with armlets fashioned from a multitude of smoke-colored nāgas,
and her hands shone with bracelets made of golden-colored nāgas.
[He beheld] the great god Śubhravarṇa, who had prepared a truly pure seat;
likewise, out of fear of constraint, [he saw her] whose body was contracted down to the tips of her toes.
With her left foot mounted upon the two feet of a corpse, she looks upward with great intensity;
she has three eyes and wears a girdle of snakes as white as jasmine that adorns her waist.
Her sprout-like anklets were made of blood-red serpents;
she was adorned with blood-red ornaments consisting of freshly severed heads from which blood still flowed. (628)
The Supreme Goddess is adorned with a great garland of fifty [heads], their hair interlocked with one another and their lotus-feet hanging down.
Seated in the midst of a blazing funeral pyre, with a leopard skin as her upper garment,
her matted locks bound by the Akṣobhya serpent, she is the bestower of boons.
The wise Mahādeva, the great poet, should thus address the Great Goddess, himself, and the materials for the sacrifice: 631.
In the *Tāropaniṣad*:
[I salute] the Guru, who has the luster of a fresh cloud, whose body is the sphere of the meaning of seemingly contradictory statements, and who has a prominent belly.
Extremely short and in the prime of youth, she wore beneath her a tiger skin with its head [and] hair [pointing upward].
Having seized Anaikya, who stands upon a corpse with her middle body half-encircled in an *ālīḍha* posture,
whose complexion is faded, and who is adorned with a garland made of human heads;
Her three reddish eyes are the manifestation of the triple Veda.
She is resplendent with a single matted lock of hair, tawny and undivided;
she is terrifying with ornaments of severed white bones;
she is adorned with serpents that constitute the mass of the eight great supernatural powers.
[She is] the giver of fearlessness to the worlds through her loud, intoxicated laughter.
Ananta was in her matted locks, Takṣaka in her ears, and the great serpent Padma served as an ornament upon her heart;
likewise, Karkoṭaka formed her sacred thread.
Then, in Sumekhalā, there was the divine Vāsuki.
It is held that with the Śaṅkhapāla [mudrā] there is a bracelet,
and at the feet, the Padma [mudrā] possesses the beauty of anklets.
The Kulika serpent is considered to be on the arms;
the arm is established as being half the length of the great garland. || 9-636 ||
White, red, pale-white, and dark-blue;
likewise, the serpent that is white and the one that is pale—
these are the varieties of color among serpents here.
All become [liberated] by the sages through the blazing funeral pyre. || 9-637 ||
Her fierce hair is bound with a skull and a flaying knife; she wears a garland of blue lotuses together with their stalks, and she constantly holds an unsheathed sword in her right hand.
Always bearing [them] with her arms, which arose from her own prowess.
One should meditate upon her, who is resplendent with the five mudrās and the two fangs of the categories of existence, and who wears a garland of blue lotuses— she who brings about poetic genius.
And one should recite the mantra of Tāriṇī until its meaning has been fully realized.
(Also in the *Phetkāriṇītantra*):
She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture with her foot placed upon the heart of a corpse; she possesses a terrifying, loud laugh; she is most excellent;
her arms hold a sword, a blue lotus, a flaying knife, and a skull-cup; she is born from the seed-syllable HŪṂ.
Dwarfish, with a vast blue and tawny mass of matted hair entwined by fierce serpents, Ugratārā herself, having cast her lethargy into the skull-bowl, destroys the three worlds. 9-640.

The characteristic of *pratyālīḍha* is as follows (*Saṃgītaratnākara*): In this stance, the left leg is bent with the thigh resting between [the knees], while the right foot is extended five *tāla*s in front. (9-641)
One should know that both [the positions] *astra* and *ālīḍha* possess deities;
however, by reversing the limbs of the *ālīḍha* position, it is called *pratyālīḍha*. (9.642)

A *tāla* is a span (*vitasti*). The two discs are the *asra* [discs]. "Adorned with Akṣobhya on the crown" means that here Akṣobhya is in the form of a *nāga*. This is because of the statement in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*: "Akṣobhya, bearing the form of a *nāga*, is in the female form upon the head of the Goddess.
Now follows the procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). Regarding this, first the meditation on the mantra is stated in the *Sādhanasamuccaya*:
"And in the root-cakra, one should meditate on Hṛllekhā, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns."
And one should visualize the second [syllable], yellow in color, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra].
One should meditate on the seed-syllable of the beard (Kūrcabīja), resembling a cloud and possessing great luster, at the navel;
and the seed-syllable of the weapon (Astrabīja), with a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction, in the heart.
One should contemplate the Vidyā from the base (mūla) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
resembling ten million suns and visible to the vision of yogins.
As it is said in the *Tārātantra*:
"A practitioner of mantra, intent on acting according to his own will,
should always recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while holding a secret rosary, for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*)."
(In the Surendrasaṃhitā:

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; he should offer oblations with blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter numbering one-tenth of that, and he should perform the libation with one-tenth of that amount.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with pure fragrant waters mixed with the liquid of black agallochum; the method for that is stated here.

Having invoked [the deity] in the water according to the rules, and having gratified the Goddess and her attendants one by one with ritual services such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having worshipped his own self with the thought that it is the Goddess, the best of practitioners should sprinkle water on his head while thinking, "I am consecrating Tāriṇī. (9-649)
O Goddess, the consecration is performed with the mudrā called Kumbha, ending with the word "namas.
(In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*):
The wise one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number. (9.650)
By offering lotuses mixed with the three sweets, a man becomes a master of speech.
(In the *Tārārṇava*):
Having meditated thus, one who subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times. (9-651)
Or, taking up the *Rahasyamālā*, one should recite it exactly one hundred thousand times. (In the *Merutantra*:
While engaged in sexual union, eating various foods, curd, and even honey... (9.652)
Having avoided honey, meat, and betel leaf, one should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times;
one should then perform oblations with red lotuses soaked in milk and ghee, numbering one-tenth of the recitation.
Having filled a skull-cup with [the substance], one should perform the recitation at the place of recitation;
while looking at, touching, or walking past a woman during the dead of night, one should offer the bali-oblation.
One should not harbor hatred toward women with beautiful brows; one should honor them with great effort.
There is no restriction regarding time for the recitation of mantras; one should recite at all times, whether standing or otherwise.
In a cremation ground, an empty house, a temple, or a secluded place, or on a mountain or in the middle of a forest, the knower of mantras should mount a corpse. (9.656)
Whether it be one slain by enemies in battle or a child of six months, one should quickly accomplish the vidyā; thus accomplished, it becomes fully perfected.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra is fit to perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*).
Now, regarding the varieties of this *vidyā*, it is said therein:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain [the rites] for the sake of the excellent accomplishment of the Daityas. (9-658)
Having recited "Oṃ trīḥ hrīḥ hūḥ," one should worship Tārā, who is worshipped by Brahmā, with offerings such as garlands, and [conclude] with the six-syllable mantra: "hrīḥ huḥ phaṭ. (9-659)
The sage is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Tārā;
one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) as before, and her meditation (dhyāna) is now described.
One should worship her who is white-clad, possessing the luster of the moon, with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, and holding a pair of scissors and a skull-cup in her two hands. (9.661)
Abounding in the splendor of various ornaments, three-eyed, and seated upon a lotus—one should perform all rites such as recitation and worship for her as previously described. (9.662)
Through oblation with honeyed *paramānna* (milk-rice), one becomes a treasury of knowledge;
for subjugation, [the fire] should be red; for paralyzing, golden-colored; and for killing, black.
One should visualize her as smoke-colored for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) and white for the rite of pacification (śānti).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain [the mantra] for the sake of the boon of Tāraka.
The twelve-syllable Tārā, worshipped by Brahmā, which is very difficult to obtain:
[the syllables] Vāk, Lajjā, Ramā, and Kāma, joined with Ha, Sa, Ra, Au, and Sa. (9-665)
This fifth *kūṭa*, rich with the *visarga*, has been declared as:
*huṃ ugratāre huṃ phaṭ*. This is said to be the mantra for recitation and other rites.
All of this is as before; in the Kali age, it produces conviction for him.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which was practiced by Brahmā.
To grant a boon to Hiraṇyakaśipu, [he gave] the Praṇava, the Kavaca, the Māyā, Klīṃ, and the fifth, the Kūṭa, each equal to seven oceans.
Ending with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, everything belonging to her, beginning with the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), should be performed as before.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe that which was indeed worshipped by Hari.
The twelve-syllable mantra, which bestows accomplishment for the purpose of propagating the Buddhist path and was worshipped by Brahmā, resides within its fifth peak-syllable.
Having spoken thus, he accomplished the twelve-syllable vidyā that bestows supreme intelligence;
by its power, Divodāsa was formerly expelled from Kāśī.
For this [mantra], the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*japa*), and so forth, should be understood as previously described.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the seven-syllabled mantra served by Rāma.
For the sake of destroying Lakṣmī and the others, Halin always [received it] from me;
the fifth *kūṭa* is situated in the middle of the seven syllables worshipped by Brahmā. (9.673)
Having abandoned that [other place] and spoken there, she was served by Balarāma;
for she is the destroyer of enemies and likewise the bestower of the perfection of speech. (9.674)
The meditation, worship, and so forth, as well as the preliminary applications and the rest, are to be performed as before.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is well-served by Nārāyaṇa. (9.675)
By the power of this five-syllabled mantra, the destruction of the Daityas was accomplished:
*trīṃ hūṃ phaṭ klīṃ*. This five-syllabled Vāgbhava bestows all spiritual perfections (*siddhis*).
For these three, however, the Sage Viṣṇu [prescribes] the recitation and other rites as previously described.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which has been practiced by me.
And that six-syllabled lore, "Oṃ Hrīḥ Hūḥ Hrīḥ Huḥ Phaṭ," was given by Ravi to Aditi; I am that sage, as before. (9-678)
All matters such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the preliminary applications (prayoga) are to be understood as before.
Now, I shall further proclaim another five-syllable mantra of this [goddess].
"O gods, for the sake of slaying Jalandhara, I have accomplished this *siddha* [mantra]:
*strīṃ huṃ māyāṃ huṃ phaṭ*. This is considered the five-syllabled mantra. (9.680)
Also in another tantra:

"The seed-syllable of the bride (vadhū), the armor (kavaca), the illusion (māyā), the 'tongue' (kūrca), and likewise the weapon (astra)—this five-and-a-half syllable mantra is proclaimed as the second. (9.681)
(From the Merutantra:
"O gods, I have recited [this] with five faces through the path of Dakṣa, among those who possess a divine portion, among the Brahmins, and likewise among those devoted to dharma. (9.682)
Deities other than those who abide in the Tantras of the Yamas and Niyanas are not capable of accomplishing the task, even if they have been propitiated through the Vāmamārga. (9-683)
The gods, propitiated by sacrificial fees, become allies in battle;
having slain their enemies who are repositories of splendor, they lead them to the eternal Brahman. (9.684)
For the sake of the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, I offered [the five nectars] to Rāma;
however, I substituted the five nectars for the place of liquor, and used sūraṇa for the place of meat.
In the place of the fish, Khaṇḍa is to be understood; in the wife of Dharma, Rata is the delight.
The rest is exactly as before; this secret has been revealed. (9-686)
A greedy person should not serve Tārā, for it results in the ruin of both worlds;
her worship and other rites are as before, with this specific distinction explained here. (9.687)
Through Tārā and the true guru, accomplishment is attained; otherwise, in the pursuit of women, delusion arises.
Now, therefore, O gods, I shall fully proclaim the mantra of Mahātārā.
Success is attained through both paths, according to the authority of the colored and colorless [mantras].
One should utter the great syllable: *trīṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ huṃ namas tārāyai*. (9.689)

Having uttered "tārāyai sakalet," followed by two *u*-sounds (*usvarau*), then two *tāra*s (the syllable *om*), and ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*, the syllable *svāhā*), this mantra is considered to consist of thirty-two syllables. (9.690)
One should perform all the rites, such as the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), worship (*pūjā*), and recitation (*japa*), as previously described.
(In the *Tāriṇītantra*) Īśvara said:
Listen, O Daughter of the Mountain, to this ancient tale which destroys dullness.
Knowledge, which yields the fruit of the four aims of life, bestows the accomplishment of mantras;
it consists of the first letter of the [first] class, joined with fire (ra) and adorned with the left eye (ī). (9.692)
Joined with the *nāda* and the *bindu*, it bestows the eightfold attainments (*aṣṭasiddhi*).
Furthermore, O Goddess, it has four faces and is adorned with the letter *ra*.
O beloved, the great seed-syllable marked by the fourth vowel and the crescent moon indeed bestows the fruit of the four aims of human life.
Then, having uttered the word *kṛṣṇe*, the word *devī* is remembered;
one should then give the syllable *hrīṃ* and thereafter extract [the name] preceded by oneself. (9.695)
Adorned with the letter *i*, the letter *r*, and the letter *m*,
one should then utter the Vāgbhava syllable and extract this mantra.
O Goddess, this nine-syllable mantra of Tāriṇī has been proclaimed;
this very Mahāvidyā is exceedingly difficult to obtain in heaven or on earth.
O Goddess, you are the bestower of the eight siddhis and the giver of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer and other elements: Śakti is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Bṛhatī is said to be its meter (chandas).
The deity is declared to be Tāriṇī; the seed-syllable is said to be the syllable *hrīṃ*;
the power (*śakti*) is said to be the *vāgbhava* [syllable *aiṃ*]. Thus one should perform the ritual for the seer and the other [limbs]. (9.699)
Now, the meditation:
[One should visualize her] as black, pot-bellied, and terrifying, adorned with serpent earrings;
with a red face and a lolling tongue, wearing red garments around her waist.

O Goddess of the gods, [one should meditate on her] who has full and elevated breasts, who is fierce, and who is encircled by a great serpent; she is upon a corpse, and upon that [corpse] is a skull-cup.
She is intent on meditation upon the tip of the nose, most formidable, and the bestower of boons;
she has four arms and long hair, with her upper right arm raised.

The goddess holds a single lotus in her upper left hand and a drinking vessel in her upper right; below these, she displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her right and left hands respectively.
[He saw] the Goddess, the eternal dweller on the mountain, who bestows all siddhis, drinking a stream of blood from her drinking vessel in the presence of Sadāśiva.
She is endowed with three eyes, has a serpent as her sacred thread,
possesses a long nose, long shanks, long limbs, and a long tongue.
(795) She is endowed with three eyes through the distinction of the moon, sun, and fire;
she is the goddess who destroys enemies, the greatly formidable one who bestows boons. 9.706.
With her head bound by a tiger skin, she is renowned throughout the three worlds;
she brings happiness to practitioners and strikes fear into all the worlds.
I bow down to the Great Goddess Tāriṇī who is thus manifested.
Now follows the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
having worshipped her in this manner with these substances, O Maheśvarī, [verse 9-708].
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Now, the mantra of Akṣobhya: (In the *Brahmasaṃhitā*) "If, having abandoned the mantra of Akṣobhya, one should recite the goddess Tārā... (9.709).
His spiritual success will perish and he shall go to the Raurava hell;
O Brahmin, this mantra of Akṣobhya is the armor and the supreme essence.
This supreme meditation is extremely secret and the highest among all meditations;
first I shall proclaim the mantra, and after that, the meditation itself.
And after that, I shall describe the armor (kavaca) in due order;
it is unsurpassed, extracted [from the source], and free from the elaborations of conceptual proliferation (prapañca).

"Akṣobhya" and "svāhā," with "ramā" at the beginning and end, constitute the great mantra (mahāmanu). It is declared that its seer (ṛṣi) is Svayaṃbhū, and the Virāṭ is said to be its meter (chandas). || 9-713 ||
Akṣobhya is declared to be the deity; he possesses three forms and assumes the shape of a serpent.
His application is fixed for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
Now I shall describe the meditation that bestows all prosperity—
auspicious, bearing the form of a serpent, and resembling a thousand suns.
His face is like ten million flashes of lightning, his eyes are radiant as fire,
he is endowed with three and a half coils [of matted hair], and [the crescent moon] rests at the tip of the crest of his matted locks.
Endowed with great beauty, saluted by gods and asuras, possessing a radiance like that of the sun and lightning, [he stands] upon the crest of a great jewel. (9.717)
This form, possessing a great body and well-worshipped even by the gods, is described in another tantra:
"Having first worshipped Akṣobhya, the wise one should thoroughly worship Tārā. (9-718)
Likewise: "One should perform the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth for this [deity] just as for Tāriṇī.
Thus ends the section on Tārā.
Now, the Śrīvidyā.
Therein, first is the Kāmarāja-vidyā (at the Candrapīṭha): Smara, Bhaga, Vindumatī, and the letter La; this is considered the Vāgbhava. (9.719)
Śiva, Jīva, Smara, Śambhu, and Lalitā constitute the *kāmakūṭa*;
Bhṛgu, Kāma, Kṣamā, and Māyā are considered to be the one named *kāmarāja*. (9.720)
The designations for the three peaks (kūṭas) as Vāgbhava and so forth are stated in that very same place:
"The first peak is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmakūṭaka, and the third shall be Śaktikūṭa; the mantra has the body of these three peaks. (9.721)
Now follows the Vidyā known as Lopāmudrā (*Jñānārṇava*):
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Vidyā named Lopāmudrā; she is the Śakti of the Vidyā called Kāmarāja, [and her] fourth... (9.722).
Having abandoned [the vowels] at the beginning, Lopāmudrā, enriched by Śiva (H) and the Moon (I), is revealed.

This means that in the *Vāgbhava* portion of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, one should place the letters Ha and Sa at the beginning, having removed the letter E and the letter I. This is the one practiced by Agastya.
Now, the Ṣoḍaśī (according to the *Yoginītantra*).
The seed-syllable of Śrī, Māyā, the Power that is the source of Smara, Tāra, Māyā, Kamalā, and then Vidyā. || 9-723 ||
And by the recitation of the seed-syllables of Śakti and the others in reverse order, this venerable Ṣoḍaśī was taught by Śiva in another Tantra. (p. 717)
The seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, the seed-syllable of Kāma, and the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable].
Then, O Supreme Goddess, there is the seed-syllable situated at the end of the *bāla* [mantra], followed by the *praṇava*,
the seed-syllable of Śakti, Ramā, and the Vidyā.
O beautiful one, having placed either Lopāmudrā, Kāmarāja, Trikūṭā, or the supreme [Vidyā],
along with the five seed-syllables preceded by the Praṇava.
One should install the supreme Ṣoḍaśī in the reverse order alone.
(Also in the Māyātantra: Lakṣmī is the supreme Śakti joined with Madana and Yoni.
The Stāra, Parā, and Kamalā, and then the Mūlavidyā. || 9-727 ||
And the Śrī Mantrarāja, which has been taught as the reverse of [the sequence beginning with] Śakti and so forth, is declared to belong to the Supreme Deity.
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a science superior to this. 9-728.
"She has not been cursed by anyone, nor has she been pinned down by anyone—
even with thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of tongues" (Jñānārṇava 9.729).
This sixteen-syllabled Śrīvidyā cannot indeed be fully described;
for it is the very nature of the knowledge of Brahman, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (9.730)

O Goddess of gods, by a single utterance [of this mantra], there are ten million Vājapeya sacrifices, thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices, and likewise the merit of circumambulating the entire earth. (9.731)
Pilgrimages to Kāśī and other sacred sites, numbering three and a half crores, do not equal it, O Goddess of gods; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (9.732)
O Girijā, if even a single utterance [of this] is so, how much more so the entire Brahman?
This great vidyā of sixteen syllables must never be revealed.
O auspicious Pārvatī, you must guard [this] as you would your own womb;
even one's most beloved children, wife, wealth, and so forth may be given away. (9.734)
The kingdom may be given, the head may be given, but the sixteen-syllable [mantra] must not be given.
O Dear One, seven hundred thousand [recitations] of the Mahāvidyās have been declared at the beginning of the Tantras.
This great vidyā, which is more essential than the essence itself, is well-guarded.
Now, regarding the assignment of the seer and other elements, it is stated in that very place:
"O Maheśānī, its seer is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (9-736)
The meter is declared to be Paṅkti; the goddess is Tripurasundarī.
Vāgbhava is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), while Śakti is the Śakti-kūṭa. (9.737)
Kāmarāja is the *kīlaka* (stake); this is declared to be the Ṛṣyādinyāsa.
The reason why the Vāgbhava and other [syllables] take the form of *bījas* (seeds) is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Great mantras emerge like sparks from a great fire. (9.738)
In the same way, O Dear One, the letters of the Mātṛkā emerged from the Vāgbhava;
for this very reason, the seed-syllable of this deity is called Vāgbhava.
The Mother of the Universe, manifesting as a woman in the form of a man, O Queen of the Gods, pierces the three worlds with great delusion. (9.740)
Therefore, O Goddess, she is that *kīlaka*; because she protects the entire world while being pregnant with good fortune (*saubhāgya*), she is called this *śakti*.
Now, regarding the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*), it is said in another Tantra:
"The seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of *a*, *ā*, and *sau* is declared to be the threefold supreme [seed].
Having repeated this seed twice, [one should place it] on the middle and other fingers. (9.742)
One should perform the purification of the hands, the palms, and also the backs;
the fourth [prostration] is joined with a bow, performed separately for each with the name-mantras.
O Maheśvarī, the names of the fingers are declared in order as follows: the middle finger, the ring finger, the little finger, the thumb, and the forefinger. (9.744)
(Regarding the Lord of the Nine Jewels:
Omniscience, eternal satisfaction, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, unimpeded power, and infinity—these six, beginning with Śivā, are said to be the limbs [of the powers] within Śiva. (9.745)
In this regard, the various networks of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) should be consulted in works such as the *Jñānārṇava*.
Now, for the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[one should meditate on her] shining like the orb of the rising sun, four-armed, and three-eyed.
I take refuge in Śivā, who holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows.
And [in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* within the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*]:
"In the midst of the ocean of blood-red nectar, agitated by the rising of the moon, there is a golden ground adorned with jewels and rubies. (9.747)
In its center was the great Nandana garden, which intoxicates with passion,
resplendent with a mass of moonlight from the ever-risen full moon.
It is always protected by Kāmadeva dwelling together with Vasanta,
and by Kadamba, Cūta, Punnāga, Nāgakeśara, and Campaka trees.
[It was adorned] with *vakula* and *pārijāta* trees, radiant with flowers of every season,
with bees buzzing with their humming, and with cuckoos and parrots warbling.
It was frequented by various other groups of twice-born men of diverse complexions,
and it was filled with various birds such as peacocks, kāraṇḍava ducks, and swans.
It was adorned with clusters of trees strewn with various flowering creepers,
and surrounded by long ponds filled with blossoming lotuses and water lilies.
Having thus meditated upon the Nandana garden, which is thoroughly served by the Malaya breezes and grey with pollen, one should then visualize the courtyard within it.
Having thus visualized the courtyard, frequented by gods and siddhas, as adorned with grounds resembling pure gold; (9.754)
In the center of that, one should meditate upon a pavilion that pervades the entire circle of the universe, resembling a thousand suns in brilliance, square-shaped, and most beautiful. (9.755)
The quarters of the sky were turned tawny by the mass of the radiance of jewel-splendor;
it was devoid of a central pillar and provided with pillars at the corners. || 9.756 ||
Adorned with great rubies, lapis lazuli, jewels, and gold,
it was enriched with canopies of pearl strings and embellished with jeweled stairways.
It was permeated by a gentle breeze, rippled with fragrant incense,
and adorned with canopies of jeweled chowries, bells, and other ornaments.
With *jātī*, campaka, *puṇnāga*, *ketakī*, *mallikā*, and other such flowers; with red lotuses, white lotuses, *mādhavī* vines, and beautiful blossoms.
It was adorned everywhere with various garlands bound together,
