and embellished by ten million red figurines shimmering both horizontally and vertically.
Constructed by Viśvakarman with various divine jewels and other materials, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a beautiful *parijāta* tree in its center. (9.761)
And [he saw] a ground of gold and other jewels, with sands of golden luster,
resembling the rising sun, pervading the pavilion of the entire universe.
The supreme palace of light was a hundred yojanas in extent,
provided with four gates and adorned with golden walls.
It was adorned with eight doorpanels beautifully fashioned from jewels,
and possessed lofty gate-towers and archways constructed from the nine precious gems.
It was adorned with rows of banners hanging from crests of golden staffs,
and it was furnished with pillars set in the middle corner made of the nine precious gems.
Adorned with great rubies, lapis lazuli, and jeweled whisks,
that parasol was positioned above the pavilion on the side of the mountain near the wish-fulfilling tree.
In the center of that [palace], fashioned with golden threads, is a pavilion of jewels;
in the center of that, one should meditate upon the supreme light, shimmering with three peaks. (9.767)
In its center, one should visualize a great wheel filled with nectar,
and in the middle of that altar, a beautiful jeweled lion-throne.
The four feet consisting of the forms of Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśa are directly composed of Sadāśiva; within that, they are of the nature of Paraśiva.
In the midst of that flower-couch, upon a glorious garden-seat,
she shone resplendent, seated upon a svastika throne with her legs crossed in the paryanka posture.
One should meditate upon the goddess Tripurasundarī, seated on the lap of Paraśiva, her form radiant in the center of a lotus, and as red as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling the hibiscus flower, comparable to the pomegranate blossom,
resembling a ruby, and similar in hue to saffron-red.
Adorned with a network of tiny bells from the rubies of her shimmering crown,
she possesses sprout-like, curling locks of hair resembling a swarm of black bees.
Her lotus-face was adorned with a glow like the rising dawn,
and her soft forehead-band was slightly curved like the crescent moon.
The Supreme Goddess, whose creeper-like eyebrows have the form of the Pināka bow, who is the play of joy, delight, and exuberance, and whose eyes are tremulous; 9.775.
She whose golden earrings gleamed with a mass of shimmering rays,
and who surpassed the orb of the moon with the expansive curve of her own cheeks.
Her nose was clearly defined by the lines of creation fashioned by Viśvakarman;
her lips were red like copper, coral, or the bimba fruit, resembling nectar.
She was adorned with rows of teeth as beautiful as rows of pomegranate seeds,
and she surpassed the ocean of the sweet flavor of nectar with the sweetness of her smile.
The Great Goddess, adorned with a jaw-region graced by incomparable qualities, possessed a neck like a conch shell and arms resembling lotus stalks. (9.779)
Her delicate arm has the form of the petals of a red lotus,
and the radiance from the nails of her lotus-like hand illuminates the expanse of the sky.
Her lofty breasts were adorned with strings of pearl necklaces,
and her waist was beautifully graced by the three folds of skin that encircle it.
Adorned with a deep navel that was like a whirlpool in the river of loveliness,
she possessed hips graced by a girdle fashioned from priceless gems.
The Goddess, whose hips are like two elephant globes, whose line of hair is like a choice goad,
and whose thighs are as tender as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree.
Her knees were beautiful, shaped like the buds of the *lāvaṇya* flower,
and she was adorned with a pair of shanks resembling the stalks of the *lāvaṇya* plantain tree.
Her two feet had hidden ankles, and her foreparts surpassed the tortoise;
her slender body was adorned with long fingers that concealed the rows of her nails.
Her lotus feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
she was radiant with a continuous stream of splendor resembling a hundred moons.
She possesses the hue of the Japā flower and the redness of the pomegranate, surpassing even the vermilion of the Lauhitya river;
she is clad in red garments, with her hands raised, holding a noose and a goad.
Seated upon a red lotus, adorned with red ornaments,
she is the one who generates delight for the world and causes the world to be enamored.
She has four arms and three eyes, holds five arrows and a bow,
and her mouth is filled with betel leaf mixed with pieces of camphor.
Her body is reddened by the intense saffron of great musk;
she is enriched with all the attire of amorous passion and adorned with every ornament.
She who generates joy for the world, who causes the world to be enamored, who effects the attraction of the world, and whose form is the cause of the world. (9.791)
I worship her who consists of all prosperity, who is eternal, and who consists of all powers.
Now, regarding the Dīpinī-vidyā, it is stated in that very same place:
"One should apply the seed-syllables of Vāc, Māyā, and Kamalā at the beginning of the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (9.792)
Having recited Tāra, Lakṣmī, the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), Manmatha, and Bhuvaneśvarī,
one should thereafter utter that which is called the Vāgbhava.
Having then recited the Praṇava, Bhuvaneśānī, Ramā, Kāma, and Vāgbhava, followed by the Kāmarāja, which causes the agitation of the three worlds. (9.794)
O Great Goddess, being composed in meditation, one should there recite the syllable Oṃ, the seed-syllable of speech, Ramā, Manmatha, and Māyā, along with Svapnāvatī. (9.795)
Having then recited the Praṇava, the syllable Kāma, Ramā, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Madhumatī, one should [recite] the Māyā, Śrī, and Kūrca seed-syllables.
O Goddess of the Gods, preceded by the Praṇava and encapsulated by the Haṃsa-bīja—
having uttered this seed-syllable, one should then recite the Śaktikūṭa.
Now, regarding the Japanese [mantra]:
one should recite it at the beginning and recite it afterwards seven times in succession;
one should also perform the illumination of the seed-syllables beginning with Kāmarāja.
Now, the procedure for *puraścaraṇa* (according to the *Vāmakeśvaratantra*):
Having stayed there, assuming the very form of the Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
and, O fair-faced one, one should perform an oblation with *kiṃśuka* flowers consisting of one-tenth that number.

Or else, with safflower blossoms mixed with the three sweets, one who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times; (thus it is stated) also in the Siddhāntasāra. (9.800)
One should perform a *homa* sacrifice with one-tenth the number of *kiṃśuka* flowers soaked in honey.
Thus, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected is fit to perform the ritual applications (*prayoga*). — 9.801 —
Now, the mantra of Tripurabhairava (according to the Vāmakeśvara):
Māyā, Lakṣmī, Haṃsa, and the seed-syllable of Prāsāda; this mantra, ending with the wife of fire (Svāhā), is that of Tripurabhairava. (9.802)
The offering of oblations, worship, and so forth should be performed with the six-limbed root mantra.
Now, the meditation: [He is] one-faced, three-eyed, and endowed with four arms. (9.803)
The Lord, red in color, is seated upon a bull and holds a goad and a sword in his right hands, and a shield and a noose in his left hands.
O Great Goddess, one should meditate upon Tripurabhairava in this manner: with hair standing erect, adorned with necklaces and garlands, and endowed with a garland of skulls. (9.805)
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] is identical to the sixteen-fold preliminary rite (*ṣoḍaśī-puraścaraṇa*).
Now, the Bālā-mantra (from the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*):
[the mantra] of her whose command is honored by the three worlds...
I shall declare the three seed-syllables of Ambikā; this must be guarded by those who know the Kula-dharma, for her sake and for their own spiritual attainment. (9.806)

The best of men who recites on earth this mantra known as Vāgbhava— which contains the word *kānta* and others, has the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) at the end of *ka*, and is joined with the letter situated in the ocean (*ja*) preceded by the end of the teeth (*ta*)— [attains success].
He attains perfection in speech that is like the essence of nectar.

The syllable ending with *kānta* (ha), joined with the fifth of the preceding *kula* (pa), and conjoined with *netrānta* (i) and *daṇḍa* (ra), is declared to be the mantra named *Kāma*; through its recitation, this mantra directly causes the agitation of the world.
The *kula* named *Saṃmohana* consists of [the same] joined with the end of *danta* (ta), together with *daṇḍin* (ra) and *sakala* (la).
By constant recitation, his eightfold qualities and the siddhi of moving through the sky are accomplished. (9.808)
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is the high-souled one named Dakṣiṇāmūrti; its meter is Paṅkti;
and Sarasvatī of inconceivable power is declared to be its deity.
The deity whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods is honored by the wise.
The seed-syllable (bīja) of this mantra is joined with the letter *ra* at its end, accompanied by the staff (*daṇḍa*), preceded by Nakulīśa (*na*).
The Śakti, however, is preceded by Khaṇḍala-karṇa (*kha*) and ends with half of the moon (*ja*) and the face (*ma*). (9.810)
In the Merutantra, however, it is stated:
"The seed-syllable of Bālā is Vāgbhava; the third is said to be Śakti;
Kāmarāja shall be the Kīlaka; and by repeating [these] twice, the six-limbed [mantra] is formed. (9-811)
In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*:
"The color of this king of mantras, which is honored by the three worlds, is white;
its musical note is said to be Gāndhāra by those whose intellects have reached the further shore of the Āgamas. (9.812)
This origin of the root of the Vidyā has been told by me; it must be understood in every way by those who desire accomplishment,
since this primordial Vidyā was cursed by the Goddess.
Previously, she had been deprived of her life by him. || 9-813 ||
By the word "jñātavyā" (to be known), however, it is indicated that [the mantra] is to be recited (*japtavyā*).
By the phrase "by the Goddess's curse," the reason for the prohibition is shown. The manner of liberation from that curse is stated in that very same place:
"Therefore, the seed-syllable of Śiva-Śakti was [revealed] by Śambhu..."
Akula was placed above those two former seeds, and Kulopari above that; then, from that point on, she became the blazing one in the middle of the lower [element]. (9.814)

He states the distinction in terminology: "If the Bhairavīya [Vidyā] begins with *udita* and is preceded by *kula*, and if it is preceded by *kula* according to the teachers, that very [Vidyā] bestows swift fruit on earth; it is called *vidyā* and is to be kept strictly secret from the common folk. (9.815)

The meaning is as follows: *Akula* is the letter *ha*; if it is preceded by that [the letter *sa*], it is *Bhairavī*. *Kula* is the letter *sa*; if it is completed by that [the letter *ha*], it is called *Vidyā*. Since there is an absence of the fire-seed (*ra*) in the initial and final seed-syllables, one should understand that this [Vidyā] differs from the *Tripurabhairavī* which is to be described later.
Her visualization is stated in the *Merutantra*: "She holds in her hands the gesture of fearlessness, a book, the goddess Bālā, and the gesture of granting boons."
[One should meditate on her] as rosy-red, seated upon a rosy lotus, wearing red garments, and [worshipping] the Lord of the Twice-born (Brahmā).
But in another tantra it says:
"One should remember the youthful Tripurā, whose radiance is equal to the autumn moon"—
thus she is described as being white in color.

In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*, the specific weapons are described as follows: "Her lotus-hands are raised, holding the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). (9-817)

Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): "One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable and perform a fire sacrifice (*havana*) consisting of a tenth part of that;
thereafter, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites, and thus become a possessor of all good fortune. (Jñānārṇava, 9.818)
Thus ends the section on Śrīvidyā. Now follows the Vidyā of Bhuvaneśvarī (from the Śāradā): Now I shall describe Bhuvaneśvarī, the sustainer of the universe, [Madhu].
Even Brahmā and the other gods, having known her, attained exalted prosperity.
Nakulīśa is mounted upon fire, possessing a left eye and a half-moon;
this is declared to be her seed-syllable, practiced by those desiring spiritual accomplishments. (9.820)
The sage is Śakti, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the mantra is said by the assembly of gods to be Bhuvaneśvarī, who is served throughout the world. (9.821)
One should perform the six limb-protections (aṅga) in sequence with the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels.
Now, the visualization: [She] has the luster of the rising sun, wears a crown of moons, possesses high breasts, and is endowed with three eyes. (9.822)

One should worship Bhuvaneśī, who has a smiling face and whose hands display the gestures of granting boons (*varada*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the noose (*pāśa*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhīti*).
Next is the *puraścaraṇa*:
the knower of mantras should recite the mantra thirty-two hundred thousand times. (9.823)
One should perform oblations with eight substances endowed with the three sweets, in ten parts [of the total number].
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"The Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, and Ramā—this consists of the three seed-syllables. (9.824)

The practitioner of mantra should extract the mantra that accomplishes the fruits of the three aims; he should fashion it with the Vāgbhava syllable at its beginning, using the middle [syllable] endowed with the six long vowels.
The knower of mantras should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of this mantra, conjoined with the [seed] syllable of its origin.
Now, the meditation (dhyāna):
[He visualizes her] with a body as red as vermilion, three eyes, and a crown shimmering with rubies.
She has Tārā as the crest-jewel upon her head, a smiling face, and full breasts.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is gentle, holding in her two hands a jeweled goblet filled with gems and a red lotus, and whose left foot rests upon a jeweled jar.
Now, the *puraścaraṇa*:
one should recite the mantra one million times while offering milk-rice (*pāyasa*) soaked in sweet substances. (9.827)
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations amounting to one-tenth [of the total recitation] and worship on the seat previously described.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
this three-syllabled vidyā is considered to be the Māyā syllable enclosed by the Vāgbīja. (9.828)
The best of mantra-knowers should fashion the limbs, joined with their respective seed-syllables, in sequence by means of the long-conjoined speech-vessel.
Now, the meditation:

[One should visualize] the eternal goddess with a dark-blue body and a moon upon her crest, holding in her own hands a gesture of generosity, a red lotus, a jewel-encrusted goblet, and the supreme protection from fear.
I bow to the consort of Hara, worshipped by the gods, who rests upon a red lotus, whose breasts are radiant with strings of pearls, and who shines with three eyes.

Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each *tattva*, and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, using *pālāśa* flowers mixed with honey, or flowers from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree. (9.831)
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
Ananta joined with the Bindu, possessing Māyā, Brahmā, Agni, and Tāra;
this three-syllabled mantra beginning with Pāśādi bestows the fruit of subjugating all. (9.832)
The sages and other [limbs] have been mentioned previously; the ritual application of the limbs is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable. Now, the visualization:
She holds a boon-granting gesture, a goad, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, and is seated upon a lotus throne. 9-833.
I worship that primordial Bhuvaneśvarī, who resembles ten million rising suns and possesses three eyes.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and with senses subdued, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the *tattva* (the number of elements). (9.834)
At the conclusion of the recitation, the most excellent knower of mantras should offer six thousand oblations with fuel-sticks from milk-trees smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. (9.835)
Then, one should offer oblations with that same number of pure sesame seeds soaked in milk.
For this [goddess], the Great Lord (Mahādeva) is the male deity; his mantra is the five-syllabled one, which has been stated in that very context. Thus ends the section on the Bhuvaneśvarī-vidyā.
Now, the Bhairavī-vidyā.
First, the Tripurabhairavī-vidyā is proclaimed therein (in the Śāradā):
"Now I shall declare the supreme vidyā, the Tripurā, which is exceedingly well-guarded. (9.836)
By knowing which, a man becomes the sovereign of the hosts of Siddhas—the elemental being who resides in space, Mercury, and Fire, and who has the Bindu as his crest. (9.837)
The letter *vi* (the sky) is situated in the first center (the east), in fire (the southeast), and possesses the point of the left eye (*i*).
The mantra is situated in space (the zenith), Venus (the west), and fire (the southeast), and is endowed with the crescent moon of creation (*u*). (9.838)
The first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmabīja, and the third is known as Śaktibīja; thus she is described by means of these three seed-syllables. (9.839)
The Vidyā consisting of five peaks is to be known as Traipurabhairavī;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is declared to be the metre (chandas).
The deity has been declared by the teachers to be the goddess Tripurabhairavī; likewise,
the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the first seed-syllable (bīja) conjoined with the six long vowels.
Other methods of nyāsa have been omitted for fear of prolixity, as it is the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) alone that is to be described here. Now, the meditation (dhyāna):
[She] possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wears a reddish silk garment, and has a garland upon her head.

I worship the Goddess seated upon a lotus, who wears a crown of jewels like the cool-rayed moon, whose face is as beautiful as a lotus adorned with three eyes, and who holds in her lotus-hands a red-stained breast, a rosary, the Vidyā-mantra, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa):
having received initiation, one who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one million times according to the principle (tattva).
One should offer oblations with flowers from the Brahma-tree (palāśa) for thousands of suns (thousands of days).

Or, with flowers produced from the *karavīra* tree smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one should perform one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa*)— that is, three hundred thousand recitations. Now, the mantra of Caitanyabhairavī (according to the *Merutantra*):
Now the three-syllable mantra of Caitanyabhairavī is being described.
The first seed-syllable is said to be joined with *sahā* and *aikāra*.
The second seed-syllable is declared to be joined with *sakalā* and *hrīḥ*. (9-845)
The third [syllable] consists of the letter *saha* joined with *rā*, followed by *au*, and ending with the *visarga*.
Here, the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) should be performed using these three seed-syllables (*bīja*) repeated twice. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*).
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns and is adorned with various ornaments.
She wears a crescent moon shimmering atop her crown, is adorned with red garments, eternally holds a noose and a goad, and carries a skull-cup in her left hand. (9.847)

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who is richly adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and whose thick breasts are full and elevated, one should worship her as she sits upon the eastern lion-throne.
One should accomplish the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and other applications as before;
"as before" means as in the case of Tripurabhairavī.
Now, the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarabhairavī is found in that very same [source].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī. 849.
The first seed-syllable is said to be *hasau* joined with *aikāra* (ai).
The second seed-syllable is declared to be *hasakalā* conjoined with *hrīṃ*.
The six limbs are said to be formed by the seed-syllable joined with *hasau* and *aukāra*, ending in the *visarga*, and combined with the middle of the six long vowels. (9.851)
Now, as for meditation:
[She is] resembling the *japā* flower, with the luster of the pomegranate blossom;
she has a mass of matted hair adorned with a crescent moon, possesses three eyes, and wears red garments. (9.852)

I take refuge in the auspicious Śivā, who is beautiful with various ornaments, whose breasts are full, elevated, and firm, and who holds the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Whatever has not been stated here that is meaningful should be understood as being like Caitanyabhairavī.
Her *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) is to be understood as being like the *puraścaraṇa* of Tripurabhairavī.
Now, Kamaleśvarībhairavī is mentioned in that same [source].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Bhairavī Kamaleśvarī;
having said "saha" in place of "hasa," all the mantras and so forth are as before.
Then, having been discovered by the king, she was cursed and became a river in the snowy mountains;
out of fear of the king, she abandoned the left-hand path for my sake.
The suffering she has obtained will become renowned in the Kali age;
and when the gods have perished, she will become manifest.

p. 811) Even those of low caste and those of high caste shall become bestowers of boons, provided they abandon the fivefold [worldly] manifestation, perform worship, and remain devoted to recitation. (9-857)
On its bank, the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) becomes perfectly successful after nine [days];
for Bhuvaneśī and Bhairavī have assumed another form of mine. (9.858)
For the sake of accomplishing his purpose, many disciples were made into Kaulikas and Vāmins;
her meditation, worship, and so forth are as before, according to the Southern Path.

Now, regarding Tripurabhairavī, the bestower of prosperity (*Jñānārṇava*): "Just as this Bālā is Tripurā, so too is Tripurabhairavī; she is named Saṃpatpradā (Bestower of Prosperity). Listen to [this] concerning her, O you of pure mind. (9.860)
Śiva [the letter *ha*] situated in fire [the letter *ra*], followed by Vāgbhava;
likewise, O Goddess, Kāmabīja, then Śiva conjoined with Candra [the letter *i*]. (9.861)
The seed-syllable of the Earth (La) enriched with Fire (Ra)—listen to this third one, O beloved!
O Maheśānī, one should join Śiva (Ha) and Fire (Ra) into the seed-syllable of Śakti (Hrīṃ). || 9-862 ||
O Supreme Goddess, O Beloved, having abandoned the creation of Vaindava, the goddess Tripurābhairavī bestows great prosperity upon the maiden.
Tripurabhairavī, when devoid of the *visarga*, becomes the bestower of prosperity.
All rites, such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship (*pūjā*), are identical to those of Tripurābhairavī. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
She possesses the luster of a thousand slightly copper-colored suns, and her matted hair is adorned with a shimmering crescent moon.
Adorned with a crown variegated by shimmering jewels and diverse pearls,
she was resplendent with a garland of severed heads dripping with the mud of blood.
She was enriched with the beauty of three eyes, possessed a face like the full moon, and had full,
elevated, firm breasts shining with a string of pearl necklaces.
Clad in red garments, her form intoxicated with youth;
she holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right. (9.867)
One should meditate upon her, who is eternally intent on granting boons and bestows great prosperity.
Her *puraścaraṇa* ritual is also to be understood as before.
Now, Kauleśabhairavī is in that very same place.
Know Kauleśa-Bhairavī to be like Saṃpatpradā-Bhairavī.
O Pārvatī, O Goddess of the gods, this [mantra] beginning with *hasara* is among the three seed-syllables;
it begins with *sahara*, and its meditation, worship, and so forth are likewise performed.

The phrase "like Tripurabhairavī" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. By the word "etcetera," the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is also included. Now, regarding Kāmeśvarabhairavī, it is stated in that very same place:
"And Kāmeśvarī, consisting of the letters of Rudra, is situated upon the eastern throne."
Of this very vidyā, two seed-syllables have been proclaimed. (9.870)
At the end of that, O Supreme Goddess, [are the words] *nityaklinne madadrave*.
O Supreme Goddess, the third syllable of this very [mantra] consists of the letters of Rudra.
O Goddess, meditation, worship, and so forth are prescribed until the attainment of consciousness;
the same applies to the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
Now, regarding Ṣaṭkūṭābhairavī (*Jñānārṇava*).
The pair consisting of Lākinī and Kākinī is located in the seed-syllables of Ḍākinī and Rākinī.
O beautiful goddess, having extracted the seed-syllables of Śākinī and Hākinī, the first is joined with the letter *ai* and the other is adorned with the letter *ī*. (9.873)
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, one should write the third seed-syllable endowed with the sound of Śakra, pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā. (9.874)
O Supreme Goddess, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by repeating [the mantra] twice,
the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is as before. Now, Nityābhairavī is in that very same place.
The six syllables of this very vidyā are established in their respective order. (9.875)
O mature woman, speak [the mantras] in reverse; this knowledge bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
One should perform all the rites for it, such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship, as previously described. (9-876)

Now, O Dear One, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] of Rudrabhairavī is right there: the syllables Śiva (Ś), Candra (C), and Mādana (M) ending with Pānta (P), joined with Vahni (R), pierced by Śakti (H), and enriched with Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. (9.877)
That indeed is the seed-syllable of Kāma belonging to Bhairavī, the bestower of prosperity;
it is also the seed-syllable of Sadāśiva and of the Great Lion Throne.
The seed-syllable of Sadāśiva is the seed-syllable of the preta;
O Maheśānī, this vidyā cannot be fully described.
The ritual placement of the seers and other elements is the same as that for Tripurabhairavī.

Now, as for the meditation: [One should visualize her] possessing the luster of a thousand rising suns, with the moon upon her crest and three eyes, beautiful with various ornaments, and the destroyer of all enemies. (9.879)
She is adorned with a garland of blood-dripping severed heads and is clothed in red garments;
she holds a trident, a hand-drum, a sword, and likewise a shield.
[One should visualize her] holding, in sequence, the Pināka bow, arrows, a goddess, and a noose with a goad;
[and further] a book and a rosary, seated upon the lion-throne of Śiva.
In another tantra:
"All [rites] such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship are identical to those of Tripurā-Bhairavī;
the same applies to the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*). Here, Bhairava is Vaṭuka, and his mantra-puraścaraṇa is taught in the section on Śiva."
Thus ends the section on Bhairavī. Now follows the Vidyā of Chinnamastā (in the Viśvasāra and the Yāmala).
I shall now describe Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, who bestows the fruits of all desires.
By the mere grace of her, a man becomes Śiva himself;
one without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth shall attain wealth.
One attains poetic skill and great scholarship; there is no doubt about this.
He states the extraction of the mantra:
"Then [place] Lakṣmī, Lajjā, and Māyā, followed by the twelfth vowel. (9-884)
When the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is joined with *vajravairocanīye*, *māye*, *phaṭ svāhā*, and is placed first, then Śrī becomes manifest in every direction. (9.885)
By means of the first seed-syllable of *Lajjā*, women come under one's control;
by means of the first seed-syllable of *Māyā*, there is the destruction of great sins.
The first seed-syllable, consisting of twelve measures (*mātrā*), is the bestower of liberation.
Here, the term "shame" (*lajjā*) refers to the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*).
Thus it has been said:
"In this regard, O Goddess, the word for modesty (lajjāpada) follows the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja);
thus is proclaimed the extraction of the mantra that brings auspiciousness, according to the Mahākālamata. — 9.887.

There is no contradiction even if the word *māyā* in the verse concerning the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) refers to the *māyā-bīja*, since we observe that in some instances the *kāma-bīja* appears after the *śrī-bīja*, while in others the pair of *māyās* appears. Furthermore, in certain cases the word *māyā* is seen to refer to the *kūrca-bīja*, as it is proclaimed: "The *māyā* is the two left ears [the *sa* and *ha*] together with the bindu, along with the sky [the *i*]."
The Vāgbhava [syllable] consists of twelve measures.
(In the Viśvasāra:
Another sixteen-syllabled [mantra] beginning with Tārā would be seventeen syllables long.
This is the knowledge, the great knowledge, which always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
As it is said in the *Merutantra*:
"The Praṇava, Ramā, Lajjā, the pair of seeds, and Vāgbhava;
'Vajravairocanīye hrīḥ hrīḥ phaṭ svāhā'—this is the mantra of dense syllables. (9-889)
Bhairava is declared its sage (muni), and Samrāj is cited as its meter;
Chinnamastā is the goddess who bestows perfection through the left-hand path.
(p. 815) (In the *Yāmala* and other texts:
"I am Bhairava, the seer (*ṛṣi*) of these [mantras]; by name, however, I am Krodhabhūpati.
The sovereign meter (*samrāṭ-chandaḥ*) and the deity (*devatā*) are proclaimed to be Chinnamastā. (9-891)
The seed-syllable of Māyā is "svāhā," which is declared by the one born from Brahmā to be Śakti;
its application is proclaimed for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 9-892 ||
Ā for the sword is declared for the heart; Sukhaḍga for the head. Oṃ Vajra is said for the crest-lock; Ai for the noose for the body armor. 9-893.
"Aum Aṅkuśāya" is for the eye, and "Aśvāsura-kṣayāya" is for the weapon;
"Hūḥ Hūḥ" is the nine-syllable mantra of the weapon. All [these mantras] should begin with the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 9-894 ||
All of these [mantras] end with *svāhā*; thereafter, one should perform meditation (*dhyāna*).
As for the meditation:
[one should visualize her] situated in the center of a radiant orb, in the posture of inverted sexual union.
Mounted upon Rati and Kāma, with all her ornaments scattered,
she again held her own severed head in her left hand.
She was drinking the blood flowing from her own throat through her own mouth,
and she was surrounded by two female companions, a Ḍākinī and a Varṇinī.
Now another mantra (from the Mahākālasaṃhitā):
"Therefore, I shall now proclaim to you the mantra of Chinnamastā;
by the mere desire to grasp it, even a practitioner shall attain the eight supernatural powers. (9-898)
There shall be no goddess more fierce than this;
therefore, this [mantra] must never be grasped by men who are not detached.
Either success or even death—only one of these two shall occur. [The mantras are:
the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Ramā, the Lañjā, and the Vāgbhava.
And "vajravairocanīye"—thus one should extract [the mantra] from there.
Then follow two wrathful deities (krodha), and then the weapon-mantra (astra) ending in svāhā; this is the sixteen-syllable [mantra]. (9.901)
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other procedures for this [deity] should be performed as before.
Now, regarding the meditation:
I shall proclaim her meditation; fix your mind thereon.
One should meditate on a pure, blooming, white lotus within one's own navel.
In the center of that lotus calyx, however, is the mandala of the fiercely radiant one,
resembling the hibiscus flower and like the red bandhūka.
It resembles the circle of the yoni, marked by the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas;
in its center is the Great Goddess, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
She holds her own severed head in her left hand;
she has a wide-gaping mouth, is terrifying, and her fierce tongue is lolling out.
And she was drinking a stream of blood arising from her own throat;
her mass of hair was disheveled and adorned with various flowers.
And in her right hand she holds a flaying knife, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
she is naked, most terrible, and stands in the pratyālīḍha posture.
The Goddess, who wears a garland of bones and has a serpent as her sacred thread,
is eternally sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts.
She who has serpent-armlets, serpent-girdles, and is endowed with serpent-anklets;
she who is joined with serpent-earrings and accompanied by eight serpents.
She is intent on perverse sexual pleasure, established in the desire for delight, and joined with Ḍākinī and Varṇinī through the union of the left and right [channels]. (9.910)
One should meditate on Varṇinī on the right and Ḍākinī on the left side;
Varṇinī is crimson-dark, with loose hair and naked.
Holding a skull-cup and a curved knife in her left and right hands respectively, she is drinking the stream of blood gushing from the neck of the goddess. (9.912)
The goddess wears a garland of bones and has a serpent as her sacred thread;
she is a Ḍākinī on the left side, resembling the blazing fire at the end of an aeon.
Her eyes flashed like streaks of lightning, her rows of teeth were like a flight of cranes,
her face was formidable with fangs, and her breasts were full and high.
To the Great Goddess, most terrible, with disheveled hair and naked,
pot-bellied, the Night of Doom, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
She has a large tongue that lolls out, is adorned with a garland of severed heads,
and holds a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her left and right hands respectively.
She is exceedingly terrifying, drinking the stream of blood gushing from the goddess’s throat with a skull held in her hand that is itself most fearsome.
While these two are being practiced, the wise man should meditate upon the Goddess, who is difficult even for the mind to behold, yet bestows the fruits of all desires. (9.918)
Now, another mantra [from the Yāmalatantra]:
Bhuvaneśī, the Kāma-bīja, the Kūrca-bīja, and the Vāgbhava;
then Bhuvaneśī, the Kūrca-bīja, and the Vāgbhava. (9–919)
And then follows "Vajravairocanīye ca huṃ phaṭ svāhā. After that, there is another mantra:
"Hṛllekhā, Vāgbhava, Kūrca, Vāgbhava, and Kūrca again. (9.920)
Chinnamastā, who ends with the weapon (astra), is proclaimed as the Great Vidyā;
and a Vidyā equal to her is not found even within the worlds.
This six-syllabled mantra directly bestows liberation; there is no doubt about this.
For both of these, the assignment of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth, as well as the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), should be performed as previously described.
As for the distinction regarding meditative absorption (dhyāna): "I shall describe her meditative absorption; listen, O lotus-faced one. (9.922)
Always assuming the *pratyālīḍha* stance, holding a severed head and a flaying knife,
clad in the directions as her garment, joyfully drinking the stream of nectar-like blood from her own trunk;
with a serpent bound as a crest-jewel, three eyes, and adorned with a blue lotus at her heart— Please perform the translation.
One should meditate upon her who is firmly seated above the Mind-born (Kāma) when he is attached to Rati, appearing as if she were engaged in silent recitation (japa).
In her right hand, she holds a razor with hair released from it, and likewise a skull-cup in her two hands; born of the quality of rajas, she is known by the name Varṇinī,
joyfully drinking the stream of blood falling from the severed headless trunk of the Goddess.
She whose crest-jewel is bound by the Nāgas should be meditated upon in that manner by those who know the Manu-mantras, as well as by the gods.
On the left, she likewise has a dark body, holding a sword and a skull-cup; standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, she joyfully drinks the blood dripping from the headless trunk.
She is that very Tāmasī power who is capable of devouring the entire universe at the time of dissolution.
That power also is the Goddess who is higher than the high, known by the name Parāḍākinī.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"O Vajravairocanī, [the mantra] with the pair of *kūrca*s, together with *phaṭ* and *ṭhaṭhaḥ*.
This great vidyā, beginning with Tārā, is the remover of all splendor. (9-926)
One should perform all [rites], such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), just as in the *Ṣoḍaśī* [vidyā].
Another mantra: O Dear One, [the syllable] "vi" joined with the two ears (the letter *śa*) and then joined with the bindu and the nāda. (9.927)
The single-syllable great vidyā brings the three worlds under its control;
this great vidyā, ending with the two *ṭha*s, deludes the three worlds. (9.928)
And this [goddess] beginning with Tārā becomes the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life;
all [the rites] such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna) have been proclaimed as being as before.
p 819) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), [the *Viśvasāra* states]:
"In the ritual of the preliminary rite, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations;
and in the case of the Great Vidyās as well, the recitation should measure one hundred thousand. (9-930)
This has been stated everywhere in all the tantras by the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
(Also in the Rudrayāmala:
"One should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, and thereafter offer oblations (*homa*) ten thousand times. (9-931)
One should perform the fire-offering (homa) with bilva wood smeared with ghee,
or one may perform it with udumbara fuel-sticks or with palāśa sticks.
One should offer oblations with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks—or, according to another reading, with *apāmārga* and *śamī* wood—for the sake of accomplishing the mantra.
(Also in another *Yāmala*):
Having meditated upon the Goddess, one who subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣyabhuk*) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. (9.933)
One should perform oblations with wood of the *vilva* tree soaked in clarified butter, using a tenth part of that [number].
(In the *Vārāhītantra*, however, it says:
"In an empty house, in a cremation ground, in a place devoid of bulls, or in a temple of Śiva. (9.934)
"One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times; then success will certainly be attained"—so it is said.
(Also in the *Gandharvatantra*:
"During the day one should observe celibacy, but at night one should be accompanied by a woman. (9.935)

O Goddess, having placed the fivefold maṇḍala before one, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times with a rosary of large conch shells, according to the requirements of the Kali age.
A person devoted to faith should recite another hundred thousand verses;
when three hundred thousand have been completed, one should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
In the Kali age, which is filled with evil and devoid of truth and dharma, the ritual practice should be recited fourfold; by that means, success is attained, without a doubt.

The procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇavidhi*) consists of practicing with the right-hand conduct during the day and the left-hand conduct at night; this is the domain of the Kaulikas. (In the *Merutantra*:
"In this manner, worship should be performed, and one should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times."
One should offer oblations with flowers or fruits from either the *pālāśa* or the *bilva* trees.
Then one should perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth; in this way, the mantra becomes perfected.

Regarding this, they say that for the sixteen-syllable mantra mentioned in the *Viśvasāra*, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*); for other mantras mentioned in other tantras, it is three hundred thousand recitations; and for the seventeen-syllable mantra mentioned in the *Merutantra*, it is four hundred thousand recitations.
(From the *Bhūtabhairava*).
Having first recited [the mantra] of Bhairava, one should then recite the mantra of this Wrathful One.
Having taken up a garland of bones, one should follow the Vajravairocanī mantra.
The Krodhabhairava mantra is stated in that very same place:
"Now I shall declare the wrathful mantra by which even the unattainable is accomplished. (9-941)
Having taken the seed-syllable Hālāhala, and thereafter the seed-syllable of Wrath,
one should address the terrifying-syllabled Asitāṅga, who has the luster of blood.
Having addressed the great flame of the fire of dissolution, one should extract the mantra;
thus uttered, the Wrathful One (Krodha) becomes spontaneously perfected.
Then, with the wrath-mantra, one should perform the six-limb placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
One should place Viṣa, Vajra, Yuta, Bodhi, and Mahākāla upon the heart.
One should place Viṣa, Harayuga, and Vajrakūrca and the others upon the head;
one should place Hālāhala together with Deha and Vajrakāla upon the topknot (śikhā).
One should place the weapon-vajra and the armor conjoined with the three uneven syllables;
the vajra conjoined with the seed-syllable of Tārā [is placed] for Mahākāla in the two eyes.
Having grasped *viṣa* joined with *hanu*, followed by *daha* and *gṛhya* accompanied by *para*;
likewise, having grasped *krodha* joined with *vajra*, one [subdues] all wicked beings thereafter. (9.947)
Then, perform the six-limbed rite beginning with the binding of the directions and ending with the *vajrāstra* weapon. Regarding the visualization, it says:
"In that [mandala], one should place the Terrifying One (*Bhīma*) in the center, filled with blazing, molten flames. (9-948)

Laughing with a loud roar, most fierce, resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, four-armed, holding a vajra in the right [hand] and a discus in the left. || 9-949 ||
With his left hand he makes the threatening gesture (tarjanī), and he is terrifying with sharp fangs;
he wears a crown of skulls and jewels, the leader of the three worlds.
Resembling ten million suns, adorned with eight nāgas,
he stands upon the unconquerable ground, possessing the mudrās and endowed with strength and vigor.
Having joined the two ring fingers and bent the two index fingers,
one should likewise [hold] the little and middle fingers with the thumb in successive order.
Thus, the bearer of the mudrā is formidable, the accomplisher of that which is unattainable even in the three worlds.
The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra is like the preparatory rite for Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā.

And regarding the procedure for recitation (*japa*) and fire-offering (*homa*), they know it to be equal for Śiva and Śakti—according to the statement: "The Ramā-kāma [syllable], likewise the Lajjā [syllable], the Vāgbhava [syllable], and the Vajra-vai-pada [syllables]..."
In the *rocanīya* [mantra], the pair of shame-mantras (*lajjādvandva*) is joined with *svāhā*.
This is that which is called the Sixteenth, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
all these auspicious Vidyās have been declared as the most essential of the essential.
[Note: These two verses are seen as an interpolation. || 9-953 ||
Thus ends the section on Chinnamastā.
Now follows the Dhūmāvatī-vidyā (from the Mahātharvaṇasaṃhitā).

The two letters *da* and *ta*, along with the moon on the left ear (*sa*), smoke (*ma*), *avati* (*a*), fire’s wife (*ra*), and the eight-syllabled great vidyā bestows all accomplishments upon those who worship it. (9.954)
In the *Merutantra*:
"The sage is Pippalāda; the meter is Nivṛt; its deity is Jyeṣṭhā.
The six limbs [are performed] with the letter *Dha* joined with the six long vowels and the bindu. (p. 822) 9-955.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the six syllables situated within the first two seed-syllables, upon the six limbs beginning with the thumbs; then one should again meditate upon the Goddess.
And likewise for meditation:
she who is discolored, fickle, black, tall, and dressed in soiled garments;
she with loose, long hair, a widow, and sparse teeth. (9.957)
Mounted upon a chariot with a crow-banner, with pendulous breasts,
holding a winnowing basket in her hand, with extremely harsh eyes, shaking her hand, and full of haste.
Her hair was thick and matted, her eyes were crooked, she was constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, and she was always intent on quarreling. (9.959)
One should always meditate upon her in this manner and then perform the ritual action.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite [the mantra] in an empty house, by day and by night, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
And one devoted to fasting shall likewise attain perfection in a single day;
or else, remaining silent, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times in a cremation ground or a forest.
Wearing a turban and moist garments, the mantra is thereby mastered;
here, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with ghee alone, and thereafter one should carry out the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites.
Alternatively, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times in a cremation ground while naked;
eating only at night, one should perform a fire offering with sesame seeds consisting of a tenth part of that number.
Now, another mantra from another tantra:
Having uttered the three seed-syllables *dhūḥ*, one should recite the pair *dhura*.
Having uttered the word *Dhūmāvatī*, it is joined with *kroḥ svāhā phaṭ*. (9.964)
The first mantra has been declared; now listen respectfully to the second.
One should utter the Praṇava, the seed-syllable Dhūmra, and the word Dhūmāvatī. (9-965)
"Devadatto dhāvati svāhā"—this is the king of mantras;
its seer is known as Kṣapaṇaka, and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter. (9-966)
The deity is Dhūmāvatī, and the seed-syllable *dhū* is declared to be the seed (*bīja*).
*Svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the purpose of eradication (*samuccāṭa*). || 9-967 ||
With the six groups of consonants [beginning with] *dh*, there are the six limbs; listen to the meditation, O fair-faced one:
she is mounted upon a crow, extremely black in luster, with broken teeth, and devoid of passion.
With disheveled hair and very smoky eyes, afflicted by hunger and thirst, distressed by haste, fickle, and excessively pained by lust, she was emaciated yet full-bodied and tawny in hue.
The supreme Dhūmāvatī should be meditated upon as a soiled female ascetic, passionate, manifesting foul odors, antagonistic, and holding a winnowing basket in her hand.
He describes the *puraścaraṇa*:
"O Maheśānī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; thus one effects the eradication of the world.
Now, the Aghora mantra (according to the *Śāradā-tantra*):
Now I shall duly declare the supreme mantra of the Aghora weapon.
By the mere recollection of which all calamities perish:
*hum* is the mantra for paralyzing (*stambhana*), *krom* for attracting (*ākarṣaṇa*) and for seating (*āsana*).
The mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ* is for concealment; ending in *namaḥ*, it is for an uneven seat (*viṣamāsana*).
For the destruction of planets, thieves, and enemies, those ending in *huṃ* and *kroṃ* are prescribed.
Ending with *śakti* (phaṭ) for all desired purposes, ending with *kṣaum* (huṃ) for killing, and ending with *phaṭ* for the destruction of spirits—this mantra is a wish-fulfilling tree. || 9.974 ||

In the *Īśvarakalpa*, however, there are two instances of *prasphurat* and two instances of *bandha*. This mantra, consisting of forty-one syllables, is extracted [as follows] in the *Padārthādarśa-ṭīkā*:
"Then there are two instances of *māyāsphurat*, followed by two instances of *prasphurat*;
at the end are 'ghora-ghoratarā', and again the word *tanurūpa*. (9-975)
At the end of that, there should be two *caṭas*, followed by two *pracaṭas*;
then two *kahas*, two *vamas* [the variant reading in manuscript 2 is *vahayugmaṃ vadadvandvam*], and then again two *bandhas*. (9.976)
The two *ghātaya* syllables followed by *varma* and ending with *phaṭ* are thus proclaimed;
this is the great mantra of the Aghora weapon consisting of fifty syllables.
Aghora is declared to be its sage (muni), and Triṣṭubh is stated to be its meter; Aghora Rudra is designated as its deity by those most skilled in mantras.
The heart is said to consist of five [syllables], the head is declared to consist of six;
the crest (śikhā) is described as having ten, and the armor (kavaca) is considered to have that same number.
The eye is said to consist of the *vasu* (eight) and *varṇa* (nine) syllables; the weapon is declared to consist of the *āśā* (ten) and *arṇa* (sixteen) syllables.
Meditation:
[One should meditate on the deity] who has the luster of a water-laden cloud, fearsome fangs, and three eyes.
He who wears serpent ornaments, who is not terrible, and whose garments and body are smeared with red pigment.
I meditate upon him bearing an axe, a hand-drum, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a trident, and a human skull.
Now, regarding his preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), it is stated in that very same [text]:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with auspicious sesame seeds sprinkled with ghee. (9.981)
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra.
Thus ends the section on Dhūmāvatī. Now follows the Vidyā of Vagalāmukhī.
(Merutantra) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the paralyzing Vagalāmukhī.
Having uttered *tāram* and *māyā*, one should say *vagalāmukhi*;
after that, the words *sarvaduṣṭānām*, followed by *vācam* and *mukham*.
"Stambhaya" (Paralyze), "jihvām kīlaya" (Nail the tongue)—after that, "buddhim vināśaya hrīḥ oṃ svāhā. This consists of thirty-six syllables. || 9-984 ||
The sage is Nārāyaṇa, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and the goddess is Vagalāmukhī; Hṛllekhā is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and Svāhā is the power (śakti). || 9.985 ||
Its application is renowned for the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha).
Hṛllekhā is declared to be the heart, and Vagalāmukhī is the head.

The *śikhā* [mantra] is for all the wicked; then [one says] "paralyze the speech, the mouth, and the steps. The *varma* [mantra] is said [to be used with the words] "pin the tongue and the eyes. (9.987)
Having destroyed the intellect, the weapon becomes the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa); this is what has been taught.
Now, the meditation: [one should meditate on her] as deep and intoxicated with passion, resembling molten gold. (9.988)
Four-armed and three-eyed, seated upon a lotus throne,
she holds a mallet in her right hand and a noose, a tongue, and a vajra in her left hands.
She wears yellow garments, possesses full, round, and plump breasts,
is adorned with golden earrings, and has a crescent moon as her yellow crest-ornament.
Adorned with yellow ornaments and seated upon a golden lion-throne;
now, the *puraścaraṇa*:
wearing a garland strung with turmeric, he himself dons yellow garments. (9.991)

One should visualize [the deity] seated on a yellow throne; one should perform ten thousand recitations (japa) of the yellow [mantra], and having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that, one should satisfy [the deity] with yellow substances.
The mantra of the practitioner is accomplished through entirely yellow ritual services.
As stated in the *Vajrayoginīmiśrakṛtasaṃgraha*:
"Having donned yellow garments, one should stand facing the eastern direction."
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times using a rosary made of turmeric knots.
"Always joined with celibacy, restrained, and intent on meditation, one should perform the fire-oblation even with *priyaṅgu* preparations and yellow flowers"—so it has been said. (9-994) p. 826)
Now, another mantra [from the Yāmala]: "Vahni-hīna-indra-yugmāyā vagalāmukhi sarvayuk;
having uttered 'the speech of the wicked,' one should recite 'paralyze the mouth'. (9-995)
"Pin the tongue and destroy the intellect"—one should utter this mantra;
it begins with the previous seed-syllable, followed by the *tāra* (oṃ), and ends with the wife of fire (svāhā). || 9.996 ||
Vagalāmukhī, who is superior to Tārā, consists of thirty-four syllables;
Nārāyaṇa (in some readings, Nārada) is her sage, the metre is Paṅkti, and she is the auspicious Vagalāmukhī.
The deity is the seed-syllable contained within the mantra; the power is Pāvakasundarī.
This application is proclaimed for the purpose of paralyzing the mouths of all enemies. || 9.997 ||
The ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is taught by means of the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels.
Now, the visualization (dhyāna): In the center, upon a jeweled altar in a pavilion of gems within an ocean of nectar—
Seated upon a lion throne, she is of a deep golden-yellow complexion.

[The reading "her limbs adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands" is also heard in many places. I worship the Goddess, who wears yellow garments and is beautified by golden ornaments and garlands, who holds a mallet to the tongues of her enemies; holding the tip of a tongue in her left hand, she torments her foes. (9-999)
And by the striking with the foot, I bow to her who is adorned with yellow garments and possesses two arms.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) in that very context:
O Goddess of the gods, the rosary for the recitation (*japa*) should be made from turmeric knots. (9–10)
Seated upon a yellow seat, intent on yellow meditation, one should daily perform worship with yellow flowers and recite the mantra ten thousand times. (9–1001) p. 827)
A Homa performed with ten parts of that [number] using beautiful yellow substances [is prescribed].
Regarding this [deity], the man Mṛtyuñjaya and the preliminary ritual (puraścaraṇa) for her mantra have been explained in the section on Śiva.
Thus ends the section on Vagalāmukhī.
Now, the Mātaṅgī-vidyā. (In the Yāmala:
Now I shall declare the Great Goddess Mātaṅgī, the bestower of all accomplishments. 9–1002.
Merely by practicing this, one certainly attains perfection of speech.
Then [one should recite] the Praṇava, followed by Māyā, the Kāmabīja, and the Kūrcaka.
The mantra consists of *mātaṅgī* joined with the weapon (*astra*) and ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is said to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Virāṭ meter is declared to be its meter (*chanda*).
Mātaṅgī is the goddess, the deity who bestows all accomplishments;
the practitioner of mantra, being composed, should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa).
One should fashion [the mantra] with a seed-syllable preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and endowed with six long vowels. Now, the meditation:
[She is] dark-limbed, moon-crested, three-eyed, seated upon a lion-throne of excellent jewels.
The city was adorned with various jewel ornaments, yet its central areas were completely depleted.
One should meditate upon her, whose face is smiling and whose breasts are like circles of water,
holding in succession with her four arms a goad, a sword, a small dagger, a noose, and likewise a shield.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite).
During the time of the *puraścaraṇa* rite, however, one should recite the mantra six thousand times.
The practitioner, together with the Śaktis, should offer oblations ten times that amount using clarified butter along with sugar and honey, and with fuel-sticks made from the wood of the Brahma-tree.
Having thus performed the preliminary honors, one should carry out the ritual procedure.
Now, another mantra [from the *Merutantra*]:
"Next, I shall proclaim the Ucchiṣṭā Mātaṅgī, who has the color of a cow. (9-1009)
One should utter the words "Oṃ Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍāli Mātaṅgi," followed by "Sarvavaśaṅkari Svāhā. This mantra shall delude the world. (9–1010)
The meter is Nivṛt with the Gāyatrī; the sages are Nārada and Tumburu;
and the deity here is Mātaṅgī, [arranged] by two, three, three, three, six, and two [syllables]. 9–1011.
The limbs [of the deity] should be [assigned] according to the words of the mantra; thereafter, one should meditate upon her in the lotus of the heart.
As for the meditation:
she is clad in black garments, her feet moist with red lac, and her breasts are full. (9–1012)
[She is] richly adorned with garlands of pearls and coral, and wears conch-shell earrings.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"Now I shall fully declare another wonderful mantra of Mātaṅgī. (9-1013)
"Kāminī Rañjinī Svāhā"—this is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra. Sammohana is its seer (ṛṣi), Nivṛt is said to be its meter (chandas), and it is its deity. (9–1014)
And the limb that deludes all consists of words repeated twice. Now, for the visualization:
she has a dark-complexioned body, is beautifully adorned, and plays the lute with her two arms. (9–1015)
She who has the moon as her crest-jewel, who deludes the world with various songs—
[this is] the preliminary rite for these two.
One should mutter [the mantra] twenty thousand times, and then perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that.
With [offerings] made from *madhūka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one may delude the entire world.
Now, regarding the mantra of Rājamātaṅgī, it is stated in that very same place:
"Now I shall proclaim another [mantra], consisting of fifty-four syllables. (9–1017)
Oṃ hrīḥ! Homage to you, O Brahmaśrīrājite, who are worshipped by kings; to Jayā, Vijayā, Gaurī, and Īśā; one should then utter the word "Gāndhāri. (9-1018)
"O subduer of the three worlds! O [subduer] of all women and men! O subduer! Su-su du-du ghe-ghe vā-vā, wife of Agni! (9–1019)
The sage is Aja, the meter is said to be Nivṛt-Gāyatrī, and the deity is Rājamātaṅgī; as for the six limbs and so forth, they are formed by means of Māyā.
Now, regarding meditation:
[The reading enclosed within these brackets is found additionally in manuscript 5.
In the beautiful Jewel Island situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar,
Enclosed by a golden rampart, it was fashioned from jewels and gems.
At the gateway of Kadamba and Bilvaka, adorned with wish-fulfilling trees,
upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne well-spread with comforts in the center of the altar.
A great eight-petaled lotus, rich with filaments and possessing a pericarp;
in its center there should be a triangle, and outside of that, another eight-petaled [lotus].
Furthermore, there should be a sixteen-petaled [lotus], and outside of that, a four-petaled one;
this mandala, possessing four corners and four gates, is declared to be the most excellent.
In its center, she sat comfortably— dark-complexioned, with a pure smile,
adorned with garlands of Kadamba flowers, and worshipped by both gods and demons.
She is adorned with long, hanging locks of hair and a crescent moon as her ear-ornament;
she bears a tilaka mark upon her forehead, and her face is slightly smiling.
Her forehead-slab was radiant with the sweetness of a few drops of perspiration;
she shone between the waves of her folds, adorned with a line of body hair.
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments, decorated with pearl necklaces,
and embellished with waist-bands bound with clusters of various jewels.
Adorned with bracelets inlaid with jewels and armlets embellished with gems, she is a young woman with two arms, her eyes rolling with intoxication. (9.1029)
Her breasts were full, round, and elevated, possessing the expanse of a circle;
she was adorned with long, variegated ornaments and graced by ear-ornaments.
The young woman was as dark as a *tamāla* tree, intoxicated by spring,
possessing the form of the sixty-four arts, with a parrot and a sarika bird at her side.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mātaṅginī as resembling ten million rising suns, or like a hibiscus flower, or likewise of yellow color. (9–1032)
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): [The reading enclosed within these brackets is found as an addition in manuscript 5.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*) and perform fire oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number.
The mantra-practitioner [should offer] bandhūka flowers mixed with the three sweets. || 9-1033 ||
Now, the mantra of Sumukhī (from the Guhyātantra):
Listen, O Great Goddess, to the mantra; I shall tell it to you exactly as it is:
one should utter the word "ucchiṣṭa" and likewise "cāṇḍālinī. (9–1034)
Then one should proclaim the goddess as "Sumukhī," immediately after that;
from her comes "Mahāpiśācinī," and after that, the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Then, O Great Goddess, there are three *ṭha* syllables joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, along with the *visarga*; this bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
This knowledge is a great knowledge that destroys all sins;
it is the knowledge that bestows heaven, bestows liberation, and bestows all prosperity [as well as the prosperity of sovereignty], so it is said. (9–1037)
Having had the remnants of the food on his face, he should meditate upon the Goddess who bestows victory;
then, O Goddess, he becomes purified by the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), even without having performed the rite.
Indeed, the unfortunate shall surely become fortunate, and the sorrowful shall become happy;
even a barren woman shall obtain a son who lives for a hundred years. (9.1038)
The weak shall attain strength, and the fool shall acquire knowledge;
whatever perfection he strives for with persistence, that very thing he shall obtain.
And I shall describe the procedure here; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance: there is no fault regarding women, nor any obstacle, nor impurity, nor any restrictive rule.
He in whom this mantra abides is not afflicted by obstacles. Likewise: Aja is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi), and its meter is Gāyatrī. 9-1041.
The deity is said to be Sumukhī; the six-limbed [protection] is performed with the Māyā-mantra. Now, the visualization:
Seated upon a corpse, clothed in red garments... 9-1042.
Adorned with red ornaments and decorated with a necklace of *guñjā* berries,
she is a young woman of sixteen years, with full and elevated breasts.

The best of those who know the mantras should meditate upon her, who holds a skull and a flaying-knife in her hands and whose nature is supreme light, through the union of the left and right [channels]. 9–1044.
Having offered the bali-oblation with the remnants [of food], one should recite [the mantra] with the mind fixed upon it;
one who desires success should perform the recitation of this [mantra] using only the remnants.
For one who performs the recitation while remaining in a state of ritual impurity (ucchiṣṭa), all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis) arise.
The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this mantra consists of eight thousand recitations.
This is because of the previously cited statements beginning with: "In whose recitation and in whose fire-oblation... (9-1046).
Now, the mantra of Vaśyamātaṅgī (from the Merutantra):
"Hereafter, I shall fully declare the mantra of Vaśyamātaṅgikā:
Oṃ rājamukhi rājādhimukhi vaśyamukhi. (9-1047)
One should then utter "Māyā Śrī Klī Devadevi Mahādevi," followed by "Devādhidevi Sarve" and the name of the person's mouth. (9-1048)
"Bring me under your control, O couple, svāhā"—this is the mantra for the limbs (*aṅga*), ending in *svāhā* and consisting of seven syllables.
The assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*) is performed using the syllables of the mantra repeated seven times for each of the directions. (9–1049)

One should understand that worship, recitation, and so forth are equal to the *rājamātaṅgī*; one should also know the ritual applications (*prayoga*), for this [vidyā] is especially effective at subjugating.
He states another mantra:

"Māyā (Hrīṃ), *namas*, the pair *hilid* (*hilid-hilid*), and *Caṇḍamātaṅginī svāhā*. Its letters correspond to the lunar days; its ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth should be performed accordingly. (9–1051)
The recitation should be ten thousand times, equal to that of the *Rājamātaṅgikā*;
there should also be an oblation of ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and the ritual applications (*prayoga*) and so forth are as previously described.
Now, the mantra of Karṇamātaṅgī:
Hereafter, I shall fully proclaim the Karṇamātaṅgikā-mantra.
One should utter the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], then the Heart [mantra], and then the word "Śrīmātaṅgī. (9–1053)
O infallible speaker of truth, then [recite] my ear-word;
next, the descent-word in two ways—speak the pair of truths.
"Come, come, O Śrī! Salutation to Mātaṅgī"—this mantra consists of three oceans [twelve syllables].
Here, the limbs [of the deity] are worshipped with the Vāgbhava [syllable], whether the worship and other rites have been performed or not. (9–1055)
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
a hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) and an oblation (*homa*) with milk-rice and other offerings shall bring the mantra to completion.
Then the Goddess shall whisper the auspicious and inauspicious [outcomes] into the ear of the inquirer.
Thus ends the section on Mātaṅgī. Now follows the Lakṣmī-vidyā (according to the Śāradā-tantra).
Now I shall declare the mantras of Śrī, which bestow the fruits of fortune and good luck;
by whose mere sidelong glance even the three worlds flourish. (9-1057)
The letter *va* mounted upon fire (*ra*), conjoined with the moon of the left eye (*i*)—this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śrī, like another wish-fulfilling gem. (9.1058)
The seer is Bhṛgu, the metre is Nivṛt, and the deity is declared to be Śrī.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of the seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels. (9–1059)
Now, for the meditation:
one should visualize the Goddess Śrī, who resembles gold in her luster, being sprinkled by four elephants resembling the snowy mountains,
who lift golden jars of nectar with their trunks.
I bow to her who stands upon a lotus, radiant with a crown, her hips graced by a silken garment, and holding in her hands a boon-granting gesture, a pair of lotuses, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
the initiated practitioner, having conquered his senses, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable (*bhānulakṣa*).
He should daily worship Śrī with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
One should offer that thousand-fold oblation with lotuses smeared with honey;
at the conclusion of the recitation, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with honey.
Or the best of practitioners should offer oblations with three fruits of the *vailva* tree.
Now, another mantra for that same [rite] is as follows:
*vāgbhava*, *vanitā*, Viṣṇu’s [seed-syllable], *māyā*, and the dolphin-bannered god (Kāmadeva).
The mantra consisting of four seed-syllables bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
The knower of the Tantra should fashion the limbs with the seed-syllable *ramā* (śrīṃ) and [the vowels] beginning with *dīrgha* (long).
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[One should meditate on her] possessing a luster like that of a ruby, [seated] upon four lofty elephants white as snow.
She is constantly being sprinkled with water from jeweled jars held by the tips of the hands of the *r̥bhus*.

I bow to the lotus-faced beloved of Hari, who holds the gestures of granting boons (*varada*), the pair of lotuses, and fearlessness (*abhaya*) with her lotus-like hands, and who yearns for the *pārijāta* creeper.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa*.
Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; at the conclusion, [one should worship] with lotuses.
One who has conquered the senses should offer a thousand oblations with blossoming reddish flowers.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"Brahmā, Bhānu, and Vasundharā, beginning with a long vowel and ending with the visarga. (9-1066)
The ten-syllable mantra of Agni, beloved of Śinī, is proclaimed;
Dakṣa is the seer, Virāṭ is the meter, and Śrī is declared to be the deity. (9–1067)
The Heart has been declared for the Goddess; the Head is proclaimed for Padminī;
the Crest-lock (Śikhā) is spoken for Viṣṇupatnī; and the Armor (Tanucchada) for Varadā.

The weapon-mantra (astra) is for the one whose form is a lotus; these mantras, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with the word "namaḥ," are declared to be the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras). One whose mind is focused elsewhere should meditate upon the Goddess.
Now, for the meditation:
Seated upon a lotus, her face smiling, holding with her lotus-hands the gestures of generosity, the pair of lotuses, and fearlessness; in her form she is like the beloved of lightning.
May Kamalā protect you—she who shines with her broad, lofty breasts adorned with a magnificent string of pearls, and who gladdens Hari with the splendor of her sidelong glances. 9-1070.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one who knows the mantra and has conquered his senses should recite this [mantra] one million times.
The practitioner of the mantra should then perform oblations (*homa*) ten thousand times with lotuses smeared with honey.
Now, the mantra of Mahālakṣmī is given in that same place:
Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, Ramā, Makaraketana, the third [seed-syllable], and Jagatpārśva, blazing with the fire-seed (vahnibīja). (9–1072)
This twelve-syllable heart-mantra of Mahālakṣmī, beginning with Om and consisting of the syllables "Bhṛgu" (Sa) and "Arghīśa" (Ha), is declared to bestow all spiritual perfections. (9–1073)
The seer is declared to be Vidyā; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
and the deity is proclaimed to be Mahālakṣmī, the primordial source of the worlds. (9–1074)
Having purified both hands with the mantra from *tāra* to the heart, one should place the five seed-syllables upon the fingers in their proper order. (9–1075)
The practitioner of mantras should place the remainder of the mantra upon both palms;
then, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the mantra from the head down to the feet.
One should place the five seed-syllables on the head, eyes, chest, private parts, and feet;
one should place the remaining seven syllables in the heart upon the seven bodily constituents.

The limbs [of the mantra] are formed from five seed-syllables, and the weapon-mantra (astra) from the remaining syllables; these are joined with the qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty, ending in the dative case and accompanied by their respective classes of sounds.
Knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and one's own splendor—these six, beginning with knowledge and sovereignty, are said to be joined as limbs in their respective order. (9–1079)
He describes meditation: Having thus cast off his body, he should recollect a wonderful garden, adorned with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *pāṭala* trees. (9–1080)
With *lavaṅga*, *mādhavī*, *bilva*, *devadāru*, and *nameru* trees, and with well-flowered *kalpavṛkṣas* such as the *mandāra* and *pārijāta*; || 9-1081 ||
With sandalwood trees, karṇikāras, mātuluṅgas along with vañjulās, pomegranates, lakucas, aṅkolakas, betel nuts, and kuravakas as well.
It was adorned with plantains, kunda, mandāra, and coconut trees,
and embellished by other groves of fragrant flowers and such.
With *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *jāti*, *ketakī*, and *śatapatraka* flowers, as well as with as many *tulasī*, *nandyāvarta*, and *damanaka* plants as there may be.
It was adorned by trees bending under the weight of blossoms from every season,
stirred by gentle breezes, and filling the quarters of the sky with the fragrance of flowers.
In its center, it was always filled with blossoming flowers— blue water-lilies, lotuses,
fragrant *saugandhika* lilies, white water-lilies, and fresh blue lotuses.
It was graced by swans, cranes, ducks, bees, and ruddy geese, as well as by other birds whose cries formed a sweet, tumultuous symphony. (9.1087)
In the midst of that great lake, upon an exceedingly beautiful sandy bank,
was a jeweled pavement adorned all around by pārijāta trees and other celestial trees.
Resplendent like the rising sun, cool as the moon,
provided with four gates, and adorned with golden ramparts.
It was joined with eight door-panels of exquisite beauty fashioned from jewels,
and its lofty gate-towers and arches were adorned with the nine precious gems.
It had golden staffs hanging from its crest, was preceded by rows of banners,
and was resplendent with rows of pillars set with the nine precious gems.
It was resplendent with lamp-stands joined by a thousand lamps,
and enchanting with windows fashioned from refined gold.
It was adorned with hundreds of millions of golden ornaments bound with cloths of various jewels,
and with banners provided with rows of small bells.
Made of gold, variegated with jewels, and exceedingly vast,
they were adorned with garlands of strings of rubies, diamonds, lapis lazuli, and gold.
It was adorned with canopies fashioned from various colorful designs, featuring gems linked together at intervals that were pleasing to the sight.
It was joined with all kinds of jewels, possessed a brilliant golden floor,
and was adorned with ketaki, mālatī, jātī, campaka, utpala, and kesara flowers.
The surface of the earth was adorned with these beautiful flowers: jasmine, tulasī, vāsā, nandyāvartaka, and kadamba.
The quarters of the sky were made fragrant by lotuses, saffron, musk, tamālaka, sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. (9.1098)
Having thus reflected with his mind upon a most beautiful pavilion,
the mantra-practitioner should visualize a lovely *parijāta* tree in its center.
Below that, the mantra-practitioner should visualize a great jewel-throne;
upon it, he should contemplate the goddess Mahālakṣmī, who is captivating to the mind.
She possesses the radiance of the rising sun, is brilliant with a crest-jewel and a necklace shimmering like a crescent moon,
and is adorned with ornaments of precious gems; she bears the grace of budding mango trees in her breasts and clusters of blossoms in her hands,
while constantly holding two lotuses and the Kaustubha jewel, and is graced with a gentle smile.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Deity, who possesses three eyes like full-blown lotuses.
She is resplendent with lotus-feet beautified by tinkling anklets,
and adorned with a girdle-string studded with clusters of the nine precious gems.
Its waist-band was set with pearls, rubies, and lapis lazuli;
it shone brilliantly at the center, adorned with three folds.
Her navel was adorned by a whirlpool of the waters of the Ganges,
and her breasts were embellished with sandalwood paste, camphor, and saffron.
She wore an upper garment fashioned from fine silk, which was more magnificent than a string of pearls released from a rain cloud.
Her armlets and ornaments were made of vaidūrya set with refined gold;
her lotus-like hands were enriched with golden bracelets shimmering with rubies.
Adorned with rings set with fragments of rubies,
and graced by necklaces and armlets fashioned from refined gold.
Adorned with various and manifold ornaments, her neck was like a conch shell,
and she was graced by jeweled earrings that had the appearance of the rising sun.
Adorned with shining golden ear-ornaments marked with jewels,
her bud-like lower lip was charming with the loveliness of hibiscus flowers and coral.
Her rows of teeth were adorned like the seeds of a pomegranate fruit,
and her face resembled the autumn moon, free from both blemish and waning.
Adorned with three eyes shaped like the petals of a white lotus,
her creeper-like eyebrows surpassed the graceful play of the excellent bow of Kandarpa.
Her nose was uplifted in victory, possessing the beauty of a blooming sesame flower;
she surpassed the half-moon with the splendor of the radiance of her forehead.
Her forehead is marked with a tilaka of musk endowed with intense fragrance,
and her lotus-face is rich with petals that shimmer with swarms of intoxicated bees.
She whose braided hair bore the beauty of *pārijāta* blossoms,
and whose head was adorned with earrings set with priceless gems and pearls.
One should meditate upon that Mahālakṣmī, the abode of all loveliness, the dwelling place of the splendor of grace, and the birthplace of all radiant energies.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
Having meditated thus upon the Goddess, the practitioner, subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and with senses subdued,
should recite the mantra one million times and perform oblations with sesame seeds ten thousand times.
Then, one should offer ten thousand oblations each with *śrīphala* fruits and lotuses;
thereafter, one should satisfy [the deity] with pure, fragrant waters twenty thousand times.
In the *Merutantra*, it is said:
"One who is restrained in diet and firm in his vows should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for the Sun;
he should then perform a fire sacrifice with clarified butter mixed with the three sweets, consisting of one-tenth of that number. (9.1118)
One should offer ten thousand oblations with lotuses and the fruits of the *ramādruma* tree respectively;
one should satisfy [the deity] twenty thousand times with very cool, pure waters.
p. 839) Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"The wife of Śambhu is Śrī; the two *ka*s are the Goddess Mahī;
Brahmā, Āditya, Dharā, and Dīrghā; the letter *la* is the Lord Marut. (9-1120)
"Obeisance to the pair of gracious ones, Śrī, Uddhā, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Mahālakṣmī"—this mantra begins with the Praṇava (Om) and ends with "namaḥ. (9.1121)
Abounding in twenty-seven syllables, it is declared to bestow all prosperity.
The heart-mantra is said to be "kamale," and the head-mantra should be "kamalālaye."
One should perform the *śikhā* with that same [mantra], the *kavaca* with four syllables, and the *astra* with these words, each individually encased by the *śrībīja*.
Now, the meditation:
[One should meditate upon her] whose splendor is as crimson as vermilion, who dwells within a lotus, who is a treasure-trove of the waters of beauty,
and who is adorned with a crown, armlets, necklaces, earrings, a waist-string, and other ornaments.
