One should constantly meditate upon the beloved of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who holds a vessel of eight treasures, a pair of lotuses, and a mirror in her lotus-hands, and who is surrounded by female attendants.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with bilva fruits smeared with honey,
in a consecrated fire, according to the very path previously described, for a tenth part [of the recitation].
In that interval:
"The great mantra of three syllables has its bashfulness obstructed by Indirā;
it consists of five letters within the heart, and for him, everything becomes a single ocean of sound. (9.1126)
Now, the mantra of the Goddess of Imperial Sovereignty (*sāmrājyalakṣmī*) [from the *Merutantra*]:
I shall now describe [the practice] by which I obtained the kingdom of Kāśī through Gaṇeśa.
The Goddess Lakṣmī was worshipped by me in the western direction from Śāmbāditya. (9–1127)
The goddess Sāmrājyalakṣmī is renowned there as the bestower of lost kingdoms; and the famous Gajānana, Lakṣmīvināyaka, resides there. (9-1128)
Success comes through the right path alone, not from the left.
The syllables *sa*, *ha*, and *kalarā* constitute the five letters. (9-1129)
The first peak-syllable (kūṭa) is said to be conjoined with the vowel *ī*;
the second is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) *ha*. This is declared to be the two-syllabled mantra.
The seer is Hari, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is said to be Lakṣmī Mohinī, the bestower of sovereignty; the seed-syllable is proclaimed to be the *kūṭa*. (9-1131)
One should perform the six limbs with the six long vowels, [beginning] with Śakti and Śrī. Now, the visualization: [She who is] like the *ataśī* flower, adorned with jewel ornaments... (9-1132)
With her six hands, she holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and arrow; with two hands, the Goddess of the Gods is graced by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having thus meditated upon her as eight-armed, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
for the sake of attaining imperial sovereignty, he should perform oblations with lotuses numbering one-tenth of that amount.
In this way, one should propitiate Lakṣmī; sovereignty will undoubtedly be attained.
The mantra of Nārāyaṇa, however, has been stated in that very section.
Thus ends the section on the Lakṣmī-vidyā.
Now, regarding the Blue Sequence and others (*nīlakramādayaḥ*).
In the *Śaktisaṅgamavīratantrasārasaṃgraha*,
the Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that which is the most secret of secrets.
O Lord, O Master, those ten sequences of the ten sciences which were previously mentioned— please state those sequences now.
Śiva said:
Out of devotion, I shall tell you this most secret of secrets:
according to the Mahānīla-krama, Kālikā bestows spiritual perfection.
(841) O Goddess, the Mahānīla-krama is proclaimed to be twofold:
as *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts). Listen to that sequence, O Pārvatī. (9-1138)
With a sword in hand and his head adorned [with ornaments], he always has his hair disheveled; ever delighted by meat and wine, his eyes are rolling with *vijayā*.
A tilaka of vermilion on the forehead, wine in the hand, wandering about at night, and the worship of Śakti at night. || 9.1140 ||
How can that man who does not perform the act of kissing the vulva, nor likewise the embrace of the consort (*śakti*), be a worshiper of you? (9.1141)
The *tāmbūlayonicakra*, the garland of severed heads, the corpse-seat,
vermilion, the sword, and the essence of *saṃvit* and wine.
Whoever, having abandoned these [preliminary practices], endeavors to accomplish Kālī, will encounter agitation in this world and go to hell in the next.
O Goddess, Kālikā is not indeed accomplished even in tens of billions of aeons, [unless one possesses] a drop of vermilion between the eyebrows and the self-arisen leaf of the sage. (9.1144)
Or likewise, having applied a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with red sandalwood paste upon that, O Maheśvarī, a drop of collyrium should be placed on the petal.
O Goddess, in the Mahānīla-krama, the sectarian mark (tilaka) is thus proclaimed:
one who sleeps in the cremation ground, who eats meat, and whose mind is filled with the bliss of pure consciousness.
Whether seeing, touching, or walking with a woman, one should perform recitation at all times;
devoted to a courtesan, staying in a cremation ground, and wearing soft hair-tufts.
O Goddess, having fashioned a rosary from ivory with a tusk of an elephant as its central bead (meru),
one should always recite the mantra while chewing betel, O Goddess.

Adorned with a garland of skulls, intent on kissing his beloved, he finds bliss in the power [of the goddess] within the pair of eyes, wine in the mouth, and [the play of love] in the courtyard of the house. (9.1149)

Having kissed the vulva of a courtesan—who is like a garland in the palm of a young girl, whose play is power, and who is the lotus of the *bhaga*—one should perform the recitation (*japa*) at all times. (9.1150)
The power (śakti) is Bharga, who is to be saluted; all this, both moving and unmoving, belongs to Him.
The qualified practitioner, with a joyful soul, devoted to women, and having conquered his senses— || 9-1151 ||
O Goddess, such a man is considered to be of the Mahānīla lineage;
his garland consists of the teeth of kings and is made from elephants, camels, and horses.
For those who are incapable, there is the partless [form]; listen to that sequence, O Pārvatī:
having drunk the milk of the yellow one, with a mind absorbed in the bliss of Being-Consciousness.
Having fashioned a rosary of crystal, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) in a monastery;
there is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor is there any restriction regarding posture and so forth.
There is no restriction regarding time for the recitation of the great mantra in its practice;
whatever the conduct prescribed for a particular mantra, such is the dharma therein.
No error should be made therein regarding heaven or even liberation;
O Goddess, [the offering] may be soft and tender, whether it has a crest or is without a crest.

Having assumed the corpse posture (śavāsana), the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), or the vulva-skin posture (yonitvagāsana), O Goddess, as well as the posture of assuming any form at will (kāmarūpāsana) and the posture of sexual union (suratāsana).
The Sindhūrāsana, O Goddess, and the Parvatāsana as well;
the Prayogāsana, O Goddess, and likewise the Mahāprayogāsana. || 9-1158 ||
Or else, O Goddess, there is the Śrīmuṇḍasurata or the Śrīvīrasurata,
[performed] on the five seats (pañcavīrāsana) in the sequence of the directions beginning with Surendra (the East).
Thus ends the sequence of Nīla.
(p. 843) The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the supreme Mahācīnakrama."
Śiva said:
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is now being described by me.
Tārā bestows swift results precisely through the Mahācīna method.
There are three [traditions]: Brahmacīna, Vīracīna, and Divyacīna as the third.
Mahācīna and Niṣkala are considered the fivefold Cīna;
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is proclaimed to be twofold.
It is both with parts and without parts; that which has parts is the domain of the Buddhists, while the second, which is without parts, is proclaimed as belonging to the Brāhmaṇas.
Likewise: mental purification such as bathing and the like, mental recitation is the most excellent, mental worship is divine, and mental libations and so forth [are likewise supreme]. (9.1164)
The mental restraint is declared to be the mental cleansing of the teeth;
every time is auspicious, for no inauspicious moment exists anywhere.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the dead of night;
one should not perform purification here, but rather let the mind move in a state free from conceptual construction.
In this [mantra], there is no requirement for ritual purity, nor is there any defect such as impurity;
whoever contemplates the mantra in this way shall obtain the fulfillment of all desires. (9.1167)
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, arises in the assembly;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants are considered shorn of their luster. (9-1168)
Even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people?
One should always worship the Goddess, even if one has not bathed or has already eaten.
At midnight, in a pure place, one should cause an offering to be presented with the mantra.
One must not harbor hatred toward women; indeed, the worship of women is especially important. (9-1170)
Having placed a large conch shell at the place of recitation, one should perform the recitation while holding it above.
Even while approaching a woman, touching her, or looking at her, wherever one may be, as long as one has not yet performed the *acūḍaka* rite.
Having eaten betel and other edible substances according to their desire,
[they partook of] meat, fish, curd, honey, and the essence of fermented liquors and spirits.
Having given all kinds of food and eatables and having eaten, one should perform the recitation;
there is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor any restriction regarding standing and so forth.

In the practice of this great mantra, there is no restriction regarding time for recitation, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings; here, it is said that one may follow one's own will.
O Goddess of the Gods, having purified clothing, seats, houses, the body, and objects both touched and untouched with water, and having washed the oil, one should always consume betel.
Wearing various garments, one should wipe the body with a cloth;
thus, O Goddess, one should always perform the bath with one’s mind intent upon that.
O Goddess, one should always cause the hair to grow while it is nourished with oil; O fair-browed one, no unrighteousness exists therein, rather, great merit shall accrue.
In this state, acting according to one's own will is prescribed; one should move about with a joyful mind, considering oneself to have accomplished the goal and having satisfied one's own heart.
One should not utter the name of Hari, nor touch a leaf of tulasī;
one should avoid the bilva leaf and diligently avoid the desert (maru).
One should not engage in thinking of anything else, nor ever criticize anything else;
one should not mutter any other mantra, O Goddess, but should always remain free from conceptual construction.

O Goddess, one who enjoys dalliance with Mātaṅgīs should drink liquor immediately; kissing, licking, and gazing upon her vulva, he should perform his recitation (japa) with undistracted mind. (9.1181)
Having reflected upon the vehicle [of practice], one should recite [the mantra]; success will be attained in just a year.
Otherwise, there will be no success at all, even with ten million recitations. (9-1182)

O Goddess, after performing a hundred thousand *puraścaraṇa* repetitions and ten million *homa* offerings and other rites, one should then apply vermilion (*sindūra*) between the eyebrows and upon the hair.
One should wear false sandalwood paste as a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and a lotus with its filaments;
a garland of severed heads should be worn around the neck, and a skull held in the hand.
Thus, one who is constantly devoted to right conduct becomes a follower of the Mahācīna-krama;
that which is situated between the ear and the eye is proclaimed as the Great Conch (Mahāśaṅkha).
O Maheśānī, one should make a garland from fifty gems or from the bones of cows and elephants; by making such a garland, one becomes a master of the eight siddhis.
She alone is Tārā, O Maheśānī; no deliberation should be made here.
Whatever conduct exists in a particular mantra, such is the dharma therein.
By that, one becomes fulfilled, whether it be heaven or even liberation.
(In the Svacchandabhairavatantra:
Rituals such as purification and so forth, enjoined by the Smṛti scriptures, are not to be performed. 9-1188.
Those [mudrās] which have been proclaimed, such as "one on the linga, five on the anus," and so forth—
these should not be performed by the best of practitioners if they desire long life.
(Also in the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*):
"There is no restriction of place or time, nor indeed any restriction regarding food and the like;
there is no requirement for ritual purity and so forth in the accomplishment of the Great Mantra. (9-1190)
Whether by day or likewise at night, at the end of the night or at the onset of night,
having eaten meat, drunk liquor, and gone to a woman, one should perform the recitation.
(From the *Śaktisaṅgama*):
O Pārvatī, I have described the *sakala* [form]; now hear about the *niṣkala*.
O Śivā, the hand is below the wrist, and the feet are below the ankles. (9.1192)
O Goddess, one should wash the face; this is known as the *cīna-snāna*.
Having gone to the ground on one's knees, one should bring the head down to the earth. (9–1193)
O Goddess of the Gods, I have proclaimed to you the homage of the Cīna path; O Mistress of the Gods, the sequence of the former transmission has been presented by me as its representative.
O beloved, having performed bathing, giving of gifts, and likewise worship and other rites,
my body is no longer withered, nor indeed do I possess any sin.
What is bathing for anyone? One who has not bathed may eat his meal;
for everything is established within me, in the lotus of the heart.
The perfection of mantra has been born within me; the gods are the granters of boons to me.
The entire universe is of the nature of radiant energy, and Tāriṇī assumes that very form.
Having rendered his body healthy through that splendor, he should perform the recitation (japa);
having come under the power of such contemplation, the yogi becomes a great poet.
For a Brāhmaṇa, however, the liquor should be made from molasses and fresh ginger;
in its absence, O Goddess, one should perform the worship after consecrating water.
With his heart ever close to that state and his mind always absorbed in it,
having abandoned the sense of duality, he shall become a master of all accomplishments.
Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise other lords of sages,
constantly worship Śivā by means of the path of the partless sequence (niṣkalakrama).
O Great Goddess, those Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to Tārā are highly praised;
the Brahmavidyā, the Great Vidyā, is difficult to obtain everywhere in the Kali age.
"This is the supreme secret, most secret of all, and must be guarded in the presence of the uninitiated (paśu).
Thus ends the Mahācīnakrama.
Now, the Divyacīnakrama is found in that same place.
The Goddess said:
O Goddess, tell me quickly the procedure for the rite of Chinnamastā.
Śiva said:
"Chinnamastā, the bestower of boons, [is worshipped] precisely by the divine Cīna-krama.
O Maheśānī, both systems have already been revealed."
O Goddess, there should be a tilaka mark made of kuñcandana between the eyebrows;
at its end, one should apply a tripuṇḍra with divine-colored marks using leaves of gorocanā.
O Dear One, O Śivā, one should cause a drop of cremation-ground ash to be placed in the center of that;
having joined mouth to mouth, one should recite [the mantra] at all times.
Whatever a man performs after beholding the *yonicakra*,
he obtains that very thing as inexhaustible, by virtue of the severance of ignorance.
There is no restriction of space or time, nor indeed any restriction of duration and so forth;
[he dwells] in the netherworld, in caves, in difficult terrains, on mountains, and on the banks of rivers.
One should perform the recitation everywhere—in the intermediate space as well as on the earth;
this specific rule, O Goddess, is declared for the protector of the Śakti-tattva.
Thus ends the sequence of the Divine Cīna. Now follows the sequence of the Gandharvas.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O God, tell me the sequence known as the Gandharva.
Śiva said:
"By means of this very sequence called the Gandharva, Sundarī bestows accomplishment (siddhi)."
O Goddess, the sequence known as the Gandharva is now being told; listen.
O Goddess, there is saffron between the eyebrows, and in the middle of that is sandalwood and agallochum.
A man adorned with the three lines of eight fragrant substances, the middle of which is infused with musk, and decorated with fragrant white and red flowers, [attains the highest state]. (9-1212)
Adorned with the fragrance of various perfumes by means of incense made from the eight scents,
wearing red garlands and garments, and graced with a necklace of pearls.
Since the head has been consecrated with the full ablution (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), there is no shaving there;
one should always bathe with warm water, or in its absence, with whatever water is available.
The house was beautifully adorned with various paintings, resembling the surface of a mirror;
it was enriched with the ornaments of canopies and banners, and graced by the resonant sound of bells.
Accompanied by the five kinds of musical instruments and endowed with various sounds,
it was adorned within with fine silken garments and embellished with golden vessels and the like.
He was always adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and finger-rings,
and [served] with various kinds of sweet foods and many varieties of milk drinks.
"Endowed with various enjoyments, this sequence called the Gandharva comes into being.
Thus ends the Gandharva sequence. Now follows the Bhairava sequence.
Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; now hear the Krama known as Bhairava.
Through the yoga of the sequence of her own flower (svapuṣpa), Bhairavī is difficult to find on earth.
O Goddess, the sequence called her own flower is now being told; listen.
A young woman, beautiful and charming, whose very form is the nectar of youth,
always longing for sexual union and with her mind intent upon intercourse.
O Maheśvarī, having brought her who is joined with mantras and yantras,
and having first made her naked, one should oneself perform the recitation while naked.
And mutual gazing must be performed between one another;
O Goddess, when [the practitioner] is unchanging, he is fit for the sādhana, and not otherwise. (9-1222)
And when a transformation occurs, the practitioner perishes in an instant;
O Goddess of the God of Gods, if she too should become subject to transformation.
O Goddess, by means of the Puṣpiṇī mantra, one should forcibly bring forth flowers;
O Goddess, by means of the Drāviṇī mantra, one should forcibly cause [the object] to melt through one's gaze.
O Goddess, due to the fault of the palate, this yoga will not be possible;
therefore, O Śivā, the Bālā [mantra] is now recommended according to the ritual procedure for the bound soul (pāśava).
In the case of a young woman, both practices are indeed valid, though the right-hand path is primary.
Likewise, if one desires swift accomplishment, one should practice the gavākṣa yoga. (9-1226)
Where there is a gathering of women at a river, stream,
or lake, one should have a window constructed there so that they may perform their ablutions.
Having beheld that [mark], one should perform the recitation (*japa*) continuously with great effort.
Thus has it been briefly declared; now hear, O Pārvatī, concerning the *tilaka*.
O Śivā, having carefully inscribed the yantra on the palm of the left hand,
O Supreme Goddess, one should apply a tilaka with unrefined [substance].
On the forehead, one should apply a drop of musk, a leaf of the *muni* plant, and a small *candana* paste;
in the center of that, a white dot should be placed, and the hair and other features should be fashioned as before.
O Goddess, in the ritual of the ten sciences, the increasing of the hair is proclaimed.
Thus ends the Bhairavakrama. Now begins the Kamalākrama.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching on the sequence of the lotus.
Śiva said:
O Goddess, [one should apply] saffron between the eyebrows, and after that, vermilion.
O Queen of the Gods, O Śivā, one should then apply a white *tripuṇḍra* with *keśara* powder in its center. (9.1232)

Having bathed and wearing white garments, a man who is fond of sweet food should perform his ablutions at the three junctions of the day, subsisting on sacrificial offerings (haviṣya) and sleeping upon the ground.
O Goddess, one should worship daily until the second Saturday with the sounds of various musical instruments.
One should perform it every day until the sixteenth day;
then again, O Maheśvarī, starting from that day until the end of that same day.
One should worship constantly with self-restraint, intent upon the state of the deity;
and circumambulation should be performed according to the sequence of the parts and states.
Lamps should be offered there according to the sequence of increasing digits (kalā),
and one should daily feed Brahmins according to the sequence of the presence of those digits.
Thus, devoted to right conduct, that illustrious man becomes the very form of Viṣṇu;
with self-restraint, he should always worship all the royal insignia.
He shall undoubtedly become the lord of all imperial sovereignty;
the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) shall reside in his home, and even the King shall become his servant.
Thus ends the sequence of Kamalā.
Now follows the sequence of the Brahma-path. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, I wish to hear the sequence of the path of Brahman.
Śiva said:
"One should apply collyrium to a prostitute and the *tripuṇḍra* with vermilion."
Turmeric should be applied to the pair of eyebrows, and one should fashion a white petal.
And one should always remain focused upon that drop of blood in its center;
whether eating, sleeping at night, or engaging in sexual union, one should always be so.
O Goddess of gods, one with soiled hands should offer the oblation (bali) with what remains [of the meal].
The food of the Śakti and the food of others is to be eaten at all times. (9-1242)
O Maheśānī, one should perform the recitation; indeed, one should practice the recitation at night.
Having consumed betel and having eaten meat, and after eating, one should perform the worship.
One should recite with hands still soiled by food remnants; this is proclaimed as the Brahma-path.
Thus ends the sequence of the Brahma-path. Now follows the sequence of the Great King (Mahārāja).
The Goddess said:
O Lord, O God, tell me the procedure for the Great King (Mahārāja).
Śiva said:
O Goddess, the procedure for the Great King (Mahārāja) is now being told; listen.
It takes place in a variegated pavilion adorned with various wonderful staircases.
Adorned with palaces and watchtowers, beautified by canopies and banners,
endowed with various groves, and graced by swans and peacocks.
With various and diverse sounds, resplendent with elephants and horses,
endowed with auspiciousness on all sides, and adorned with various ornaments.
In a place filled with the fragrance of incense, adorned with various lamps,
upon a beautiful jeweled lion-throne decorated with precious ornaments.
It was beautified by the fragrance of *jātī*, campaka, *puṇnāga*, and *ketakī* flowers,
and was endowed with camphor, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, and saffron.
Adorned with fragrant ointments such as *jaṭāmāṃsī* and other perfumes,
accompanied by the sounds of bells and other instruments, he is at all times pure in mind.
His heart immersed in bliss, adorned with divine garments,
wearing celestial garlands and robes, and embellished with divine ornaments.
With his mouth filled with betel, he shone like the Lord of the Gods;
he resounded with the vessels of the Vedas, the vessels of dance, and the vessels of enjoyment. (9.1252)
It resounded with dances, songs, and instrumental music performed by twenty-four musicians,
filled with the sounds of musical compositions, melodies, and rhythmic beats.
Adorned with prose and verse in the languages of various regions,
the supreme practitioner is embellished with diverse and wonderful ornaments.
Deluding the royal consorts with all the modes of royal conduct,
she is the illustrious Mahārājamātaṅgī, who utterly fascinates all the gods.
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen as the tilaka for that [deity] is described:
there should be kucaṃdana between the eyebrows, and the essence of guggulu within it.

O Śivā, O Goddess, the method of the Great King (Mahārāja) has been described by me to you: a mark of musk (kastūrikā) with a triple line (tripuṇḍra), and in its center, a tuft of hair (keśara). 9-1257.
Alternatively, O Goddess of the gods, one should personally become intent on singing.
This is the sequence of the Mahārāja. Now follows the sequence of the divine state (divyabhāva).
The Goddess said:
"Tell me the ritual procedure of Śrī Bhuvaneśānī, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain."
Śiva said:
By the very sequence of divine states, Bhuvaneśī bestows swift accomplishment.
The syllable *ha* is the form of Śiva; the syllable *ra* is the destroyer of sins.
The letter *ī* is Kāmarūpa; therefore, it is proclaimed as Māyā.
O Goddess, this entire universe is enveloped by Māyā.
O Goddess, without whose illusion nothing whatsoever appears;
and that which is devoid of her light never appears anywhere at all. (9.1261)
O Goddess, this world shines forth accompanied by that light;
for without it, O Maheśānī, the world would be like something insentient. (9-1262)
O Goddess of the gods, by practicing in this manner with a mind always fixed upon that, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
O Goddess, listen attentively as the tilaka of this [mantra] is now described:
one should apply a drop of white sandalwood paste between the eyebrows. (9.1264)
At the end of that, there should be a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with divine colored powders;
and in its center, red unbroken rice grains (raktākṣata). By means of this, one becomes a lord of supernatural powers (siddhīśvara).
Thus concludes the sequence of the divine state.
Now follows the sequence of smoke.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, I wish to hear the *krama* of Dhūmāvatī.
Śiva said:
"O Goddess, O Pārvatī, listen as the *krama* of Dhūmāvatī is being told."
O Goddess, there should be collyrium between the eyebrows, and within that, a drop of ash;
there should be a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, and within that, the ash of a corpse.
Wearing black garments and adorned with black perfumes,
he is joined with fragrant flowers and seated upon the cremation ground.
The entire world is smoke-colored; the practitioner of mantra should become composed of smoke.
A crow’s wing shall be his seat, and he should hold black substances.
A celibate student, moderate in diet, free from conceptual construction, with senses conquered, truthful in speech, firm in conduct, sleeping on the ground upon a mat of *kuśa* grass. || 9-1270 ||
One intent on the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) should perform ablutions three times a day;
having made one's own mind like a crow, one will certainly eradicate the world.
p. 854) "One should be devoted to such conduct and enter the sequence of smoke (dhūmrakrama).
Thus ends the sequence of smoke.
Now, the sequence of good fortune (saubhāgyakrama) is in that same [text]:
Vagalā bestows swift accomplishment precisely through the sequence of worship for good fortune.
The minister, wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow ornaments,
clad in yellow garlands and robes, was seated in a yellow house.
He partakes of yellow substances and is endowed with a yellow seat;
he performs oblations with yellow offerings, uses yellow flowers, and is possessed of yellow devotion.

One should apply yellow pigment (rocanā) on the eyebrows, saffron and *munipatraka* [on the forehead], and a triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with turmeric; in its center, O Śivā, one should place a piece of *khadira* wood.
O Supreme Goddess, she was perfumed with the incense of yellow sandalwood;
she was beautiful in every limb, lovely, and adorned with all her members.
One should not solicit a Brahmin girl who has not yet reached puberty, nor one who is already menstruating;
likewise, one should avoid a maiden on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the full moon day.
Alternatively, on a Tuesday or on a Friday at night,
one should likewise perform an oil massage with well-perfumed oil.
Having brought a bed with a cotton mattress and spread it out facing north,
he then spreads [offerings] upon it with *jāti* and *campaka* flowers accompanied by mantras.
The wise man should apply a paste of camphor mixed with musk and sandalwood over all his limbs while reciting the Lakṣmīsūkta.
Upon the couch, having anointed that maiden with sandalwood paste,
he [should place] the maiden facing southward with the mantra beginning with "dhruva" and so forth.
One should cause the young girl to lie upon the bed facing upward while reciting the Śrīsūkta;
then, having extended her feet, one should perform the secret worship. (9.1282)
Having placed the two groups of six, one should place the five-fold Vagalā;
one should also place the Goddess Kanyā and recollect their respective limbs.
One should purify the city of Ananyajapura with the root mantra;
one should apply musk ointment with the mantra beginning "gandhadvārā."
One should offer a garland of consciousness with the root mantra;
then one should present the purification of the ritual substances and perform the recitation.
This practice bestows accomplishment upon men and is the supreme means for achieving mantra-perfection;
O Goddess, without this sequence, the practice will never succeed anywhere.
Therefore, O Goddess, one who desires accomplishment on this earth should strive with every effort to abandon the eightfold pride and indeed the three defects.
Having abandoned attachment to the five senses, one should practice the Saubhāgyakrama.
Thus ends the Saubhāgyakrama. Now, the divine, heroic, and animal states (divya-vīra-paśubhāva).
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, the Goddess said:
"O Lord, the state of being (*bhāva*) is threefold, according to the sequence of the Divine, the Heroic, and the Fettered. (9-1288)
In this regard, there are three kinds of gurus, and likewise of mantra-deities;
O Mahādeva, the Śakti-mantra is especially the bestower of mantra-perfection.
O Mahādeva, the first state is the most excellent, bestowing all prosperity;
the second is middling, and the third is censured by all.
The phrase "condemned by all" refers to those other than Brāhmaṇas; for regarding a Brāhmaṇa, no such censure is heard when he resorts to the state of a beast or any other [lower] state. Likewise:
"By a hundred thousand recitations, by burnt offerings, and by extensive physical austerities..."
O Lord, without the *bhāva*, the tantras and mantras do not bestow their fruit. (9-1291)
What is the use of the *vīrasādhana* alone for those whose lineages are agitated by all manner of worldly views?
What is the use of the worship of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*) alone, or of the feeding of virgins and so forth? (9.1292)
What is the use of giving pleasure to one's own wife, and likewise to others?
What is the use of self-control over the senses, or of performing the duties of family tradition?
If one who is devoted to the family were not pure in being,
one attains liberation through being, and through being, the increase of the family.
Through devotion there shall be the increase of the lineage; through devotion the lineage becomes illustrious.
What is the use of elaborate ritual deposits? What is the use of extensive purifications of this or that?
If the state of being does not arise through such worship alone, by what is the Vidyā worshipped? And if it is not worshipped by anyone, by whom is it recited? || 9-1296 ||
And the absence of fruit, O Lord of Gods, arises from the non-existence of [divine] being;
likewise, the first is said to be divine being—listen with respect. (9-1297)

Having visualized the entire world as consisting of light— filled everywhere with masses of light belonging to whichever deity corresponds to the particular color— one should perform the mental construction of the form.

Furthermore, within the mantra consisting of that particular form, having perceived oneself as identical with it and likewise all existence as being of that same nature, [one should meditate]. (9.1299)
Having meditated upon all that within a woman, one should contemplate with a restrained mind:
"She is endowed with an entire lineage, born from various castes. (9.1300)
Or even those born in various countries, endowed with virtue and beauty, from after the second year until the eighth year [of age]. (9.1301)
To that extent, the maiden should be understood as the bestower of the fruits of mantras and yantras;
indeed, through the worship of the maiden and also through feeding the maiden, [the results are attained]. (9.1302)
Seeds numbering one, two, three, and so forth, undoubtedly bestow their fruit here;
from them [come] flowers, fruits, or likewise unguents and the like. (9-1303)
Having offered an oblation dear to Bali and being filled with that state of being,
he should offer himself upon his body, acting in the manner of one who has become an offering to Bali.
By engaging with them in conversation, play, curiosity, and so forth—performing such acts as they desire—one will become a master of supernatural powers (siddhīśvara). 9-1305.
Therefore, up until the sixteenth year, she is declared to be a "young woman" (yuvati).
In that regard, if there is the manifestation of passion (bhāva), it is considered the supreme state of being (sadbhāva). || 9-1306 ||
They must be protected with great effort; one should not cause them to be violated.
Thus, O God, has this divine state that brings happiness been described to you.
"It must not be given to just anyone; it should be guarded with great effort from animals.
This is the divine state (*divyabhāva*). Now, the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*) is described in that same [text]:
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, the state of the Hero is being described; listen, O Bhairava. (9.1308)
Having become one whose mind is free from dualities, with the body as the form of the digit of desire (kāmakalā) within the heart,
worship during the nights is indeed the most excellent and likewise endowed with its proper cause.
Having established one's own lineage, one should personally assume the form of Bhairava;
the lineage is the form of Bhairavī, and its detailed placement (nyāsa) is upon that body.
One should likewise perform the placement (nyāsa) consisting solely of the nine-yoni form;
"consisting of the nine-yoni form" refers here to the Śrīvidyā.
[This should be done] in the midst of a bed of flowers, provided with a profusion of blossoms.
Having drawn the yantra with family substances (kuladravya) amidst a variety of perfumes,
one who is capable should worship it after first performing the ritual installation of the water jar (ghaṭasthāpana).
p. 858) Having drawn a hexagon on one's own left side with the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) in its center, one should place there a water-pot made of gold or likewise of silver. (9-1313)
One should place a vessel for the support of the pitcher, made either of copper or of earth, provided it is free from base metals and has been perfumed with fragrant scents.
One should fill the causal substance (*hetudravya*) according to the distinctions of the *brāhmaṇa* and so forth.

The phrase "according to the distinctions of the *brāhmaṇa* and so forth" means that it should be filled by the *brāhmaṇas* and others with substances consisting of milk, clarified butter, honey, and wine. And thus, for a heroic *brāhmaṇa*, milk alone is to be used in the place of the causal substance; however, it should be understood that even that is not for the animal (*paśu*).
Having first drawn the diagram (*yantra*) there, whatever originates from the family [should be placed]. (9–1315)
Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, having displayed the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās, that [mantra] is said to be fully accomplished.
Having seen the nectar in their own vessels, the hosts of yoginīs indeed dance;
all the Bhairavas dance, and the Mothers also dance.
All the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy. (9–1318)
Having divided the vessel for the *argha* offering into three parts, one part should be given to the Guru;
likewise, having given [another] to the Kula, the propitiation of the deity is performed with the remaining one.
Having drunk the essence of the clan (kularasa), adorned with various garments and ornaments,
if the Guru is not personally present, then one should discharge it into water.
Having become one whose nature is bliss, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
one should worship her according to the specific ritual procedure for each [deity] and with the corresponding effort.
Having performed the ritual dismissal at the end, one should then unite with one's own family;
by drinking the essence of that *vimba*, I consume the nectar of immortality.
From tasting the juice of that *cakra* fruit, a state of intoxication arises within me;
by the mere grasping of its fruit, one descends from the peak of Mount Meru.
By the mere embrace of the creeper, his body becomes washed with nectar;
when the root-yoga has been performed there, he should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times. (9.1324)
In the case of constant recitation and in the fire-oblation (homa), where no specific number is prescribed, this calculation is declared:
one thousand and eight [repetitions].
Then, having taken the sacrificial substance purified with water, one should perform the libation;
O Lord, having performed the libation, one should follow [the deity] in circumambulation.
Having praised and prostrated, one should then offer praise with the hymn prescribed in the Kalpa.
Thus, O God, is the Vīrakula, which is beautiful and worthy of worship by the gods.
In the Kali age, one must wander at night and worship the Śakti at night;
O Īśāna, how could one who is my devotee become a Kaulika without doing so? (9.1328)
(From the Merutantra:
O Goddess, one should conceal the *kula* like the juice within a coconut;
the wise man should reveal the guru, but he should guard the mantra with great effort. (9.1329)
(In the Kulārṇava):
"The Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas are as clear as courtesans;
but this Śāmbhavī Vidyā is hidden like a virtuous wife. (9.1330)
The deities favor those who keep the Kaulika conduct well-guarded;
they bestow the fulfillment of one's desires, but destroy it through disclosure.
One should not serve a woman during the day, nor should one gaze at her private parts.
Even if a woman has committed a hundred offenses, one should not strike her even with a flower.
One should not enumerate the faults of women, but rather manifest only their virtues. Likewise:
"Maidens, young girls, naked women, and even those who are intoxicated... (9.1333).
One should not revile, loathe, laugh at, or insult a solitary tree, a cremation ground, or even a gathering of women. (9.1334)
And seeing a woman dressed in red garments, one should salute her with devotion. Likewise:
"The *Kulayoginīs* always reside within the *Kula*-trees. (9.1335)
One should not eat from its leaves, especially from the leaves of the Arka plant;
one should not sleep beneath a family tree, nor should one cause any harm.
Having seen [these trees], one should pay homage with devotion, but one should never cut them down:
the *śleṣmātaka*, *karañja*, *arka*, *nimba*, *aśvattha*, and *kadambaka*.
The bilva, the vaṭa, the udumbara, and the ciñcā—these are recorded as the ten [trees].
[One should avoid] the expiation of Bhṛgu, falling from a cliff, renunciation, and the observance of vows.
A follower of the Kaula tradition should avoid five things, including visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrthayātrābhigamana*).
Expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and the like differ from those prescribed in the Tantras. (In the *Raudra* [Tantra]).
O Maheśānī, one should never disclose the state of a hero in any way whatsoever.
(Vīracūḍāmaṇi) O Maheśānī, if anyone should enter here at the time of worship,
one should show them the Vaiṣṇavī mudrā, as well as the Viṣṇu-nyāsa and the hymn. 9-1340.
Śākta within, Śaiva without, and considered Vaiṣṇava in the assembly;
the heroes, assuming various forms, wander upon the surface of the earth.
(Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
O Bhairava, in whatever region or even in whatever family a Vīra resides, there shall be no fear of pestilence, nor any fear of kings and the like. (9.1342)
There, O Mahādeva, there is always auspiciousness that increases wealth and sons; there, prosperity remains firmly established for certain. (9.1343)
The mantra of the Svapnaprabodhinī must necessarily be applied with effort at the foot of a tree, and no obstacle shall arise. (9-1344)
That [attainment] is not fit for any other hero, even by means of seizing the deities;
it is not lost to the Yoginīs, nor is one stained by sin thereby.
If one goes to a cremation ground on any day whatsoever,
provided it is a Tuesday, the fruit of the worship there shall be equal to that of seven days.
If one goes there on the fourteenth day, one obtains the fruit of a fortnight’s worship;
otherwise, by not going to that place, one becomes a mere beast—of this there is no doubt.
Thinking, "O God, there is none superior to me," he becomes devoted to such thoughts;
through intoxication, he becomes a consumer of wealth and one who is intent on his own lineage.
"When the practitioner falls into agitation, my own agitation arises.
Therefore, the excellent hero, endowed with enjoyments, should strive to remain happy. (9.1349)
Through enjoyment one attains liberation; through enjoyment one achieves the goal of the lineage.
O Maheśvara, without tasting it without cause, one remains possessed by agitation.
Neither worship nor contact with me, nor meditation or reflection, [is required];
therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
In this state, there is no fault of falling away, nor is there any other defect to be adorned;
whatever he speaks, whatever he sleeps, whatever he does, and whatever he worships—[all is pure]. (9.1352)
Having meditated upon all that as the form of the *kula*, one should dwell happily—alone in a secluded place, such as a cremation ground, a mountain, or a forest. (9.1353)
One should dwell joyfully and without attachment in an empty house or on a riverbank;
for heroes, every time is praised as the proper time for recitation.
This should be performed in every land and at every sacred seat (pīṭha), without a doubt;
even if a Brahmin should be fallen, provided he is devoted to the duties of his lineage. (9-1355)
Then, according to that procedure, the pleasing of the Kula must be performed;
for within the interior of another's flower lies the enchanting seat of the Kula.
There, the face of all the gods is of the nature of the great art of desire;
in the Hayāri flower, the Lord Sadāśiva himself is ever present.
Taking a small amount from that [substance] and placing sandalwood or a red flower in the center of the flower, one should meditate upon oneself as being of the nature of Śiva.
One should unite [the two] through the intellect, contemplating the oneness of Śiva and Śakti;
having meditated for a moment right there, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Having recited [the mantra] over that very substance called *kuṇḍa*, which is most difficult to obtain—
wherein the *aparājitā* flower and the *japā* flower are found, O Bhairava— 9.1360.
The red and white *karavīra* and the *droṇapuṣpa* flower remain there;
the Goddess dwells eternally in that place, and one should worship me in that yantra.
By offering even a single hibiscus flower (*japāpuṣpa*), one obtains the fruit of silk garments;
the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils is certainly destroyed in an instant.
But, O Maheśvara, it is indeed impossible to describe the majesty of Aparā;
furthermore, the rite of *vīrasādhana* must be performed by heroic men.
It should be performed even by the gods, but not by beasts or commoners;
it is certain that the work of a commoner is better than that of a beast.
If the convention regarding the accomplishment of mantras was not previously explained by me, the hero of great power should perform [the rites for] collyrium, pills, and so forth. (9.1365)
There is no difference between the divine and the heroic; that which is described as a difference is as follows:
[the divine hero] is peaceful, humble, sweet, and endowed with artistic grace and beauty.
The divine one is like a god, while the hero is generally high-minded;
(in the *Kularatnāvalī*):
"O Mistress of the Gods, the divine and the heroic are both devoted to the service of Śakti. (9.1367)
Each of these is traditionally held to be twofold, according to the divisions of Vāmika and Kaulika.
(In the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi:
He may be adorned with ashes as ornaments or smeared with sandalwood paste. 9-1368.
Whether he conceals his outward form or has abandoned it, O Kulabhairava;
whether he is smeared with red sandalwood paste, a Vaiṣṇava or even a non-Vaiṣṇava.
Whether he is intent on reviling the deity or intent on worshipping it, he should always remain joyful and well-nourished in the face of both insult and honor. (9.1370)
Free from those [distinctions], established in the Kula and Akula doctrine, and endowed with his own innate state, he should wander upon the earth like a god. (9.1371)
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) must be performed at night within one's own lineage and not otherwise;
O God, just as there can be no discourse on the Vedas for a twice-born man who is devoid of Vedic knowledge.
Just as devotion to the Goddess cannot flourish without devotion to Viṣṇu, so too, without the knowledge of Śākta [reality], one's liberation would become an object of ridicule. (9.1373)
Just as one has no entitlement whatsoever to the tantra without a guru,
so too is a woman deprived of all ritual actions when she is without a husband.

"O follower of the Kaula path, one who lacks the [proper] lineage has no authority whatsoever in my practice regarding the rites of the gods; therefore, one should be devoted to the inner disposition."
How can one whose family is undisciplined be a worshiper of me?
Therefore, one must act with such effort that [the family] becomes endowed with discipline.
In the Kula scripture, there is no qualification whatsoever regarding existence or non-existence;
therefore, a practitioner who is pure in his state of being becomes a true follower of the Kaula path.
Thus ends the sequence of the Heroic State (vīrabhāva).
The Goddess said:
"I shall explain the State of the Fettered (paśubhāva); listen with focused attention, my child."
Having received the knowledge of the sacrificial animal according to the prescribed rule, he should be devoted to its true nature.
First, for the sake of preliminary service, one should diligently practice purification;
one should eat facing north and not recall a woman even in one's mind.
One should not be covetous of another's property, nor should one set one's mind upon enjoyments;
whether on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, and in a beautiful, sacred field,
one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual], and one should diligently abandon all crookedness.
The deity of auspicious complexion should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed;
one should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day and practice the recitation of mantras at the three junctions of the day.
At night, one should never touch the mantra or the rosary;
nor should one recite the mantra after eating; one should remain observant of silence during all ritual acts.
On the occasion of a festival day, the best of practitioners should never approach a woman;
he should worship by personally bringing flowers, incense, and water.
One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it;
furthermore, one should not approach a woman with passion except during her fertile period.
O Supreme Lord, one who has faith in listening to the Purāṇas and is devoted to the meaning of the Vedas and Vedānta should not eat at night, O Wise One, nor should he consume betel leaf.
Whatever has been commanded by the Guru, all that one should perform with diligence;
likewise, O Bhairava, one's own birth-flower and the causal substance [should be offered].
Having touched [such a person] or likewise smelled them, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One who is devoted to the Goddess should not accept red garments.
O auspicious one, in the Viṣṇu-tantras, one should perform only that [prescribed] practice;
O you who are worshipped by heroes, one should not engage in talk concerning the deeds of heroes. (9-1389)

One devoted to dharma should perform the daily śrāddha, the śrāddha at Gayā, the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana), bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), and visiting the sites of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
In the *Merutantra*:
"At a temple of the deity, at the abode of the guru, in a cremation ground, and at a crossroads, one should avoid sandals, seats, excrement, urine, and sexual intercourse. (9.1391)

One should not revile a woman of the lowest caste who is intoxicated, a maiden in her menses, one whose breasts have fallen away, one who is deformed, one with disheveled hair, or one afflicted by passion.
One should not look at a maiden’s private parts, nor engage in animal-like play with her while she is naked or has exposed breasts; one should avoid the property of others and the wives of others.
One should never stretch out one's feet toward grain, cows, teachers, deities, fire, kusha grass, or books, nor should one step over them.
One should avoid laziness, intoxication, delusion, curses, malice, strife, envy, self-adulation, and the censuring of others. (9.1395)
(From the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*):
"Bhāva, however, is a mental state; how indeed could it be verbal?
Therefore, bhāva should not be spoken of [in this context]; only a mere indication has been provided. (9-1396)
Just as the sweetness of sugarcane or molasses is known through eating it, O Lord,
so too is the aesthetic emotion (bhāva) and its determinants (vibhāva) experienced by the mind.

In another tantra it is said: "The divine state (*divyabhāva*) is supreme; the heroic state (*vīrabhāva*) is middling; the animal state (*paśubhāva*) is declared to be inferior. One should rely upon a single state. (9-1398)
Thus ends the sequence of the animal-nature (*paśubhāva*).
(In the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*) I shall now describe the traditions of Gauḍa, Kāśmīra, and Kerala.
Following the offering of flowers as worship for the resolve to accomplish all goals.
The fire-oblation (havana) is prescribed at the end of the food offering (naivedya), and the ritual offering (bali) at the end of the betel-nut offering (tāmbūla).
Worship is performed with the left hand, while the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with the right hand.
Direct giving when there is no [external] cause, and the dismissal of the Goddess within the heart—
this is the Gauḍa-Akṣa tradition, always practiced by those who follow the Left-hand path (Vāmīs).
Following the worship of the pedestal, the bali offering is for the purpose of ritual application (viniyoga);
after the five-fold service (pañcopacāra), there is the fire sacrifice (homa), followed by the worship of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the libation (tarpaṇa).
Cow's products kept in a copper vessel are like liquor (vāruṇī), except for ghee;
likewise, the pentad of salt, fresh ginger, oil-cake, onion, and black gram [is so regarded].
O Great Goddess, garlic is remembered as a substitute for meat;
in the absence of fish, betel nut and betel leaf may be used, as well as whatever else constitutes meat.
In the absence of jaggery, one may use fried rice or roasted chickpeas and the like;
in the absence of the fifth [item], one should draw a triangle containing the seed-syllable of Śakti.
On the left thigh, the practitioner who knows the ritual procedure, having worshipped the Śakti with red sandalwood paste,
should recite her Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times right there.
In the absence of Svayambhū flowers, one should offer red sandalwood;
Śambhu has declared that the Hayāri flower is the Śakti and Aparājitā is the other [Śakti].
One should take the *kulāmṛta* (clan-nectar) produced from the union of those two.
Likewise: "In a copper vessel, [one should place] oil-cake from cow-products, garlic, milk-rice, and milk. (9-1408)
These are the secondary forms of the principles (*tattvānukalpa*) within the thousand-spoked [mandala], and their emission;
this is the Kashmiri tradition, which should be known as dear to the Kaulikas. (9.1409)
*Piṇyāka* is sesame paste; *gṛñjana* is garlic. Likewise:
"The resolve for the propitiation of the deity is indeed the very contemplation of the principles (*tattva*)."
The Self, Knowledge, Śiva, and the All—these are [the stages] in sequence. (9.1410)
At the conclusion of the fivefold worship (pañcopacāra) and at the end of the worship, there should be an offering (bali).
Worship is performed with the right hand; libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with the left hand.

The fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed at the conclusion of all rites, and the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) is traditionally held to take place within the heart; this is the tradition known as Kerala, which has been practiced by the sages.
Such is the sequence of the tradition.
It honors the confluence of rivers of compositions, abounding in the stream of nectar— the wonderful variety of words that purify beings and possess marvelous splendor.

Thus, the ninth beautiful wave, which possesses the reasoning of the analogy of the "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta), has come to an end in this new ocean of preliminary rites composed by the lord of all kings. 9.1413.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purascarana Rites for the Ten Mahavidyas," in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Maharajadhiraja Shri Pratap Singh Sahib.
Now, the mantras beginning with Sarasvatī and their specific preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) are demonstrated.
And so it is said in the *Śāradā*:
The mountain [is represented by] *a*, and the two syllables *ṭha* and *ṭha* are for Vāg-vādini;
this ten-syllable mantra of Vāgīśvarī bestows the power of speech. (10.1)
The seer is Kaṇva, the metre is Virāj, and the deity is Speech as it is uttered;
these [syllables] are placed in the head, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, anus, and genitals. (10.2)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables and the limbs as previously described, according to what is taught in the *Mātṛkā*.
Now, the meditation:
She possesses a white luster and bears the crescent of the young moon.
Her body bent by the weight of her breasts, she is seated upon a white lotus.
May the Goddess of Speech protect us, she whose splendor consists of the pen and book held aloft by her own lotus-like hands, for the attainment of all prosperity.
Now, another mantra from that same source follows:
One should recite the mantra one million times and then perform the fire oblation (homa) with one-tenth of that number.
[One should offer] white lotuses smeared with milk, or sesame seeds soaked in sweet [substances].
Now, another mantra for that same [rite] is given therein: at the end of the *hṛdaya* [mantra], the word "bhagavati," followed by the pair of words "vada vada. (10.5)

One should extract the mantra of the Goddess of Speech, beginning with Vāgbhava and ending with the wife of Agni (Svāhā), enriched with sixteen syllables, which bestows the fruit of mastery over speech. (10.6)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the six parts of the *mantra* joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*).
Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[She is] white, adorned with white unguents, garlands, and garments, and radiant with a crescent moon.
Holding in his lotus-like hands a commentary, a rosary, a jar filled with nectar, and sacred knowledge. (10.7)

I bow to the goddess of speech, who sits upon a lotus, whose breasts are full, who smiles beautifully, who possesses three eyes, who bestows the power of eloquence, and who grants the wealth of good fortune.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite).
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should properly recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
At the end, one should perform a *homa* offering of one-tenth [the number of recitations] with sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter.
Now, another mantra for that same purpose is given:
*Tāra*, *Māyā*, *Dhara*, *Bindu*, *Śakti*, *Tāra*, and *Sarasvatī*. (10.9)
The eleven-syllable mantra is declared to be the ultimate secret;
it resides respectively in the aperture of Brahmā, between the eyebrows, and in the nine apertures. (10.10)
The practitioner of mantra should place the syllables of the mantra; the assignment of the limbs is performed with the Vāgbhava syllable. Now, the visualization:
[One should meditate upon] Vāṇī, whose face is radiant as the full moon, possessing the luster of camphor and the kunda flower.
Her head was marked with the crescent moon, and she respectfully held [the offerings] with her own hands.
I worship her who holds a lute, a rosary, and a jar of nectar, who possesses the knowledge of lofty breasts, whose body is adorned with divine ornaments, and who is mounted upon a swan.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite).
One should recite the mantra twelve hundred thousand times and offer a thousand white lotuses.
Or the supreme practitioner should perform the oblation with *nāga* and *campaka* flowers.
Furthermore, another mantra for that same purpose is stated therein: "O Vācaspati! O Amṛta! Again, *pluvaḥ pluvaḥ*—thus one should recite. (10–13)
The mantra consisting of eleven syllables, proclaimed by the sages as "vāgāḍhya," should duly form its limbs (aṅgas) with the five words beginning with "vāk. (10.14)
Now, the meditation:
Seated upon a lotus, holding a rosary, two lotuses, and a book in her hands;
wearing a crown bound with the young moon, she possesses the luster of pearls, moonlight, and jasmine.
May the Goddess of Speech, whose eyes are half-closed by her brow, who is burdened by the weight of her breasts, and who is constantly attended by hosts of sages, lead you to prosperity. || 10-15 ||
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for Rudra and offer oblations of clarified butter amounting to a tenth part of that number.
One should worship her upon a pedestal fashioned according to the *mātṛkā* system, as previously described. (10–16)
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"The bed of Viṣṇu situated in water, together with the four-faced one alone;
joined with Bindu and Arghīśa, Vahni, Bindu, Sadya, Ambumān, and Bhṛgu. (10.17)
The wise have declared three seed-syllables for those seeking the grace of Sarasvatī;
one should fashion the limbs [of the mantra] using these seeds repeated twice and joined with the jāti-mantra.
Now, the meditation:

[One should visualize her] white as a string of pearls, adorned with a crescent moon upon her head, holding in her own arms a book, a rosary of colored beads for recitation, a jewel-encrusted vase, and [the gesture of] exposition.
I praise for a long time the Mistress of Speech, who sits upon a lotus, whose waist bends under the weight of her full and lofty breasts, and who is bowed down by the three worlds.

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and perform oblations (*homa*) with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) sprinkled with clarified butter (*ājya*) into the consecrated fire in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that recitation. (10.20)
Now, the mantra of Cintāmaṇi-Sarasvatī (from the Merutantra):
Next, I shall first fully explain the Cintāmaṇi-Sarasvatī [mantra]: Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and the letters Ha, Sa, Ra, Na, enriched with the letter E and provided with the bindu (Ṃ). (10.21)
Furthermore, one should utter "Māyā" (Hrīṃ) and "Tāra" (Oṃ), followed by Sarasvatī in the feminine nominative singular;
this mantra, ending with the heart-seed syllable (Namaḥ), is thus proclaimed. || 10.22 ||

The *triṣṭubh* is the meter, Kaṇva the sage, and Cintāmaṇi-Sarasvatī the deity. *Hsaiḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *hrīḥ* is the power (*śakti*) for the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpana*). (10.23)
The assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) should be performed with the consonant groups beginning with *ka*, each encapsulated by its own vowel.
Now, the visualization (dhyāna): She is mounted upon a swan, possesses the luster of a pearl, and has a gentle smile and the moon as her crest-jewel. (10.24)
[One should meditate on her] holding a lute, a jar of nectar, a rosary, and a garland in her radiant hands, born from the lotus-seated [Brahmā].

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): having stated that "one should recite twelve hundred thousand [times]," one should then offer oblations of white lotuses or campaka flowers by the thousands. (10.25)

Now, the mantra of Pārijātasarasvatī (from the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā): The knower of mantras should write the seed-syllable Vāgbhava of Saṃpatpradā Bhairavī, having encased it with the Tāra [Om] and the supreme [Hrīṃ], O Goddess. (10.26)
This mantra, ending with the heart [seed-syllable] of Sarasvatī and consisting of eleven Rudra-syllables, has been proclaimed;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas). (10.27)
The goddess Vāṇī is proclaimed as Pārijāteśvarī;
the third and second [syllables] are the seed-syllable (bīja) and the power (śakti), along with the Tāraka.
O Supreme Goddess, the *kīlaka* bestows the great power of Sarasvatī;
one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-vinyāsa*) with the seed-syllables conjoined with the six long vowels.
Now, the meditation:
Seated upon a swan, laughing with a beautiful smile, as white as the moon or a kunda flower, Vāṇī has a face graced by a gentle smile and a crescent moon bound upon her head.
May Bhāratī, her hands radiant with the lute of knowledge, the jar filled with nectar, and the rosary, seated upon a white lotus, grant you the attainment of your desired goals. (10.30)

Now, regarding the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) according to another tantra: one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable, and thereafter perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with one-tenth that number, using *kiṃśuka* or *campaka* flowers, or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and honey. (10.31)
Regarding that nine-syllable mantra as well, first is the *praṇava*,
then the *āghora* [mantra] which bestows prosperity, and then the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjābīja*).
(From the *Śāradā-tantra*)
When these mantras have been thus spoken, the initiated one, with a restrained mind, [should practice].
He who worships with devotion this One shall possess both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
in the rite for Sarasvatī, worship is performed with very white perfumes and flowers. (10.33)
Sprouts from dūrvā grass seeds, flowers produced from the rājavṛkṣa tree, excellent utpala lotuses, and sprouts of the sindhuvāra plant [are recommended]. (10.34)
Constantly resorting to Sarasvatī, one should avoid these:
the āmrātaka, the gṛñjana, the bimba, the karañja, and likewise garlic.
Oil, onion, oil-cake, and even meat along with its eight accompaniments—
everything that has turned stale must always be abandoned by one who seeks the grace of Sarasvatī.
One should not consume betel leaf at night, nor should one approach a woman during the day;
one should never sleep during the two twilights, nor should one utter anything while impure. (10.37)
At dusk, one should remain silent and not look at a woman clad only in a garment of directions;
one should not approach a woman in her menses, nor should one revile a beautiful-eyed woman.
A wise person should not speak false words, nor should they step over a book;
one should neither neglect nor tread upon leaves rich with syllables. (10.39)
On the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, on festival days, on the first day of the month, during eclipses, and at all transits of the sun, a person should never recite the vidyā.
During the exposition, a wise person should abandon sleep, laziness, yawning, anger, spitting, and likewise touching the lower parts of the body. (10.41)
If humans, snakes, cats, frogs, mongooses, or the like should pass between [the teacher and the student], then one should cease the exposition. (10.42)
One should immediately cease recitation during the nights or when the lamp goes out.
Having correctly understood these defects, he who worships the *Bhāratī* with devotion [is truly devoted]. (10.43)
One attains perfection of speech, becoming like a second Vācaspati.
Thus ends the section on Sarasvatī.
Now follows the mantra of Tvaritā.
In that very place:
"Then I shall describe Tvaritā, who swiftly bestows her fruit. (10.44)
Tāra, Māyā, the seed-syllable of Varma, and Ṛddhi joined with the vowel of Īśa;
Kūrma at its end, followed by the Lord Bhaga, the letter Kṣa, and the long Tanucchada. (10.45)
The Blessed One Saṃvarta is the twelve-syllable mantra ending with *māyā* and *phaṭ*;
he is declared to be the Sage Arjuna, and Virāṭ is said to be the meter. || 10.46 ||
Tvaritā is declared to be the deity who bestows the fruits of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
Likewise, [the mantra is formed] with the five syllables beginning with *kūrma*, each successively deprived of its preceding [consonant]. (10.47)
The supreme practitioner should arrange the six limbs by means of two [syllables] each.
Now, the meditation: [She is] dark-complexioned, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, and wearing a garment of woven leaves.
She bore eight serpents upon her heavy breasts, which shone with garlands of *guñjā* berries.

I worship the three-eyed Goddess, who wears earrings, armlets, and a girdle, whose anklets have attained the quality of sweetly tinkling, who holds a deer-skin, and whose hands are raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa*.
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, the knower of mantras, with his senses subdued, [attains success]. || 10-49 ||
One should offer oblations ten times the number [of recitations] with the best fuel-sticks made of bilva wood, anointed with the three sweets.
Likewise, the practitioner whose mantra has been thus perfected is honored by women, men, and kings. (10.50)
"Within a year, he will be honored as one who has surpassed the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) in prosperity"—
this is the mantra of Tvaritā.
Now, the mantra of Nityaklinnā is found in that same [text] on page 874.
*Tāra*, *māyā*, and *vāgbhava* at the end, followed by *nityaklinne madadrave*. (10.51)
The fifteen-syllable mantra consists of the word *vāṅmāyā* followed by the consort of Fire (Svāhā);
it is divided into syllables two by two, then again two by two, and finally five. (10.52)
Then, even without words, one should perform the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga).
Now, the meditation: [One should visualize] an island, vast and triangular, enchanting with the celestial tree (kalpavṛkṣa). || 10.53 ||
Rich with the warbling of cuckoos, fanned by gentle breezes,
strewn with bees and flowering creepers, it was illuminated by the rising moon and sun.
Having recollected [the Lord] situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, within that pavilion of rubies, upon a jeweled throne whose radiant pericarp is formed by a triangle; 10.55.
One should contemplate the Goddess, who directly fascinates the three worlds, within a lotus;
I worship the Eternal One, whose crest is adorned with the young moon, and who holds a noose, a goad, a wish-granting creeper, and a skull-cup. (10.56)
With her hands she was holding a reddish [lute], three-eyed,
and striking that sweet-sounding *vallakī* lute.
Now follows the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and then perform oblations with clarified butter.
"The tenth part" is the understood remainder.
Thus ends the mantra of Nityaklinnā.
Now follows the mantra of Annapūrṇā.
(Merutantra) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the great mantra of Annapūrṇā:
having first uttered "Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Klīḥ Namaḥ," one should then speak the word "Bhagavati. (10.58)
"O Māheśvarī, O Annapurṇā, Svāhā"—this mantra consists of twenty syllables. Its meter is Anuṣṭubh, its sage is Brahmā, and its deity is indeed Annapurṇā. (10.59)
The seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*, the power (*śakti*) is *śrīṃ*, and the peg (*kīlaka*) is proclaimed as *klīṃ*.
The *hṛllekhā* mantra, joined with the six long vowels, is prescribed for the six limbs. (10.60)

Now, as for the meditation: [One should meditate on her] resembling molten gold, with the young moon as her crest-jewel, her crown radiant with the luster of nine gems, and reddish like saffron. (10.61)

Seeing the Supreme Goddess, who was filled with bliss, dancing incessantly— she who was clothed in variegated garments, possessed eyes like those of a fish, and breasts like water-jars— and beholding the Lord likewise dancing, [he was struck with wonder].
She whose face is joyful and whose eyes are tremulous, whose hips are adorned with a girdle,
who is eternally devoted to the giving of food, and who is saluted by the Earth and the Goddess of Fortune.
One should meditate on the Goddess holding in her left hand a vessel filled with milk-rice and adorned with jewels, while in her right hand she holds a golden ladle.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while observing the restrictive rules, and then perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with ten parts of that amount using delicious milk-rice and clarified butter; in this way, it becomes a bestower of success. (10.65)

Now, another mantra (in the *Śāradā-tantra*): Māyā, Hṛt, followed by the word "Bhagavatī," then the word "Māheśvarī," and then "Annapūrṇe" with a pair of Ṭhas; this is the seventeen-syllable mantra. (10.66)
One should fashion the [mandala] lines with *māyā* and then contemplate the Goddess. Now, the meditation:
[She is] red, wearing variegated garments, and has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel.
Devoted to the giving of food, she was bowed down by the weight of her breasts.
I worship the Goddess, the remover of the suffering of worldly existence, who is delighted upon seeing the dancing [Śiva] adorned with the crescent moon.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa*.
One should recite the mantra eight thousand times according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oblations of food with clarified butter, followed by ten parts of the subsequent [mantras].
This is the mantra of Annapūrṇā. Now follows the mantra of Pratyaṅgirā.
(Merutantra) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain [the rite] that wards off the malevolent acts of others. 10-69.
One should recite the goddess named Pratyāṅgirā, who wards off all calamities: Oṃ a ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa bha ho hrīḥ. (10.70)
Having uttered "huḥ," the sixteen-syllable weapon-mantra ending in "svāhā" is thus declared; its sage is Vidhātṛ, its metre is Uṣṇih, and six deities are proclaimed for it. (10.71)
The great wind, the great earth, and likewise the great space;
that which is named the great ocean, and the great mountain as well. || 10-72 ||
Mahāgni is "huṃ," and the seed-syllable is "hrīḥ"; this is proclaimed as the power (śakti).
One should perform the six limbs with the syllable of modesty (lajjā), conjoined with the six long vowels. (10.73)
Then the mantra-practitioner, with a perfectly steady mind, should meditate upon the Mantra-goddess. Now, the visualization:
[She is] pervaded by the radiance of various jewels and endowed with streams of water flowing from trees. (10.74)
One should visualize the mountain as being filled with beasts such as tigers and the like,
together with their offspring, abounding in seeds such as fish and tortoises, and endowed with the nine gems.
One should contemplate the ocean with its dense shade and its waves, and the wondrous triple world pervaded by garlands of flames. (10.76)
For the pacification of enemies, one should meditate upon the great fire of yellow color,
which is turbid with a flood of sounds arising in haste and which obstructs both earth and heaven.
One should contemplate the purifying wind, the life of the universe, in its form as the vital breath (prāṇa), which is filled with the tips of rivers, mountains, trees, and so forth. (10.78)
The practitioner of mantra should here meditate upon the Earth as the support of the world, together with the sun and other planets, the lunar mansions, and the wheel of time (kālacakra). (10.79)
One should meditate upon the stainless sky, the abode and refuge of all living beings.
Regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), he says:
"Having thus meditated upon the six deities, [one should recite] sixteen thousand [times]. (10.80)
One should recite the mantra ten times the number of oblations and perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with six substances:
rice grains, husked rice, clarified butter, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds. (10.81)
Having offered oblations with these according to their respective portions, one should worship on the seat previously described.
Now, the *mālā-mantra* for that very [deity] follows; next, the accomplished *mālā-mantra* of Pratyaṅgirā is proclaimed: 10.82. [The mantra follows].
Oṃ Hrīḥ! Homage to the one clothed in black, who dwells as the lord, the subduer of the thousand-fold universe;
O thousand-faced one of great power, you who are unconquered! || 10.83 ||
In the *pratyaṅgira* [rite], one should utter the words "parasainyaparakarma";
then one should say "vidhvaṃsini paramantrotsādinī. (10.84)
One should then say "sarvabhūta" and "damani," followed by "sarvadevān.
Then [one says] "bandha" twice, "sarvavidyā," "dviśchindhi," and "kṣobhaya" twice. (10.85)
One should say "parayantrāṇi," then utter "sphoṭaya dvitayam," followed by "sarvaśṛṅkhalāḥ troṭaya troṭaya jvala. (10.86)
One should recite "O you whose tongue is a flame! O terrible one! before the face;
"Gire hrīḥ namaḥ"—this consists of one hundred and twenty-five syllables. (10.87)

Brahmā is considered the sage, Anuṣṭubh the metre, and the goddess Pratyaṅgirā the deity; the seed-syllable and power-syllables are Tāra and Māyā, and the application is "Kṛtyānāśa" (Destruction of Magic). || 10-88 ||
p. 878) Herein is the procedure for the six limbs, performed with the *māyā* [syllable] conjoined with the six long vowels.
Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*): [One should meditate on her] mounted upon a lion, with exceedingly black limbs, a face of flames, and terrifying. (10.89)
I worship her who holds a trident and a sword in her hands and wears fresh garments.
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and offer a thousand oblations of sesame seeds and black mustard. (10.90)
Having offered oblations, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra should recite it one hundred times during ritual applications;
while reciting the mantra, he should sprinkle water to ward off the misfortunes caused by planets, spirits, and other such malevolent forces.
One shall destroy the mechanical devices, mantras, and other means employed by others.
Now, another mantra (from the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*):
Oṃ! Whatever cruel magic (*kṛtyā*) our enemies fashion against us, like a bride [to be discarded], [may it be destroyed]. (10.92)
"May that [impurity] be driven away by the Brahman; may it seek the agent in the west.
Hrīḥ! From the Munya-mantra to the end of the viniyoga, however, this [rite] is like the mala-mantra. (10.93)
One should perform the six limbs with a quarter, a half-quarter,
and a full quarter, encased within the *hṛllekhā* mantra preceded by the Vedas and the six long vowels.
Then, one should place [the syllables] step by step upon the head, between the eyebrows, the face, the throat, the two arms, the heart, the navel, the sides, the hips, the knees, and the feet.
Having made her all-pervasive throughout the entire [body], one should meditate upon Maheśvarī—
black, holding a sword and a shield, with loose hair and naked.
One should meditate upon her whose face is formidable with fangs, who is terrifying to behold, adorned with all ornaments, and who devours her enemies, impelled by the splendor of Śiva. (10.97)
He describes the *puraścaraṇa*:
"The mantra-practitioner, with a restrained mind, should mutter this [mantra] ten thousand times;
thereafter, he should offer oblations consisting of one-tenth that amount of *apāmārga* wood and black mustard seeds. (10.98)
When combined with clarified butter (sarpiṣ), the mantra then becomes perfected;
for its applications, the wise one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
"By that much alone, through the oblation, the work of others is destroyed.
Thus ends the mantra of Pratyaṅgirā. Now follows the mantra of Kubjikā.
(In the Kulālikāmnāyatantra) the venerable Kubjikā said: "O Lord Laghvikā, tell me how [the lineage] is endowed with the words of mantra. (10.100)
O Goddess Laghvikā, who are all-knowing and always endowed with auspicious marks, Bhairava spoke thus: "Listen, O Laghvikā! (10.101)
But you must not speak until the child has been commanded;
"ce-vī" is the first word, and "ṇikiṇiki" is the second.
*Chī*, *chā*, and the third word; *khimuragha* as the fourth;
*menaṇañaṅa* as the fifth; and *hrau*, *hrā*, *hrī* as the sixth word. (10.103)
That which has *kābjikuśra* as the seventh and *tyaivagabha* as the eighth—this is that goddess Samayā, garlanded with thirty-two syllables. (10.104)
Joined at the beginning and end with five *praṇavas*, it is endowed with the defining characteristics;
and with the forty-second [syllable] of the *Mālinī* at the start and conclusion of the *kūṭas*.
O Goddess, one should recite this in reverse order according to the instruction from the mouth of the Guru;
this *kūṭa* consisting of the letters *ra* and *sa* is remembered as the seventh of the Vidyā. (10.106)
O Kubjikā, my life must be dedicated to the preservation of Śrī; otherwise, by virtue of my own intellectual conceit, it shall be destroyed by the rays of the *iṣṭomara* weapon. (10.107)
This must be kept secret, most strictly secret, for it is the delight of the heart of the Yoginīs;
because it is called "Bhasmāra," it is the very essence of the entire Yoginī-kula. (10.108)
Now, if this Mother, whose nature is the pledge (samaya), resides in all the seats (pīṭhas), then by the mere remembrance of her, the three worlds become utterly overwhelmed. (10.109)
"O lady of excellent vows, by a single recitation [of this mantra] from the heart up to the weapon, the mother is well protected; of this there is no doubt. (10.110)
I shall now describe the path of accomplishment (*siddhimārga*) in reverse order, from the end back to the beginning:

*Yastrā-a yairvāṇākakko ccevi ṇikiṇiki yayātratrane keritāhaṃmajalaku chā/ chī/ yacāvakayaipārūhubakhīmuragho-a me naṇañaṅa yaikhāśi kheśirarvava hrī/ hrā/ hrau/ seraśi yaipādīlaku yaikābjikuśrī yayādahṛ yailāmatkahṛtyaivagabha mona |* The heart mantra consists of fifteen syllables, and the head mantra consists of thirteen. (10–111)
