The *śikhā* (crown) is known to consist of eleven *rudrākṣas*; the *kavaca* (armor) consists of nineteen; the *netra* (eye) should be fifteen in number; and the *astra* (weapon) consists of fourteen.
The five *praṇavas* are at the beginning and the end; as is the first [knowledge], so is the last.
This has been told to you with supporting evidence in the Kaulika terminology. (10–113)

That which resides clearly in the mouth of the Guru, yet remains in reverse order, does not succeed; this has been fully declared in the Kaulika tradition, being extremely difficult to attain on the path of accomplishment.

Now, as for the meditation (*dhyāna*): [one should visualize] the deity established upon a bull in the *Paratantra* [mandala], adorned with the color and form of the sky, having one face, three eyes, and bearing eighteen arms. (10–115)
In his right hands, he holds a battle-axe, a hand-drum, an arrow, a sword, a goad, a thunderbolt, a conch, a flute, and the gesture of granting boons.
In the left [hands], he holds a khaṭvāṅga, a trident, a bow, a shield, and a noose;
a bell, a skull-cup, and a flute; and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) which destroys fear. (10–117)
Her knees and thighs are bound with a cloth, and she is hunchbacked;
she has one face and three eyes, and is described as being of the nature of supreme compassion.
The goddess has two arms; she bestows boons and grants fearlessness with her right hand;
her body is adorned with various ornaments, and she wears the crescent moon as her crest-jewel. (10–119)
With a mass of curly hair and beautiful, full, firm breasts—
such is Kujā, the mother to be meditated upon, the mistress of the Western Tradition.
Now, regarding the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite): (In the *Kulālikāmnāyatantra*) one should join the succession of syllable upon syllable by the count of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*).
Such a person becomes equal to the qualities of the Lord Laghvīśa; he is himself the master, the destroyer, and the creator. (10–121)
For he indeed beholds the station of the Khecarīs through non-discursive contemplation,
meditating upon Maheśvarī by means of yoga that is free from ritual conduct.
Thus ends the Kubjikā mantra.
Now, the Gaṅgā mantra (from the Merutantra).
Now I shall declare other mantras residing in the head of Rudra:
one should utter the Tāra (Oṃ), then "namo śivāyai," and the word "nārāyaṇyai. (10.123)
The mantra ending with "svāhā" for Daśaharā Gaṅgā consists of twenty syllables;
Vyāsa is the sage, Kṛti is the metre, and the goddess Gaṅgā is proclaimed as the deity. (10–124)
The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed with syllables numbering three fires, Vedas, arrows, fires, and eyes.
Now, the visualization (dhyāna): [She is] four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with all ornaments. (10.125)
Her hands are beautifully adorned with a jewel-jar, a white lotus, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she is being fanned with chowries and graced by a white parasol. || 10-126 ||
(p. 882) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with ghee amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Furthermore, another mantra is mentioned in that same source:
Now I shall further explain another [practice], which destroys the sins of the left-hand path (vāmācāra).
By the power of which the practitioners of external sacrifice become Siddhas, [that mantra is]:
Tāra, namo bhagavati, Vāgbhava, and Hilid twice. (10.128)
One should utter the two syllables "mil" and the two purifying syllables "gaṅge," ending with "svāhā"; this six-syllable *mantra* is the savior that destroys all sins. (10.129)
The sage of this [hymn] is Īśvara; the meter is Amita; and Gaṅgā is the deity.
The arrangement of its limbs consists of eighteen syllables, corresponding to the number of Rāmas (seven), Vedāṅgas (six), fires (three), and eyes (two). 10.130.

Now, the meditation: She is dressed in red garments and is red in color; she holds a trident, a jar, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her hands; she is smiling and stands upon a tortoise, surrounded by gods and other beings. (10.131)
For the destruction of one's own sins, she should be well-served with mantras of that same form.

Now, regarding the *puraścaraṇa*: one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for each syllable; the fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed as a tenth part of that, performed with lotuses. (10.132)
Thus, having accomplished the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should go to a waterless region such as Marutādi and perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for the sake of obtaining water.
Having completed all [rites] beginning with the fire-oblation (homa), one should then invoke the Gaṅgā;
having constructed a well or similar structure there, it shall become like nectar.
It is unfathomable due to its persistence for an eon (*kalpa*) and is the destroyer of all diseases.
Likewise: "Having omitted this first group of seven syllables, it is called the 'Nail-syllable' (*nakhākṣarī*). (10.135)
As before, one should worship the sages and others with five, four, three, three, and three arms;
the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are formed by the syllables of the mantra, and the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
One who has mastered the mantra should perform the oblation materials and so forth as previously described;
having stood in the midst of water and recited the mantra ten thousand times, he should carry out the ritual application. (10.137)
Even during the non-rainy season, abundant rain falls within three days.
Now, another mantra for that same purpose is given in that very [text]:
"Tāra, *hilimili* in the dual, *gaṅge devi*, *namaḥ*" is the mantra (10.138).
The color of this [deity] corresponds to the lunar day (tithi), and the worship of the sages and others is declared as before.
The procedure for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared by means of three, two, three, two, four, and four syllables.
By venerating this, a living being shall not meet death in an improper place.
He then states another mantra: Tāra (Oṃ), Lajjā (Hrīṃ), Ramā (Śrīṃ), Hārda (Namaḥ), and then the word Bhagavatī.
"Huṃ! Salutation to the one who is fully awakened, O beloved of the Gaṅgā! Likewise, there is the Astra-mantra.
This mantra consists of eighteen syllables; its sage and other attributes are considered to be as previously stated. (10.141)
Thus ends the mantra of Gaṅgā.
Now follows the mantra of Maṇikarṇikā;
it is in that very same place.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the non-dual mantra of Maṇikarṇikā: Tāra (Om), Vāk (Aiṃ), Hrīṃ, Ramā (Śrīṃ), Kāma (Klīṃ); this is the Tāra-mantra of Maṇikarṇikā. || 10-142 ||
Namaḥ oṃ—this mantra consists of the letters of the lunar days (tithis) and is extremely difficult to obtain.
Vyāsa is the sage, the Atiśakvarī is the meter, and Maṇikarṇikā is the deity. (10.143)
The deity’s six limbs [are consecrated] with the three syllables of *candra-netrākṣi*. Now, the visualization:
in the right hand is a citron, and in the left, a garland of blue lotuses. (10.144)
With palms joined in reverence, clad in white garments, possessing three eyes and a face like the moon,
she faces the west, smiling, seated upon a lotus, and wearing a garland of lotuses.
Śrī Maṇikarṇikā, enriched with various ornaments and finery, should be meditated upon. (p.
884) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount. (10.146)
"One should worship her with lotuses smeared with the three sweets, as equal to the Gaṅgā.
This is the mantra of Maṇikarṇikā. Now follows the mantra of Vāgmatī.
In that very place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the two mantras of the Vāgmatī. (10.147)
The first mantra is the seed-syllable Vāk; Nārada is considered its sage (ṛṣi), the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is proclaimed to be Vāgmatī. (10.148)
Now, regarding meditation: [One should visualize] the Śvetāmbarā goddess, white in color, anointed with white perfumes, holding a jar of nectar, a lotus, a lute, and a book. (10.149)

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who holds [objects] with her hands, is seated upon a fish, and is adorned with ornaments of pearls, one should worship her in the pericarp of a six-petalled lotus.
[One should worship] Rudradhārā, Maṇimatī, Phalgu, Viṣṇumatī, as well as Prabhāvatī and Bhānumatī; and in the Bhūpura, the lords of the directions.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and likewise offer oblations (*homa*) with the five types of edible foods.
Then, having performed the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites, the mantra becomes perfected (*siddha*). || 10-152 ||
One should write the seed-syllable on the tongue of a newborn infant with honey using a golden stylus; such a child shall become a poet at the age of eight.
He who performs the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) at the Vāgmatī or the Gaṅgā—refraining from accepting gifts, subsisting on alms, and observing silence—[attains success]. || 10.154 ||

A celibate student who sleeps on the ground, wears white garments, and remains pure, will certainly attain mastery over speech; he shall be a giver and an enjoyer, yet remain a non-seeker of alms. (10.155)
Now, another mantra is given in that same place: "One should utter the seed-syllables of Ramā, Māyā, and Vāk, ending with the word 'vāgmatyai';
then the words 'namo mama', followed by 'dhāraṇām' and then 'dhiyam'. (10.156)
Bestow the wondrous speech, ending with "svāhā," characterized by the phonemes of the principles (tattvas).
Likewise, the worship of the sages and so forth, as well as the preliminary ritual service (puraścaryā), are to be performed as before.
Thus ends the mantra of Vāgmatī.
Now, the mantra of Candra (according to the Śāradā-tantra):
Now it is said: the mantra of the Moon bestows all prosperity;
it consists of the letter Kha (kha), followed by the Lord of Swords (īśa), then Bhṛgu (bha), the Moon (u), and the vowel Svara (ā). (10.158)
This six-syllabled mantra, ending with "to Soma, [the heart]," has been proclaimed;
Bhṛgu is said to be its seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti its meter (chandas), and Soma its deity (devatā). (10.159)
The mental visualization of the limbs [of the deity] is considered to be performed with one's own seed-syllable, which possesses long vowels.
Now, as for meditation:
[one should visualize the deity] whose face is like the orb of the full moon, eternally pure like camphor and crystal.
With a body adorned with strings of pearls, he utterly eradicates darkness.

I worship the Moon, who holds a white water-lily and a boon-granting gesture in his two hands, who is illuminated by dark curls of hair, and who possesses the quality of being the refuge for the deer dwelling upon his own lap; [I worship] the ocean of nectar.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite).
The practitioner, having conquered his senses, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should offer that thousand-fold oblation with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
Now, another mantra (in the *Merutantra*):
*Oṃ Ā Śrī Śru*, with the nasal bindu, followed by *sa somāya*; this is the consort of Agni. (10.162)
This ten-syllable mantra of Candra should be recited ten thousand times by the king;
all procedures such as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth should be performed as previously described. (10.163)
Thus ends the mantra of the Moon.
Now follows the mantra of Mars;
in that same [text]:
Now I shall declare the mantra of Bhauma (Mars), which wards off all diseases:
*Aṃ Aṅgārakāya ṅe*, ending with the heart [seed-syllable]; it consists of eight syllables. (10.164)
The seers and so forth for this Brahma-Gāyatrī are declared to be the sons of the Earth (the Vasus);
the six ancillaries (aṅgas) of this mantra are considered to be formed with its own seed-syllable.
Now, the meditation: I bow to Aṅgāraka, who is red, adorned with red garments and ornaments, whose left hand rests upon his knee, and whose other hand displays the gesture of fearlessness. (10.166)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):

it is taught that there should be one hundred and eight thousand recitations (*japa*). One should offer oblations (*homa*) with fuel-sticks made of *khadira* wood mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*). One should perform the act of satiation (*saṃtarpaṇa*) with red sandalwood and other such substances.
Now, another mantra is mentioned in that very same place:
"Now I shall declare another mantra that grants success for the Bhūmi-mantra:
Oṃ hāḥ haḥ saḥ khaḥ khaḥ; this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. (10.168)
The sage is Virūpa, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the son of the Earth (Dharātmaja).
The practitioner should perform the six-limbed ritual of the mantra with six syllables.
Now, the meditation:
I bow to that son of the Earth, who resembles a hibiscus flower, who holds a spear, a trident, a mace, and a boon-granting hand, who is seated upon a ram, and who is clad in red garments. (10.170)

The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of six hundred thousand recitations; for it is stated in that very same source: "One should perform the recitation one million times and offer oblations with fuel-sticks of the Khadira tree."
Oṃ krā, krī, krau—accompanied by the nasal bindu and the wife of Kuja (Kuja-patnī)—is Agnigehinī. (10.171)
This ten-syllable mantra of Bhauma should be recited nine thousand times.
He then states another mantra:
having uttered "Oṃ Śrī Klī Hrī," [the name] Bhauma follows in the dative case (Ṅe-ending) and ends with the word "Hṛdaya" (Heart). (10.172)
The ten-syllable mantra is proclaimed; Virūpākṣa is considered its sage (ṛṣi).
Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas), and Maṅgala shall be its deity (devatā). (10.173)
*Hrīḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *śrīḥ* is the power (*śakti*), and *klīṃ* is fashioned as the wedge (*kīlaka*).
Having uttered [these] along with *Kālādi* and so forth, this is the application for the destruction of debt. (10.174)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) on the fingers and other parts using the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
Now, for the meditation: thereafter, one should meditate upon [the deity] as red in color, adorned with red garlands and garments. (10.175)
Adorned with a lotus garland on the neck and holding a spear and trident in his hands, he is the most auspicious among all auspicious things and the bestower of the fruits of all desires. (10.176)
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with many *karavīra* flowers—
specifically *javā* blossoms— mixed with the three sweets.

One should worship the Son of the Earth (Mars), who is adorned with red ornaments and bestows all desired fruits, according to the prescribed rite with offerings rich in the fragrance of red sandalwood.
Thus ends the mantra of Kujā.
Now follows the mantra of Bhauma;
it is in that same [text].

Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the most wonderful mantra of Budha; it consists of six syllables, beginning with "buṃ," ending with "ṅe," containing the word "Budha," and concluding with the "heart" [syllable]. (10.179)
The sage and others of this [mantra] are considered wise in the lineage of Brahmā;
having thus performed the placement of the six limbs with their own seed-syllables, one should meditate as follows. (10.180)

Now, regarding meditation: I ever revere the wise Lord, beautifully adorned with yellow garments, whose left lotus-hand rests upon his knee and whose other hand displays the gesture of fearlessness. (10.181)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one thousand times and offer oblations of clarified butter in the tenth part of that number.
Furthermore, another mantra is mentioned in that same context:
Oṃ brā, brī, brū—accompanied by the nasal bindu and the word "sabudhāya"—is the consort of Agni. (10.182)
The gentle mantra of ten syllables is to be recited one hundred thousand times;
thus ends the mantra of Budha.
Now follows the mantra of Bṛhaspati.
In that very same [text]:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the guru-mantra which effects the state of being a guru. (10.183)
For Bṛhaspati, the heart-mantra and the eight-syllable mantra are considered [as follows]: the metre is Anuṣṭubh, the sage is Brahmā, and the deity is said to be Bṛhaspati. (10.184)
*Bṛ*: The seed-syllable is for the Lord; the power (*śakti*) is likewise [formed] with the seed-syllable, as is the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpana*).
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): [He is] golden-hued, wearing yellow garments, or red, gold-colored, and other such robes. (10.185)
With his right hand he scatters that heap, while with his left hand he touches another [heap] consisting of gold and other goods in the marketplace.
Abounding in the splendor of various ornaments and having crossed the ocean of knowledge—now follows the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
having recited [the mantra] eighty thousand times, one should offer oblations with cow's ghee. || 10.187 ||
One should worship him upon the pedestal of dharma, adharma, and so forth, with the limbs and the deities of the directions.
Now, another mantra for that same [deity] is given therein:
Oṃ jrā jrī jrū; Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the nasal bindu and ending in the dative case. (10.188)
p. 889) This mantra of Bṛhaspati, consisting of fire (RA), woman (Ī), and all colors (KṢA), is to be recited fifteen thousand times. Now follows the mantra of Śukra.
In that very place:
"Give me a garment for Śukra; [beginning with] *śu* and so forth, within the heart. (10.189)
The mantra consists of eleven syllables; the Virāṭ meter is proclaimed for it.
Brahmā is the sage (ṛṣi), and the deity is Śukra, who is worshipped by the Daityas and others. (10.190)
With six words, one should then contemplate the deity with six limbs. Now, the meditation:
"I bow to Śukra, who stands at the marketplace, adorned with ornaments of pearls. (10.191)
With both hands rendered delighted by streams of gold, garments, and jewels—now follows the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and offer oblations of clarified butter one thousand times. (10.192)
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"Oṃ hrāḥ hrīḥ hrauḥ, with the bindu, for the one accompanied by Śukra"—this is the wife of Agni.
This ten-syllable mantra of Śukra should be recited twelve thousand times. (10.193)
One should perform oblations with fuel-sticks of the Udumbara tree; all calamities caused by kings will perish, and happiness from women will arise. (10.194)
Thus ends the mantra of Śukra.
Now follows the mantra of Śanaiścara;
it is in that same [text].
The heart mantra for Śanaiścara consists of eight syllables beginning with *śam*. The sage and other attributes are as follows: the Brahman is the Gāyatrī, and the deity is named Śanaiścara. (10.195)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*): I salute Śanaiścara, who has curved fangs and blue adornments. (10.196)
With his left knee resting on the ground, his left hand placed upon it, and bestowing a boon with his right hand—[this reading is found only in manuscript 5]—in the *Mārtaṇḍabhairavatantra*:
"His divine form is graced by the splendor of a blue mountain; he holds a sword, a triple staff, and a bow and arrow in his hands. (10.197)
"Śambhu, Mahākāla, Śani, and Purāri—victory to him who effects the destruction of all asuras!
Thus another meditation has been described.
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) [on Mount Meru]:
One should recite the thousand syllables and perform a fire oblation with clarified butter consisting of one-tenth that number.
For those devoted to Śanaiścara, there shall be no misfortunes nor poverty resulting from the worship of the six limbs, the planets, the guardians of the directions, and their weapons. (10.199)
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:

Having uttered "Oṃ prā prī prau sa," one should speak the word for Śanaiścara in the dative case, followed by "svāhā. This twelve-syllable recitation is considered to be performed ten million times (prayuta). || 10.200 ||
"By means of fuel-sticks of *hunecchāmī* grass, all eunuchs shall come under his control.
This is the mantra of Śanaiścara. Now follows the mantra of Rāhu.
In that very place:
"Furthermore, I shall state the mantra for Manu; one should utter 'Obeisance to Rāhu'. (10.201)
This six-syllable mantra is preceded by *rā*; the assignment of the limbs (*aṅga*) is performed with these very syllables.
The sages and so forth, as well as the deity, the meter, and the seed-syllable, are proclaimed to be Brahmā, Gāyatrī, and Rāhu respectively. (10.202)
Now, the meditation:

I praise Rāhu, smoke-colored, with his entire body joined in añjali, with a distorted face and red eyes, adorned with smoke-colored ornaments—thus [I praise him] every day. (10.203) [Note: This reading is according to the variant in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and Pu.]
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times according to the number of its syllables and perform oblations with cow’s ghee.
Worship with the planets, the lords of the quarters, and weapons is declared to be the mode of practice. (10.204)
A king who is a worshipper of Rāhu shall be victorious in battle.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
*Oṃ sāḥ sīḥ sauḥ* (with the nasal bindu), she who dwells with fire is [the consort] of Sarāhava. (10.205)
This ten-syllable mantra of Rāhu should be recited ten thousand times;
having performed oblations with dūrvā grass and having gratified the twice-born brahmins, it becomes perfected.
Thus ends the mantra of Rāhu.
Now follows the mantra of Ketu;
it is in that same [text].
"Ke / Ketave hṛdi"—this is the six-syllabled mantra of Ketu;
Brahmā is considered its sage, Paṅkti its metre, and Ketu its deity. (10.207)
*Ke* is the seed-syllable, while *ve* is the power (*śakti*). By means of the seed-syllable alone, the six-limbed [mantra] is formed. Now, the meditation:
I bow to the Kula, black in color and adorned with black garments. (10.208)
With his left hand resting on her left thigh and his other hand displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*),
he should then perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
He should recite [the mantra] one thousand syllables and offer oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) ten times that number.
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
*Oṃ prā prī prau* (with the nasal bindu), followed by *saketave vahnigehinī*.
This ten-syllable mantra of Ketu should be recited twelve thousand times. (10.210)
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with kuśa grass smeared with clarified butter, as well as the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites;
for the banners of this [deity] move before the lay practitioners (upāsakas). || 10.211 ||
Thus ends the Ketu-mantra. Now follow the Graha-mātṛkā-mantras.
In that very same [text]:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the excellent method for propitiating the Mothers of the Planets (Grahamātṛs).
When the Mothers of the Planets are satisfied, what need is there for the planets or even for misfortunes? (10.212)
When the Mother of the Planets is satisfied, what need is there for auspicious planets?
Maṅgalā, Piṅgalā, Dhanyā, Bhrāmarī, and likewise Bhadrikā—[these are the Mothers]. (10.213)
Ulka, Siddha, Saṃkaṭā, Vikaṭā, and Garbhapālikā—these eight daśās follow the sequence of the birth asterism, beginning from the Rudra asterisms. (10.214)
The fruit should be commensurate with the cause; from the accumulation of one, there is that of two.
Piṅgalā is the mother of the Sun, the bringer of great mental and physical afflictions.
If she is pleased, she brings satisfaction to the enemy faction; if enraged, she acts against the practitioner.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *bje*, O Piṅgalā, O you who have the color of an enemy! (10.216)
"Prasīda Phaṭ"—thus uttered, these three syllables consist of fire (Ra), power (Hūṃ), and phonemes (Kṣa).
Together with the first seed-syllable conjoined with the six long vowels, one performs the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka). || 10.217 ||
Now, for the meditation: I worship her who is tawny in color, with tawny hair and tawny eyes, holding a bow and arrows and a pair of lotuses in her two hands. (10.218)
Now I shall describe the procedure for worship according to all the tantras:
hibiscus flowers are recommended, and the incense should be derived from guggulu resin. (10.219)
Ghee lamps, sweet food offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like, red ornaments, likewise red garments, and sandalwood. (10.220)
O Supreme Goddess, one should satisfy [the deity] a thousand times with golden ornaments and excellent materials of the five kinds, while reciting their respective mantras.
Having fashioned a beautiful, flawless golden plate measuring one cubit in length,
one should worship the Yoginī there according to the prescribed method.
Having recited that supreme mantra a thousand times for the pacification of obstacles, the warding off of the three kinds of portents will be accomplished within seven days. (10.223)
Then, having constructed a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules, or else upon a pure altar (sthaṇḍila) well-smeared with cow-dung and water; || 10-224 ||
With a steady mind, one should prepare [the site] measuring four cubits; having established the fire for the Yoginī and performed the rites previously described. (10.225)
For other [deities], it should be done ten times; for a hostile one, a thousand times, using bilva leaves, its fruits, lotuses, and nāgakeśara flowers.
One should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) together with the family substance (kulavastu),
either one thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand times, according to the sequence of one's desires.
Now I shall describe the worship: one should worship the Goddess in the center;
one should worship the powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action in the three corners. (10.228)
One should worship the five Manmathas below that in the five corners;
afterwards, one should worship the six limbs and the other Yoginīs on the eight petals.
One should worship the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the outer enclosure (bhūpura) surrounding that;
for this indeed is the method of worship and the fire-oblation (homa) for all [the deities].
Furthermore, there is a specific distinction here regarding the malevolent rite for the destruction of enemies:
one should meditate on her as holding a sword and shield, fierce and possessing six arms. (10.231)

Seated upon the Garuḍa posture, performing the subjugation of enemies, one should first recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; indeed, one should then offer libations one hundred thousand times.
There shall be the destruction of all enemies, and one shall encounter no suffering anywhere.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Candramātṛ. (10.233)
Beginning with *māyā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) and ending with *vahnijāyā* (the word *svāhā*), this eleven-syllable mantra is proclaimed for Maṅgalā, the abode of auspiciousness. (10.234)
Having performed the six limbs by means of this [mantra] joined with the six long vowels, one should meditate upon her as three-eyed and resembling the rising sun. (10.235)
Her lotus-face was gently smiling, her lips were beautiful with vermilion,
and she held a pair of lotuses, a bow, and arrows in her sprout-like arms.
O Maheśānī, having meditated thus upon her who is resplendent with tinkling, soft anklets and a girdle-string, one should worship her as before.
Then, having recited the mantra obtained [from the guru] preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *māyā* (hrīṃ),
one should offer the bali-oblation to the Yoginīs, the Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and the Lord of the Gaṇas.
At the conclusion of all worship, Maṅgalā alone becomes pleased.
Now he describes the *puraścaraṇa*:
"For the sake of obtaining the grace of the Yoginī, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable. (10.239)
To counteract adverse circumstances and for the sake of favorable results, one should recite the mantra ten million times;
this is for the attainment of auspicious fruits that have been obstructed by unseen forces. (10.240)
For the sake of attainment, one should perform the daily recitation of the mantra a thousand times until the wicked Yoginī has been reduced to a hundred syllables.
When she is satisfied, one should consecrate the patient with ten syllables;
with a mantra consisting of syllables equal in number to her own, he who is intent upon her service [shall be healed].
The cessation of her suffering shall occur within the days corresponding to the [number of] syllables;
O best of gods, such is the procedure for the nine [vowels] to be understood. (10.243)
The Yoginī bestows equal fruits on both the left path and the right;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain Bhrāmarī, the mother of the earth. (10.244)
Having uttered "kṣī bhrāmari pada" and "jaya tānme adhīśvari," followed by "bhrāmaya klīḥ"—this sixteen-syllable mantra of hers has been proclaimed. (10.245)
Just as in the case of Piṅgalā, for her success, one should consecrate ten pieces of sugar with this [mantra] and cast them upon the path in the ten directions. (10.246)
Then, at dawn, one should set out on the road; for all those situated upon the path—tigers, serpents, and robbers alike—fall into a state of delusion.
One should always behave in this manner toward tax-collectors and wicked kings;
having written one's name on the sole of a sandal, one may then depart. (10.248)
He who recites the mantra for one yojana shall wander the earth.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Bhadrikā, the mother of Budha. (10.249)
First, one should utter the seed-syllable *plū*, which arises from its abundance of water;
then again, the phrase: "O Bhadrikā, grant me, [your] Bhadra. (10.250)
And one should say "vadecca parabhadrāṇi"; then, destroy the pair.
This mantra of Bhadrikā is considered to consist of the syllables of the Jina ending with "svāhā. (10.251)

The ritual of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is proclaimed by means of the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels; meditation upon Maṅgalā bestows auspiciousness, whereas [meditation upon] Śubhā yields evil results. 10-252.
The recitation and other rites for Piṅgalā have been taught according to the prescribed method;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the one named Dhanyā, the mother of the Guru. (10.253)
Having recited "Śrī Dhanade," the eight-syllable mantra "Dhanye Svāhā" is employed;
the ritual for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared by means of the first seed-syllable enriched with the six long vowels.
There is nothing in this world equal to Dhanyā as a bestower of fruits;
having performed the three-fold *puraścaryā*, one's sins accumulated in previous births [are destroyed]. (10.255)
Having become steadfast, Dhanyā bestows the state of being blessed upon the practitioner;
one should behold Dhanyā in Kāśī to the west of Bṛhaspatīśvara. || 10-256 ||
By performing the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) there, a Vaiśya is born truly fortunate.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the perfected mother of Śukra. (10.257)
Hrīḥ! Having uttered "may all my pride be accomplished," the mantra of Siddhā is proclaimed as ending with the heart [syllable] and consisting of the color of a friend (mitra). (10.258)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllable (*bīja*) itself, and carry out the recitation (*japa*) and other rites as previously described.
For those who worship the perfected ones (*siddha*), there is no failure of their ritual action (*karma*) anywhere. (10.259)
Whatever tradition the lay practitioners of Siddhā follow, everything indeed comes to fruition for them through the maturation of the deities of that very tradition. (10.260)
The sixfold ritual action is accomplished for him even without the propitiation of Manu;
now, therefore, I shall explain it further after having addressed the Mother of the Dull-witted One. (10.261)
Oṃ, destroy my disease, shatter it—this eleven-syllable mantra removes all diseases through its recitation for seven days. (10.262)
For one whose Ulkā-mantra is perfected, no disease shall exist in his residence;
during the great pestilence of Śītalā, [he should offer] a buffalo endowed with all auspicious marks.
Having released that [effigy] for the pleasure of Ulkā, one should carry it around the city again,
surrounded by various musical instruments and adorned with garments and other ornaments.
One should release it in whichever direction the pacification of misfortune may occur.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe Saṃkaṭā, the mother of Rāhu. (10.265)
Hrīḥ! O you who possess the two supreme forms, destroy my disease even in times of distress!
This sixteen-syllable mantra is the dispeller of all suffering. (10.266)
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times in prison, liberation from bondage occurs.
To the north of Vīreśvara in Kāśī is where Saṃkaṭā is situated. (10.267)
Having recited sixteen hundred thousand [times] there, one should perform the fire-oblation with *dūrvā* grass;
then that mantra will become perfected if it should issue forth from his mouth. (10.268)
(897) The suffering of such-and-such a person has gone; it is indeed destroyed.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Vikaṭā, the mother of Ketu. (10.269)
*Tāra*, *namo bhagavati vikaṭe vīrapālike*, and *prasīda*—this pair is proclaimed as the mantra consisting of sixteen syllables by nature. (10.270)
In Kāśī, situated near Vīreśvara, Vikaṭā resides to the west;
having recited this mantra there, children afflicted by the planets [are cured]. (10.271)
The womb of a barren woman, as well as the head of one who has given birth;
infants abandoned by their fathers and others, as well as those deprived of their mothers. (10.272)
"By the touch of the practitioner's hand, [the planets] become free from disease and long-lived.
Thus end the mantras of the *grahamātṛkā*.
Now follow the mantras of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*).
In that regard, first, the mantra of Śakra is stated in that very same place:
"Jñam indrāya namaḥ"—this is the six-syllabled mantra of Śakra. (10.273)

The metre is Paṅkti, the sage is Brahmā, and Indra is proclaimed as the deity; Māyā is the Śakti, *i* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and by means of that very seed-syllable, the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) is performed. (10.274)
Now, for the meditation:

I bow to Indra, the lord of the guardians of the directions, who is yellow in color, possesses a thousand eyes, holds a vajra and a lotus in his hands, is all-pervading, and is adorned with every ornament. (10.275)
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this [mantra] is described in that very same place:
"One should recite it one hundred thousand times (one lakh), and then perform oblations with sesame and clarified butter.
Once the mantra is thus perfected, the practitioner of mantras is fit to perform the ritual application (prayoga). (10.276)

Now, the mantra for Agni (in the *Śāradātilaka*): "The three *vyāhṛtis* shall belong to Agni: 'O Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here! Having addressed all rites, accomplish them, O beloved of Agni! (10.277).
This mantra beginning with "Tārā" is said to consist of twenty-five syllables;
Bhṛgu is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī its meter (chandaḥ), and Agni its deity (devatā). (10.278)
The ritual application of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) of the root mantra is declared to be divided by five, six, four, five, three, and two syllables, respectively. (10.279)
Now, for the meditation:

[He is] adorned with a golden garland draped over his shoulders and decorated with red wreaths and sandalwood paste; his crown shines with a mass of matted locks (*jaṭā*) like a cluster of flames, and he wears fine pearls and garments.

I worship Agni, who is red in hue, whose three eyes are slightly closed, and who holds with his arms the Śakti, the Svastika, a handful of Darbha grass, a rosary for recitation, the Sruk and Sruva ladles, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): Having received the mantra from the guru, the practitioner, having fasted on the fourteenth day, being pure in conduct and with senses subdued, should recite it one thousand times for each syllable of the sun. (10.281)
On the new moon day, one should feed the Brahmins with foods consisting primarily of sweets, according to one's ability; one should also give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) on this occasion.
Having enjoyed the offerings and brought together the materials for the oblation, one should purify them;
then, beginning from the following day, one should perform the homa without weariness.

The wise practitioner should continuously offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each of the following in sequence: banyan wood, rice, sesame, black mustard, clarified butter, and sacrificial offerings. (10.284)
Having thus completed the ten-day rite according to the prescribed rules, the knower of the ordinances,
having properly offered the final oblation on the eleventh day, [honored] the best of the twice-born.
Having worshipped him, one should satisfy him with wealth according to one's means and with due respect;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, consisting of a reddish-brown, milch cow.
Having given garments, wealth, grain, and so forth, one should fully satisfy the guru.
Now, regarding the mantra (in the *Merutantra*):
"Oṃ kroḥ hrīḥ āḥ," one should state that seed-syllable followed by the name "Vaivasvata" in the dative case ending in *-ṅe*. (10.287)
One should utter "Salutation to Dharmarāja, who bestows grace upon his devotees.
This twenty-four-syllable mantra of Yama grants all desired objects. (10.288)

One should meditate upon Yama, who is dark as a cloud, with a gracious countenance, adorned with various ornaments, and possessing six limbs through the twelve syllables of the *siddhi* mantra. (10.289)
One should worship Yama, who is mounted upon a buffalo, holds a staff, is praised by the ancestors,
surrounded by messengers assuming various forms, and is clad in white garments.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable and perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
Furthermore, the mantra of Nairṛta is found in that very same place.
Oṃ kṣaḥ! One should utter the word "pada" for Nirṛti, the lord of the rākṣasas. || 10-291 ||
To the smoke-colored one, with a sword in hand, whose vehicle is a preta;
ending in the dative case (ṅe), this thirty-syllable mantra is considered the heart-mantra.
Oṃ; with the five words beginning with *kṣamā* and ending with *hṛt*, one performs the five-limbed rite. Meditation:
[One should meditate on him] as wearing a crown, with tawny eyes, smoke-colored, and having a corpse for a vehicle. (10.293)
I worship the one served by various hosts of Rākṣasas, who bears a sword and shield.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for that very deity is as follows:
one should recite [the mantra] thirty thousand times and then offer oblations of guñjā seeds and clarified butter. (10.294)
Now follows the mantra of Varuṇa.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the mantra whose deity is Varuṇa:
one should utter the *tāra* (om), then *vaḥ*, then *varuṇāya*, and say *jalādhipataye* (to the lord of waters). (10.295)
And one should speak thus: "Salutation to the white-colored one, holding a noose in his hand;
salutation to the vehicle, the crocodile"—this consists of eleven syllables. (10.296)
The metre is Triṣṭubh, the seer is Vasiṣṭha, and Varuṇa is considered the deity.
With the five syllables beginning with *oṃ vaṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga*) is performed using the five words. || 10.297 ||

In meditation, he wears white garments; with his hands he holds a noose, a goad, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he dwells upon a clear lotus and is adorned with ornaments of pearls. (10.298)
May Varuṇa, who has a protruding belly and a serene countenance, be the bestower of treasures upon me.
[This is] the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One should recite the mantra one thousand times; the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed with lotus seeds.
Alternatively, the mantra for Vāyu is given in that very same place:

"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the most wonderful mantra of Vāyu. One should utter the Tāra (Oṃ), then 'Yaḥ', then 'Vāyave', followed by the word 'Prāṇādhipataye' (Lord of the Life-breaths). (10.300)
"O dark-colored one, O goad-holder, O you who have a deer as your vehicle—salutation to you. This is declared to be the mantra of Vāyu, who is of the color of a cow's hide. || 10-301 ||
The sage of this mantra is Gaṇaka, its metre is Nivṛt, and its deity is Vāyu.
Its five limbs consist of the words beginning with the seed-syllable *oṃ ya*. (10.302)

Dhyāna: [One should visualize] a black-colored [deity], running, mounted upon a deer, exceedingly swift, holding a noose and a goad in his hands, and accompanied by the scent of the Pretas and Kṛtyās. (10.303)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times and perform oblations (*homa*) with parched grain and clarified butter.
At that time, one whose mantra is perfected shall become superior in strength upon the earth. (10.304)
Now, the mantra of Kuvera is given in that very same place:
"Next, therefore, I shall fully declare the auspicious mantras of the king of kings;
one should address them to Yakṣa, to Kuvera, and to Vaiśravaṇa. (10.305)
To the Lord of Wealth and Grain, one should utter the words "Wealth and Grain";
one should say "Grant me prosperity," ending with "Cause [it] to be given, O Beloved of Agni. (10.306)

The sage Viśravas is said to consist of thirty-five syllables; the meter is Bṛhatī, with six limbs [in the first half] and eight limbs [in the second], consisting of three, four, eight, and eight [syllables]. (10.307)
Meditation: [He is] peaceful, resembling an emerald, adorned with a crown and other ornaments, holding a boon-granting gesture and a mace, pot-bellied, and attended by yakṣas. || 10.308 ||
Regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds ten thousand times.
One should worship [the deity] upon the seat of Dharma and so forth, along with the limbs, the world-protectors, and the weapons. (10.309)
One should mutter the mantra ten thousand times in a temple of Śiva for the increase of wealth;
muttered one hundred thousand times while seated at the root of a bilva tree, it bestows an abundance of riches.
Now I shall declare another mantra: one should utter "Oṃ Śrī" and "Oṃ Hrīḥ.
Then [one should recite] "Śrī Hrīḥ Klīḥ Śrī Klīḥ," followed by "Namaḥ Vitteśvarāya" (Salutation to the Lord of Wealth). || 10-311 ||

This [mantra] consists of sixteen syllables; its sage and other [constituents] are as before. The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed with [the mantras] consisting of three, two, two, two, five, and two [syllables]. Meditation, worship, and so forth are as previously described. (10.312)
Now, another mantra for that same [deity] is given there:
"Now I shall declare another mantra of Kuvera consisting of six syllables:
*Tāra* (Oṃ), *vaiśravaṇāya*, and *svāhā*; herein, however, there are five limbs. (10.313)
With the five mantra-syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*, he describes the visualization:
"A golden jar full of wealth, as well as a casket of jewels. (10.314)
Holding [the child] with both hands, he was short-limbed, pot-bellied,
seated upon a jeweled throne beneath the earth, and possessed a smiling countenance.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for each syllable; the fire-oblation and worship are as before, and it yields great wealth.
By practicing this, the Yakṣiṇīs and others likewise become submissive. (10.316)
Now, the mantra of Īśāna is as follows:
Having uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the *haṃsa*, one should then say "to Īśāna," and then "to the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyādhipataye*)," and then say "sphaṭika" (crystal). (10.317)
To the one of fair complexion, holding a trident in his hand, ending with the vocative particle *ṅe*, and having the bull as his vehicle;
this mantra, ending with *namaḥ*, is declared to consist of thirty-one syllables. (10.318)
The five-limbed [mantras] consisting of five words, beginning with *oṃ haṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, as well as those which are the mantras of the Śaktis—these are proclaimed as the Vidyās. (10.319)
And those mantras of yours, O Puruṣas, would not bear fruit without a Puruṣa, just as a woman [is barren] without a man. (10.320)
Where the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) is not mentioned, one should employ Īśāna.
In another Tantra, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this is stated to be eight thousand recitations.
Now, the Brahma-mantra (in the *Merutantra*):
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme mantra of Brahmā.
One should utter the syllable TĀRAṂ, followed by PĀŚAṂ, and then say "to Brahmā, the Lord of the World";
thereafter, one should say "to the red-colored Guardian of the Upper World."

And for the one with a lotus in hand (Padmahasta), the word ending in the dative case (padma-hastāya) followed by the syllable "syāt" and the vehicle (ardha-savāhana), ending with "namaḥ," and containing the phonemes of Bāṇa and Rāma—this is proclaimed as the mantra. (10.323)

With the six words beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and *pāśa*, ending with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the heart (*hṛd*), there is no worship for this [mantra] due to my curse; its recitation (*japa*) alone is prescribed. (10.324)
By merely reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed color, one becomes capable of both restraint and grace.
One should worship this [deity] upon a ten-petaled lotus; on the petals starting from the east and ending with the northeast, the gods [are to be worshipped].
My curse does not apply there; the curse applies only to [the omission of] worship. Now follows the mantra of Ananta: "Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the wonderful mantra of Śeṣa. (10.326)
One should utter "Tāram" and "Māyā" for Ananta, the lord of the Nāgas,
and for the seven lords of the worlds, beginning with Atala, who are golden-hued.
"Salutation to the one with a discus in hand, whose vehicle is Garuḍa; [this] ends with 'namaḥ'.
Thus, the forty-syllable mantra of Ananta has been proclaimed. (10.328)
On each fourteenth day, one should recite the mantra one thousand four hundred times;
one should offer milk into the fire and feed fourteen Brahmins.
One should observe the fourteenth lunar day with devotion, and one shall become endowed with wealth and grain;
one fallen from a kingdom shall regain his kingdom, and one desiring knowledge shall become a scholar. (10.330)
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, special worship is prescribed.
Thus ends the section on the Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas). Now begins the procedure for the Purascaraṇa of Gāyatrī and other rites.
(Merutantra) Now I shall proclaim the Gāyatrī of the Lord of Mantras, the Mother of the Vedas. (10.331)
But that [wisdom] by which Brahman with attributes is sung and expounded—without which liberation does not arise for anyone—is [the wisdom of Brahman without attributes]. (10.332)
Mahākāla himself should perform the sacrifice within the one whose essential nature is Mahāmāyā;
by her power, both you and I have become like another Jātakāla. (10.333)
"Saguṇabrahma" means that which consists of the nature of light situated within the solar orb and composed of the three qualities (*guṇas*). As it is said in the *Bṛhatsiddhāntasāra*:
"That light residing in the solar orb which consists of the three qualities—that is this Saguna Brahman, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (10.334)
"Without qualities" (*nirguṇam*) means being devoid of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the three qualities (*guṇa*).

"Without whom" (*yāṃ vinā*) refers to the fact that this very [Vidyā] is the cause of liberation, since it establishes the quality-less Brahman by means of designating the Brahman of qualities (*guṇabrahma*).
(In the *Śāradā-tantra*)

The seven vyāhṛtis, beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, followed by the words *tat* and so forth, together with the *gāyatrī* consisting of twenty-four syllables and the *śiras*, [constitute the mantra]. (10.335)
This mantra is proclaimed as the essence extracted from all the Vedas;
Brahmā, the Goddess, the Gāyatrī, and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) are declared to be its components. (10.336)
These sages and others have been proclaimed by the seers as the Ṛṣis of the Praṇava:
Yamadagni, Bharadvāja, Bhṛgu, Gautama, and Kāśyapa. (10.337)
They know Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha to be the ṛṣis of the vyāhṛtis;
furthermore, [the meters] are gāyatrī, uṣṇih, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, and paṅkti. (10.338)
The Triṣṭubh and Jagatī are declared by the wise to be the meters;
the seven-flamed fire, Vāyu, Sūrya, Vākpati, Varuṇa, and Vṛṣa [are their presiding deities]. (10.339)
The Viśvedevas are proclaimed as the deities of these [goddesses] in succession. (In the Merutantra:
Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic, is declared to be the sage (ṛṣi) of the Gāyatrī. 10-340.
The Gāyatrī is said to be the metre (chandas), and Savitṛ is remembered as the deity.
In another tantra: "Agni is the mouth, Brahmā is the head, Viṣṇu is the heart, and Śiva is the forehead. (10.341)
Sāṅkhyāyana shall be the lineage, and the three worlds are the three feet. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
Brahmā is remembered as the sage of this [mantra], and Devī-ādikā as its meter. (10.342)
The Gāyatrī is said by the wise to have the Supreme Self as its deity. (In the Merutantra:
The seven Vyāhṛtis, beginning with Bhūḥ, [should be placed] on the heart, the face, the two shoulders, and the pair of thighs. 10-343.
And one should place [the mantras] in the abdomen in sequence; this is remembered as the first nyāsa.
It should be at the joints beginning with the toes of the feet, and at the joint of the ankle and the foot. (10.344)
One should place the phonemes in sequence upon the ankles and knees, at their joints, as well as at the joints of the knees and thighs, on the genitals, the navel, the heart, and the throat. (10.345)
At the joints at the bases of the fingers of the hand, at the wrist, at the elbow, at the base of the arm, and also on the face, the nose, and the two cheeks. (10.346)
One should place the syllables in sequence upon the eyes, ears, eyebrows, head, the lower left ear, the right ear, the mouth, and the crown of the head. (10.347)
The second [method], the placement of the syllables of the Gāyatrī, has been fully proclaimed.
The ten words of the Gāyatrī are placed on the head, between the eyebrows, the eyes, and the mouth. (10.348)
Then one should assign [the syllables] to the throat, heart, navel, secret place, knees, and feet;
the third assignment is the placement of the head of the Gāyatrī upon the region of the head.
The heart is declared for Brahmā, the head is said for Viṣṇu;
the tuft (śikhā) is for Rudra, and the armor (kavaca) is proclaimed for Īśvara.
The eye is said to belong to Sadāśiva, and the weapon is remembered as belonging to the Soul of All;
this is proclaimed as the fourth six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
One should place the *vyāhṛtis* in sequence upon the knees, the shins, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the forehead; and "Supreme Brahman" is to be placed upon the head. (10.352)
Furthermore, this fifth method of placement (nyāsa) by means of the vyāhṛtis is proclaimed:
"Tat savituḥ" is for the heart, and likewise "vareṇyam" is for the head.
"Bhargo devasya" is the Śikhā; "dhīmahi" is remembered as the Kavaca;
"dhiyo yo naḥ" is declared to be the Netra; and the remaining portion is proclaimed to be the Astra. (10.354)
This, indeed, is the sixth nyāsa; these six are the removers of sin.
Having performed three rounds of prāṇāyāma, one should then practice meditation. (10.355)
As for the meditation:
one should meditate upon her who possesses three eyes with faces having the luster of pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white;
who is adorned with a jeweled crown bound with lotuses; and whose nature consists of the colors corresponding to the principles (tattvas).

I worship Gāyatrī, who carries in her hands the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the goad, the kusha grass, a radiant skull, the triple-strand cord, the conch, the discus, and a pair of lotuses.
The *Dhyānāntara* is described in another tantra:

"Brahmāṇī has four faces; she holds a rosary, a water-pot, and a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle in her hands; she possesses a reddish luster, a moon-like face, and the form of a young girl embodying the *Ṛgveda*."
May Gāyatrī, adorned by the orb of the sun—the delight of the sky who sports upon her swan-mount—be meditated upon within our hearts for the perpetual attainment of abundant prosperity. 10.357
Now I shall describe the distinction in meditation for midday and the final twilight. Likewise:
[one should meditate on] Rudrāṇī, who is in the bloom of youth, three-eyed, and clothed in a tiger skin.
Ambikā holds a skull-topped staff, a trident, a rosary, a bracelet, and the gesture of fearlessness.

She whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon shimmering amidst a mass of matted locks like a cluster of lightning, who is always accompanied by Sāvitrī, who rides upon a bull, whose body is dark-hued, and who takes the form of the Yajurveda— she should be meditated upon as the aged goddess, radiant with the luster of a dark cloud and adorned with yellow garments.
Then, with divine ornaments upon her lotus-like limbs, she bore the conch and the mace.
Seated upon the shoulders of Tārkṣya, she is the supreme Vaiṣṇavī who is worshipped by the entire world;
she is indeed the Goddess Sarasvatī, whose nature is always that of the Sāman chants, and who is to be meditated upon.
Her worship yantra is described in the *Merutantra*.
An eight-petaled lotus should be drawn, with the syllable *hrīḥ* situated in its pericarp. || 10-360 ||
One should draw two vowels each toward every cardinal and intermediate direction;
on the filaments and at their tips, one should write the syllables of the Gāyatrī three by three.
But within the space between those two outer circles, one should draw the letters beginning with *ka*, as well as "Umā," "Apo," "Jyoti," "Rasa," "Amṛta," and "Brahman. (10.362)
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ"—this [mantra], when used in the yantra, bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (In the Śāradā-tantra:
Having first performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Gāyatrī at the two twilights. (10.363)
Reciting three times the Gāyatrī joined with the seven Vyāhṛtis and accompanied by the Śiras, one should restrain the vital breaths (prāṇas) with a focused mind and a controlled intellect. (10.364)
This is declared to be breath control (prāṇāyāma), which removes all evils;
one who is initiated should recite the Gāyatrī joined with the three Vyāhṛtis.
Now follows the procedure for her worship (in the *Merutantra*):
"Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess together with her ten enclosures;
having first worshipped the Mistress of the Gods, one should then worship [the deities] at the tips of the corners. (10.366)
Starting from the fire-corner (southeast) of the triangle and proceeding clockwise, the deities Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and Vaiṣṇavī constitute the first enclosure. (10.367)
In front of him, one should worship eight [deities] in the eight directions in sequence:
Āditya and the others—Ravi, Prajñā, Bhānu, and likewise Prabhā.
Bhāskara and Sandhyā constitute this second enclosure;
thereafter, one should worship the six limbs upon the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus.
And within the middle of the third pada of the Gāyatrī, one should worship these:
Prahlādinī, Prabhā, Nityā, Viśvaṃbharā, and Vilāsinī.
Prabhāvatī, Jayā, and Śāntā—this is the fourth enclosure;
thereafter, one should worship Kānti, Durgā, and Sarasvatī at the tips of the petals.
Viśvarūpā, Viśālā, Īśānī, Vyāpinī, and Vimalā— these are declared, in sequence, as the worship of the fifth enclosure.
In the eight-petalled lotus immediately following that, these Śaktis are to be worshipped:
Tamo’pahāriṇī (the Dispeller of Darkness), Sūkṣmā (the Subtle One), Viśvayoni (the Source of the Universe), and Jayāvahā (the Bringer of Victory).
The sixth [enclosure] shall be Padmālayā, who possesses supreme splendor and has the form of a lotus;
and in front, there are the seven Mothers beginning with Brāhmī.
The eighth is declared to be Aruṇā; this indeed is the seventh enclosure (saptamāvaraṇa). [The deities are] Ravi, Sita, Kuja, Rāhu, Śani, Candra, Budha, and Guru. (10.375)
This eighth enclosure is in the eight directions of the square;
the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) are declared in the ninth, and their weapons in the tenth.
In this manner, one should worship the Goddess and display her mudrās to her;
the mudrās are explained in that very same place. Now, the twenty-four mudrās of Gāyatrī shall be described. (10.377)
One should show these [mudrās] at the beginning of the recitation (japa) and likewise the deities and their fruits.
With the hands joined together, the fingers are slightly bent and turned upward; this is the Sumukha [mudrā]. (10.378)
There, the power is the refreshing one that bestows bliss upon the practitioner;
the two hands, resembling the interior of a lotus bud, are joined together in a hollow embrace. (10.379)
His power is eternally universal and brings joy to the entire world.
His two hands are extended and joined together, palms upward with long fingers.
The power named Hṛdayā is that which goes to the hearts of all.
It is formed by joining the two hands with the palms spread wide and the two index fingers released from each other. (10.381)
Power (*śakti*), however, is stainless; by its influence, one becomes free from fault.
That which is called "two-faced" (*dvimukhā*) consists of two [hands] joined together facing each other. (10.382)
The union of the two little fingers alone is Śakti; its constant form is as follows:
in the [mudrā] called Trimukhī, the two hands are joined with the two ring fingers interlocked. (10.383)
The remaining fingers joined together constitute the Śakti mudrā;
it shines forth when the four faces [of the hands] are joined with two hands, with the middle fingers meeting. (10.384)
The remaining fingers joined together is proclaimed as the *lolāśakti*;
likewise, the *pañcamukhī* mudrā is that in which there is a joining of the two index fingers. (10.385)
When the fingers are separated and not turned away, it is the Śakti-mudrā; when it brings about peace, it is the Śānti-mudrā.
When the fingers are joined completely, that becomes the Ṣaṇmukha-mudrā. (10.386)
Excluding the pair of little fingers, this is proclaimed as the *śakti* [mudrā] of Durgā.
The mudrā named *adhomukha* consists of the two hands turned face down. (10.387)
With the fingertips contracted and joined, Sarasvatī is its power;
such hands form the mudrā named Vyāpikāñjali.
The distinction here, however, is that the hands are turned upward; Viśvarūpa is the deity here. That is the mudrā called Śakaṭa, formed with the fingers of both hands joined at the tips.
When the two fists are bound with palms facing downward, it is Viśākhā;
here, however, when the two bound fists are joined together, it is Yamapāśa.
The two index fingers should be placed palm-down there; the deity to be known here is Granthitā, provided that the fingers are joined together at their joints. (10.391)
With the palms facing upward and the thumbs raised, the left hand is declared to be Śakti;
the Sammukhonmukha mudrā consists of the two hands joined with the fingers pointing upward.
The right hand should face downward and the left upward;
this is the mudrā named Vilambā, with the tips of the fingers raised and turned upward. (10.393)
In that [mudrā] in which the two hands are stainless, its power is proclaimed as Śakti. When the two fists are joined with one another, it is the Muṣṭika [mudrā].
With the two hands turned upward, the Śakti mudrā consisting of Tamas is said to be formed; when the little fingers are joined and facing each other, it is the Matsya mudrā.
The remaining [limbs] have their joints turned upward and are curved; the Śakti is made of gold.
The tortoise faces downward on the left, while on the right it is likewise positioned on the back.
His subtle Śakti, which accomplishes subtle purposes, has stepped upon him;
Vārāhī is on the upper right hand, while the left hand is turned upward.
Having placed it face down, one should bend it with the Viśvayonikā;
this is the mudrā named Siṃhākrāntā, when the two hands have their fingers extended. (10.398)
Placed above the ears, its power brings victory;
this is the mudrā named Mahākrāntā, with the tips [of the fingers] bent as before.
The two hands placed at the ears are declared to be the mudrā named Padmālayā;
when the left index finger is raised slightly upward, it becomes the Mudgara.
Held in the right hand, the supreme deity here is Śobhā;
the mudrā is called Pallava, wherein the fingers are made into sprouts. (10.401)
One should display the Śakti before the Goddess; she is celebrated as being in the form of a mace (gadā).
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for that very [mantra]:
twenty-four lakhs [of recitations] are said to constitute the puraścaraṇa. (10.402)
For the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, one should offer three thousand oblations each of milk-rice, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, cooked rice, and excellent sacrificial fuel sticks.
Then, having performed the libations and other rites, and having diligently satisfied the gurus,
the wise one should carry out the ritual applications preceded by their permission.
Thus ends the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* of the Gāyatrī.
Now follows the exposition of the *vyāhṛtis* (from the *Prapañcasāra*).
The *vyāhṛtis* begin with the word *bhūḥ*; the word *bhūḥ* exists as that very state.
That state is declared to be "Being" (*sat*), because it is the ground (*bhūḥ*) of the six measures. (10.405)
The word *bhuvaḥ* is connected [to the deity] because it denotes existence (*bhūtatva*) and because it is the cause;
the word *svar* is said to be so called because it brings about all prosperity (*sarvaśrīkaraṇa*) and because it serves its own purpose (*svārthatā*). (10.406)
Because of its greatness, it is called *mahaḥ*; it is impelled by that [Brahman].
Precisely because it gives birth to all, it is therefore the *vyāhṛti* known as *janaḥ*.
It is remembered as austerity because of its nature as knowledge and likewise because of its nature as heat;
it is truth because of its supremacy, its selfhood, and its own infinite knowledge. (10.408)
The unification of the *vyāhṛtis* with the *praṇava* is stated in that very same place:
"The internal connection of the *praṇava* with the *vyāhṛtis* is now declared:
the letter 'A' is *bhūḥ*, the letter 'U' is *bhuvaḥ*, and the letter 'M' is said to be *svaḥ*. (10.409)
Bindu, Mahas, as well as Nada, Jana, Shakti, and Tapas are remembered;
Shanti and Satya are proclaimed—this is the existent, that supreme state. (10.410)
Now, following the explanation of the Gāyatrī, the identity of the Praṇava with the Vyāhṛtis and the Gāyatrī has been stated in that very same place.
Here too, the identity of the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Gāyatrī is now being declared; the subject matter already mentioned previously is here further described. (10.411)
By this second singular case ending,
[it is indicated that] the cause of the creation and so forth of all things is that which has the nature of light within the solar orb.
The subject to be expressed is the Supreme Brahman, who is eternal bliss;
that which is expressed by the phrase "of the Sun" (*savitṛ*) is [the word] *tat* in the nominative singular. (10.413)
The word "dhātu" arises from that which denotes the procreation of living beings;
it refers to the progenitor of all classes of living beings at all times. (10.414)
It is remembered as *vareṇya* because it is worthy of being chosen, and likewise because it is to be served, worshipped by all, and prayed to. (10.415)
Thus, for the first eight-syllable [mantra], the *vyāhṛti* is remembered as "Bhūḥ"; it is called "Bharga" because it burns away sin and because it is affectionate toward its devotees. (10.416)
Of the god who is eternally endowed with qualities such as the bestowing of rain, or likewise, who shines by means of his sovereignty and splendor. (10.417)

The word *dhīmahi* is derived from the verbal root *dhyai*, meaning "to contemplate. O Goddess of Gods, one should contemplate with the divine eye, which consists of the form of the Vidyā and begins with the sacred syllable (*oṃ*). (10.418)
The visible golden deity is eternally established within the sun;
he whose splendor is devoid of inferiority is "golden" (hiraṇmaya). (10.419)
We indeed always contemplate: "He who is subtle, that am I. This is declared to be the manifestation of the second eight-syllable mantra, namely *Bhuvaḥ*. (10.420)
The word *dhiyaḥ* is explained as being synonymous with *buddhiḥ* and *manaḥ* due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*);
furthermore, a change of gender has been made [from feminine to masculine] according to the rule regarding suffixes, verbal endings, and voice (*sūptiṅupagraha*). (10.421)
That which is incomparable splendor, consisting of the essence of all the gods, is said to be the cause for the destruction of the sins of those who worship it. || 10.422 ||
The substitute "naḥ" is prescribed for the sixth case of the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*;
therefore, it means "of us," and [the word] *pracodayāt* is used in the sense of a prayer. (10.423)
The third [foot] of the eight-syllabled [pāda] is also declared to have a svarita accent.
Thus, it is remembered that this [verse] has ten words, three of which consist of eight syllables. (10.424)
There are four [mantras] consisting of six syllables each, making twenty-four syllables in total; such is this [mantra] of the all-pervading Lord Savitṛ. (10.425)
May that supreme Bharga, the most excellent, which effects the destruction of the sins of those who worship it, and which has been meditated upon by us—may it impel our intellects. (10.426)
Thus the Gāyatrī has been explained here; now its head is described:
"Water, light, essence"—by these, the splendor of Soma and Agni is expressed. (10.427)
The entire world is composed of that; it is known as the two-fold essence and light.
Because it is imperishable, it is called *amṛta* (nectar); because of its vastness, it is designated as *brahman*.

When Brahman, whose nature is bliss and which is characterized by existence, knowledge, and so forth, is expressed as "Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ," that which is proclaimed as "So 'ham" (That am I) is Om. (10.429)
This, however, is like the Veda; it is called the head of the Veda.
As indicated by its characteristics, it is established within the essences of the Vedas. (10.430)
"He who seeks fruit obtains fruit; he who seeks liberation attains liberation.
This is the explanation of the Vyāhṛtis. Now follows the Praṇava mantra.
(From the *Prapañcasāra*):

Now I shall proclaim the excellent mantra known as the *praṇava*, together with its recitation (*japa*), its worship (*arcana*), its ritual preparation for oblations (*huta-kḷpti*), and its meditative practice (*upāsana*). (10.431)

It removes all sins without exception, is a wish-fulfilling tree for various desires, bestows the attainment of the fruit of liberation, and is served by those with pure minds; it is the primordial vowel joined with the immortal [letter *m*] and the seventh [vowel] together with the bindu. (10.432)
In this context, the Praṇava is said to consist of three morae and to be the embodiment of all mantras.
The sage of this mantra is Prajāpati; its metre is declared to be the Gāyatrī beginning with the Goddess; and its deity is known as the Supreme Self throughout the worlds. (10.433)

The practitioner of mantra should form the limbs (aṅgas) by means of the vowels joined with the *jāti* syllables, or else with the *vyāhṛtis* excluding *satya*, combined with the *aklīvas* (the non-neuter vowels), the pair (*yuga*), the middle (*madhya*), and the *dhruva* (the fixed vowel *m*), in due order. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*).

Viṣṇu, whose body is adorned with a radiant crown, armlets, bracelets, necklaces, waist-bands, anklets, and hip-ornaments, and who is embellished by divine earrings shaped like jewels and sea-monsters; || 10.434 ||

I bow to Him who holds in His uplifted hands the stainless discus, conch, lotus, and mace; who is clothed in radiant yellow silk; whose splendor shines like the rising sun; and who is seated upon a lotus.
For this [mantra], the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of ten million recitations (*koṭijapa*).
It is stated in that very same [text]: "The initiated one should mutter this mantra one million times and offer oblations in the homa ten percent of that amount. (10.435)
At the conclusion of that, one should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee, or else fuel-sticks produced from the trees sacred to the Brahmins.
He who offers into the fire clarified butter, milk-rice, rice, sesame, fuel-sticks, and ghee— || 10.436 ||

Having described the ritual of worship: "In this manner, the practitioner of mantra, having performed recitation, oblation, and worship with the *tāra-mantra*, shall obtain the desired fruit pertaining to both this world and the next before long."
And having accepted the various divisions, one may also employ the yogas.
"Having attained complete prosperity here through these [practices],
that yogi reaches the abode of Viṣṇu at the end and attains the Truth.
Thus ends the preliminary ritual for the Praṇava.
Now follows the Vedic Mṛtyuñjaya mantra. (In the Merutantra:
"Fear of death, however, always exists for everyone in all undertakings. (10.438)
When that [mind] is conquered, a person may accomplish everything from the state of the gods down to liberation;
for that purpose, I shall fully explain the mantra known as Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death).
There would be no worship of Him, and one born in such a lineage would be short-lived and afflicted by disease.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. (10.440)
"May I be released from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, into immortality.
Vasiṣṭha is the sage, the Anuṣṭubh is the metre, and Tryambaka is the deity. (10.441)
He describes the meditation on the six-limbed [mantra] consisting of three, four, eight, five, two, and three syllables:
[he visualizes the deity] bathing the head with the nectar-fluids from two jars held in his two hands.
With two [hands] they bear rosaries of dead men's eyes, and with two others they carry the Supreme.
I worship Lord Śiva, who resides on Kailāsa, seated upon a pure lotus, wearing a crown of the new moon, possessing three eyes, and holding two nectar-pots placed in his folded hands.
[This is] the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One who has conquered the senses should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times while meditating in this manner.
One should perform the oblation ten thousand times with ten substances saturated with ghee.
Those ten substances are mentioned in that very same place:
*vilva*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *vaṭa*, sesame, and mustard seeds. (10.444)
Having gratified [the deity] with milk-rice, curd, and dūrvā grass one thousand times each, and having performed the consecration, one should then satisfy the brahmins and honor the guru.
When this has been performed, this Great Mantra becomes fit for practical application.
Thus concludes the Vedic *puraścaraṇa* of Mṛtyuñjaya. Now follows the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* of the Rudrādhyāya.
In that very place, the illustrious Viṣṇu said:
"O God of gods, O Great God, O you who bestow grace upon your devotees! (10.446)
"You are Time for the worlds, and this supreme Mahāmāyā is yours;
tell us, then, which mantras and hymns bring satisfaction to both of us."
"By which [means] there is both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and indeed neither affliction nor [even that]?
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Viṣṇu, you have asked about a secret; it must not be spoken to a twice-born who is a follower of Tantra. (10.448)

In this Tantra, which is the supreme among the four Vedas and the sole abode of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, you have asked about my *tāmasa* form, even though [this work] is *sāttvika*. (10.449)
Know that this mantra, the Lord of Hymns, is my Śatarudriya;
its meters are the Anuṣṭubh and others, and Aghora is considered its sage.
Its deity is Rudra, and the Supreme Person is Āditya.
(In the Paddhati:
The application is for the recitation of the Śatarudriya for the pleasure of Śrī Rudra. 10-451.
Now, the placement of the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) is as follows:
*oṃ agnihotrātmane aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*;
*oṃ darśapaurṇamāsātmane tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ*. (p. 916)
Oṃ, salutation to the self of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice with the two middle fingers.
Oṃ, salutation to the self of the Nirūḍhapaśubandha sacrifice with the two ring fingers. Oṃ, salutation to the self of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice with the two little fingers.
Oṃ, salutation to the essence of one hundred and forty thousand [pores] with both palms and backs of the hands.
In this manner, the placement (nyāsa) of the heart and other limbs is performed.
The great placement (mahānyāsa), however, has been omitted for fear of excessive prolixity.
Now, concerning meditation:

with the nectar vomited by the full moon shimmering upon the crest of the crystal *liṅga*, whose light flashes throughout the universe from the depths of the netherworld (*pātāla*) to the heights of the sky, filling the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

For the sake of attaining his desired goal, a Brahmin should constantly mutter the Rudrānuvākas while meditating upon the Lord, the wondrous-footed one, who is the sole master beyond all measure; he should thus consecrate Śiva.
(From the Merutantra:
Then one should perform the worship of the *liṅga* according to the method described for the earthen [liṅga]:
"Worshipped by humans, by the *siddhas*, and by gods, asuras, and others... (10.453).
I propitiate you with devotion; accept me, O Maheśvara!
Let the wise bay horses bring you hither together with their conscious, bannered steeds. (10.454)
Come quickly with powerful winds and waters, swift as thought, for my oblation; salutations to Śarva!

O Rudra, pass beyond the Mūjavat mountains with that which is your own portion; with bow unstrung, carrying the Pināka, clad in skins, wearing a tiger-skin garment, and being auspicious, pass by safely.
He has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands;
bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly. The great god has entered into mortals. Be gracious, O Lord of Gods; be well-disposed, O Śaṅkara! (10.455)
Be at peace here and remain facing me, O Lord, Sovereign of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship. (10-456)
For that long, remain present within this liṅga with a state of loving devotion;
thereafter, perform the consecration with the five nectars in due order.
Then, after purifying with pure water, one should perform the worship;
thereafter, one should perform the "Raudrī" stream-offering, according to its prescribed ritual procedure.
By reciting the two chapters beginning with "namaste rudrāgnāviṣṇu," this is declared to be the "āvartana" rite, which bestows the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
The man who performs the ritual ablution at the whirlpool every day shall have his daily sins and those born of fate destroyed. (10.460)

If that [karma] born of previous births is diminished by the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana), then a single recitation of the first [Anuvāka] and a full Anuvāka of the second shall remove it. (10.461)
Thus may there be obeisance to Bhava; likewise, Agni and Viṣṇu individually.
This is declared to be Rudrī, which cuts away fierce sins.
Whoever performs this daily consecration of the Liṅga, the sins committed throughout birth after birth perish year by year. (10.463)
When the sins committed over seven lifetimes are destroyed, prosperity increases, the lineage attains stability, and fame spreads to the ends of the earth. (10.464)
And just as its form is produced, so it perishes in the water;
this is proclaimed as the Laghurudra by means of the eleven Rudrīs. || 10.465 ||
Those by whom the *liṅga* has been consecrated with these eleven [mantras] do not behold the son of the Sun (the Lord). By means of these eleven, Mahārudra is proclaimed.
This fire-oblation, performed for indigent twice-born men, is remembered as the destroyer of great sins; its fruit is said to be equal to that of the Soma sacrifice.
p. 918) Because of the lack of eligibility for initiation in the Kali age, this is the accepted view:
the Atirudra is proclaimed as consisting of eleven Mahārudras. || 10-468 ||

Likewise: "In whichever Vedic school both [mantras] are recited according to one's own traditional study, they should be recited by him in that manner; he should not effect a division of the Vedic school. (10.469)
He under whose branch Rudra does not recite the Taittirīya—
that branch belongs to the sacrificer, established through the mediation of the Brāhmaṇa.
Alternatively, the Taittirīya [branch] alone should be employed, and no other branch;
a ritual action performed by mixing branches would bring destruction upon the sacrificer. (10.471)
That Brahmin who, out of greed for wealth, consecrates me for the sake of another shall be known as a Cāṇḍāla and remain destitute for seven births.
If, however, a householder performs worship with effort for the sake of sowing seeds,
the expiation for that is one-tenth of the number of recitations and offerings performed.
Likewise:
"He in whose branch Rudra is not included, accompanied by the Pariśiṣṭas—he, having lost his own branch, should indeed recite that Taittirīya Rudra. (10.474)
Now the Rudrādhyāya, together with its ritual application (prayoga) and mantras, shall be explained; it must never be spoken to one who is unrefined or to a follower of Tantra.
Therein, first:
beginning with *oṃ namaste rudramanyave* and ending with *mā hiṃsīḥ puruṣaṃ jagat*.
The procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
The wise man, having conquered his senses, should recite these verses one million times;
he should offer oblations one hundred thousand times, verse by verse, with [fuel sticks] the size of a hollowed palm.
Whatever task one undertakes while consuming barley, wheat, honey, sesame, clarified butter, and curd, its accomplishment is brought about. (10.477)
In the same way, if one performs a thousand oblations on the eleventh day, the infant mortality occurring in the village will perish; there is no doubt about this. (10.478)
