The epidemic that kills children in a village perishes in twelve days;
however, a fire-oblation performed for fifteen days destroys calamities affecting the entire kingdom.
Through twenty nights of fire-offerings, the calamities of the land are destroyed;
through fire-offerings for a full month, the calamities of the earth shall perish.
When a calamity has befallen the cattle, one should then offer oblations in the middle of the cow-pen with fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood ten thousand times; thus peace is produced.
"By performing twenty thousand *homa* offerings, great peace will certainly be attained.
By the word of Śiva... and so forth. One should recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times, and liberation from the curse will arise. (10.482)
In the cold season, however, by chanting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times in the water at dawn, one shall become happy. It has been said:
"One hundred thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite (puraścaryā); the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with white mustard seeds. (10.483)
This other application for the transmission of disease is now described:
having consecrated seven mustard seeds with mantras, [one should apply them] to the patient. (10.484)
One should scatter [the mustard seeds] in the four directions; thus protection arises from the ten directions.
Having consecrated seven mustard seeds with mantras, one should go on the road. (10.485)
If one constantly casts [the water] in the ten directions, safety on the road is produced;
one is protected from Brahma-rākṣasas, yakṣas, and others, as well as piśācas, pretas, and bhūtas. (10.486)
Those seeking wealth should strike [the target] repeatedly with mustard seeds infused [with power] and consecrated seven times, preceded by the recitation of the mantra. (10.487)
Taking the wealth, they depart; and that [wealth] is quickly placed in their hands.
Having stepped upon the crest-lock (śikhā), one should sacrifice and strike with white mustard seeds. (10.488)
Throughout the entire night, the afflictions caused by Skanda and other planetary spirits are destroyed;
having consecrated it with this mantra, one should administer the medicine prescribed in the scriptures.
At that time, for the sake of those qualities, he should otherwise, according to the ritual, consecrate water with mantras and give it; [this cures] the disease arising from all living beings.
One may remove the afflictions of all seizing spirits by striking with mustard seeds;
likewise, one shall conquer the suffering arising from all elemental beings by wearing sacred ash.
Day and night, one should consecrate the trident with mantras;
one thousand times each, one should cast it into a lake inhabited by nāgas.
Accompanied by their kin, the serpents go to destruction;
having consecrated ashes with mantras, one should place them in a house infested by serpents. (10.493)
One should cast [the mantra] with the sound of a clap of the hands (*tāla*); this becomes the destruction of serpents.
"He who is copper-colored," and so forth;
with these two [verses], one worships the Sun at its rising and setting. (10.494)
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for three years, there shall be the arising of inexhaustible food.
One should bathe Śiva with milk over which the mantra has been recited one thousand times.
One becomes pleased by a single oblation, and there is a shower [of benefits] from a bath with ghee.
One should offer flowers of linseed in a number of ten thousand.
One who is powerless shall attain mastery, and the Sun-god shall become a granter of boons;
one should perform oblations with milk extracted from *arka* trees after they have been soaked [in it]. (10.497)
One should offer ten thousand fuel-sticks of the *arka* tree along with parched grain and water;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the Blessed Sun will release rain, and not otherwise. (10.498)
The two mantras bestow the desired accomplishment upon those who recite them:
"Obeisance to the Blue-necked One" (namo 'stu nīlagrīvāya), and so forth.
Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (kṛśara) for the ritual site (sthaṇḍila), together with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa), [one should offer it]. (10.499)
Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should bathe [the deity] every day with [water] consecrated a thousand times.
One should offer a thousand kārṣāpaṇas to that deity;
when the mantra is perfected, profit arises from exertion—of this there is no doubt. (10.501)
If that is not achieved, however, half of it may be obtained even from a sun-crystal stone;
furthermore, through offering, there is a gain of one hundred thousand, with honor being the foremost.
The fire-oblation (*homa*), however, performed with milk-rice and clarified butter, is a practical application that need not be further described;
beginning with "O Dhanvan, release [the arrow]," one should consecrate the weapons a thousand times with these six [mantras]. (10.503)
Having bound them, one should go to battle; thus do the enemies go [to their defeat].
One who desires to create enmity should offer ten thousand oblations of *garbhakaṇṭakī*. (10.504)

Having raised a ball of jaggery with his mouth while recollecting the name of the enemy, he should perform the recitation (japa) in the very posture known as "recitation" (japāsana); by this, he shall utterly destroy the enemy instantly.
Chanting the *sampūrṇāhaṃ* mantra, one may indeed destroy a city or a village;
by chanting it for a day and night, one may even destroy a king.
One should wait for half a day for a prince, for three parts of a day for a Kṣatriya,
for four parts for a Vaiśya, and for six parts for one of the single caste (Śūdra).

One who desires the subjugation of Brahmins and the other castes should, in sequence, offer [the leaves] of the *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, *bilva*, and *apāmārga* trees, combined with curd, honey, and ghee. (10.508)
One hundred thousand fuel sticks (*samidh*) should be used for the accomplishment of one's purpose;
to bring those of lower caste under control, [fuel sticks] of *varuṇa*, *arka*, and *kaveta* [should be used]. (10.509)
One should offer oblations of *sākhoṭaka* wood after seeing those who live by the profession of Brahmins and others; one should present fragrant *utpala*, *kumuda*, and other lotuses. (10.510)
By offering one hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood-anointed [substances] with devotion at the Svayambhū-liṅga,
using each of the six mantras individually, a king who has been deprived of his kingdom shall regain his sovereignty.
One who desires wealth shall obtain riches; thus, being capable, one should perform worship.
He who offers one hundred thousand sesame seeds upon Śiva with separate mantras [attains his goal]. (10.512)
He shall always stand upon the heads of his enemies;
he who offers ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree [shall achieve this]. (10.513)
He who offers six thousand pieces of guggulu incense in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti will swiftly conquer his enemy in battle, in the royal court, or at a game of dice. (10.514)
Whatever purpose for which one performs the oblation, its accomplishment arises swiftly;
even that which is otherwise impossible to achieve shall be accomplished by performing eight thousand oblations.
Just as one might offer food prepared in a great kitchen, so too,
eight thousand recitations of this [mantra] become an inexhaustible substance.
One *ṛc* remains of this [hymn], which they recite hereafter:
"Salutation be unto you, O Blessed One.
Whoever should mutter this ten thousand times with *bilva* leaves smeared with ghee— || 10.517 ||
Having offered oblations with each of the thousand names, one shall be honored by the world.
"Obeisance to Hiraṇyavāhu," and so forth;
eight thousand repetitions of this are declared to be the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One who has entered into battle should recite this for the sake of skill;
by the power of the recitation, he will not be harmed by enemies with weapons and the like. (10.519)
p. 923) Prior to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the *paśi* mantra is declared as follows:
"Obeisance to Rohita, the Architect (*sthapati*)".
Its preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is said to consist of five thousand recitations. (10.520)

For one who recites this, there is no fear in the forest arising from tigers, thieves, and the like. "Obeisance to the Conqueror, the Unpierced," and so forth—eight thousand repetitions of this are said to be the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). (10.521)
The recitation (*japa*) of this [mantra], beginning with "Obeisance to those who possess arrows" (*nama iṣumadbhyaḥ*), is known to be the destroyer of intense pain from wounds and the like.
Its preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of nine thousand repetitions. (10.522)
One should recite this mantra—"Obeisance to the Āvyādhinīs," and so forth—for the pacification of the fourfold army.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of sixteen thousand recitations. (10.523)
Having offered an oblation to the malevolent planets and having recited the mantra, one becomes free from disease.
[The mantra begins with] "Namo bhavāya" and so forth. For the sake of prosperity, one should perform its preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) ten thousand times. (10.524)
One should recite this at the three junctions of the day; within a year, one will become fortunate.
"Salutation to the Foremost One" (namo 'gryāya), and so forth—five thousand [recitations] of this are said to constitute the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). (10.525)
One attains leadership of the assembly and is honored even by others;
[this is taught] in the mantra beginning with "Obeisance to the Eldest" (namo jyeṣṭhāya ca).
A preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) of ten thousand repetitions is prescribed. (10.526)
When this is recited, one attains preeminence among knowers; of this there is no doubt.
"Obeisance to Āśuṣeṇa," and so forth.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā), however, is prescribed as five thousand [recitations]. (10.527)
By reciting this, lameness is destroyed and one attains the perfection of the *pādukā* (divine sandals).
"Obeisance to Dundubhya," and so forth;
twenty thousand recitations of this are prescribed as the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
This section is proclaimed to bring victory in battle, beginning with "Obeisance to Kūpya" and so forth.
A preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) of six thousand recitations [ensures success]; a treasure (*nidhi*) presided over by a planet [is attained]. (10.529)
Water consecrated with this [mantra] releases that treasure.
"Salutation to Soma," and so forth.
One should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) by reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times, plus one hundred and eight.
One should consume and likewise smear ashes with water three times a day;
within three months, consumption (rājayakṣmā) is cured, and within a year, leucoderma (kilāsa) and vitiligo (śvitra).
The body shall perish and become divine; minor diseases [shall vanish] within three days.
"Salutation to the Tīrthya," and so forth.
One should perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*) six thousand times and recite [the mantra] for six months while visiting sacred sites (*tīrtha*). (10.532)
As it has been said: "They enjoy the fruit of that sacred ford (tīrtha) in this very birth," beginning with "Obeisance to Irinya" and so forth.
A preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) of nine thousand [repetitions] is thus prescribed. (10.533)
The alchemy of silver is accomplished through its power;
here there is indeed only one remaining section (anuvāka). 10.534.
One should recite this [mantra], ending with "namas," preceded by "rajasyāya ca caitasya. Then one should recite "namo nandikāya ca," and so forth.
Eight thousand recitations of this are said to constitute the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite).
Child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) perish by being wiped away with a stream of peacock feathers.
[The mantra] beginning with "Obeisance to the Wide One" (*nama ūrvyāya ca*) and so forth is declared to be the equivalent of four thousand preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*). (10.536)
Having consecrated water with mantras, it should be given to one who grieves for the sake of pacifying their sorrow,
[reciting] "Obeisance to you, the Kirikas," and so forth.
By performing ten thousand *tila* oblations, [the merit is equal to] a thousand *kārṣāpaṇa* coins.
Or else, from the exertion of the king himself, he shall obtain [the kingdom] within the middle of the year;
having offered ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, he becomes a lord of wealth.
The accomplishment of one's own [desire], equal to a thousand pieces of gold, shall occur at once;
having fashioned an image of guggulu resin, one should cut it with a razor.
One should perform eight thousand oblations and obtain a well-adorned maiden;
or, having thus performed the fire sacrifice preceded by recitation, one who seeks wealth shall attain it.
Within the course of a year, one shall obtain a hundred gold pieces;
furthermore, one should offer eleven thousand portions of cow-dung.
Indeed, by offering eleven cows anointed with ghee for one month,
preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite, one obtains the fruit of reciting a hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds and rice.
In the house of one who performs the fire-oblation (homa), the goddess of royal fortune (rājyalakṣmī) shall dwell of her own accord;
and likewise, through oblations of sesame and grain, fortune becomes stable. (10.543)
Having fashioned an image in the form of a king out of *śatapuṣpa* flowers, one should offer a thousand oblations; the king will certainly become submissive. (10.544)
By offering a hundred thousand lotuses and water-lilies, one shall further obtain prosperity;
by offering a hundred thousand chickpea-shaped pills made of guggulu resin, one should perform the fire-oblation.
He shall certainly obtain a kingdom with remembered neighboring realms, and not otherwise.
One should offer oblations of *bilva* wood fuel-sticks in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (10.546)
Then, one will certainly obtain a kingdom of one hundred thousand villages from a neighboring vassal.
A liṅga made from the earth of an anthill should be installed at a great crossroads. (10.547)
One should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrate it with the Rudrādhyāya;
one should also sprinkle the offering with the mantra beginning with "mā nastoke."
One should offer milk-rice with ghee and likewise present an oblation to the spirits;
by doing this for three months, one shall attain great sovereignty.
Either a *pala* or even half a *pala* of white cloth, having ground it in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should place it in a copper vessel.
Having stirred it with Kapila ghee and consecrated it with the index finger,
one should then drink eight thousand [drops] while reciting this mantra.
His speech shall be unimpeded and authoritative everywhere;
one should offer ten thousand oblations of Udumbara wood fuel smeared with curd.
That master shall possess many cows, and his milch-cows shall never diminish;
one should offer eight thousand oblations of bilva fruits smeared with ghee.
One who has not attained perfection obtains eight pieces of gold, or indeed eight pieces of silver;
in the absence of bilva fruits, however, one uses āmalaka, and in its absence, udumbara.
In its absence, [one should offer] Himalayan sandalwood; in its absence, Vibhītaka;
or one hundred thousand lotuses smeared with *śrīkhaṇḍa* and cow’s ghee.

Prosperity comes to him of its own accord who offers oblations with the mantra beginning "drāpe andhasaspate. With this, one should offer clarified butter for ten thousand (*ayuta*) up to a million (*niyuta*) offerings. (10.556)
And his garments become inexhaustible in that very manner, as in the passage beginning with "O Rudra... (p. 927).
The wool should be taken from the body of one who is still living, after the body has been discarded. (10.557)
One should prepare eleven arrows and a single thread for each arrow;
having consecrated them a thousand times, eleven knots are prescribed.
Having thus worshipped that cord and offered incense, one should bind it;
when tied upon the left hand of the pregnant woman, she will give birth easily and safely.
The child remains comfortably with its hand on the right side;
the owner should wear this either at the base of the arm or around the neck. (10.560)
At times, no fear arises for that creditor;
[this is taught] in the passage beginning with "imā rudrāya... and so forth.
One should offer sesame seeds into the fire one thousand and eight times every day. (10.561)
By him, wealth is obtained from people in the world without having to ask for it; and he who should offer ten thousand oblations of *dūrvā* sprouts smeared with clarified butter. (10.562)
Even when struck by a great fever, he lives as if dead;
one who eats honey, milk-rice, and ghee should, being pure, offer ten thousand oblations.
One is liberated from great planetary afflictions, fevers, and the like, as well as from malevolent spells;
one should offer ten thousand fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood into the fire with clarified butter.
Suffering arising from fever and other ailments perishes instantly; likewise, when one is overcome by mild means for the sake of wealth and such, [the affliction likewise ceases]. (10.565)
Then, one should offer husks ten thousand times; thus one’s happiness increases.
Likewise, one may offer fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood, *audumbara* wood, or sesame seeds. (10.566)
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations with this; it is remembered as bringing peace to all.
Indeed, in the event of an affliction among cows or other livestock, one should perform it at that very spot.
Having established the fire, one should offer ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from the *vaikaṅkata* tree soaked in curd;
likewise, ten thousand oblations of *pālāśa* sticks shall bring him peace. (10.568)
One should offer oblations of [substances] smeared with ghee; thus the planets headed by Mahājvara, as well as Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, Pretas, and Piśācas [are pacified]. (10.569)
They leave behind people, elephants, and horses,
and depart from afar from any house where the birth of children occurs frequently.
In that case, either death or loss is proclaimed;
however, a twice-born man should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with ghee. (10.571)
In whatever region there is a great pestilence, or fear of tigers and the like, or where there is fear of gods and demons, there I shall declare the rite of pacification. (10.572)
In the central part of the city, one should perform the installation of the fire;
moreover, in the four directions, there should indeed be four guards, fully equipped and well-concealed.
Then, having established the men [in their positions], one should perform the ritual with vigilance;
one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with ghee.
Then, at the time of midnight, [one should offer] boiled rice with ghee, sesame seeds, ground flour,
black-gram rice, kṛśara, and excellent cooked rice.
When the people have fallen asleep, one should then offer oblations at various places;
first to the Rudras upon a Palāśa leaf, and immediately thereafter to the Rākṣasas.
One should perform this for one fortnight, which destroys all calamities;
beginning with the mantra "mṛḍāno rudra," one should recite it a thousand times in the water and worship Śiva on the bank. (10.577)
"However far away one's beloved may be, within three days they will meet.
"One should offer sesame seeds for the sake of the health of the attendants and children," and so forth. (p. 929) [Verse 10-578]
Ten thousand [recitations] of the *Śītalā* and other [mantras] quickly produce health.
Regarding the *Mānastoka*: this great *kalpa* is hidden in all the tantras. (10.579)
I shall speak to the Sage for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods,
[through] the Atikṛcchra, the Kṛcchra, and likewise the Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Having first purified oneself, one whose body is cleansed should perform the recitation (*japa*). While reciting this, one should consume vegetables, barley-gruel, or milk. (10.581)
While reciting the mantra while begging for alms, it shall amount to ten thousand repetitions;
a mere thousand-fold oblation (homa) shall render the mantra fit for practical application.
At the conclusion of the ritual application, however, recitation should be performed continuously for a day and night;
one should offer oblations of udumbara wood soaked in ghee, numbering one-tenth of that [recitation].
Afterwards, one should likewise offer ghee with the Mahāvyāhṛtis; having consumed the portion of the residue, one shall not suffer exhaustion through ritual applications.
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual action and the expiatory rite again and again;
and one should bathe with pungent oil that has been consecrated seven times.
There shall be liberation from the sin of the practices of killing and so forth;
however, one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer oblations eight thousand times.
And with fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished in all rites;
likewise, for one who has fasted for ten nights, [the rite succeeds] with lotuses smeared with clarified butter. (10.587)
One who desires prosperity, or one who wishes for a vision of Śiva, should offer ten thousand oblations of rice grains produced from the apāmārga plant. (10.588)
For the fulfillment of all aims, one should offer oblations of rice mixed with curd and ghee;
and for the acquisition of a thousand cows, one should sacrifice with cow's froth. (10.589)
Having fasted for ten days, one should then reverently offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter and bilva fruits.
And one shall obtain ten thousand [offerings] smeared with ghee, eight thousand in number;
when the mantra is perfected, one gains gold, but when it is not yet perfected, silver.
"May such-and-such a woman become my wife"—for this purpose, one who is pure should offer oblations of *jātī* flowers mixed with clarified butter and honey. (10.592)
When a tawny cow, or even a white cow that has calved for the first time,
has given birth, one should take her first milk and cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) with it.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, or likewise eight thousand, and having consecrated that sacrificial porridge (caru) with mantras, he, together with his wife, should consume it.
One will undoubtedly give birth to long-lived sons who are firm; one should offer oblations of young *dūrvā* shoots combined with curd, honey, and ghee. (10.595)
One who desires long life obtains a long lifespan by offering eight thousand flowers of *dadhī*, honey, and ghee, along with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses. (10.596)
If one desires minor animals, one should offer eight thousand oblations;
having fasted for three nights, one should go to a great crossroads. (10.597)
Having smeared the ground with cow dung and likewise [anointed] the mouth with ghee,
and having performed worship, one should offer oblations upon the ground one thousand and eight times.
By this rite, the king will undoubtedly become submissive.
With that [substance], having consecrated sharp oil seven times, both hands [should be smeared]. (10.599)
For he who has been touched by that [fire] which has crossed over correctly shall come under its control.
One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), however, [should offer oblations] combined with curd, honey, and ghee. (10.600)
Having offered one hundred thousand fuel-sticks of *vilva*, one becomes a treasury of splendor;
one should also offer sticks of *udumbara* wood mixed with curd, honey, and clarified butter. (10.601)
One who desires food shall likewise obtain ten thousand measures of abundant food;
one who desires wealth [should offer] fuel-sticks of the *palāśa* tree mixed with clarified butter.
If one performs one hundred thousand oblations, his wealth shall become eternally inexhaustible;
[using] fuel-sticks of Apāmārga combined with pungent oil. (10.603)
If one recites it eight thousand times, the eradication of the enemy occurs;
"eradication" (uccāṭana) means expulsion from one's country and so forth.
For the purpose of destroying all calamities, one should take seven pieces of sugar. (10.604)
Having recited the mantra a thousand times, one should then scatter [the substances] in the four directions, as well as above and below near it; this destroys all calamities.
Having done this, one may travel on the road; it removes the fear of thieves and tigers.
"O you who have recently killed a cow," and so forth.
When great danger has arisen—such as the fear of tigers, thieves, and the like—(one should recite this). (10.606)
One should remember these four verses in the mind, which destroy their respective fears, beginning with "vikiri... and so forth.
One should recite them ten thousand times in the event of conflict with great men.
"Or by the king, peace is attained and joy arises," and so forth; "But when there is the death of great beings, or a calamity for the king," (10.608).
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the best fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata*,
or those of *udumbara* or *śālmali*, or even with sesame seeds or barley.
Having consecrated each [offering] eleven times with mantras, one should then present the bali offering—
either kṛśara or pāyasa— and thereafter worship the bhūtas.
One should offer an oblation of cat-flesh, and all calamities will perish.
One should recite these nine verses, beginning with "The Rudras by the thousands, by the thousands," together with the *Pariśiṣṭa*. (10.611)
Therefore, those [mantras] devoid of that [quality] are considered givers of enjoyment, while those [possessing it] are considered givers of knowledge.
"Obeisance to the Rudras," and so forth.
At midday, one should offer ten thousand oblations of thorny wood with clarified butter. (10.612)
One should perform the ritual of the Pratyaṅgirā mantra; this is the manual.
The completion of this [rite] is with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra: "Obeisance to you. (10.613)
In another branch, the Taittirīya, there are seven supplementary sections (*pariśiṣṭas*):
the five beginning with *sadyojāta*, and "We worship Tryambaka" (*tryambakaṃ ca yajāmahe*). (10.614)
And thus, O Rudra, this is called the *Tvarita-mantra*:
"O Agni and Viṣṇu," and so forth.
Standing at the conclusion of the daily twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), one should recite it during the three periods of the day. (10.615)
By reciting one thousand and eight times for six months, one becomes a speaker of truth.
[One should recite] "vājaśca me prasavaśca me," and so forth; with these seven *anuvākas* and likewise with the five beginning with *āna*, [one attains the result]. (10.616)
Having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter and entered into water, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times; then eye disease will never arise. (10.617)
For one who has been born, there shall be tranquility and the luster of the eyes increases.
"And for me fuel, and for me sacrificial grass," and so forth.
Thus much is declared to be Rudra, the bestower of the fruits of all desires. (10.618)
A recitation in various forms, free from syllables, has been performed for the pacification of those defects:
"iḍā devahūḥ," and so forth.
One should mutter this remainder; this is remembered as the ritual procedure for Rudra. (10.619)
One should perform an empowerment for the sake of prosperity; one desiring pacification should perform fire offerings (homa);
and one desiring success should recite [the mantra] according to the number of syllables. (10.620)
Right here he is the Vajra-body, Śiva himself and none other;
through recitation with an equal number of repetitions of the *pada*, the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) arises. (10.621)
By reciting the mantra a number of times equal to the number of words, all sin is destroyed;
by reciting it a number of times equal to the number of verses (*ṛc*), all minor sins are destroyed. (10.622)
Having recited [the Rudrādhyāya] as many times as there are sections (anuvākas), one shall conquer the afflictions caused by malevolent planets.
Thus concludes the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of the Rudrādhyāya.
Now follows the preliminary rite of the Gaṇeśasūkta.
In that very place:
"Now, O Viṣṇu, I shall proclaim the supreme hymn (sūkta) of Gaṇapati. (10.623)
Since all mantras are obstructed by impediments even without [proper] means of accomplishment, one should first propitiate Gaṇeśāna and then perform the rite again. (10.624)
Sleep, laziness, hunger, anger, greed, delusion, and lust—these are remembered as the obstacles for those who worship Gaṇeśa. (10.625)
Therefore, that hymn is taught according to the prescribed ritual; for those who recite it, their undertakings shall be unimpeded.
The seer of this hymn of twelve verses dedicated to the high-souled Gaṇeśa is indeed proclaimed to be the sage named Gṛtsamada. || 10.627 ||
The meter of the first three triplets is proclaimed to be Triṣṭubh;
the meter of the subsequent nine is said to be Gāyatrī. (10.628)
Mahāgaṇapati is proclaimed as its presiding deity;
the application (viniyoga) should be declared according to the specific purpose at hand. || 10-629 ||
"Of the hosts, thee, the Lord of Hosts (Citra)"—and so forth. (p.
934) "Of the hosts, sit down for us; likewise, [know] that brilliant host.
O Indra, we know thee as one who is never deficient, nor indeed one who has abandoned the trident. (10.630)
Beginning from the tip of the thumb, one should place [the mantras] on the back of the hand and other parts;
and with the six verses beginning "gaṇānāṃ tvā," one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) for the heart and the other limbs.
Having thus performed the two types of nyāsa, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the six limbs.
Having described the other nyāsas and the ritual of worship, he speaks of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
"Twenty-one thousand [recitations] of this hymn constitute the preliminary rite. (10.632)

The fire-oblation (*homa*) should consist of one-tenth the number of recitations (*japa*), performed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), clarified butter (*ghṛta*), sugar, the five kinds of edible foods, and *karavīra* flowers. (10.633)
With bilva leaves, stalks of sugarcane, pomegranates, and plantains,
as well as with delightful sweetmeats and *laḍḍuka* balls cooked in ghee.
In the absence of all [other] substances, one should perform the oblation with sesame seeds and clarified butter;
one should satisfy [the deities] with cow's milk equal to one-tenth of the number of oblations.
Alternatively, in the absence of that, one may use sugarcane juice or molasses water;
having performed the libation with a tenth part [of the quantity], one should perform the ritual sprinkling with pure water.
One should feed many Brahmins with a tenth part of the quantity used for the ritual sprinkling,
providing them with milk-rice, the five kinds of edible foods, sweetmeats, and prepared *laḍḍukas*.
And with cakes, pancakes, and the like, accompanied by ghee and mixed with sugar,
together with mango juices as well as plantain fruits.
When this hymn has been thus accomplished, the fruit thereof is now declared:
unsurpassed great sovereignty, wisdom, knowledge, fame, and strength. (10.639)
One attains perfection of speech and, at the end, shall go to the state of Brahman.
Thus ends the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Gaṇeśasūkta.
Now begins the procedure for the Puruṣasūkta.
In the Merutantra, I shall declare the procedure for the Puruṣasūkta, which is hidden therein. (10.640)
The meter of this hymn is Anuṣṭubh, its deity is Triṣṭubh, and the seer is remembered as Nārāyaṇa, who is Puruṣa, the seed of the universe. (10.641)
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite, facing eastward with a pure mind,
one should place the first [syllable] on the left hand and the second on the right hand.
One should place the third [syllable] on the left foot and the fourth on the right;
the fifth on the left knee and the sixth on the right knee.
One should place the seventh on the left hip, the eighth on the right hip,
the ninth at the region of the navel, and the tenth at the heart.
One should place Ekādaśī at the region of the throat, Dvādaśī on the left arm,
Trayodaśī on the right arm, and Caturdaśī at the region of the mouth.
One should place the fifteenth [syllable] on the two eyes and the sixteenth on the head;
having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), one should thereafter perform the worship.
In water, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial ground, and in images—in these six, the fitness for the perfect worship of Hari is declared. (10.647)
For water is his abode; therefore Hari is always present within them. For those who perform ritual acts, Hari is in the fire; for yogis, Hari is in the heart.
For the wise, Hari is the sun; for those of purified soul, he is on the sacrificial ground;
for those of limited intellect, he is in images—these six modes are traditionally taught.
I shall describe the characteristics of those [images] which are both unartificial and artificial, immovable and movable, and both lifeless and endowed with life. || 10-650 ||
The unartificial [liṅga] is of two kinds; the Śālagrāma is exceedingly purifying.
In its absence, the discus of Dvārakā is likewise purifying. (10.651)
Artificial [images] are said to be of ten kinds; among them, each preceding one is superior to the following.
The first may be inlaid with gems, or made of gold, or even of silver. (10.652)
The copper-born, the brass-born, the crystal-born, the red-cool-born, the granary-born, the clay-born, and the multiform—these are [the types] in sequence. (10.653)
Those that are in the form of sacred fields are immovable, just as Haridvāra and Gayā are;
those which have been established by the deities as physical forms are both movable and immovable.
Jagannātha, Veṅkaṭeśa, Pāṇḍuraṅga, and others are indeed Brahmins who are endowed with life; the Pippala tree is considered to be devoid of life. || 10-655 ||
First, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon one's own body and upon the deities;
having placed the limbs [of the mantra] with the Gāyatrī and the syllable Oṃ, one should worship the imperishable Viṣṇu.
One should invoke the Lord Puruṣottama with the first ṛc;
one should offer a seat with the second, and offer water for the feet with the third.
The *arghya* should be offered with the fourth [mantra], the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*) with the fifth;
one should perform the bath with the sixth, and the clothing with the seventh. (10.658)
On the eighth day, the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) should be offered; on the ninth, unguents;
on the tenth, flowers; and on the eleventh, incense.
On the twelfth day one should offer a lamp; on the thirteenth, the food offering (naivedya);
on the fourteenth, prostration; and on the fifteenth, circumambulation.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) after the bath, the clothing, and the food offering;
and one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given according to one's ability, specifically with the sixteenth [verse].
Then, having performed a circumambulation, being composed and reciting the mantra,
one should offer that hymn to him after having recited it according to one's ability.

On the right side of the deity, one should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) prepared with the first [mantra], while the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is performed with the second. (10.663)
With the third [verse] one should take up the fire; with the fourth, the kindling wood;
with the fifth, the heating of the clarified butter, and likewise the heating of the sacrificial porridge (caru).
With the sixth [syllable], one should imagine a lotus seat in the midst of the fire;
one should meditate upon the Lord of the Gods, whose radiance is equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.

Then, having requested permission for the offering of incense, flowers, and the presentation of incense smoke and lamps, one should perform the rites beginning with the seventh day in their proper sequence.
First, one should offer as many fuel-sticks (samidh) as there are, sprinkled with clarified butter; then one should offer oblations of ghee, and after that, again with sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having performed the oblation in this manner and then having obtained permission from him, one should recite a hymn of praise in due order in the presence of that Blessed One, Agni.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe.
Let there be salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa.
I always go for refuge to your pair of feet, which are common to both the gods and the dānavas as their presiding deity. (10.670)
You alone are the creator of the world and likewise its destroyer;
you are unmanifest and the witness, veiled by the *māyā* of the *guṇas*.
Having obtained refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is a vessel for infinite afflictions. (10.672)
You have no form, nor appearance, nor weapons, nor abode;
nevertheless, you manifest in the form of a person for the sake of revealing yourself to your devotees.
Nothing is hidden from you, nor are you hidden from anyone;
nothing is impossible for you, nor are you subject to anyone else. (10.674)
The cause of all effects is prior; the object of speech is the supreme.
Yogis know that to be the highest perfection and the ultimate state.
"I am a being in this world, O Lord of Gods, amidst this great terror;
protect me, O Lotus-eyed One, for I do not know the supreme state. (10.676)
O Acyuta, at all times and in all directions, and even within my own body, you have entered; yet a great fear persists within me.
Apart from your lotus feet, I have no other [refuge] even in future births; for it is by attaining these that this realization has been gained and this state has been won. (10.678)
"O Lord, may there never be a loss of this [faith] for me even in another birth;
for even if I am born into an evil state, you have become the fulfillment of my heart's desire. (10.679)
If I do not meet with destruction, by that alone I am always content; I desire only the feet of Viṣṇu in all my births.
This hymn of Puruṣa Hari leads to heaven, brings wealth, and confers glory;
it is this meritorious knowledge of the Self, this supreme knowledge of Yoga. (10.681)
Having thus praised the bearer of oblations, one should thereafter dismiss him;
for by this alone, a person does not become free from sin. (10.682)
Having offered oblations as before, one should purify [the site] and then commence the ritual applications during the bright fortnight,
on an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion, and in a propitious planetary alignment.
The husband and wife should observe a fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the temple of the Lord;
on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), for one desiring a son, they should prepare a Vaiṣṇava sacrificial oblation (caru).
Having properly worshipped Janārdana with sixteen *ṛg* verses, one who desires a son should cause [the deity] to consume the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
One shall indeed obtain a Vaiṣṇava son who is capable of perpetuating the lineage without delay;
one should properly offer a caru-oblation with milk on each twelfth lunar day.
He who offers a thousand oblations goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
Keśava is to be worshipped in the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa in their proper sequence.
Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu;
he is called Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, and likewise Dāmana.
Having worshipped Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Janārdana, one should then recite the hymn one hundred and eight times.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) as previously described and shall attain all desires;
this applies to those who are childless, those whose children have died, and those who give birth only to daughters.
I shall now describe the means by which she may become possessed of beautiful feet:
one should offer a hundred pieces of fuel-sticks from the Aśvattha tree for each verse.
One should offer eight additional oblations of ghee into the fire;
then, having worshipped Viṣṇu once more, one should perform the oblation of ghee.
Being pure and restrained in speech, one should perform one hundred and eight [recitations] for each image;
having set aside the residual ghee (saṃpātājya), it should be given to that noble woman for consumption.
She should give [the food] and, having paid homage to Viṣṇu as her husband, she should eat it herself;
she should properly satisfy the twice-born with offerings, eat light food, and go to bed for the night. (10.694)
At most, after seven cycles of recitation, she will certainly become pregnant. Now, the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should dwell constantly in the forest and perform ablutions three times a day. (10.695)
One should recite this hymn one hundred and eight times at the three periods of the day for one month, subsisting on fruit and offering libations with water for one month. (10.696)
One should constantly worship the Sun with this root-mantra;
having offered a thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should recite it three times every day for three years. (10.697)
Devoted to Him, with his mind fixed on Him, disciplined, and intent on no other for ten years,
he beholds directly that Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction.
Thus concludes the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the Puruṣasūkta.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the Śrīsūkta;
it is found in that very same [text].
Now I shall declare the Śrīsūkta, the most excellent of all, together with its ritual procedure;
in the Kali age, there is nothing else like it for men to destroy poverty. (10-699)
"Hiraṇyavarṇām," and so forth.
For this verse beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇām," Lakṣmī is considered the seer (ṛṣi).
For the remaining fourteen [verses], Ānanda and Kardama are likewise [the seers]. (10.700)
The four sons of Lakṣmī are considered to be the sages;
for the three beginning with Hṛdayā, the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh.
May the *kāṃsa* [tone], the *ṛc*, the *bṛhatī* [meter], and the moon-like and sun-colored [deities]—may the *triṣṭubh* meter of the eight verses of the gods come to me today. (10.702)
The meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh; the Ṛc verses are "tām ma āha vaḥ.
The Prastāra is indicated as Paṅkti, and the deities are Śrī and Vibhāvasu.

The consonants are said to be the seeds, the vowels are declared to be the powers (śaktis), and the nasal bindus are called the pins (kīlakas); these constitute the six limbs beginning with the thumb.
Hiraṇyā, and likewise Tandrā, the third being Rajataprabhā;
Hiraṇyasrak, Hiraṇyākṣā, and likewise Hiraṇyavarṇikā.
One should perform the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*) with these [mantras] ending in *namaḥ*.
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
She is seated upon a reddish lotus, her complexion like a mass of its pollen.
And she holds in her lotus-like hands the pair of gestures known as *iṣṭa* and *abhaya*, along with a lotus. || 10-706 ||
May Śrī, the Mother of the World, adorned with a jeweled crown and a multitude of various ornaments, be ever for our prosperity. Now follows the *puraścaraṇa*.
One should always sprinkle [the image] three times with those hymns during the ritual of bathing.

Facing the sun, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and likewise the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for as long as [the period lasts], beginning from the first lunar day (*tithi*) of the bright fortnight until the eleventh day arrives. (10.708)
During that time, the wise person, devoted to celibacy, with pure clothing, teeth, and so forth, and with a steady mind, should recite the mantra twelve thousand times. (10.709)
One should offer three hundred oblations each of lotuses mixed with the three sweets, of milk-rice sprinkled with ghee, and of *śrī-samidh* wood fuel with clarified butter.
Furthermore, on the twelfth lunar day, one should feed twelve Brahmins;
by that, the mantra becomes perfected—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The *kunda*, *mandāraka*, *kumuda*, *mālatī*, *padma*, *ketaka*, the one called *nandyāvarta*, *jātī*, *kalhāra*, and likewise the *campaka*. || 10-712 ||
For red lotuses and other such flowers are indeed exceedingly dear to Lakṣmī;
the practitioner of mantra should offer them as oblations three times every day according to the prescribed ritual.
He who performs this for six months shall himself become the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Thus concludes the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Śrīsūkta.
Now follow the Vedic mantras of the nine planets.
In that very same [work]: "There, for the mantra of Bhāskara, Hiraṇyastūpa is the sage. (10.714)
The *triṣṭubh* is proclaimed as the meter and Savitṛ as the deity:
"Moving through the dark expanse, establishing the immortal and the mortal, the divine Savitṛ comes on his golden chariot, beholding all beings.
One should recite the six limbs, beginning with the thumb, accompanied by the six long vowels. (10.715)
Then, one should perform the placement of the words (padanyāsa) for the mantra of Bhuvaneśī;
thereafter, in the place of the verses mentioned in the Śrīsūkta, one should meditate upon the Sun.
As for the meditative absorption:
[He is] in the lotus posture, with lotus hands, possessing a radiance like the interior of a lotus;
wearing a crown and armlets, adorned, and shaded by a red parasol. (10.717)
Mounted upon his chariot on the left side, presided over by the presiding deity Agni,
and joined on the left by the lord of the counter-deity, he faces the east.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable, and perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number.
The recitation should be performed in equal measure to the oblations, including for the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and the secondary deity (*pratyadhidevatā*). (10.719)
The libation for the Lord of Day should be performed with karavīra and other flowers mixed with red sandalwood, along with sprouts of dūrvā grass and unbroken grains of rice.
Now, the mantra of Candra:
Now I shall declare the mantra of Candra; Gautama is considered its sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas), and Soma is proclaimed as its deity (devatā). (10.721)
"Then, O Soma, let virility come to you from every side; be present in the gathering of strength.
With the letter *sa* joined by a nasal drop (*bindu*) and lengthened sixfold, one performs the six-limbed rite. (722)

Now, the meditation: [One should meditate upon him] wearing a crown and white garments, having ten horses and white ornaments, holding a noose in his hand, two-armed, and born of the Atri lineage. (10.723)
It was born in the land of the Yavanas, characterized by white perfumes and ointments; its metre is Anuṣṭubh, its seer is Atri, and it is the Śvetātapatraka. (10.724)
Abounding in white banners and flags, adorned with armlets and jewels,
it was made stable, mounted upon a chariot, and joined with its presiding deity and water.

Facing the northwest, with Umā as the presiding deity, one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; this is the rule for all [the mantras] beginning with *sarvaśveta*. (10.726)
Now, the mantra of Bhauma:
I shall proclaim the mantra of Bhauma; Virūpa is considered its sage (ṛṣi), Aṅgāraka is the deity here, and Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas). (10.727)
Agni, the head of heaven, the lord of the earth, he whose seed is wondrous, quickens the waters. 10-728
The six limbs [of the body] and the assignment of the fingers should be performed with the seed-syllable;
the second [stage], the assignment of the steps, should be performed in the locations of Rudra. || 10.729 ||
Now, the meditation: [He is] clad in red garments, red in color, and anointed with red perfumes; he is worshipped with red flowers, has four arms, and wears a crown. (10.730)
One should meditate on Mars, who holds a boon-granting gesture, a shield, a mace, and a trident in his hands,
is seated upon a ram, belongs to the Vasiṣṭha lineage, and has Yamadagni as his seer.
Having meditated upon the deity as being of the Jagatī meter, red in color, with red banners and pennants, and born in the region of Avanti, one should worship him.
When a triangular mandala has been fashioned with rice grains mixed with red sandalwood,
it should be joined with the deity presiding over the earth (Kṣmādhideva) and with the six-month-old [deity].
Having invoked [the deity] there along with the presiding and secondary deities, one should worship them. (p.
944) Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times per syllable, combined with the three sweets. (10.734)
The *svāhā* ending for the oblation of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth is like that of the Sun.
Now, the mantra of Budha: I shall proclaim the mantra of Budha; his sage (*muni*) is considered to be Bauddha. (10.735)
The Triṣṭubh is its metre; its deity is considered to be Budha, the bestower of intelligence.
"Awake, O Agni! Be watchful for me! Through this sacrifice and through pious works, may he release me from sin. (10.736)
"Making you anew, the father, the youth—O Citra, may you follow this thread of yours.
With the seed-syllable, the six limbs are meditated upon; thus his visualization is described. (10.737)
Clad in yellow garments, yellow in complexion, and anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents, he is worshipped with yellow flowers; he holds a sword, a shield, and a mace as his excellent weapons.
One should meditate on the one who holds [the conch] in his hands, seated upon a lion, born of the Atri lineage,
descended from the sage Bhāradvāja, and appearing as Kirīṭin in Magadha.
He is endowed with the Bṛhatī meter, possesses yellow parasols, banners, and flags,
is richly adorned with armlets and jewels, and has Viṣṇu as his presiding deity.
I meditate upon the Knower (Jña) joined with that presiding deity.
Now, for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (varṇalakṣa) and perform oblations (homa) amounting to one-tenth of that.
One should then perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.
Now, the mantra of Bṛhaspati:
I shall declare the mantra of Bṛhaspati; the sage is considered to be Bṛhaspati Mada. (10.742)
The *triṣṭubh* is its meter; the Lord of the Gods (*Devapati*) is its deity. [The mantra:

"O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the enemy, which is worthy, which shines radiantly among men with wisdom, and which has shone forth through power, born of the Truth (*ṛta*)—bestow upon us that wonderful wealth.
(p. 945) One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllable *Bṛ*. (10.743)
I shall describe his meditation: he is yellow in color, wears a crown, and holds in his hands a boon-granting staff, a rosary, and a water-pot. (10.744)
[He is] the sage Vasiṣṭha, born in the land of Sindhu, clothed in yellow garments;
[he is] in the Anuṣṭubh metre, of the Aṅgiras lineage, and wears a diadem. (10.745)
Abounding with yellow banners and flags, with yellow parasols and ointments,
adorned with the splendor of armlets and bracelets, it was joined by the presiding Indra.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as joined with Brahmā as the presiding deity (pratyadhideva), one should invoke him.

As for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the number of its syllables; the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with offerings mixed with the three sweets (trimadhura).
The satiation should be performed with five yellow *pippala* fuel-sticks.
Now follows the *śukra* mantra: "I shall proclaim the *śukra* mantra; Bhāradvāja is considered its sage. (10.748)
The *triṣṭubh* is declared to be the meter, and the preceptor of the Daityas (Śukra) is the deity.
"One [nature] of yours is bright, the other is sacrificial; you are like the sky, possessing day and night within yourself. (10.749)
O self-dependent one, you protect against all illusions; O Pūṣan, may your bounty here be auspicious.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable *śu*, one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*). || 10-750 ||

He describes the meditation: [One should meditate on] the sage Śaunaka, wearing white garments, white in color, anointed with white perfumes, being worshipped with white flowers, and adorned with a crown. (10.751)
Four-armed, holding a staff, a rosary, and a water-pot; having the Paṅkti meter as his vehicle, granting boons, and born in the Kīkara country. (10.752)
He who possesses a white umbrella, banners, and flags, born of the Bhārgava lineage,
adorned with armlets, mounted upon a chariot, and decorated with white ornaments.
(p. 946) Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables and perform oblations with *udumbara* wood fuel sticks mixed with the three sweets.
The libations (*tarpaṇa*) and subsequent rites should be performed as described for the Moon. (10.754)
Now, the mantra of Śani:
I shall proclaim the mantra of Śani; Sindhudvīpa is considered its sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas), and the deity is indeed Śanaiścara. (10.755)
"May the divine waters be auspicious for our desire and for our purification; may they flow toward us for our well-being.

With the seed-syllable *Śaṃ*, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and then practice meditation [on the deity] who holds a bow and arrows and a trident, possessing a luster like that of a sapphire. (10.756)
He is said to be born in the land of Saurāṣṭra, the bestower of boons, having the vulture as his vehicle;
he was born in the year of Bhṛgu, in the lineage of Kaśyapa, and is also known as Kirīṭin.
He wears black garments, is black in complexion, and is anointed with black perfumes;
he has the Gāyatrī as his meter and is adorned with black-colored ornaments.
Adorned with armlets and a crown, bearing a black banner and pennant,
he was mounted upon a chariot accompanied by Prajāpati as its presiding deity.
Having meditated upon [the deity] joined with the secondary presiding deity (pratyadhideva) of the lotus, one should worship him.
Now, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
with musk and those [other substances], on a circular mandala of two finger-breadths in size, at the appropriate time... 10-760.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with *samī* fuel-sticks; the libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be with half the amount of iron [filings].
There should be black flowers, sandalwood, *kālīya*, and *aguru*. (10.761)
Now, the mantra of Rāhu:
I shall proclaim the mantra of Rāhu; Vāmadeva is considered the sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas), and Saiṃhikeya is the deity (devatā). (10.762)
By what means has he become a manifold splendor, the ever-increasing friend? By what most powerful assembly [of attendants]?
(p.947) His meditation is described as having the seed-syllable *rāḥ* and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*):
bearing a terrifying face and carrying a sword, a shield, and a trident. (10.763)
Clad in black garments, black in complexion, and anointed with black perfumes,
he was being worshipped with black flowers and adorned with armlets and a crown.
This planet originated in the eastern region; it is the cruel one whose seer is Aṅgiras, who belongs to the Pāṭala lineage, and whose meter is Auṣṇih.
He has a black parasol, is mounted upon a chariot, and possesses black banners and flags;
his presiding deity is the serpent, and his secondary presiding deity is the ancestral time (Kāla).
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

having reflected thus, one should invoke [the deity] with *śyāmā* flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) upon a winnowing-basket-shaped mandala in the southwest (*nairṛtya*), measuring twelve finger-breadths in width. (10.767)
An oblation for him is prescribed with *dūrvā* grass smeared with honey;
the Kaulikas should satisfy the twice-born with substances such as those used for libations (*tarpaṇa*). (10.768)
Now, the Ketu-mantra.
In that very same [text]:
"I shall proclaim the Ketu-mantra; Madhucchandas is considered its sage."
The deities are said to be the banners (ketavaḥ), and the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed [as the meter]. || 10-769 ||
"Creating a banner for the bannerless, O youths, a form for the formless, you were born together with the dawns.
The meditation on this [deity] is described by means of its six limbs:
they have smoky eyes and arms, hold nooses, and possess distorted faces. (10.780)
Wearing crowns, borne by vultures, born in the Middle Country, and firm;
they wear variegated garments, possess variegated complexions, and are anointed with variegated fragrant unguents.
They possess various meters, have Gautama as their seer, and are born of the Jaimini lineage;
they bear black and tawny banners and flags, and likewise wear crowns.

One should contemplate here the heroic deities beginning with Brahmā, adorned with armlets and mounted upon chariots, along with Citragupta as their respective presiding deities (pratyadhidevatā). (10.783)

Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable; *kuśa* grass is prescribed for the fire-oblation (*homa*), and one should satisfy [the deity] with various substances combined with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*). || 10.784 ||
Thus end the Vedic mantras for the nine planets.
Now follows the mantra of Agnidurgā;
it is in that same [text].
I shall declare that which accomplishes all aims and bestows victory in battle;
listen to that which I remember for the sake of slaying Jalandhara. (10.785)

We press the Soma for Jātavedas; he shall lay low the wealth of the one who acts with hostility. May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as one carries a boat across a river, leading us beyond all misfortunes.
Triṣṭubh is the metre, and Marīci Kāśyapa is considered the sage.
Jātavedas Agni is the deity; one should perform the six ancillary rites (ṣaḍaṅga). (10.786)
With nine, six, seven, eight, and seven mantra-syllables; now, the meditation:
[one should visualize her] possessing a radiance like a garland of lightning, seated upon the shoulders of the king of beasts, and terrifying.
She was attended by maidens whose hands resounded with the sound of swords and shields.

One should meditate upon Durgā, whose nature is fire, who wears the crescent moon, and has three eyes; she holds in her hands the discus, sword, shield, arrow, noose, goad, and the gesture of threatening (tarjanī).
Now follows the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
One should recite thousands of mantra syllables and perform the fire-oblation separately for each.
One should perform [the rite] with the number of offerings equal to four times the number of Vedic branches (forty-eight), using sesame, white mustard, and various grains,
as well as roots and sacrificial fuel-sticks from the banyan, udumbara, and pippala trees.

One should also offer oblations with clarified butter produced from *arka* and *plakṣa*, with sacrificial offerings, and with all types of food smeared with ghee; finally, there should be an oblation of sesame seeds mixed with ghee. (10.790)
Then, having offered libations with sesame seeds and performed his own ritual ablution,
and having propitiated the excellent deities, he should honor his own preceptor.
Thus concludes the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) for the mantras of Agni and Durgā.
The Vedic sacrificial procedure (*homavidhi*) required for the preliminary ritual of Vedic mantras is not written here for fear of prolixity.
Now, the quantities of the sacrificial materials (*homadravya*).
(From the Śāradā-tantra:
Now, the measure of the substances for the fire-oblation (homa) is declared here: one karṣa of ghee is prescribed for the oblation, and one śukti of milk is traditionally taught. (10.792)
The wise have declared that these five substances are equal;
honey, milk, and food of that same measure are said to be equal to an *akṣa*. (10.793)

The curd should be the measure of a handful (prasṛti); the parched rice grains (lāja) should be equal to a fistful; the flattened rice (pṛthuka) should be of that same measure, and the roasted flour (saktu) is likewise considered to be so. (10.794)

Jaggery should be half a *pala* in measure, and sugar is considered to be the same; the portion of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should be half a mouthful, and sugarcane is considered to be measured by the joint.
One should prepare each leaf and flower, as well as cakes; likewise, they know that plantain fruits and orange fruits should be offered one by one. (10.796)
The wise know that the mātuluṅga fruit should be divided into four pieces, the jackfruit into ten, and the coconuts into eight. (10.797)
The fruit of the bilva tree should be cut into three parts, and the wood-apple (kapittha) should be split into three pieces;
other fruits should remain uncut, and the sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, as well as guḍūcī and caturaṅgulā; there should be a handful of vrīhi rice, and likewise mudga beans, māṣa beans, and barley.

Rice grains should be one-fourth [of the measure], while *kodrava* grains are measured by a handful (*muṣṭi*); wheat and red *kalama* rice are likewise prescribed according to the measure of a handful. (10.800)
Sesame seeds should be the size of a handful; mustard seeds are of that same measure. Salt is the size of a *śukti* (a small shell), and black peppers are twenty [in number].
A *pura* should be the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*), and *rāmaṭha* is recorded as being equal to that;
likewise for sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron.
The seeds of the tamarind have been specified by the teachers;
their characteristics, beginning with the *karṣa*, are stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: ten *guñjās* make one *māṣa*, and four *māṣas* make one *śāṇa*.
Two śāṇas make a vaṭaka; [these are also called] kola, badara, and kṣudravrata. || 10-803 ||
Two of those [māṣas] are a pāṇitala; four [pāṇitalas] are a karṣa; four [karṣas] are a suvarṇa; and eight [suvarṇas] are a graha.
A picu, a viḍālapadaka, a tinduka, and an akṣa are each equal to two of those [grahas].
Two *śukti*s are one *aṣṭamikā*; two of those are one *pala*, which is four *niṣkas*.
A *muṣṭi* is the measure of a *prakuñca*, and likewise, two *palas* are one *prasṛti*. (10.805)
According to Agastya, however:
"Five *guñjās* are proclaimed to be one *māṣaka*;
sixteen *māṣakas* constitute a *suvarṇa* and also a *karṣa*. (10.806)
It is stated: "A *pala* is proclaimed to be four or even five *suvarṇas*.

According to this view, one *karṣa* consists of eighty *guñjās*, and that same measure is also called a *suvarṇa*. *Pṛthukas* are flat rice cakes; *guḍūcī* is a specific type of creeper; *pura* is *guggulu* resin; *rāmaṭha* is asafoetida (*hiṅgu*); and *soma* is Śambhu.
When no sacrificial substance is specified, sesame seeds and clarified butter are said to constitute the oblation. (10.807)
When no specific substance for the collyrium is mentioned, they know that ghee alone is the collyrium;
when no number is mentioned, it shall be one thousand, and likewise, when no substance is mentioned, it is ghee.
Regarding the matter of fuel-wood not specifically mentioned, those made of *pālāśa* wood are prescribed;
likewise, the oblation of parched grain and other substances is ordained to be performed with the hand together with the fingers. (10.809)
The oblation (*homa*) of fuel sticks, flowers, fruits, and so forth should be performed with the *mṛgamudrā* gesture;
for liquid substances, the *śruva* ladle is prescribed by those expert in mantra and tantra. (10.810)
Thus end the measurements of the substances for the *homa* offering.
[This work] is highly esteemed as a confluence of rivers of compositions, abounding in streams of nectar variegated by the wonderful diversity of words that purify beings through marvelous splendor.

The tenth beautiful wave has passed in this new ocean of preliminary rites performed by all the earthly lords and leaders, which possesses the logic of the analogy of the "Six Liberated Ones" (Ṣaṇmukta). 10.811.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Performance of Vedic Mantras such as the Gāyatrī, Preceded by the Performance of Mantras such as Sarasvatī," in the *Puraścaryārṇava* composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha Sāhi.
Now, the various types of Durgā mantras and their specific preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) are described.
And so it is said in the *Śāradātilaka*:
Next, I shall declare the mantra of Durgā, which bestows both seen and unseen fruits:
the syllable *māyā* (hīṃ) repeated three times, enriched with the seed-syllable of the ear (kṣa), and again followed by that same syllable with the vowel *sarga* (*visarga*). (11.1)

Ending with the five [vowels], possessing a foundation, having Māruta as its seed-syllable and Bhūtika as its seat, this mantra consists of eight syllables, beginning with the letter *Tā* and ending with the Heart. (11.2)
The seer is Nārada, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu;
Durgā is proclaimed by the virtuous as the remover of the afflictions of misfortune. (11.3)
The practitioner, using the root mantra devoid of the *namaskāra*,
should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) together with the syllables beginning with *drām* according to the prescribed rule.
Now, for the meditation:
Seated upon a lion, crowned with the moon, and adorned with three eyes, she holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her four arms which resemble emeralds.
Adorned with armlets, necklaces, bracelets, jingling girdles, and tinkling anklets,
and shining with jeweled earrings, may she who removes all misfortune from the difficult path be for your protection.

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one who has conquered the senses should mutter the mantra eight hundred thousand times, or offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with honey or with milk, one thousand times.
Thus ends the mantra of Durgā.
Now follows the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī;
it is in that same [text].

The syllable *bhānta* (bha), followed by *viyat* (ha), *sanayana* (na), and *śveta* (sa), then *mardini* (ma), and the pair of *ṭha* (ṭha ṭha)—this is declared to be the eight-syllabled Vidyā known as Mahiṣamardinī. (11.7)
This mantra consists of nine syllables, enriched by any one of the seed-syllables beginning with Māyā and Praṇava.
As it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, the *Viśvasāra*, and other texts:
"At the end of the seed-syllable that constitutes the three worlds, there follows the word of address."
The two syllables [representing] creation and destruction are Vidyā and Mahiṣamardinī.
The wise practitioner should recite the vidyā beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), or he may recite it enriched with Māyā (Hrīṃ);
likewise, he may also recite it beginning with the seed-syllable of the bride (Śrīṃ) and enriched with the Kavaca (Huṃ). || 11.9 ||
(From the Śāradā-tantra: "O Slayer of Mahiṣa! Huḥ Phaṭ! is proclaimed as the heart mantra.
"O Enemy of Mahiṣa! Sārṣi Huḥ Phaṭ! is declared to be the head limb mantra. || 11-10 ||
"Obeisance to Mahiṣa, [conquer] the pair of hatreds, huḥ phaṭ"—this is the mantra for the crest-lock (śikhā).
"O Goddess, obeisance to Mahiṣa, slay the pair [of enemies], huḥ phaṭ"—this is the armor-mantra (tanucchada). || 11-11 ||
At the end of "mahiṣāntesūdini," the weapon-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ" is proclaimed; with these mantras joined by their respective seed-syllables (jāti), one should fashion the five limbs.
Now, the meditation: I bow to her who resembles a garuḍa-stone, adorned with a jeweled crown and earrings, possessing an eye on her forehead, and seated upon the head of the buffalo-demon.
She bears in her own arms a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a trident,
and a raised index finger, and she has the moon as her crest-jewel.
Regarding the *puraścaraṇa*:
one should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times; the remainder [of the instruction] is that one should offer oblations with auspicious sesame seeds a thousand times for each [recitation].
Thus ends the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī. Now follows the mantra of Śūlinī;
it is in that same [text].
At the end of the word *jvalajvala*, one should utter the word *śūlinī*.
The mantra for a malignant planet is *huṃ* at the end followed by *svāhā*;
it is said that with five or ten recitations, it destroys enemies among the planets. (11-15)
The seer (ṛṣi) is declared to be Dīrghatamas; Kakubh is cited as the meter (chandas);
and Śūlinī, who is worshipped by all the gods, is declared to be the deity (devatā). || 11-16 ||
"Durge" is the heart-mantra; "hṛdvarade śīrṣa" is the head-mantra for her who dwells in the Vindhya mountains;
"asurānte mardinī" is the weapon-mantra (śikhā); and again, "yuddhapūrvapriye" is [the armor-mantra]. (11.17)
The two-triangle armor, O goddess highly honored by the Siddhas, is Nandinī; then follow the pair of protections, Mahāyogeśvarī, in sequence. (11–18)
The five limb-mantras are known to begin with *śūlinī* and end with *phaṭ*. Now, the visualization (*dhyāna*):
[She] is mounted upon a lion, dark as a water-laden cloud, with her lotus-hands...
She who bears the trident, the arrow, the sword, the lotus, the mace, the bow, and the noose.

I meditate upon the wielder of the trident, who is adorned with the moon as her crest-ornament, possesses three eyes, and is served by maidens bearing swords and shields— she who strikes fear into rival warriors.
Now follows the preliminary ritual (puraścaraṇa).
The wise practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times.
The oblation with clarified butter (ājya) should be one-tenth the measure of that [total].
Thus ends the mantra of Śūlinī. Now, the mantra of Vanadurgā. [Note: In most manuscripts, "Vanadurgā" appears as "Navadurgā."]
Having uttered the word "uttiṣṭha" (arise), there should then be the word "puruṣi" (O woman). || 11-21 ||
"O Grandfather, if you sleep with our eyes open, there would be fear for me;
therefore, having uttered [this], it should be done immediately if possible. (11.22)
Or else, O Blessed Lady, tell me that which is impossible for me;
then the mantra consisting of thirty-seven syllables is the wife of the Fire-god Śamaya. (11.23)
The seer is Āraṇyaka, and the meter is said to be Atyanuṣṭubh;
the deity is Vanadurgā, the liberator from all difficulties. (11.24)
The arrangement of the limbs (aṅga) should be performed according to the sequence with the six, four, eight, eight, and six syllables of the mantra, joined with the seed-syllables (jāti). || 11-25 ||
Now, for the meditation:
[One should meditate on her] seated in the center of a golden lotus, three-eyed, resembling a flash of lightning,
holding a conch, a discus, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and bearing a digit of the moon.

One should meditate upon the moon-faced Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains, who wears necklaces, armlets, strings of pearls, and earrings; who is praised by Indra and the other gods; and who has a lion standing at her side. (11.26)
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):

having meditated in this manner, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times; then, as a tenth part of that, he should offer oblations of sacrificial food, *śāli* rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
Thus ends the mantra of Vanadurgā.
Now follows the mantra of Cāmuṇḍā, who is identical with the nine Durgās (according to the Merutantra).
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Cāmuṇḍā, which consists of the nine Durgās; by the service of which come both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By whose grace Suratha, having obtained a kingdom, became Manu;
and by whom, through meditative absorption (samādhi), knowledge that destroys the bonds of saṃsāra was attained. (11.29)
I shall now declare that mantra which bestows the fruit of recitation and other rites upon this triad of life-stories and hymn as told in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
One should utter the seed-syllables of speech (*vāg*), modesty (*lajjā*), and desire (*kāma*), followed by the word *cāmuṇḍāyai*.
"Vicce"—this is the nine-syllable mantra, the most excellent of all Śakti mantras. (11.31)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are proclaimed as his sages;
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, and Anuṣṭubh are declared to be his three meters. (11.32)
His deities are Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī; Nandā, Śākambharī, and Bhīmā are declared to be the triad of Śaktis. (11.33)
His three powers are Durgā, Bhrāmarī, and Raktadantikā;
one should assign the principles of fire, wind, and earth, as well as the seers and so forth, as previously described.
Likewise: "Then one should perform the six-limbed [mantra] using the distinct root-syllables:
with one, one, one, four, and a pair. (11.35)
One should perform the six limbs in sequence with that very same mantra.
Now, the meditation:
thereafter, one should meditate upon the triad of goddesses; the meditation on Kālikā is now described. (11.36)
One should meditate upon her who has ten faces, ten feet, and ten hands, praised by the Creator,
possessing the luster of sapphire, and holding a sword, a discus, a conch, a severed head, and arrows.
Holding a mace, a trident, and a *bhuśuṇḍikā* in her right hands, and holding an iron club and a bow in her left hands—she who is praised by Brahmā. || 11-38 ||
For the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha, [he visualizes] the three-eyed [Lord] adorned with ornaments.
Also in another Tantra:
"A sword, a discus, a mace, arrows, a bow, a bludgeon, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī*, and a head."
Holding a conch shell with her hands, she has three eyes and is adorned with ornaments on all her limbs.
I worship Mahākālī, who possesses the luster of a blue gem and ten faces and feet—
the one whom the lotus-born Brahmā sought out while Hari was asleep, in order to slay Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Thus ends the mantra of Cāmuṇḍā.
Now, the meditation on Mahālakṣmī (from the Merutantra):
Then one should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura. (11.40)
Born from the splendor of all the deities, seated upon a lotus throne, she has eighteen arms; [she holds] a rosary, a lotus, and arrows. (11.41)
She holds a sword, a vajra, a mace, and a discus in her right hands,
and a water-pot, a conch, a spear, an axe, and a bow in her left hands.
A skin, a staff, a vessel for liquor, a bell, a noose, and a trident; and elsewhere:
a rosary, an axe, maces, arrows, a thunderbolt, a lotus, a bow, and a water-pot.
A staff, a spear, a sword, a shield, a lotus, a bell, and a vessel for wine.
I worship here Mahālakṣmī, who sits upon a lotus, possesses the luster of coral, and holds a trident, a noose, and the Sudarśana discus in her hands as she tramples Śarabha.
Now, the meditation on Sarasvatī:
Then, one should meditate upon Sarasvatī, whose radiance is equal to the autumnal moon. (Merutantra 11.44)
She bears the conch, the mace, the discus,
and arrows in her right hands, and she bears the bell, the trident, the plough, and the bow in her left hands.
Born from the body of Gaurī, she bestows bliss upon men;
she is the foundation of the universe and the destroyer of Śumbha and his ilk.
One should always remember her as the presiding deity of the third conduct (*caritra*).
Also, in another tantra:
"The bell, trident, plow, conch, pestle, discus, bow, and arrow..."
Holding with her lotus-hands a radiance as white as the cool-rayed moon shining at the end of the rainy season.

I worship Sarasvatī, who emerged from the body of Gaurī, who is the foundation of the three worlds, the Great One (Mahāpūrvā), and the crusher of the Daityas headed by Śumbha. Now follows the *puraścaraṇa*.
Starting from the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, up until the eighth day.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with edible offerings soaked in the three sweets;
one should worship the Goddess Caṇḍī every day and recite [the hymn] at the beginning and at the end.
By propitiating Brahmins and one's gurus, one quickly obtains what is desired.
Now follows the mantra of Jayadurgā (from the Śāradā-tantra):
Tāra, the pair "durge," the red [syllable], the final [letter] and the one ending in ḍha, together with the eyes. || 11-50 ||
This ten-syllable Vidyā of Jayadurgā ends with two *ṭha*s;
it is to be known as beginning with *Tārā* (Oṃ), with *Durge* as the Heart (*hṛdaya*) and *Durge* as the Head (*śiras*). (11.51)
The *śikhā* mantra is for Durgā, while the *varman* is proclaimed as Bhūtarakṣiṇī;
the pair beginning with Tārā and Durgā is declared to be the weapon (*astra*) of Rakṣiṇī. (11.52)
Now, for the meditation:
[One should meditate upon her] who resembles a dark cloud, who strikes fear into the hosts of enemies with her sidelong glances, who has the crescent moon bound upon her crest,
who bears in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident, and who possesses three eyes.

One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is mounted upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire three worlds with her splendor, surrounded by the thirty gods, and served by those desiring spiritual accomplishments.
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one million times (some read "one hundred thousand times according to the number of syllables"), and thereafter perform oblations with clarified butter.
One should offer a tenth part of that into the consecrated fire and also feed Brahmins. (54)
Thus ends the section on Durgā. Now, the procedure for the Durgā festival is presented (from the Bṛhatsiddhāntasāra).
During the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, those who seek the fruits of the four aims of human life should propitiate Śrī Durgā with various kinds of great festivals.
(In the Kālikāpurāṇa):
By means of the Durgā-tantra mantra, kings and others should perform the great festival of Durgā; on the Mahānavamī day in autumn, they should offer the bali-oblation. (11.56) p. 959)
On the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
the Great Goddess accepts worship through various forms for the sake of prosperity.
O child, when the sun is situated in Virgo, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (Śukla-pakṣa) on a Nandā tithi, one should remain free from begging,
subsisting on food at night, eating only once a day, or else giving food as alms, while consuming only air.
"Bathing at dawn, having conquered the pairs of opposites, and worshipping Śiva three times a day on the Mahānavamī"— thus it is said.
That has been stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, during the triad of lunar days beginning with the seventh.
