"The great sound (*mahāśabda*) is to be employed [only] there and not elsewhere; this is the settled conclusion. Regarding "beginning": the meaning is "beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*). Regarding "giver of food" (*annada*): the meaning is "having fed the Brāhmaṇas. In the reading *vāyvada*, however, the meaning is "one who subsists on air" (*vāyubhakṣa*). Regarding "one who has conquered the pairs of opposites" (*jitadvandva*): the meaning is "one who endures cold, heat, and so forth. In the term "worshipper of Śiva" (*śivapūjaka*), one should understand that a *ekaśeṣa* compound is intended. (From the *Rudrayāmala*)
But by increasing by one each time, it continues indeed up to the ninth.
One should recite the Caṇḍī-pāṭha oneself or have it recited according to the prescribed rules;
likewise, one should thus propitiate all the Brahmins who are learned in the four Vedas.
And their selection must indeed be made for the purpose of reciting the Vedas to completion.
In another Tantra it is said: "O Maheśvarī, among the Vīrarātris and others, Mahārātri is the most excellent. (11.62)
Having observed the fast, one should worship Durgā, the destroyer of the distress of those in difficulty.
These are declared [in the *Śaktisaṅgama*] as Vīrarātri and so forth: "Vīrarātri, Mahārātri, and likewise Kālarātri. (11.63)
The great night, the terrible night, and likewise the night of wrath;
likewise the immovable night, and likewise the starry night. (11.64)
O Supreme Goddess, Śivarātri is described as the Divine Night and the Terrible Night respectively; listen and be attentive. (11.65)
On the fourteenth day, during a transit [of the sun], under a *kula* asterism, on a *kula* day,
or at midnight according to the proper conjunction, it is proclaimed as the "Night of Heroes" (*vīrarātri*).
The eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is indeed the Navarātra;
it is the Mahārātri, O Maheśānī. Listen, my beloved, to [the description of] Kālarātri.
On the fourteenth day of the festival of lamps (Dīpotsava), when it coincides with the new moon (Amāvāsyā) yoga,
she is Kālarātri, O Maheśānī, the beloved Tārākālī who bestows grace.
O Great Goddess, Janmāṣṭamī is proclaimed as the Night of Delusion (Moharātri). Likewise,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, O Son of the Earth (Bhūsuta), || 11-68 ||
O Maheśānī, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, Krodharātri will appear in the form of a star, O Maheśvarī.
And Ghorarātri is proclaimed to have the very nature of Mahākāla;
she is the eleventh day of the dark fortnight when the month of Phālguna has arrived.
If the tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha is joined with Venus and Mars, it is declared to be Acalārātri. (11.71)
O Supreme Goddess, if the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is joined with the ten yogas, that lunar day is proclaimed as a divine night.
The tenth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, when endowed with the ten yogas,
is declared to be the sacred day (tithi) of Vaṭuka, which brings about the manifestation of Vaṭuka.
If there should be an eclipse on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā) conjoined with Mars, occurring at a solar transit (saṃkrānti), and associated with the Kula constellation; || 11-74 ||
The Tārārātri is said to be obtained only through good fortune;
it occurs at midnight on a Friday during the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, O Śivā. (11.75)
Śivarātri has indeed arrived, bestowing all spiritual perfections;
it is the new moon joined with a Friday, occurring simultaneously with a solar eclipse.
When the conjunction occurs in the afternoon on the Mṛtasaṃjīvinī lunar day, all acts from bathing and giving gifts up to the performance of fire-oblations shall yield infinite fruit. (11.77)
The eighth day of the month of Caitra, when conjoined with a solar transit (saṃkrānti), is renowned as Siddhirātri; in the Kali age, it is equal to Tārākālī.
The third [lunar day] in the bright fortnight of Mādhava, conjoined with the asterism and weekday of the Kula,
is proclaimed as the supreme Goddess Dāruṇā, the sovereign of all accomplishments.
And there are the *kulavāra*s (family days) and so forth: the Sun, Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are considered *akula* (non-family).
Mars and Venus are known as *kula*, while Wednesday is *kulākula*. (11.80)
The second, tenth, and sixth lunar days are declared to be *kulākula*; all the odd-numbered days are *akula*, and the remaining lunar days are *kula*. (11.81)
Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Ārdrā, Abhijit, and Mūla are declared to be both *kula* and *akula*.
Those constellations that possess an even number of stars are *kula*, while the remaining ones are *akula*.
Thus it is declared in the Rudrayāmala: "Likewise,
O Pārvatī, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of every month,"
Whether conjoined with Mars, or likewise conjoined with a lunar mansion, or even alone.
The goddess known as Rātri bestows all accomplishments;
she is joined with the lunar mansions, specifically joined with the Kula-mansion.
Likewise:
O Great Goddess, that which occurs every month as Budhāṣṭamī— 11.84.
p. 962) It is especially renowned as Viṣṇurātri in the month of Bhādrapada;
in that very context (in the *Navarātranirṇaya*), it is called Navarātra because it is endowed with the nine Śaktis. || 11-85 ||
O Goddess of the lords of gods, she who is one alone is established in nine ways;
the Navarātra becomes twofold, consisting of the periods known as Śayana (Sleeping) and Bodhana (Awakening).
The Lord’s reclining occurs in the month of Caitra, and His awakening in Āśvina;
by fasting on both occasions, a person shall attain all perfections.

One should practice according to one's capacity: abstaining from food, subsisting on fruits, eating only once a day, observing the vow of water, eating only at night, or consuming sacrificial oblations (haviṣya). || 11-88 ||
Now, regarding the characteristics of the pavilion used for the worship of the Goddess (*Devīpūjopayukta-maṇḍapa-lakṣaṇa*), [it is stated in] the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"In the northeast or in the eastern part, one should construct a temple for the Goddess that is pleasing to the mind and endowed with all auspicious characteristics, so as to achieve success. (11.89)
Beginning from ten or twelve cubits up to a hundred cubits,
a very beautiful square temple for Durgā should be constructed (according to the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa). || 11-90 ||
The secret [mandala] is smeared with svastikas and other designs, adorned with cloth,
encircled by rows of lamps, and beautified by garlands at the entrance.
It is declared that it is auspicious when smeared with white clay and cow dung;
in its center, a level and beautiful altar measuring four cubits should be constructed.
Upon that [throne], there should be a gentle lion-throne provided with woolen and deerskin covers;
having installed Durgā there, who is endowed with all auspicious marks.
She consists of all the gods, is radiant with the intoxication of full youth,
and is adorned with either four or ten beautiful arms.
Her limbs have the color of molten gold; she has three eyes and the moon as her crest-jewel;
she is clothed in yellow garments and draped in dark blue silk. (11.95)
Adorned with necklaces, strings of pearls, armlets, and anklets,
she was resplendent with a crown variegated with various jewels.
She was resplendent with her matted locks strewn with many flowers,
and she made a tinkling sound from the small bells fastened to the curve of her hips.
She holds a trident, a discus, a staff, a spear, a vajra, a bow, and a sword;
her hands shine with a bell, a rosary, and a skull-cup vessel.
Before him was a buffalo with its head severed, drenched in blood,
with half its body protruding from the throat, holding a shield and a sword.
The Daitya, whose neck was seized by the hand of the Goddess, was struck in the chest with her trident;
his mouth was filled with formidable fangs, and the hair on his head was tawny like lightning.
He was cast down by the serpent-noose and pursued by the tawny-eyed lion; with blood flowing from his mouth, he shook off half of the enraged lion's mane.
She is served on all sides by the circle of Mothers and likewise by the gods, with her staff-like upward-pointing tail beautified by the presence of the Goddess.
A man, being self-restrained and established in his observances, should worship the Goddess.
Regarding the installation, a specific rule is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Durgā facing south bestows auspiciousness; facing east, she increases victory."
"It should always face west; it must not be placed facing the north. || 11-103 ||
The meditation on the ten-armed [form] as described in the *Matsyapurāṇa* is as follows:
"I shall describe the ten-armed form of Kātyāyanī, who brings about the dharma, kama, and artha of all three deities. (11.104)
She is endowed with a mass of matted hair marked by the crescent moon, possessed of three eyes, and has a face resembling a lotus or the moon. || 11-105 ||
Having the complexion of an *atasī* flower, well-established, with beautiful eyes, endowed with fresh youth, and adorned with all ornaments. (11.106)
Likewise, [he saw] Mahiṣāsuramardinī, who possesses beautiful teeth, full and elevated breasts, and is poised in the tribhaṅga posture.
One should place a trident in the right [hand], and below it, a sword and a discus in succession;
likewise, understand that a sharp arrow and a spear are on the left. (11.108)
One should place a shield and a full bow, a noose and an elephant-goad above;
and on the left, one should arrange a bell or even an axe. (11.109)
Likewise, one should depict below it a buffalo that is headless;

and likewise, the head should be shown as having arisen from that [buffalo], belonging to the Dānava who holds a sword in his hand. [Note: Regarding the term *khaḍgapāṇikam* here, the reading *khaḍgapāṇinam* is found in all manuscripts. || 11-110 ||
One should depict the lion of the Goddess as having its mane grasped by Durgā with her left hand, which holds a noose, and with blood flowing from its mouth.
The goddess’s right foot is placed evenly atop the lion,
while her left foot is slightly raised, with the big toe positioned upon the buffalo.
And while that form is being praised by the immortals, one should install it.
Now, the meditation on the sixteen-armed [form] (from the Kālikāpurāṇa): Yoganidrā, Mahāmāyā, the sustainer of the world, whose nature is the world... 11.113.
Endowed with sixteen arms and known as Bhadrakālī,
she assumes a vast body upon the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
She has the luster of the color of an *atasī* flower, wears blazing golden earrings,
and is adorned with a mass of matted hair, the unbroken moon, and three crowns.
Accompanied by a necklace of serpents and adorned with a golden chain, she likewise holds a trident, a sword, a conch, a discus, and an arrow. (11.116)
The goddess, with eyes ever-bright and radiant, constantly bears in her right arms a spear, a thunderbolt, and a staff.
He holds in his left hands a shield, a shield-skin, a bow, a noose, a goad, a bell, an axe, and a pestle.
Seated upon a lion, with three red eyes blazing with fire,
the Supreme Goddess stands piercing the buffalo with her trident.
Having stepped upon that place with her left foot, the Goddess who is identical with the universe—
whose meditation with eighteen arms has already been described— [remains there].
Now, the meditation on Caṇḍikā is as follows in that very same [text]:
Her hair was bound in a *dhammilla* braid, like the crescent of the moon turned downwards.
Bearing a beautiful tilaka above the hairline,
her cheeks were brushed by jeweled earrings, and she was adorned with a crown.
Her ears were filled with two ear-ornaments that were glowing lamps;
she was adorned with necklaces of gold, gems, rubies, and serpents.
Wearing jeweled armlets, that most beautiful woman always bears upon her neck a garland of ever-fresh and exceedingly lovely, fragrant lotuses.
With her beautiful, tender arms, round and as long as lotus stalks, she shone, adorned with a bodice and possessing full, elevated breasts.
With a slender waist, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with three folds across her midriff,
she likewise holds a trident, a thunderbolt, an arrow, a sword, and a spear.
Holding [the weapons] with her left hands in the sequence starting from the top,
Kauśikī stands upon a tiger skin atop a lion.
Bearing an incomparable form that enchants both gods and asuras—(p.
966) now, the meditation on Sarvamaṅgalā (from the Devīpurāṇa):
Brahmā said:
In the incarnation, Sarvamaṅgalā has been described in brief. || 11-127 ||
I shall correctly describe the characteristics of the image as they should be:
she should be seated upon a lion-throne or a lotus-seat, serene in appearance, and adorned with a crown of matted hair. (11.128)
The auspicious one with four arms is described as holding a trident, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and a water-pot in her hands; likewise, hear now about the eight-armed one.
In the right hands, he holds the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a sword, and a rosary;
in the left, there should be a mirror, a trident, a bow, and a fourth [hand] holding a shield.

Thus the eight-armed goddess is Maṅgalā, the source of all auspiciousness. Now follows the determination of the time for awakening the Goddess. In that regard, the specific times for awakening the single goddess Mahiṣamardinī through various meditations on her eighteen arms and other forms are stated in the *Mahātharvaṇasaṃhitā*:
"Durgā, who is remembered as Ugracaṇḍā, possesses eighteen arms. (11–131)
This very same goddess, when endowed with sixteen arms, is celebrated as Bhadrakālī;
when endowed with ten arms, she is remembered as Kātyāyanī.
She who crushes the demon Mahiṣāsura is differentiated by meditation according to the distinction of the Kalpas;
she is to be awakened at the specific time during the rites of the Durgā festival.
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, having worshipped with devotion during the day, one should awaken Ugracaṇḍā on the Khaḍga-nakṣatra under the constellation Ārdrā.
"During the dark fortnight of Āśvina" means during the dark fortnight of Āśvina ending with the full moon.
Thus,

the meaning of the sentence is that one should awaken Ugracaṇḍā by worshipping her with a sword during the day on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina ending with the full moon, when it is conjoined with the lunar mansion Ārdrā.
(From the Liṅga Purāṇa and also the Devī Purāṇa:
When one worships the eighteen-armed Mahāmāyā during the dark fortnight of the month of Kanyā, on a day when the moon is in the constellation Ārdrā, by day; 11-135.
On the ninth day, one should awaken the Goddess with the sounds of songs and musical instruments;
on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, however, is the loosening of the Goddess’s hair.
On the morning of the fifth day, they should bathe [the image] with auspicious waters;
on the seventh day, there is worship of the foliage (patrikā), and on the eighth day, the fast (abhyupoṣaṇa).
On the ninth day, there shall be worship, a vigil, and the offering of oblations according to the rules;
on the tenth day, however, there is the dismissal [of the deity] accompanied by play, festivities, and auspicious rites.
(Also in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"O Dear One, those mortals who desire to worship the goddess named Ugracaṇḍā, who possesses eighteen arms, are considered her devotees. (11.139)
Likewise, on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, those who are well-composed should awaken Karavāla at midday with the sounds of conch shells. || 11.140 ||
Midday (madhyāhna) is the third part of the day divided into five parts.
The first portion of the day is known as the morning (prātaḥkāla);
the second is called the forenoon (saṅgava), and the third is midday (madhyāhna). (11–141)
"Midday is the fourth [period], and evening is recorded as the fifth"—according to this statement.

The phrase "with the sounds of conchs" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); it means "with the sounds of various musical instruments such as conchs and others. In this matter, on whichever day of the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) the *Ārdrā* asterism is obtained during the day, the awakening (*bodhana*) should be performed on that very day. However, if the *Ārdrā* asterism is not obtained during the day on the ninth lunar day for two consecutive days, then by the force of the scriptural injunction regarding the *yugma-vidhi* (the rule of pairing), the awakening should be performed on the ninth lunar day even if it is overlapped by the eighth (*aṣṭamī*). Thus, even when the *Ārdrā* asterism is not obtained, the determination is made solely through respect for the *yugma* rule; so says the author of the *Varṣakriyākaumudī*.

In reality, however, because the statement of Mahākāla—“At midday, with the sounding of conchs”—indicates that midday is the time for awakening, the determination [of the proper time] is made by its very pervasion.

This is according to the declaration of Bṛhadyājñavalkya: “Whichever lunar day (tithi) pervades the specific time of a particular rite, that lunar day [is to be taken]. When [the asterism] pervades midday on both days, or does not pervade it at all, [the decision depends on] the asterism. Regarding the asterism:
The statements regarding the *yugma* (pairings) have been stated in the *Nigama*:

"Of the pair [of tithis] beginning with Agni (the third), the pair of Yugas (the fourth and fifth), the pair of Bhūtas (the ninth and tenth), the pair of Ṣaṇmuni (the seventh and eighth), and the pair of Vasu and Randhra (the eighth and ninth);
likewise, the twelfth joined with the thirteenth, and the full moon joined with the fourteenth. (11.142)
"The first lunar day (pratipad) and the new moon (amāvāsyā)—this pair of lunar days yields great fruit;
the wise declare that these, when separated [from their proper sequence], cause great harm.
Here, the words beginning with "pair" (yugma) and ending with "navel" (randhra) denote the lunar days starting from the second and ending with the ninth. Rudra is the eleventh. The rest is clear.

Although statements such as "the pair [of tithis] beginning with the two fires" (*yugmāgni*) have been explained by the *Nirṇayāmṛta* and others as referring to the bright fortnight— on the grounds that the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), the new moon (*amā*), and the pair consisting of the first lunar day (*pratipad*) cannot occur in the dark fortnight— nevertheless, because Mādhava states that "in both fortnights, the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) is indeed joined with the preceding one," even in the dark fortnight, the ninth must be accepted only when conjoined with the eighth (*aṣṭamī*). However, the authors of the commentaries on the legal digests (*nibandha*) maintain that these "pair" statements apply to both fortnights, since they cite another Smṛti text which reads "the fourteenth and the full moon" (*caturdaśyā ca pūrṇimā*) instead of "the thirteenth and the fourteenth" (*trayodaśyā caturdaśī*).

The author of the *Nirṇayasindhu* also stated that because of the mention of the new moon (*amā*) and the first lunar day (*pratipad*) in pairs, and due to the indicative marks of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), this [rule] refers to both fortnights; however, by means of specific statements regarding particular lunar days in the dark fortnight, he declared that [the rite] is restricted to those specific occasions.

As for the mention of the conjunction with the *Ārdrā* asterism in the verse, "Having worshipped during the day under *Ārdrā*," this is intended to indicate the possibility of the conjunction as being auspicious.
Thus, the conclusion is that, when possible, one should perform the awakening ceremony on the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) which extends through midday and is conjoined with the *Ārdrā* asterism.
When there is a conjunction of a lunar day (tithi) and a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), both must be observed.

"In the absence of a [favorable] yoga, the lunar day (tithi) alone should be accepted for the rite of worshipping the Goddess"—so says Devala as cited in the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Furthermore, the conjunction with specific asterisms (nakṣatras) serves to increase the fruit [of the rite]. And from the words of Mahākāla: "In the event that the [asterisms] are not obtained, however, the lunar day alone is highly recommended."

The authors of the *Nirṇayāmṛta*, however, state that because the suffix *ktvā*—in the word "having worshipped" (*pūjayitvā*)—indicates a prior time relative to another action performed by the same agent (as in the rule *samānakartṛkayoḥ pūrvakāle ktvā*), and since the instruction to "awaken on the ninth day" (*navamyāṃ bodhayet*) establishes the awakening as occurring on the ninth day, the worship must necessarily take place on the eighth day; thus, they maintain that worship is on the eighth and the awakening is on the ninth. This is established in the *Nirṇayasindhu*, where it is noted: "Having worshipped on the eighth day"—[this is a variant reading found in some manuscripts]. (Note: *iti 4 pu0 pā0* refers to a specific manuscript reading).
As for the view that worship should be performed on the eighth day conjoined with the lunar mansion Ārdrā and the awakening [of the deity] on the ninth day, that opinion is trivial.
"The ninth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina which is joined with the asterism of Śiva (Ārdrā)... (11.144).
"Having awakened the Goddess, one should begin the autumnal worship in her"—for thus Mahākāla has declared that the conjunction with the *Ārdrā* asterism occurs on the ninth lunar day itself.

Thus, beginning from the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina until the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, there is the festival according to the tradition of the eighteen-armed [form].
Now, the tradition of the sixteen-armed [form] (from the *Mahātharvaṇasaṃhitā*):
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, having awakened Bhadrakālī who is endowed with sixteen arms, one should worship her until the ninth day.

(Also in the Mahākālasaṃhitā: "On the very first day of the bright fortnight, having awakened the Goddess of the Gods, one should worship her for nine days according to the procedures of the Tantras and the Purāṇas. (11.146)

However, when the festival is to be performed according to the purely Puranic tradition, the awakening of the sixteen-armed [Goddess] should be performed specifically on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
This is stated in both the *Kaumudī* and the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"When one worships Mahāmāyā with sixteen arms..."
Listen now to the specific [instruction] regarding that [rite] by means of the Durgātantra mantra.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Kanyā,
one should take a single meal on the twelfth day and observe the nakta vow on the following day.
On the fourteenth day, having awakened Mahāmāyā according to the prescribed rite with the sounds of songs and musical instruments and the offering of various food oblations, || 11-149 ||
"A wise man should observe a fast on the following day even if it has not been specifically requested;
in this very manner he should perform the vow until indeed the ninth day arrives. (11.150)
Regarding the installation of the jar (*kalaśasthāpana*), it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
"The installation of the jar must likewise be performed on the first lunar day (*pratipad*).
However, according to the third position, the installation of the jar will be described as taking place on the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*).

Now, the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina is determined. In rites such as the worship of Durgā, that [tithi] should be taken when it is joined with the following day (*paraviddhā*).

"Whichever first day of the bright fortnight occurs in the month of Āśvayuja and is conjoined with the *Bhadrā* [nakṣatra], my worship performed on that day bestows the fruit of a hundred sacrifices. (11.151)
Thus, because the *Devīpurāṇa* prescribes the excellence of the [tithi] overlapped by the next day:
"If the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is overlapped by the previous [day], the Navarātra vow should not be performed on it by one desiring auspiciousness. (11.152)
In that place where my worship is performed on the Nandā day joined with the lunar mansion Darśa, the destruction of the country will occur and a famine shall arise. (11.153)

Thus, because of the prohibition of the *pūrvaviddhā* (the first lunar day overlapping with the previous day) in both the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and the *Devī Purāṇa*, and because it is stated in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"The first lunar day (*pratipad*) that is always joined with the new moon (*amā*) is considered censurable."
In that case, one should not place the water-pot; a famine will certainly arise.
The first lunar day (*pratipad*) is auspicious for the work of placing the water-pot (*kumbha*),
but one should avoid the *pratipad* tithi when it is joined with the fourteenth day (*kuhū*) or the eighth day (*kāṣṭhā*). (From the *Kalpataru*, 11.155)
She was declared to cause the destruction of the kingdom; therein, worship is censured.
(In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain the procedure for the worship of Caṇḍikā. (11.156)
Beginning with: "On the first day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, on a most auspicious day," it continues:
"The rite should be performed on a pure lunar day, specifically one that follows immediately after the first day (pratipad). (11.157)
Having omitted the first sixteen or even twelve nāḍīs, those who desire a pure lineage should perform [the rite] during the afternoon. (11.158)

The excellence of the *yoginī* [tithi] in the afternoon should be understood as applying when there is no *pratipad* on the second day. In that very same [text], the *Uḍḍāmaratantra*, there is the statement of the Goddess:
"The *pratipad* joined with the new moon (*amā*) must not be used for my worship.
It should be performed even if it lasts for only a *muhūrta*, provided it is endowed with the qualities of the second day. (11.159)
If a man performs the installation of the ritual jar (kalaśasthāpana) having obtained the first sixteen channels (nāḍī), misfortune will certainly arise there. (11.160)
In the *Śaktisaṅgama*, it is said:

"The first sixteen ghaṭikās of each lunar day (pratipad) should be avoided; one should perform the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*) during that time, and then prosperity arises. (11.161)
Likewise,
it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The first lunar day (pratipad) joined with the new moon (amāvāsyā) must not be used for the ritual worship performed at the prescribed time."
O King, one should avoid with great effort a day joined with the new moon (amāvāsyā).
The first lunar day (pratipad), when endowed with the qualities beginning with the second [tithi], grants all desires.
(From the Devīpurāṇa) These are the words of the Goddess:
"Whoever worships me with devotion, endowed with the qualities beginning with the second [tithi]," (11.163).
Having understood the first day of the autumn month [Śarad-pratipad], he attains imperishable happiness;
provided that he establishes the first day as joined with the new moon (Amāyukta-pratipat) for me.
Having given him ten thousand curses, I shall bring about the destruction of his lineage—
he who, out of obstinacy, performs my first installation.
For him, there will be the destruction of his prosperity and his eldest son will perish;
therefore, the first lunar day (pratipad) joined with the new moon (amāvāsyā) must not be used for the worship of Caṇḍikā.
Especially for those seeking wealth, a loss of lineage occurs;
the first lunar day (pratipad) joined with the digit of the new moon (darśakalā) is not suitable for the worship of Caṇḍikā.
Even if it lasts for only two muhūrtas at sunrise, it should be accepted if it extends to the sunrise;
this applies elsewhere as well:
"The pure first day of Āśvina that is overlapped by the next [tithi]... (11.168).
"In that regard, one should perform the festival of Durgā, avoiding [the day] joined with the new moon (amā).
Now, as for these statements: "The pair consisting of the first lunar day (pratipad) and the new moon (amāvāsyā) yields great fruit. (11.169) p. 972)
If it is argued that these [rules] contradict the statements regarding the *yugma* (paired dates), we say no; for those *yugma* statements refer to *pratipads* other than this specific *pratipad*.
As it is stated in the *Nandikeśvara Purāṇa*: "Therefore, it is said in the *Devī Purāṇa*:
'The great annual worship (*mahāpūjā*) which is performed in the autumn season...'"
"In that case, when the result is to arise [on the following day], there is no pairing of lunar days (tithi-yugmatā) therein. — 11.170 ||
And having fully worshipped Navadurgā, one should perform the rite known as Navarātra at night with a concentrated mind;
this is remembered as the Naktavrata.
Thus, since it is established from the *Skānda* that this Navarātra vow is a *nakta-vrata* (a vow to be observed at night),
one must state that only the [lunar day] overlapping with the previous [tithi] is to be accepted, according to the scriptural statement: "In all *nakta-vratas*, connection with the night is praised."

Because of specific prohibitions such as "it should not be performed when joined with the new moon" (amā), and furthermore, because this is not merely a nakta-vow; thus [it is said]: "In this way, by fasting during the nine nights for Vindhyavāsinī... (11.172).

By means of eating once a day, by eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is unasked for, people should worship the Goddess in various places and in every city according to their own capacity. (11.173)
(From the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* in the *Hemādri*: because four vows have been mentioned [the reading in the fourth manuscript is "because of the mention of various vows"];

for this very reason, Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa stated: "This is a restatement of the optional night-fast" [the reading in the fourth manuscript is: "Even though many rites such as fasting are mentioned here, the worship of the Goddess alone is the primary element—so say those who know the secret"].

Regarding this, some hold that because of the scriptural injunction for the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*) found in the *Rudrayāmala*, *Devīpurāṇa*, and other texts, it is that [installation] alone which is prohibited on the first day, and not the fasting and so forth; for the [rule of] the *yugma* states: "The first lunar day (*pratipad*) is like the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)."

They say that because Mādhava states, "In the bright fortnight, [the day] pierced by the new moon [is the one to be taken]," there is no authority for setting aside this [rule] when it applies to the previous day.
However, in reality,

since the worship of the Goddess is the primary element here and is prohibited on the previous day, it is logical that even for its ancillary elements such as fasting (*upavāsa*), the subsequent day alone should be observed.

For this very reason, Devala has stated: "In the case of vows, fasts, and observances, even a single *ghaṭikā* [of the lunar day] that occurs on a day makes that *tithi* worshipable on that day; however, the opposite is the rule for ancestral rites (*paitṛka*). (11.174)
Regarding this, the Gauḍas maintain that the word *ghaṭikā* refers to a *muhūrta*. Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, however, states:

"The phrase 'one *ghaṭikā*' means it should be performed for at least one *muhūrta*, and the mention of 'two *muhūrtas*' is a commendatory exaggeration (*stuti*). Therefore, the first lunar day (*pratipad*) occurring at sunrise should be accepted if it lasts for two *muhūrtas*; otherwise, the injunction regarding two *muhūrtas* would result in being purposeless."

However, when [the new moon] becomes complete and pure on the previous day and increases on the following day, then the previous day alone is to be accepted because of its completeness and the absence of conjunction with the *amāvāsyā* (new moon).

As for those statements that some recite which prohibit conjunction with the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*), they say that these too are intended to prohibit [conjunction with] a pure *adhika* (intercalary) day. Furthermore, since even the statement regarding "two muhūrtas" is a praise of "three muhūrtas," the author of the *Samayaprakāśa* maintains that if on the following day the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is less than three muhūrtas, then the previous day alone is to be accepted, even if it is joined with the *darśa*.
In reality, however, the rule of three *muhūrtas* is the primary one; the rule of two *muhūrtas*, on the other hand, is a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).

That even two *muhūrtas* should be observed is because the word "also" (*api*) was used by Dakṣa [in the passage: "Even if it is for two *muhūrtas* at sunrise..."]. Thus, in the present case as well, since the word "also" is used in the phrase "even if it is for two *muhūrtas* at sunrise," it should be understood that the rule of two *muhūrtas* is a secondary alternative. (Note: This is the reading in the fourth manuscript.)
If the first lunar day (pratipad) does not exist on the following day, then that which is joined with the new moon (amā) should be accepted;

for it is stated in the commentary on the Nibandha: "It should be performed even if joined with the new moon, provided it does not exist on the following day. [The ten statements cited from other texts prescribing the first lunar day as joined with the tenth day (daśamī) refer to this very subject; thus reads the manuscript in the fourth volume.]
On this point, some say:
"When [the moon] increases, the completion [of the lunar day] occurs on the eighth; when it decreases, it occurs at night on the new moon or the first day. (11.175)
"The commencement of the Navarātra is indeed the Navacaṇḍī; therefore, the Navarātra is meaningful" (p.

974)—from this statement cited in the *Nirṇayasindhu* from the *Devīpurāṇa*, it follows that the word "Navarātra" refers to nine days and nights. This is because of the statement cited in the *Nirṇayasindhu* from the *Devīpurāṇa*: "In the case of the waning or waxing of a lunar day (*tithi*), the prior overlap (*pūrvavedha*) is not a defect. Furthermore, as stated in Tantric texts: "In the case of the waning or waxing of a lunar day, the prior overlap is not a defect" (as noted in the Puṇya-pāṭha).

As for those statements prohibiting the first lunar day (*pratipad*) when conjoined with the new moon (*amā*), they apply to cases where there is no decrease in the duration of the lunar day, so they say.
And this is the tradition of the land of Nepal;
however, in reality:
"The installation should not be performed at night, nor should the consecration with the water-pot. (11.176)

Thus, because the statement from the *Matsya Purāṇa* prohibits the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and other rites at night, and because it declares that "the commencement of the Nine-Śakti (*Navacaṇḍī*)" refers to the performance of worship and other acts for the first time, this statement concerns the recitation of the *Caṇḍī* text in nine repetitions over nine days.

The term *navarātra*, however, refers exclusively to the nine lunar days (*tithis*). In passages such as "the commencement of the *navarātra*," the word is used figuratively to denote the ritual action itself; for if it were taken to mean nine full days and nights, there would result a deficiency or excess [of days] due to the decrease or increase of lunar days.
Therefore it has been stated in the *Nirṇayāmṛta* and in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"In the case of the increase or decrease of lunar days (*tithi*), the Navarātra [calculation] becomes inconsistent;
this fault arises in the Navarātra when there is a loss of lunar days within the eight-night period. (11.177)

"Indeed, even if there is a decrease in the lunar days (tithi), the worship must be performed during the eight nights, excluding only the full moon; [it should be done] on the first day (pratipad) of the bright fortnight of Āśvina. — 11.178.
The prohibition regarding the conjunctions of Citrā and Vaidhṛti on the first lunar day (pratipad) is stated in that very same source:

"If the first lunar day is joined with the asterism of Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā) or with Vaidhṛti during the worship of Caṇḍikā, the installation of the water-jar (kalaśa) in the home should be performed in the interval between those two. || 11-179 ||
Likewise: O King, when the first day of the month of Āśvina is full and pure, the Navarātra should be commenced, avoiding the Citrā and Vaidhṛti constellations. (11.180)
But when the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) can be obtained by avoiding Citrā and Vaidhṛti, then Kātyāyana says:
"In the month of Āśvina, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, a man should avoid the first quarters of the constellations Vaidhṛti and Citrā and begin the Navarātra. (11.181)
(Also in the Rudrayāmala:
"In Vaidhṛti there shall be the loss of a son; in Citrā, the loss of wealth.
Therefore, one should not install the water-pot in Citrā, nor likewise in Vaidhṛti. (11.182)

O Goddess, when the first lunar day (pratipad) is complete and conjoined with the Citrā asterism, or even if it is conjoined with the Vaidhṛti yoga, then at midday on the sun [that day is auspicious]. (11.183)

If the moment Abhijit occurs therein, it is desired that [the image] be installed; O King, this applies if the first lunar day (pratipad) is fully joined with the asterism Citrā and the conjunction Vaidhṛti. (From the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa) 11.184.
Indeed, the first three quarters [of the lunar day] are to be abandoned, while worship is performed during the fourth quarter.
Even if the second [lunar day] is joined with Citrā and so forth, it is not considered defective if it is conjoined with the first; thus it is said in the *Durgotsava*:
"If the first lunar day is obtained even when accompanied by Bhadrā, or even though joined with adverse yogas... (11.185).
"Indeed, that [rite] should be performed by the wise in the afternoon; it is the cause for the increase of prosperity, sons, kingdom, and so forth.
Now follows the procedure for sowing barley (*yavavapanavidhi*) [from the *Rudrayāmala*]:
"Having performed an auspicious bath, one should then worship the Goddess. (11.186)
Having first constructed an altar with auspicious clay,
one should sow barley there, combined with wheat as well.
In another tantra:
"Having carefully collected sand originating from rivers and streams, one should diligently construct a square altar that brings about auspiciousness. (11.188)
The altar should be two cubits for the best, one and a half cubits for the middling, and one cubit for the lowest; one should not allow it to be either less or more than these measures.
Having recited the mantra "bhūrasi," the person, having touched the Goddess and pronounced the fire-mantra over the waters, should sprinkle her with scented water.
In the center of that, one should inscribe the supreme mantra known as Jayadurgā;
having invoked the Goddess there, one should worship the supreme deity who possesses eighteen arms. (11.191)
Having worshipped with the five offerings, one should also worship the guardians of the directions;
thereafter, one should worship the Weapon-Mātṛkā with the nine-syllable mantra.
Having purified the heap of barley while reciting the mantra "yavo 'si," he should cast it into the center of the altar while muttering the mantra that is about to be described.

Oṃ! Since you are barley, possessing the form of barley, created by the Ordainer for the sake of sacrifice, and because you bring satisfaction to the gods, therefore, may you be a granter of boons. (11.194)
O Jayantī, Maṅgalākālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā— salutations be to you!
Likewise,
one should celebrate a great festival with the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, hand-drums, bells, and war-drums during the rite of sowing barley.

When the tenth day has dawned, one should indeed consider whether it is auspicious or inauspicious; however, this consideration applies elsewhere [to other days]. If the sprouts have emerged properly, are long, and straight, they are auspicious. (11.197)
Those that do not rise up, have blunt tips, are short, dry, and brittle; those eaten by insects or mice, those that are decayed, and those that are uneven are considered inauspicious. || 11-198 ||
However, other deliberations written within this compendium have been disregarded because they are rooted in fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
(In the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Therein, one should establish the water-pot (*kumbha*) according to the ritual procedure preceded by mantras."
It may be made of gold, or silver, or copper, or even of clay. || 11-199 ||
(Matsya Purāṇa): One should not place the water-pot at night, nor should there be an ablution with the pot at night. — Viṣṇu.
Starting from the rising of the sun until ten nāḍikās have passed. || 11-200 ||
The morning time is prescribed for the rites of installation (*sthāpana*), consecration (*āropaṇa*), and so forth.
The procedure for installing the water-pot (*kalaśa*) will be explained in the *Vaiṣṇavīkalpa* section concerning the ten-armed form.
One should perform worship for nine days according to the rules prescribed for occasional rites (*naimittika*). (11–201)
The wise man should observe the fast on the eighth day, perform abundant offerings of oblations on the ninth day,
and then perform the ritual dismissal on the tenth day.
One who has sons, however, should not observe a fast on the Mahāṣṭamī.
"One who possesses sons should not perform a fast on the Mahāṣṭamī;
rather, with his mind restrained, he should worship the Goddess while observing the vow. (11.203)

Thus, from the *Kālikāpurāṇa*: "On the ninth day, there is the offering of abundant *bali*. By this, it follows that the offering of *bali* as an ancillary part of the worship (*pūjāṅga*) applies to the eighth day and so forth. Some recite a statement devoid of a name: "By the offering of *bali* on the eighth day, the destruction of one's son will certainly occur. The source for this must be sought. If it is asserted to have a source, it should be understood as a prohibition against the offering of abundant *bali*. The procedure for the offering of *bali* during worship, the dismissal (*visarjana*), and so forth, will become clear further on.
Now, regarding the ten-armed aspect (as described in the Kālikāpurāṇa):
"On the sixth lunar day, one should awaken the Goddess upon the branches of the bilva tree and among its fruits. (11.204)
On the seventh day, having brought that bilva branch, one should worship it;
furthermore, on the eighth day, one should perform the worship with special care.
One should personally observe a vigil and offer oblations during the great night;
and on the ninth day, one should perform the offering of abundant oblations according to the prescribed rite.
Engaged in recitation and fire-offerings, one should indeed feed young maidens;
one should meditate upon the ten-armed Goddess and worship her according to the Durgā-tantra.
On the tenth day, one should indeed perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) with the *Śāvara* festivals.

Regarding "in fruits" (*phaleṣu*), it means on branches endowed with fruit. "By the *Durgā-tantra*" means by the previously mentioned *Jayadurgā-mantra*, which is designated as the *Durgā-tantra*. Regarding "with the *Śāvara* festivals," it will become clear later that these consist of dress and speech appropriate for the *Śavaras*, the scattering of dust and mud, and so forth. On the sixth day, the awakening (*bodhana*) should be performed either in the evening or at twilight:
"In the evening, on the sixth day, one should awaken the Goddess upon a *vilva* branch. (11.208)
Thus it is stated in the *Mahākāla-ukta*;
and from the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*: "On the sixth lunar day, one should cause awakening [of the deity] at the bilva tree during the evening twilight."
The evening (*sāyāhna*) is the fifth part of the day divided into five portions. The twilight (*sandhyā*), however, is a *muhūrta* at the junction of day and night.
(In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"On the sixth lunar day conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, one should consecrate the *vilva* fruit.")
On the seventh lunar day conjoined with the Mūla asterism, the entry of the leaf [patrikā] should take place;
such is the excellence of the result when the lunar mansion is so joined.
Even in the absence of Mūla, one should cause the entry to occur on the seventh alone. (11–209)
Thus, from the Nandikeśvara Purāṇa: "And in this manner,
having awakened [the deity] specifically in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should cause [the disciple] to enter by means of the Mūla-mantra."
Having worshipped with the [mantras] ending in "pūrva" and "uttara," one should perform the dismissal at the conclusion of the recitation.

In all such cases, it should be understood that the abundance of fruit results from the conjunction of the lunar day (*tithi*) and the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). Regarding the phrase "by the preceding and the following": this means on the eighth day conjoined with Pūrvāṣāḍhā and on the ninth day conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā. The entry of the *pattrikā* (the sacred leaf) and its dismissal must not be performed at night merely out of deference to the lunar mansion.
"If one should perform the entry of the *pattrikā* or the dismissal at night merely out of deference to the conjunction of the lunar mansion, he perishes along with his entire kingdom. (11.211)
Thus, from the statement written in the *Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī*: "And likewise,
when the final quarter of the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra] occurs during the portion of the night..."
Then, on the tenth day, at the arrival of the [lunar] portion, there is the rising of the Goddess.

Because of this statement, and in accordance with such injunctions as "one should perform the dismissal at the end of the *śravaṇā* [nakṣatra]," it is stated in that very same source that the dismissal should not be performed at night. Regarding this, the threefold worship prescribed for the three lunar days (*tithi*) during these three days is the general rule; however, sometimes due to the waning of a lunar day, the threefold worship may be performed in two days, and sometimes due to the waxing of a lunar day, the threefold worship may be performed over four days. But when all three lunar days are obtained, the arrangement is beyond dispute. "The observer of the vow should worship the Goddess during the three days beginning with the seventh [lunar day], or in two [days] or four days, depending on the waning or waxing of the lunar day. (11.213)

Thus, according to the statement in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* (p. 979), even in this view, the daily duties beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*) are prescribed in the *Bhaviṣya*: "On the first lunar day, one should provide substances for the grooming of the hair."
On the second day, a silk cord is used for the purpose of binding the hair.
On the third day, a mirror, as well as vermilion and lac;
on the fourth day, however, honey-mixture (madhuparka), a tilaka, and eye-ornamentation.
On the fifth [day], one should apply body ointments and ornaments according to one's capacity;
on the sixth, one should perform the awakening of the Bilva tree during the evening twilight rites. || 11-216 ||

In this matter, if the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is absent on the evening preceding the day of the entry of the manuscript, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) should be performed on the day prior to that. However, if the sixth is entirely non-existent on the evening, there is an omission of the preliminary consecration, according to the statement in the *Kalpataru*: "On the evening of the sixth, one should perform the preliminary consecration at a *vilva* tree. This same rule applies to the awakening of the Goddess (*devībodhana*) as well.

In reality, however, since the awakening of the Goddess—whose ritual requirements are taught in numerous Tantras—is mandatory, the awakening should take place on that very day when the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) occurs at the time of evening twilight. If the sixth lunar day occurs during twilight on both days, the determination is made according to the principle of pairing (*yugmādara*). If the sixth lunar day does not occur during twilight on either of the two days, then the opinion of the author of the *Kaumudī* alone should be followed, as the sixth lunar day exists at the time of *pradoṣa* (early night) and so forth; for there is the presence of the secondary period (*gauṇakāla*).
As it has been said:
"A time subsequent to its own [prescribed] time would be secondary (gauṇa) for the preceding rite"—

for this very reason, the teacher Cūḍāmaṇi maintains that the scriptural injunction regarding evening is intended for the excellence of the fruit, and not to suggest that the omission of the rite should be performed.
As for Pradoṣa:
When the sun has set, the evening (pradoṣa) shall last for three muhūrtas.
Thus it was stated by Vyāsa in the *Madanaratna*.
However, Vatsa has said: "Pradoṣa is desired as the two ghaṭikās following sunset."

Thus, for the commencement of writing manuscripts and similar rites, the seventh lunar day (saptamī) that spans seven *tithis* must be taken, and not one that spans six or eight according to the rule of the "pair" (*yugma-vākya*).
For it is said: "The beginnings of the Yugas, the anniversary of a birth (*varṣavṛddhi*), and the seventh day dear to Pārvatī—these desire the rising of the sun;
in these cases, the rule of the 'pair' of lunar days does not apply. (11.218)
Thus, according to the statement written in the *Kṛtyatattvārṇava*:
"A wise person should perform all the rites of the Blessed Lady, from her entry until her departure, on the lunar day that is rising [at dawn]. (11.219)

Thus, according to the *Tithitattva* and the *Nandikeśvarapurāṇa*, the *adhivāsana* rite must be performed on the evening of the day immediately preceding the entry of the *patrikā*, even if the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is absent; for it is said:
"Whether it be Jyeṣṭhā or the sixth lunar day, if they do not occur in the evening..."
Nevertheless, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) should likewise take place that very evening at the bilva tree.
"One should avoid the sixth lunar day [of the dark fortnight] even if it arrives at evening, provided that the preceding [day] is still joined with its asterism.
Likewise, the Jyotiḥśāstra states:
"The Navapatrikā [ceremony] performed in the forenoon brings auspiciousness and bestows success in all undertakings."
The auspicious Caṇḍī, entering at dawn, bestows health, wealth, and victory;
at midday, she causes no affliction and brings no destruction to men; but at twilight, she will grant slaughter, imprisonment, initial strife, and total ruin.
If, on the seventh lunar day as it reaches its end, a leaf-stalk, a wood-apple, or similar object enters the palace,
it destroys the seven-limbed kingdom of the king along with the happiness of his people, according to the authority of the *Mūla* [astrological] treatises.
Therefore, having reached the goddess-like seventh day situated at sunrise, which bestows auspiciousness upon the lord of men—
The king should cause her, who is for the welfare of all people, to enter [the city], avoiding the asterism of Rākṣasa (Mūla).
According to the words of the Matsyasūkta:

"On the evening of the day prior to the entry of the bird [the sacrificial arrow], the wise man should invoke Caṇḍī as Vilvavāsinī; there is no preliminary rite for the sixth lunar day (Ṣaṣṭhī) here. (11.223)
Thus, according to the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*,
the procedure for the entry of the invitation letter for the *vilva* tree and so forth will be explained further on.
The one-day (*ekāha*) option is also mentioned in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*.
"But the practitioner who, on either the eighth or the ninth day of the lunar fortnight,
should worship the boon-granting Goddess with extensive displays of great opulence— " so it is said.
(Rudrayāmala) Sarasvatī should be worshipped beginning from the Mūla asterism. (11.224)
One should worship the Goddess every day until the Vaiṣṇava asterism;
during this time, one should never teach, write, or study [the scriptures].
O Goddess, when a book has been placed [before him], the best of the twice-born who desires knowledge [should worship];
and during the bright fortnight of Āśvina, one who desires intelligence [should worship] Sarasvatī. (In the *Saṃgraha*) 11.226.
One should invoke the Goddess with the *Mūla* [nakṣatra] and dismiss her with the *Śravaṇa*.

Now, the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī) is determined. In matters such as worship and fasting, it should be taken as joined with the following day, according to the rule of "the Vasus and the Apertures" (*yugmavākya*). As it is said:
"The eighth day of the bright fortnight, and likewise the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight... (11.227).
"One should not perform [the rite] on a day pierced by the previous [tithi]; it should be performed when joined with the following one.
Thus [it is stated] in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa, and likewise in the Smṛtisaṃgraha.
The Great Eighth Day of the month of Śrāvaṇa should always be honored when it is conjoined with the ninth day.
When the seventh lunar day is constantly joined [with the eighth], it causes grief and torment;
however, when the seventh is joined with Jambha, that great eighth day (Mahāṣṭamī) is indeed honored.
Jambha, that foremost of Dānavas, was slain by Indra;
therefore, with every effort, the eighth lunar day conjoined with the seventh should be observed.
Those who desire their own welfare should avoid, through discernment, the seventh [day] which is fraught with thorns, whether out of delusion or even ignorance. (11.231)
One who observes the Mahāṣṭamī on a day where the seventh lunar day exists even for a single moment and the eighth day follows thereafter, falls into hell. (11.232)
Therefore, this has been declared as a thorn that brings about the destruction of sons and grandsons.
Likewise: "It destroys sons, it destroys cattle, and it destroys the kingdom along with its king. (11.233)
"The eighth lunar day joined with the seventh destroys both those who have been born and those yet to be born" (*Nirṇayāmṛta*). This is a statement from another Smṛti:
"The eighth [day] joined with the seventh is not [to be observed]; the seventh is not [to be observed] when joined with the eighth. (11.234)
The eighth [lunar day] should always be observed together with the ninth by the wise;
for it is said in that very same source:
"The eighth joined with the ninth is a great festival of immense splendor. (11.235)
Thus, in the Devīpurāṇa:

"Those by whom the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī) is observed when the seventh lunar day is conjoined with the Vedha [transit], shall wander here like a Piśāca, deprived of sons, wives, and wealth. (11.236)
In the *Bhojarājīya*:
"The ninth lunar day is declared to belong to Umā, and the eighth to Hara;
when these two coincide, it is the highly meritorious lunar day of Umāmāheśvarī. (11.237)
In the *Madanaratna* and the *Smṛtisamuccaya*:
"The seventh [tithi] pierced by a *śalya* (the sun's shadow) should be avoided for the Great Eighth (*mahāṣṭamī*).
Even if it is very brief, that [eighth] on which the sun rises possesses great merit. (11.238)

"Even a small amount" means even for the duration of a single *ghaṭikā*. For this very reason, even a single *ghaṭikā* of the eighth day occurring at sunrise is to be accepted; as stated by Devala: "In the observance of vows and fasts, even a single *ghaṭikā* [of the tithi] which may occur [at dawn] [is sufficient]. This is the view of the author of the *Nirṇayasindhu*. The Gauḍas also say exactly the same.

Thus, it should be understood that even the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*) conjunction, when it takes the form of a *kalā* (one-thirtieth of a day), is the cause for the exclusion of the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), and not merely the duration of three *muhūrtas*.

However, the authors of works such as the *Samayaprakāśa* maintain that only an *aṣṭamī* lasting three *muhūrtas* is the cause for the exclusion of the *saptamī*, and not one less than that. They argue that statements such as "even if small" (*stokāpi*) praise the three *muhūrtas* by way of its constituent parts; therefore, if on the following day the *aṣṭamī* is less than three *muhūrtas*, then the preceding [day] alone, joined with the *saptamī*, should be accepted.
The author of the *Nibandhavyākhyā* also stated that the terms *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *ghaṭikā*, *muhūrta*, *dvimūrti*, and *vacaḥ* are intended as praises for the *trimuhūrta* period.
As for that which was said:
"In the month of Āśvina, the bright eighth day (*aṣṭamī*) is the bringer of auspiciousness. (11.239)

The statement, "It should also be joined with the seventh [tithi], especially with Mūla," refers to a case where there is no eighth [tithi] on the following day. This has been stated in the *Devīpurāṇa* (in the *Nirṇayāmṛta*).
O lord of men, those lunar days which are the latter half of the month undergo waning.
Then one should perform the eighth day of the waxing moon; otherwise, it will be inauspicious. Thus [it is said].
And as it is said:
"When the sun sets having reached the eighth lunar day, one should perform the Durgā festival on that very day, and not on the following day. (11.241)
"One should know that there will be famine in that place where [the goddess] is worshipped on the ninth day.

This statement, which prescribes the previous day [as the proper time for worship] even when the eighth day exists on the following day, refers to a situation where the ninth day does not exist on the following day. As it is said: "When the ninth day does not exist at sunrise on the subsequent day... (11.242).
"Therefore, O King, one should observe the eighth lunar day together with the seventh," as stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*.
However, as for that which says:
If the eighth lunar day occurs after the sun has risen on the seventh day, [it is considered the following day]. || 11-243 ||

Regarding this, the statement from the *Viśvarūpa-nibandha*—"One should perform the festival of Durgā there [on the eighth day], and not on the following day"—which prohibits an eighth day overlapped by the next, refers specifically to the worship of the Goddess performed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the awakening of the Goddess prescribed for the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina. [As it is said:
"The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight... (11.244).
It should be observed when joined with the preceding [tithi], and never when joined with the following;
this is the eternal rule regarding rites such as fasting. || 11-245 ||
Thus, the authors of the commentaries on the *Nibandhas* maintain that this is because the excellence of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī is prescribed only when it is overlapped by the following day (*paraviddhā*).
And as for those [verses]:
"I am Bhadrā and Bhadrā is I; there is never any difference between us two."
Even when I am worshipped by Bhadrā, I shall bestow all accomplishments.
Likewise, when the Blessed One is worshipped on the Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī) day, which is also the day of Bhadrā,
she bestows long life and health, because she is the very embodiment of Bhadrā.
These and other such statements from the *Devīpurāṇa* are intended for the purpose of prescribing worship during the period of *viṣṭi*.
"He who performs my worship on the Great Eighth (*mahāṣṭamī*) after having abandoned the *viṣṭi*, his fruit of worship shall not be realized; by him I am insulted. (11.248)
Thus, from the words of the Goddess:

"The ritual of worship for Bhadrakālī should take place on the Bhadrā [tithi], which occurs between [the two seventh days]. Therefore, the Durgā-aṣṭamī should indeed be observed by the wise as being joined with the seventh day (saptamī-viddhā). (11.249)
It is universally agreed that this statement refers to cases where the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) is absent on the preceding day.
If the Great Eighth (*mahāṣṭamī*) is conjoined with Tuesday (*bhaumavāra*), it is exceedingly auspicious.
Thus it is said in the *Madanaratna*:
"If the eighth [tithi] occurs when the sun has risen and the ninth [tithi] should exist at the end of the day, and it falls on a Tuesday,
it should be worshipped with great effort."
It has been stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* that "this [Aṣṭamī] joined with Mūla is exceedingly praiseworthy":

"The Mahāṣṭamī joined with Mūla is very difficult to find even in the three worlds. Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Durgotsava* that even when joined with Mūla, if it is pierced by the seventh lunar day (*saptamī-viddhā*), it must be rejected.
For even when conjoined with Mūla, the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) should always be avoided by the wise.
"If [the seventh stage] were even slightly defiled, it would be [only] by a mere fraction."

However, when the [Ekādaśī] is complete on the previous day and increases on the following day, then because it is complete and lacks conjunction with the seventh lunar day (saptamī), the former alone is to be accepted and not the latter;
for there is a Smṛti statement: "When a lunar day consisting of sixty *daṇḍas* departs into the next day, that impure lunar day is unfit for ritual action, except for Ekādaśī."
And likewise:
the eighth day of the great [fortnight], when joined with even a fraction of the seventh, should be avoided. (11.251)

By such statements as these, since the *pūrvaviddhā* (the eighth day overlapping with the seventh) is prohibited, it is established that the *mahāṣṭamī* is indeed the *paraviddhā* (overlapping with the ninth).
However, regarding the *śuddhā* (pure, uncombined) [eighth], there is no doubt whatsoever.
Some, however—
There, on the eighth day, the most terrible Bhadrakālī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
manifested together with ten million yoginīs.
For this reason, she should be worshipped by men on that day;
one should worship the Goddess at the three junctions of the day, being devoted to recitation and hymns of praise.
In the daytime worship prescribed by such passages as these, the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) that is overlapped by the following day (paraviddhā) should be accepted:
"On that eighth lunar day which occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, she [the Goddess] is to be worshipped at night with extensive and magnificent offerings. (11.254)
Regarding the night-worship prescribed by such statements as these, on the eighth day (the *aṣṭamī*), the conjunction with the night alone is to be respected:

"For whatever rite there is a specific time, one should perform that rite during the lunar day (*tithi*) that pervades that time; the waning or waxing [of the moon] is not a cause [for changing the time]. (11.255)
Thus they say, on account of this scriptural statement. The ritual for the Mahāṣṭamī will be explained later.
Now, the Mahānavamī is determined. And that [Navamī] should be accepted as joined with the preceding [Aṣṭamī], according to the rule of pairs (*yugma-vākya*):
"That lunar day, the Mahānavamī, should be performed together with the Aṣṭamī."
Thus, according to the *Bṛhatsiddhāntasāra*, the Riktā tithi is never joined with the eighth day when it is followed by another [tithi]. (11.256)
Thus [it is stated] in the *Laghutithinirṇaya* and the *Matsyapurāṇa*; Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"The first lunar day (*pratipad*) and the ninth day (*navamī*) should be observed as the 'facing' (*saṃmukhī*) lunar days."
It is present when it extends through the evening.
(In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"The eighth [lunar day] joined with the ninth should be observed by those desiring the fruit. (11.257)
(Padme) The eighth [tithi] joined with the ninth, and the ninth joined with the eighth.
(Mātsye), p. 985.
The Riktā [lunar day] should always be observed together with the eighth [day] by the wise.
At that time, one should perform the *pūrṇā* (full-moon) conjunction; there is no [conjunction] with the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*). (As stated in the *Hemādri*, citing the *Padma Purāṇa*):
"The *Śrāvaṇī*, the *Durgā-navamī*, the *Dūrvā*, and the *Hutāśanī*. (11.259)
Śivarātri should be observed on the day overlapping with the previous [tithi], as should the day of Bali. (In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"The eighth lunar day in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja which is conjoined with the Mūla asterism... (11.260).

That [day] is called Mahānavamī, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds; the meaning is that it is joined with the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) and the Mūla asterism. The mention of "Mūla" is illustrative. Thus, it is said in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa* (in the *Madanaratna*):
In the Durgā-pūjās, the ninth lunar day (navamī) conjoined with the three asterisms beginning with Mūla [is auspicious].
On that [day], Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, is said to be "great";
the ellipsis is that one should worship her.
An eighth [tithi] pierced by a ninth, and likewise a ninth pierced by an eighth; || 11-262 ||
"The primordial [goddess], worshipped even throughout the three worlds by means of the triad of root-mantras and the others."
In this context, a penetration (*vedha*) consisting of three *muhūrtas* is to be understood.
Thus said Paiṭhīnasi:
"On both fortnights, the lunar days (*tithis*) [penetrate] the preceding as well as the succeeding lunar day."
"They pierce it in three muhūrtas; this is remembered as the general rule."
Even though it is said:
"The rite for the gods [should be performed] when the sun has risen, and that for the ancestors when the sun has set. (263)
"Whatever [time] of the day consists of two or three *muhūrtas*, that is the *tithi* for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).

(Viṣṇudharma in Hemādri). Although piercing (*vedha*) is thus stated to consist of even two *muhūrtas*, nevertheless, it occurs only in the morning; however, in the evening, piercing occurs only when it lasts for three *muhūrtas*.
As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
On whichever lunar day the sun, the lord of the lotuses, goes to its setting; || 11-264 ||
That lunar day (tithi) is said to belong to that very day on which it exists for even three muhūrtas.
Even at sunrise, the duration of two muhūrtas is merely a secondary alternative (anukalpa).
This is because Dakṣa also used the word "even" (*api*) in the statement: "That lunar day which is increasing in duration should be observed even if it lasts for only two muhūrtas."
The author of the Nirṇayasindhu also maintains that when there is a conjunction of three muhūrtas, the ninth [tithi] is the earlier one, based on the previously cited statement:
"O dear one, one should never perform [the rite] on the ninth tithi when it is joined with the tenth. (11.265)

Thus, because of the prohibition of the later [tithi] in the *Skānda*, when there is an absence of a connection of three muhūrtas, the later [tithi] should be accepted even if it is prohibited: "In the observance of vows and fasts, even a single ghaṭikā that occurs at sunrise [is sufficient]; that [vow] should be performed on the [day when the tithi] is present at sunrise. (11.266)

They say that such statements as these refer to lunar days other than the ninth, because there is a specific injunction regarding the ninth day (*navamī*). Even though this determination has been made by authoritative scholars, nevertheless:
"If on that [occasion] the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja lasts for even a single *muhūrta* or a *kalā*..."
That lunar day (tithi) should be known as complete by those who seek fortune, knowledge, and victory. || 11-267 ||
Thus, from the *Saurapurāṇa*:

"If on the eighth day the sun has risen and at the end of the day there should be a ninth day, then even if only a small portion [of the ninth] is obtained at dawn for the offering of the bali-oblation... (11.268).
"Having worshipped Durgā, the destroyer of the distress of those in difficulty, there on the ninth day"—according to this statement cited from the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*:
"If the Riktā [tithi] extends beyond sunrise, it shall be considered full thereafter. (11.269)
An offering bringing auspiciousness should be made in that place;
O King, if an offering is made on the eighth day, there will be the ruin of one's sons.

Thus, from the *Devīpurāṇa* as well, it should be understood that for the offering of food (*validāna*), the excellence of the [Ekādaśī] overlapping with the next day (*paraviddhā*) is indeed to be recognized; however, for the fast (*upavāsa*), only the preceding day is [to be observed], according to the collection of previously cited statements.

(p. 988) "If the Ekādaśī should be pierced by the ninth [tithi] even by a single digit (*diśā*), then it must be avoided with great effort, just as the water of the Gaṅgā is [avoided] when mixed with liquor. (11.271)

"The ninth and the tenth [lunar days] should not be observed as fasts when conjoined with another [day]," according to the *Padma* and *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇas*, because of this prohibition of fasting on the *parā* (the following day). Furthermore, the offering of the oblation (*bali*) as an ancillary part of the worship must be performed even on the eighth day:
"On the eighth day, more should be given than the offering of the oblation on the seventh. (11.272)
Thus it is stated in the Mahākāla-śāstra.
However, the offering of abundant sacrificial oblations (*bali*) is prohibited therein:
"One should not perform the offering of abundant sacrificial oblations except on the ninth day (*navamī*)."
Thus it is stated by Bhairava.
Regarding the ninth [lunar day] that extends into the sunrise, the offering of abundant *bali* is prescribed in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*:
"Having thus passed the night joyfully, at dawn, when the sun has risen... (11.273).

"One should cause buffaloes and rams to be slaughtered while they are bleating with their necks bent down—either a hundred, fifty, or even half of that, according to one's desire. "Night" refers to the eighth night. "Aruṇodaya" means the rising of the sun.
At sunrise on the ninth day, one should unweariedly present the bali offering.
Thus, from the corroboration of other tantras;
and also from the *Amarakośa*: "The term *aruṇa* may also apply to the sun."
But as for those [days]: "On the Nandā, fire blazes; on the Pūrṇā, there is the slaughter of animals. (11.275)
If the *gokulakrīḍā* (cowherd’s play) occurs on the Bhadrā day, it leads to the destruction of the kingdom;
however, the offering of a sacrificial oblation (*validāna*) in the afternoon on the ninth day is highly recommended.
"One should avoid the tenth [lunar day] therein; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.

Such statements from the *Brahmavaivarta* and other Purāṇas are intended to prohibit [the practice] when the [ninth lunar day] is deficient or merely equal [to the tenth]; such is the direction [of the argument].
The ritual procedure for the ninth lunar day will be explained further on.

Now, the Vijayā-daśamī is determined. In rites other than the dismissal of the Goddess (devī-visarjana), that [tithi] which pervades the time of the rising of the stars (tārakodaya) is to be accepted. (p.
989) "When the twilight has slightly passed and the stars have just begun to appear... (11.277).
"This time is called Vijaya, which bestows success upon all undertakings," according to the words of Nārada in the *Jyotirnibandha*.
When the tenth lunar day exists as pervading the rising of the asterism on two days, the preceding one [is to be taken].
On that full ninth lunar day joined with [the asterism] Aparājita, Aparājitā is to be worshipped.
For the sake of security and for the sake of victory, men should perform [the rite] according to the previously stated procedure on the tenth lunar day conjoined with the ninth. This is Aparājitā.
"The Goddess, when worshipped as the increaser of victory, bestows victory.

Thus [it is said in the *Skanda-purāṇa* cited in the *Hemādri*]; however, according to the *Nirṇayasindhu*, the *uttarā* [Aśvinī] is preferred. On the tenth day, Aparājitā should be properly worshipped by men. (11.280)

"Taking recourse in the north-eastern direction with effort during the afternoon"—thus [it is stated] because of the predominance of the afternoon's duration. However, if that were not the case, the day that extends through eleven muhūrtas should be taken.
"As for the lunar day which is the tenth in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina... (11.281).
"That [Ekādaśī] lasting eleven muhūrtas, when conjoined with Śravaṇa, is to be accepted"—so says Dhaumya.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, an auspicious journey may be undertaken at any time throughout the night, or in the evening, or during the day at a moment of victory.
The eleventh muhūrta is also proclaimed as Vijaya;
on that occasion, a journey should be undertaken by all who desire victory. (11.283)
This is also because of the statement of Bhṛgu:
"When [the asterism] spans two days, the previous one is preferred due to the greater duration of its conjunction with the rising of the stars.
However, when on the following day even a small portion is conjoined with Śravaṇā, then for the purpose of a journey, the latter alone should be adopted.
If, at sunrise, the tenth lunar day has passed slightly and the eleventh is complete,
and the Śravaṇa asterism occurs at that time, that lunar day is known as Vijayā.
Since the descendant of Kakutstha set out when the full moon was in the constellation Śravaṇa, men may cross boundaries on that day under that same asterism. (11.285)
Thus, according to the statement of Kāśyapa in the Hemādri:
"If the tenth day, characterized by the aforementioned marks, exists on the following day, then even for the dismissal of the Goddess (devīvisarjana), the later [tithi] alone should be taken;
for the dismissal on that [earlier] one is defective, causing the loss of fortune and power. (11.286)
(Regarding the determination of lunar days in the Devīpurāṇa: Because of the prohibition of the preceding [day], for this very reason Nārada says:
"O King, when the tenth lunar day is seen at sunrise..."
The wise know that Vijayā occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina.
Thus, the ritual dismissal (visarjana) should be performed on the tenth lunar day conjoined with [the asterism] Śravaṇa, or on the tenth alone;
however, when there is a conjunction with those respective asterisms, an abundance of fruit arises.
But in the absence of the asterisms, one should perform it on the lunar day alone. (11.288)
Thus it is stated by Mahākāla;
and from the words of Lalla: "The lunar day (tithi) is the body, the lunar day alone is the cause, the lunar day is the authority, and the lunar day alone is the means."
However, if the tenth day does not exist on the following day, the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) must be performed on the preceding day during the portion of the tenth day itself.
As stated in the *Nandikeśvara Purāṇa*: "The sending forth [of the deity] on the tenth day should be accompanied by play, festivities, and auspicious rites."
Regarding the auspicious times for installation and dismissal, he says: One should install the Goddess during a fixed (sthira) lagna, but one should move her during a movable (cara) lagna. (11.289)
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
For the ritual of the autumnal worship of the Goddess, her installation and dismissal should be performed during a movable lagna or a movable degree for the sake of all prosperity. (11.290)
"If [the ritual is performed] under another ascendant or in another degree, it yields contrary results"—thus it is stated in another tantra.
Thereafter, one should dismiss the Goddess after praising and bowing to her again and again. (11.291)

It has already been stated that on the tenth lunar day, during the final quarter of the Śravaṇa constellation, the ritual dismissal (visarjana) must not be performed at night along with the Śāvara festivals, even if following the [specific] requirement of the Śravaṇa constellation;
this is according to the Devīpurāṇa in the Tithitattva.
One should invoke the Goddess in the morning, and one should cause her to enter in the very morning.
One should worship only in the morning and dismiss [the deity] only in the morning.
This dismissal is to be understood as occurring on a day that is not overlapped by another lunar day (*paraviddhā*).
Likewise:
Every year, the installation and the dismissal should be performed.
In another tantra:
"Then, having performed worship in the afternoon under the asterism of Śravaṇa and the Aparājitā plant, the king, together with his ministers, army, and vehicles, should set forth. (11.294)
The procedure for these two will be explained further ahead.
Furthermore, the departure should not be made on the portion of the eleventh day after having bypassed the tenth;
for the king who makes his departure having completely bypassed the tenth [day]...
During that year of his reign, he shall meet with no victory anywhere.
Thus, from the *Nirṇayāmṛta* (citing the *Skānda Purāṇa*):

"If there is even a slight [presence] of the tenth at sunrise," and so forth; according to this statement by Kāśyapa, it appears that even the pervasion of the tenth by the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) is not required. Therefore, this statement from the *Skānda* refers to a case where the tenth is devoid of the *Śravaṇa* nakṣatra.
Thus concludes the determination of the tenth day (*daśamī-nirṇaya*).
Now, regarding the specific rule for impurity (*āśauca*), [it is stated] in the *Viśvarūpanibandha*:

"When the nine-night festival (*navarātra*) has commenced during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, and a death-impurity (*śāva-āśauca*) arises, how should the rites be performed by the wise? (11.296)

And when one is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), if [the festival] should occur there, the worship of the Goddess must be performed according to the ritual procedure for animal sacrifice (paśuyajña). || 11-297 ||
During a period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), worship and especially the giving of gifts are prescribed;
these should be performed with the Goddess in mind, for no fault is found therein.
Viṣṇu:

"In the case of a vow, a sacrifice, a marriage, a śrāddha, a fire-oblation, a worship, or a recitation—if these have already commenced, there shall be no birth-impurity (sūtaka); however, if they have not yet commenced, there is indeed impurity. (11.299)
Also in the Tantra:
"When this birth-impurity (sūtaka) has arisen, the wise man should not abandon what has been commenced.
Here, "commenced" refers to the undertaking in the form of a formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
"Saṅkalpa [is required] for vows and sacrificial sessions"—so it is stated in the Viṣṇu-saṃhitā.

Once [the ritual] has begun, the worship of the Goddess and so forth should be performed by oneself; however, if it has not begun, it must be caused to be performed by another, just like the Agnihotra and other rites—this is the consensus of all authorities, as there is no specific statement to the contrary that a woman in her menses should have it performed by another.
As it has been stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*:
"But if there is an occurrence of menstruation in the interval, one should have the worship performed by another.
