In that regard, rites such as worship, which are of the nature of active engagement (*pravṛtti*), may be carried out through the agency of a son or others; however, fasting and the like must be performed by oneself alone, because impurity (*āśauca*) pertaining to cessation (*nivṛtti*) is ineffective [in delegating such acts].
Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
"When a woman established in her observances should see menstrual blood in the interval," (11.300)
"Having fasted during those nights and bathed, one should perform the remainder of the vow."

Regarding this, some maintain that if one encounters impurity due to birth or death (*sūtaka*) on the day of breaking the fast (*pāraṇāha*), one should disregard it and perform the breaking of the fast; however, that is incorrect.
For it is said: "One should perform the breaking of the fast on the ninth day during the period of impurity, preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*);
at its conclusion, one should feed the Brahmins and give gifts according to one's capacity. (11.301)

This is because the *Rudrayāmala* states that the rule for breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) applies even during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Furthermore, the mention of "on the ninth day" is made with reference to the tradition known as Gauḍa.
As it is said in the *Prakaṭayoginīmata*:
"In the tradition known as Gauḍa, however, the breaking of the fast shall take place on the ninth day."
One should avoid that direction which is pierced; however, in Kashmir, that very same direction is auspicious.

In the tradition known as Kerala, the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) occurs on the tenth day alone; it is the same in the *Śaktisaṅgama*. "That very [day] is auspicious" means that in the Kashmiri tradition, the ninth day joined with the tenth is indeed recommended. However, according to the Gauḍa tradition, the breaking of the fast must not be performed on the ninth day when it is joined with the tenth. As it is stated in that very same source: "He who, out of delusion, worships Caṇḍikā on the ninth day when it is pierced by the tenth, and should perform the breaking of the fast [then], his merit becomes fruitless."

(p. 993) The prohibition of performing the sacrifice (*yajana*) on the preceding day should be understood as applying when the ninth day (*navamī*) is obtained as being fit for the ritual. As for the statement from the *Muṇḍamālā*—"One should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the tenth day"—that refers specifically to the subject of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*). The differences in the procedures (*itikartavyatā*) resulting from the various branches of the tradition have been clarified in the ninth chapter (*navamataraṅga*). However, the author of the *Nirṇayasindhu* maintains that these and similar statements prescribing the breaking of the fast on the ninth day are entirely baseless (*nirmūla*); even if one were to assume they possess a basis, they actually refer to the *lohābhisārika* rite, since that is stated to last only until the end of the eighth day.

Since the vow of Navarātra must be performed until the end of the ninth day, they say that the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) along with the observance of the rules should be done on the tenth day itself. Now, some maintain that this autumnal worship (*śāradī pūjā*) is obligatory (*nitya*), because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) for its non-performance;
others hold that it is occasional (*naimittika*), as it is occasioned by the arrival of autumn.
Others maintain that it is "optional" (kāmya) because various specific fruits are mentioned;
however, in reality,
it takes the form of both obligatory (nitya) and optional (kāmya), but it is not occasional (naimittika).
Otherwise, because time is a cause for every effect whatsoever, even an obligatory rite (*nitya*) would incur the status of being occasional (*naimittika*); as it is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*:
"Now I shall explain specifically, along with its secret [teachings], verse 11.303."
Wise men perform worship during the autumn and spring seasons, which bestows various fruits; regarding this, they engage in further reflections. (11.303)
All those who move within the path of mindfulness, and all the Kaulikas as well—among these three categories, what is the nature of this worship? (11.304)
That from the non-performance of which sin always arises is [an obligatory rite];
and that from the performance of which a desired fruit arises is [an optional rite]. (11.304)
That sin which arises for someone from non-performance, or that fruit which arises even from performance, is called "occasional" (naimittika). || 11-305 ||
Regarding this autumnal worship that is spoken of, what is its nature?
Some say it is for the sake of specific desires (kāmyā), while others say it is occasional (naimittikī).
Some who follow the path of the Kula say that this [practice] is eternal, because the fruit was previously heard [to result] after the arrival of autumn. (11.307)
Likewise, the words that the Queen of the Gods spoke before the Destroyer of Tripura:
"Those men who shall not perform this autumnal worship... (11.308)
"Those wicked ones who steal offerings shall fall into hell"—from such statements and from the declaration of eternality in the Śruti [it follows that the image is eternal]. (11.309)
And its desirability is also appropriate; I shall tell you the reason for that here as well:
it is equal to the nectar produced from the lotus-face of Caṇḍikā.
O auspicious lady, consider these words which establish the desirability [of this practice]:
those who, imbued with devotion, perform the autumnal worship... (11.311)
O Śambhu, being satisfied, I shall grant them their wives, sons, enjoyments, wealth, health, and prosperity, as well as eternal residence in the heavenly world.
Thus, because various descriptions of its fruits are heard, there is also a sense of it being desirable;
and those wise ones who, having set forth the arrival of autumn as the cause for this [practice]— || 11.313 ||
Those whose intellects are not wise declare that [time] is merely contingent;
for what entity could time ever be the material cause? (11.314)
If that [result] were the cause for its own arrival, then even for that which is eternal, there would be no eternality;
for sin would not arise when unperformed, and there would be no fruit when it has been performed. (11.315)
O beloved, when those who speak thus describe the characteristics of an omen, why are both [the auspicious and inauspicious] words not seen to produce their respective fruits? 11.316
Therefore, O Sovereign Lady, it should be understood here that there is both a permanent and an optional nature,
just as the autumnal worship is exactly like the springtime worship.
Not even the slightest difference exists between these two in the Vedas and other scriptures.
Regarding the cause of the autumnal festival, it is said:
(p. 995) "In former times, there was only the Great Vāsantī worship throughout the three worlds. (11.318)
When the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa took place during the interval of the Tretā Yuga,
Rāma was unable to slay him because he had assumed the form of Kālika.
Then, having been thus meditated upon by the hosts of gods, Brahmā, surrounded by them,
awakened Kālikā, whose abode is on the Himalayas.
O Goddess, come and behold the training in weapons and the agility of your two devotees as they fight fiercely in battle.
Thus entreated and awakened at an untimely hour, the Goddess went together with Brahmā to Laṅkā to witness the battle between those two.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the Sovereign arrived at that place;
for seven nights she remained without food, while a great battle raged day and night.
As those two were intent on the employment and withdrawal of divine weapons,
Rāma was unable to slay the Rākṣasa who was a devotee of Kālī.
And even though he was unable to reach Rāma, who had approached Viṣṇu himself,
the Rākṣasa rejoiced at the sight of the Goddess’s power of arms.
Considering him to be his own devotee, Brahmā showed partiality toward him; and seeing the favor bestowed upon the Rākṣasa, Brahmā, together with all the gods, [acted accordingly].
With his neck bowed in devotion, he praised him with divine hymns,
using plaintive cries, prostrations, salutations, and further eulogies.
Satisfied, she said to Brahmā, "O child, choose a boon that dwells in your heart.
Thereupon, the four-faced one chose a boon together with the gods.
Out of even a slight trace of grace toward me, and also out of respect for Viṣṇu, abandon this wicked Rākṣasa who is devoted to your feet.

(996) And by his compassionate glance, for the sake of establishing the Dharma among the gods, may the three worlds become well-settled; may the gods who partake of sacrificial offerings be secure. (11.330)
"Let the sages perform their austerities, and let the fourfold order of society proceed.
Let this Vīrajit, purified by the sword, go to the worlds. (11.331)
"I shall perform worship for you, O Goddess, together with the immortals, beginning from this first lunar day until the slaying of the Rākṣasa occurs. (11.332)
For nine days, your worship shall prevail throughout the three worlds,
once the hero Rāvaṇa, the thorn of the universe, has been slain on the ninth day.
We shall produce joy for you with abundant offerings;
on the following day, the tenth, we shall perform for you the great festival of the lustration rite (nīrājana).
By means of songs, dances, and instrumental music; by playing in water and with mud; by indecent dress and speech; and even by the composition of treatises and weapons. (11.335)
On the surface of the earth, both gods and humans will likewise set in motion chariots, elephants, and vehicles according to the prescribed rules for the well-born.
O Kālikā, just as this Rāvaṇa is devoted to your feet,
so shall Rāma always be your worshiper.
And there shall be a certain mantra of yours, O Goddess, known as the "Rāmopāsita," which will instantly produce delight for you and attain renown throughout the world. (11.338)
Having spoken thus, Kālī turned her face away from him at Brahmā’s command;
thereafter, Rāghava struck Rāvaṇa in battle with divine weapons.
From that time onwards, O Goddess of the Gods, the autumnal worship was inaugurated;
for this very reason, both the spring and the autumnal rites should be performed.
Regarding the Vāsantī [consecration], there is no difference of opinion among any [authorities].
However, three varieties of the Śāradyā [consecration] are now described by me. (11.341)
On the ninth day of the waning fortnight of Āśvina, conjoined with the asterism Śiva (Ārdrā),
one should awaken the Goddess and perform the autumnal worship.
"The worship continues as long as the ninth day of the bright fortnight;
thus one position has been declared—now attend to the second. (11.343)
On the very first day of the bright fortnight, having awakened the Queen of the Gods,
one should worship her for nine days according to the procedures of the Tantras and the Purāṇas.
This second [chapter] has been declared; now I shall speak of the third:
one should awaken the Goddess on the sixth lunar day at the time of sunset upon a bilva branch.
The worship commences at dawn during the three days beginning with the seventh;
regarding this threefold mode of worship, the wise dispute among themselves. (11.346)
I shall state therein the definitive conclusion by which darkness may be severed:
long ago, in the *Rambha-kalpa*, the Goddess [confronted] that which arose from the body of the demon Rambha.
Having assumed eighteen arms and a most terrifying form,
Ugracaṇḍā, by her very nature, slew the demon Mahiṣāsura.
With his bright sword, he likewise abandoned this dead man;
and as he fell upon the earth, his body shattered into pieces.
In the Nīlalohita Kalpa, however, he was born once again,
causing agitation among the gods and likewise bringing about the destruction of the sacrifice.
Having thus assumed the form of Bhadrakālī, Mahāmāyā appeared with sixteen arms, indeed most exceptionally sharp.
He slew him again, yet he released him when he had fallen to the ground;
for indeed, he was born once more at the beginning of the Śvetavārāha Kalpa.
(998) By the grace of Jaigīṣavya, he came to remember his former births;
having previously realized that he himself had been slain twice by the Goddess, the Asura [attained this knowledge]. (11.353)
And having learned from the dream-vision that she herself, as well as the people there, were to be slain by a woman due to the curse of the sage Kātyāyana, [he departed]. (11.354)
Resorting to threefold devotion in solitude, Mahiṣāsura propitiated Kālī for the sake of the ultimate purification of his own future.
After twelve thousand divine years had passed, the Goddess appeared before him in person and said, "Choose a boon."
Then that asura, beholding her standing before him, said to her:
"O Goddess, I shall later receive from you the boon desired by my heart."
First, sever the doubt that has arisen in my heart;
you slew me twice on the battlefield against the enemy of the gods.
Having assumed what form—whether non-terrible or terrifying—will you take again in this birth, O Kālikā? (11.359)
"You shall slay me, the wicked one, the thorn in the side of all the immortals. Hearing these words of his, the Mother of the World laughed.
Shaking her head slightly, she spoke in sweet syllables:
"The fruit for you has come from seeing such a form as mine."
"What will happen, O Lord of Daityas? You shall indeed experience terror if you wish to behold that formidable form of mine. (11.362)
Saying "Behold!", the Mother of the World cast off her graceful form and revealed to the Dānava the appearance of her fierce and terrible body.
With a face formidable with flames and endowed with eighteen arms, he is equipped with divine weapons and missiles, and is terrifying with a garland of severed heads. (11.364)
With the pair of its corners split apart, it was terrifying with its formidable fangs;
its tongue flickered like a moving flash of lightning, and it let out a dreadful roar.
Beholding that form, the son of Diti closed his eyes;
then, with palms joined in reverence, he replied to Kālikā.
I am unable to behold such a terrible form of yours;
O Goddess, withdraw, withdraw this form that terrifies the three worlds! (11.367)
Having spoken thus, the king of the asuras again assumed his ordinary form and showed it to him; thereupon, he became composed.
Assuming the form of Bhadrakālī once more, that Supreme Goddess gazed upon the second form, which was life-taking.
Even upon seeing that form, he again fell into terror;
yet when even that was transformed, he became his former ordinary self.
Having gone to that goddess, the lord of the Daityas said:
"O Goddess, how can [this be] with you who bear such a form? (11.371)
Intoxicated by the pride of my boon, I was unable to fight in battle,
just as a small frog has no desire for combat with Garuḍa.
As by forest fire for moths, by the sun for darkness, by the lion for deer, and likewise by the wind for trees; || 11.373 ||
Just as [there is a great conflict] between frogs and snakes, or through the destruction of living beings, how was it that there occurred such a great battle between you and me? (11.374)
That which was past is now past; therefore, I choose these three boons from you. Grant them to me, for they transcend the reach of mere desire.
"O Goddess, having assumed a gentle form in this birth, you shall slay me for the sake of protecting those who partake in the sacrifice. (11.376)
A second lotus-foot of yours shall always rest upon my head,
as long as I am endowed with life and behold the radiance of your face.
"O Goddess, I shall receive some portion of the sacrifice as the third.
When these words had been spoken by Mahiṣa, the enemy of the gods, [the goddess replied: 11-378.

In the Ramkalpa, your father Rambhāsura, having performed most severe austerities on Mount Himālaya, gratified Śaṅkara.
Pleased, Hara spoke these words: "O illustrious one, choose a boon.

Restrained by devotion because of the course of events, that Maheśvara granted a boon, having indeed assumed the form of a son for himself.
For you were born from the womb of the queen by one deluded by passion;
you are indeed Rudra himself in person, not a mere ordinary form of Hara.
Likewise:

Henceforth, you who possess the body of a son of Diti must not dwell here;

And due to the curse of Kātyāyana, which caused the severing of your head,

"Due to the curse of a pigeon, it became like this"—thus were the five causes stated.
Having given such a boon to Mahiṣa and having told the ancient tale, [he spoke]. (11.387)
Kālī vanished instantly, like lightning during the rainy season;

He became as wicked as before toward sacrifices, gods, and the twice-born;
his unwavering devotion to the Goddess also perished.
"Having lost the intelligence previously bestowed upon her, she wanders with her knowledge obscured.

For this autumnal worship is considered threefold according to the different forms [of the deity]; presiding over various substances, it accepts the adoration of men.

Now, regarding the ritual for the seventh [day], it is in that very same place:
"Then, at dawn on the seventh day, the wise man, having performed his daily obligatory rites... (11.464).
Having worshipped the Goddess upon a bilva branch as before, the person, taking up a sharp knife, should recite this mantra: (11.465)

"Cut this branch, sever the pair of yokes, and likewise seize that pair of weapons and the head, holding them both in your two hands. (11.467)
With palms joined in reverence, O beloved, one should recite the four ancient mantras on the mountain peak of Mount Meru, Maṇḍala, Kailāsa, and Himavat.
You were born as the Śrīphala tree, ever dear to Ambikā;

"The gods took hold of your branch; you are renowned as 'Ambā' (Mother).
Then the practitioner should again recite another mantra in the form of a verse: || 11-472 ||

Come, O Goddess Caṇḍikā, for the sake of all auspiciousness;

And then one should proclaim: "I shall perform the installation.

I shall indeed proclaim to you that which is both ancient and Vedic:
one who is capable should perform it for three days, but if incapable, for two days.
In the absence of all [other options], bathing on the ninth day is considered mandatory;
one should also perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) here, O beloved, because this is for the sake of a desired result (kāmya).
It is first remembered for liberation from the sins committed over a hundred births;
likewise, indeed, for those [sins] limited to eight thousand years. (11.482)
Having performed the ritual for the stability of Durgā’s world, which is endowed with the attainment of the fruit of a hundred sacrifices,
one should then bathe the nine leaves with pure water.
Each [mantra] is addressed by its respective name, both in form and in thought;
at the beginning of the mantras in verse form, there are the *tāra* (om), *trapā* (hrīṃ), and *smara* (klīṃ).
O Goddess, in the sequence of the Tantric ablution, one should offer Ramā, Medhā, Rāva, Rauṣā, and the eight Ḍākinīs—these nine—to each [deity] individually. (11.485)
O you who reside upon the chest of Śambhu, you are like the trunk of a plantain tree;

Are you indeed become stable, bestowing success immediately?
By means of your form as Durgā, bring victory everywhere through bathing.
O Haridrā, you who are ever dear to Śaṅkara, remove my miseries! O Goddess, you are the very form of Rudra; grant me all-pervading peace.
O Jayantī, you are of the nature of victory and the bringer of triumph to the worlds;
O Goddess, I establish you here; grant me victory in my home.

O beloved of Umā, you were created in ancient times by the Creator for the destruction of pomegranates, ghee, and consumption among men; be gracious! (11.491)
Be firm forever in the world, O destroyer of the sorrow of Durgā;

O Lakṣmī, you are the form of grain and the giver of life to living beings;

Then, having placed water from two or three rivers into the interior of a jar and mixing it with sandalwood paste, one should bathe Caṇḍikā with that.
The Śītā, the Alakanandā, the Cakṣu, the Bhadrā, the Ṛṣadvatī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Kṛṣṇavarṇā, the Payoṣṇī, and likewise the Narmadā. (11.495)

Nirukta, Jyotiṣa, and all the Purāṇas;
as well as Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, Vedānta, Akṣapāda, Sāṅkhya, and Patañjala. || 11.512 ||
All the treatises on memory (Smṛti), as well as both forms of the science of government (Daṇḍanīti), the Gandharva, Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and the sixty-four arts; || 11-513 ||
All missiles, all weapons, vehicles, as well as kings, all medicinal herbs, or the sciences of the arts and so forth— (11.514)
Pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, diamonds, and emeralds, as well as hessonite, rubies, coral, and sapphires. (11.515)
Whatever other jewels there are, as well as the divisions of time—
the entire span of all the Manvantaras and indeed the four Yugas.
The year, month, season, fortnight, day, night, solstice, and the subtle divisions of time such as the *kalā* and *lava*;
as well as the zodiac signs, lunar mansions, planetary conjunctions, and minute degrees—these are the subtle [divisions]. (11.517)
Rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, clouds, and streams;
gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas. (11.518)
May these lakes, renowned on earth such as Sindhur, Raivata, and Śoṇa, consecrate you for the attainment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
Let all of them, becoming well-disposed, bathe you with golden jars;
as do the Nāgas, Takṣaka and others, who dwell in the depths of Pātāla.
O Sustainer of the World, let them bathe you with well-perfumed golden pitchers.
Now, I shall tell you the different mantras according to the specific substances used. (11.521)
In the great ritual of bathing according to both the Purāṇas and the Tantras,
the presiding deity for all is the one known by the name Īśāna.
May Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident, bathe you thoroughly;
he shall bathe you with water from a conch shell while pronouncing this mantra: || 11-523 ||
May you have a bath with the water of the Mandākinī, which is supreme in removing all sins and originates from the stream of heaven.
One should bathe the Goddess with Ganges water while reciting this mantra:
"The warm [water], which provides a pleasant touch and is endowed with the light of fire. (11.525)
It is wholesome and removes impurities; therefore, perform your bath with it.
O beloved, bathe [the deity] with warm water while reciting this mantra: 11-526.
May this water—rich in fragrance, beautiful, cool, and most enchanting, which removes all sins—be suitable for your bath. || 11.527 ||
With this jar of fragrant water— one whose water is meritorious, pure, clear, cool, and sweet— one should bathe Śivā.
"May that [water] be fit for your bath, and likewise for the allaying of your fatigue;
bathe the Mistress of the Sage with pure and cool waters. (11.529)
Cows are indeed pure and sinless; cows are the mothers of the universe.
Cows are the sustainers of sacrifices, and everything is established in cows. || 11-530 ||
"Then, O Dear One, having recited the general mantra: 'I bathe you with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) flowing from its various limbs,' thereupon—" (11.531)
One should bathe the Mother of the World with the five products of the cow individually,
using the meritorious urine of the cow, which steals away all sins.
I bathe the Mother of the World for the increase of my son's lifespan and wealth;
with this [mixture], one should bathe the Goddess slowly, drop by drop, using cow’s urine.
Cow dung purifies the earth, is the supreme cause of prosperity, and destroys all sins; with it, I bathe you.
One should recite this mantra and bathe the Goddess with cow-dung water;
for that which is produced from the limbs of cows is indeed the cause of the sacrificial oblation.
May this curd serve to produce luster for your limbs;
with this curd, the most excellent preceptor should bathe the Blessed One.
I bathe you, the beloved of Hara, with such milk as this, in which the entire collection of sacrificial rites is established.
Chanting [her name], one should bathe that Mother of the World with milk from cows,
which is celebrated in the Vedas and other scriptures as the means for performing fire-offerings (homa).
Furthermore, since all the gods consume [offerings] through Agni alone as their mouth, there is nothing more purifying than this, nor anything that bestows such strength and vigor. (11.539)
Therefore, I bathe you today with cow-derived oblation, O Sovereign Goddess Kālī;
the wise one should bathe her with clarified butter using these two mantras. (11.540)
Then, having combined all five products of the cow together,
O Dear One, stir them with the ring finger or with the root of a *kuśa* blade.
Since there is nothing purer than this, which, having entered the body, destroys all sin,
and since there is nothing more heart-pleasing than this, may these five products of the cow serve as your bath.
One should bathe Kālikā with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting this mantra:
cow’s milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and white sugar. (11.543)

This is declared to be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta); with this one should bathe Umā, which was fashioned by the Creator for the sake of sacrifice, having extracted the essence of the three worlds. (11.544)
O Mother of the World, may that fivefold nectar (pañcāmṛta), which is sweet and pleasing, serve as your bath;
with this very mantra, one should bathe the auspicious Goddess (Śivā) with the fivefold nectar. 11-545.
Likewise:
"Oṃ, we know Kātyāyanī; we meditate upon the Blessed One; may Durgā inspire us.
With this [mantra], one should bathe the Goddess of the Gods with sugarcane juice alone.
In another tantra: "With all the great medicinal herbs, for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims. (11.546)
One should bathe the Mother of the World with the mantra beginning "yā auṣadhī.
(The great medicinal herbs are mentioned in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*:
"Sahadevī, as well as Vyāghrī, Balā, and likewise Atibalā. (11.547)
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, siṃhī, vacā, and suvarcasā—
these are declared to be the eight great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadhy-aṣṭaka), which one should employ in the great ritual bath (mahāsnāna).
Vyāghrī is kaṇṭakārikā; balā is vāṭyalaka. Furthermore, the medicinal herbs have already been mentioned previously. Likewise:
One should bathe the Mother of the World with a thousand-streamed pitcher.
(From the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*): "All the oceans, all the rivers, as well as the celestial streams and rivers... (11.549)
There are thirty-five million sacred sites on the surface of the earth—wells, lakes, springs, natural pools, and pits. (11.550)
And there were canals, mountain torrents, ponds, and all manner of reservoirs,
consisting of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
The seven oceans and those seven islands which are proclaimed—namely Jambū, Plakṣa, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, Śālmali, and Puṣkala—[are situated there]. (11.552)
May all those who have been brought under control by the recitation of mantras consecrate you with the mantra "Agnimīle," which is the first verse of the Ṛgveda.
Let one bathe Caṇḍikā with a pitcher of cow’s milk using the mantra beginning with "iṣe tvā," and let one bathe her with the juices of sugarcane.
The Yajurveda, joined with its eighty-six divisions, [worships] the Queen of the Gods;
the Sāmaveda, endowed with a thousand branches, [worships her] with flowing honey.
May the Atharvaveda, accompanied by many branches, bathe you, O Caṇḍikā, with the oblation and with the mantra "O Agni, come hither. (11.556)
"May the Goddess [Sarasvatī] consecrate you with the mantra 'śanno devī';
indeed, those eighteen Purāṇas which were spoken by Vyāsa—" (557)
And may those Upapurāṇas indeed bathe you with curd,
as well as those Dharmaśāstras composed by the great seers.
Let the hundred and eighty forms bathe Maheśvarī;
let the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you with their sprinkling.
With this first jar, filled with the waters of the celestial river—the water of the Gaṅgā—one should bathe the Supreme Goddess. (11.560)
And may the Maruts, full of devotion, consecrate the Queen of the Gods with a second pitcher filled with the water of rain from the clouds.
With this jar, rich with rainwater, one should bathe Śivā;
and with the waters of the Sarasvatī, O Caṇḍikā, which are clear and pure. (11.562)
Let the Vidyādharas bathe [her] with the third pitcher;
one should drench Śivā with a jar filled with the waters of Sarasvatī.
May Śakra and the other guardians of the world, having assembled together,
bathe you with a fourth pitcher filled with the waters of the ocean.
One should bathe the Goddess with water that is devoid of [physical] substance, using this mantra,
with water completely full and fragrant with the pollen of lotuses.
"Let the Nāgas indeed consecrate you with the fifth pitcher;
let this mantra accompany the water-pitcher joined with lotus flowers. (11.566)
May the mountains Himavat, Meru, and Kailāśa consecrate [you] with the sixth pitcher, filled with the water of mountain torrents.
With these waters from the mountain stream, one should bathe the Supreme Goddess;
with a pitcher filled with the waters of all sacred fords, one should bathe the Queen of the Gods.
"Let the seven ṛṣis who move through the sky consecrate him with this seventh [mantra].
One should perform the ritual bathing with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) in a jar while reciting this mantra. (11.569)
May the Vasus consecrate you with the eighth vessel, with water from the lake; O Goddess Durgā, salutations be unto you!
One should sprinkle the Goddess with the water of a pond while reciting this mantra:
"Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, austerity, truth, forbearance, and fortitude. (11.571)
Fame, solitude, self-restraint, celibacy, compassion, self-control, tranquility, silence, as well as purity, contentment, and moderation in speech. (11.572)
Whatever Upaniṣads there are that establish the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), and whatever exists in the three worlds, both stationary and moving— || 11.573 ||

Whatever has arisen from the creation of Brahmā, both manifest and unmanifest, whether immobile or mobile, and that which consists of speech as well as that which does not consist of speech. || 11-574 ||
May they all indeed bathe you with a new pitcher;
one should bathe Caṇḍikā with pure water while reciting this mantra: || 11-574 ||
Thus has the great ablution been described to you, O beloved, for the ritual of autumnal worship;
if a devotee is permeated by devotion, he may perform it even on another day.
Whoever bathes the Mother of the World according to this rite shall be liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, one shall dwell in the world of the gods for eight thousand divine years;
furthermore, the great ablution on the ninth day increases wealth and progeny.
One obtains the fruit of a thousand sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter.
A king attains his kingdom, and likewise the destruction of his enemies. (11.574)
Others, O Pārvatī, attain their own desired goals through the great ablution (mahāsnāna).
Following the great ablution, one should then offer a bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūtas).
Having taken meat and wine for the Kaulas, and black gram food for those who abide by the Smṛtis,
he should indeed offer that bali-oblation with both hands.
"May the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas who dwell here upon this earth accept this prepared bali-offering given by me. (11.577)
Honored with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and likewise satiated with offerings, may they depart from this place and behold the worship performed by me. (11.578)
*Tāra*, *rāva*, *kūrca*, *bhūta*, *bhyasanta*, and *bhūta*—this is the *vali* together with the *sandhi*; these two are declared to be the *hṛdaya* mantras. (11.579)
The sound *phre* is for *rāva*; *sphro* is for *bhūta*.
Likewise, if the offering of the *bali* has not been performed, it should be done immediately after the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*).
O Goddess, that [offering] would become fruitless, and likewise the constituent part of the worship is lost.
The greedy always plunder, and the deities do not accept [the offerings];
therefore, one must diligently perform the expulsion of the elemental spirits.
Having taken parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and so forth, one should utter the *tāra*, *roṣa*, *anuniḥśreṇī*, and *astra* mantras.
May those spirits depart who are present here during the autumnal rites;
without causing any obstruction to the spirits, I perform the worship of the Goddess.
May the vetālas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and reptiles flee everywhere, struck by the weapons in the form of mantras.
Before those Manus, one should recite "hūṃ aḥ phaṭ";
then, having driven away the bhūtas and others, as well as the gatekeepers.

Immediately after that, O Pārvatī, one should offer a *kūrca* and the weapon (*astra*) mantra with this following verse to her who dwells within the branch of the *vilva* tree at the heart of *trapuṣa*: 11-586. [The mantra follows: "To her who dwells within the end of the *vilva* branch at the heart of *trapuṣa*, to Durgā, [I offer] the *kūrca* and the weapon. With this mantra, O Pārvatī... [586].
Having worshipped [the deity] with water for the feet and other offerings, one should perform the rite of *nīrājana*.
*Nīrājana* means the act of waving lights (*nirmañchana*).
Having brought [the deity] to the doorway, one should then perform the *nirmañchana*. (11.587)
Thus, according to the statement in another Tantra:
"Then, having assumed the posture, [one should worship] the Goddess, whether she be represented by a leaf or even made of clay."
Having moved the singing, musical instruments, and so forth, one should recite this mantra.
Then, one should establish her in a very firm form upon the imagined seat;
[there she is] with Tārā, Trapuṣā, Rāvalakṣmī, Yoginī, and Kāmayoṣit.
Ḍākinī and Phetkārī, Caṇḍikā and Bhagavatī; move the two moving ones, twice, O Vajrakāpālinī! (11.590)
Enter the house of worship twice: *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. After that:
"Come to my home, O Goddess, together with your eight powers (*śakti*). (11.591)
"Accept this worship according to the rules for the sake of all auspiciousness;
with this, one should install the Goddess who bestows all auspiciousness. (11.592)
For the purpose of worship for three days, [the mantras] for the altar, the seat, and so forth are as follows:
Trapā (hrīḥ), Rāva (phreṃ), Yoginī (chrīṃ), Kāma (klīṃ), Yoṣit (strīṃ), Ḍākinī (khphreṃ), and Phetkārī (hskhphreṃ). Likewise:
O Ambikā, you likewise abide as Tārā, Cidrā, Vaṭuka, and Ḍākinī.
One should stabilize [the vessel] with the mantra "sthirībhava śiraḥ" and thereafter stabilize it further with the *cidvāgbhava* [mantra].
Now, he describes the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*).
Then, furthermore, when the Sarvatobhadra mandala has been fashioned again, || 11-594 ||
It was painted with five colors, provided with curd, unbroken rice, and fruit,
and adorned with five jewels, gold, and a central gem.
O Dear One, having placed [the image] upon rice or barley, its neck wrapped in a silken cloth and adorned with sprouts; 11-596.
One should perform the installation of the water-pot according to the Vedic injunctions.
Having touched the ground, O fair-faced one, one should mutter the mantra beginning with "bhūr asi. (11.597)
Then, having said "Dhānyamasi," he should consecrate either rice or barley;
while reciting the mantra "Ājighra," he should place the water-pot there.
One should fill it completely with water while reciting the mantra "varuṇasya...";
then, having recited "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt...", one should place a sprig [of durvā grass] therein.

Having said "phalaṃ vā phalinī," one should offer a lotus; having said "śrīśca," a flower; then, having said "gandhadvārā," the perfume; and with "sahasraśīrṣā," one should place the unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
One should perform the rite of stabilization with the mantra "sthirībhava" [using earth] from an anthill, an elephant's tusk, a confluence of rivers, or a mountain. (11.601)
Having brought earth from Gokula and also from the gate of the king of the gods,
one should place it into each jar individually while reciting the Hārdamantra.
With the heart-mantra, namely the mantra "namaḥ," one should indeed perform the purification of all objects and so forth as before,
using the previously mentioned mantra and likewise with the visualization.
Whatever defilement of offering materials and the like that one has not personally condemned, or even the touching of the untouchable, or whatever has been acquired through unjust means; (604)
Likewise, whatever is touched by floral remains (nirmālya) or defiled by the climbing of insects—all those defects perish through [the Lord’s] glance. (11.605)
Having performed the expulsion of obstructing spirits and having carried out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
one should worship one's own seat, as well as Gaṇeśa, the Guru, and the deities.
Having bowed, the wise one should then perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma);
thereafter, with a restrained mind, he should perform the rite of the ṛṣis and so forth for the leaf-manuscript (patrikā).
O Nārada, for this ritual of the worship of Durgā in the autumn season, the seer is [the same], the metre is Gāyatrī, and Śrī Durgā is considered the deity. (11.608)
The seed-syllable (bīja) is taught as *hrīṃ*, and the power (*śakti*) is also *śrīṃ*, O Pārvatī;
the pin (*kīlaka*) is declared to be *klīm*, and this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the worship.
For at this very juncture, some perform a formal resolve (saṅkalpa);
others do not, because this [rite] is optional (*kāmya*), unlike the obligatory daily duties (*nityakṛtya*) which are mandatory. (11.610)
If the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) is made for even a single three-day period, it is indeed one [rite],
because of the unity of the performance and its conclusion, as well as the unity of the fruit resulting from the final dismissal (visarjana).
One should always perform that Ṛṣi-veneration for him upon the pedestal (pīṭha) and the image (mūrti).
Listen now to the mantra along with its Ṛṣi in the case of an earthen image or a leaf-image.
First, having written the beginning of the Vedas, one should utter the name of Durgā twice;
then, one should recite the vocative case of the Protectress together with the word "Śiras" (the Head).
For the purpose of offering the leaf, the image, the services, and so forth, O Manu, you [should recite] one, two, two, three, two, and the entire mantra. (11.614)
These mantra-syllables are to be deposited on the hands, fingers, heart, and so forth;
likewise, one should perform the respective meditations as previously described for the eternal seats (nityapīṭha).
O Dear One, contemplate the meditation on the side of the Māheya-pīṭha:
[the goddess] possessing the luster of refined gold and endowed with fresh youthfulness. (11.616)
Her face has the luster of the full moon; she is adorned with a crown of matted locks;
her three eyes are large, long, and black; and she wears a crest bound with a crescent moon.
She was adorned with rows of teeth shaped like pomegranate flowers,
possessed lofty and full breasts, and was graced by three folds on her waist.
The goddess, whose waist was exceedingly slender and who shone with the fullness of her hips, stood in the *tribhaṅga* posture as if her middle were being bent. (11.618)
Endowed with ten arms and adorned with all ornaments, she holds in her right hands a trident, a sword, a discus, an arrow, and a spear. 619.
Furthermore, she holds a noose, a shield, a goad, and a bow in her left hands;
her lotus-like right foot is placed upon the back of a lion.
She stood face-to-face with the severed head of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
while the mass of hair from the crowns of the Daityas rose up from her lotus-stalk-like throat.
The Supreme Goddess, holding a noose with her left hand alone,
gazed with fury upon the Dānava whose heart had been pierced by her trident.
His belly and arms were encircled by great serpents in the form of nooses;
his appearance was terrifying with a frown, and his body was moist with blood.
The great-souled Hari forcibly drew back his arm, its elbow locked as he seized his sword, while blood flowed in streams from his face.
She was being praised by all the gods, headed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
having slain the Dānava with ease, she had a slight smile upon her face.
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Caṇḍikā. || 11-626 ||
One should meditate upon such Durgā, who constantly surrounds herself with these eight powers and bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation. (11.627)
Having meditated thus and performed worship with purely mental offerings,
one should establish the *argha* water according to the very procedure previously described.

Where the detailed procedure according to the specific occasion has been proclaimed, one should, provided there is the capacity, arrange the water for the feet (pādya) and the other offerings individually. || 11-629 ||
To the north of the *argha* offering, the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, *snānīya*, and *madhuparka* should be prepared; such are the services provided by me. (11.630)
At this very moment, the worshipper of the fivefold abode of the Goddess should perform sacrifice with the prepared offerings for Gaṇeśa, Arka, Hari, and Īśāna.
Then the wise practitioner should first perform the general worship of the seats (pīṭhārcana);
at the conclusion of everything, the Jewel of Yoga (yogaratna), augmented by the remaining mantra, [should be performed].
Having performed the meditation once more, the practitioner, with eyes closed, should then perform the invocation accompanied by the distinct gestures (*mudrā*). (11.633)

Then, having made [the deity] possessed of limbs by means of the root mantra and through meditative visualizations, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with the syllables of the mantra while touching those respective parts.
In the consecration of the primary pedestal, whatever mantra was previously declared,
with that very same [mantra] one should perform the stable installation of the yantra and the image.
O Dear One, some desire that mantra even for clay images, paper, jars, tridents, faces, and so forth; however, the Kāpālikas and others do not accept it at all.
One should utter other worldly mantras as well as certain Vedic ones over the pedestal, the water-pot, the image of Mahesha, and so forth. (11.637)
I tell you this, O fair-limbed one, from the words spoken by Nandikeśvara:
having placed the hand upon the leaf, [one should say] "Tārā" and so forth, ending with "tatsat. (11.638)
Having uttered [the invocation] three times, one should recite these very mantras at the two stable seats:
"Come to my house, O Goddess, together with the eight Śaktis. (11.639)
Accept this worship according to the rite, O you who bring about all auspiciousness! Come, come, O Blessed Mother, bestower of victory and the destruction of enemies!
I worship you with devotion, O Navadurgā, honored by the gods. O Goddess Durgā, come hither and grant me your presence. (11.641)
"Accept your sacrificial portion along with your eight Śaktis;
O you who are worshipped by the thirty gods, I perform this autumnal worship."
Command me, O Great Goddess, destroyer of the pride of the Daityas,
for I am perpetually fallen into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross.
Protect me, O boon-granting goddess; salutations to you, beloved of Śaṅkara!
For whatever gods and goddesses there are, they indeed tremble when you tremble.
I invoke them all, O Caṇḍikā, Supreme Goddess!
Protect my life-breaths, protect my fame, and protect my wife, my son, and my wealth.
Since you, O Goddess beloved of the world, are the provider of all protection,
please enter and remain within this sacrifice while I perform the worship.
O Goddess who brings joy to Menā, grant me all perfections;
come, O Goddess Caṇḍikā, for the sake of every auspiciousness.
Accept this worship, O fair-faced one; salutations to you, beloved of Śaṅkara!
O Goddess, I invoke you here into this earthen image and likewise into this bilva fruit.
On the trident, the jar, the sword, the mandala, and even in a painting—
from the peak of Kailāsa, O Goddess, from the Vindhya mountains, and from the Himalayas— (649).
Having arrived, O Caṇḍikā, establish your presence upon this bilva branch;
you have been installed by me, O Goddess—worship you, be gracious to me. (11.650)
O fierce one, O you whose nature is fierce, O fierce lady, O bearer of a fierce form!
O Goddess, take refuge in the branch of the bilva tree and remain there together with your hosts.
Alternatively, [one may perform it] upon an earthen jar, a trident, or even a sword;
likewise upon a painted cloth, or upon the severed head of an enemy, or within a circle of fire.
O omnipresent one, having arrived, grant your presence here!
O Goddess, Mother of the worlds, you who effect creation and destruction! (11.653)
O Caṇḍikā, manifest your presence in all the maṇḍalas,
numbering twenty-four, which are to be consecrated.
Having arrived, accept this autumnal worship, O Goddess; be gracious to me.
You have been invoked, O Goddess, throughout the entire mandala dedicated to you.
Having become stable right here in my house, O Caṇḍī, you who are born from the splendor of the gods, be the granter of desires; for you are of fierce form.
Having gathered with your retinue, quickly establish yourself here;
O beloved, one should recite these eighteen mantras from the Purāṇas.
Then, "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," likewise "pra tad viṣṇu stavate," and similarly "viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu"—these are declared as the third [round]. (11.658)
One should recite these five Vedic mantras: the Gāyatrī preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ) and followed by the Tāra, and likewise "Tryambakam. (11.659)
One should not even conceive of [the deity] upon a stable seat or in an image;
therefore, one should indeed perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) with the extensive mantras.
By the first [verse], which is eternally renowned and states the cause, that [result] follows;
immediately thereafter, by the third verse, its state of being about to be explained [is indicated]. (11.661)
And that [should be performed] during the autumnal worship, never at any other time;
likewise for the pedestal and the image, as well as in the mandala, but not elsewhere.
*Tāra*, *maidhātṛ*, *pārā*, *vayoginī*, and likewise *ḍākinī*; *phetkārī* and *kūrcavanitā*—these indeed are the nine seed-syllables.
"Come, come, O Blessed One!"—thus one should then utter these three words;
likewise, from the thirty-three crores of words, by means of the word "tridaśa. (11.664)
From the word *tejaḥkalpita* one should likewise imagine [the goddess] in the body; from the word *padāt*, as well as from *mahiṣāsūra*, [one derives] *mardinī*. (11.665)
Then, having uttered "jagattraye," one should recite "pālini";
thereafter, "kāmaprasāda-pāśāḥ" and "nṛsiṃha-kamale."
The two who are arriving and the two who are manifesting their presence, having entered the place of worship and spoken, remain thereafter as a pair. (11.667)
Then, one should speak the mantra surrounded by the eight power-words (*śaktipada*) at the end of each *sandhyā*:
"Jvala-yugmam, Prajvala-yugmam, Sphura, Prasphura"—it is thus.
Then follow Aṅkuśa, Preta, Bhairavī, Amā, Hāra, and Pralaya;
then Vidyun, Mahākrodha, and Tārā; and after that, Śiraḥśeṣa. (11.669)
In this Manvantara, there are indeed one hundred and eighteen syllables;
with these very three mantras, one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
A person other than a Kaula should recite the final mantra, "mano jūtiḥ," from the Śruti over clay images, leaf-manuscripts, water-pots, and so forth. (11.671)
Then, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) as instructed by the ritual specialist;
this is done three times with the mantra, but only upon the seat (pīṭha), not on the ancestral plate (patryā).
Then, O Dear One, at this juncture, the Kaulas and others should perform the excellent installation of the vessels according to the occasional (naimittika) rite.
Having placed before oneself the floods of ritual depositions (nyāsa) prescribed by the occasional rites,
one should indeed perform all five pentads in the case of the Śakti, as well as the triad of sixfold [depositions].
One should never perform this [rite] with vessels made of earth or leaves;
rather, one should arrange the vessels according to one's own preference.
The method of investigation for these is indeed declared to be occasional;
that conceptualization, those mantras, that sequence, and that very state of being [are all such]. (11.676)
Those [five] deposits (nyāsa) constitute purification, and that [purification] consists of either the substance or the satiation;
this occurs through the occasional worship of the pedestal and the image during the autumnal rite.
In the opinion of some, O Īśānī, not even an atom is divided;
therefore, I have distinguished between these two methods: that of the Tantras and that of the Purāṇas. (11.679)
He is generally called Manu, being within the scope of the intellect of the wise;
for in the *patrikās* and other texts, it is indeed the *pīṭha* that is both ancient (*paurāṇa*) and tantric (*tāntrika*). (11.680)
O Pārvatī, those mantras which were previously declared for each individual offering of the substance should also be employed here in the ritual of occasional worship.
I shall now declare those individual mantras which are established in the ritual manuals and other texts, for the purpose of the procedure of offering those respective substances.
O Goddess of the gods, just as [the mantras] are recited following the utterance of their respective *mūla-mantras* for the purpose of bestowing the [desired] object, so it is here as well.
Having recited the Purāṇic mantra, one should then proclaim at its end the thirty-two-syllable mantra uttered by Bhairava.
The ten-syllable mantra of Jayadurgā worshipped by Kātyāyana—by those two, through the extraction of the gift of the substance during the ritual worship according to the Purāṇas. (11.685)
If one is unable to perform both, one should perform at least one out of necessity.
I shall now describe their extraction; first, that which was worshipped by Nandīśvara.
From *tāra* and *trapā*, ending in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, there is *dakṣayajñavināśinī*;
likewise, from the word *yoginīkoṭi*, there is *mahāghorā*. (11.687)
In the same manner, it should be surrounded; thereafter comes the seed-syllable of Māyā.
As before, Bhadrakālī follows, and the heart-mantra is placed at the very end of all.
Alternatively, one should recite "Tārā" or "Durgā" twice; then [one should recite] the vocative form of "Rakṣaṇī," followed by the *tarjanī* and the end of the *anura*. (11.689)
O Goddess, although these two mantras are declared to be Tantric,
they should nevertheless be employed at the conclusion of the Paurāṇika rite for their respective offerings.
Now I shall declare the ancient mantras for all ritual services;
those pertaining to the Tantras have already been mentioned previously in connection with the worship of the causal signs.
These very same [deities] should be appointed here for the individual offerings;
those belonging to the Purāṇas for the parchments and so forth, while those belonging to the Tantras are for the pedestal and the image.
Then [he offers] a seat, water for the feet, and the arghya; thereafter, water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), bathing water, clothing, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
Flowers, incense, a lamp, and collyrium for the eyes; furthermore, lac-dye, as well as food offerings, circumambulation, and prostrations. (11.694)
These ritual services have been proclaimed as those which bring satisfaction to the Goddess;
whatever substance is offered, such as ornaments, gold, and so forth. (11.695)
Having invoked their respective deities and performed the sprinkling and worship, one should offer [the oblation] by uttering each deity's name along with its specific mantra.
One should perform the complete purification according to the ancient sequence with the earth-mantra:
"This seat is offered by me to you, O one worshipped by the best of gods. (11.697)
"Please remain seated here while I perform the worship;
[here is] water mixed with dūrvā grass, parājitā, lotuses, and śyāmāka grain. (11.698)
O Goddess, it is suitable for the water for the feet (*pādya*) specifically during special forms of worship, and not otherwise:
"Accept this water for the feet given by me, which removes all suffering. (11.699)
"O Goddess, granter of boons, protect me from this terrible ocean of existence.
When the bathing, the garments, and the food offering have been presented, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya). (11.700)
And one should offer that madhuparka with the word *svadhā*, O beloved;
likewise, the *argha* with the word *svāhā*, and everything else with words of *namaḥ*.
Pure water combined with fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, bilva leaves, milk, and dūrvā grass.
Having placed it within a conch-shell vessel, one should offer it to Kālikā, together with dūrvā grass, unbroken grains (akṣata), and bilva leaves. || 11-703 ||
O beloved of Hara, accept this beautiful arghya-water placed in a conch vessel,
consisting of water from various sacred fords and prepared with all necessary substances.
Accept this *argha*, O Goddess, Mother of the World; salutations be unto you!
This water is accompanied by camphor, nutmeg, cloves, and *kakkola*.
One desiring fruit should indeed offer this most excellent special water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) to the Goddess, made fragrant with aromatic substances. (11.706)
Please accept this water for sipping (ācamanīya) offered by me with devotion;
these waters have been placed by me with devotion at the soles of your feet. (11.707)
"O Great Goddess, drink [this] water; being pleased, grant me peace.
In the absence of wine, one should offer ghee, curd, and honey in a bronze vessel. (11.708)
That which is intended for the gods is called *madhuparka*; it is to be requested [of them], O Maheśānī, and was fashioned by Brahmā as *madhuparka*. (11.709)
I have presented this to you; accept it, O Sovereign of the World!
Following the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), here again is the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
At the conclusion of the consumption [of the water], he should be given [water] so that he may become free from the state of being impure from remnants:
"O Vārida, this water is pleasing to me, clear, and indeed pure. (11.711)
"O Goddess of the Gods, bathe with this [garment] offered by me with devotion, which is fashioned from silk thread and other materials endowed with various colors. (11.712)
O Goddess of the Thirty-three, accept these garments—both white and red—which beautify the body, are pure, and are dyed with substances from the serpent realm. (11.713)
"O Mother of the World, clothe yourself with this garment offered with devotion.
After the garment has been put on, there is again water for sipping. (11.714)
It should be given with a spirit of devotion, because it is prescribed by the Smṛtis, just as in the case of humans;
[the recipients] are endowed with divine jewels and possess a radiance equal to fire and the sun. (11.715)
May these ornaments beautify your limbs, O Sovereign of the Gods!
This unguent of yours is exceedingly fragrant and cooling.
"O Goddess, take this fragrant flower that has grown in both villages and forests which I have offered, and smear it upon your limbs. (11.717)
"Please accept this heart-pleasing refreshment for the vital breaths offered by me;
it is produced from the essence of trees and blended with camphor and agallochum. (11.718)
"O God and Goddess, please accept this incense offered by me;
[may there be] the light of fire, the light of the sun, and likewise the light of the moon. (11.719)
May this lamp, the supreme light among all lights, be accepted;
you [are] the lights of the moon and sun, as well as those of lightning and fire.
You alone are the light of the worlds; let this lamp be accepted, for it is smooth, warm, most pleasing to the eyes, and a source of beauty for you. (11.721)
O Pārvatī, take this collyrium immediately and anoint your eyes;
it is as beautiful as the luster of the rays from the toenails of your lotus-feet.
"O Queen, please accept this lac-dye given by me;
it is of various kinds, beautiful, delicious, and flavorful. (11.723)
"O you who are worshipped by the gods, please accept these offerings given by me—every kind of fruit and grain-garlands grown in villages and forests. (11.724)
O Supreme Goddess, accept these various forms of fragrant food;
O Goddess, this fourfold offering is endowed with the six flavors.
Please accept this delightful food, which provides constant satisfaction, combined with cow’s ghee and milk, and mixed with various sweets. (11.726)
"O Goddess, please accept this supreme food (paramānna) offered by me;
it is divine, composed of nectar, and prepared with ghee and sugar-candy."
O beloved of Hara, accept these various kinds of delicious flour-cakes, and this sweet, charming *modaka* confection seasoned with camphor and other ingredients. (11.728)
Having accepted this mixture of various substances, let it be consumed quickly;
[it consists of] sidhu liquor placed in a copper vessel, or else cow's milk here.
O beloved of Śaṅkara, accept this coconut water in a bronze vessel;
it is cool, pure, clear, and mixed with camphor.
O Goddess, may this which brings satisfaction in eating be graciously accepted;
at the conclusion of the meal, the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be offered once again.

O lady of pure smiles, in every instance, one should use the very mantra previously mentioned [for] that which is combined with fruits and leaves and well-scented with camphor and other fragrances. (11.732)
"Please accept this betel leaf, which beautifies the face and is pleasing to the heart.
Then, the best of practitioners should offer a blade of dūrvā grass to the Goddess. (11.733)
Salutations to you, O omnipresent Goddess; salutations to you, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
Accept this *dūrvā* grass, O Goddess, and deliver me from distress. (11.734)
Then one should offer a bilva leaf to the Goddess separately, saying:
"Born of nectar, endowed with beauty, this is always dear to Mahādeva. (11.735)
I offer you this sacred pavitra, fashioned from the leaves of the Bilva tree,
adorned with various flowers, bound upon the breast, and fragrant.
O Goddess, I inform you that even if it has fallen or is hanging down,
the vermilion (sindūra) must be offered at the very end of the worship of the leaf-strips (patrikā).
At the time of applying the ointment, however, one should offer [the offering] to the pedestal and the image;
it is the cause of the arising of passion that brings about the beauty of the forehead and other parts.
"O one of excessive passion, accept this intensely beautiful red lotus, white yak-tail fan with a golden handle and fine hair. (11.739)
Please accept this royal insignia, the fly-whisk offered by me,
fashioned from the feathers of a peacock with its shaft made of bamboo.
"O Goddess, please take this fan to remove the sweat from your body—by which you terrify the Daityas and by which you fill the sky. (11.741)
I give you that bell; take it, O slayer of Mahiṣa!
This auspicious ārātrika has been prepared with many lamps.
I inform you, O Goddess: withdraw the darkness born of ignorance.
At the conclusion of everything, three handfuls of flowers should be offered.
O lady of excellent hips, the *tanmantra* is proclaimed as the *Gāyatrī* of Durgā:
"Oṃ, may we know Caṇḍikā; may we meditate upon the Blessed Lady; may Gaurī impel us.
O Pārvatī, he who [performs this] by this rule and with these mantras— || 11-744 ||
One should worship Mahiṣaghnī, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), upon leaves;
having obtained the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, he shall go to the abode of Caṇḍikā.
And here too, O lady of noble limbs, he shall immediately become a vessel for auspicious things; such is the method of worship for both the sacred seat and the image.
The disclosure of mantras should be known as the supreme [transgression], as well as the improper placement of vessels;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the individual leaf-tablets (patrikā). || 11-747 ||
To the extent that it can be performed through ritual application and even through mantras individually, each respective presiding deity is proclaimed as one. (11.748)
O Dear One, one should invoke and worship each [deity] with their respective name in the dative case;
first, however, Brahmāṇī is proclaimed as the presiding deity of Rambhā.
Kālikā is presided over by Kaccī and was spoken of by the Destroyer of Tripura;
Durgā is presided over by Haridrā, as is Kārttikī at Jayantī. || 11-750 ||
Śivā is the presiding deity of the bilva tree, and likewise Raktadantikā is the presiding deity of the pomegranate;
she should be known as the destroyer of hosts of enemies. (11.751)
She who is free from sorrow has been proclaimed by the sages as the presiding deity of Aśoka;
likewise, Cāmuṇḍā is celebrated as the presiding deity of pride.
Lakṣmī, the presiding deity of grain, was presented by Nandīśa;
Kātyāyanī, the presiding deity of the nine leaves, has also been mentioned.
O Goddess, just as their names have been declared to you by me in sequence,
so now I shall proclaim each mantra in its proper order.
O Brahmāṇī, come hither and grant your presence here;
in the form of Rambhā, bring peace everywhere. Homage be to you! (11-755)
O Kālikā, you became the girdle during the battles with the demon Mahiṣāsura;
for the sake of favoring mankind, you have come to this world.
O Goddess Haridrā, bestower of boons, you are Durgā in form, O beautiful one;
for the destruction of my obstacles, accept this worship and be gracious to me. || 11-757 ||
In the past, during the slaying of Niśumbha and Śumbha, you were worshipped by the hosts of gods led by Indra; as Jayantī, grant us boons. (11.758)
O Bilva tree, who always brings pleasure to Mahādeva, who is ever dear to Vāsudeva,
and who always causes delight to Kālī— salutations be unto you!
In former times, during the battle with Raktabīja, you brought joy to Cāmuṇḍā; therefore, I worship you. (11.760)
The aśoka tree indeed brings delight to Hara and destroys sorrow;
by bringing delight to Durgā, make me forever free from sorrow.
O Goddess, beloved of Śacī, you who dwell upon the leaf of the mango tree;
for the sake of my very grace, accept this worship, O Queen of the Gods.
Created of old by Brahmā for the sake of protecting the life-breath of the world, you are the grain that brings pleasure to Umā; therefore, protect me always. (11.761)
O Patrika, O Navadurga, you who are enchanting to Mahādeva,
having accepted this complete worship, protect me, O Sovereign of the Thirty Gods.
Having thus worshipped each one individually with these uttered mantras, as well as by means of their two previously mentioned names ending in the feminine suffix *ṅi* (e), [one should proceed].

One should also [worship] the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), accompanied by their mounts and weapons as described in the daily rites, using the names stated in the general *pīṭha*-nyāsa, augmented with the nominative case-ending (-ṅ).

One should worship the Supreme Goddess with the materials prescribed for the daily and occasional rites, as well as with the elaborate expansions of the preliminary and formal worship, using both the pedestal and the image.
Whatever constant duties have been described by me,
one should apply both of them likewise even in the case of occasional rites.
In the ritual procedure for the ancestors (āvaityaka), they have declared that there is no recitation of mantras during the formal conjunction;

One who is motivated by specific signs is to be gathered; all others possess a dual nature.
For whatever the ritual application may be, the act of propitiation is indeed of that same nature.

If one is capable, however, one should worship the ten weapons during the leaf-worship (patrikārcā), using the syllables of each respective weapon ending in the suffix -Ṅa, preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ) and the Hṛdaya-mantra (Namaḥ), and positioned in their respective centers. || 11-769 ||
Thereafter, at the conclusion of all the worship, one should worship Mahiṣāsura;
and according to one's own capacity, one should offer oblations consisting even of animals and birds.
"The procedure for that occasional rite has already been proclaimed to you.

The purification of the various ritual substances as well as the seat and so forth, along with breath control (prāṇāyāma), the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the ritual placement of the alphabet (mātṛkānyāsa). || 11-773 ||
Likewise, having performed the two known as the Pīṭha and Ṣaḍaṅga nyāsas, as well as the other nyāsas, according to the previously stated method, and likewise the great bath (mahāsnāna).

Having diligently worshipped the five deities beginning with Sūrya,

One should worship Mahāmāyā with the sixteen types of offerings,
O Pārvatī, using those respective mantras in their proper sequence.
