The Kaulika [practitioner], however, [should worship] them with mantras consisting of garlands of mantras, and with mantras in the form of verses as declared in the Nandikeśa Purāṇa. || 11-783 ||
O Dear One, O Beautiful One, those who travel the path of the Śruti should worship Ugracaṇḍā and the others; I shall now tell you their mantras.
First the Tārā-hṛdaya-mantra, then the name in the middle with the feminine suffix -ī, and finally the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu); thus indeed is the sequence proclaimed. (11.785)
May Ugracaṇḍā, who bestows fearlessness and possesses a radiance equal to the midday sun, always grant me boons; to her, eternal salutations, salutations! (11.786)
O fierce one, O mother, who are always surrounded by the fierce hosts;
O goddess who bestows joy upon the world, be forever gracious.
O fierce and terrible one, you are the form of the spirits and the bestower of fear upon all beings;
O beautiful one, be always gentle toward me and grant me boons.
O Goddess of the Gods, you who have been revealed by the Lord of Gods under the name "Siddhi"—you are that very one; O Goddess, salutations to you, Caṇḍanāyikā!
O Goddess, fierce one whose nature is wrath, you who grant victory over the fierce enemies;
you are the bestower of dharma and liberation—be forever the granter of boons to me.
Salutations again and again to Caṇḍavatī, who is endowed with the three qualities of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and than whom there is neither higher nor another.
Fierce in form, the Great Fierce One, the Fierce Leader, the Fierce Goddess;
O Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, salutations, salutations eternally to her! (11.792)
May that Caṇḍikā, whose eyes are as red as the rising sun, who is always affectionate toward her devotees,
and who is the crusher of the demon Caṇḍa, be the bestower of boons.
Then, by means of eight repetitions, one should worship on the petals of the eight-petaled lotus the sixty-four [deities] who take the form of the assembly of Yoginīs.
Having first uttered the three *tāra*s, and then the word "namaḥ," one should place the name of each of them ending in the nominative case (*ṅe*) in between and join them together. (11.795)
With the fivefold services, or with flowers, or even with unbroken grains alone, one should worship Brahmāṇī, Caṇḍikā, Raudrī, Gaurī, and likewise Indrāṇī. (11.796)
Kaumārī, Bhairavī, Durgā, Nārasiṃhī, Kālikā, Cāmuṇḍā, Śivadūtī, Vārāhī, and likewise Kauśikī. (11.797)
Māheśvarī, Śaṅkarī, Jayantī, Sarvamaṅgalā, Karālinī, Muktakeśī, Śivā, and likewise Śākambharī. (11.798)
Bhīmā, Śāntā, Bhrāmarī, Rudrāṇī, Caṇḍarūpiṇī, Kṣamā, Dhātrī, Svadhā, Svāhā, Aparṇā, and Mahodarī. (11.799)
Ghorarūpā, Mahākālī, Vidyujjihvā, Kapālinī, Kṣemaṅkarī, Mahāmāyā, Meghamālā, and Balākinī. || 11-800 ||
Śuṣkodarī, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Mahāpretā, Priyaṅkarī, Kharatuṇḍī, Ṛkṣakarṇī, and likewise Balapramathanī. || 11-801 ||
Likewise, Manomathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, Umā, Tārā, Mahānidrā, Vijayā, and Jayā. (11.802)
Śailaputrī, Maholkā, Triśūlinī, Añjanaprabhā, Kūṣmāṇḍī, Viśvasaṃtrāsā, and likewise the supreme Kātyāyanī. (11.803)
Kālarātri and Mahāgaurī—these sixty-four are considered [the goddesses];
one should worship them at the edge of the maṇḍala for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. (11.804)
Furthermore, O Dear One, ten million yoginīs should be worshipped under a single name upon the tips of the lotus petals, using the same ritual arrangements of mantras as before.
Then, in the presence of the Goddess, one should worship the eight forms of Durgā who truly bestow fruits, two by two in the sequence starting from the northeast, or nine in the center. || 11.806 ||
The mantra for these [deities] is proclaimed to be like that of Ugracaṇḍā and others;
one should worship them with water for the feet and other offerings as before, using their respective mantras.

(1040) Then, by those who abide in the *mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra] and in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), as well as by the followers of the Purāṇas, the former position belongs to the Kaulikas, while the latter belongs to those who are learned in the Śrutis. (11.808)
I shall now declare her mantra; listen with attention.
She is four-faced, the sustainer of the world, mounted upon a swan, and the bestower of boons. (11.809)
I bow to that illustrious Brahmāṇī, the creator of the universe;
the auspicious Śivā, mounted upon a bull, the benevolent one with three eyes, the bestower of boons, the gracious one.
I bow to Māheśvarī, the cause of the dissolution of the universe;
and to Kaumārī, clad in yellow garments and borne by an excellent peacock.
I always bow to her who holds a spear in her hand, whose body is crimson,
who bestows boons, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and whose form is dark blue.
I bow to Vaiṣṇavī, whose form is stability, who dwells upon the king of birds;
I bow to the Goddess in the form of the Boar, who lifted the earth with her tusks.
I bow to that Vārāhī, the bestower of auspiciousness, who wears blue garments,
who possesses the form of Nṛsiṃha, who is formidable, and who slays the Daityas and Dānavas.
I bow to the radiant Nārasiṃhī with formidable claws;
to the auspicious Indrāṇī, who dwells upon the frontal globes of elephants and possesses a thousand eyes.
I bow to the boon-granting goddess, who is saluted by all the gods—
to Cāmuṇḍā, the crusher of skulls, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
I bow to Kātyāyanī, who possesses ten arms and tramples upon the demon Mahiṣāsura, for the sake of my own spiritual power—she who has arisen with a loud, echoing laugh. (11.817)
I bow down to the goddess with a serene countenance, the bestower of boons;
O Caṇḍikā, O Navadurgā, you who are ever beloved by Mahādeva.
"Accepting this entire worship, protect me, O Goddess of the Thirty-three!
These two mantras are considered to belong to Kātyāyanī and Durgā. (11.819)
O Goddess praised by the gods, one should worship these with that very same mantra;
furthermore, one should worship the eleven goddesses according to the previously stated procedure.
One should worship Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svadhā, and Svāhā.
Then, O Sovereign of the Gods, one should perform the worship of the weapon (astra-pūjā), which is superior to the worship performed on the seventh day,
using mantras indeed beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ."
First, however, one should worship the tridents and other implements on the right side, and then on the left,
using water for the feet and so forth, or simply with unbroken grains (akṣata).
You were fashioned as the foremost of all weapons by the wielder of the Pināka bow; having extracted the essence of the trident and formed a firm grip with your fist, you are auspicious.
The sword that slays the unassailable, sharp-edged and difficult to approach;
the womb of prosperity and victory itself—O Protector of Dharma, homage be to you! (11.825)
O Discus, you are the form of Viṣṇu; you are ever stationed in the hand of Viṣṇu.
You have come into the hand of the Goddess; O King of Discuses, salutations be to you!
You are the best among all weapons, O destroyer of the Daitya armies;
protect us always from all fears, O wielder of sharp arrows—salutations be to you!
O Śakti, you are the power of all the gods, and especially of Guha;
in the form of Śakti, grant protection everywhere. Homage be to you! (11.828)
O Kheṭa, you who act as the destroyer of enemies in the form of a protector;
always held in the hand of the Goddess, protect me from many perils. (11.829)
O great lord of all weapons, destroyer of all asuras,
protect me on all sides with your bow together with your most excellent arrows.
O noose, you are in the form of a serpent, filled with poison and having a poisonous belly;
you are eternally unbearable to enemies. O serpent-noose, homage be to you! (11.831)
You are the goad; salutations to you, the controller of elephants.
For the protection of even the gods, you have been held in the hand of Pārvatī.
O Ghaṇṭā, protect us from various kinds of fear—you, upon hearing whose sound the hosts of Daityas discharged excrement and urine. (11.833)
O axe, you are exceedingly sharp, the crusher of all enemies;
you have come into the hands of the Goddess—salutations, salutations to you forever! (11.834)
Whatever principal and renowned weapons there are here,
which cause the destruction of enemies and are famous throughout the three worlds—
Whatever Ambikā always holds in her own hands—bhuśuṇḍīs, nooses, iron clubs, bhindipālas, and cudgels—[she carries them all]. (11.836)
Spear-tips, javelins, and lances, as well as sharp-edged spears and clubs; maces, śataghnīs, kuṇapas, churikās, and weapons with the shape of a kartarī. || 11.837 ||
I worship all of them today, especially on the Great Eighth Day;
may they all protect me constantly and grant me every accomplishment.

From the syllable *tārā* and the *kūrca* mantra, one should utter the words "to Durgā, who holds all weapons," followed by "to the Sustainer, obeisance" (*dhāriṇyai namaḥ*), and offer three handfuls of flowers.
Then one should worship the goddess’s ornaments, beginning with the crown,
using their names preceded by *tārā* (oṃ), ending with *namaḥ*, and followed by the suffix *ṅe*.
Then one should worship the unsurpassed lion-throne of the Goddess, having indeed proclaimed:
"To Tārā, whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs."
"Hu! To the Great Lion!"—with this, one should worship the lion in the heart with the offerings as they have been prepared, such as flowers and unbroken grains. (11.841)
At the end of that, one should worship the lion-throne of the Goddess with this mantra:
"O Sword, you are the throne of the Goddess, endowed with formidable and fierce fangs. (842)
O King of Lions, whose form is like the peak of the Himālaya mountain, salutations be unto you!
By virtue of the boon granted by the Goddess, you have especially [slain] the demon Mahiṣāsura.
On the eighth and the ninth [days], one should worship with extensive offerings,
employing various services such as water for the feet and so forth, to the best of one's ability.

Beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, and having the word "mahiṣāsura" ending in the suffix *-ṅe* (dative), one should offer all the ritual services (*upacāra*) to him with this mantra. || 11-845 ||
O Dear One, one should not worship with an ordinary demonic mindset, but rather with the very mindset of Rudra;
at the conclusion of the worship, one should recite these mantras with palms joined in reverence.
O King of Asuras, you are Rudra, the destroyer of the pride of the gods;
born from the womb of your mother through the prayer for a boon from your father.
Who possesses the capacity to fight against Kātyāyanī?
By which asura was Madhusūdana held captive in battle? (11.848)
By whom else were the gods conquered in battle and made into servants? By whom was a kingdom enjoyed without any thorns for three *manvantaras*? (11.849)
Whose army could there have been, numbering even a hundred parārdhas, that came forth assuming the form of Rudra? O Mahiṣāsura, salutations to you!
Then, O Goddess, one should also worship the four Vaṭukas:
Siddhaputra, Jñānaputra, and likewise Sahajaputraka.
In the remainder, there is the Samayaputra; listen now to their mantra:
at the beginning of the lotus-seed syllable of the Vedas, and likewise at the end, there is also "namaḥ."
O Goddess of the Universe, in that same manner, Vaṭuka is embodied along with each respective name; these mantras for them should end in the suffix -Ṅ. (11.853)
One should worship these Vaṭukas with all the ritual offerings arranged according to one's means, while listening to the worship performed during the recitation.
One should worship the Kṣetrapālas in the center, on the filaments, and on the petals:
Hetuka, Tripuraghna, and likewise Agnijihva. (11.855)
And [the lords] named Agnivetāla, Kāla, Karālaka,
Ekapāda, and Bhīmanātha, in the sequence beginning from the north.
Now I shall speak the mantra for these; listen, O Pārvatī! This triad of seeds—Tāra, Kūrca, and Kṣetrapāla—is placed at the beginning. (11.857)
Furthermore, the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla) together with this name is proclaimed to be likewise endowed with a physical form and exceedingly terrifying. (11.858)
O fair-faced one, the wrathful deities are located in the heart and the head; one should worship two of each of these mantras in the four directions of the mandala and two in the center.
O Goddess of the Gods, there are nine Bhairavas in the ritual of the autumnal worship:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmatta; ||| 11-860 ||
Ānanda, Kapālī, and Bhīṣaṇa immediately after that;
Saṃhārī shall be at the very end—these are proclaimed as the nine Bhairavas.
Then follows the seed-syllable of intense shame and passion (*tāratrapāroṣa*), after which comes each respective name;
it should end with *bhairava*, be provided with a body [in the feminine], end in the suffix *ṅi*, and be conjoined with the heart-mantra. (11.862)
Outside the lotus, in the eight directions, one should worship the eight lords of the quarters:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and likewise Varuṇa. (11.863)
Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna are established under these names;
likewise, the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and the goad. (11.864)
The weapons of these [deities] on the banners and tridents have been described to you;
Nairṛta and Varuṇa are also mentioned, with Ananta situated in the center. || 11-865 ||
Then that weapon, the discus, arose from between Indra and Īśāna;
Brahmā with his lotus—these are declared to be the ten lords of the directions.
O beautiful lady, now fashion the manner of the mantra:
having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning, follow it with the respective name. (11.867)
Thereafter, each respective weapon appeared, accompanied by sound and surrounded [by its attendants], together with its vehicle, retinue, and implements.
These four words ending in the suffix -ṅī should be formed, followed by the word *namaḥ*;
thereafter, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) to the Goddess according to the previously stated procedure.
On the eighth day, one should give an offering greater than that given on the seventh.
In another tantra: "Then, having performed recitation according to one's ability, one should recite the hymn. (11.870)
The ritual for the offering of betel and the hymn of praise will be explained further on.
Likewise:
"Devoted to devotion, one should prostrate with the eight limbs upon the ground before the Goddess."
(In the *Nirṇayāmṛta*, from another Purāṇa:
Then, having paid homage to the sword for the sake of accomplishing the slaughter of enemies... (11.871)
If a king desires victory in his kingdom and abundance for himself, he should repeatedly bow to the Noble Lady and remember the auspicious one in his heart. (11.872)
Having performed all this, O descendant of Kuru, one should hold a great festival at night on the eighth day with the sounds of actors and dramatic performances. (11.873)
Now, at the junction of the eighth and ninth [lunar days], there is the worship of Cāmuṇḍā.
(In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
"Some perform the worship at the junction of the eighth and ninth [days]."
This is proclaimed in the Purāṇas and other texts as "the worship of the junctures" (tatsandhipūjana).
Some Tantrikas maintain that worship should be performed on the ninth day, or at midnight, or even on the following day; however, they hold that success is attained through worship in either case.
The worship of the Goddess there is prescribed for her while she assumes the form of Cāmuṇḍā; it is not performed for her in any other form—such is the settled conclusion.
Now, contemplate that mantra and its visualization;
we shall explain the mantra and visualization of Cāmuṇḍā in the section on the Eight Mothers as taught in another Tantra. Likewise:
Having meditated thus and having performed worship with various offerings and the like, || 11-877 ||
If possible, however, one should fill earthen vessels with measures of cooked food,
raw meat, and the blood of birds to be offered.
And one should worship them with perfumes, red flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as with incense, lamps, and enemy-subduing mantras.
One should offer an oblation with that [mantra], and thereby one enjoys great prosperity.
After that, at the hour of Śakti, some Kaulikas perform [the rite].
The procedure for that has been stated previously; one should conclude this very rite with that same [procedure].
Now follows the ritual for the ninth day (from the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa).
On the ninth day, she is endowed with glory and is well-worshipped by all the gods.
Having received the consecration on the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the Giver of Boons slew the wicked Mahiṣa, who was incapable of being slain by the gods.
Therefore, on that ninth day, the wise should worship Caṇḍikā there, for it was there that the goddess Sarasvatī attained her greatness. (11.883)
For that purpose, this ninth day is always proclaimed as great by the wise;
having worshipped the Great Goddess Mantracaṇḍikā on the ninth day, [one attains success].
O hero, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise the immortals attained greatness [through it];
therefore, this ninth day is highly meritorious and the destroyer of sins.
O King, this fast should always be observed with great effort by all rulers according to the prescribed rites, when [the moon] is conjoined with the constellation in the northeast (Pūrvottarā).
Especially by kings and others—by children, the elderly, and those in their youth;
by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other servants. || 11-887 ||
Thus it is stated in another tantra, the *Durgotsavapaddhati*.
Then, on the Mahānavamī day, one should worship the Mother of the World.
Whatever extensive worship has been described for the eighth [day], [it should be performed]. || 11-888 ||
On the ninth day as well, O fair-faced one, it should be performed for that same duration;
however, a specific distinction must be made there: the offering of abundant sacrificial oblations (bali).
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
One should perform the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and the forms (mūrti) according to the occasional (naimittika) sequence;
however, if capable, the practitioner should perform the worship according to the eternally manifest (nityodita) procedure. (11.890)

O lady of beautiful hips, there is no other worship; this is the rule declared by Śiva for one who is permeated with devotion toward the sacred seat (pīṭha), the image (mūrti), the leaf-image (patrikā), or the earthen image (mṛnmūrti).
Then he performs the two prescribed types of worship:
first the worship before the leaf-manuscript (patrikā), and thereafter the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha) and the image (mūrti).
The entire Tantric method has been declared regarding the sacred seats (pīṭha) and the forms (mūrti);
however, in the *Patrikā* and other texts, the Paurāṇic method was taught by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva). (11.893)
Having separated these two which were previously combined, I have thus spoken them;
thereafter, O Queen of the Gods, one should either cause [the disciple] to recite or recite [them] oneself.
One should recite either the entire hymn of praise to the Blessed Lady contained within the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, or else the account of the slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha.
In this case, one should perform both rites for Mahiṣāsura as well as for Madhu and Kaiṭabha, preceded by the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa).
Having invited the Brahmins with garments, ornaments, and seats, one should perform the inscription of the desired [mantra] and worship the book according to one's ability. (11.897)
The reciter should also read slowly, preceded by the clear pronunciation of each syllable;
it should be very distinct, neither too disjointed nor like a song with the head shaking. (11.898)
Neither swaying his body, nor laughing, nor weeping as he walked;
neither eating nor conversing with others, and likewise not cutting off [his speech] in the middle. || 11-899 ||
Having sipped water and performed purification, and wearing upper garments on his feet,
she who is the Mother of the World is pleased when one studies according to this rule.
And she becomes the bestower of the fruits as described, O beloved of life;
by this recitation, the Goddess, the Sovereign, shall quickly be pleased. (11.901)

Neither by extensive offerings of incense, lamps, garlands, unguents, and food oblations, nor even by reciting or teaching it, is there such [merit] as that which comes from the diligent study of this [work]. (11.902)
One who desires the satisfaction of Kālikā should perform the autumnal worship;
for indeed, this [worship] is constant within the Goddess’s autumnal rite.
In the same way, these two should be understood as the primary limbs of the fire-oblation (homa).
First, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit with clay and faith.
There, O Dear One, having established the fire with Vedic mantras, one should offer oblations of clarified butter, or else those mixed with sesame seeds. (11.905)
One should offer bilva leaves, barley, lotuses, or milk-rice mixed with honey;
the mantra to be employed therein is the sixteen-syllabled Bhāratī.

Alternatively, regarding the mantra of Jayadurgā which is well-established—the sixteen-syllabled Bhāratī—this is stated with reference to the specific context [of this work]. However, it should be understood that the Jayadurgā mantra is common to all [practitioners].
Likewise:
Likewise, the Goddess [is praised] by the Saptaśatī, or even by each individual verse. || 11-907 ||
In the case of a mantra, the number should be one thousand; in the case of a Śakti, it should be ten thousand.
In both instances, auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) must be given at the conclusion of the rite.
O Goddess, one should perform these two rites before the image;
nor should this pair be performed at night, except during the day. (11.909)
Whatever is performed in that [time] becomes fruitless according to the Vedic injunction;
however, the Goddess accepts the recitation of the Saptashati when it is performed according to the prescribed rules. (11.910)
Whether performed according to the prescribed rule or even without it, one offers the oblation again;
therefore, the oblation must be performed with great care during the autumnal worship.
Homa, the recitation of the Saptashati, the offering of bali, and the playing of musical instruments—
this quartet is recommended for the worship of Kālikā during the month of Āśvina.

And an abundant offering of oblations (bali) should be performed according to one's prosperity. Now, the procedure for the offering of oblations is as follows: then one should offer the living oblation (jīvabali), according to what is available and according to the prescribed rule.
Ritual procedure is said to be of two kinds: that which is Vedic and that which is Āgamic.
The Vedic is performed with mantras declared in the Śrutis, while the Āgamic is performed with mantras declared in the Tantras. (11.914)
Even that which is prescribed by the Śruti is offered according to the specific rules stated in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;
therein, moreover, there exists a further distinction based on the particular species of animal. (11.916)
In the Merutantra, it is stated:
"The *vali* is to be known as threefold: the Tantric, the Smārta, and the Vaidika.
Among these, first, the Tantric is recorded as being of eight kinds. (11.917)
The human, the buffalo, the boar, the goat, the sheep, the crane, the pigeon, and the cock—these are the [animals] in order of increasing commonality from the first to the last. || 11-918 ||
Likewise: Having wrapped a kūṣmāṇḍa gourd, a coconut, a bilva fruit, or even sugarcane in cloth, one should cut it with a knife or similar weapon. (11.919)
Thus has been declared the *smārta* bali offering for those who follow the *dharmaśāstras*.
Likewise: "One should offer the Vedic bali with boiled rice mixed with cooked mung beans. (11.920)
"Accompanied by *vaṭaka* offerings for the exceedingly fierce deity Sarocana"—thus it is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*.
This is the Vedic [rite], which is to be applied in the *śrutis* and prescribed for the sacrifices (*adhvara*). (11.921)
I shall explain everything pertaining to the scriptures that has come down through the sequence of sacrificial sites:
there is no such god, no such goddess, nor any such distinction among the classes of divine beings.
There is no time and no being, O beloved, that does not desire an offering;
nor do the formless entities—time, space, months, years, and seasons—exist [without it]. (11.923)
The fortnights, solstices, days and nights, lunar days, watches, and transits—even these desire an offering; how much more so the classes of divine beings?
Trees, herbs, creepers, shrubs, mountains, and so forth—both the immobile and the mobile—likewise manifest a desire for strength. (11.925)
For whatever deity whatever offering (bali) has been proclaimed, in this context, O Śivā, each one of those is now being described. (11.926)
The sacrificial offering for Svayambhū is a lion; for Viṣṇu, it is said to be a rhinoceros;
for Indra, it is declared to be a horse; and for Parameṣṭhin, it is a rhinoceros-beetle.

The author of the *Uktāvalī* states that, with reference to Viṣṇu and others, there is only the release (*utsarga*) of a *vārghrīṇasa* animal and so forth, and not an injunction for killing (*hiṃsā*).
The definition of a *vārghrīṇasa*, however, will be stated later.
Likewise:
A boar is dear to Bhairava, a jackal to the Pramathas,
a leopard to Brahmā, and a tiger is desired as an offering for Bali.
The bear is the animal of Gaṇādhyakṣa; the red deer is that of the Yakṣas;
the monitor lizard is that of Skanda; and the yak is also that of the Viśvedevas.
The sacrificial offering for the Vināyakas is said to be the black antelope;
for the Vetālas it is the buffalo, and for the Guhyakas it is the peacock.
Śalya is said to be the [portion] of Śacī; Rohiṣa is proclaimed as that of the Tuṣitas;
Kṛkalāśa belongs to the Dānavas, and Śyena is said to belong to the Daityas.
The eightfold offering (balis) of Hiraṇyagarbha is proclaimed;
the footprint of Īśāna is praised with hymns, and the Ruru [deer] is celebrated as belonging to Rudra.
Bali is my [vehicle], Gokarṇa is that of the Sādhyas, and likewise the Gavaya is that of the Bhāsuras; the Sṛmara is desired for the Vasus, and the Ṛkṣa is prescribed for them.
The Gavaya belongs to Bṛhaspati, and the elephant to Prajāpati; the Kuraṅga is said to belong to the Sādhyas, and the camel to Tvaṣṭṛ.
The bull is proclaimed as the representative of the Viśvedevas at the Śrāddha;
the bird Kuṭaru belongs to Agni, and the Cakravāka to Pracetas.
The parūṣṇa is for the gārhapatya fire, while the cīnaka is for the dakṣiṇāgni;
the camūru is declared for the āhavanīya, and the śaśa for Aryaman.
The crane belongs to Vāyu, the swan to Soma, and the Lava bird indeed to Candra;
likewise, the crocodile belongs to Varuṇa, and the Kulīyaka bird to Mitra. || 11-937 ||

The blue jay (cāṣa) is to be known as belonging to Agni and Soma; the curlew (krauñca) belongs to Indra and Agni; the water-hen (madgu) is for Mitra; and the wagtail (kulīka) indeed belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ. (11.938)
Likewise, O Īśvarī, the nyaṅku is for the Ādityas, the black antelope is for Yama,
and the two types of wild oxen (gomṛga) are the sacrificial offerings for Prajāpati and Vāyu.
The peacock is said to belong to the two Aśvins, while the jackal belongs to Pūṣan;
the donkey belongs to Nirṛti, and the pigeon to Mitra and Varuṇa. (11.940)
Godhā is the chief among the wives of the gods, as is Mālika of Savitṛ;
Kulīka is the foremost among those of divine birth, and Rājajña likewise among the Apsarases.
The yoktra is of the intermediate space, the rat of the earth, and the whip of the sky;
Balī is of the cardinal directions, and the mongoose is indeed of the intermediate directions.
The fish is the [essence] of the waters; the serpent named *homīya* is that of fire;
the water-snake is that of ordinary time; and likewise, the chameleon is that of [specific] time. (11.943)
The *suparṇa* and the *dātyūha* are the lords of the year and the month respectively;
the *kapiñjala* is the lord of the spring season, and the *kalaviṅka* is the lord of the summer.
Tittiri is to be known as the bird of the rains; likewise, the quail (varttikā) is that of autumn;
the krakara is of the winter season, and the vaikakari is of the cool season.

The *khañjarīṭa* bird represents the fortnight (*pakṣa*); the *sārasa* crane represents the solar transit (*ayana*); the *pārāvata* pigeon represents the day; and the *sīrāyu* bird is said to represent the night.
It is declared that for the *jalaukā* [sandhyā], for the *sandhyā*, for the *yajñarāja* lunar day, and for the watch (*yāma*), the *sukhilīka* [period] is that which follows the *saṃkrānti*. (11.947)
Kirīṭaka was the master of the planets and the target-shooter among the lunar mansions; Sākalya was the expert in the zodiacal signs, and Cuñcuṭa was the specialist in the ascendants. (11.948)
The Śiśumāra is the lord of the ocean and of rivers; Timiṅgila is the lord of whirlpools; Makara is the lord of waves; and Śaṅkha is likewise the lord of shells.
The camel is the deity of the netherworld (pātāla), while the stake (śaṅku) belongs to Tāṇḍava;
the frog is the deity of the rain-clouds (parjanya), and the creepers of the earth belong to the rain itself.
Sambūka was the son of Vidyut, Bhāradvāja of Aśani, and Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati were born in succession [from the other wives]. (11.95)
The śara, kaṅka, hārīta, and jīvañjīva birds are proclaimed [as suitable for offerings];
bali and kalañja are for the pretas, and the vaka bird is also for the piśācas.
The kurara bird is the foremost among spirits (bhūtas), the cock among the brahmarākṣasas, the cuckoo among the gandharvas, and the crow among the ghoṇakas. || 11.953 ||
The quail is for the guardians of the fields, and the cock is for the *vaṭukas*;
the *bhāruṇḍa* is said to be for as many [deities] as there are who carry away their [victims'] species.

The musk shrew (chucchundarī) is the offering for the Aśmanis; the śarabha is the offering for the waters; the cilla is the offering for the ḍākinīs; and the takṣaka is the offering for the kinnaras. || 11-955 ||
The bhūliṅga bird is the offering for the yoginīs; the ṭiṭṭibha bird is the offering for the treasures (nidhis).
Now I shall speak of the senses: the gnat is the offering for the two eyes. (11.956)
A bee is also [the deity] of the two ears, and likewise wasps of the nose;
Bali is the deity of the tongue, as are the *cikkā* and the fly; and Bali is the deity of the skin. (11.957)
The grasshopper is considered the offering for the mind, and the moth for speech;
the cricket is the offering for the two hands, and the firefly for the two feet.
The louse of the anus is designated as Samuddiṣṭā; Sinīpati is that of the generative organ.
Madhuka is the presiding deity of the trees, and Tailapāyikā is that of the creepers. (11.959)
Bedbugs are the [emanations] of medicinal herbs, young ants are those of trees; the sulphur-insect is that of shrubs, and likewise, those born from the earth are those of mountains. (11.960)
A corpse is the offering for Pūtanā; a snake is the offering for the Rākṣasīs;
a newborn infant is the offering for Ṣaṣṭhī; and a conch shell is the offering for Bālagraha. (11.961)
The *cakora* bird is the enemy of even Garuḍa; the *tailapāyikā* is the enemy of mothers; the boar is the enemy of the Vidyādharas; and the parrot is the enemy of sacrifices. (11.962)
The vulture was the tribute of Aruṇa, the kareṭuka animal that of Naraka; the monkey was the tribute of King Bali, and the flying bird that of Kāntāra. (11.963)
Buffaloes, goats, and other such animals are specifically prescribed as sacrificial offerings for all the gods alike.
Those born in water and those born on land, as well as those born in villages and those born in the forest—beasts, birds, insects, and indeed all creatures of the animal realm. || 11-965 ||
These have been ordained by the Creator as the sacrificial offerings for the dwellers of heaven;
the deities are not so pleased by other preparations of food offerings.
Just as it is for animals and likewise for birds, so indeed, O Goddess of Gods, is it even for the Mīmāṃsā and the Vedas. (11.967)
The term *devānāṃ priya* is said to be a synonym for "beast";
having understood this established conclusion for the sake of pleasing the Goddess, [one should proceed]. (11.968)
One should offer as sacrificial oblations even pure animals and birds;
likewise, all those classified as lower creatures, such as worms and insects. || 11.969 ||
"O beloved, they were not ordained by the Creator to be the sacrificial offerings for you, O Goddess;
one might indeed sacrifice a white bull in a rite named Gomedha. (11.970)
In the human sacrifice, he likewise offered a man; in the elephant-conquest, an elephant;
in the horse sacrifice, a horse; and at Śaṅkhacūḍa, an elephant.
Where even the Veda speaks thus, what need is there for further deliberation?
Therefore, O beloved, an offering (bali) is essential for the occasional worship.
It should be offered especially for the sake of pleasing the Goddess;
indeed, without the *bali* offering, the Goddess does not accept the worship at all.
In that regard, both the buffalo and the goat are praised; any other suitable sacrificial offering will suffice—what is the use of further deliberations? (11.974)
I shall now describe that contemplation by which Kālī is satisfied;
whatever animal species have been ordained for Guhyakālī— 11.975.
Whether they be wild or domestic, as well as the species of aquatic birds— I shall first describe those very types of birds to you.
Fish, deer, boars, tortoises, and likewise buffaloes; crocodiles, iguanas, water-monsters, tigers, and even lions. (11.977)
O beloved, there are also mongooses, śarabhas, gavayas, and goats; likewise, humans and birds, as well as their very sheaths. 11-978.
These have been designated as offerings by the Creator for the sake of the Blessed Lady;
by offering these oblations, one shall accomplish all undertakings. (11.979)

He states the fruits of making offerings: "Indeed, through offerings life is increased; through offerings disease is pacified; through offerings one conquers enemies; and through offerings wealth is obtained. (11.980)

One attains success through powerful offerings; with even more powerful ones, one shall go to the third heaven. When an offering is given by those free from desire, even liberation is attained, just as in a formal sacrifice.
He states the different species of fish and other animals: "Now I shall describe the different species; understand them in brief.
Fish are of eighteen kinds, and wild animals are of twenty-four kinds. (11.982)
Boars are said to be of five kinds, and tortoises also have three varieties;
buffaloes likewise have two types, and rhinoceroses are of four kinds. (11.983)
The *godhikā* is of three types, and the crocodile (*grāha*) is of two types;
the tiger and the lion are each of three types, and the mongoose (*nakula*) is also of two types. (11.984)
The śarabha is of a single species, O fair-faced one, and there is no division of it;
the gavaya is said to be of three kinds, and the chāga is considered to be of five kinds.
There are four kinds of humans and thirty-six species of birds;
O beloved, I shall now declare their names to you in order.
Śaṅkula, rohita, śāla, pāṭhina, and rāghava; proṣṭhī, nāla, śiśu, dhyāṅga, mereṭā, aṅguli, and ambaṭa. || 11-987 ||
The *timi*, *mākūṭa*, *rājīva*, and *gaḍaka* are esteemed species;
as are the *gokarṇa*, *kṛṣṇasāra*, *eṇa*, *ruru*, *nyaṅku*, and *camūra*. (11.988)
The priya, vāta, pramīcīna, samūha, sṛmara, and kraṣā;
the raṅku, śambara, kandali, sukharo, rohiṣa, and vaṭa. || 11-989 ||
The Kadalya, Viśālākṣa, Pataṅga, Ullāṭa, Rohita, Varāha, Stabdha, Kroḍa, Kuśākṣīṇa, Jalasvana—[these are the rivers]. || 11.990 ||
The tortoise is of three kinds: *citrī*, *citrakaṭa*, and *vāmana*;
the *akera* and *kṣīrila* are also considered, while the buffalo is regarded as being of two types.
The *kauñjara*, *vārila*, *carmī*, *vaiśa*, and *khaḍga* are the four kinds [of tortoises].
The *hiraṇyā*, *kilikā*, *mīnā*, and *godhikā* are considered to be the three kinds [of lizards]. (11.992)
The long-necked one, the leather-filled one, and the crocodile—these are the two types [of snakes].
The hyena, the *taruga*, and the variegated tiger are said to be the three types [of beasts]. (11.993)
The *śarala*, the *kṛkayu*, and the *medī*—even the lion—is considered to be of three kinds; likewise, the *sthūla* and the *kaliṅga*, as well as the *nakula*, are said to be of two kinds. (11.994)
Except for the *ekajāti*, no other *śarabha* is produced;
the *lāṭika*, the *viṭcara*, the *sāsni*, and the *gavaya* are likewise said to be of three kinds.
The *tripiva*, *pālita*, *kṣaurī*, *varkara*, and likewise the *māriṣa*—these are the five varieties of the goat (*chāga*). The sheep (*avi*) is also considered to be of three types. (11.996)
Listen also to me regarding the *ūrmika*, the *pāriśa*, and the *bheṭa* among human beings;
for within the commonality of being human, there does not exist a fourfold division. || 11-997 ||
Its diversity is conceived through the distinction of its modes;
[this occurs] for one who is favored by Caṇḍikā and is free from thirst within the ocean of existence. (11.998)

And for one who is eager to hear of the fruit consisting in the attainment of various worlds, there is a spontaneous inclination; may I become the form of the offering (bali) for that goddess. (11.999)
And having arrived in person, he says: "Appoint me as the sacrificial offering (bali), right before the eyes of everyone, and especially that of the king."
O Goddess, that one has been described; now attend to the second:
he who is a thief of much wealth, such as jewels and the like, and who is held in contempt by the world. (11.1001)
Having been determined in the midst of the assembly and proclaimed previously due to his past karma,
O Goddess, he is called the second because he is to be beheaded.
An enemy who has been defeated in battle and held captive, appearing as a warrior but fighting with deceit—this is designated as the third; now understand the fourth. (11.1003)
He who is an assassin of travelers, whether in the wilderness or at home, and who is known and established as such by truthful witnesses; ||| 11-1004 ||
For that is declared to be the fourth; a fifth is not possible. (p. 1058) I shall now describe the birds which have been designated as offerings for the Goddess. 11-1005.
Pigeons, red-crested cocks, swans, vārdhrīṇasa birds, owls, iron-backed birds, sarvāghāṭas, and cranes; || 11.1006 ||
Kalaviṅkas, cakoras, cakravākas, and parrots as well; śatapatras, bharadvājas, bhūliṅgas, and sparrows likewise. || 11-1007 ||
Kāraṇḍavas, cakravākas, pāruṣṇas, and kulīyakas; also plavas, kuṭaravas, varttakas, and kukkubhas as well. || 11-1008 ||
The *tittiri*, *uru*, *krauñca*, the nine types of *cāṣa* and *śikhaṇḍin*, the *yoktra*, *dātyūha*, *sākalya*, *paiṅgarāja*, and *vāyaka*. (11.1009)
The *jihvika*, *sukhilika*, *mudgu*, *harita-varttaka*, *jihvin-jiva*, *harita*, *koyasthi*, *asmat*, and *titibha* birds; || 11-1010 ||
Crows, cuckoos, vultures, kareṭus, unakas, khanjanas, cirīkas, jahikas, sīcāpuñjantas, and ekalas; || 11-1011 ||
The Kaśās, Suparṇas, Bhāruṇḍas, and also the Hāmāyas, O Pārvatī—all these sixty varieties of birds have thus been described to you. || 11-012 ||
No other birds are mentioned here as being suitable offerings for the Goddess;
however, the various distinctions among these species are found in the *Ḍāmara* and other texts.
Because they are numerous, they are not mentioned here for fear of making the text too voluminous:
the Kapotabhrāmakas, the Vaṅkamanitthas, the Turukas, and so forth. (11.1014)
The pigeons are of ten kinds, and likewise the swans are of five types:
the royal swans (rājahaṃsa), those called mallikā, the dhārtarāṣṭras, and the parisphuṭas. || 11-1015 ||
The Māheyas and other such beings of mixed birth should be understood in this same way.
Likewise, I shall now fully explain by which specific [deities] one becomes powerful. || 11-1016 ||
Throughout whatever period Kālikā remains satisfied, Caṇḍikā likewise [remains so] with eighteen kinds of fish and tortoises. (11.1017)
For indeed, by means of an offering consisting of a cock, or even a swan or a crane, one is satisfied for the duration of a month. (11.1018)
She becomes satisfied for two months by the flesh of the leopard and the jackal;
she would be satisfied for four months by the flesh of the kalaviṅka bird and the owl. (11.1019)
For five months she shall be satisfied even with parrots and pigeons;
for six months she shall obtain satisfaction from woodpeckers and cakora birds.
She is satisfied for seven months by *jihīka* and *kulīyaka* fish,
as well as by the twenty-four varieties of *kuraṅga* and *gavaya* antelopes.
The goddess shall be satisfied for eight months by [offerings of] mangoes, for nine months even by cuckoos,
and she is satisfied for ten months by the offering of a green parrot.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, by the offering of gallinules and lordly elephants, the auspicious Goddess, the bestower of perfection, attains satisfaction for eleven months. (11.1023)
By the offering of a lizard as a sacrificial gift, one remains satisfied for a year;
likewise, by the offering of a mongoose or even a rat, one shall remain satisfied for three years.
She may be satisfied for five years by a goat or even by a strong bull;
she is satisfied for eight years by a *jīvañjīva* bird offered in a row of five.
With the meat of the spotted deer and the meat of the powerful boar, Kālikā remains satisfied for a period of twelve years. (11.1026)
The goddess is pleased for twenty-five years by the gift of that bird named Hāmāya, which has the form of a lion and is reddish-brown. (11.1027)
By means of three kinds of tigers, two kinds of buffaloes,
and likewise four kinds of rhinoceroses, offered as sacrificial oblations (bali), || 11-1028 ||
For as long as a hundred years, Caṇḍikā enjoys satisfaction;
however, a single *vārdhrīṇasa* goat is proclaimed to be a special offering.
Another, belonging to the species of birds, dwelt at the foot of the Himavat;
he was old, possessed a beard, was white, had cracked feet, and was devoid of sense faculties.
The *raktarāsana* is of three kinds: the *niḥśṛṅga*, the *svarabhaṅgyaja*, and the one with a yellow beak, red veins, white wings, and black feet. (11.1031)
The blue-necked bird, or the vārdhrīṇasa with a pale-red throat; (also in the Kālikāpurāṇa: "One who drinks from three [streams], whose senses are decayed, white, aged, unborn, and supreme. (11.1032)
One should recognize the *vārdhrīṇasa* as prepared for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*);
it has a blue neck, a red head, black feet, and white wings. (11.1033)
That bird is the *vārdhrīṇasa*; it is dear even to me and Viṣṇu.
(In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
"By means of goats and *vārdhrīṇasas*, [the deity] shall be satisfied for thirty years. (11.1034)
When she is worshipped as the power (*śakti*) by means of the hair-ends of those who have no marks (*niraṅka*), that Guhyakālī becomes satisfied for five hundred years. (11.1035)
When offered with śarabhas, lions, and blood produced from one's own body,
Kālī is satisfied for a thousand years.
O beloved, by the ritual procedure involving the offering of a *vārdhrīṇasa* bird,
the Mother of the World remains satisfied for twelve thousand years.
In the form of a powerful thief or assassin,
she remained as a Guhyakālī for three hundred thousand years for the sake of his pleasure.
p. 1061) These, O Goddess, have been declared to you as the offerings for the purpose of satisfaction.
Now, regarding the prohibited offerings, it is said in that same place:
"I shall now describe those animals and even birds that must not be given. (11.1039)
Bears, monkeys, jackals, snakes, otters, as well as dogs, camels, wild asses, porcupines, and village-pigs; || 11.1040 ||
Among aquatic creatures as well, there were frogs, donkeys, porpoises, crabs,
long-backed fish, and many other kinds of fish in great numbers.
Among birds, there are crows, blue jays, durvidas, and also kulikas;
in this same way, others as well are to be understood from various scriptures and traditions.
Likewise, I shall describe certain things that are prohibited even among the prescribed offerings: namely, the domestic and wild animals, as well as the beasts and birds. (11.1043)
The practitioner should never employ a woman in the rite of the offering;
having given the offering with prior knowledge [of her identity], he falls into hell. (11.1044)
Even if one has committed some slight sin through ignorance, one still incurs its consequence;
however, one should not offer an animal born within the last three months.
One should never offer to the Goddess a bird that is smaller than half that size, nor one with broken horns, broken teeth, or a severed tail. (11.1046)
One who is one-eyed, deformed, diseased, or likewise pierced by a horn;
one who is wicked, with fallen hair, a milk-drinker, or with a drooping beard. (11.1047)
One should not offer such an animal, nor likewise one that is flightless—such as one with a severed beak, severed wings, broken limbs, or deprived of food. (11.1048)
One should not give away a domestic animal or a bird that is either unable to fly or is situated upon its mother's lap, even if they have been prepared for sacrifice.
In another tantra:
"If a sacrificial offering (*bali*) is black in color but has a white tail, the wise man should avoid such a goat from afar. (11.1050)
Thus, a wise person should always avoid one that is white with a black tail.
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
That which is prohibited for each specific [person] is now being described. 11-1051.
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, offer human beings, lions, tigers, blue jays, or wagtails, nor his own blood or wine.
Having given away two birds, as well as a lion, a leopard, and likewise a human being,
a sick person becomes short-lived and experiences hell.
A twice-born man incurs self-destruction by giving his own blood;
by giving liquor to the Goddess, a twice-born man becomes fallen from the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Deprived of all ritual duties, he attains the status of a Cāṇḍāla;
nor, O lord of men, should a king bestow the skin of a black antelope or a peacock feather.
O Goddess, O Sovereign, the second caste who gives a black antelope skin to the Goddess incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and is excluded from all ritual acts. (11.1056)
Vaiśyas must not give a pig, nor a quail, nor a kulīyaka;
for those who give these, at that very moment, the state of a great sinner (mahāpātaka) shall arise.
A Śūdra who gives another skin—such as that of a lizard, a parrot, or a rhinoceros—as well as the skin of a rat, a cat, or a blue jay, falls into a low state. (11.1058)

For those who give out of delusion or through force, the state of being a slayer of a Brahmin occurs instantly; yet this applies except for one devoted to compassion, whether he be a forest-dweller, a student, or a householder. (11.1059)
One who is sattvic, established in Brahman, and free from violence—
by him they should not offer an animal sacrifice, even if they are practicing according to the secondary rule.

It was stated previously that even in the case of a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*), only one who is qualified for the primary rite (*mukhya*) is entitled to perform it. The rule regarding the secondary alternative is stated in that very place as follows:
"A person of sattvic nature (*sāttvika*) must never, under any circumstances, commit the killing of a living being."
As well as sugarcane, pumpkin, and wild fruits and the like. || 11-1061 ||
Having fashioned an animal out of balls of milk and rice powder, one should perform the bali offering;
according to the specific fruit desired, one should bring forth that particular animal.
Likewise:
one should offer a *kuṣmāṇḍa* pumpkin as a buffalo, a *karkaṭī* gourd as a goat, a *vṛntāka* eggplant as a cock, and a *tumbikā* melon as a ram. (11.1063)

In the Kali age, the *rambhā* flower becomes the seed-vessel (*bījapūra*), and the *piṇḍa* becomes the *jīva*; through human existence it becomes the *panasa* fruit, and through the state of a fish it becomes the sugarcane stalk.
One should regard *śūraṇa* as Śambara, likewise *kośātaka* as Mṛga, *pāyasa* as an elephant, and *kulittha* as a cat. (11.1065)
O Maheśānī, the paṭola fruit represents the state of a boar, likewise the sugar-cane and sand represent the state of a rhinoceros, and the plantain fruit represents the state of a fish.
O Supreme Goddess, one should prepare a radish for the state of a mouse, a kaliñjaka for the state of a deer, and a coconut for the state of an elephant. (11.1067)

O fair-faced one, for the sake of obtaining the respective fruits for those who offer various animals, all types of beans (māṣa) are used as the sacrificial offering (bali), surpassing even the kṛśara-rice for everyone.
With ghee, wheat, sugarcane products, molasses, and likewise with foods derived from grains; || 11.1068 ||
"Having sacrificed such and such an animal, they shall obtain such and such a fruit.
Now, the characteristics of a praiseworthy animal (in the *Ratnāvalī*): "One with upright horns, long ears, of a single color, and very fat..."
Free from disease, with a nourished body, full of pride, and endowed with great strength. || 11-1069 ||
Neither possessing extra limbs nor lacking any limbs, and being one, two, three, or more years of age—such a praiseworthy animal is auspicious and brings delight to the Goddess. (11.1070)
In another tantra:
"If a black-colored goat has a white backbone, one should know that it is auspicious; one should avoid the opposite. (11.1071)
"Contrary" means white in color; the meaning is that it is blue on the surface of its back. (In the *Traipurapaddhati*):
"At the conclusion of the offering, O Goddess of the Gods, [present] the goat-offering as well as the ram."
One should offer [it] at all times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
In rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for a specific desire, one should offer an oblation of buffalo meat for the sake of victory,
for the fulfillment of all desires, and for the attainment of success in the world of the Goddess.
(In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"O Goddess, wherever there is an abundance of animals according to one's wealth, there one [animal] should first be chosen, endowed with all auspicious characteristics. (11.1074)
One should release an animal that is vigorous, beautiful, and strong. Likewise,
for all animals here, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is performed in exactly this same manner.
There is a specific distinction regarding the fruit in the general rite when invoking the gods and so forth.
(In the *Traipurapaddhati*):
Having bathed the sacrificial animal (*paśu*), which is endowed with all auspicious marks, according to the mantra... 11-1076.
Having placed it before the Goddess, one should then sprinkle it with argha water;
then, having protected it with the Astra mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca mantra.
Having recited the root mantra and consecrated [the offering] with the nectar of the *dhenumudrā*,
one should properly worship it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other ritual services.
One should recite this mantra for the liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu-pāśa) into his ear:
*Oṃ paśupāśāya vighnahre viprakarṇāya dhīmahi, tanno jīvaḥ pracodayāt.* This is declared to be the Gāyatrī that liberates one from the bonds of the bound soul. (11.1079)
One should recite this into the right ear for the sake of achieving his liberation. One should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with the root mantra itself;
one should sprinkle him three times with the pure water from the *argha* vessel using the root mantra. (11.1080)
Thus it is stated in the *Mahākāla-ukti*.
Another version is mentioned in that same work:
"We know the form of the offering (*bali*) as ending in the letter *ṅa*, derived from the seed-syllable of the Yoginīs."
Then, as before, one should meditate upon "the beloved of the Goddess" (devīpriyam), followed by "dhīmahi."
Having said, "That [is] our animal," he should then say, "May it impel [us]. Thus [it is taught].
The seed-syllable of the Yoginī is *chrīṃ* (according to the *Traipurapaddhati*).
Then, the practitioner of mantras should worship the sword on the right with this mantra:
one should write the *Tāra* (oṃ), Bhuvaneśvarī, and a pair of Kālīs. (11.1090)
Following the station of Vajreśvarī, then Lohadaṃṣṭrā, ending in the feminine suffix -ī;
this mantra is considered to consist of nine syllables, with the heart-mantra [Oṃ] and the pair of Vasus (eight). (11.1091)
With these [substances], such as perfumes and flowers, the wise one should worship the sword;
then, in its hilt, middle, and tip, respectively.
With perfumes, flowers, and consecrated rice, the mantra-practitioner should worship the triad of couples:
Brahmā together with Vāgīśī, and likewise Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
And Umā and Maheśvara—thus is the triad of couples proclaimed.
Thereafter, one should consecrate that sword with this mantra: || 11-1094 ||
O Lord of the Sword, you who are intent upon the destruction of the asura Khaḍga and the accomplishment of that task, may the sacrificial animal be swiftly slain by you; salutations be unto you!

Then, taking the kuśa grass, unbroken rice, water, and so forth contained in a copper vessel, and having recited the root mantra and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should release the sacrificial animal. || 11.1096 ||
Having taken unbroken rice grains, water, and other items, he should cast them upon the head of the sacrificial animal;
then, with that very sword and the root mantra, the practitioner [should proceed].
One should perform the severance of the sacrificial animal while personally recollecting the Goddess;
when one has been seized, one may move the limbs as one desires. (From the *Merutantra* and the *Siddhāntasāra*) 11.1098.
As long as one does not move the body, the animal is not killed;
having turned toward the north, one should likewise offer the oblation facing the east.
Having gazed [at him], the practitioner should thereafter utter this mantra:
"O beast, you have appeared before me by my good fortune in the form of a sacrificial offering."
I bow, therefore, to Him who possesses all forms and who takes the form of Bali;
who, through the gift that pleases Caṇḍikā, brings about the destruction of the donor's calamities.
Salutations again and again to you, O Bala, who are the sacrificial offering for Cāmuṇḍā!
For the sake of sacrifice, animals were created by Svayambhū himself.
Therefore, I cause you to be slain today; thus, in this sacrifice, killing is no killing. Having cast off this body, you shall assume a divine form.
Rejoice together with the first [Indras] as long as there are fourteen Indras,
by means of the mantra "Ai Hrīḥ Śrīḥ," you who are the sacrificial offering (bali) in my own form.
Having reflected thus, one should place a flower upon his head while holding the breath (*kumbhaka*).
(From the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
O fair-faced one, having first taken up a flower, one should meditate upon it as a sword. (11.1105)
He was dark-complexioned, with the Pināka bow in hand, appearing like the Night of Destruction (Kālarātri);
he was fierce, with a red face and eyes, adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Wearing red garments, holding a noose in his hand, and accompanied by his family, he was drinking blood and eating a mass of raw flesh. (11.1107)
Agitating the entire world by means of the movement of earthquakes and other such phenomena,
he is surrounded on his left and right sides by Death and Time.
In another tantra:

"Then the mantra-knower, the practitioner, should worship the sword with offerings such as water for the feet (pādya), and with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, using this mantra. (11.1109)
The mantra, however, is the one previously mentioned. (In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he should indeed recite the mantra while gazing at the sword.
And you, Rasanā, are the embellisher of the world of the gods for Caṇḍikā.
"Drink the blood of this sacrificial animal and eat its mass of flesh! Cut down this enemy of mine as you have cut him; grant me auspicious blessings! (11.1111)
"O you who are intoxicated by the blood of Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, obeisance be to you!
Having thus addressed the sword while reciting these eight names of its own, [one should worship it].
One should seize a sharpened sword by which death may be instantaneous;
[for] the sword is a slayer, a blade, keen-edged, and difficult to approach. (11.1113)
O Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and Dharmapāla, homage be to you!
Reciting the mantra "Ā HŪṂ PHAṬ," one should cut the sacrificial offering (bali). (From the Merutantra)
With a single blow alone, it was severed for the satisfaction of the deity.
(Also in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
One should cut with the Candrahāsa sword in a single stroke;
one should perform the striking while standing, never while seated. (11.1115)
(Kālikāpurāṇa) 11.116: Cutting with a *candrahāsa* sword or a razor is said to be the primary [method];
cutting with a sickle, a small knife, a saw, or a *śaṅkulā* is middling.

The small dagger (asidhenu), the short sword (svalpakhadga), the spearhead (śaṅkulā), the discus (cakra), the scissors (kartarī), the razor (kṣura), the crescent-headed arrow (kṣurapra), and the broad-headed arrow (bhalla) are proclaimed as the middle [weapons]. (11.1117)
The *bali* offering must never be cut with anything other than these, such as spears or arrows;
for the Goddess does not eat that *bali*, and the giver shall meet his death.
If a practitioner cuts an animal or a bird with his hand instead of performing the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa),
he incurs the unbearable sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having consecrated the sword, the wise practitioner should employ it as an offering.
In that regard: "Of all [weapons], the Candrahāsa sword is the most excellent and brings happiness. (11.1120)
It should be made fifty finger-breadths long, or perhaps three spans (tāla);
it may be shaped like a karavīra petal or have the form of a lotus petal.

Alternatively, one should pierce [the target] with the Kubjakhaḍga or the Daṇḍakhaḍga [mantras], even when thousands, tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands of offerings are available. (From the Mahākālasaṃhitā) 11.1122.
Two, three, five, eight, ten, or even twelve; one should not make more than these, established as deities through the state of being (bhāva). || 11-1123 ||
Facing the eastern direction, the best of preceptors should simultaneously utter the mantra; by means of this single ritual formula (tantra), he should sprinkle all the offerings.
O lotus-faced one, many more cuttings should also be made:
those of the Haridvipa, the goat, the jivajivaka bird, the crane, the buffalo, and the sky-goer.
One should give these, as well as various drinks, on the left side.
"Urabhro" means a ram. Likewise:
Fish, crocodiles, hares, rhinoceroses, tortoises, and porcupines; || 11.1126 ||
Indeed, one should offer as many varieties of animals as possible directly before [the deity];
according to the *Śrīkramasaṃhitā*, one should diligently offer that sacrificial oblation (*bali*) and must not kill them oneself. (11.1127)
If one should kill [an animal] through negligence, one will go to the Raurava hell.
Even Mahākāla,
having slain a sacrificial animal with his own hand, would attain the state of a beast.
In another tantra:
"Whether it be oneself, a brother's son, a brother, or even a friend—if one whose inner organ (antahkarana) is pure, even a sapinda may perform the severance. (11.1129)
"One should not employ an enemy, nor one who is deficient in limbs, nor one who is one-eyed, nor even one who is hunchbacked, in the work of cutting the enemy's forces"— so it has been said.
A specific detail regarding the offering of a buffalo sacrifice has been stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*;
I shall now describe that particular point which is additional [to what has been said] concerning the buffalo. (11.130)
Then one should worship all the deities in their respective limbs with flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
using words beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namaḥ," as well as words ending in the ṅa-pratyaya in the center.
I shall describe to you in due order the locations and the deities as well:
in the aperture of Brahmā, in the nose, in the two ears, and likewise in the tongue.
In the two eyes and the face, then on the forehead, on the right cheek, on the left cheek, on the neck, and indeed on the hair. (11.1133)

and on the lower lip, on the shoulder, on the heart, and indeed on the back. (11.1134)
In the belly, the feet, the tail, and indeed throughout the entire body, there is Brahmā, as well as the earth, space, and that which faces in every direction. (11.1135)
The luminaries, Viṣṇu, Candra, Śakra, Vahni, Maheśvara, Nirṛti, Mitra, Varuṇa, as well as Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī. || 11-1136 ||
Dhaneśvara, the King of Serpents, Āditya, and Sādhya;

In this very manner, one should also worship a human being;

In former times, the son of the Asura Rambhā, deluded by pride, assumed your form and engaged in battle with the Blessed Lady.

therefore, O Bhṛṅgura, you now carry Caṇḍikā upon your head."
There is no other offering besides you that so greatly pleases the Goddess;

Regarding the human sacrifice, he states a distinction:

not shedding tears, free from arrogance, neither dejected nor with face cast down. (11.1145)

First, one should sprinkle [the victim] in the form common to all sacrificial animals;

Among all living beings, you are established as the most excellent, being human; O fortunate one, best of the strong, you are endowed with the splendor of a divine embryo.
Protect me from all fears; grant me supreme accomplishment. Grant me sovereignty, grant me glory, and grant me the unsurpassed state.
Health and long life, increase of progeny, victory in battle, auspiciousness, abundant enjoyments, and even wives desired from the heart. (11.1150)
Having bestowed firm devotion toward Kātyāyanī and even greater, stable prosperity,

Go quickly to the world of the gods, together with your kinsmen, children, and relatives,

Go to that place which cannot be reached by worldly beings, O bull among men;
you have been claimed by Mahākālī through her desire for flesh and blood.
"Having gone quickly, may you attain the world of the goddesses, which is so difficult to reach;
having gone there, O Lord of the World, meditate upon Śiva, who is mine. (11.1154)
"O Goddess, by your grace, such a desirable course for the world of gods shall be yours;
and by your grace, may I conquer my enemies at the forefront of battle. (11.1155)
"O Goddess, one should recite these eight verses at the moment of offering the human *bali*.
Furthermore, a specific rule regarding the *gaṇḍaka* is stated in that very same place:
'I shall fully declare the mantra of the sword (*khaḍga*), by which the *gaṇḍaka* is given. (11.1156)
O sword, whose body is indestructible by weapons, when you take the form of a two-footed being,
may the ancestors and even the gods be satisfied by your flesh.
And there is no one more pure than you upon the surface of the earth;
skull-cups from your hand are recommended for use in the rite of *śrāddha*. (11.1158)
"Today you have been offered by me as an oblation to the Goddess;
having dispelled my obstacles, immediately become one among the host of the Goddess.

Having thus slain the sacrificial animals, he likewise [drank] their blood immediately.
One should take the warm, frothy [liquid] in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
(From the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Oṃ hrīḥ aiḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ! May Kauśikī be nourished by this blood. Thus.
One should place the red [substance] in a vessel and apply it as a lamp upon the head.
(In the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*):
Now I shall describe the vessels in which blood is to be placed;
the King should take up the blood in one made of gold, silver, or copper. (11.161)
By feudal lords and provincial governors, it should be made of copper, bell-metal, or brass;
and by poor householders, it may be made of clay or wood.
Alternatively, one should never [perform it] in a leaf-cup, nor in iron, nor in tin,
nor in lead, nor even on the rind of a coconut fruit.
Among all the vessels of the Kaulas, the skull-cup (kapāla) is held to be the most excellent.
The satisfaction that is said to arise from the flesh of these bound souls (paśus) [is attained through it]. || 11-1163 ||
O beloved, even with blood, the satisfaction of the Blessed Lady Kātyāyanī is likewise great during her constant or occasional worship.
One should never offer raw meat, blood, or even the flesh of an animal, a bird, or especially a human, without first performing the *bali* offering. (11.1165)
Now, regarding the result of the head falling, it is stated in that very same place:

"Having thus offered the oblation to the Goddess according to the procedure for giving an offering, one should discern the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of both the kingdom and the king. (11.1166)
If it falls upon the head in the direction of Vāyu, or in the south-west, or even in the south, one should predict loss in this case. (11.1167)
Listen now to the results in all the remaining directions and intermediate points:
if the head falls in the eastern or northern quarter, [the following occurs].
One should know that this knowledge brings all prosperity; the king shall declare it as the attainment of sovereignty when the head, having whirled around, falls indeed upon the right ear.
Then, at the end of the month, there will be success; however, misfortune shall arise in the left ear.
There will be loss before the king, but for householders, it will be auspicious.
If the head falls in the northeast or in the center,
or if a severed head is seen fallen along with its face, [it portends misfortune].
One should recognize his sovereign power; the king shall then designate him as ruler.
Then, in a short time, all success will certainly be attained.
Success occurs on the first occasion; on the second, it is said there is loss.
This should be understood for householders, but for kings, it is the reverse.
When tears are seen in the eyes, one should then predict loss;
when the sound of teeth grinding is heard at any time, [the same is indicated]. (11.1174)
At that time, one should declare death and the destruction of knowledge in all cases.
(In the *Traipurapaddhati*:
Success occurs when it falls to the right, while the left side is censured. (11.1175)
When the cutting [of the blade] falls on the left, the wise one should recollect the mantra of the Goddess;
then, having offered oblations into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth with fifteen offerings, [he should proceed]. || 11.1176 ||
One should pacify the defect indicated by the sound "dhūṅ" as characterized by the signs of the *bali* offering.
According to the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, the practitioner of mantra should personally offer the head of the *bali* in the direction of the Rākṣasas. (11.1177)
To the south of that, one should not join a red vessel upside down;
having placed it facing the deity, one should arrange the severed portion.
One should know that very [offering] to be the best; that which has been described is the middling.
This is the designation for the offerings (*bali*); one should place the head in front.
Likewise: One should not place the head on the ground, nor should it be inverted; one should present the head with its blood facing forward, and not otherwise. (11.1180)
At the time of taking the blood, however, one should place a little rock salt and exactly one fruit in a vessel obtained according to one's own means.
That blood shall indeed be the oblation, and that head the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa);
for, having cut off the nose, neck, cheeks, tail, and flesh [from the body]. (11.1182)
Having thrown it into the mouths of the animals, one should then place it before them;

O lotus-eyed one, one should also place [the offering] on the head of the one who moves like a beast;
one should place a lamp and an incense wick upon the heads of the bali-offerings.
The fragrance that arises from the burning of body hair and nails—the Goddess Caṇḍikā smells it, and she becomes truly satisfied. (11.1185)
At that very moment, O Goddess, one who is intent on devotion should increase the offering of incense and lamps according to one's means. (11.1186)
Furthermore, when there is an excess of strength, rows of letters representing the head should be arranged accordingly,
accompanied by incense and lamps, as well as heaps of flowers and unbroken grains.
Likewise, one should place the head facing forward, provided with a lamp and devoid of a vessel; and it should be anointed with clarified butter or sprinkled with sesame oil. || 11-1188 ||
One should not offer mustard oil, nor that produced from other fruits;
one who has been consecrated with the head-anointing (mūrdhābhiṣikta) and possesses many accomplishments [should use] ghee or oil. (11.1189)
One encounters disease, grief, and death arising from seeds other than one's own; therefore, men should act with such diligence that even a single hair is not burned. 11-1190.
In another tantra: "One should provide a wick made of thread; a wick made of cloth is highly praised.
Its thickness should be the measure of a thumb, and its length should be six finger-breadths. (11.1191)
One should provide twenty-one threads made of cotton;
one should prepare that with fragrant substances such as camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
O Śivā, one should not cause a lamp to be offered for crocodiles, turtles, and especially for monitor lizards, nor for fish or birds.
For as long as the lamp burning above the head continues to burn, for that long one shall dwell in heaven; therefore, one should cause it to be offered with great effort.
Having smelled the fragrance arising from the burning of hair, the Goddess becomes pleased;
therefore, one should increase the lamp, and for that reason, one should avoid [using] a vessel.

One attains death in Nirvana when the lamp is being offered (from the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*). Then, having placed the vessel before the Goddess, [one offers] the blood of the sacrificial animal. (11.1197)
One should administer great clarified butter three times with sugar and dūrvā grass;
likewise, rock salt, ginger, and plantain fruit. (11.1198)
The practitioner, aiming for the fulfillment of his desires, should cast [the offerings] of sweet substances;
he should divide the directions into eight parts and place one in the center with kuśa grass and other materials.
Having offered some ghee there, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the *tarpaṇa-mudrā*;
the libation for the goddesses who partake of their shares should indeed be performed twice each.

At the beginning and the end are *tāra* (oṃ) and *hārda* (namaḥ); in the middle is the first mantra as well, conjoined with the words "I satisfy [the deity] by name" according to each respective name. (11–1201)

The second form ends in the suffix -ṅ, and that which is uttered as the second word is situated in the middle; the ritual action resides in the seat like a vessel called Śrī, which is eternally manifest.
Cāmuṇḍā is in the eastern direction, while Yoginī is in the southern;
