Vidārikā is in the southeast, Pāparākṣasī in the southwest,
Pūtanā in the northwest, and likewise Kālikā in the northeast.
Then, with palms joined in reverence before her, one should offer praise:
"Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World! Victory to you, O Dispeller of the Multitude of Sins! (11-1205)
Victory to you, who appear like a forest fire to the grass of birth, old age, and disease!
Victory to the destroyer of all calamities! Victory to you, who are worshipped by the gods!
Victory to you whose form is eternal bliss! Victory to you, the bestower of auspiciousness!
Victory to you, the destroyer of enemies! Victory to you, the eradicator of disease!
Victory to you, O Bhīmā! Victory, O Aghorā! Victory, O Deliverer from Peril!
Victory to you, whose fierce grasp is swollen with the savor of the essence of nectar!
O three-eyed one with a terrifying face, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
you who cause the destruction of all asuras and wield the sword and the khaṭvāṅga staff!
O Greatly Terrible One, O Loudly Roaring One, O Destroyer of the Pride of the Daityas, O Goddess Kālarātri, having accepted this animal offering! (11–1210)
Be pleased, O Mahācaṇḍā; protect me who have come to you for refuge.
Grant me long life, grant me wealth, and grant me fortune and fame.
"Grant me a wife, grant me sons, and grant me all my desires!
O Ugracaṇḍā, you are Pracaṇḍā, the fiercely powerful one with the mane of a lion! (11–1212)
O Goddess of the Universe, whose arms are great, fierce, and formidable, salutations be unto you!
Protect me, who have come for refuge and have offered my mind at your feet.
Remove evil, remove affliction, remove sorrow, remove unhappiness;
remove disease, remove agitation, remove wretchedness, O Beloved! (11-1214)
Having recited this hymn of praise in this manner, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff, [saying]:
"O Guhyakālī, O Mother of the World, O Sovereign who dwells within all! (11-1215)
Having accepted this animal offering, grant the fruits as previously described;
through body, mind, and speech, I have no other refuge but you.
"You move within all beings; you are the Seer, O Supreme Goddess. (In the *Yāmala*:
O Kātyāyanī, O Great Illusion, O Durgā, who delivers one from misfortune! (11-1217)
"Salutations to you, O Sustainer of the World, whose nature is that of Kālarātri.
Having thus praised the Great Goddess and offered handfuls of beautiful flowers, [he spoke].
One should prostrate on the ground with eight limbs and a mind imbued with devotion.

Regarding the plural form "sumano'ñjalīn" (handfuls of flowers), according to the *kapiñjalādhikaraṇa* principle, it is restricted to the number three. Thus, the meaning is that one should prostrate after offering three handfuls of flowers.
This concludes the procedure for the offering of oblations (*balidāna*).
Now, regarding the presiding deities of domestic animals, birds, and other objects (from the Mahākālasaṃhitā): "Of animals, birds, and other things as well... (11-1219).
(1078) I shall declare all the deities in their proper order for the rite of release:
the elephant is said to have Prajāpati as its deity, and the horse has Yama as its deity. || 11-1220 ||
Likewise, all single-hoofed animals are said to have Yama as their presiding deity;
the buffalo is likewise associated with Yama, while the camel is considered to belong to Nirṛti.
The two bulls have Rudra as their presiding deity; the goat is said to belong to Agni;
the ram is to be known as belonging to Varuṇa; and the boar is considered to belong to Viṣṇu.
The two goddesses Gaurī and Devī, the tiger and the lion, and the Gaṇḍaka are presided over by Brahmā;
however many species of deer there may be, they are said to have Vāyu as their deity.
All birds whatsoever are proclaimed to belong to Vāyu;
likewise, fish belong to Prajāpati, and tortoises have the Sādhyas as their deity.
The iguana has Varuṇa as its presiding deity, and crocodiles are likewise;
similarly, the mongoose and the locust have Āditya and Īśāna as their presiding deities.
A maiden, a male slave, and likewise a female slave belong to Prajāpati;
human beings have Abhaya as their deity; the earth has Viṣṇu as its deity.
Likewise, gems, pearls, and so forth have the ocean as their presiding deity;
likewise, all reservoirs of water, water-jars, and water-pots [have the same].
The water-drawer, the pitcher, and the small water-jar are to be known as having Varuṇa as their deity;
gold has Agni as its deity, and iron has Bhairava as its deity.
Pūṣan and the two Aśvins are proclaimed as the deities of bell-metal (kāṃsya);
the stage (raṅga) has the Nāsatyas as its deity, and lead (sīsaka) has Vāyu as its deity.
Copper has the Sun as its presiding deity; brass has Mars as its presiding deity;
silver has the Moon as its presiding deity; and the earthenware bowl has the ancestors as its presiding deity.
p. 1079) Molasses has Kuvera as its presiding deity, while sugar has Mitra as its presiding deity.
However, elsewhere it is stated: "In molasses, the waters (Āpas) are the deities."
Likewise: Jāṅgala has Agni as its deity; honey has Yama as its deity. (11.1230)
The deity of betel is to be known as Śakra or a Vidyādhara; as stated in another tantra:
"In betel, the deities are Śakra, the Vidyādharas, and Vināyakas. (11-1231)
Mahākāla;
likewise, the goddess Mṛtyuñjaya is established in clarified butter (ghṛta).
Oil has Rāhu as its presiding deity, and cotton has Ketu as its presiding deity. || 11-1232 ||
Milk has Tārā as its presiding deity, and curd has the medicinal herbs (oṣadhi) as its presiding deity.
However, elsewhere it is stated: "Nārāyaṇa is declared to be in milk, and the serpents are proclaimed to be in curd."
Likewise, O Pārvatī, ground sindūra dedicated to the deity Śacī [should also be used]. || 11-1233 ||
In another tantra: "In all other [tantras], the deities are various; in the Piṣṭa [tantra], the deity is Prajāpati Mahākāla."
Salt has the ocean as its presiding deity, and water has Varuṇa as its presiding deity.

The deity of the *smara* flower is Smara; the deity of the *gandharva* flower is Gandharva; the deity of the *madhuparka* is Madhuparka; the deity of the sandalwood is Candana; the deity of the flower is Lakṣmī; and the deity of the incense is Vanaspati.
All items such as musk and the like should be known as having the Apsarases as their presiding deities;
the lamp has Agni as its deity, and the food offering (naivedya) has Viṣṇu as its deity.
The sandals have Soma as their deity; the parasol should have Indra as its deity.
O Sovereign of the Thirty-three Gods, the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) is the deity of the fly-whisks. (11-237)
The fan has Vāyu as its presiding deity; Indra is the deity of the lion-throne;
the garland has Rati as its deity; and the liquor has Ḍākinī as its deity.
Meat has Nirṛti as its presiding deity; a canopy has Candra as its deity;
and all kinds of grain-crops and cooked foods belong to Prajāpati.
Garments for Vācaspati are white or black;
those for Mayu are red; but for Durgā, it is a silk cloth.
The Brahma-vidyā has been fully described, as well as the various sections concerning knowledge;
those pertaining to Sarasvatī, such as books and so forth, are to be known, O Pārvatī. (11–1241)
Viśvakarman is the presiding deity of all vessels as well;
according to the Yāmala, the fourfold musical instruments are to be known as having Rudra and the Gandharvas as their deities. (11-1242)
Mahākāla is the deity to be known as the lord of trees, creepers, vegetables along with greens, and indeed of all fruits. (11–243)
Likewise, deer skins, beds, chariots, seats, sandals, swings, and whatever else is devoid of living beings [may be used]. || 11-1244 ||
The wise declare that the *uttāna* is presided over by Aṅgiras;
the banner is indeed presided over by Dharma, and the plough is presided over by Parjanya.
Stone and the like, as well as gems, are said to have Śakra as their presiding deity;
but the house, O beloved, has all the gods as its deities, even though it was not mentioned by me.
All that should be known as having Rudra as its presiding deity in the rite of consecration (utsarga).
Thus end the deities. Now follows the procedure for the worship of the maiden (kumārī-pūjā-vidhi).
p. 1081) (In the Mahātharvaṇasaṃhitā:
Then the best of practitioners should perform the worship of the maiden. 11-1247.
When this is performed according to the prescribed rule, the ritual action becomes complete in all its parts;
whereas if it is not performed, there will be a deficiency of limbs, especially in the autumnal worship.
(Mahākālasaṃhitā) Having completed the worship, when evening has arrived and the onset of night is present,
one should perform the beneficial fifth worship of the maiden according to the prescribed rite. (11-1249)
Likewise,
O Sovereign of the Gods, having herself assumed that form and entered into a state of delusion, she anoints both the auspicious and the inauspicious for her devotees.
The auspicious Śivā approaches, desiring to see [him], equipped with the provisions for devotion and worship;
therefore, one who understands the nature of devotion should show her respect there. (11.251)

O Goddess honored by the gods, just as deities indicate benefit or harm for specific locations through three kinds of portents, so too do they indicate the [conditions] for these regions throughout the year.
For the sake of realizing that [reality], this [scripture] should also be honored with effort by all four types of Kaulas: the Smārttas and the Ānukalpinas.
In this matter, there is no difference of opinion, nor even any distinction in worship; there are neither opposing positions nor any room for the conception of doubt. (11-1254)
There shall be an abundance of fruits as well as satisfaction for the Goddess;
furthermore, by this [rite], the future auspicious and inauspicious is specifically known. (11–1255)
When auspiciousness is known, there should be satisfaction; otherwise, one must contemplate other means.
Likewise, Śivā is not so satisfied by offerings, fire-oblations, praises, or incantations as she is by [the knowledge of auspiciousness]. (11-256)
Just as she becomes instantly pleased here through the worship of a maiden, one should not only worship her, but also feed her with diligence. (11.257)
Likewise, it is proclaimed that physical deformity results from the failure to perform worship;
yet, through the worship of a young maiden here, one is immediately propitiated. (11.1258)
For even when another [rite] has not been performed, completeness may still be achieved through its performance;
likewise: "For the Kaulas, worship is prescribed at night; for the Smārtas, it is in the afternoon. (11.1259)
The daily [worship] is performed with the *śārada* hymn; the optional and the occasional are otherwise.
He describes the characteristics of the maiden: "Well-bathed, wearing garments radiant with various colors such as red and yellow... (11.1260).
Her limbs were adorned with all manner of ornaments, yet she was unaware of the gestures of the God of Love;
she had never experienced attachment in the minds of men, being only seven, eight, or nine years of age.
One who is not of low birth, fair-limbed, and whose father and mother are known;
who has no protruding teeth, whose teeth are not too large, and who is free from any deficiency in her limbs. || 11-1262 ||
One who has not long hair, is radiant, possesses a beautiful smile, and lovely eyes—regarding those with prohibited characteristics, it is stated in that very same place:
"A dark-complexioned woman with long teeth, dog-like eyes, and tawny hair. (11-1263)
One who is emaciated, slow-moving, angry, humpbacked, lame, or has a goiter; one whose eyebrows and hair are sparse, and likewise one with oozing sores. || 11-1264 ||
One should diligently avoid a woman who has reached puberty and whose passion is aroused.
In another Tantra: [One should avoid] one with extra limbs, one with missing limbs, one who is diseased, and one marked by sores. (11–1265)
One should reject a girl who is blind, one-eyed, squinting, misshapen, or excessively hairy.
(From the Mahākālasaṃhitā) A maiden other than these [defective ones] is to be chosen for the sequence of worship. 11-1266.

(Merutantra) One should worship a Brahmin woman for the complete accomplishment of all desired aims; a Kṣatriya-born woman for fame; a Vaiśya-born woman for the acquisition of wealth; and a Śūdra-born woman for the attainment of sons. (11–1267)
In the *Skānda*:
"A man should worship an Antyaja girl in a formidable manner according to the prescribed rite.
In the *Yāmala*:
The practitioner who should always worship a maiden on all festival days.
By him the Great Goddess was worshipped; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
She who is one year old is called Sandhyā, and she who is two years old is Sarasvatī.
Kālikā is threefold in form and three years old, while she who is four years old is Subhagā; this Umā is five years old, and at six years she becomes [the goddess] Bhavānī.
Mālinī is seven years old, and the eighth is considered Kubjikā;
Kālasaṃkarṣā is nine years old, and Aparājitā is ten years old.
Rudrāṇī is eleven years old, and Bhairavī is twelve years old;
beyond that is Mahālakṣmī, and beyond her is the Kulanāyikā.
The Kṣetrajñā is said to be devoted to that [deity], while Caṇḍikā is sixteen years old;
in this sequence, the Kumārikā should be understood as being without flowers.
(In the Skanda Purāṇa, within the Hemādri):
One should worship each maiden individually, or likewise with an increase of one;
or even double, triple, or nine for each. (11–1274)
Likewise: "By nine he attains the stages; by double that, sovereignty;
by increasing by one, he obtains security; and by each [subsequent] one, he obtains prosperity. (11.1275)
However, one should avoid a maiden who is only one year old for the purpose of worship;
she possesses no delight in perfumes, flowers, fruits, and the like.
(vāḍavānalīye) That [cow] which is seven, eight, or nine years old is to be known as the best;
the five-year-old and the six-year-old ten-year-old [cows] are the middling ones. || 11-1277 ||
"One, two, three, or four years is remembered as the minimum [age] for the Rudra-abda and other [initiations] (Mahākālasaṃhitā,
11.1278). [This should be performed] with the sounds of singing and musical instruments, preceded by joy and reverence."
Having led those unmarried maidens— either five, or seven, or nine, or eleven— she should place them at the door of the hall of worship.
Among them, one principal [image] should be made, which is beautiful in all its limbs;
indeed, even in the absence of [all] the fires, there should be at least one young maiden.
In rites for specific desires and occasional rites, as well as in the autumnal worship, there may be one or many [deities], arranged in rows, standing, or even with faces bowed down. (11–1281)
Having established these [deities] in sequence and having first appointed the principal one,
the practitioner, free from haste, should conceive of this [principal deity] as the Goddess.
Intoxicated by the wine he has taken, having prepared the materials for the ritual worship,
he first performs breath control (prāṇāyāma) and then the expulsion of the elemental spirits (bhūtāpasāraṇa).
Having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇapati on the left and right,
and likewise to Kumārī in the center, who is the very embodiment of the Root Goddess (Mūladevī).
Likewise, one should perform the binding of the directions with finger-snaps and three claps of the hands;
then, one should wash the feet of the maiden who serves as the root.
Likewise, one should place that water upon the head with the wisdom that it is the water from the Goddess’s feet;
then, one should offer the water for the feet using one's own upper garment.
Furthermore, O Dear One, taking up unbroken rice grains, one should dispel the obstacles while reciting the mantra, preceded by three claps of the hands. (11.1287)
First, one should utter the weapons consisting of the *tāra*, the noose (*pāśa*), the digit (*kalā*), and the brush (*kūrca*);
and also say, "Drive away the spirits" and "Destroy the obstacles."
One should place [the seed-syllables] at the heart and the head; this is the mantra of twenty-one syllables.
All [the deities] are accompanied by Kumārī, who is the very embodiment of the Goddess.
As many beings as there are of divine origin who come for the sake of seeing [him]—
pretas, bhūtas, piśācas, gandharvas, and even guhyakas.
The Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and others who perform cruel deeds,
having entered together with Kaumārī into the pavilion for the autumnal worship of Śāradā.
They crush the image of the maiden and destroy the worship;
therefore, O beloved, the expulsion of obstacles must be performed twice.
Then, having taken the maiden's right hand with his own left hand, preceded by the placement of his right foot, [he should proceed].
Reciting the mantra in the form of a verse, he should cause those maidens, arranged in rows,
to enter slowly into the interior of the worship chamber with their heads bowed.
O primordial one of all the worlds, whose form is the support of the universe,
assume the form of a maiden and enter this house of mine.
"O Mother, I do not know what your true form is;
with my human eyes, I see only this form of a young maiden. (11.296)
O Śivā, having recognized my devotion to your lotus feet,
you have manifested such a form for the attainment of all perfections.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, my gaze must not be fixed upon sinful things or the path of the wicked; it should be directed solely toward firm devotion. (11.1298)
Indeed, even Śiva and the others do not know what your true form is;
how then could I, a wretched being with a body composed of the five elements, know it? (11.1299)
Thus, reciting these five verses, O Goddess, one should carry [the disciple] across on one's own back,
without even looking at him, preceded by song and instrumental music.
(Based on the *Yāmala*:
Having bathed her with scented oil and adorned her with various ornaments, the wise one should bring her to the side of the deity and establish her there. (11.1301)
(Also in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"That worship is declared to be primary, as is its mantra for the Primary [Goddess] alone.
By worshipping her alone, all of them are worshipped; of this there is no doubt. (11.1302)
Likewise,
O Supreme Goddess, having offered oblations to the divine beings,
one should, free from laziness, begin the supreme ritual installation of the Kumārīs.
Indeed, at the beginning, the names are considered to be Mahācaṇḍayogeśvarī;
then Siddhikarālī, and again Siddhivikarālī. (11–1303)
Then Mahantā and Māryathā are to be known as Vajrakāpālinī; Muṇḍamālinī and Aṭṭahāsinī—these two are proclaimed. (11-1304)
Immediately following [her] is Caṇḍakāpālinī, the sovereign of Kālacakra;
then Guhyakālī, followed by Kātyāyanī together with Kāmākhya.
Cāmuṇḍā, Siddhilakṣmī, and Kubjikā follow after that; thereafter Mātaṅgī is to be known, and then Caṇḍeśvarī is proclaimed.
Finally, at the end of all [the others], there is Kaumārī; these eighteen have been described.
These belong to the domain of Guhyeśī. But elsewhere:
First, I shall utter her names: Durgā, Nārāyaṇī, Śivā. (11.1307)
Mahāmāyā, Yoganidrā, Kālarātrī, Kapardinī, Ugracaṇḍā, Bhadrakālī, Ajitā, and Aparājitā. || 11-1308 ||
Kātyāyanī, Mahākālī, Kāmākhyā, Kulanāyikā, Bhairavī, and Bhuvaneśī— these are remembered as the eighteen Kaumāryas.
Thus other names have also been stated.
Likewise: "Therefore, I shall state the limbs: first the head, then the face, and after that the two eyes."
The two ears, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, and again their two bases. || 11-1310 ||
The lower lip, the rows of teeth, the shoulders, the heart, the two arms, the belly, the back, the thighs, and likewise the knees.
The shanks, the feet, and all the limbs— these many locations as well—
as well as [the principles] from Kalā to Kalānta, the wise one should worship them according to the prescribed rule. (Triśaktiratna, 11–1312)
Having seated the young maiden upon a divine seat, the most excellent practitioner should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon her body according to the procedure to be described.
The first should be Kumārikā, the second is considered Nāyikā;
the third is known as Bhairavī, and the fourth shall be Vāgīśvarī. (11–1314)
The fifth [syllable] is declared to be *pālikā*; ending with the perfective suffix (*sambuddhi*), they are the [mantras] beginning with the *kula* [syllables].
These are to be deposited by means of the application of the five limbs (*pañcāṅgayoga*) within the bodies of the young maidens.
One should worship the four faces in sequence, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.
Then [the goddesses] Siddhā, Jayā, the other Jayā, and Kubjikā are worshipped in order.
The fifth is declared to be Kālikā; these [deities] are to be known as awakened.
They are joined with the faces starting from the east, ending in the dative case, and concluding with "namas. (11.1317)
One should install [the deities] in their respective places according to one's own intellect and in due order,
employing the five *praṇavas* together with the mantra of consciousness.

The best of practitioners should perform the previously mentioned network of nyāsa-s (Mahākālasaṃhitā). Then, he should perform the placement of the arghya offering as it has been described for the daily rites. 11–1319.
The purification of the ritual implements is also stated as previously described.
Likewise: "Then one should perform the meditation on the maiden as it will be explained. (11.1320)
In another tantra:
[She who has] a serene lotus-face, possessing the radiance of the rising morning sun, clad in red garments and red garlands, adorned with various ornaments. (11.1321)
One should meditate upon the youthful maiden, smiling, intent on the delight of play with divine maidens, and the bestower of the desired perfections upon her devotees. (11-1322)
Likewise: "Then one should offer all [the items], beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and ending with praise"— this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
She should be worshipped either by the previously mentioned path or again by the one that will be described hereafter. (Yāmalatantra, 11.13–23).

The mantra-practitioner should worship these deities, endowed with their proper characteristics, in the western direction using their own names in the dative case, preceded by the three stars (oṃ āḥ hūṃ) and ending with "namaḥ. || 11-324 ||
The first is Śuddhā Kālikā, the second is remembered as Lalitā;
the fourth is known as Mālinī, and the fifth shall be Vasundharā. (11–1325)
Sarasvatī, Ramā, Gaurī, and Durgā shall be the ninth;
a wise man should worship the Child [Bāla] for five years or nine years. (11.1326)
A five-year-old is declared to be a *vaṭuka*, and a nine-year-old is *gaṇeśvara*. Likewise:
"One should offer a seat with words; with modesty (*hrī*), one should present water for the feet (*pādya*). (11–1327)
Having offered the *argha* with the *ramā* mantra, one should then present sandalwood paste with the *strī* mantra;
one should offer a collection of flowers to the maiden (*kumārī*) with the *śakti* seed-syllable.
The practitioner, with the *caitanya* mantra, should place the incense, lamps, and so forth;
these are declared to be the *tāra*s, and *bhṛgu* conjoined with *bhava*. (11–1329)
The *manu* (seed-syllable) of consciousness, pervaded by the *bindu* and the *nāda*, is proclaimed [as such];
in some places, however, the fifth *praṇava* is considered to be the seed-syllable of Bhairava. (11–1330)
It should be understood that when worshipping a single deity alone, the offering of all the ritual services (*upacāra*) is performed using the mantra beginning with the *tritārā*.
This is because of the statement in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "One should offer everything to her with the mantra beginning with the *tritārā*."
Ornaments, silken garments, vermilion and lac-dye, as well as collyrium, mirrors, renowned palm-leaf fans, and a casket.
The preparatory rite, the support, the *cola*, the small stool, the seat, the swing, the doll, the chest, the wooden sandals, the rug, and the cloth mat. (11.13–32)
A moon-lamp, a vessel for ointment, a bed, a pillow, a couch, a casket, and a cosmetic box. 11-1333.
A water-vessel, a swing, as well as a parting-line comb, gorocanā, musk, camphor, and saffron; || 11-1334 ||
O Sundarī, other such items as these, as many as possible, should be given so that the maiden may be satisfied. (11.1335)
Likewise: (p. 1090) Then, one should present the vessel that has been set aside to the maiden;
she should accept it right there and likewise apply herself with effort. || 11-1336 ||
If that vessel is not accepted, a great fault arises;
therefore, one should exert such effort that it is indeed accepted by her. (11.1337)
Then, having taken flowers and unbroken rice grains, one should worship fifty Śaktis in succession upon her body.
I shall now proclaim them; listen with attention:
the first is Jayā, then Vijayā, Ṛddhidā, and Māyānvitā.
Kalā, Sūkṣmā, Siddhidā, Prabhā, Suprabhā, Vidyutā, Viśuddhi, Nandinī, and Viśuddhiyuk. (11–1340)
Aparājitā, Lalitā, Lakṣmī, and likewise Gaurī;
then Medhā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and again Svadhā.
Svāhā, Icchā, Kriyā, Vidyā, Prajñā, Dīptā, Cetanā, Bhadrā, Jyeṣṭhā, Umā, Śivā, Muditā, and Kṣamā. || 11-1342 ||
Then there is Śraddhā, Vimalā, and indeed Viśadā Kaumudī;
thereafter Aśokā, Jñānadā, Baladā, and Rājyadā as well.
Following that are Maitrī, Rudrāṇī, Bhavānī, and also Mṛḍānī;
then Sarvajñā, Caṇḍikā, and Kumārī, who resides at the very end of all.
These fifty maidens are known as the Śaktis;
thereafter, one should worship the eight Bhairavas with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings.
Then [offerings] to the Bhairavīs, and likewise to the Vighnas and Vināyakas, to Vaṭuka and Kṣetrapāla, and similarly to the Yoginīs. || 11-1346 ||
One should perform this worship for the *bhaṭas*, the *pretas*, the *yakṣas*, and likewise for the *ḍākinīs*, using *dūrvā* grass, parched grain, and sandalwood paste. (11.1347)
Furthermore, O Dear One, at the very end of all, one should worship eight goddesses ending in the dative case:
Mahāmāyā, Kālarātrī, and then indeed Sarvamaṅgalā.
Next, Ḍamarukā is to be worshipped, and likewise Rājarājeśvarī;
thereafter, the Goddess Kumārī, the bestower of prosperity. (11.1349)
In the *Yāmala*, one should worship her within the *kula*; one should worship these [goddesses] in the corners of the *kula*: Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśī, and the third, Bhagamālinī. (11–1350)
Above, in the corners of the pair of families, one should worship these:
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamanmathā, and [the goddess] preceded by Anaṅga.
The fourth [day] begins with Madanānandaśabda and ends with Kusumottarā;
the fifth begins with Anaṅga and ends with Anaṅgapadādikā, characterized by the state of being afflicted by passion.
These powers, numbering six, are indeed declared to be cool;
by this procedure, the Kumārī should be worshipped by the most excellent practitioners.

(Mahākālasaṃhitā) Having thus completed the worship of the maiden, one should draw a circular maṇḍala on the ground with water in front of her, and in its center [place] the beloved of the Kula. 11-1354.
Having drawn [the mandala] with water, flowers, unbroken rice, sandalwood, and nāgaja [incense], one should worship that mandala and utter "Obeisance to the Giver of Auspiciousness. (11.355)
Having placed all that food contained in the vessel there, as well as various kinds of provisions consisting of things to be licked, sucked, and so forth; || 11-1356 ||
Having placed a vessel filled with meat, fish, and wine, and stocked with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten,
one should place the right hand of a young maiden upon the top of the food.
p. 1092) One should offer the food face-upward with the mantra to be recited hereafter.

The mantra for the offering of food is as follows: *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ strīṃ sauḥ! To the Blessed Lady Kumārī, whose nature is all powers (*sarvaśaktisvarūpā*) and who bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhidā*), I offer this great feast-offering (*mahābhoga-naivedya*) consisting of various kinds of foods—both solid and soft—endowed with the six flavors; please accept it, accept it! Eat it, eat it! Be gracious, be gracious! Grant me all accomplishments, grant them! Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ svāhā!*
Thus it was stated by the author of the *Paddhati*.
Likewise: "One should perform the worship of each of the other maidens individually. (11.1358)
With perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of cooked rice.
Likewise: "Indeed, such foods as were prepared for this principal [goddess]," (11.1359).
Only those [mantras] similar to those already practiced by others should be given; this is the certainty.
However, the wise person should understand here that the presence or absence of fruit depends on the primary [mantra]. (11.360)
While the young girls are eating, one should not play the sound of musical instruments;
one should not direct the mind elsewhere, nor should one create any crowding.
One should suppress clamor and whatever things are inauspicious;
one should carefully avoid weeping and the downward wind (flatus).
One should be attentive in this matter: what do they eat first? What do they whisper to one another? Or where is the seizing of objects? (11.1363)
"Where do they cast their gaze when frightened, or what do they say?"—such various kinds of gestures as these were observed by him with great care. (11–1364)
One should attentively recognize those [omens] as indicators of good or bad fortune;
while they are thus devouring [the offerings], one should recite that hymn without haste. (11.1365)
With palms joined and head bowed, casting his eyes upon their mouths, he said:
"Victory to you, O Kālī, most terrible one, of fearsome roar, remover of fear! (11.1366)
O you who are like a cresting flame in the forest fire of saṃsāra, who enable one to cross the ocean of misfortune,
and who are worshipped by the immortals beginning with Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and Bhūteśa!
O Guhyakālī, who brings about the creation, protection, and destruction of the world, and whose form is filled with the essence of supreme bliss! (11.1368)
She who bestows the bliss of liberation through the tasting of the essence of the Supreme Brahman;
she who, though transcending all qualities, appears as if possessing qualities; and she who dances at the end of the great cosmic cycles.
Assuming the form of a maiden, O you whose very nature is discernment and wisdom,
you have come to my abode for the completion of the Śārada rite.
To indicate the auspiciousness of the annual festival, and likewise:
"I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose; my life has become fruitful. (11.1371)
Since you, having assumed such an excellent youthful form,
have arrived here in secret with the desire to receive the annual worship.
In former times, you were indeed entreated by the gods in this very form;
you granted them sovereignty as well as the boons they desired.
O Goddess of gods, well-worshipped, grant a boon to me today as well;
for in the past, you granted the power of creation to Brahmā.
And you alone gave the power of protection to Viṣṇu;
likewise, O Śivā, you bestowed the agency of destruction upon Mahārudra.
O Sovereign Lady, you are the inner controller even of the gods, and you possess the skill to destroy the Daityas;
you are likewise the inner controller of all who dwell within the three worlds.
(1094) What shall I report to you, the sole witness of all actions—whether it be the destruction of enemies, the attainment of a kingdom, or even the health of the body? (11.377)
I pray for devotion to your lotus feet; grant me these four boons. Salutations to you, O Blessed Mother; salutations to you, O lover of devotion.
Salutations to you, whose form is the support of the universe; protect me always. I know you as my Mother, yet your true nature is neither body nor quality.
With single-minded devotion, I recognize your worship through the devotion residing within my heart;
you are the mother, you are the father, and you alone are the kinsman, O Sovereign Lady of the World.
You are the goal, you are the refuge, you are heaven, and you are indeed liberation; O Mother of the World, having abandoned you, I know no other deity.
"Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again!
O fair-faced one, having performed this praise with these verses for the young maidens," (11.1382)
One should indeed offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) with haste at the conclusion of the meal;
thereafter, one should present betel-leaf (tāmbūla) scented with musk and camphor.
Having followed him for a while accompanied by musical instruments and other offerings, one should dismiss him.
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall tell you of the auspicious and inauspicious results [of this].
In that regard, I shall first describe the auspicious rite, and then its opposite;
thereafter, one should give the remnants of that to the jackals upon the ground.
Or, O Goddess, one should bury it in water, or having stirred it well, one should cast it away.
If it is first placed upon the hand along with the food, there will be abundance of food in the realm.
Through milk-rice (pāyasa), the increase of cattle for the sacrificer is produced;
through clarified butter (ghṛta), there shall be longevity and health; and through worship, it is for the increase of sovereignty.
Likewise, there will be an abundance of a continuous succession of sweetmeats and cakes; from fish one gains wealth, and from rice-and-sesame porridge (kṛsara), the excellence of vehicles. (11.1388)
In the case of meat, there shall be the gain of a son; in the case of cooked food, one shall obtain a woman.
I shall now describe the distinct and mixed fruits of specific types of meat.
In the Vārāha [mantra], there is the gain of wealth; in the Khāṅga, victory in battle;
and by means of buffalo meat, the attainment of a kingdom will certainly occur.

Through the meat of a black antelope one quickly attains health; through that of a spotted deer, eloquence; through the meat of a hare, one attains intelligence; and through that of a goat, even freedom from old age.
O Goddess, by eating meat from the belly of a sheep, one shall obtain all auspicious things;
by eating that of a tortoise, there is the acquisition of land; and by eating that of a deer, there is an abundance of food.
In the case of the vārdhrīṇasa, there is the destruction of enemies; in the haṃsa, the subjugation of men;
in the taittira, the attainment of desired objects; and in the varttaka, the total destruction of sins.
Satisfaction of the mind is found in the crane; mastery over all things is in the fruit of the sugarcane;
great fame resides in curd; and unsurpassed prosperity is in milk.
From flour comes the attainment of a son; from vegetables, the destruction of enemies;
from wine, an increase in merit; and from dry food, prosperity and eloquence.
There is the acquisition of wealth through molasses, and an increase in strength through inspissated milk;
likewise, [prosperity comes] from the gourd, the eggplant, the pumpkin, the karellaka, and the patola. (11.1396)

O Goddess, when an ointment is prepared with ghoṣa, śūraṇa, long-rooted radish, and garlic, there shall be the acquisition of knowledge; moreover, if it is mixed with buttermilk (takra), there is also eloquence of speech.

If a reflection appears in an object made of wheat flour during the battle, liberation will be attained upon seeing the sacrificial altar; likewise, there will be exaltation within the pavilion. (11.1398)
The best fortune lies in the sight of the yak-tail whisk and the parasol, as well as the palm-leaf fan and the couch, and also the bell and the mirror. (11.1399)
(1096) In the case of ornaments for the body, tactile sensations, movements, and visual perceptions, there are various kinds of substances that are dear to the Great Mother. (11-1400)
Many such activities and omens of this kind arise as auspicious portents; now hear from me about those that are the opposite.
If the principal maiden vomits two or three times, famine will certainly arise and the subjects will also be afflicted. (11.1402)
If a maiden weeps, the king comes to ruin;
if she voids excrement, there is a great pestilence; if she voids feces, there is the burning of the city.
By not eating, there is danger from enemies; by eating too much, there are calamities. By not speaking, there may be diseases; by speaking too much, there are misfortunes.
Various kinds of physical movements of the hands and feet are [indicative of] calamities;
excessive modesty leads to ruin, whereas a lack of modesty is auspicious. (11.1405)
If various portents occur while she is silent, there will be destruction of the arms;
if she is frightened, there is total ruin, and if she is angry, there is death itself.
Upon possession, the king dies at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
When she is suspected, there is fear of an enemy; when she is pacified, there is fear of death.
If [the mantra] is merely thought upon, it should be known that the very kingdom will fall;
through delusion there is loss of wealth, and through dullness worship becomes fruitless. (11.1408)
If there is fickleness, the fortune of the worshipper alone becomes fickle;
furthermore, if a girl possessed of dejection is born there. (11-1409)
Then the kingdom, along with its ruler and its subjects, perishes, O Pārvatī;
the king dies of disease if the subjects become afflicted by illness.
If there is a threat of famine or pestilence and it sheds tears, then total destruction will occur; but if it shakes its head, [it is otherwise]. (11.1411)
When she is terrified, fear from enemies is ordained for that king;
when there is trembling, the Supreme Goddess Kālikā becomes averse.
If the Goddess is dissatisfied and lowers her head, then the life of the lord of the earth will be diminished; likewise, if she speaks with a faltering voice, it shall be so. (11.1413)
If the worshipper becomes distressed or agitated, it will lead to wretchedness; but if she who is to be enchanted becomes agitated, the entire city will fall into turmoil.
If she feels ashamed, disease will arise; if there is perspiration, there will be the destruction of wealth and grain;
and if, by the turn of fate, the downward wind should issue forth from the maiden, [these results follow].
At that time, the city will be oppressed by a foreign army,
if a young girl there sings a song devoid of ritual action.
If the death of a king who has sons and a wife is accompanied by the leading queens, and they should ever quarrel among themselves, [it portends misfortune]. (11.1417)
Then, a most terrible enemy army will suddenly arrive,
either with anyone at all or by means of anything whatsoever.
The maiden speaks fearlessly, free from bashfulness and trepidation;
then, the six calamities arise within his realm. (11.1419)
O beloved, if they perform a reversal of the food with the movements of their hands,
everything that is desired by the mind becomes consumed.
Whatever object was presented as an offering to the Goddess in the pavilion,
if the king touches it with both hands, he shall become terrified and flee in all directions.
If a young girl should extinguish a lamp with the breath from her mouth, then there will be a derangement of the intellect and the lamp of knowledge will perish. (11.1422)
And if, by the turn of fate, young maidens dance while filled with spirits, the entire kingdom along with its king becomes like a cremation ground. (11.1423)
If the maidens there should cast off their garments and become naked,
then the king will be seized by his enemies at the forefront of the battle.
If they leap while blowing and whirl about while clutching their hands, the king will be possessed by a spirit; of this there is no doubt.
"If the young girls say, 'We shall laugh' or 'We shall speak' thus at the time of eating, then there will be the fear of a great pestilence. (11-1426)
Whether on the left or on the right, with her eyes whose pupils are trembling and which are red and fierce, the young maiden causes her own head to whirl.
Or she may let out a loud, boisterous laugh by which men are terrified;
then there may be possession by spirits, or ghosts may dance in the city.
Grinding his teeth against each other, he makes a rattling sound;
accompanied by his wife, sons, and kinsmen, he goes to the abode of Death.
Having fixed her unblinking gaze and bit her lip with her tooth,
the young girl threatens him while shaking her head.
That very fruit which occurs when there is a crunching sound is prescribed;
one should observe silence from beginning to end and should not touch food with the hand.
One should bend the head excessively and scratch the ground with the thumb;
one may draw lines upon the earth with fingernails for no purpose at all.
One should not scratch one's head with both hands joined together, nor should one cut grass without cause, nor snap one's fingers. (11.1433)
One may cover the two eyes with both hands, or close the two ears;
one may perform the *bāhurikā* gesture or rub the heels together. (11.1434)
He takes a large mouthful, stands with his mouth wide open, and repeatedly suppresses a sneeze or yawns over his food. (11.1435)
Or if, having taken food with his hand, he throws it in the four directions;
or if he stands up or moves about, having abandoned the food as well as the act of worship. (11–1436)
Vomiting may occur for her, or there may be horripilation and trembling;
or alternatively, pus and blood may emerge from her limbs even in the absence of an internal cause.
If she suddenly utters a plaintive cry without cause, speaks indecorously, or weeps for the sake of her own kin, [she is to be known as such]. (11.1438)
Standing in that place, she should either cast off her ornaments and finery, or say, "I am going home," or she should utter insults toward whomever she may encounter. (11.439)
Or she might reproach someone who has approached her together with him;
or she might break the bond, or [seize] the rings from his own hand by force. (11.1440)
When some kinsman has died, that young maiden grieves there; or she prattles something or other without any apparent cause. (11.1441)
O you who are worshipped by the thirty gods, all of this should be known as inauspicious:
famine, loss of wealth, disease, and likewise the fear of pestilence.
At every step there shall be calamities, grief, diseases, and the rise of enemies; there shall be the sudden arrival of a foreign army, and the burning of cities and houses by fire.
Fear of death, poverty, and separation from one's kinsmen, as well as possession by spirits, ghosts, and demons, prevail in every household. (11.1444)
The death of living beings occurs through eight great diseases;

The annual fruit for the king shall be victory or defeat, death, suffering, wealth, happiness, fear of enemies, or the increase of power. (11.1446)
The prosperity of the kingdom, the oppression of the subjects, physical deformity, and the destruction of the army—all this is known from the worship of the maiden and even from her meal. (11.447)

When an auspicious birth has occurred, worship for specific desires (kāmyārcā) with abundant materials is appropriate; however, in other circumstances, one should avoid the fault arising from such [desire-driven] practice.
Even if the maiden returns home from her illness on that very same day, there will still be no auspicious result.

Taking the form of a beast, she arrives together with her retinue;

At that very moment there is auspiciousness for him, and not otherwise, O ornament of the family;

If one does not worship the goddess Śivā in the form of a female animal in a secluded place, everything of his will certainly perish quickly due to her howling. (11-1476)

With every effort, one should perform this great worship when confronted by fear of kings and the like, or fear arising from foreign lands and so forth.

The mantra previously mentioned brings about accomplishment; with it, one should offer the bali-oblation.

(From the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*):
"O child, if it is not taken, then there will certainly be no auspiciousness. (11–1492)

One should personally prostrate like a staff, regarding all [the goddesses] with the thought that they are one's own chosen deity;
then, taking up a handful of flowers smeared with fragrant sandalwood paste.
Having risen, with disheveled hair, eyes closed, and naked as the sky,
he was full of devotion, free from fear, and with his neck slightly bowed.
One should perform praise with these hymns, preceded by a prayer for boons:
"O Goddess who bears the form of Śivā, O Guhyakālī, salutations be to you! (11-1496)
O Ulkāmukhī, O Lalajjihvā, O Ghorarāvā, O Śṛgālinī!

Be gracious, O Goddess of gods, toward me, your devotee, O Caṇḍikā!
You who cross the ocean of saṃsāra, victory to you, the maker of all that is auspicious!

"O Vikaṭā, grant me sovereignty, wealth, long life, sons, and a wife;
O Goddess, may you become gracious through this offering of the Śivā-bali. (11.503)
"Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, homage be to you"—

Thereafter, O Pārvatī, one should carefully bury all of that remaining food, as well as the vessel or any other item, in the ground.

Grant me long life; grant me glory; O Blessed One, grant me fortune. Grant me sons; grant me wealth; grant me all my desires.
O Pracaṇḍā, O Putradā, who are ever well-pleased, O leader of the gods, O fierce one who illuminates the lineage, grant us victory; homage be to you!
O Ugracaṇḍā, you are Pracaṇḍā, the destroyer of fierce strength.
Homage to you always, O Goddess; O Sovereign of the Universe, let there be homage to you.

O Goddess Durgā, you are the deliverer from difficulty; you are the destroyer of all that is inauspicious. O Goddess, bestower of virtue, wealth, and liberation, be forever the granter of boons to me.
O Goddess Durgā, O highly fortunate one, protect me who have come to you for refuge;
I bow down before you, O you who are intoxicated by the pride of the blood of Mahiṣa—be gracious to me.
Take away evil, take away affliction, take away sorrow, take away the inauspicious;
take away disease, take away agitation, take away pride, O Beloved! (11-1515)
O Kālī, O Mahākālī, O Kālikā, O remover of sins!
O Goddess who bestows dharma and desire, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be unto you! || 11-1516 ||
Grant victory in battle; grant wealth always within the home.
Grant the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha; O Goddess, salutations be to you!
O slayer of Mahiṣa, O Great Illusion, O Cāmuṇḍā, O wearer of a garland of severed heads!
O Goddess, grant me long life, health, and victory; homage be to you.
May Kālī grant me long life; may Sadāśivā also grant me sons;
may Mahāmāyā grant me wealth and desire; and may Sarvamaṅgalā grant me prosperity.
May Caṇḍikā protect my head; may Sureśvarī protect my throat;
may Cāmuṇḍā protect my heart; and may Kālikā protect me from all sides.
Brahmāṇī, Kaumārī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Māheśvarī, Nārasiṃhī, Indrāṇī, and Śivadūtī. (11-1521)
Mahākālī, Cāmuṇḍā, Bhairavī, and likewise Kauśikī;
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.

Protect me together with them in battle and in times of distress,
according to the words of various Purāṇas and the utterances of various divine sages.
By the command of Sadāśiva as well, you alone are my refuge;
O Śivā, leaving you aside, I do not seek shelter with any other deity.
Therefore, O Mother, you ought to do whatever is appropriate hereafter,
[to dispel] mental agitation, poverty, disease, and terrible grief.
O Durgā, remove the distress caused by separation from kinsmen and relatives;
may his kingdom and his standing be established, and may his prosperity remain forever firm.
His sovereignty is his power, over which you preside upon my head;
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and my life is fruitful.
Since you have come to my abode, O Maheśvarī, who are difficult to approach,
[accept] the water for honor, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and likewise the sacrificial oblation.
"Accept [this], O goddess, bestower of boons; grant me prosperity at all times.
Having performed this according to the prescribed rite, preceded by prostrations with a staff-like body and hymns of praise, || 11-1530 ||

O Caṇḍikā, I bow to you today; may this worship be accepted.
In body, mind, and speech, I have no other refuge but you.
"You move within all beings; you are the knower and the witness of all.

O Goddess of the Gods, beginning at dawn and continuing until the third watch of the night,

O beloved, having abandoned the three weapons on the eighth day, this very same procedure applies;
thereafter, whatever remains following the grace of the Goddess [should be performed].
One should eat the incense, flowers, and food offering—whether it has been prepared or not—with one's kinsmen, preceded by laughter and merriment. (11.1537)
Thereafter, he should present singing, dancing, and so forth before the Goddess;
the wise man should also engage in play together with his kinsmen.
If one is unable to perform the complete worship as prescribed in the ritual manual, this concise worship has been taught [in the Kālikāpurāṇa]:
"One may offer perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, or even food offerings alone. (11.1539)
"In the absence [of these], with water and flowers; and in the absence of those, through devotion—the abbreviated worship has been described."
Thus concludes the ritual for the ninth day.
Now follows the procedure for the worship of Revanta and others from the second day through the ninth.
This is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
For the peace, the prosperity of the horses, and for one's own victory. || 11-1540 ||
O King, one should worship Revanta from the second day until the ninth.
As stated in another text:
"Indeed, throughout the bright fortnight of Āśvina, up to the ninth day. (11.1541)

(In the Śālihotra)
During the seven nights beginning with the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja.

It completely suppresses their splendor, vitality, and strength;
consequently, painful diseases arise, accompanied by great calamities. (11.1545)
Therefore, when Svāti is afflicted, there will be great suffering among horses;
thus, the conjunction of Svāti is specifically indicated to last for seven nights.
In that regard, the horses should be protected from being touched by the rays of the sun;
they should be kept in a stable that has been smeared with cow dung, is pleasing to the mind, and is shielded from the sun's rays. || 11-1547 ||
One should have it adorned with various kinds of flowers and fumigated with incense.
On the second day, the horses, having bathed, being well-fumigated and honored, [should be led forth]. (11.1548)
And it must be guarded for seven days by men with weapons in their hands. Likewise:
"On an auspicious day and at an auspicious moment, the lord of the earth, together with his domestic priest... (11.1549).
One should worship the mounts that have been consecrated with auspicious rites in the stable;
as it is also stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "The wife of the Sun named Svātī, who is beautiful and a granter of boons, [approaches] the chariot. (11.1550)
Flowing during the month of Āśvina and supported by the rays of the sun, she may afflict horses for seven days; thereafter, they should be bathed and honored in the home. (11.1551)
Then, having worshipped Revanta and tied a small bundle around his neck,
one should likewise protect the stable by encircling it on the second day of the bright fortnight. || 11-1552 ||
When the sun has set, one should remove the mats, cloths, and other such items from the draft animals that were driven [to pasture] by means of the sun's rays. || 11-1553 ||
Furthermore, one should provide protection against the wind until twilight arises;

Rubbing, whirling, and likewise turning back [the vessel] should be performed at the end of the night, as long as the sun remains far away.
One should perform this every day for seven nights without sloth;
one should also have Brahmins perform rites for peace and prosperity.
(Also in the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Then, for the performance of rites for peace and prosperity day after day, [one should offer] grain, bhallātaka, kuṣṭha, vacā, and likewise siddhārthaka. (11.5–8)
One should bind a five-colored thread around their necks with mantras dedicated to Vāyu, Varuṇa, Sūrya, Śakti, and Viṣṇu.

one should place the goddess upon the head and always worship Revanta. (Śālihotra, 11.1561)

one should offer various kinds of edible foods and sacrificial oblations to Revanta.

At the front of the hall,

"Arise! Accept this oblation; may there be peace for him and for his horses. With this mantra, "Svāhā," one should offer the first oblation there.

To the Ādityas, as well as to the Aśvins, the Rudras together with the Vasus, to Viṣṇu, to the Viśvedevas, and to the Sādhyas together with the Maruts. || 11-1567 ||

One should offer oblations with the utterance of "svāhā" to the goddesses, the rivers, the oceans, and the lords of the forest, and a third offering into the sacrificial fire.

One should always cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be performed, accompanied by benedictions, blessings, and auspicious rites;
as well as [the entertainment of] actors, dancers, celestial musicians (*gandharva*), heralds (*sūta*), wandering bards (*cāraṇa*), and panegyrists (*māgadha*). (11.1572)
One should attend to the horses for seven days for the sake of performing pacification rites;
upon hearing pleasant and sweet sounds, the planetary spirits depart.
One should always employ musical instruments in the stables for the mounts;
and having passed seven days, one should have them bathed on the eighth day.
Having offered the bali-oblation to Varuṇa, one should afterwards immerse oneself in the water.
"On the eighth" means starting from the second lunar day until the eighth lunar day; as stated in another text:
Having adorned those horses and brought them into the stable, || 11-1575 ||
One should worship the god Revanta with various collections of offerings in an image, on a painted cloth, on a sacrificial mound, or in a mandala.
Homage to the God Supreme among Gods, who moves with the strength of horses, to the divine Son of the Sun, and to the benefactor of horses. || 11-1577 ||
The horse of Turaṅgaparīṣadya runs upon the back of a man;
protect the lord of horses along with his steed—I go to you for refuge.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers, one should present an oblation to Revanta:
"O son of the Sun, O great-armed one, O delighter of Chāyā’s heart! (11.1579)
"Bring peace to the horses; salutations to you, O Revanta!
Having praised him thus according to the prescribed rite, one should then worship Uccaiḥśravas.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "On the auspicious conjunction with the asterism Svātī during the bright fortnight of the month of Aśvayuja, Uccaiḥśravas first brought forth the Sun. (11.1581)
Therefore, he should always be worshipped there with faith by men together with horses;
indeed, the horses themselves should be worshipped until the ninth day. (11.1582)
In another text:
"O Uccaiḥśravas, salutations to you; salutations, O delight of the Ocean of Milk!
Increase the mounts, O lord of steeds, and destroy all calamities. (11.1583)
Having thus praised Ucchaiḥśravas, one should then worship the horses with various offerings;
for them, one should recite this whispered prayer into their ears: || 11-1584 ||
"You are born of the Gandharva lineage; may you not be a defiler of your family, by the word of truth of Brahmā, Soma, and Varuṇa. (11.1585)
By the splendor of the sun, by the ascetic power of the sages,
by the celibate discipline of Rudra, and by the strength of the wind.
And by the power of the sacrificial fire, remain steady, O horse;
remember that you are a prince, and remember the Kaustubha gem.
Formerly, Uccaiḥśravas was born from the Ocean of Milk while it was being churned by the gods and demons for the sake of nectar and other treasures; remember that you were born from him. (11.1588)

The destination that a killer of a Brahmin reaches, as well as a killer of a father or a mother, and one who speaks falsehood for the sake of land, or he who turns his back in battle—[he shall go to that same state]. (11.1589)
As far as the sun, the moon, and the wind perceive your evil deed, go quickly to that destination; thereafter, that sin shall be yours.
O horse, if you should suffer any injury on the path in battle,

O horse, live long, unobserved by the weapons of the enemy;
always protect me in battle and always fulfill the master's task.
In the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "One should not worship with water-born flowers during the ritual for the offering (*argha*) to the vehicle;
one should especially avoid giving *saugandhika* flowers among them at all times. (11.1593)
The fire-oblation for the planets must be performed, as well as the worship of the planets;
he who celebrates the horse festival according to this procedure [attains the fruit]. (11.1594)
For that lord of steeds, no fear shall ever arise.
The worship of the elephant is also prescribed [in the *Brahma Purāṇa*]:
"Formerly, during the conjunction with the month of Jyeṣṭha, eight elephants of great strength were there. (11.1595)
In former times, Kumuda, Airāvata, Padma, Puṣpadanta, and Vāmana bore the earth together with its mountains, groves, and forests.
Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla—one should worship them there;
beginning from Śakra and Ṛkṣa up to the ninth, as before.

May the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts protect you! O King of Elephants, protect your master; let your vow be observed. (11-1598)
Obtain victory in battle; go at this time for our well-being.
Prosperity comes from the Moon, strength from Kṛṣṇa, splendor from the Sun, and speed from the Wind.

May the serpents protect you in battle with steadfastness like Mount Meru, victory from Rudra, and glory from the god Purandara; may the quarters of the sky, together with their presiding deities, also protect you.
"May the Aśvins, together with the Gandharvas, protect you always from all sides"—

This concludes the procedure for the worship of Revanta and the others.
Now, the specific rites for desired results as taught in the Śaktisaṅgama are written down:
one who is devoted to the vow of Navarātra will certainly become a Navanātha. (11.1601)
It may be of three kinds according to the Gauḍa, Kāśmīra, or Draviḍa traditions.

O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who bestow grace upon your devotees!
The eight Śaktis of the Sun, beginning with Brāhmī, reside in his chariot. (12.1)
O Śaṅkara, tell me those [rites] which grant heaven to those who die in battle, to those who die through yoga, and to those who die as companions [of the deceased]. (12.2)
Śiva said:
Brahmaśakti is proclaimed as the leader of all powers;
she is considered the bestower of liberation to yogins and the giver of enjoyment to those who seek worldly pleasure. 12-3.
The single-syllable seed-mantra is "Brām"; the sage is considered to be Vasiṣṭha; Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter; "Baḥ" is the Śakti, and "Vacaḥ" is the Kīlaka.

Then one should meditate upon the goddess Brāhmī, who stands upon a lotus, is mounted upon a swan, has four arms, and holds a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, the gesture of fearlessness, and a water-pot; she is of a reddish hue. || 12-5 ||
The six limbs [are performed] with the seed-syllable itself—[thus it is said].
Regarding its preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it is stated in that very same source:
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with *palāśa* wood-sacrificial fuel."
One should offer libations with water mixed with those flowers and purify [the area] with kuśa grass.
Now follows the mantra of Māheśvarī.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the correct ritual procedure for Māheśvarī:
"Oṃ Hrīḥ! Homage to the Blessed Māheśvarī; hi" is what one should utter. (12.7) p. 1131)

The mantra ending with "svāhā" for Īśvarī is formed by uttering "parame pade," beginning with the Tārā (Oṃ), consisting of twenty-one syllables; that which follows is considered the one mounted on a horse. (12.8)

I worship her who is in the state of meditative absorption, mounted upon a bull, adorned with the crescent moon, possessing three eyes, and radiant like the moon; she who bears a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, and great serpent-bracelets. (12.9)

Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for each syllable; one should offer oblations with *vilva* leaves soaked in ghee in a tenth part of that number, and thus one shall become possessed of great sovereignty. (12.10)
Now, the mantra of Kaumārī:
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme rite of Kaumārī.
"Krauṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī"—this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. (12.11)
The sage is Brahmā, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Kaumārikā; Kaumida is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and Kaumāryai is called the power (śakti).
One should meditate upon the six limbs with the syllables of the mantra and upon the deity in the heart. As for the visualization:
"She who holds a spear, a rosary, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, resembling the bandhūka flower... (12-13).
She has a peacock as her banner, wears red garments, and stands upon an udumbara tree;
she is clad in a beautiful green bodice and adorned with various ornaments.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
A recitation (*japa*) of six hundred thousand [times] is prescribed, and likewise one should perform oblations (*homa*) with the five foods to be eaten;
when combined with the three sweets, the mantra then becomes perfected (*siddha*). (12–15)
Having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), as well as the feeding of virgins, [one should proceed].
Now follows the Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the wonderful Vaiṣṇava mantra. (12–16)
The mantra of Vaiṣṇavī is said to be *akacaṭatapayaśā*.
Its eight-syllable seed-mantra (*manu*) has Nārada as its seer and the Anuṣṭubh as its meter. (12–17)

The meter belongs to the goddess Vaiṣṇavī; the ritual placement (nyāsa) preceded by the Praṇava should be performed with three syllables at a time from the letters of the root mantra in their proper sequence.
Thereafter, one should recite each [mantra] individually, followed by the six limbs in their proper sequence.
Now, the meditation: [She who is] resembling a red lotus, with her hair loose and hanging down... (12-19)
She was radiant and resplendent with earrings fashioned from shimmering gold,
and she wore a crown-string set with gold and jewels.
She was beautifully adorned with three eyes— black, white, and reddish-brown—
and possessed lips the color of the bandhūka flower and a nose with the luster of the śirīṣa flower.
She had a neck like a conch shell, large eyes, and a radiance equal to ten million suns;
she was four-armed, well-clothed, and possessed full, elevated breasts.
She holds a sword and a rosary in her two right hands,
and likewise displays the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting with her two left hands.
With thighs like the trunk of a large elephant, with concealed ankles and beautiful heels,
she stood firmly, leaning perfectly against her body against a jeweled pillar.
She repeatedly uttered the words, "What do you desire?",
while gazing at the five-faced one standing before her and at her own mount.
One should meditate upon Caṇḍikā in this manner—this is the remainder [of the instruction].
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times in the rites of preparatory practice.
The fire sacrifice (homa) with clarified butter, as well as the libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites, should be performed using one-tenth [of the number of recitations].
Now, another mantra is given in that same place:
"Oṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī"—this is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra.
Here, the limbs [of the ritual] are formed by the syllables of the mantra; the remainder should be performed as before. (12.27)
Now, the Aparājitā-Vaiṣṇavī mantra is given in that very same place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the Vaiṣṇavī Aparājitā. One should utter the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), then the word *Ākarṣiṇī*, and then say *Āveśinī*. (12.28)
Having uttered "Jvālāmālini," "Ramaṇi," "Rāmaṇi," "Dharaṇī," "Dharaṇi," "Tapanī," "Tāpinī," and "Manonmādini. (12-29)
Having uttered the word "Śoṣiṇī," and then "Saṃmohinī," likewise "Nīlapatākā," "Mahānīlā," and "Mahāpriyā. (12.30)
One should address her as Mahāgneyī, Mahācaṇḍā, Mahāraudrī, and Mahā; likewise, one should speak of her as Vajriṇī, Ādityaraśmi, and Jāhnavī. (12.31)
One should utter the words Yamaghaṇṭe Kilikili Cintāmaṇi, and then the word Sarasvatī for Surabhi and Surotpannā. (12.32)
Having declared, "O you who yield all desires, may that which is my wish be accomplished for me," this mantra is considered to end with "svāhā. (12.33)
The mantra consisting of six or twelve syllables, beginning with "Muni" (the sage), bestows happiness as before;
one should recite it a hundred times and perform the fire-oblation and other rites as previously described.
Now follows the mantra of Vārāhī.
Next, I shall describe Vārāhī in the form of Vārttālikā, the slayer of enemies.
Aiṃ / Lauṃ / Ṭhaḥ / Ṭhaḥ / Ṭham / Huṃ / Svāhā—this eight-syllabled mantra ends with *svāhā*. (12.35)
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the sage is Kapila, the deity is Vārttālikā,
and here [in the Vārāhī-mantra] the six limbs are assigned in order by the numbers two, one, one, one, one, and one.
Then, with two [hands], one should meditate upon the Goddess, radiant as lightning, holding in her lotus-like hands a goad,
a noose, a mallet, and a spear.
[She is] radiant as lightning, three-eyed, and likewise destroying enemies.
Now, regarding the *puraścaraṇa*: having recited [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times, at the end, one should offer oblations with *bilva* leaves and *hayārija* (Arjuna tree) flowers. (12.38)

A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with dhātrī fruits, bhṛṅgarāja, and kuśa grass in the tenth part [of the number of mantras recited]; one should also perform libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth, and provide a meal for the brāhmaṇas.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra is fit to perform the ritual applications. Now follows the Śyāmalā-mantra.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) which bestows perfect accomplishment. (12.40)
Having first uttered "Oṃ Ai Glau Ai Namaḥ," and then "Bhagavati," [one should recite] the pair "Vartali Varahi" and "Varahamukhi Abhavam. (12.41)
Glau! Homage to Andhā and Andhinī, to Rundhā and Rundhinī;
homage to Bhañjā and Bhañjinī, to Mohā and Mohinī.
Oṃ, namas-stambhe, stambhinī, namaḥ, ai, glau, and vāgbhava—by this, one shall cause all the wicked and malicious beings to fall silent with their speech. (12.43)
The mind, eyes, mouth, gait, tongue, and the two pillars—quickly bring them under control, *kuru kuru ai glau ai*, with the four *ṭha*s. (12.44)
"HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ"—this mantra is remembered as consisting of the syllables of the Vedic Rudra;
Śiva is its sage (ṛṣi), Jagatī its meter (chandas), and the goddess Vārtālikā its deity (devatā). (12.45)
The six limbs of Vārāhya are as follows: Vārtālī is remembered as the heart;
the head of Vārāhya is proclaimed [as the head], and Vārāhamukhī is the crest-lock (śikhā).
Andhe andhini, varma is declared; rundhe rundhini protects the eyes.
Bhañje bhañjini shall be the weapon-mantra; thereafter, one should meditate upon Caṇḍikā.

Now, for the meditation: [One should visualize her] seated upon a corpse on the pericarp of a red lotus, her neck radiant with a garland of severed heads, blue in complexion, and holding [attributes] in her hands. (12.48)
She holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as a pestle, a plow, and likewise a boon-granting gesture;
she has the face of a boar, high breasts, three eyes, and wears crimson garments. (12.49)
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra a thousand times; one should offer oblations with *bandhūka* flowers and sesame seeds—thus [it is said].
Now follows the mantra of Svapnavārāhī:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Vārāhī, known as Svapna. (12.50)
Oṃ hrīḥ! Homage to Vārāhīghorā, joined with the dream [syllable] and the visarga, followed by two *ṭha*s and ending with the wife of fire (svāhā); this is the fifteen-syllable mantra. (12.51)
The sage of this [mantra] is declared to be Īśvara; Jagatī is said to be its meter;
the deity is Svapnavārāhī; and the seed-syllable is proclaimed to be the Tāra (Om). || 12.52 ||
The power (śakti) is declared to be Hṛllekhā, and the two syllables "Ṭha" are considered the peg (kīlaka). Now, the meditation:
Then one should meditate upon her who is dark as a rain-cloud, three-eyed, and with uplifted breasts. (12.53)
One should meditate on Kolāsyā and Candrabhālā, who lifted up the earth with their tusks;
they hold a sword and a goad in their right hands, and a shield and a noose in their left hands.
And one should visualize Kolāsyā mounted upon a horse, adorned with various ornaments.
Now follows the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with blue lotuses and sesame seeds in the tenth part of that number.
Now follows the mantra of Indrāṇī.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain Indrāṇī, who bestows lost sovereignty.
"Indrāṇyai namaḥ" is declared to be the six-syllabled mantra. (12.56)
The Guru is the Sage; the Gāyatrī is the metre; the Goddess Indravallabhā is the deity;
"I" is the seed-syllable; "Indraṇī" is the power; and "Namaḥ" is said to be the pin. || 12-57 ||
Now, the meditation:

[She] has in her hands the vajra, noose, varada mudrā, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is clothed in dark blue garments; she stands with a shadow like that of a four-tusked elephant; she possesses a golden luster. (12.58)
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times and perform oblations with *mālatī* flowers.
For the sake of attaining a kingdom, one should likewise offer oblations with the wood of royal trees (*rājavṛkṣaka*) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). (12.59)
Now, the mantra of Cāmuṇḍā is found in another tantra:
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, [one says] "Cāmuṇḍā" followed by the dative suffix (ṅe), and ending with "namaḥ"; this mantra, consisting of seven syllables, accomplishes all aims. (12.60)
Śiva is the sage, Gāyatrī is the meter, and Cāmuṇḍā is the deity of this [mantra]; by repeating the syllables of the mantra twice, the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed.
Now, the meditation: She is dark-complexioned like the petal of a blue lotus and endowed with four arms;
she holds a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) and a crescent-shaped sword (candrahāsa) in her right hands. (12.62)
In her left hands she holds a shield and a noose, and above them, she likewise holds a garland of severed heads; she is clothed in a tiger skin.
She was lean-limbed with long fangs, exceedingly tall and most terrifying;
her tongue was lolling, her sunken eyes were red, and her form was fearsome to behold.
Seated upon a headless trunk (kabandha) as her vehicle, with ears and mouth spread wide;
now follows the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and perform the ten-part oblation with offerings soaked in honey.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of milk-rice; then the mantra will become effective.
Now, regarding the Mahālakṣmī mantra, it is stated in that same source: "Having extracted the *māyā* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*), one should then extract one's own seed-syllable. (12.66)
Then follows the eight-syllabled mantra: *ṅentā mahālakṣmīr namo’ntaḥ*.
Śiva is declared to be its sage (*ṛṣi*), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (*chandas*). (12.67)
The deity is Mahālakṣmī; the six-limbed [protection] is performed with the syllables of the mantra.
(p. 1137) Now, the visualization: Her limbs are radiant with a golden hue, she has three eyes, and she is borne by a lion. (12.68)
The goddess has a slight smile, her eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus;
she is endowed with sixteen arms and adorned with all ornaments.
Holding a sword, a bell, an arrow, a thread, a goad, a trident, and a lotus in her right hands, she bestows boons upon those who are protectorless.
Likewise, with his left lotus-hands, he holds a shield, a ḍiṇḍima drum,
a bow, a water-pot, a serpent-noose, a skull-cup, a book, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Blazing with splendors, she is exceedingly delightful.
Now, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and perform the *daśāṃśa* (tenth-part) offering with oblations soaked in honey. (12.72)
One should perform the fire-oblation with milk-rice (*pāyasa*); thus the mantra becomes perfected.
This concludes the section on the Eight Mothers (*Aṣṭamātṛkā*).
Now follows the mantra of Gorakṣanātha.
In the Kalpadrumatantra, Garga said: "Now I shall proclaim the mantra; listen, O delighter of the Yadus. (12.73)
The heroic practitioners, endowed with faith, recite those mantras;
by the command of Śiva, accomplishment indeed swiftly comes to those practitioners. (12.74)
Likewise:
"By chanting the mantra of Gorakṣa, a man shall become a lord of yogis;
without the mantra of Gorakṣa, the perfection of yoga does not arise. (12.75)
By the grace of Gorakṣa, one shall accomplish all undertakings.
The mantras are as follows:
Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ goḥ gorakṣa huḥ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ goḥ gorakṣa huḥ huḥ nirañjanātmane hūḥ phaṭ svāhā | oṃ śrīḥ goḥ hrīḥ haḥ hāḥ gorakṣanāthāya nirañjanātmane haḥ saḥ phaṭ hasaḥ |
Thus are the four mantras. Now the Gāyatrī: Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! We know the seed-syllable of the Cow; we meditate upon Gorakṣa; may Nirañjana inspire us.
Now, the seer and so forth for the mantra of Gorakṣanātha: Bṛhadāraṇyaka is the sage (muni). || 12-76 ||
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is the Lord known as Gorakṣa.
The ritual placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) is as follows:
*Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ goḥ, salutation to Gorakṣanātha with both thumbs*, and so forth.
Now, regarding meditation: [He is] like pure crystal, with matted locks and three eyes. (12.77)
Stainless, formless, free from conceptual construction, and free from affliction.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*): having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand plus one hundred times, the practitioner, with a purified mind, [attains success]. (12.78)
One should accomplish all tasks; there is no need for deliberation here.
This is especially true for the man who constantly maintains this mantra. (12.79)
He attains perfection in yoga through the grace of Gorakṣa.
Now, regarding the mantra of Śītalā (in the Merutantra):
I shall now declare that which is the washerwoman of Maheśa’s garments. (12.80)
She is renowned as Śītalā and Cipiṭeśvarī by means of Masūrī.
*Tāra*, *Māyā*, *Ramā*, *Śītalāyai*, and *Hṛt* constitute the nine-syllable mantra. (12.81)
In the *Yāmala*, however, it is stated: "The eight-syllable mantra consists of *māyā* (hrīṃ), *śrī*, *śītalā*, ending with *ṅe*, and ending with the heart [seed-syllable]. (In the *Meru*).
The sage is Upamanyu, the metre is Bṛhatī, and the deity is Śītalā;
the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed with the two seed-syllables of Trapu and Lakṣmī, joined with the six long vowels.
Now, regarding meditation (as found in the *Yāmala* and other texts):
I bow to the goddess Śītalā, who is mounted upon a donkey, naked, holding a broom and a water-pot, and whose head is adorned with a winnowing basket. (12.83)
One should meditate upon the goddess Śītalā, mounted on a donkey, naked,
holding a broom and a winnowing basket in her hands, and worshipped with red flowers and snow. || 12-84 ||

One should worship the goddess within a triangle, visualizing her as having a head wrapped in a cloth bundle stained with oil, filth, and other impurities, and possessing a complexion like that of kodrava grain or lentils.
One should place the Śarāvikā [seeds] in the corners and the eight Bhairavas in the outer enclosure (bhūpura).
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with milk-rice (pāyasa) in a tenth part of that number.
Having performed the fire oblation, the libations, and other rites, the perfection of the mantra arises.
He who stands in water reaching up to his navel and recites the mantra a thousand times [attains this]. (12.87)
By that [application], even severe boils are destroyed in that very instant.
In the lineage of one by whom this mantra has been mastered, no smallpox shall ever appear. (12.88)
In that house where the ashes consecrated by him are present, she indeed does not [dwell].
This mantra for the husband is also stated in that very place:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme mantra of her husband. (12.89)
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *prāsādabījaṃ* (Hrīṃ), *ya*, *va*, *vyomavyāpine*, and *dviṭhaḥ* (Svāhā).
This eleven-syllable mantra is for the rites of placement (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*arcana*), and so forth. (12.90)
It should be known that the preliminary rite (*puraskriyā*) consists of one hundred thousand and five thousand recitations, like those for the *Prāsāda* mantra;
one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) ten times that number, and thereafter perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites. (12.91)
Thus ends the section on Śītalā.
Now, the worship diagrams (*pūjā-yantras*) of the aforementioned deities are presented.
Among them, first is the diagram of Vighnarāja (from the *Merutantra*).
On a pedestal made of *śrīparṇī* wood and other materials, one should fashion a beautiful triple square with four gates using saffron and similar substances. (12.92)
In the center of that, one should construct the eight-petaled worship-seat (pīṭha) of Gaṇeśa.
Now, the Lakṣmī-Gaṇeśa yantra is described right there:
two eight-petaled lotuses, radiant with pericarp and filaments. (12.93)
Provided with four gates and surrounded by three squares, [it consists of] Śakti, Gaṇeśa, Kṣiprasāda, Hara, Ambā, and Haridrā; this is the Gaṇeśa yantra, similar to the Vighnarāja yantra.
Now, the Mahāgaṇapati yantra is described in that same place:
In the previously mentioned [set of] dharmas and so forth, which are conceived as possessing the nine powers such as intensity and the rest.
The worship diagram of Gaṇeśa is said to be a lotus of the Mātṛkās,
provided with four gates and surrounded by three squares.
In its pericarp is a hexagon, and within that, a triangle;

this is the Yantra of Virañcigaṇanāyaka, similar to the Yantra of Vighnarāja. The Yantra of Vakratuṇḍa is like the Yantra of Lakṣmīgaṇeśa; likewise, the two following [Yantras] are also equal to those of Vighnarāja.
Now, the Sūrya Yantra (according to the Saurapaddhati):
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus, and outside of that, one should draw another eight-petalled lotus.
Then, outside of that square, this is known as the solar yantra;
(according to the *Mahākramārcanapaddhati*), there is an eight-petaled lotus in the center, and beyond that, eight peaks. (12.97)
