It has been stated: "The lotus indeed has twelve spokes and four gates. In some places, however, only an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by a square is mentioned;
in others, a twelve-petaled lotus is mentioned.
Now, regarding the Viṣṇu-yantra in that very place:
one should draw an eight-petalled lotus, radiant with a pericarp and filaments, surrounded on the outside by a square; this is the worship-altar of the Slayer of Madhu.
Now, the fish-mechanism (*matsyayantra*):
One should draw a six-petaled lotus, and outside of that, a four-petaled one;
outside of that, however, a seven-petaled one, and outside of that, one should draw an eight-petaled one. (12.99)
Then, outside of that, is a fourteen-petaled [lotus], and beyond that, a sixteen-petaled one;
outside of that is an eight-petaled [lotus], and beyond that, a square.
The tortoise diagram (*kūrmayantra*), however, is simply an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by a square enclosure.
Now, regarding the boar diagram (*varāhayantra*) [in the *Prapañcasāra*]:
having duly fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with a radiant pericarp, according to the rules...
One should worship the Boar there for the sake of accomplishment in a mandala resembling a thousand suns.
Now, the Nṛsiṃha Yantra (from the Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā):
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments.
Outside of that, an eight-leaved [lotus] should be drawn, and outside of that as well, a sixteen-leaved one. (12.102)
Then, outside of that, is the four-cornered *yantra* of the glorious Nṛsiṃha.
However, elsewhere it is stated that the previously mentioned Viṣṇu-yantra itself is the Śrī-Nṛsiṃha-yantra. Now, the Vāmana-yantra.
Having drawn a six-petalled lotus, one should draw a sixteen-petalled one outside of it.
Outside of that is an eight-petaled lotus, and outside of that a twelve-petaled one;
beyond that is an eight-petaled lotus, and outside of that are three concentric enclosures (bhūpuras).

p. 1142) Now, the Paraśurāmayantra: First, one should draw a four-petalled lotus; outside of that, an eight-petalled one; then, outside of that, an eight-petalled one; and outside of that, a ten-petalled one. (12.105)
Outside of that is a twelve-spoked wheel, and outside of that is a sixteen-spoked one;
outside of that is a pair of earth-fortresses (bhūpura) adorned with four gates.
Now, the Yantra of Raghunātha:
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp radiant with six triangles; furthermore, one should draw another eight-petalled lotus outside, beyond the three circles. (12.107)
Outside of that is a twelve-petaled lotus, and outside of that is a sixteen-petaled one;
outside of that is a row of teeth-leaves, surrounded by three enclosures of earth-fortresses.
On this point, some say:
"Just as there is a distinction between the body and the self, so too is there a distinction between the mantra and the deity;
therefore, having written the great mantra upon the seat (pīṭha), one should worship it there."

They say that according to the words of Vasiṣṭha, even on this *saparyāyantra*, one should write the syllables of the mantra as prescribed for the *sādhāraṇayantra* in their proper places and worship Śrī Rāma. However, the method of writing the mantra on the *dhāraṇayantra* is stated in the *Rāmatāpinī*: as follows.
Having drawn a container consisting of three lines, one should write two *tāra*s (oṃ-kāras) in the center.
Having written the seed-syllable in the center of that, one should write the object of accomplishment (sādhya) below it;
[the name of] the object should be in the accusative case, and likewise the practitioner (sādhaka) above it in the genitive case. || 12.110 ||
One should draw two *kuru*s on its sides with the syllable *ramā* (*rī*) between them;
one who possesses intelligence and prosperity should encircle all of that with two *praṇavas*. (12.111)
In the six long-sided hexagons, one should write the seed-syllables beginning with the heart-mantra;
on the sides of the corners, one should write *ramā* and *māyā*, and at their tips, one should inscribe *anaṅga*.
One should write the syllable *krodha* within the corners of the triangles surrounding the mantra;
then, one should draw three circles with eight petals upon the lotus and inscribe the vowels thereon. (12.113)
Then, one should write the *vagaṣṭika* [mantra] upon the filaments and the eight petals; therein, one should inscribe the syllables of the *mālāmantra* forty-five times. (12.114)
Having thus written the five syllables at the front, one should again draw an eight-petaled lotus;
upon those petals, one should write the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa, and the syllable *Ramā* in its pericarp.
Outside of that, one should draw a twelve-petaled lotus for the twelve-syllable mantra:
"Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," which is imperishable.
One should inscribe the letters from *ā* to *kṣa* in a circular form upon the filaments;
outside of that, one should draw a sixteen-petalled lotus, and upon its filaments, the syllable *hriḥ*.

The practitioner of mantra should inscribe the twelve-syllable mantra, conjoined with armor (*varma*), weapons (*astra*), and delight (*rati*), upon the petals; he should also write the mantras of Śrī, Rajā, and the others in the junctions between them.
One should correctly write the syllables *hṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, *ḷ*, *ṣṛ*, and *jṛ* outside of that;
[this is] the great lotus in the twelve-spoked [mandala], conjoined with the *nāda* and *bindu*. (12.119)
One should carefully inscribe the syllables of the king of mantras upon those petals;
likewise, one should meditate upon the eight Vasus and the eleven Rudras.
With the twelfth [syllable], one worships Dhātṛ and Vaṣaṭkāra outside of that;
then there is the earth-pavilion, enriched with vajras and tridents, and provided with three lines.

Having thus drawn the mandala, complete with its gates, adorned with the [nine] heaps and so forth, and joined by the hooded serpents, one should [place offerings] in its cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should likewise draw the Nārasiṃha and Vārāha [mantras], as well as the two mantras,
joined with the peak-syllable (kūṭa), the letter ra, the favoring moon (anugraha-indu), the nasal sound (nāda), the power (śakti), and so forth.
That which is known as Nṛsiṃha for the rite of slaying the planets is the boar-seed mantra (Śaukara), formed with the final letter, Arghīśa, Vyoman, Bindu, and Nāda. (12.124)
And here, the *hūṃ* syllable is the seed-mantra of Rāma; the garland-mantra is now proclaimed as follows:
the *tāra* (oṃ), the salutation (*namaḥ*), the sleep-seed (*hrīṃ*), the memory-seed (*smṛtiḥ*), the Veda-seed (*vedam*), and the desire-seed (*kāmikā*). (12.125)
Accompanied by Rudra, adorned with fire, intellect, and the gods;
then Dīrghā joined with Krūra, Āhlādinī, and likewise Dīrghā with Samānadā.
Kṣudhā, Krodhinī, Amoghā, and Viśvā, as well as Medhā; furthermore, Yuktā, Dīrghā, Jvālinī, Sūkṣmā, and Mṛtyurūpiṇī. (12.127)
Sapratiṣṭhā, Ahlādinī, Tvak, Kṣveḍa, Prīti, and Sāmarā;
Jyotis, Tīkṣṇā conjoined with Agni, Śvetā conjoined with Anusvāra. (12.128)

The *kāmikā* [syllable] ends with the fifth [vowel], ending with *sta*, ending with *nta*, and then ending with *dhā*; likewise, ending with *sa* and *na*, joined with a long vowel, [is] *vāyu* joined with *sūkṣma*, [and] *viṣā*.
Kāmikā joined with Kāmika, then Rudra joined with Asthira; Tāpinī joined with Dīrgha, Bhū, Anīla, Anantaga, and Anala. (12–130)

Time is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa; it is the vital breath (prāṇa), water, joined with knowledge (vidyā). It is yellow, as well as delight (rati), ending with the letter *la*, joined with the womb (yoni), and likewise with obeisance (nati). || 12-131 ||
Consisting of forty-seven syllables, it is within the qualities yet itself devoid of qualities;
one should write this for Rāma, consecrated in the kingdom, according to the stated sequence.
This all-encompassing yantra, previously described and practiced by the sages, grants liberation to its practitioners and increases their lifespan and health. (12–133)
It grants sons to those who are childless; indeed, what need is there for further elaboration?
For here, they duly obtain even dharma and the other goals of life in an instant.
This supreme secret is difficult even for the Lord to traverse;
this yantra has been fully described, and it must not be given to an ordinary person.
The yantra for Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma is indeed the same as the previously mentioned Viṣṇu-yantra.
The Buddha-yantra, however, is a lotus with thirty-two petals surrounded by a square enclosure (bhūpura).
Having meditated thus, one should worship in the lotus consisting of thirty-two petals.
Thus, according to the statement in the *Meru-tantra*:
"The Viṣṇu-yantra is indeed the Kalki-yanttra;
the Hayagrīva-yanttra and others are also the Viṣṇu-yanttra itself."
The Gopālasundarīyantra is the Śrīcakra, which will be described further ahead.
Now, the Śivayantra (in the Prapañcasāra):
It is surrounded by eight petals, three circles, the zodiac signs, paths, and kalpataru trees. (12-136)
Having prepared the mandala, one should worship the Trident-bearer with the seat-mantra and the nine Śaktis.

In some cases, however, the Śaiva yantra is said to consist of three eight-petaled lotuses surrounded by three enclosures of squares (bhūpura). One should draw [the central lotus] shining with a pericarp, filaments, and eight petals. (12–137)
It is provided with four gates and surrounded by three squares—thus [it is described].
In the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*:
"Within the three outer squares, one should draw three eight-petaled lotuses;
one should arrange filaments on the first petals and a bindu in the center. (12.138)
Now, regarding the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Yantra (in the Merutantra): "Endowed with three lotuses, provided with three subterranean chambers, and possessed of four gates... [and so forth].
Now, regarding the mantra and yantra of the Pāśupata weapon, right there:
having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments. (12–139)
Provided with four gates and surrounded by three squares—this is the *vaṭuka*-yantra; there, on the Śaiva pedestal, one should worship the God within the eight-petalled inner void. (12–140)

An upward-pointing triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and surrounded by a square—this is the *kṣetrapāla* yantra. On that very same [lotus], one should worship on the Śaiva pedestal, which has eight petals adorned with the vowels of the directions. (12–141)
Now, regarding the Bhavānī yantra in another tantra:
Having first drawn a triangle, outside of that an eight-petaled lotus, and also a square enclosure (bhūpura) outside of that, one should worship the mantra of Bhavānī. (12–142)
This very triangle, when empty, is another yantra.

As for the Garuḍa-yantra, it is indeed the Mātṛkā-yantra which is about to be described, according to the statement in the *Merutantra*: "One should worship Garuḍa, whose form is the Vedas, within the Mātṛkā-lotus."
The Kārttavīrya yantra is indeed the same as the Viṣṇu yantra mentioned previously.
Regarding the specific procedure for optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*), it is stated in the *Merutantra*:
"Now, therefore, the optional worship shall be described according to the Southern Path."
On a pure ground, one should draw the yantra with the eight fragrances; that is what is taught.
One should draw a ten-petalled lotus and inscribe [the seed-syllables] within the pericarp;
on the petals, one should inscribe the syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), namely *plauḥ*, *klīm*, and *om*.
One should then write the nine seed-syllables of the mantra, as well as the ten syllables beginning with *phaṭ*, within other yantras of that very mantra. (12–145)
One should write the letters śa, ṣa, sa, and ha, as well as the vowels, twice each upon the filaments;
one should then encircle them with the letters beginning with ka, excluding śa, ṣa, sa, and ha.
Outside of that, one should enclose a square with the colors of the elements;
these are air, fire, earth, water, and space, according to the distinction of the desired aim.

There are five short vowels, five long vowels, and five beginning with *e*; likewise, there are five groups of five consonants starting with *ya*, followed by *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *ra*, and *ha* in sequence. (12–148)
For immobilization, one uses earthy [mantras]; for pacification, watery; for subjugation, fiery; for eradication, airy; and for causing enmity, also ethereal.

For killing, one should use fiery [mantras]; for pacification, watery ones; and for nourishment, earthy ones. In this yantra, which is a water-filled jar, one should worship the King (the deity). (12.150)
Having touched the water-pot, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times and sprinkle [the water] upon it;
then the person to be treated will become possessed of sons and free from disease. || 12-151 ||
He shall be illustrious and long-lived, possessed of a virtuous wife who brings him joy;
he shall also be perfected in speech, radiant, majestic, and one who has conquered his senses.
One who has encountered an attack by enemies— whether in a village, a pavilion, or a city—
should install this yantra for the sake of removing the fear of foes.
Now I shall describe the various types of yantras for those who follow the left-hand path; listen to that.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus with the name of the target (*sādhya*) in the center, along with the syllable *phroḥ*. (12–155)

One should write the two [syllables] *yau* at the beginning and end of that [mantra], and the eight seed-syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the petals; furthermore, *phaṭ* should be written on the final petal.
On another petal, one should write the remaining letters at the end; and on the filaments, one should write the vowels in pairs, accompanied by the two types of sibilants.
And outside those two circles, one should place the letters beginning with *ka* within the path (*vīthi*) between them;
[the ground] is square, provided with eight vajras, and devoid of the sibilants (*ūṣman*). || 12–158 ||
Outside of that, one should draw there the figures of the elements as before;
another jar for the purpose of bathing should be brought, as previously described.
Now, the Hanumat Yantra is described in another Tantra:
"One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, radiant with a pericarp and filaments; then, having drawn a square enclosure (bhūpura) outside of that, one should worship therein. (12.160)
Now, regarding the *smarayantra* in that very context:
Then the wise one should draw an auspicious eight-petaled lotus diagram;
outside of that, a sixteen-petaled one, joined with a square. (12–161)
(p. 1148) Now, the *mātṛkāyantra* (according to the *Śāradā-tantra*):

Upon the moon of the void (*vyomendu*), the pericarp consists of the letters of the tongue (*rasanārṇa*); it has a shimmering filament formed by pairs of vowels (*ac*), and within the yantra, there are the three groups beginning with the letters *ya*, *śa*, and *la*, along with the five groups [of consonants], arranged in sequence.

In this [mandala], worship that deity whose nature consists of the phonemes—a lotus situated within the three quarters (āśās), surrounded by the city of the earth (kṣoṇīpura) joined with the letters *la* and *laṅgali*. 12.162.

*Vyoma* is the letter *ha*; *indu* is the letter *sa*; *au* is its own form; the letter of the tongue (*rasanārṇa*) is the *visarga*. Thus, it becomes *hsauḥ*. Regarding "in the quarters" (*āśāsu*) and so forth: "in the quarters" means in the cardinal directions; "in the corners" (*asriṣu*) means in the intermediate points. *Lānta* is the letter *va*; *lāṅgalī* is the letter *ṭha*. Thus, the meaning is that in the four directions and in the corners joined with *va*, [the letters] are joined with *ṭha*. The rest is clear.
As for the *bhūtalipi* yantra, it is stated in the *Śāradā-ṭīkā* that there is a sixteen-petaled lotus above an eight-petaled one, and above that, a square provided with four gates.
Next is the yantra for the ritual of Śyāmā according to the *Kālītantra*:
Having first inscribed a triangle, one should then place another triangle outside it;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should indeed draw three excellent triangles.
Then, having drawn a circle, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus;
having drawn another circle according to the rule, one should then draw a single outer square enclosure.
Another yantra is described in the Kumārīkalpa:
"Having first laid out a triangle, one should place another triangle outside it;
having drawn a triangle on the exterior, one should place a hexagon outside that. (12.165)
In the center, however, is the Vaindava-cakra, adorned with the seed-syllable;
outside the hexagon is a lotus, joined with a single enclosure of walls.
Knowing this, one attains liberation through this yantra; of this there is no doubt.
[It consists of] an eight-petaled lotus and a square enclosure (bhūpura) provided with four gates. As it is stated in the Bhairavatantra:
With the two [lines of] Śakti and Agni, one should draw a hexagon; therein, one should write the three Śaktis.
Then, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus on the ground, provided with four gates.

Regarding the phrase "by means of Śakti and Agni": *Śakti* is a downward-facing triangle; *Agni* is an upward-facing triangle. The meaning is that once a hexagon has been formed by these two, one should draw three downward-facing triangles within it or in its center.
Likewise: [in] a vessel made of gold or other materials, smeared with red sandalwood...
Or it may be smeared with *svayambhūkusuma*, or otherwise smeared with red [pigment], being pure.
The meaning is that the diagram (*yantra*) should be drawn by a *vīra* with a stylus made of red sandalwood or a golden rod,
upon a surface smeared with red sandalwood and adorned with self-arisen flowers (*svayambhukusuma*) and the like;
thus it is stated in the *Kumārīkalpa*.
One should engrave this, however, upon copper smeared with the *kuṇḍagola* substance.
In the *Svatantra-tantra*, it is said: "Endowed with self-arisen flowers and attended by those reddened with saffron;
the 'self-arisen flower' consists of [the substances] produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, along with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and agallochum (*aguru*). (12.170)
Saffron, musk, wine,
and sandalwood— this fragrance is proclaimed to be always dear to Caṇḍikā.

With this application of fragrances, one should draw the sequence of the wheel of the womb (yonicakrakrama) in a copper vessel, a skull, or one fashioned from wood in a cremation ground. (From the *Muṇḍamālā*) 12.172.
Or on a Saturday or a Tuesday, when a hero has met his death,
the discus should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite upon gold, silver, or iron.
In this case as well, it should be understood that the injunctions regarding the skull-cup and other implements refer to the *vīra* [state].
Now, the Guhyakālī yantra (from the Mahākālasaṃhitā) is endowed with nine corners, divided by three spokes and five spokes, together with the bindu.
Thereafter, within the space between the two circles, one should draw an eight-spoked wheel. || 12-174 ||
Then, it should be provided with the forms of the sun, the earth, the king, and the lotus,
both internally and externally, and further endowed with eight thunderbolts.
It is endowed with eight tridents and eight severed heads, surrounded by a cremation ground filled with flames of fire, and at its base, it is encircled by a flow of blood. (12.176)
O Goddess, this king of yantras has been prepared for worship.
Bharata, Cyavana, Hārīta, and Javālaka [are its guardians]. (12.177)
And these five persons, being skillful, worship Ambikā with this [mantra];
the *bindu* resides within the five-spoked, six-cornered, three-cornered, and nine-cornered [diagrams]. (12.178)
O Dear One, it is joined with a lotus of sixteen petals accompanied by eight circles; at the end, it is again endowed with circles as before—this is the complete [mandala]. (12.179)
O lady of beautiful countenance, she is worthy of worship by Rāma, Yakṣeśa, and Nahuṣa.
Now, regarding the *kāmakalāyantra* in that very context: "I shall proclaim her *yantra*; fix your mind thereon, O beloved. (12.180)
Within the *bhūpura* (the outer square), one should fashion a lotus enriched with eight petals,
complete with filaments and a pericarp in its center.
Indeed, there should be three separate triangles within the pericarp;
one should write the three auspicious seed-syllables on the corners of the triangle outside.
The seed-syllable of Māyā should be on the left, while the seed-syllable of Krodha is on the right;
having indicated the noose below, the syllable of Kandarpa is in the middle.
The Goddess resides within that; everything is established therein.
O Great Goddess, this is the Yantra that bestows the fruits of all desires. (12.184)
All other yantras are not worth even a sixteenth part of this one.
Now, regarding the Śmaśānakālī-yatra (in the *Svatantra-tantra*):
there is an eight-petalled lotus within a circle, and outside of that, the eight groups of consonants (*aṣṭakavarga*). 12–185.
One should first draw four groups of four [squares] upon the ground, extending from the eastern edge to the northern edge; in the center, one should worship the Goddess.
(p. 1151) Now, regarding the Yantra of the Fortune of Success (*siddhilakṣmī*) in the *Kālānala-tantra*:
"O twice-born one, listen as I describe the layout of the Yantra of the Fortune of Success:
it is a square with four gates, encircled by three circles. (12.181)
One should draw an eight-spoked [wheel], then a twelve-petaled one, and again an eight-petaled one;
within the center of the hexagon, one should contemplate a triangle and therein a bindu.
Now, one should draw the Tārāyantra (in the Pheravīya tradition): an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp radiant with triangles.
Having placed the Māyā syllable on the eastern petal, one should place the second seed-syllable on the southern petal.
Likewise, one should then write the syllable *phaṭ* in the north and the west;
having written the seed-syllable in the center— [iti].
(In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*):
With cow-dung containing its [natural] yoni, one should prepare a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus. (12.184)
The Bhūpura (earth-city) is enriched with eight jewels and vajras; this is the Yantra consisting of Ekajaṭā. (From the Merutantra:
Then one should worship her upon the pedestal, on a lotus whose pericarp is a hexagon. (12.185)
First, the pedestal (pīṭha), together with its Śakti, should be worshipped within the enclosure of the earth-chamber (dharāgṛha).
For these two, the city of the earth (*bhūpura*) is said to be superior.
Likewise, there is an option regarding the triangle and the hexagon in the *Nīlatantra*:
"Upon the moon in the sky, [is the lotus] whose pericarp has six syllables, with filaments shimmering from the pairs of vowels."

This supreme yantra of the Blue-Body (Nīlatanu), which bestows the accomplishment of all aims, is described as having beautiful petals blooming in groups, encircled by the abode of the Earth (the square), and graced by corners shining with the color of the lord of stars (the moon). || 12-186 ||
And this *Nīlasarasvatīyantra* is so called because it is designated as "the blue-bodied" (*nīlatanu*).

According to the masters of the tradition, the *yantra* mentioned in the *Phetkāriṇītantra* belongs to Ekajaṭā, while that mentioned in the *Pheravīya-merutantra* belongs to Tārā. However, some maintain that the *dhāraṇāyantra* beginning with "in the moon of the sky" (*vyomendu*) and so forth has been stated [here], and they assert that the previously mentioned *yantras* are common to Tārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī.

(Matsyasūkta) 12.187: In a ritual procedure where no specific diagram has been mentioned, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus within a circle; it should have a hexagonal pericarp and be adorned with four gates.

Now, regarding the Śrīyantra (in the *Yāmala*): it consists of a point, a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, two sets of ten petals, a sixteen-petaled lotus joined with an eight-petaled lotus, and a twelve-petaled lotus.
The three circles and the three abodes of the earth constitute the Śrīcakrarāja, which has arisen from the Supreme Deity.
In this yantra, filaments (kesaras) must not be drawn.
O Maheśānī, the Bhairavas, together with the Yoginīs, inflict violence upon him who fashions filaments in this yantra. (12.189)
Thus, according to the statement of Bhūtabhairava,
the fruit of this vision is declared in the *Yāmala*:
"Whatever fruit one might obtain by perfectly performing a hundred sacrifices..."
One obtains that fruit by performing the vision of the Śrīcakra with devotion.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the great sixteen-fold gift and other such acts,
that same fruit one attains by performing the visualization of the Śrīcakra.
Whatever fruit one enjoys by bathing in three and a half million sacred fords (tīrthas),
one obtains that same fruit through devotion by performing the vision of the Śrīcakra.
Now, the fruit of worship:
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the consecration of ten million liṅgas, that fruit one certainly obtains from the worship of the Śrīcakra. (12.193)
Now, regarding the fruit of giving:
whoever, having had a *śrīcakra* fashioned, should give it to a practitioner, by him indeed the entire circle of the earth—with its mountains, forests, and oceans—has been given. (12.194)
Now, regarding this majesty of the water from the feet:
[The merit gained] at Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, Narmadā, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, Godāvarī,
Gomatī, Gaṅgādvāra, Gayā, Prayāga, Badarī, Vārāṇasī, and Sindhu—

The water from the feet of the Śrīcakra is multiplied by thousands of crores of baths at sacred fords within the interior of the vessel of the universe, such as the Revā, Setu, Sarasvatī, and others. (12.195)
Now, the method for constructing this wheel, as taught in another tantra, is demonstrated:
Having drawn a circle with a desired measurement, one should drop a thread through the center so that its two ends touch the eastern and western points; it shall consist of forty-two parts. (12.196)
A line should be drawn from the eastern direction to remove defects;
leaving aside one-sixth part, the first line shall be oriented from south to north.
Then, having set aside five parts, the second [line] should likewise be made;
thereafter, three [parts] should be at a distance from the four corners of the sections. || 12-198 ||
Then, having set aside three parts, the fourth line should be drawn;
then, having set aside two parts from there, the fifth line should be made.
Then, by means of four parts, the sixth line shall likewise be formed;
the seventh shall consist of three parts, and the eighth likewise of four parts.
Having thus laid out the lines by means of five parts for the ninth [line],
there should be an interval of six parts between the first and last lines from the circle.
One should inscribe the names of the nine planets, beginning with the Sun, in their proper sequence;
furthermore, the tips of the lines on both sides must be wiped away.
In both of the two outer [lines], three parts each would be omitted;
five parts would be omitted on the second [line] at both sides.
In this manner, there shall be a wiping away at the tips of the two foremost lines for Śani and Bhauma;
one should carefully erase sixteen parts at the tips of the lines of Budha. (12.204)
One should erase eighteen parts from the two uppermost rows of the Guru,
and likewise, one should erase sixteen parts from both sides of the two uppermost rows of Bhṛgu.
In the case of Rāhu and Ketu, there shall be the removal of one-eighth and one-sixth [of the debt] respectively;
when Venus kisses the tip of the Sun, it is the middle [case], and again when it kisses the tip of the Moon.
When the circle at the tip of Mars touches the center of Ketu, and likewise when the circle at the tip of Mercury touches the center of Rāhu; || 12-207 ||
The two front portions of Jupiter touch the middle of Saturn;
the middle of the circle in the east touches the front of Saturn as well.
In the same manner, he kisses the sun situated at the tip of Rāhu;
likewise, he kisses Mars at the tip of Ketu, and he kisses the moon at the tip of Bhṛgu.
"Having thus drawn the wheel, it shall become exceedingly beautiful"—
this refers to the *bālā* diagram, which is like the *tripurabhairavī* diagram to be described [later].
Another diagram is stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.
Having drawn a triangle, then a circle, and beyond that a pentagon of petals;
again, a six-petaled lotus, and also a circle on the outside.
One should draw eight petals, and also outside of that.
Now, regarding the *bhuvaneśvarī* yantra (*Śāradā-tantra*):
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus on the outside, followed by a circle with sixteen petals;
in the center of the pericarp, one should draw a most beautiful hexagon. (12.211)

One should draw a mandala that is square and possesses four gates. Then, according to the *Śāradā-tantra*, one should draw the Tripurabhairavīyantra, which consists of an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp enriched by nine triangles. (12–212)
Then, one should draw an underground chamber (bhūgṛha) provided with four doors.
Next, O fair-faced one, [one should draw] the Caitanyabhairava yantra, which consists of a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus (*jñānārṇave* 12.213).
One should draw a mandala that is square and has four gates;

this same yantra applies to Bhuvaneśvarī-Bhairavī and Kamaleśvara-Bhairavī as well. The yantra for Sampatpradā-Bhairavī is like that of Tripurabhairavī. The yantra for Kāmeśvara-Bhairavī is like that of Caitanyabhairavī. Now, the yantra for Ṣaṭkūṭā-Bhairavī (from the Jñānārṇava):
O lady of beautiful hips, one should draw her yantra as a triangle enclosed within a casket.
Then one should draw an outer eight-petaled lotus with petals like the sun;
thus one should delineate the mandala as a square with four gates.
Now, regarding the Rudrabhara-vīya yantra in that very same [text]:
"A triangle, a circle, a lotus with eight petals within a circle, and a circle representing the earth-mandala... and so forth.
Now, regarding the Yantra of Chinnamastā (in the Yāmala):
one should first lay out a triangle, and in its center, three mandalas. (12.216)
In the center of that, one should draw a yoni provided with three gates;
outside of that, an eight-petalled lotus, and again, a triad of earth-mandalas.
One should write the *kūrma* seed-syllable in the center of the triangle, accompanied by the syllables *ha* and *sa*.
(In another Tantra:
Now, O Great Goddess, the king of diagrams (*yantrarāja*) of Vairocanī is described. 12-218.
First, a hexagon should be drawn; in its center, a triangle;
then one should place the solar disc, and after that, a square.
Then the preceptor should offer the terrestrial globe, and after that a square;
then he should offer an eight-petaled lotus in its proper place.
Then one should offer the lunar disc, and after that the solar disc;
then one should offer the terrestrial globe, and after that the triple enclosure of the earth. (12.221)
One should place a chisel joined with a vajra-spike in the corner;
one should apply the syllables of the mantra upon the filaments and the pericarp within the triangle.
Thus one should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess Vairocanī above the [syllable] *kāma*.
(In another tantra) I shall describe the *yantra* spoken by Bhairava, which bestows all prosperity. (12.223)
First, a triangle should be drawn, and it should be surrounded by hexagons;
then one should provide three circles that bring about the transformation of the qualities (guṇas).
One should construct three concentric square enclosures provided with vajras and spikes;
then, in the corner regions, one should place the most beautiful ṭaṅkā weapon.
The wise one should draw the auspicious *kartṛkharparaka* in its proper place;
above Rati and Kāma, he should meditate upon the auspicious goddess Vairocanī.
(From the Merutantra:
A triangle, or a hexagon, or an eight-petaled lotus, followed by a square enclosure;
then, the Dhūmāvatīyantra according to another tantra.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by a perimeter of protective enclosures (bhūpura).
Now, regarding the Vagalāmukhīyantra (in the Merutantra):
[It should be drawn] on gold, or silver, or copper, or on birch bark, using camphor, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and saffron. (12-228)
One should diligently draw the yantra with a pen made of gold or silver;
having drawn the yoni in the center, one should then draw a six-cornered figure (ṣaḍasra) outside of it.
Outside of that is an eight-petalled lotus, and outside of that is a sixteen-petalled one;
on the exterior are three squares, adorned with four gates.
Now, regarding the Mātaṅgīyantra in another tantra:
One should draw a beautiful yantra consisting of a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus.
On this seat, one should worship these nine Śaktis in their proper sequence. (12.231) p. 1157)
Now, another yantra (*Merutantra*):
One should draw a triangle and a pentagon; outside, two eight-petalled lotuses, a sixteen-spoked wheel, an eight-petalled lotus, and three earths and three waters. (12.232)

Both of these belong to Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī. As for the Yantra of Rājamātaṅgī, it has already been described previously through her meditation. The same Yantra should also be understood for the various divisions such as Vaśyamātaṅgī and others.
Now, the Yantra of Sumukhī:
a triangle, a pentagon, a circle, and surrounded by eight petals.
And outside of that, a square is declared to be the Sumukhīyantra.
Now, regarding the Lakṣmīyantra (in the Merutantra):

On a pedestal fashioned from Dharma and the other [virtues], adorned with gates and a perimeter wall (*bhūpura*), one should worship this [goddess] upon the pericarp, within the eight petals known as the filaments (*keśara*). (12.234)
A yantra consisting of three eight-petaled lotuses surrounded by a square enclosure is described elsewhere.
Now, the Sarasvatī-yantra is described in another tantra:
"An auspicious eight-petaled lotus should be drawn, surrounded by a square."
O lady of excellent hips, this yantra is proclaimed to belong to Vāgdevī.
The yantra for Tvaritā and Nityaklinnā is like the previously mentioned yantra of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Now, the yantra of Annapūrṇā (in the *Merutantra*):
first a triangle, then a four-petaled lotus, and after that an eight-petaled one.
And the petal of the digit (kalāpatra) and the orb of the earth (bhūvimba) are surrounded by three squares. || 12-236 ||
The *pratyaṅgirā* yantra is like the *annapūrṇā* yantra.
Now, the *kubjikā* yantra:
[it consists of] a bindu, a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus with filaments.
The Yantra of the illustrious Kubjeśvarī consists of three Bhūpuras with a central door.
In another tantra: "A bindu, a triangle, a hexagon, and likewise an eight-petaled lotus;
an eight-petaled [lotus] with the seed-syllables of the Mothers, and an eight-peaked [mountain] together with the outer enclosure. (12.238)
The Gaṅgāyantra is like the Sarasvatīyantra. The Vāgmatīyantra consists of a six-pointed star surrounded by a square enclosure (*bhūpura*).
The Candrayantra consists of two eight-petaled lotuses.
Now, the Bhaumayantra (according to the *Merutantra*):
Having first drawn a triangle, one should then divide it into five parts;
one should mark the third line with two signs at equal intervals.
One should place the two tips of the first line upon the two third marks;
having drawn [a line] from the tip of the second [mark], one should place it upon the two third marks.
The third line, being equal, should then be divided equally;
the fourth [line] is marked by two points, and the fifth by three points.
One should draw the third line at the tip of the first, and the fifth line at the mark of the center;
one should properly join the fourth line to the two marks of the fifth line.
Then the wise one should apply two threads across the pair of fish;
in this way, there will be twenty-one squares perfectly formed.
The yantra for Mercury and the others consists of an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by a square enclosure (bhūpura). Other yantras for them are not written here for fear of prolixity.

The *piṅgalādi-grahamātṛ-yantro* consists of a triangle, a pentagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure. The *indrayantro* has an eight-petaled lotus outside of a six-petaled one. The *agniyantro* is the same; however, there is another form of the fire-mantra consisting of a mere eight-petaled lotus. The *yamayantra* is like the *indrayantro*. The *nairṛtayantra*, however, is an eight-petaled lotus with a pentagon at its center. The *varuṇayantra* has an eight-petaled lotus outside of a six-petaled one. The *vāyuyantra* has three eight-petaled lotuses outside of a six-petaled one. The *kuverayantra* is a mere eight-petaled lotus. The *īśānayantra* is like the *śivayantra*. The *brahmayantro* is a ten-petaled lotus. The *viṣṇuyantra* is itself the *anantayantra*. The *brāhmīyantra* is a sixteen-petaled lotus with a hexagon in its pericarp. The *kaumārīyantra* is an eight-petaled lotus with a pentagon at its center. The *vaiṣṇavīyantra* is an eight-petaled lotus; that very same [mantra] is also the *vārāhīyantra*.

As for the *mālāmantra*, another diagram (*yantra*) described in the *Merutantra* is as follows: [It consists of] a womb (*yoni*), a pentagon, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a hundred-petaled lotus, surrounded by a thousand-petaled lotus and the orb of the earth, and adorned with gateways. (12.244)
One should contemplate this *pīṭha* situated in the midst of Mount Kailāsa.

The *Svapnavārāhī* yantra, consisting of a triangle, a sixteen-petaled lotus, an eight-petaled lotus, and two ten-petaled lotuses, is described in that very [text]. The *Aindrī-Cāmuṇḍā-Mahālakṣmī* yantra consists of an eight-petaled lotus within a hexagon. Furthermore, the *Cāmuṇḍā-mantra-yantra* embodying the nine Durgās is found in another [source]. (p. 1159)
One should draw a triangle surrounded by these mantras, together with a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus.

Outside, there is an auspicious twenty-five-petalled [lotus] surrounded by a square; now, according to the *Merutantra*, the Durgā-yantra consists of two eight-petalled lotuses surrounded by three squares. (12.246)
One should draw [the diagram] provided with four gates using saffron and other substances.
Now, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the yantra, it is said therein:
"First, for the sake of accomplishing the yantra, one should perform the preparatory service (*puraskriyā*) of its mantra. (12.247)
Having performed [the preliminary rites] ten thousand times, one should subsequently proceed with the yantra;
having carefully drawn the yantra upon its proper support with the appropriate materials.
Having invoked that deity there and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
and having meditated upon him, performed the bali offering, recitation, and fire-oblation, one should dismiss the deity.
Repeating it once each time while recollecting that mantra, the wise one [proceeds];
thus, when the yantra has been perfected through japa and other means, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished.
The ritual worship should be performed upon a yantra measuring one thousand digits.
Now, the practice for the *dhāraṇā*-yantra has been stated (in the *Merutantra*).
Next, I shall describe the procedure for the yantra, which is concealed in all tantras. (12–251)
By the mere writing of a perfected [mantra], the success of the yantra is produced;
however, that for which the effect is not yet to come shall occur even when it is perfected. || 12-252 ||
If one has previously seen an evil dream, then one should not have the yantra made; rather, on an auspicious day, the practitioner should worship his chosen deity.
One should sleep on the ground for three days, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and devoted to recitation.
"I shall perform this yantra; what will it be like for me, O Lord? (12.252)
O Goddess of gods, having performed this worship as an ancillary part of the dream at the time of dusk, one should draw [the mandala] on the ground for three days. (12.253)
On the third day, at night, just as a dream arises,
so too, having received the command, one should draw [the mandala] upon the ground during a virtuous dream.
Whether in a dream or in a nightmare, one should certainly not perform [the rite];
rather, one should draw it upon a yantra and perform the installation of the life-force (jīvasaṃsthāpana) therein, by which one obtains the fruit.
One should write the word denoting the practitioner (sādhaka) ending in the genitive case above the central seed-syllable;
the word denoting the target (sādhya) ending in the accusative case below it; and the pair of "do" (kuru) syllables on the two sides. (12.256)
The *jīva* of the solar machine (*sūryayantra*) should be written below the middle portion;
one should write each individual syllable of the mantra "Haṃsaḥ So’ham" there.
One should write the two syllables "īd" in the corners beginning with Īśāna and on the right side,
and the two syllables "ud" on the left side, in sequence starting from the eastern direction.

One should write *la*, *ra*, *ma*, *kṣa*, as well as *va*, *ya*, *sa*, and *ha* in the directions starting from the east; [and] between the northeast and the east, one should write *ā* and *hrīḥ*; and between the northwest and the north. (12.259)
In this manner, one should place the seed-syllables of the guardians of the directions (dikpāla) in the ten directions in sequence.
"We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Bestower of Boons; may that Yantra inspire us.
On each cardinal point of this [yantra], one should write three syllables each.
One should surround the mantra for the external installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) everywhere;
thus written, the yantra shall be a bestower of success.
If no specific location is mentioned, one should draw the yantra on birch bark, linen, or a copper plate;
having bound it into a pill, one should wrap it with thread.
One should cast [the yantra] onto gold, silver, or copper covered with lac;
and one should worship that yantra of the deity with the solar mantra (arkamantra) and its seed-syllable (bīja). || 12-263 ||
In its absence, one should perform the worship of the yantra with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Having recited the root mantra one thousand and eight times, one should offer clarified butter as an oblation. (12.264)

Having sprinkled the yantra with that [liquid] by means of its discharge, one should apply it to the head, the arm, or even the throat, for the sake of accomplishing each respective desired object. (12.265)
(From the Merutantra:
Or else, the Bhūtalipi may be worshipped as that which effects the accomplishment of yantras;
by it alone, one shall attain the success of all yantras without any difficulty. (12.266)
Now follows the determination of the Bhūtalipi (according to the Śāradā): "Now I shall declare the Bhūtalipi, which is difficult to obtain even though it is well-guarded;
having obtained which, the sages attained all their desires from Śambhu. (12.267)
The five short vowels are the phonemes of conjunction: Vyoma (Ā), Īra (I), Agni (U), Jala (Ū), and Dharā (Ṛ);
these correspond respectively to the final, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle [consonants]. (12.268)

The letters of the five groups, together with the *va*-ending [consonants] and the white moon [the letter *ma*], constitute what is called the "earth-script" (*bhūtalipi*), consisting of forty-two letters. (12.269)

The five short vowels are *a* and so forth. The four conjunct vowels (*saṃdhi-varṇa*) are *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*. Space is *ha*; fire is *ra*; water is *va*; and earth—the ground—is its seed-syllable, *la*. Regarding the phrase "the end," etc., the word "of the class" (*vargasya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The end of the [first] class is *śa*; the white one is *ṣa*; the moon is *sa*. Likewise: "The first, fifth, and best letters of the classes, joined with the letter *śa*."
These nine Durgās are to be known as beginning with the [letters of the] classes; they are thus remembered. || 12-269 ||

Regarding the phrase "āyaṃvarārṇāḥ": *ā*, *i*, and *aṃbarārṇa* (the letter of the sky) constitute *āyaṃvarārṇāḥ*; this means the letters *a*, *i*, and *ha*. The fifth letters of the classes (*varga*) are *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*. *Śārṇaḥ* refers to the letter *śa*. These letters are the first of the nine classes;
this demonstrates their nature as the "earth-alphabet" (*bhūtalipi*). It is said:
"One should know the letters of the classes of space, air, fire, water, and earth to be distinct."
In the second group there would be no earth, but in the ninth, it would be possessed of water.
"Earth would not exist"—the meaning is that this is because the second letter consists of four letters. The same should be understood for what follows as well.
Likewise:
"Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Aśvins, Prajāpati, and the lords of the directions."
The nine lords of Durgā are remembered as being endowed with the powers of action and the rest.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the metre is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity declared by the virtuous is the supreme Parā herself, the Mistress of the Letters. (12.272)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the six root-syllables together with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), according to the *Merutantra*.
These five groups of five mantra-syllables should begin with the letter *ha* and be devoid of vowels. (12.273)
Now, regarding meditation (*dhyāna*):

"The wise declare that at the root of the tree of letters, one should meditate upon the Goddess within a lotus composed of those [letters]; they say this auspicious tree is eternally composed of phonemes. (Śāradā, 12.274)
The great seed of supreme consciousness has the bindu and nāda as its great roots;
it expands in all directions with the syllables of the earth as its branches. (12.275)
With its own water-like syllables as leaves, it covered the three ages;
blazing with sprouts the color of fire, it was like a celestial tree adorned with jewels.
Illuminating the beauty of his form with flowers radiant as the color of the Maruts,
he is bowed by fruits whose measure is the sky, the supreme refuge of all beings.
He sprinkles the Supreme Goddess with the honey known as supreme nectar,
[a tree] made beautiful by its lofty growth fashioned from the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures.
Consisting directly of Śiva and Śakti, it is the refuge of the three worlds and their shadows;
by taking recourse to this, the wise have attained all their desires. (12.279)
With her three eyes rolling from the intoxication of wine, her head adorned with the crescent moon, and her full, lofty breasts resembling ten million moons emerging from their craters,
she constantly holds in her hands a boon, a rosary, a sacred knowledge, and a skull-cup.
I take refuge in Vāgīśvarī, who is proud of her youth, whose body is inscribed with letters, and who resides in the eastern quarter. || 12-280 ||
Now, regarding the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*):
the wise practitioner should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) one hundred thousand times, recite [the mantra] that many times, and likewise offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds;
he should worship the Goddess daily upon the pedestal previously described. (12.281)
(Also in the *Merutantra*):
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and offered ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
In this way, the Earth-Alphabet (*bhūtalipi*) should be practiced, whereby the perfection of the yantra arises. (12.282)
"A man also becomes capable of worshipping Śrīvidyā.
Thus concludes the *bhūtalipi-puraścaraṇa*.
Now follows the *mātṛkā-nyāsa-puraścaraṇa* (according to the *Śāradā-tantra*).
Having been initiated, one who is composed should perform the placement (nyāsa) a hundred thousand times according to the prescribed path.
The wise one should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times with that same number [of oblations], using sesame seeds soaked in honey;
he should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds and recite the Mātṛkā daily.
Thus concludes the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the placement of the *mātṛkās*.
Now, regarding the seal (*mudrā*) of the three metals, it is said in that same [text]:
"The phonemes are of the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and likewise are the three metals."
Silver is remembered as the moon, gold as the sun, and copper as the sacrificial fire.
The proportions of the metals are specified by the number of the letters beginning with 'Sva' (the vowels);
with those metals, one should have a mudrā fashioned, joined together without being soldered.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times plus one, the practitioner of mantras should then touch it and offer oblations into it;
he should pour clarified butter into it with the previously mentioned number.
Having placed that seal (mudrā) into the jar according to the procedure prescribed for consecration,
one should, with a concentrated mind, invoke the Goddess and worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras).
Having performed the consecration, the Guru should give that ring to the disciplined disciple.
This is a protection that destroys minor ailments, poisons, and fevers. (12.288)
One should provide special protection against beasts of prey, thieves, wild animals, and the like;
by wearing this, a lord of men attains victory in battle. (12.289)

"Having the forms of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni" means that the vowels beginning with *a* have the form of Soma; the consonants from *ka* to *ma*, the "contact letters" (*sparśavarṇa*), have the form of Sūrya; and the "pervasive letters" (*vyāpakavarṇa*) beginning with *ya* have the form of Agni—this is the meaning. "In the same way" means that likewise the three metals also have the forms of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni. He clarifies this very point with the words beginning with "silver" (*raupya*). "Parts" (*bhāga*) means portions (*aṃśa*).

"By the number of the letters beginning with the vowels" means: sixteen for silver, twenty-five for gold, and ten parts for copper. "Uncombined yet united" means: uncombined, having not attained a single uniform form; yet united, being mutually connected.
"Having recited" (saṃjapya) refers here specifically to the recitation of the letters of the Mātṛkā.

"In that [mudrā] one should perform the *saṃpāta*": the meaning is that, having uttered "Vāha," one should pour the *saṃpāta*-clarified butter into that mudrā. "By the path stated for the consecration" means by the method described for the optional (*kāmya*) consecration.
The optional consecration, however, is found in that very same [text].
Having fashioned the lotus as previously described and having established the pitcher as before,
the practitioner of mantra should fill it with the decoction of milky trees according to the prescribed rule.
Having stirred the eight fragrances within this [vessel] endowed with the nine gems,
one should invoke and worship the Goddess Mātṛkā according to the path described.
One should sprinkle the beloved man with a thousand prepared waters on a Sunday at an auspicious moment, and one should also feed the Brahmins. (12.292)
Filled with devotion, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to one's own capacity;
for this specifically brings about protection and the pacification of malice.
"This consecration, which generates sovereignty for men and grants the attainment of all good fortune,
is said to be the supreme means of enchanting the entire universe."
"The Goddess Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī" means:

"Having consecrated [her]"—the consecration (abhiṣeka), however, should be performed with the letters of the Mātṛkā in reverse order. (p. 1165) "One should consecrate her in reverse order until the end of the sādhya, having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (12.294)
Because this is stated in that very same place within another consecration (*abhiṣeka*):
"Now, regarding the *navaratna-mudrā*, in that very same place [it says]:
'The mantra-practitioner should divide the *mātṛkā* into nine groups in their proper order.'"
There are eight vowels each, and the consonants (sparśas) are fivefold, as are the pervasive ones (vyāpaka).
The nine groups have arisen as the planets who are lords of the nine jewels: the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. (12.296)
Ruby, pearl, beautiful coral, emerald, topaz, glittering diamond, sapphire, and auspicious hessonite; || 12-297 ||
One should fashion an auspicious seal from beryl and the nine precious gems;
one should perform all rites such as recitation and fire-offerings according to the path previously described.
For whoever wears this mudrā, the planetary spirits (grahas) shall come under his control;
good fortune attends him, and even prosperity (lakṣmī) shall remain unassailed.
Malevolent spells and acts of treachery perish; all calamities vanish.
Rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, and the like, overwhelmed by fear, do not even look upon him. (12.300)
"Wealth, jewels, and other riches increase higher and higher"—
thus is the *navaratnamudrā*. Now, the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) is described in another Tantra:
Endowed with the state of being a Goddess, one should be intent upon the sixfold ritual placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
In the ritual of the ten vidyās, she is divided into ten distinct forms;
for each one, he should perform the meditation on that respective six-syllable ṛṣi-mantra. (12.302)
O Supreme Goddess, wherever the seer, meter, and so forth are explicitly mentioned, that very [set] is prescribed there; where they are not mentioned, it is as in the case of the Root Deity.
Meditation, the preliminary rites beginning with desire (*chanda*), and the hymn of praise—all these are exactly as for the Goddess. (p.
1166) The *puraścaryā* consists of ten thousand recitations, along with the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) performed according to that sequence. (12.303)

Thus concludes the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the sixfold placement (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*). Now follows the preliminary practice for the hymn of a thousand names (*sahasranāmastava*) and the armor-verse (*kavaca*), in that very same context.
The Lord said:
O Pārvatī, in the hymns of a thousand names as well as in the protective charms (kavacas), that preliminary rite which is prescribed at the beginning of the kavaca must indeed be performed. (12.304)
Where the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is not mentioned, what indeed is prescribed there?
For it is proclaimed that ten thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite for a mere hymn (stotra). (12.305)
This preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is prescribed for the armor of the Thousand Names;
having thus performed the preparatory service, one should perform the oblations and other rites ten times the [required] portion.
O Goddess, libation (tarpaṇa) and purification (mārjana) are proclaimed in some places;
according to the Mahākāla-mata, one should perform them if they are prescribed therein. (12.307)
O Pārvatī, by simply satisfying the Brahmins, everything is accomplished;
likewise, the fire-oblation (havana) as well as the preliminary ritual service (puraścaryā) and so forth should be performed.
O Supreme Goddess, what indeed is the nature of the Thousand Names?
And likewise, O Goddess, what is the form of the Armor (Kavaca) that has been proclaimed?
The dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess is proclaimed as the *brahmarandhra*;
other verses are said to be like hair, and the *ṛṣi* is declared to be the head. (12.310)
O Goddess, the *chandas* (meter) is the mouth, and the deity is the heart;
the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is declared to be the secret, while they know the power (*śakti*) as residing in the words. (12.311)
O Goddess, every limb is indeed proclaimed as a *kīlaka* (stake);
whatever is situated within the hymn, all that takes the form of the hymn. (12.312)
Thus, O Goddess of the gods, has the form of the hymn been proclaimed;
likewise, O Beloved Goddess, having understood the armor (kavaca), one should recite its reading.
O Supreme Goddess, if even one limb is deficient, there will be total destruction.
O Goddess, the praise of the fruit and so forth is designated as an "aṅga" (limb). (12.314)
O Goddess, without the beginning and the end, the fruit is proclaimed to be half;
in this matter, O Goddess, the proof is as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and others are traditionally remembered.
The oblation for the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and others may be prescribed at the end of the verse;
however, it is considered that one should first recite from the beginning to the end, and only thereafter perform the oblation.
O Maheśvarī, having first recited the complete [mantra], and likewise at the end, one should place the names and the *pādya* offerings in between; this is proclaimed as the *puraścaryā*.
The oblation is prescribed at the end of each verse, as is the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) and so forth;
there, one should perform the preparatory rites (puraścaryā) and other duties according to the procedure stated for the hymn.
Having recited the hymn in its entirety, one should perform the rite for the Gaṇas at its conclusion;
O Priyaṃvadā, this method for the complete fire-oblation has been described to you.
Sārūpya is called Kavaca, and Sāyujya is declared to be the Stotra;
Sānnidhya is the Sahasranāma—this triad has been proclaimed.
The armor (kavaca) shall take the form of armor, and the hymn (stotra) shall become the companion;
however, the Thousand-Name Hymn (sahasranāmastotra) is proclaimed as the place of worship.
Worship is the very form of Durgā, while the offering of the sacrificial victim (bali) is her slaying;
the mantra is the king, and the preliminary ritual (puraścaryā) is declared to be the attainment of sovereignty.
O Maheśvarī, a king does not shine without prosperity;
for this is proclaimed to be the very root of all prosperity. (12.323)
The human being is declared to be the mantra; the rain-cloud weapon is the libation (tarpaṇa);
water is indeed the nature of the fortress, and it is proclaimed as the consecration (abhiṣeka). || 12-324 ||
The feeding of the Brahmins is indeed the devouring of the wicked army;
and having contemplated the oneness of the deity, the guru, and the vidyā, as well as the oneness of the self, [one should proceed]. (12.325)
Having become the Lord of All Siddhis, one shall become the sovereign of the three worlds;
yet, as in the case of a king's kingdom and so forth, there may be fear of enemy armies. || 12-326 ||
O Great Goddess, it is likewise proclaimed that the kingdom of accomplishment (siddhirājya) is established;
O Goddess, the Durgā-yanttra and other such [devices] are considered to be in the kingdom of the region (deśarājya).
In the same way, the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth are considered the means for the attainment of sovereignty;
the mantra is the king, the guru is the minister, and the Gaṇeśas are the gatekeepers. (12.328)
The ritual means for the corpse and the skull is said to be the lion-throne;
the practitioner should act in such a way that everything is accomplished. (12.329)
The horse and the elephant are considered to be for occasional rites (*naimittika*) and rites for specific desires (*kāmya*).
There should be oblations, incense, and banners; victory, however, is the ground of accomplishment (*siddhabhūmikā*).
O Queen of the Sovereign of Siddhis, O Goddess, what on this earth is not accomplished?
The installation of the sixfold division (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*) and so forth is the army that bestows the kingdom of the deity. (12.331)
The Yantra is indeed the Vajra-fortress, and the Jīvacakra is indivisible;
the armor and so forth, as well as the preliminary ritual (puraścaryā), have been declared—what do you wish to hear?
Thus concludes the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the hymns, protective verses (*kavaca*), and the thousand names.

This is the preparatory rite for those hymns, protective verses, and so forth, for which no specific preparatory rite has been mentioned. However, for those for which a preparatory rite has already been stated, that very rite as prescribed in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpa*) must be performed.
Now follows the preparatory rite for the Camphor Hymn (*karpūra-stava*) according to the *Vīra-tantra*.
The Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, please tell me the ritual application (prayoga) of this hymn called Karpūra, which you previously described as the means for accomplishing the six rites (ṣaṭkarma)."
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the practice of the Karpūra-stava;
O Mistress of the Gods, even if performed but once, Kālī shall always be pleased. (12.334)
O Goddess, having bathed on a Saturday or a Tuesday with a restrained mind,
one should worship the goddess Kālikā and properly perform the formal ritual resolve (saṅkalpa).

O Goddess, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sixteen-fold worship, the wise one should recite this unsurpassed hymn ten thousand times and perform the fire oblation at one-tenth that measure.
Then one should perform the libation and the ritual bathing, and feed the Brāhmaṇas;
thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose, one should likewise carry out the ritual applications (prayogas).
O Maheśānī, when fear of a king has arisen, in times of famine, in the perils of enemies, when terror has been produced, and likewise in the fear of disease and grief. (12.338)
One should recite the hymn of Mahākālī; it bestows all peace.
At the conclusion, the worship of a young maiden should be performed with a well-concentrated mind. (12.339)
When this has been performed, O Great Goddess, perfect accomplishment will certainly be attained.
Thus concludes the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the Camphor Hymn (*Karpūra-stava*). Now follows the procedure for the Seven Hundred Verse Hymn (*Saptaśatī-stava*).
(In the Muktāvalī:
Listen, I shall explain with diligence the procedure for the Saptaśatī. || 12-340 ||
"By knowing which, the best of practitioners shall attain all perfections;
indeed, I alone know the entire reality of the *Saptaśatī*. (From the *Merutantra*, 12.341)
Śrī Hari knows three-quarters of it; Prajāpati knows half;
Vyāsa knows a fourth part; and other people know but a ten-millionth part.
In the *Vārāhītantra*:
"Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and so forth, the wise one should recite the hymn.
The placement of the seers and other elements is described in the *Merutantra*.
But in the first narrative of the *Saptaśatī*, the sage Padmabhū [is mentioned]. || 12-343 ||
The meter is said to be Gāyatrī, Mahākālī is the deity, the seed-syllable is Vāk, the principle is Fire, and its application is for the sake of Dharma and Artha. (12.344)
The sage of the middle conduct is declared to be Viṣṇu;
the meter is Uṣṇik, the deity is Mahālakṣmī, and the seed-syllable is Adrijā.
The wind element (vāyustattva) is declared as the application for the attainment of wealth;
the sage Śaṅkara is said to be the author of its ritual procedure (caritra). || 12-346 ||
The goddess Mahāsarasvatī is declared to have the Triṣṭubh metre;
Kāma is the seed-syllable, Ravi is the principle (tattva), and the application is for the attainment of desire. || 12-346 ||
In another tantra:
"One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the syllables of the nine-syllable mantra.
The meditations on the three deities have been explained [in the Durgā section]."
Now, regarding the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), [it is stated] in the *Vārāhītantra*:
"Having placed the book upon the support, one should then read it. (12.347)
O Goddess, because only half the fruit is obtained by merely placing [the hand] upon it,
one should not cease reciting until this chapter is completed.
O beloved, if an interruption occurs during the recitation due to negligence,
one should begin the recitation from the beginning and repeat the entire text again and again.
O Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] in due order and abandon shaking the head and other such gestures.
(From the Mahākālasaṃhitā) Having thus honored the Brahmins with garments, ornaments, and seats... (12.350)
One should perform the recitation of desires and worship according to one's capacity toward the book;
the reader should also recite slowly, preceded by the clear pronunciation of each syllable.
Neither clearly manifest nor yet separated, his head was not like that of a corpse;
he did not sway his body, nor did he laugh or weep as he walked. (12.352)

He should not eat while conversing with others, nor should he break off in the middle; likewise, having sipped water and performed purification, and wearing his upper garment over both shoulders. (12.353)
When one studies according to this rule, the Mother of the World is pleased;
O beloved of my life, she becomes the bestower of the fruits as described. (12.354)
"In the Vārāhī Tantra, having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning, one should recite the hymn or the *saṃhitā*;
and at the end, one should place the *praṇava*—thus spoke the Primordial Being. (12.355)
Likewise: "That which is written by oneself, that which is written by a Śūdra, and that which is written by one who is not a Brāhmaṇa—that too shall be fruitless. (12.356)
Wherever it is not seen in the hymn, there one should insert the *praṇava*; this should be understood to apply throughout the recitation, for otherwise it would be fruitless. (12.357)
(From the Devīpurāṇa):
O King, having honored the reciter with extensive offerings according to one's means, one should then have him recite the supreme *Devīmāhātmya*. 12.358.
At the conclusion of that, the word "peace" (śānti) is uttered for the people and the king as well.
O King, whoever should recite or even listen to this according to this ritual procedure—
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who either contemplates or recites it:
it is equal to that of a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices and a hundred Aśvamedha sacrifices. (12.360)
"O dear one, whatever fruit one obtains, that fruit shall become a hundredfold"—and so forth.
In the *Marīcikalpa*, the sequence is as follows: one should first recite the *Rātrisūkta*, in the middle the *Saptaśatī* hymn, and at the end, indeed, the *Devīsūkta* should be recited. (12.361)
Thus, this combined hymn is for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
Herein is also the *Rātrisūkta*, and the *Devīsūkta*—
beginning with "Thou art *svāhā*, thou art *svadhā*"— which takes the form of a praise situated within the first *caritra*.
"Namo devyai" and so forth constitutes a hymn (*stuti*) situated within the third chapter; this is the view of Nāgojibhaṭṭa and others.
Others, however, maintain that these two *sūktas* are purely Vedic. (In the Merutantra:)
One should recite the daily Caṇḍī-stava as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Chanting [the mantra] encased by the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one attains what is desired;
the root-mantra is the nine-syllabled one mentioned in the section on Durgā.
Now, the *puraścaraṇa* (according to the *Marīcikalpa*):
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
That [mantra] should be recited with an increment of one for each repetition, encapsulated by the previous [syllables].
Thus, O Goddess, the procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* has been declared by me. (12.364)
At the conclusion of that, one should perform an oblation with milk-rice (pāyasa) for each verse of the Rātrisūkta,
as well as for each verse of the Devīsūkta.

Regarding the phrase "verse by verse": this refers to the division of mantras as taught in the *Kātyāyanītantra*. However, the traditionalists maintain that if one lacks knowledge of those [specific divisions], the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed using only the verses.
An alternative method for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) during the nine nights (*navarātra*) is stated in that very same work:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the nine nights."
One should recite with an increase of one [mantra] per day for a period of nine days.
Then, having performed worship according to the ritual of the nine-syllable mantra, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra one thousand times for each [deity], following the prescribed rule.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part [of the total], one shall attain success therein.
Thus concludes the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). Now, as an incidental matter, the procedure for the Śatacaṇḍī rite is written down.
And likewise, in the *Merutantra*:
"I shall now proclaim the procedure for the hundred-fold *Caṇḍī* sacrifice for the delight of men. (12.368)
When there is an affliction by the king, during famine, an earthquake, excessive rain, drought, fear of a foreign army, or destruction; (12.369)
When the rite of Śatacaṇḍī is performed, all obstacles perish;
there is the destruction of diseases and enemies, and the prosperity of wealth and sons. (12.370)
Near the shrine of Śaṅkara or Bhavānī,
one should construct an auspicious pavilion, richly adorned with gate-altars (dvāravedī), banners, and archways (toraṇa).
There, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) either to the west or in the center;
having bathed and performed the daily rites, one should employ ten brāhmaṇas.

Those who have conquered their senses, who follow virtuous conduct, who are of noble birth, who speak the truth, who are proficient in learning, devoted to the recitation of the Caṇḍikā hymns, and possessed of modesty and compassion. (12.373)

According to the procedure for the madhuparka offering, one should give them garments, gold, and other gifts; furthermore, one should provide them with a seat and a rosary for the purpose of recitation, as well as food.
Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), with their minds fixed on the meaning of the mantras,
and sleeping upon the ground, they should each recite the hymn of Caṇḍikā.
Those who possess a focused mind should recite ten times the Navārṇa Caṇḍikā mantra as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, or in some cases, they should chant it ten thousand times.
The *vāḍavas* are the Brahmins.
And in this regard:
"By five, or by seven, or likewise by nine or eleven."
Within a short time, one should quickly perform the sacrifice to Caṇḍikā.
The rite should be performed by an odd number of Brahmins, repeated one hundred times for the sake of perfect accomplishment;
it may take three, five, seven, or nine days, or even a fortnight.
Furthermore, any recitation of the Devīmāhātmya performed by Brahmins during the Yugas shall become entirely fruitless, and they shall incur the destruction of their prosperity. (12.379)
These three statements, which are recited under the name of the *Kroḍatantra*, are indeed baseless; for the tantra is not found and it contradicts many other tantras. Likewise:
"The patron should worship a group of ten auspicious maidens."
One should worship young girls who are between two and ten years of age.

Likewise: "One should worship a Brahmin woman for the accomplishment of all desired goals; a Kṣatriya-born woman for fame; a Vaiśya-born woman for the acquisition of wealth; and a Śūdra-born woman for the attainment of sons. (12.380)
The names for each of the ages beginning with two years are as follows:
she who is two years old is called a *kumārī*; one of three years is a *trimūrti*; a four-year-old is a *kalyāṇī*; and a five-year-old is a *rohiṇī*. (12.381)
Kālikā is said to be six years old, Caṇḍikā seven years old, Śāmbhavī eight years old, and Durgā nine years old. (12.382)
A girl ten years old is said to bestow auspiciousness; one should worship her with mantras.
A one-year-old girl lacks affection, while a eleven-year-old girl is to be avoided. (12.383)
I invoke the maiden who is composed of the syllables of mantra, who assumes the forms of the Mothers, and who is the manifest embodiment of the nine Durgās.
I shall now declare the worship mantras for virgins, such as young girls:
"O you who are worthy of worship by the world, O you who are swiftly to be saluted, O you whose very nature is all-pervasive power! (12.385)
Accept this worship, O Daughter of Kaśyapa; salutations to you, the Mother of the World!
You are Tripurā, the support of the three cities, whose form is the knowledge of the three aims of life.
I worship the Goddess who is adored by the three worlds, the triple-formed one,
whose essence consists of the creative powers yet who transcends them, the auspicious Śivā whose heart is compassion.
I worship the eternal Kalyāṇī, the mother of all that is auspicious, the support of qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, whose essence consists of the letters beginning with ‘A’. (12.388)
I worship Lakṣmī, who possesses infinite power, Rohiṇī,
the auspicious beloved who moves at will, whose very nature is the wheel of time.
I worship Kālikā, the bestower of desires, who is noble with compassion;
she whose seed-syllable is fierce, who is composed of fury, and who is the shatterer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
I always worship the Goddess Caṇḍikā, who possesses fierce valor, who bestows eternal bliss, who is peaceful, and who is saluted by all the gods. (12.391)
I worship Lakṣmī, who is the self of all beings, who belongs to Śambhu,
and who destroys the suffering of existence in difficult and insurmountable undertakings.
I always worship with devotion Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune—
she who is beautiful, possessing a golden complexion, and the bestower of happiness and good fortune.
"I worship the goddess Subhadrā, the mother of Subhadra.
With these mantras, one should worship each such maiden who is endowed with auspicious marks.
With perfumes, flowers, various kinds of food, garments, and even ornaments,
upon a beautiful *sarvatobhadra* mandala fashioned upon the altar.
Having placed a water-pot according to the prescribed rite, one should invoke and worship Śivā therein;
furthermore, one should feed young maidens and Brahmins in front of it.
Having likewise performed the previously mentioned enclosures with various ritual services for four days, one should perform five fire-oblations.
By this it is meant that on the first day there is one repetition each; on the second, two each; on the third, three each; and on the fourth, four each. As it is said in the *Rudrayāmala*:
"One, two, three, and four—one should recite [the mantra] during the four days."
On the fifth day, in the morning, one should perform the *prātarhoma* according to the prescribed rule.
Now, the sacrificial materials for the Brahmin are also stated in the *Merutantra*:
"With milk-rice mixed with honey, and also with grapes and plantain fruits. (12.398)
With citron fruits, pieces of sugarcane, coconuts, dates, sesame seeds, nutmegs, mangoes, and other delightful sweet substances. || 12-399 ||
One should perform oblations for each verse of the *Saptaśatī* ten times over;
and ten thousand oblations with the nine-syllable mantra should be offered into the consecrated fire according to the prescribed rite.
The specific details regarding the fire sacrifice (homa) shall be explained by me further on;
having performed the homa for the deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇadeva) using their respective name-mantras. (12.401)
Having properly performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and having bid farewell to the divine fire,
the assembly of brahmins should consecrate the sacrificer with the waters from the ritual jars.
The initiation mantras (abhiṣeka-mantra) are as follows:
"O Sovereign of the Universe, Sustainer of the World," and so forth;
and "By which Goddess this [universe] was pervaded," and so forth.
"Salutation to the Goddess, the Great Goddess"—and so forth.
"O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge, be gracious"—these are the four verses.
One should then bestow a gold coin (*niṣka*) or gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for each.
In the *Mārīcikalpa*, however, there are five gold pieces for a hundred repetitions; for a repetition of twenty-one thousand, three of those;
for a repetition of five thousand, one gold piece; and for a repetition of three thousand, half of that. (12.403)
It is stated [in the Kātyāyanītantra]: "In the case of a single recitation, a wise man should give one quarter [of the gift], or according to his capacity;
he should give a pair of cows equally to ten Brahmins."
Endowed with three gold coins, and adorned with garments and ornaments.
In that tantra, one should feed the Brahmins separately with various kinds of foods and edibles;
having given them sacrificial fees as well, one should likewise receive their blessings. (12.405)
When this is performed, the world is brought under control and all calamities perish;
one shall obtain a kingdom, wealth, fame, sons, and desired food. (12.406)
(Kātyāyanītantra) Whatever task is undertaken with the aim of performing the Śatacaṇḍikā rite,
Mahālakṣmī truly bestows that very thing upon him swiftly. (12.407)
Now, the procedure for the Sahasracandī rite has been declared;
one should perform the ritual for a thousand Candīs ten times that [scale]. One should select one hundred Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and of virtuous conduct. (Meru, 12.408)
Every day, they should perform ten recitations of the Caṇḍikā;
each of them should mutter the nine-syllable mantra ten thousand times.
The auspicious maidens previously mentioned should be worshipped with the previous mantras a hundred times;
having thus performed this for ten days, they should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa).
By reciting the *Saptaśatī* one hundred times according to the prescribed rite for each verse,
one should also perform one hundred thousand recitations of the nine-syllable mantra using the previously mentioned collections of ritual materials.
Having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Hotṛ priests, one should feed the twice-born previously mentioned—
virtuous men numbering a thousand who are devoted to the propitiation of the Goddess.
When the ritual of Caṇḍī has been performed by men in this manner a thousand times, everything desired is accomplished and the flood of suffering is destroyed. || 12-413 ||
Māris, epidemics, diseases, and other such calamities perish;
[as stated] in the Rudrayāmala:
"In the loss of a kingdom, during great portents, in a pestilence among people, and in times of great fear... (12.414).

In the case of the death of an elephant or the death of a horse, in fear of an enemy army, and likewise in various other misfortunes such as the danger arising from consumption and other diseases— (12.415).
One should perform or cause to be performed the recitation of the *Sahasracaṇḍikā* one thousand times;
however, one should not speak of this rite to a wicked person, a rogue, a thief, or one who betrays the guru. (From the *Merutantra*, 12.416)
One should declare this supreme rule to a virtuous person who has conquered the senses and is self-controlled;
for thus, when Caṇḍikā is pleased, she protects both the speaker and the listener. (12.417)
Now follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*):
