In a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) that is level, measuring one cubit on all sides, provided with a single enclosure, and adorned with a vulva-shaped mandala (*yonimaṇḍala*). || 12.418 ||

One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the rule of the ten-fold portion using the aforementioned oblations; such is the prescribed sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for both the Nityacaṇḍī and the Navacaṇḍī rites.
A pit twice this size is prescribed for the Śatacaṇḍī rite;
having consecrated the pit with the eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras), one should establish the fire within it.
Having wiped the ground within the pit with *darbha* grass, one should smear it;
then, one should draw three lines with their tips pointing eastward using the base of the *sruva* ladle.
Afterward, having removed the dust, there is the sprinkling of the lines;
then comes the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which is the sixth [rite], and the seventh is performed with the seven mudrās.
The eighth consecration is remembered as the "enveloping with weapons" (astrāvaguṇṭhita) performed within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should establish the fire named Aṣṭamaṅgala within the sacrificial pit.
In all these cases, the seed-mantra of Māyā is used.
When the recitation of the Caṇḍikā is complete, one should honor a Brāhmaṇa with a sacrificial fee to the south;
thereafter, one should adorn that fire-pit containing the fire with a new cloth. (12.424)
To the north of the *kuṇḍa*, the *praṇītā* vessel filled with water should be placed. (p.
1179) All the various vessels should be placed in sequence starting from the *praṇītā* vessel. || 12-425 ||
The vessel for clarified butter, the vessel for the sacrificial porridge accompanied by cow's milk, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, cow's ghee, rice grains, and the roots of *kuśa* grass. (12.426)
Three fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, followed by a full vessel;
having meditated upon the Mistress of the Seven Islands and taken hold of the root of *kuśa* grass.
One should pour it into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the seed-syllable of Varuṇa;
with that bundle of *darbha* grass, numbering one hundred, O Goddess, [one should sprinkle].
Sprinkling the vessels in sequence with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel,
one should place ghee and rice into the *ājya* vessel and the *caru* pot.
Then, in the proper sequence, the placing [of the vessels] upon the fire should be performed for those two;
first, the milk-rice (pāyasa) must be prepared, followed by the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) for those two.
Having placed the two *sruva* ladles on the left with a *palāśa* wood stick and three blades of *darbha* grass, they were set out shining brightly; then their placement was made on the right.

Having first caused [the deity] to depart from the fire, one should bring it back from the east and place it between the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the preceptor (ācārya), moving clockwise, out of respect for the recitation of its own seed-syllable (bīja).
One's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*) is the nectar-seed (*amṛtabīja*).
Having sprinkled [the oblation] with one's own seed-syllable, one should place the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in the northwest.
Standing silently, one should cast *pālāśa* fuel-sticks into the Vaiśvānara fire. (12.433)
Having sprinkled water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel mixed with the roots of *kuśa* grass around the fire in a clockwise direction,
one should discard the roots of the *kuśa* grass into the *praṇītā* vessel.
Having placed his right knee upon the ground, he should offer oblations with the fire as the mouth;
while the disciple maintains contact, he should pour clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle into the smokeless bearer of the offering.
Prajāpati, Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī—this is declared to be the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), preceded by the seed-syllable of Māyā. (12.436)
One should pour the remnants into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and set aside the implements of the sacrifice;
one should provide the prepared oblation for the *homa* with clarified butter and *śamī* wood.
"Kalpita" means that which is mentally conceived (*saṅkalpita*).
Then, one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the sacrificial food (*havis*) into one's own blazing fire, [reciting]:
"To Māyābīja, to Brahmāṇī, Āheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī, and Cāmuṇḍā—*vicce viṣṭe*—*svāhā*."
This mantra of Mahādevī has been declared for the oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt.

With clarified butter, one should perform nine oblations using the seed-syllable *māyā* (hīṃ) and the names [of the goddesses] beginning with Nandā—namely, to Nandā, Raktadantikā, Śākambharī, Durgā, Bhīmā, Bhrāmarī, Kālī, Śivadūtī, and Cāmuṇḍā—and to the Prajāpatis.
Having prepared the sacrificial ladle (*śruci*), which is of the nature of the sacrifice, provided with perfume, flowers, and fruit... [12.439]
Then, being fully devoted to Mahālakṣmī, he should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with clarified butter in an unbroken stream, using the nine-syllable mantra.
Having meditated upon the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as nectar difficult even for the gods to obtain,
he consumes the remnants from the middle of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with the mantra.
Because of this, the mantra is: "I partake of the consecrated sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) which bestows happiness and merit.
Being intent on meditating upon the sacred water-source (tīrtha) of the *praṇītā* vessel, [he should consume it] with water.
One performs the cleansing with a hundred blades of darbha grass through the recitation of a hundred verses. || 12-442 ||
"Those auspicious powers and Savitṛ together with them,
and those who abide in proximity— may they all provide you with healing."
May the divine waters, the mothers of all beings, purify me—those waters which repeatedly mix with the entire universe as the seed of Prajāpati. 12.443.
"May the divine Waters purify me with the mantra: 'The Waters, through the touch of their water, wash away Alakṣmī in the form of impurity which resides within all beings.'"
Then one should consecrate oneself with the four hymns of Caṇḍikā.
The four verses beginning with "śūlena pāhi no devi" [are used] for the consecration of the officiating priests;
however, for the consecration of the patron (yajamāna), only the previously mentioned four verses are used.
One should give gifts according to the prescribed rule, such as gold, cows, garments, and so forth.

Having announced the recitation and the fire-oblation, and having bowed to Mahālakṣmī, he should circumambulate her while reciting these verses beginning with "O Goddess, protect us with your trident. (12.446)
One should perform [this] with great steadiness, intent upon the meditation on Caṇḍikā;

that is to say, by means of these verses beginning with "With the trident... and ending with "...protect us from all sides. One should be intent upon meditation with these five verses beginning with "Obeisance to the Goddess" (namo devyai). || 12-447 ||
Having performed the five prostrations and sat upon an auspicious seat, with palms joined in reverence, he recited the six verses beginning with "O you who possess all forms. (12.448)
"Bowing down, one should pray with the heart's desire to the Mother of the Worlds;
having projected [the deity] into one's own body, one should offer her dismissal.
He who performs the worship of Caṇḍikā according to this rite— || 12.449 ||
Mahālakṣmī, being pleased with him, bestows all desires. Thus ends the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*). (From the *Prayogasāra*)
O King, listen as I speak of the fruit of reciting the Caṇḍī-pāṭha.
For men who recite the texts one hundred times or more every day,
having first made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and worshipped them, they should place the mantras upon their limbs once.
Afterwards, by making an offering of oblations, a human being obtains the fruit;
for the sake of pacifying calamities, a person should recite it three times.
O fair-faced one, for the sake of pacifying the afflictions caused by planetary influences, one should recite it five times;
when a great danger has arisen, one should recite it seven times. (12.453)
Through nine repetitions, there shall be peace, and one may be released from the fear born of affliction to life;
for the subjugation of kings and for prosperity, one should recite the Rudra-repetition.
By repeating [the mantra] one hundred times, the fulfillment of desires and the destruction of enemies arise;
by repeating it one thousand times, the enemy is brought under control, and likewise, a woman comes under one's influence. (12.455)

By performing it fifteen times, a person attains happiness and prosperity; by performing it twenty-four times, they know that there will be the acquisition of sons, grandsons, wealth, and grain. (12.456)
O Dear One, for the destruction of fear of kings and for the uprooting of enmity,
one should perform seventeen or eighteen circumambulations.
A person should recite it twenty times for liberation from the great ocean;
by twenty-five recitations, there shall be release from bondage.
When a crisis has arrived, consisting of a disease difficult to cure,
when the destruction of one's lineage and the extinction of the family occurs, and when the end of life has come— (12.461)
In the increase of enemies, the increase of disease, as well as in the loss of wealth and in decline;
likewise in the occurrence of the threefold portents, and in the case of a great transgression.
One should perform this with effort one hundred times; from that, auspiciousness is attained.
His calamities perish, and in the end, he goes to the supreme goal. (12.463)
There is an increase of prosperity through a hundred repetitions, and likewise a supreme increase of sovereignty;
O Goddess, whatever is conceived in the mind shall be accomplished by one hundred and eight [repetitions].
O lady of excellent vows, one obtains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices;
Lakṣmī herself, becoming steadfast, attends upon him who recites it a thousand times.
Having enjoyed the desires of the mind, a person may attain liberation, just as the Aśvamedha is among sacrifices, or as Hari is among the gods. (12.466)
Among all hymns of praise as well, the Saptashati Stava is likewise supreme; O fair-faced one, there is no hymn whatsoever superior to this.
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is meritorious and the purifier of purifiers.
Or rather, O fair-faced one, what is the use of speaking at great length? (12.468)
Through a hundred recitations of Caṇḍikā, all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are accomplished. (In the *Merutantra*):
In the Kali age, there is nothing equal to Caṇḍī as a bestower of perfection within the three worlds. (12.469)
By means of the left and right paths, she bestows the fruits of authority;
therein, one should employ the first conduct for the destruction of disease. (12.470)
The wise person should employ the middle [method] for the destruction of calamities; however, one who desires the extraordinary should cultivate the conduct of the last [method]. (12.471)
For one who maintains the discipline of these two conducts, the lineage is never severed anywhere;
if one recites the conduct from beginning to end, their misfortune is destroyed. (12.472)
Whoever recites this beginningless [text] shall slay his enemies before long;
one should also join the verses following one's own purpose with the *Saptaśatī*. (12.473)
He who recites the Caṇḍī-mantra, encased by that [syllable] alone and with its numerical expansion at the beginning and the end, his desire is fulfilled.
Visualizing one's enemies as demons and one's friends as deities,
one should practice the worship of Caṇḍī at the three junctions of the day for a period of one month.
Without a doubt, enemies will either die or become as good as dead;
this applies to whoever [performs the rite] during the fortnight of the moon's increase, beginning from the first day until the eighth day of the month of Āśvina.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while offering food drenched in the three sweets;
one should worship the goddess Caṇḍī every day and recite [the hymn] at the beginning and the end.
By propitiating Brahmins and one's guru, one quickly obtains what is desired.
Now, some practical applications mentioned in the *Kātyāyanītantra* are written down:
one should recite the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and end of each mantra; thus, there is success in the mantra.

By placing the *saṃpraṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) and the three *vyāhṛtis* at the beginning and in reverse order at the end of each verse, one attains success very quickly through a hundred-fold recitation.
By reciting the *ṛc* "jātavedase" at the beginning of each verse, all desires are fulfilled.
To ward off untimely death, one should recite the *tryambaka* mantra a hundred times both at the beginning and at the end.

At every verse, one should recite the verse beginning with "śaraṇāgatadīnārtta... for the accomplishment of all undertakings. At every verse, one should recite the half-verse beginning with "karotu sā naḥ śubha... for the attainment of all desires.
For the sake of obtaining one's desired boon, one should recite the verse beginning with "evaṃ devyā varaṃ labdhvā...".
For the removal of all obstacles, one should recite "durge smṛtā" at every verse.
Even for this single verse alone, there should be a recitation (*japa*) of one hundred thousand, ten thousand, one thousand, or one hundred times according to one's desire.
By reciting "sarvabādhā" one hundred thousand times, the fruit mentioned in the verse is obtained.
When the mantra "itthaṃ yadā yadā" is recited one hundred thousand times, there is the pacification of the Great Plague (mahāmārī).
Then, by reciting the mantra "tato vavre nṛpo rājya" one hundred thousand times, there is the recovery of one's own kingdom.

By means of the mantra "hīnasti daityatejāṃsi," when accompanied by the offering of a lamp and a sacrificial oblation (bali) and the tying of a bell, there is the pacification of the seizing spirits of children (bālagraha).

Having recited the first rotation in the forward order (*anuloma*), then again in the reverse order (*viparīta-krama*), and then once more in the forward order—thus performing three counter-clockwise rotations—in the manner described, success (*siddhi*) is swiftly attained.

For the warding off of all calamities, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the half-verse beginning with *durge smṛtā*, followed by the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with *yad antike yacca dūrake*, and finally the half-verse beginning with *dāridryaduḥkha*. This should be done one hundred thousand times, ten thousand times, one thousand times, or one hundred times, according to the requirements of the task.
Having spoken thus for the purpose of killing, one should recite [the verses] as they arise—one verse at a time. Through the recitations prescribed for killing, the attainment of the fruit occurs.
It is established by experience that the three verses beginning with "Even the minds of the wise... cause instantaneous delusion;
however, this must necessarily be done by reciting those verses for each individual mantra.

By reciting the *pratiśloka* (counter-verse) for the verse beginning with "rogānaśeṣāḥ," there is the destruction of all diseases; even by merely chanting that [verse], the same fruit is obtained. Having said this, the Goddess then stated that by reciting the *pratiśloka* for the verse beginning with "gambhīrā," or by chanting it, one attains knowledge (*vidyā*) and the destruction of defects of speech.
The mantra consisting of one hundred and twelve syllables beginning with "bhagavatyā kṛtaṃ sarvam" grants all desires and wards off all calamities.

Regarding the verse beginning with "O Goddess, remover of the distress of those who have sought refuge," if one recites it one hundred thousand, ten thousand, one thousand, or even a hundred times according to the specific requirement, or if it is recited for each individual verse, there shall be the cessation of all calamities and the attainment of all desires.
In these practices, if one performs prostrations before a lamp for every single verse—or even just once—the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained very swiftly.
In all these applications, thirteen lamps should be offered either in thirteen separate vessels or in a single vessel.
By reciting each verse encapsulated by the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) thirty times for forty-one days, all desires are fulfilled.
By reciting it ten times daily according to the aforementioned method for twenty-one days, one achieves subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
By reciting it thirteen times for seven days, encapsulated by the *māyābīja* and accompanied by the *phaṭ*-sprout, the accomplishment of eradication (*uccāṭana*) is attained.
For one who is exactly such [as described], by reciting it eleven times over four days, there is the destruction of all calamities.
By reciting it fifteen times for a period of forty-nine days, with each verse encapsulated by the Śrī-bīja, there is the attainment of Lakṣmī.
By reciting it one hundred times, with each verse encapsulated by the Vāgbhava-bīja, there is the attainment of knowledge (vidyā).
Now, regarding the application for the sake of others:

one should recite the Vedic mantra—"Oṃ! May the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus kindle you again; may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, [kindle you] with sacrifices. May you increase your body with clarified butter; may the desires of the sacrificer come true"—at the beginning of each chapter or at each repetition.
The practice of enclosing [the mantra] within the nine-syllable mantra should be performed only for the sake of removing obstacles.
As it is said in the *Vārāhītantra* and other texts:
"One should recite the nine-syllable mantra a hundred times at the beginning and a hundred times at the end. (12.478)
Within the *Caṇḍīsaptaśatī*, this *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) has been proclaimed:
those with desires should recite the *saṃpuṭa*, while those free from desires should recite it without the *saṃpuṭa*. (12.479)
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, one should recite [the mantra] encased within the nine syllables. Thus it is said.
In this context, two nine-syllable mantras are well known. One of them has been mentioned in the section on Durgā;
the other, however, is found in the Vārāhītantra:
"The beginning of the Vedas (OM), the vāgbhava (AIM), Māyā (Hrīm), and likewise Kāma (Klīm)."
The letter *pṛ* (the earth) followed by *repha* (the letter *r*), adorned with the left eye (*i*), and further embellished by the *nāda* and *bindu*.
The root mantra is declared to be "Māyā Kāmo Namaḥ.
Regarding this, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is also stated in that very same place:
"One should recite the root mantra one hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals."
In the Kātyāyanītantra:
the sequence of maintenance is for one who desires enjoyment, and withdrawal is for one who desires liberation. (12.481)
For one desiring prosperity and for one desiring nourishment, the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama) is prescribed.
The sequence of emanation and the others are taught in that very [text]:
"One should recite starting from the beginning; this is called the sequence of emanation here. (12.482)
One should perform the recitation beginning from Śakra and ending with the slaying of the Daitya Śumbha;
this is declared to be the sequence of the maintenance [of the mantra], starting from the first Śakra and continuing to the end.
Beginning from the remainder and ending with the first, this sequence constitutes the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
(In the *Merutantra*), having stated the number of applications for the three modes of conduct in their proper order:
"Thus, seven hundred applications have been proclaimed here. (12.484)
Therefore, this [text] was called the *Saptaśatī* by the wise Vyāsa.
However, in the *Kātyāyanītantra*, it is stated that the very mantras for the seven hundred oblations (*saptaśata-homa*) are the basis for its designation as the *Saptaśatī*.
Those mantras are found in that very [work].
O beloved, [this begins] from the first verse spoken by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya.

"Arising from the letter of space (vyoman) and joined with the second vowel": *vyoman* is the letter *ha*; its "beginning" (*ādi*) is the letter *sa*. The "second vowel" (*dvitīyasvara*) is *ā*. Thus, it becomes *sā*.
Likewise.
O beloved, all eighteen mantras should be recited, ending with the word "nṛpa."
The Vaiśya said: "Then there are five mantra-ślokas beginning with 'vyoma';
the compound 'vyomādyāḥ' means those of which 'vyoma' is the first. The King’s utterance consists of the letter 'ma' as its final syllable and is joined with the twelfth vowel. (12.487)
The letter *ya* is the penultimate syllable; it is joined with the twelfth vowel, *ai*.
The letter *sa*, conjoined with the *bindu*, is at the end—such is that mantra.
The Vaiśya spoke again: "O Goddess, the eleventh vowel from the beginning... (12.488).
The eleventh vowel is *ekāra* (e). At the end should be the five mantras, including the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*) conjoined with the bindu. The seed-syllable of fire is *ram*.
The three mantras proclaimed by the sage Mārkaṇḍeya have been cited. || 12-489 ||
The supreme [seed-syllable] has the letter *tā* as its color and is joined with the vehicle of the *bhuvana*-svara;

the *bhuvana*-svara is *au*, and the vehicle joined with that is *vau*. "Thus spoke the King"—these are the six auspicious mantras beginning with *bhā* and ending with *dita*, O fair-faced one. (12.490)
Then the Sage spoke, O Sovereign of the Gods, beginning with "Knowledge exists" and so forth;
at the end are the twelve clear mantras of the Mistress of all Masters. (12.491)
The King said: "O Blessed One, best among those who know the beginning and the end, this triad of mantras is renowned. Thereupon, the Sage spoke.
She is eternal, the primordial state, the Lord, and at the end, the eight mantras.
Then Brahmā spoke: "And you, O great Asuras, [beginning with] Svāhā. (12.493)
O Supreme Goddess, these fifteen mantras should come first;
likewise, there are indeed seven mantras beginning with the hymn of praise and ending with the statement of the seer.
Then there shall be two verses spoken by the Blessed One beginning with "mānu";
and there shall be two mantras spoken by the Sage beginning with "vañcitā," O Supreme Goddess. (12.495)
The statement of the sage beginning with "tathā" and so forth is cited as a pair of mantras;
all the verses in this chapter are seventy-eight in sequence. (12.496)
In the middle, the twenty-four half-mantras are proclaimed;
all the oblations are to be known as one hundred and four.
He spoke there: "The mantras to be understood therein number as many as the worlds.
Thus ends the determination of the mantras for the first chapter.
The Lord said:
In the second [chapter], it is said that "the sage spoke," and there are ninety-six oblations in sequence.
Then, in the third chapter, it is stated by the teachers that "the sage said," and thus, O fair-faced one, thirty-six mantras are to be understood as verses (ślokas). (12.499)
The Goddess said: "At the end of this mantra, O Dear One, the verse is considered the mantra;
furthermore, the five verses spoken by the Sage are eternal mantras. (12.500)
Thus, O Goddess, there are forty-four oblations there in the fourth [stage] in sequence; the utterance of the Ṛṣi consists of twenty-six.
Again, in the same manner, there are two verses consisting of the speech of the Ṛṣi in the form of a mantra.
Thus praised, O fair-faced one, this mantra is extremely secret. (12.502)
The Goddess said: "Let this sixteen-syllable mantra be chosen.
Then the gods said: "And having spoken, one should say that it was performed by the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī)."
This mantra consists of one hundred and twelve syllables;
furthermore, it includes the words "Then the Sage said" and "Thus [he] was propitiated.
These verses are four in number, and the mantras are indeed that many.
O Supreme Goddess, there are thirty-six verses in the fourth chapter;
furthermore, by means of two half-mantras, there are forty minus two [forty-two]. (12.504)
Thus, there are one hundred and fifty for the Madhyacaritra,
and likewise five hundred mantras according to the divisions of Mahālakṣmī.
Thus concludes the determination of the mantras for the Madhyama-caritra.
The Sage said: Then the six mantras in the form of verses praised Tripurā, who is the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu; thereafter those gods spoke.

There are thirty verses beginning with "namo devyai," followed by those with bodies bowed in reverence; then there are sixty-three verses beginning with "viṣṇumāyā" and ending with "bhrāntirūpa. (12.507)
There are sixty-three separate mantras for the descents;
one should perform three oblations with the mantra in the form of the funeral pyre (citirūpa). || 12-508 ||
"Thus there are eighty mantras; so the seer said.
Why then are these [mantras], which are joined with praises and the like, not accepted by you? (12.509)
Having heard this utterance of the Ṛṣi, these seventeen mantras were indeed proclaimed;
by means of these three initial mantras, the pure divisions are made known. (12.510)
Then the messenger spoke thus: "O Goddess, the Lord of the Daityas...
and so forth; [he recited] these nine mantras, and then the sage spoke again.
With the single mantra beginning with "ity uktā" and so forth, Sarasvatī spoke; these four verses constitute distinct mantras. (12.512)
The messenger said, "Thus you are once again arrogant";
then four mantras are to be known, after which the Goddess spoke.
"Thus it is; let the powerful Śumbha do what is appropriate.
These are the two mantras, consisting of nine verses and half-verses. (12.514)
p. 1190) And there are twenty-nine [verses] in addition to the hundred, consisting of mantra-forms.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
It is said that four verses beginning with "The Seer spoke" and "Listen" have been uttered. (12-515)
Then the sage spoke again; commanded by him thereafter, these three mantras were proclaimed, beginning with "The Goddess said. (12.516)
Sent by the lord of the Daityas, one mantra was proclaimed;
then the sage said, "Thus addressed, he rushed forward. (12.517)
These twelve verses beginning with "ityādi" are proclaimed in the sixth chapter;
they constitute the offerings to the deities in their twenty-fourfold divisions in due order. (12.518)
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Regarding the sage’s address to the king and so forth: "The twenty-three Mothers...
The sage said: "Those two groups of Mothers were brought [there] in due order. (12.519)
O Goddess, there are twenty-seven oblations here in sequence;
in these two chapters, O Goddess, Dhūmrākṣī is proclaimed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
The phrase "When the Rishi and Caṇḍa were slain" marks the conclusion of the chapter.
Sixty-three oblations have been prescribed; one is considered to be a half-oblation. (12.521)
The eight deities with red eyes are proclaimed as the great Śaktis.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
The two verses beginning with "The king, Vicitra... have been cited [here]. (12-522)
The sage indeed manifested his anger in the form of verses beginning with "ityādi";
here, in this auspicious ninth [chapter], there are forty-one oblations.
"O fair-faced one, listen now to the deity Bhairavī, which is to be kept secret.
Thus ends the ninth chapter. (p.
1191) The seer [of this] is the two-mantra beginning with "Niśumbha was slain," etc. (12.524).
Then the mantra "Devī" consists of two [syllables], while "Ekaivāham" is the supreme *manu* consisting of one [syllable].
Again, by means of the single mantra "Devī," the manifest mantras are proclaimed. (12.525)
Then this sage proceeded for twenty-two and a half [ages];
there, thirty-two Manus are recognized, and one indeed as half a Manu. (12.526)
First is she who sits upon a lion, bearing a trident and a noose;
she is the principal [deity], four-armed, holding an arrow and a bow in her hands, and possessing auspicious eyes.
Thus ends the tenth chapter.
When the auspicious [goddess] was slain by the Goddess, the seer (ṛṣi) was proclaimed to be the renowned Sumedhas;
likewise, there are thirty-four verses, and the mantras are equal in number to those.
Then, O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, by means of this single mantra I am the Bestower of Boons;
thus the gods spoke, as well as [the method for] the pacification of all afflictions.
O Goddess of the Gods, after that, the Goddess spoke with a single verse;
thereafter follow fourteen verses beginning with "She was born in the Vaivasvata interval. (12.530)
O Goddess, there are fifty-five complete oblations;
for here the deity is Vaiṣṇavī, who is borne by the Great Garuḍa.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
Then the Goddess said: "With these hymns, and always with me [invoked] by the half-verse beginning with 'dūre', there are twenty-eight forms. (12.532)
Then the sage spoke, having recited this verse from the beginning;
with ten subsequent verses, the mantras are considered to be of that same number.
Thus, in the twelfth chapter, there are forty-one oblations.
This concludes the twelfth chapter.
Then, in the thirteenth chapter, the Sage said: [verse 12.533].
"O King, this which has been told to you," and so forth—this constitutes three and a half verses; the meaning is that it comprises four *manus*.
Then, after "Mārkaṇḍeya said," he chose two *manus*. (12.534)
The Goddess said: Furthermore, by means of these three very short verses, there shall indeed be six oblations here, because even the half-verses constitute mantras.
The meaning is that there are six oblations.
Then, having uttered "Mārkaṇḍeya said" and "to those two," one should recite the two mantras again: "Sāvarṇi shall become the Manu. (12.537)
In this [rite], twenty-nine oblations are prescribed;
likewise in the thirteenth chapter, regarding the fire-oblation and the rite of libation.
O Daughter of the Mountain, seven hundred [verses] have been declared to you;
this mantra, beginning with the letter *sa* and ending with the letter *na*, is most difficult to obtain.
O beloved of mine, that [mantra] must be understood according to the traditional method;
otherwise, the mantra is fruitless. This which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.

Regarding the phrase "according to the rule": this means [the ritual is performed] on the eighth or fourteenth day by means of a *kīlaka* (stake). In that context, these mantras end with *svāhā* during the fire-oblation (*homa*), end with *namaḥ* during worship (*pūjā*), and end with *tarpayāmi* during the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Some recite the specific mantra and then say, "To the deity of that particular chapter, *svāhā*.
During the oblation for each chapter, one says, "I satisfy the deity of that particular chapter," and likewise during the libation.
They say that for the purpose of worship, one should recite: "Obeisance to the deity of each respective chapter.
This applies when one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
In such cases, the oblation, worship, and libation (*tarpaṇa*) may be performed with the *Jayantī* mantra, the *namo devyā* mantra, or the *sarvamaṅgala* mantra.
"One should offer auspicious oblations to Caṇḍikā with the hymn-mantras," as it is also stated in the *Rahasya*.
Furthermore, according to such injunctions as, "Having first performed the *kavaca*, one should thereafter conquer the *Saptaśatī*," when the recitation of the *kavaca* is being performed,
no oblations should be offered with its verses.

And according to the statement in another Tantra: "In ancient times, the Daitya Andhaka, who was devoted to the *durgā-homa*, was struck down by Maheśvara with the mantra for the armor-offering (*kavacāhuti*).

Some maintain that the "armor" (*kavaca*) here consists of the four verses beginning with "O Goddess, protect us with the trident. However, regarding that [view], the division of the mantras as taught in the *Kātyāyanītantra*—which contradicts [that view]—has been clearly demonstrated by the learned authorities.
For it is thus: five hundred and seventy-eight verses. (12.541)
It is stated in the Saptaśatī Stotra that one should divide the mantra according to the count of seven hundred and offer it as oblations; this is the doctrine of Kātyāyanī. (12.542)
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Thereafter follows one [verse] concerning Sāvarṇi and others;
then seventeen verses consisting of *śloka* mantras, followed by one composed of half-verses.
Thus there would be nineteen; likewise, the statement regarding the Vaiśya is twenty.
Again, half [a verse], then another verse, three [verses], and again half [a verse] would occur. (12.544)
The number twenty-five shall be the Rāja, and likewise twenty-six;
two mantras consisting of half-verses shall each become a half [of a complete mantra]. (12.545)
Thus, twenty-nine mantra enumerations have been proclaimed; furthermore, there is a half [verse], then three verses, and then another half [verse].
Mārkaṇḍeya, moreover, consists of half-verses;
[the next] consists of full verses; the mantra consists of half-verses; and the king possesses mantras consisting of half-verses. || 12-547 ||
The mantras are exactly forty; there are four mantra-verses (śloka-mantra).
Furthermore, there are ten half-verse mantras belonging to the seer (ṛṣi), and again ten half-verse mantras. (12.548)
Again half [is] the King; again, fifty-nine is stated.
Again half [is] the Śloka; again half [is] the Ṛṣi. (12.549)
p. 1194) Again half [a verse], again verses, six mantras, and again half-verses:
the Lord [addressed] the divine Nidrā, who is peerless in the splendor of Viṣṇu. || 12-550 ||
Thus, this very reading is said to consist of seventy-one mantras;
there is one mantra of half a verse for Brahmā, and thirteen mantras of full verses.
One half-verse and one verse [make] two; the seers are indeed five verses. Furthermore, half [of that] of the mantras is recorded as ninety-five. (12.552)
The Blessed One [taught] two half-mantras; the seer [taught] one half-verse again; the verse [taught] one verse again; and the seer [taught] two verses, which constitute two mantras. (12.553)
In one hundred and seventy-four verses, at the very beginning of the chapter, the Seer says "Manu said" only once. (12.554)
Sixty-eight verses are considered to be as many *manus*;
there are sixty-nine mantras in total in this second chapter.
At the beginning, the seer spoke one [verse], and twenty-five thereafter;
the verses beginning with "nihanyamāna" have syllables agitated by the color of the speaker's face.
Thus far the Goddess spoke; then another [said], "One should roar, one should roar!
Then there is a verse, and again the Sage spoke, followed by five verses. (12.557)
Thus, in the third [section], there are exactly forty-four mantras in total;
at the beginning, the seer says "Iti," while Śakra and the others provide the verses and mantras. (12.558)
The twenty-sixth is the seer; there are two verses, and after that, the Goddess [is the seer]:
"O all you gods, let that which is desired from us be chosen. (12.559)

Then, following that, the gods spoke the mantra consisting of half a verse; thereafter, they spoke the mantra consisting of half a verse: "Everything has been accomplished by the Blessed Lady. || 12-560 ||
Since these consist of three verses and mantras that are fixed from the beginning, the four verses of the sages are proclaimed as the Manavas. (12.561)
In the thirty-sixth chapter there are forty-two verses;
in the seventy-sixth chapter, however, there are five hundred and sixty-two mantras.
In the *Kātyāyanīmata*, there are one hundred and twenty-nine [verses];
at the beginning, it says "the sage spoke," and formerly there are six [verses] concerning Śumbha and others.
Then the gods spoke the verses and mantras, and the eighth was Manu;
the five verses beginning with "Namo Devyai" are proclaimed as the mantras. (12.564)
There are exactly thirteen mantras, beginning with "yā devī" and so forth;
among those, the mantras consist of twenty-one verses ending with "bhrānti."
In every verse, three mantras are to be known, and they total sixty-three;
she is the Goddess who, within all beings, is designated by the word Viṣṇumāyā.
The mantra "namas tasyai" is said to consist of twenty syllables;
the second [mantra] "namas tasyai" is said to consist of four syllables.
The third, consisting of eight syllables, is "namatasyaiva namo namaḥ.
Thus, the wise should understand these three mantras within the twenty-two verses. (12.568)
Furthermore, there is a mantra consisting of a single verse, and again a mantra consisting of three verses;
within twenty-three verses, there are indeed sixty-seven mantras.
Together with the thirteen preceding mantras, eighty are declared;
the sage further recited two verses beginning with "Praised by the gods. (12.570)
Furthermore, there are seventeen verses by the Seer, then three verses;
the Messenger has nine verses, one verse by the Seer, and then Ambikā.
The meaning of "one" is that it consists of a single verse. Furthermore, there is the *Catuḥślokī*, and again the messenger (*dūta*), and again Śivā.
When the two verses are combined, they total forty-nine. (12.572)
Furthermore, by adding eighty and twenty-nine more, one hundred and fifty-nine oblations should be known thus in the fifth [section]. (12.573)
In the sixth chapter, consisting of twenty verses, all the verses are proclaimed to be of the nature of mantras; O Goddess, [this is] the fifth [section], and now follows the triad of seers.
Thus, it is proclaimed that there are twenty-four mantras;
these mantras are found in the seventh chapter, which consists of twenty-five verses.
All the mantras are in the form of verses; following that, there are two [sections] consisting of the words "the Seer said" (ṛṣyuvāca).
Thus, the number of mantras is proclaimed to be twenty-seven.
In the eighth chapter, sixty-one verses are proclaimed at the beginning;
there are sixty-one mantra-verses, and at the end, there is one mantra consisting of half a verse. (12.577)
At the beginning, there is one sage, and the lineage of mantras is proclaimed to consist of sixty-three,
joined with thirty-nine verses.
In the ninth chapter, there are as many mantras as there are [verses], plus two mantras; including the mantra "rājā ṛṣiśca," this constitutes forty-one mantras. (12.579)
In the tenth [chapter], which consists of twenty-seven verses, there are twenty-seven mantras in the form of verses; then follows the final one.
The collection of thirty-two mantras consists of one mantra comprising half a śloka, two instances of "the Seer said" (ṛṣyuvāca), and two instances of "the Goddess said" (devyuvāca). || 12-581 ||
It should be clearly understood that there are fifty-five and a half verses in the eleventh [chapter];
there are fifty verse-mantras, and at its end, there is one mantra consisting of half a verse. (12.582)
"Then I shall attain renown on earth as Śākambharī.
Regarding this, some wise ones say that "eṣo 'rdhamantraḥ" (this is the half-mantra) refers to this very point. || 12-583 ||
Two goddesses and one ṛṣi, and the gods as one—it is thus declared.
It should be clearly understood that there are fifty-five mantras. (12.584)
Even though this twelve-chapter work consists of thirty-eight verses,
there are forty-one mantras therein, and for each of them, two oblations are offered.
The verses consist of thirty-seven half-verses; including the single verse beginning with "The Goddess said," the total number is clearly stated as such. (12.586)
In the thirteenth [chapter], seventeen and a half verses are proclaimed, beginning with "The Sage said," and ending with "bestowing enjoyment, heaven, and liberation. (12.587)
Thus end the five mantras; after that comes Mārkaṇḍeya.
Having heard these words of his, the half-mantra is proclaimed.
Then the five śloka-mantras are to be known, followed by one half-mantra;
"The Goddess said" is this mantra, and thereafter the śloka is the mantra. (12.589)
Then the Mārkaṇḍeya mantra, then two verses, then a pair of mantras;
thereafter, seven mantras of the sixfold Devī have been proclaimed. || 12-590 ||
After that, Mārkaṇḍeya [will appear]; two mantras are traditionally remembered.
Through repetition, however, the mantra becomes superior; Sāvarṇi will be the Manu.
"Twenty-nine mantras are recorded here by the wise"—thus it is said.
Now, as an incidental topic, the procedure for questioning is stated through the words preserved in the *Tantravidhānamuktāvalī*:
"Having drawn a very beautiful lotus with thirteen petals..."
One should fill the petals with numbers in the sequence beginning with one. || 12-592 ||
The number of verses for each chapter should be written separately, line by line; one who knows the ritual procedure should worship Durgā in the book with the nine-syllable mantra.
O Goddess Durgā, salutations to you, the all-knowing and all-seeing!
Grant success to my task of accomplishment; truly manifest the power of the mantra. (12.594)
Having thus made the prayer, one should place either a fruit or unbroken rice grains (akṣata) into the lap of the sacred text from the hand of a maiden or a child.
Having understood this chapter in this way, one should place it within the mark of that verse;
then, having recognized the stanza, the minister should recite it with clear syllables.
The wise should understand the auspicious and inauspicious [outcomes] according to the meaning of the verse;
those verses which have the purpose of granting boons and those which serve to please the Goddess. (12.597)
Those verses which concern the undertaking of protection, those which concern future welfare, and those designated as "celestial festivals," are indicators of success. (12.598)
Therein is the enumeration of the Daityas, the description of the Goddess’s prowess, and the description of the Goddess’s indignation toward the Asuras on the field of battle. (12.599)
Such are the verses that grant victory in battle,
as well as those verses intended for prayer and likewise those in the form of hymns of praise.
And they indicate that the accomplishment will be delayed for a long time, provided that the following verse is intended for the purpose of granting a boon. (12.601)
Even such a verse as this promises success immediately; for it describes his misfortunes and makes them known to the gods. (12.602)
The dialogue between the mountain and the people, the description of their calamities, the words of the messenger, and the description of the prowess of the Daityas. || 12-603 ||
The description of their departure indicates the destruction of their purpose;
"calamities" refers to the description of the calamities of the gods (*suparvan*). The "perception" (*vedana*) of that calamity means its knowledge or, in other words, its narration.
By him, all those hosts of gods were cast down from heaven to the earth. (12.604)
The meaning is that they move about in such forms as these.
Some announce verses that are either desirable or undesirable;
upon obtaining such a verse, one should again perform the inquiry. (12.605)
Thus ends the section on the *Saptaśatī*. Now follows the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). As it is stated in the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the preliminary practice of breath control."
The mantra-practitioner, having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), keeps the body, head, and neck straight. || 12-606 ||

Having brought the collection of senses under control, free from distress and devoid of trembling, [one should meditate] in the *mūlādhāra*, or the *anāhata*, or in the lotus between the eyebrows. (12.607)
One should meditate on the mantra consisting of light, by which this restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*) is performed;
that is to say, the meaning is that the restraint of breath, which is breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), is to be performed with that mantra. Likewise:
One should meditate upon that auspicious nature of Śiva by the very path previously described.

The wise one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma), characterized by inhalation (pūraka) and the other stages; the term "Śiva" is used here with reference to the deity under discussion. Likewise:
Beginning from the time of dawn until two watches have passed. || 12-609 ||
Likewise, one should take a measured meal at night consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya);
one should not touch women, nor should one look upon base people.
On pure ground strewn with *kuśa* grass, one who has conquered the senses should lie down;
in this manner, the wise man should perform one hundred thousand breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
Then one should perform the fire oblation and other rites according to the path described for the preliminary service (puraścaryā).
One should cause the Brahmins to eat and likewise satisfy the Guru.
Having acted thus, liberated from all sins and possessing a pure body,
one attains the accomplishment of mantra, and especially the accomplishment of yoga.
He shall indeed be the locus even for the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*;
whatever mantra the practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*) seeks to accomplish, that mantra succeeds for him. (12.614)
Thus concludes the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Now, regarding the method for attaining mantra-perfection (*mantrasiddhi*) apart from the *puraścaraṇa*, [it is said in] the *Vīratantra*:
"Now I shall correctly explain the lineage of the perfections of the Guru."
Knowing this, one who discerns the distinction should guard it for my pleasure.
From the disclosure of this in the world, there is a great loss at every step.
The seed-syllable of Ugrāprabhā is this unprecedented pair, enriched by the fifth vowel and the final vowel [of the alphabet]: Śiva (H), Śikhin (R), and Śitabhānu (M).
Having meditated upon it within the circle of beautiful women for even a moment, [one attains success].
He exhausts his misfortune and becomes a king among the masters of debate. || 12-616 ||

*Śiva* is the letter *ha*. *Śikhin* is fire, whose seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the letter *ra*. The "white-rayed one" (*sitabhānu*) is the *anusvāra*. The fifth final vowel is *u*. Thus, *hum*—meaning the second seed-syllable of the *Ugraprabhā* mantra, which begins with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and ends with the *vahnijāyā* (*svāhā*).
Likewise: he conquers hosts of enemies and the kings of debate in dispute.

He who steals the hearts of beautiful women and possesses long life composes fine poetry unseen even by the kings of poets; yet, even a mind as sweet as honey must be abandoned, let alone the multitude of supernatural powers. (12.617)
Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra and all the letters of the Vedas— excluding those corrupted by defects such as *supta*— into the excellent womb of a noble maiden,
he who knows the ritual and has mastered the internal and external paths of the Guru’s lineage;
With a peaceful mind, one should cultivate that which is more effective when combined with honey. || 12-618 ||
O Mother, that person whose mind is intent on satisfying the lineage of ancestors through the continuous path of the family, and who would satisfy them with the waters of sacred fords—
he, it is said, [should satisfy them] with celestial flowers and corresponding fragrant garlands.
Having assumed the guise of a young woman, he is meditated upon with the thought that it is she. || 12-619 ||
He who, having worshipped in the *yonicakra* with all the well-known networks of ritual attendants preceded by the *nyāsa*s,
serves her who is born of a most pure lineage and is overcome by shame.
Having himself assumed a physical form, he causes agitation among the yoginīs.

The Lord of the Gods, who is the protector of the family of the Kulapati and whose fine garments have fallen away due to his sins, touches the central branch within the circle of the assembly of beasts and their enemies; having joined those two together—
One who is outside that [circle] should join it, having reflected upon it while it is enclosed within the *maṇi*.
O Mother, who among those possessed of wisdom— capable of assuming any form at will and whose minds are free from evil thought— could possibly describe those three aspects of yours in three ways,
you who are like the moon that has dispelled the net of darkness consisting of fear and dispute?
He should be rendered subject by means of nets produced from the power of holding [the breath] within the soles of the feet during recitation. || 12-622 ||
That wise one, whose body is fashioned from those qualities worthy of divine worship, attends upon them with the intent for the practice of liberation;
having extracted the seed and power of those who have shaken off the intoxication of passion.
Following that, [one should place] the seed-syllable Kaṭha and the world-supporting goddess within it. (12.623)
If one recites [this mantra], having attained absorption within me, he shall immediately attain the state of the city of the gods (Svarga) and be honored by the hosts of Siddhas.
One who is well-perfected [in this] possesses Śiva, Bhṛgu, Madapṛthvī, and Śakti.
Abounding in the respective supernatural powers of Hari, Hara, and Caturāsya.
Known as the Supreme Bestower of Boons, the agitator of passionate women,
the Lord of Speech, the Lord of Fortune, and the Sovereign of All—
[one should place] the seed-syllable of Desire (Kāma-bīja) beneath the syllable of Bhṛgu (Ma), and that [seed-syllable] before him.
The destruction of the world's fear occurs by joining with Kṣobhiṇī. || 12-625 ||
If Vīrasiṃha, who causes agitation within the lineage of noble young women through the state of passion, is recited or even once meditated upon,
having joined the seed-syllable of power (Śakti-bīja) beneath the creeper of the intoxication of love—
He is the form of Smara, Hara, and Hari; he is Kāmarūpa and Kuvera. || 12-626 ||
Having had the intense heat within their hearts shattered by the profuse watering from the lightning-like lotus-eyes of the deer-eyed women of the enemy clans,
they now resort to the root of the pride of Śiva-Bhṛgu— the very root of greed.
If one reflects upon the root of the path of the various gurus... || 12-627 ||
If the Lord of Treasures (Kubera), the Protector (Indra), and the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) are of auspicious mind, then this constitutes the primary sovereignty over the earth;
[the other planets] are like Varuṇa, excluding only one sense-organ, the sense of smell.
Above that is the deer-sign; this pair belongs to Bhavānī.

This seed-syllable of Bhavānī, joined with the *śiva* (H), *śamana* (S), and *naya* (Ū), is the king of mantras that bestows liberation upon all the foremost sages, is uniquely skilled in granting salvation, possesses a nature equal toward both the existent and the non-existent, and is the creator of well-being.
And those who share the same nature as Analaśiva [worship] the primordial king as independent.
O Maheśa, you alone are capable of explaining this twofold seed-syllable associated with the *samanā* state, as well as the celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
What need is there for the Lotus-born Brahmā here, with his thousands of streams of births?
Thus, by one's own good fortune, one partakes of the king of mantras among men.
O Mother, this devotee of your lotus feet never at any time abandons the Supreme Person;
indeed, no one has ever [abandoned] his body, which is beyond price.
Or having obtained it from the mouth of a guru who has been properly attended, why would one [abandon it] all of a sudden? || 12-631 ||
Beyond the city of the enemy of Smara (Śiva), beyond the shoreless practice for liberation,
dissolved in the supreme state through the enjoyments of all auspiciousness— there,
in the division of the city of fire (the triangle), is the seed-syllable of the aperture of Kālikā.
If one should perform even that for one who has been initiated, it would result in the color of a staff.
If one recites the entire mantra— which is adorned with two eyes, joined with the letter *nā* at the head,
followed by the fierce, protruding fangs, and endowed with the seed-syllable—
this is the most secret of secrets.
What is there in these three worlds that can be obtained through affliction by any means whatsoever?

If that which is accumulated in succession—the entire unprecedented [result]—is bound together, then the Manu (the cosmic being) is to be contemplated as something other than that; its form abides in the middle.
If he, who possesses the nature of consciousness and bliss, remains alone, he partakes in that state.
The foremost of the various worlds, full of curiosity, and preeminent in honor. || 12-634 ||
Thus I have told you all this most wonderful secret;
what in this world cannot be accomplished by a king among yogis through following it in due order?
Now, the *Bhairavasādhana* (from the *Merutantra*): "Next, I shall fully explain the various *sādhanas* of Bhairava.
They abide in cremation grounds, at various times, in every city. (12.636)

He who does not abandon any single rule imbued with dharma, even if he is devoted to the left-hand path (vāmamārga) and so forth, provided he feels no hatred toward those following other paths. (12.637)
If, due to fear of the world, one performs the practice with inferior materials, or when the teacher is unqualified or the ritual incomplete, that deity Bhairava becomes the ruler of that region.
The spirits and vetālas dwelling there always attend upon him;
he constantly exercises authority over those who have fallen away from their own path. (12.639)
When he, whose karma is exhausted, has departed, the village dissolves;
when another Bhairava is born, the village certainly dwells [again]. (12-640)
Since Bhairava is that tradition and his teaching is in that direction,
one should bring that very Bhairava under control by means of that path for the sake of accomplishing the task.
The seed-syllables *vāgra*, *mā*, *kāya*, *māyā*, and *tāra* shall be, in sequence,
for the lineages (*āmnāyas*) beginning from the east and ending at the zenith, respectively.
The seed-syllable of the tradition (āmnāyabīja) is the seed of the village and of Bhairava;
having then uttered the name of the village, [one addresses him] as residing in the ancestral home.
Then, one should recite this mantra of theirs ten thousand times at night in a cremation ground, and offer a bali-oblation according to the method prescribed in the tradition.
With undistracted mind, one should always offer [the oblation] at the beginning and at the end of the recitation;
one should offer the products of the cow as prescribed for Vaṭuka, and thereafter perform the libations and other rites.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra becomes capable of subduing living beings;
hear now how its direct manifestation occurs in that place.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites in the morning, fasting and with senses subdued,
he should perform the evening twilight prayers and the like, and carry out the recitation for peace.
Having gathered the necessary materials in the evening, the practitioner together with his assistant should proceed to the cemetery; listen attentively to the requirements for the cemetery. 12-648.
Likewise, [he should offer] water with ungerminated sesame seeds and mung beans, as well as lentils; similarly, chickpeas, cooked rice, milk-rice, cakes, and *śaṣkulī* pastries. (12.649)
A thread spun by a maiden and well-dyed with saffron; eight pieces of khadira wood, each a span (vitasti) in length and as thick as a closed fist. (12.650)
A single *kolā* [measure], one cubit (*hasta*) in length, as well as perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
and the sacrificial materials previously mentioned, together with fish, according to the Eastern Tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*).
In the Western Tradition it is with meat; in the Northern, it is with wine.
In the Center of the Village and in the cremation ground, in the Upper Tradition, it is with blood. (12.652)
Having offered the oblation as is appropriate, one should depart free from fear;
then, having performed the washing of the feet, one should remember that deity.
With palms joined in reverence, the supreme practitioner should utter these words:
"Whatever deities indeed dwell here in this cremation ground... (12.654)
May they grant me success, may they be gracious, and may they protect me!
May Śaṅkara protect me in the east, and likewise may the wielder of the trident protect me in the southeast.
May Kapālī protect [me] in the south; may Jaṭila protect in the southwest;
may the Lord of Pārvatī protect in the west; and may the Lord of the Pramathas protect in the northwest. (12.656)

May he richly adorned with a garland of severed heads protect me in the north; may the bull-bannered Lord protect me in the northeast; likewise, may Śambhu protect me from above, and he grey with dust protect me from below.
May Bhairava protect me from the front; may Khecara protect me from behind;
may Bhūdhara protect me on the right; and may Piśitāśana protect me on the left.
May the large-eyed one protect the hair; may the beloved of the Maruts protect the crown of the head;
may the Lord of Bhṛgu protect the skull; and may the high-minded one protect the eyes. || 12-659 ||
May Vīreśa protect my cheeks; may Gaṇḍādimardana protect my temples;
may Virūpākṣa protect my upper lip, and Yoginīpriya my lower lip.

May the Lord who destroys Dakṣa protect me in my teeth; may he who bears a human skull on his chin protect me; and may the blue-throated God, the teacher of the world, protect me in my throat. (12.661)
May Girīndreśa protect the right shoulder and Sundara the left shoulder;
may Sarvamantranātha always protect the right arm. (12.662)
May Sārvabhauma protect my left arm; may Pāṇḍura protect my heart; may Paśupati protect my right breast, and Maheśvara protect my left. || 12-663 ||
May the one who performs all that is auspicious protect me always in the north;
may the destroyer of desire protect me at the navel, and may the compassionate one protect my shanks.
May Ajāmitra protect my knees, may the Lord of Gaurī always protect my ankles,
may the Treasure of Knowledge protect the backs of my feet, and likewise may Hara protect my toes.
"May Vyomakeśa, the beloved of the world, constantly protect [me] beneath my feet.
Having thus established this protection, one should then perform the mantra-protection.
Oṃ hrā hru hru hru ca in the east;
oṃ hrī hro in the southeast (the burner); having placed oṃ hrī śrī in the south; and oṃ glu slu also in the southwest.
Oṃ plu/ mlu/ ylu/ and Tāra in the west; pro/ pru/ in the northwest (samīraṇa);
oṃ bhrā/ Bhairava in the north; and oṃ blu/ plu/ bhru/ phaṭ in the northeast (śiva). || 12-668 ||
Oṃ glau blu! At the region of the head, then srā sru sra; it is remembered that *srasta* is below.
Having thus established the protection, the stakes are [placed] at the eight directions beginning with the east. (12.669)
Then, having placed the great kila in the center, one should begin the worship of the guardians of the directions;
thereafter, filled with love, one should recite this mantra and offer a prayer. || 12-670 ||
Having uttered "Bhrā" or "Bhairava" twice, one should say "bhayaṅkarahara";
then "māṃ rakṣa rakṣa huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this mantra consists of twenty-two syllables. || 12-671 ||
Having placed black gram beans in a vessel made of *palāśa* wood, one should then go toward the east;
there, near the ritual stake (*kīla*), one should invoke Indra and worship him.
Having performed the meditation as previously described, one should offer an oblation to Indra within a square mandala using this mantra:
p. 1207) [Omitted in source] One should present the bali offering to Indra in the mandala with this mantra.
Having uttered *oṃ hrāḥ hrīḥ hruḥ*, [one says]: "O Indra, leader of the gods!
Be gracious to me quickly and grant me eternal accomplishment (*siddhi*)."
"Accept this offering, accept it, hūṃ phaṭ! [O you] of the color of fire and serpents!
Having offered water and cast forth the offering, one should bow and proceed to the fire-stake.
Having invoked the fire there and meditated upon it as before, one should worship it;
having fashioned a mandala in front of that, one should indeed offer the bali-oblation with the mantra.
Oṃ ra rā rū rū ca ri rī; at its tip, one should step upon the word "Agni.
One should speak thus: "O Leader of Radiance, quickly grant me success! (12.677)
"mudgabaliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ phaṭ"—this is the mantra consisting of seven syllables.
Then, one should worship Yama near the southern kīla.
Having invoked [the deity] with the seed-syllable *ma*, one should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra:
*oṃ prā prī pru*; then [one should utter]: *prā prī prū bho yamapadaṃ*. (12-679)
"O Lord of the Pretas, quickly become gracious and speak!
Accept this offering of lentils in the bowl for me!"—thus one should say twice. (12-680)
The mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ* is declared to be of a reddish-yellow color.
Then, one should worship Nairṛta near the kīla of the southwest. || 12-681 ||
Having invoked [the deity] with the seed-syllable *kṣa*, the mantra for the offering (*bali*) is now declared:
*oṃ pre pre pre*, then *hū hū* three times, *kha* twice, and *hrī* twice, followed by the pair *bhoyuga*. (12.682)
O Lord of the Rakṣasas, quickly from your feet, be gracious and speak!
Accept this offering of chickpeas for me—*hūm phaṭ*; thus is the mantra considered. (12.683)
Then, with the thirty-six-syllable mantra, one should proceed to the western *kīlaka*;
having invoked Varuṇa there by means of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should worship him.
The *bali* mantra is *dhruvaḥ brāḥ brīḥ bho bho varuṇa saṃvadet*.
At the end of the words for the Lord of Waters (*jalanātha*), one should say: "Be gracious" (*prasanno bhava saṃvadet*). (12.685)
"Take, take this offering of exhortation for you, HŪṂ CA PHAṬ!
This thirty-syllable mantra is declared to be that of Varuṇa Bala. (12.686)
From there, one should go to the northwest corner and worship near the kīla; having invoked Vāyu with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, hear the mantra of Vāyu from Bala: *yaṃ* (the mantra).
Or *vī*, *vū*; then *krā*, *krī*. "O Vāyu, again and again, quickly become gracious; drink this of mine! || 12-688 ||
*Baliṃ gṛhṇa yugaṃ hūṃ phaṭ* is the thirty-five-syllable mantra.
Then, having gone to Udak-kīla, [one should worship] Dhaneśvara with the seed-syllable *ku*. (12.689)

*mama apūpa-baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having gone near the Īśāna-kīla, one should invoke Īśāna with the seed-syllable *haḥ*;

Taking flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), one stands below the middle pillar;

With this mantra, one who is fearless and firm should perform worship;

Oṃ hrāḥ hrīḥ hruḥ; then one should utter hraḥ, kṣrāḥ kṣrīḥ kṣruḥ kṣraḥ.

MRŪ / MRO / MRE / MRA, then MRO / MRAU; having uttered these three groups of seven, each repeated three times as stated, one should utter PHAṬ at the end of all of them. || 12-697 ||

Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍakeśa, Caṇḍātman, Cāmara, Cāritra, Camatkāra, Cañcala, and Cārubhūṣaṇa. || 12-704 ||
Cāmīkara, Cāruvaha, and Cakita— these sixteen,

One should worship the [eight goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī on the eight petals, the lords of the directions on the outer path, their weapons on the path outside that, and these [following deities] on the path outside that.
Those named Pracaṇḍa, Caṇḍa, Ūrdhvakeśa, Bhīṣaṇa, Abhiṣaṇa, Vyomakeśa, Vyomavāha, and Vyomavyāpaka; || 12-707 ||
Having summoned these heroes, one should utter the words, "Come here!

One who has ascended [to this state] should recite this; then the divine state becomes manifest.

One should fashion the six limbs with *māyā* and draw an eight-petalled lotus;

Having worshipped the Goddess upon the pedestal, one should meditate on the Goddess, the beloved of the world.
The meditation is as follows: [One should meditate on her] with a face like the full moon, fair-complexioned, and wearing variegated garments. (12.721)

Having meditated thus upon the beautiful woman, whose breasts are uplifted by drinking [the nectar], who is the primordial of all and the bestower of fearlessness, one should offer the auspicious water for the feet and other offerings with the root mantra.

Having meditated upon the Goddess with a measure of one thousand repetitions at all times, the wise man,
