Having performed this, one should recite the mantra; at midnight, Sundarī arrives at the practitioner's abode through her majesty, perceiving the practitioner to be most steadfast.

Then, being exceedingly gracious before the practitioner and always possessing a smiling countenance—the lord of practitioners, having beheld the Goddess, should offer auspicious water for the feet and other offerings. (12.727)
Knowing that she desires excellent sandalwood and *sumanasa* flowers, one should speak to her—whether she be a mother, a sister, or even a wife—with a spirit of devotion. (12.728)
If she is the mother, then she grants day by day divine and most enchanting wealth, as well as that sovereignty over the earth which was requested. (12.729)
In this world, truth has been protected like a son; this truth is most certainly established. Furthermore, one's sister bestows a divine gift as well as celestial garments.
Bringing forth celestial maidens and nāga maidens day after day,
[he knows] whatever has happened and whatever will happen again.
She certainly offers all of that to the lord of practitioners;
whatever he prays for, she gives it all to him day after day.
If that goddess were to become the enchanting wife of the practitioner, she would be protected in the world by his desires and longings as if she were a brother. (12.733)
The lord of kings among all kings, the supreme practitioner in saṃsāra, his path is certain everywhere—in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld. (12.734)
Whatever that goddess bestows cannot be described;
and with her, the supreme practitioner enjoys union. (12.735)
"Having abandoned going to another's wife, otherwise one certainly perishes.
Thus ends the *Sundarīsādhana*. Now follows the *Manoharāsādhana* in that same [text].
Next, I shall describe another means of accomplishment, which was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times.
Having reached the riverbank, one should then perform the ritual bathing and other rites;
all the procedures should be carried out as before, and one should draw a mandala with sandalwood paste.
Having written one's own mantra there and invoked [the deity], one should meditate upon the enchanting lady.
As for the meditation:
she has the eyes of a deer, a face like the autumn moon, lips like the bimba fruit, and is anointed with the fragrance of sandalwood.
Clad in fine silken garments, with full breasts, enchanting, youthful, ever-granting desires, and most wonderful.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra for the Goddess while offering incense of aguru and padmaka.

Gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ rasaṃ caiva tāmbūlādīṃśca mūlataḥ | Tāraṃ māyā tathāgaccha manohare pāvakavallabhā || 12-739 || [The mantra for] perfume, flowers, flavors, betel, and so forth, from the root: Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and likewise "Come, O Manoharā, Beloved of Fire" (Svāhā). || 12-739 ||
Having bathed, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times every day with a serene mind;
at the end of the month, having reached that final day, one should perform the supreme recitation.
Having recognized the practitioner as firm, she recites the mantra until midnight;
then, becoming well-pleased and enchanting, she approaches the practitioner. (12.741)
"Choose a boon quickly, whatever resides in your mind.
Then the foremost of practitioners, with devotion, should joyfully honor her with water for the feet and other offerings. (12.742)
One should perform the six-limbed *prāṇāyāma* along with the *māyā* [mantra],
and having offered an oblation of fish and meat, one should worship with a concentrated mind.
Then, having been worshipped with sandalwood water, flowers, and fruit, she becomes pleased and, being propitiated, fulfills whatever is desired. (12.744)
She gives a hundred loads of gold day after day;
she would spend it with great distinction, but once she has stopped, she will not give it.
For him, there shall be no approaching another's wife; it is declared that his movement becomes unimpeded—of this there is no doubt. (12.746)

Even if the Yakṣiṇī has been accomplished according to the ritual procedure, if she does not come, one should utter words of wrathful intent, saying: "Poison! [This is directed] against such-and-such a Yakṣiṇī! (12.747)
From Bhūteśa [one proceeds] to Mādana; these two winds are joined with the weapon of Krodha.
Having stepped upon [the victim] with this Krodha, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
When this is done, she arrives and bestows the desired object.
He describes the mudrā: Having formed a fist with the hands joined together, one should interlace both little fingers. (12.749)
Extending and then contracting the two index fingers, they should be formed into the shape of a hook;
this is the Krodhāṅkuśī mudrā, capable of summoning yakṣiṇīs. (12.750)
O Sovereign of the Gods, this knowledge which is most secret has been told to you;
O Supreme Goddess, I am under your sway because of your affection and my devotion.
Thus ends the *Manoharāsādhana*.
Now, the mantra of Dhanadā is found in that same source:
"That [syllable] *tūrya* joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), and the seed-syllable of *lajjā* (hrīṃ) likewise with the nasal drop."
Then, O Goddess, one should address the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī as "O beloved of Rati."
The mantra ending with *svāhā* is declared to be the king of mantras, the most excellent of the excellent.
Another mantra is as follows:
that fourth [vowel] joined with the *bindu*, *lakṣmī*, and the *praṇava*. (12.753)
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā and awakened Ratipriyā,
[the syllable] Vahnijāyā is thus proclaimed as the most excellent of the best among kings of mantras.
Kuvera is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), the Paṅkti its metre (chandas), and the deity is Dhanada; its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the propitiation of that goddess. || 12-755 ||
The ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs is prescribed with the six long [syllables] and the Āyā mantra;
after that, the meditation: [one should visualize her] as having the luster of the interior of saffron and possessing the grace of early youth. (12.756)
Her arms were as tender as lotus stalks, adorned with armlets and bracelets,
and her two lotus-feet were set in motion by the tips of her anklets.
Adorned with necklaces of rubies, crowns, earrings, and other ornaments,
her eyes were like blue lotuses, and she was graced by her slightly swelling breasts.
She holds a lotus whirling in her lotus-hand, is clothed in red garments and anointed with red unguents,
and stands upon a jeweled lion-throne situated within a golden enclosure.
One should meditate upon that goddess, the bestower of wealth, at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
Having meditated, the most excellent practitioner, intent on devotion, should worship her. (12.760)
One should draw a wheel consisting of nine wombs (navayoni) upon the pericarp;
having drawn a lotus with petals in the cardinal directions, one should then draw a square outside of that.
Having drawn vajras in the corners, one should inscribe the seed-syllable (bīja) in the center;
having worshipped the limbs (aṅgas) upon the filaments (keśara), one should worship the powers (śaktis) upon the petals.
Lakṣmī, Padmā, Padmālayā, Śrī, Haripriyā, Harā, Kamalālayā, Abjalolā, and Cañcalā. (12.763)
Having worshipped these Śaktis, one should then worship the Goddess in the center;
one should perform the recitation [of mantras] with a thread made of jewels, following the right-hand tradition.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for the attainment of the mantra; then the wise practitioner should perform the ritual applications.
If one recites it eight thousand times at night for seven days, [the result follows]. (12.765)
By this very means, the ritual procedures such as the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) become perfectly accomplished;
O Goddess, what could be difficult to achieve here for a human being who practices it? (12.766)
Whether having eaten or not having eaten, and having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), one should perform purification ten times; or else, one may bring her into the family without performing purification.
O Goddess, by remembering that Vidyā, one is not overcome by miseries of poverty;
one should daily recite the mantra of Kāmadeva with devotion at the side of the Goddess. (12.768)
By that [offering], great joy is bestowed and the desired object is granted;
at the conclusion of the worship, the goddess Dhaneśvarī arrives in the night.
Having cast off all ornaments and given them away, she goes to her own abode;
and having bestowed abundant wealth, she fulfills the desires of the practitioner.
Having completed [the rite], O Maheśānī, the auspicious woman becomes submissive;
she herself declares: "O Mistress of Yakṣas, that man who remembers me... (12.771).
"I shall act like a maidservant to effect his renunciation of poverty.
He states the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the second mantra: "The preparatory rite is said to consist of seven hundred repetitions. (12.772)
A person, having prepared a maṇḍala in a copper vessel smeared with sandalwood paste, [should offer it] with ghee, sugar, and honey, in the tenth part [of the quantity]. || 12-773 ||
Worship of the Great Goddess should be performed for the sake of the immediate pacification of poverty;
one should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and [visualize] the deity within his own body.
In accordance with the opinion of Kuvera, her worship is likewise performed.
Thus ends the *Dhanadasādhana*.
Now follows the *Apsarassādhana* (from the *Bhūtaḍāmara*).
The frost is Śrī, the moon is the goddess Tilottamā, who is beginningless and the very essence of beauty.
Having extracted the mantra beginning with *tāra*, it is called Kāñcanamālikā; joined with *tāra*, *śrī*, and *varman*, she should be meditated upon as wearing beautiful earrings. (12.776)
The fifth is *tāraṃ varmasamāyuktaṃ ratnamālyā*; the sixth is *tāraṃ brahma* known as Rambhā; the seventh is Viṣa; and the next is Śrī-Urvaśī. (12.777)
Having bowed to Krodha, I shall now proclaim the means for attaining the accomplishments (siddhi) of these [goddesses]: Anādibījā, Mātā, Bhūtinī, and Apsarā, in their respective order.
Having ascended a mountain peak, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind;
having worshipped on the full moon day, one should offer a lamp of ghee.
One should recite throughout the entire night; she arrives at the exhaustion of one's bonds.
Satisfied by an offering of sandalwood, she says: "Choose a boon."
She becomes his beloved wife and bestows an elixir;
he lives for a thousand years, and she grants him whatever boon he desires. (12.781)
One who subsists on milk should recite [the mantra] exactly ten thousand times for seven days;
then, on the seventh day, having prepared a mandala with sandalwood— || 12-782 ||
Having worshipped with devotion on the eighth day of the bright fortnight at the eastern summit, one should perform recitation throughout the entire night; at the end of the night, she arrives.
Having arrived, she stands before him with white garments and uplifted breasts;
kissing and embracing him quickly, she becomes his wife according to his desire. (12.784)
Being well-satisfied, she grants him sovereignty and even reveals herself for three days;
having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures for five thousand years, [he attains liberation]. || 12-785 ||
Tilottamā grants birth in a royal family when one has died;
otherwise, if the ritual is performed incorrectly, one dies quickly.
Having performed the union with the downward-flowing [channel], one should draw a mandala with sandalwood paste, offer incense and agallochum, and present the bali offering. || 12-787 ||
One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times daily for a period of seven days;
on the seventh day, having performed worship, one should offer incense.
One should recite [the mantra] throughout the entire night; at the end of the night, she arrives. Satisfied by an offering of sandalwood, she says, "Choose a boon."
The practitioner should also say: "Protect me as a mother.
[The deity] bestows clothing, ornaments, and food upon the servants. (12.791)
The Kāñcanamālikā [rite] bestows birth into a royal family upon one who has died;
neither a specific lunar day, nor a constellation, nor a fast is prescribed for it. (12.792)
Having stationed oneself upon a mountain peak, one should recite the mantra for ten thousand times over the course of a month;
having offered incense and performed worship, one should then recite it again at night.
At midnight she arrives; as before, one should cause the *arghya* offering to be presented.
She becomes his beloved wife and grants [her favors] every day. (12.794)
Carrying him upon her back, she who took away his earrings showed him one hundred thousand pieces of gold, perfected elixirs, and rejuvenating potions, as well as heaven itself.
Having gone to a temple of the deities, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for one month;
then, at the end of the month, on the full moon day, one should recite it again.
Having performed worship at midnight, one hears the sound of footsteps;
he arrives and one should offer him an unsurpassed seat of flowers.
"Tell me what you desire; become my wife," says the practitioner.
She then performs the duties of a wife and bestows a kingdom according to one's wishes. (12.798)
Having prepared a mandala of sandalwood, she remains satisfied every day for thousands of years, beginning from the first lunar day.
Having offered incense and guggulu resin, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
having performed a most beautiful worship at the three junctions of the day and on the full moon.
One should recite [the mantra] throughout the entire night; at the end of the night she arrives.
She becomes one's desired wife, otherwise she will certainly die. (12.801)
It bestows desired food, perfected substances, and elixirs;
one lives for ten thousand years, and upon death at the end, [is reborn]. (12.802)
One should cause birth in a royal family; one may bestow [punishment or favor] through anger or grace.
Having gone to a temple at night, one should draw a mandala with sandalwood paste.
Having offered incense and then recited the mantra ten thousand times for each month,
one should perform a great worship at the end of the month and carry out the recitation during the night.
At the end of the night she arrives; one should offer her a seat of flowers.
Having offered a welcome, one should ask, "What do you desire? and she speaks. (12.805)
The practitioner said: "Become my wife and grant me the elixir;
the Apsaras Urvaśī herself shall remain for thousands of years."
One should avoid all the wives of others; otherwise, one will certainly die.
Remaining alone on one's bed at night, being pure, [one should anoint oneself] with saffron. (12.807)
Having written [the mantra] upon birch bark with sandalwood paste, one should fumigate it;
then, one should diligently recite it eight thousand times for the duration of a month.
Having worshipped at the end of a month, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
she arrives within half a night and becomes a beloved wife.
When satisfied, Bhūṣiṇī bestows perfected substances and gold;
however, Krodharāja spoke again: "If the practitioner does not come... (12.810)
With this wrathful yoga, one should recite the assembly of apsarases;
one should extract the initial poison-seed and the pair of pungent syllables.
Having extracted the name of [the person], the seed-syllable of wrath (krodhabīja), and the wind-syllable (vāta) conjoined with the syllable of passion (ādara),
one should recite this mantra eight thousand times.
"He dies, he withers, he bursts upon his head, and the apsarases [emerge]! With this mantra, the practitioner should pay homage to the host of apsarases. (12.813)
Having proclaimed the two poison-bindings, one should utter the pair of days;
"Amukīm"—this is the Krodha mantra that brings Apsarases under control.
Now I shall declare the supreme mantra that brings the Apsarases under control:
having uttered "viṣaṃ caladvayam," one says, "bring [the name] so-and-so under my power. (12.815)
By means of the recitation of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) together with a *kūrca* syllable, one will certainly bring the *apsarases* under control.
Now follows the *sādhana* of Jvālāmukhī (from the *Phetkāriṇītantra*):
having uttered "Obeisance to the Blessed Lady" (*namo bhagavati*), [one should follow] after that with the mantra of Jvālāmālinī. (12.816)
Surrounded by a flock of vultures, the mantra *dviṭhānta* (ending in *svāhā*) is proclaimed by Manu;
*Oṃ namaḥ* is declared to be the heart, and *bhagavati* is remembered as the head.

One should place upon the body the crest-mantra *Jvālāmālinī*, surrounded by a flock of vultures, together with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras, joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*). || 12-818 ||
Without having eaten, the victor should certainly recite this mantra of victory.
Now, another mantra for that same purpose is given therein:
"Rudrāṅganāgnijāyā" (the wife of the fire born of Rudra's consort) is also known as "Rudrajvālāmukhī. (12.819)
Immediately following [the mantra of] Jvālāmukhī, another mantra is fully explained:
beginning from the day of the Guru, at midnight, one whose feet are smeared with lamp-oil [should perform the rite]. (12.820)
One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for twenty-three days;
there is no doubt that it bestows six palas every day. (12.821)
He speaks of the greatness of the former mantra:
"It was told by Nārāyaṇa and told again by Agastya;
it should not even be uttered by name by one desiring perfect accomplishment. (12.822)
And for a son, especially for a righteous king, one should perform the rite according to the procedure for the Nine Durgās due to the gravity of the matter. (12.823)
The king, being of proper conduct and knowledgeable in mantras, should first offer various kinds of wealth according to the prescribed rite, and thereafter perform the formal reception of the mantra.
By mere recollection, one may destroy all enemies of every caste;
one should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of either a thousand or a hundred [gold pieces]. || 12-825 ||
By giving cows, gold, golden coins, or land abounding in grain, one attains all peace and becomes a provider of all protection. (12.826)
A golden ornament (*niṣka*) is the adornment.
Thus ends the *sādhana* of Jvālāmukhī. (p.
1221) Now, the mantra of Karṇapiśācī is found in that same [source].
"Kaha-yugmam kālike ca, likewise take the pair [with] 'piṇḍaṃ piśāci svāhā'—this is declared as the mantra of Dvīpārṇa. (12.827)

Meditation: One should meditate upon the Piśācī—dark green, very tall, and youthful; holding a moving trident in her hand; possessing three eyes; wrathful and discolored; with a slender, rounded waist; and wearing a necklace fashioned from Guñjā berries.
He describes the method of accomplishment: one should recite [the mantra] from sunrise until sunset for twenty-one days.
Every evening, one should cast one's own food, as a single morsel, upon the roof of the palace.
After three weeks, that female piśāca, having become pleased, went to his bed and even related stories of twenty-five countries.
O Goddess of the gods, one should relate the story of Jambūdvīpa in thirty days;
likewise, O Gaurī, one will certainly cause the three worlds to hear it in thirty-two days.
By offering a bali-oblation of the three sweets, one can cause everything to be spoken at that very moment—
whether in an assembly, in a gathering, in a game of dice, or in the presence of enemies.
She certainly speaks everything quickly; she is surely a pleased Piśācinī. She cannot be known by anyone at all, yet the practitioner beholds her.
Thus ends the sādhana of Karṇapiśācī.
Now, the sādhanas of Vibhūṣiṇī and others (in the Phetkāriṇītantra):
The first goddess is Vibhūṣiṇī, the supreme wearer of earrings. (12.833)
Hāriṇī, Siṃhinī, Haṃsinī, and then Naṭī; the goddess Kāmeśvarī and the goddess Ratipriyā have thus been described.
He states the mantra for Vibhūṣiṇī:
"The two Krodha-weapons, followed by Māyā and Bhūtinī, then the three Kūrca-syllables;
after the Oṃ, the two Lajjā-syllables, and at the end of the two weapons, comes Vibhīṣikā. (12.835)
This mantra, ending with two wrathful syllables, has been proclaimed by Vibhūṣiṇī. (12.835ef)
She is in meditative absorption;
in her other hand she holds a human head of lofty form, terrifying,
and she observes the vow of the spirits consisting of flesh, blood, and fat caught between her teeth.
May she, whose entire earth and mountains are filled with masses of hair resembling the terrifying fang-sprouts of Time’s fierce and formidable serpents, protect us. 12-836.
He states the method of accomplishment:
"Having gone to a solitary tree, one should dwell there for three nights during the night;
one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times while meditating with an undistracted mind. (12.837)
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform worship by name and offer aguru incense;
at midnight, she who is adorned with ornaments arrives.
If an arghya offering mixed with sandalwood water is presented, she will certainly be satisfied;
whether she be a mother, a sister, or a wife, she becomes joyful and gratified. (12.839)
Having become the Mother of the three worlds through the act of melting [the elements],
she is the constant ointment and ornament for the retinue of one hundred and eight.
O Great Yogin, if a sister brings a woman even from a distance of a thousand yojanas and bestows her as a divine elixir of rasa, [one attains success]. || 12-841 ||
If one's wife touches it and places it upon him, she leads him to heaven at that very moment;
moreover, he obtains a thousand jewels daily, as well as mercury and an elixir of immortality.
The word "should give" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. The Goddess Vibhūṣaṇī always fulfills all desires.
Now, the mantra for Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī is found in that very same place.
She who possesses the pair of weapons Dhruva and Māyā is called Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī.
One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times every day for the duration of one month;
she who wears earrings on her ears, she who wears moon-shaped earrings.
When she arrives, an offering of blood should be presented; being satisfied, she speaks:
"What should be done by me, my child? Become a practitioner (sādhaka), O Mother! (12.845)
Even with fifty days, he will grant even the three worlds. Now, the mantra for Sindūrahāriṇī is as follows: from the pair of Krodhas and the pair of Astras, the word "Sindūrahāriṇī. (12.846)
The mantra of Sindūrahāriṇī is declared to end with three *kūrca*s.
Meditation: She who captivates with her adornment of golden lotus-stalks, whose garment is the branches swaying on trembling leaves,
who is beautiful in her longing gestures of the body, and who possesses the radiance of the moon, the white-rayed one.
May this trident-creeper, which possesses teeth of continuous inner luster, which is the seat of the beauty of the three worlds, and which is captivating with its vermilion, protect you. (12.847)
Having gone to an empty temple, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
she will quickly come, and having arrived, she becomes the desired wife.
For twenty-five days, the goddess Sindūrahāriṇī bestows garments, ornaments, and decorations upon the lord of practitioners.

Now, the mantra of Siṃhinī is given in that same place: "The two *lajjās*, the pair of *astras*, then the word 'Siṃhinī', with the three seed-syllables of Wrath at the beginning and the end—this is proclaimed as the Siṃhinī mantra. (12.850)
Meditation:
O Durgā, whose hair rests upon the mountain peaks, trees, heavens, and the faces of Daityas,
and who strikes terror into all the bones of Viṣṇu as he falls from her feet!

May she protect [us]— she who, in the battle of holding [the skull-bowl] suspended between her teeth, causes the Siddha-women to tremble, and whose garland is agitated by the shaking of the entire multitude of thorns.
Having gone to a solitary linga at night, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times;
then, being worshipped, the delighted Siṃhinī, the bestower of supreme boons, approaches. (12.852)
"What shall I do?"—thus speaks the beloved wife;
she gives a pair of garments to the wretched man, as well as juices and elixirs. (12.853)
Now, the *haṃsinī* mantra is given in that very same place:
"The *tāra*, the three *kūrca*s, the weapon (*astra*), the pair [of *tāra*s], *haṃsinī*, and then *bhūtinī*; ending with three *kūrca*s—this is declared to be the supreme *haṃsinī* mantra. (12.854)
Meditation:
Her eyes are like white and white-lotus flowers; she is worshipped with milk and wine;
she is respectfully attended by young women who are charmed by the sounds she has begun.

May the illustrious Haṃsinī protect us—she whose face is charmingly closed as her slightly raised, tremulous side-glances are cast about, and who is graced by a shimmering necklace of strung pearls. 12.855.
Having gone to the abode of Vajrapāṇi, one should paint a beautiful image;
having worshipped it with Hayamāra, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Until midnight, the goddess certainly arrives in the form of a female swan;
delighted by the offering of sandalwood and water for the feet, she speaks to the practitioner. (12.857)
"What shall I do for you? O practitioner, become my servant!
She provides clothing, ornaments, food, and so forth, for the sake of expenditure. (12.858)
Because there is no lack of any resources, he does not give and becomes angry.
Now, regarding the means of the female servant (*ceṭī*) in that very context:
thereafter, a pair of *kūrca* [brushes] and a pair of weapons, and then the female servant. (12.859)
Having spoken the pair of Krodhas ending in *ṅe*, [one should utter] the pair of Ceṭīs and then *trapā*.
Dhyāna: Walking along, speaking with measured words, her moon-like face radiant, her upper garment slipped away,
bearing a water-pot and a pair of lotuses— such is the golden-complexioned woman.

May this maidservant protect you—she whose pure body is honored by the fragrance of sandalwood paste and other unguents, and who has offered her hand earned through some measure of religious merit. 12-860.
In any terrifying place, by the mere utterance of her name, a female servant will certainly appear and perform even the work of a servant. (12.861)
Alternatively, one should perform the recitation at his house door for three nights;
the Goddess will surely come and perform the work of a servant.

Now, the mantra of Kāmeśvarī is given in that same place: "Oṃ, Hrīṃ, Phaṭ, Kāmeśvari, Bhūti—after this, the threefold Krodha ending in Ṅ (Krodheśvari). This is declared to be the mantra of Kāmeśvarī. (12.863)
Meditation: She belongs to the realm of desire; she is endowed with the sweetness of spring flowers; she sings with a face of sweet lips and smiles; she holds a lute and is fickle.

May this Kāmeśvarī Bhūtinī, whose eyes are like red lotuses, who is intoxicated by the intoxication of honey, who wields the flower-bow, and who is filled with the fragrance of spring, protect us on all sides. 12-864.
Having approached the Mother’s abode and partaken of meat, and having offered an oblation of meat and other substances for seven days, [one should recite] a thousand [times]. || 12-865 ||
Through recitation, one certainly attains success; one should present an offering of blood.
Kāmeśvarī becomes pleased, and she becomes one's desired wife.
It certainly fulfills all hopes and bestows a kingdom with certainty.
Now, regarding the mantra of Ratipriyā in that very same context:
Tāra (Oṃ), Lajjā (Hrīḥ), joined with the two [syllables] Kūrca (Hūṃ) and Astra (Phaṭ), is Ratipriyā. (12.867)
The ritual action involving the three weapons of wrath and shame is as described for the mantra of Kāmeśvarī.
Meditation:
In the midst of a golden enclosure, upon the slope of a celestial tree, she sits enthroned upon a golden seat—
a Yakṣī whose mass of braided hair is radiant with flowers whose fragrance spreads forth.

Abounding in full and lofty breasts, with eyes like blue lotuses, red in complexion, holding two whirling red lotuses in her hands, she is joined by all the gods and adorned with divine ornaments and unguents.
Having gone to a temple at night, one should prepare a bed there;
one should offer white cloth, sandalwood, and jasmine flowers.
Having offered guggulu incense, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, she constantly arrives with kisses, embraces, and the like.
The maiden goddess, who is Truth itself, becomes his beloved wife;
then, within eight days, she shall grant him a divine pair of garments.
He will provide divine, wish-fulfilling food for his retinue;
furthermore, bringing other substances from the house of Vaiśvānara, he bestows them.
One should recite these one thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, success is attained with certainty.
"One should recite the mantra again and again," so said Krodhabhūpati. (12.873)
Thus end the sādhana rites for Vibhūṣiṇī and the others.
Now follows the sādhana of Dharitrī. As it is said in the *Vaiṣṇavīkalpa*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme sādhana of Dharitrī."
It is a supreme secret, hidden within all tantras.
It bestows all sovereignty upon men, being difficult to attain and most wonderful;
having known it, the foremost of practitioners becomes equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). (12.875)
And in the autumn season, in the middle of a field crowded with lotuses,
having constructed a beautiful hut, one should install an auspicious water-pot.
On the eighth day of the lunar month, an image fashioned at night from earth brought from the ground, smeared with fragrant pastes, and wrapped in white cloth; (12.877)
Having invoked Vasundharā there with the mantra to be recited hereafter,
the wise practitioner should worship her at the three junctions of the day with an abundance of various ritual offerings.
The seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū), followed by Tāra (Oṃ) and Māyā (Hrīṃ), and then Vasundharā in the feminine dative case (Dharāyai);
this twelve-syllable mantra is known as the Heart-mantra ending with the wife of Fire (Svāhā). || 12-879 ||
The sage of this [mantra] is Mahāvarāha, Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter, Vasundharā is its deity, and the seed-syllable *bhūḥ* is said to be its seed. (12.880)
The seed-syllable of Māyā and that of the Earth are employed for the purpose of propitiation;
having performed the six limbs with the syllables of the mantra, one should meditate upon Vasundharā.

Meditation: [One should visualize her] standing in the center of a full-blown lotus, possessing the luster of an indīvara petal, clad in yellow silk garments, and adorned with various ornaments. (12.882)
I worship Vasumatī, the sustainer of all the world, who holds in her hands a pair of blue lotuses, a cluster of rice stalks, and sugarcane.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind for four hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the goddess Vasudhā speaks from the interior of the jar.
"Choose a boon; I shall grant whatever is in your heart.
To the goddess who was speaking thus, [he replied] with three handfuls of flowers.
Having worshipped [her], the best of practitioners should prostrate on the ground like a staff, with the mantra falling upon half a verse:
"Obeisance to you, O Blessed One, O Mother of the World, O Vasundharā! (12.886)
O Consort of Viṣṇu, whose abode was made by the tip of the tusk of the Boar;
O Supporter of the Universe, salutations to you, O Earth, the refuge of all beings!
"O auspicious Earth, I desire to obtain the jewels and treasures contained within you; may I receive them through your grace. (12.888)
Thus he should pray to the Goddess; she then grants a boon, saying, "You shall see, you shall attain. Thereupon, the practitioner beholds her.
And at every step within a distance of three yojanas, there are jewels;
having taken them, one may then roam upon the earth as one desires.
At the outset, one should perform the preliminary rites and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables;
then, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire for one-tenth of that number.
One should satisfy [the deity] with milk-rice mixed with ghee for one-tenth of that amount;
one should perform the purification (mārjana) for one-tenth of that, and likewise satisfy the Vaiṣṇavas for one-tenth of that.
The practitioner of mantras should feed the brahmins and then perform the sādhana;
for without performing the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), no mantra whatsoever attains success.
Thus ends the *Dharitrīsādhana*.
Likewise, the *Sādhanas* for the Kinnarīs and others have been omitted for fear of prolixity.
[One should consult] the *Merutantra*, the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, and the *Śaktisaṅgama*.
The Vāḍavānala-tantra and the tantra named Kālānala.
The Kālītantra, the Parātantra, and likewise the Tantrarāja;
the tantra known as the Muṇḍamālā, and also the Yoginīhṛdaya. || 12-895 ||
The secret tradition of the Kumārītantra, which is most excellent and venerable, as well as the Kulikāmnāyatantra and the Kulacūḍāmaṇi; || 12-896 ||
Likewise, the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*,
the *Samayācāratantra*, and similarly the *Viśvasāra*.
And likewise, there are five Tantras respectively for Bhairavī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Yoginī, and Vārāhī. (12.898)
The Nīlatantra, the Gautamīyatantra, and also the Phetkāriṇī;
the Vāmakeśvaratantra and likewise the Vīratantra. (12.899)
The tantra called Saṃmohana, the tantra known as Gandharva, the Māheśvarīya tantra, and the tantra named Prathama. || 12-900 ||
In the same way, there is the Kātyāyanī-tantra and likewise the Bālā-tantra;
as well as the Uḍḍīśa, the Mālinī-tantra, and the Guhyā-tantra. (12.901)
The Kauleśa, the Kubjikātantra, the Kularatnāvalī,
the Viśuddheśvaratantra, and the Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī.
The Siddhasārasvata, the Śambhuvidyātantra, and likewise the Bhairavatantra, as well as the Jñānārṇava and the Kulārṇava. || 12.903 ||
Likewise, the Vaiṣṇavī-kalpa, the Kālī-kalpa, the Kulāmṛta,
the venerable Pratyaṅgirā-kalpa, and similarly the Tārā-kalpa.
The tantra called Niruttara, the tantra known as Uttara, and likewise the tantra named Svatantra, which illuminates the deities of mantra. || 12-905 ||
The Śrīkrama, the Yāmalas of Brahmā, Rudra, and the others, the Kula-āgama, the Śaiva-āgama, the doctrine of Somaśambhu, and likewise the Devyāgama.
The Ḍāmara, the Bhūtapūrva, the Yakṣaparva which is formidable, the Vaināyakī-saṃhitā, and the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā. || 12.907 ||
Likewise, the Agastyasaṃhitā, the Bṛhacchrīkramasaṃhitā,
the Surendrasaṃhitā, and the Nandikeśvarasaṃhitā.
Likewise, the Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā, the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, the Gorakṣa-saṃhitā, and the Saṃhitās of Siddhanātha and others. || 12-909 ||
The Vārāhī-saṃhitā, the Mahātharvaṇa-saṃhitā, the Tattvasārādi-saṃhitā, and the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-saṃhitā.
The Viṣvaksenīsaṃhitā, likewise the Brahmasiṃhatā, the Kriyāsāra among the nibandhas, and the Tripurāsārasaṃgraha; (12.911)
The *Prapañcasāra*, the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Mantramahodadhi*,
the *Śāradātilaka*, and also the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Likewise, [I have composed] the *Mantraratnāvalī*, the *Ācārakusumāvalī*, and,
among the well-known compendia (*sagraha*), the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*.
The *Āgamādikalpalatā*, the *Mantraratnākara*,
the work titled *Kriyāsaṃgraha*, and the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*.
The *Kālītattva*, the *Śyāmārahasya*, the *Mantracaṇḍikā*,
the commentary on the *Tārārahasya*, and the *Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī*.
The *Tantrasāra*, the *Tantraratna*, and likewise the *Tantracintāmaṇi*, as well as the *Tattvasāra*, the *Yogasāra*, and the *Śrīrāmārcanacandrikā*. || 12-916 ||
The work titled *Vidhānamālā*, as well as the *Vidhimuktāvalī*, various types of manuals (*paddhati*), and likewise the Upaniṣads as well. (12.917)
Having thoroughly examined the science of astrology, the treatise of Śālihotra, the Purāṇas, and the Smṛtis as well, with the desire to provide benefit to the world.
By the illustrious Pratāpasiṃha, the great king of kings who emulates the king of the gods and has reached the further shore of the ocean of knowledge.
In the year marked by the moon, fire, serpents, and earth (1831),
on a Sunday during the bright fortnight of the month of Tapas,
this book named *Puraścaryāṇava* was composed.

King Pratāpasiṃha shines forth—a hero whose lotus-feet are greyed by the dust from the garlands upon the heads of the most eminent hosts of kings; he is preeminent in the great battles of magnificent charity.
Opening the lotuses that are the minds of his own kinsmen, causing the night-lotuses that are the faces of rival kings to close,
and gladdening the cakravāka birds that are all the learned men;
The sun of whose majesty rises upon the earth.
When the sun of the majesty of that lord of the earth blazes forth,
other kings on the surface of the earth do not shine, appearing like the feeble light of young fireflies;
for the three worlds have been made white on all sides by the moonbeams of his fame.
The blackness of his enemies rests within the mass of the darkness of their ill-repute. || 12-923 ||
As long as the sun tirelessly creates days for the benefit of the world;

as long as the moon adorns the three watches of the night with moonlight that clarifies the night-lotuses; as long as Viṣṇu’s names are recited by people; and as long as living beings exist—so long [shall this work endure].
May the fame of that lord of the earth shine throughout the entire circle of the earth for as long as this [world endures]. || 12-924 ||
Those belonging to the Vaiṣṇava community proclaim him as Viṣṇu; the Śaivas consider him to be Śiva;
the Gāṇeśas declare him to be the four-tusked face [Gaṇeśa]; the Śauras know him as the Sun;
the hosts of Śāktas perceive him as the Power of Consciousness (Cicchakti); and the Sāṅkhyas regard him as the Supreme Puruṣa.
May that divine lion-like form protect you, which those who know Brahman declare to be both Brahman and non-Brahman.

In this new Ocean of Preliminary Rites (puraścaryārṇava) composed by Naradeva— a confluence of excellent compositions characterized by a stream of nectar variegated by the wonderful power and diverse terminology of the Bhūtas— this is the twelfth [chapter].
The wave, lofty with the luster of a mass of clear pearls of sound reasoning, has departed.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Different Types of Puraścaraṇa for Mantras, Yantras, Stotras, Kavacas, and so forth, Preceded by the Puraścaraṇa of the Brāhmī and Other Mantras," in the *Puraścaryārṇava*, composed by the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Pratāpasiṃha Deva, who is exalted in honor and resplendent with a multitude of various titles such as "Śrī Girirāja-cakracūḍāmaṇi" and "Naranārāyaṇa. || 12 ||
